For the last decade, Sara (not her real name), 25, has dreamed of becoming a doctor. She secured a highly sought after place to study medicine at Kabul University in February 2021, but in a matter of months the Taliban returned to power and imposed a ban on women studying for degrees. Sara had been searching for other options. Then the University of Glasgow offered her a lifeline.
Her visa application was made just days before the Home Office introduced a visa brake in March 2026 for students from Afghanistan, Sudan, Myanmar and Cameroon. Her teachers consider her to be an exceptionally able and dedicated student, she had secured funding and the university was waiting to welcome her on to a gateway course at its school of medicine, dentistry and nursing – a route to a full degree course to become a doctor. So why have the UK’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, and her officials gone to such extraordinary lengths to bar her?
Sara says her life has been “challenge after challenge”. She survived a suicide bomb attack on her school, swerved her father’s attempts to force her into early marriage, as well as the omnipresent Taliban who patrol Kabul’s streets. Then she made a nail-biting escape from her country and avoided capture by police in Pakistan who were searching for her. But it is the UK’s Home Office, which champions women’s rights, that has inflicted the deadliest blow.
Sara grew up in a poor household in Kabul in the period before the Taliban regained power. Against the wishes of her violent father, who wanted to see her follow the traditional path of teenage marriage and a life of enforced domesticity in service to a husband, she fought to continue her education, encouraged to aim high by inspirational female teachers at her single-sex school.
“The community I come from is a particularly traditional one,” she says. “Even among my relatives I couldn’t find any girl who has been educated. While boys were free, my mum, who has always supported me, was told by relatives that rather than pursuing an education I needed to go somewhere where I could be taught to cook. After a relative’s daughter got married I was told I was next in line.”
But at school, she saw that life could be different. “I was about seven years old when one of my teachers first encouraged us girls,” she says. “Later, my physics teacher was also very supportive. She said that we would face challenges but should never give up in pursuing our dreams.”
Sara says that she is still in contact with some of the girls she was at school with, who were similarly inspired by their female teachers. Some of them are now flying high in other countries, having been granted full university scholarships.
But there were others whose ambitions were thwarted. “I can still see the face of one 15-year-old girl who was like a supportive older sister to me at school. She wanted to continue her education but she was full of tears when she came to school one day and told us her family was forcing her to leave school and get married.”
When Sara was 15, a much-loved uncle died after his heart disease was misdiagnosed. At that moment, she vowed to become a doctor. “My uncle was such a kind soul. He always supported me when my father was being harsh. ‘It’s OK. Whatever your father is doing, I’m with you,’ he used to say to me.”
Sara always put everything into her studies at school, getting marks close to 100% in her tests and exams. Along with her love of science, she speaks multiple languages. She is Hazara and along with Hazaragi speaks Dari, Pashto, Urdu, English, as well as some Spanish and Arabic.
Somehow, despite her father’s disapproval, she continued her studies and attended an educational centre to prepare for Afghanistan’s university entrance exam, the Kankor, so she could secure a place at Kabul University to begin her medical studies. In October 2020, it was targeted by a Taliban suicide bomb attack. She was feeling unwell that day so did not go to school. Many of her friends were killed.
Against the odds, in February 2021, she passed her exam, secured her place at the Kabul University’s medical school, and was overjoyed – until she and other women at the university had their right to study brutally terminated when the Taliban came to power in August 2021.
Devastated, but undeterred from pursuing her dream, she began volunteering at medical clinics in Kabul, taken there and back by clinical staff who supported her, ducking down and hiding in the car when they approached Taliban checkpoints. When Taliban members came to the clinic for treatment, she was bundled into the staff room to hide until they had left. She continued her medical studies at home, begging friends who were studying to send her PDFs of medical textbooks because she couldn’t afford to buy them. She devoured the medical bible Gray’s Anatomy.
Despite the Taliban obstacle, she was determined to keep studying any way she could. “I was at the clinic one day in 2023. I wasn’t allowed to perform medical procedures on patients but wanted to learn as much as I could. I asked a friend to teach me how to do sutures and then practised the technique on a banana. The head surgeon came in and asked what we were doing, saw how enthusiastic I was and allowed me to observe an operation.”
By 2024, life at home with her father was becoming increasingly violent and dangerous and the pressure on Sara to marry was increasing. “The situation was deteriorating so much that we had to find a way to get out,” she says.
Sara hoped she could pursue her medical studies in Pakistan, so before she left Afghanistan she went to the medical school in Kabul to try to get her course records to prove that she had started a medical degree. “Taliban guards wouldn’t let me through the front gate and were very abusive to me so I couldn’t get them,” she says.
Sara was later able to get a reference from one of her lecturers at the university which described her as a “highly dedicated and capable student.”
“She demonstrated strong academic performance, critical thinking and a deep passion for medicine. She is a resilient, compassionate and motivated individual,” the lecturer said.
Sara, her mother, her siblings and other relatives had to leave Afghanistan in a hurry when things reached crisis point with her father. “I could only pack a few clothes,” she says. “But I took my white medical coat with me, hoping that even if I was unable to continue my medical studies in Afghanistan, I would be able to qualify to be a doctor somewhere else.”
The family managed to get together the money to escape to Pakistan by plane. Their cover story was that Sara’s mother needed urgent medical treatment. Their male escort was Sara’s brother-in-law. At Kabul Airport, they were stopped by the Taliban and taken into a room for questioning.
“We arrived at the airport at 12.30pm for a 2pm flight. We were questioned in that room until 1.50pm. My hands were shaking so much. I didn’t think they would let us go. They wanted to know why my father was not accompanying us to Pakistan. When they finally released us at 1.50pm, we all had to run to make it on to the plane before it took off. When we sat on the plane my mum said to us; ‘Our life is full of challenges. If we overcome one, another one comes.’”
Life in Pakistan was not much better. The family overstayed their visa because they had nowhere else to run to and Sara was unable to continue her medical studies. “Sometimes the police came to look for us at the place where we were staying. I hid in the kitchen cupboard when they knocked on our door so they wouldn’t find me,” she says.
A London-based English teacher, Jane Conway, became another lifeline. She taught English to refugee students and became involved in a group called Save Afghan Women. After the Taliban regained power, Conway helped with online English classes for women no longer able to physically study in Afghanistan, and got to know Sara and other members of her family who she supported as they continued their higher education.
It was Conway who found that the University of Glasgow had a gateway course for female students from Afghanistan who wanted to pursue a degree in medicine, and helped her apply. “It was teacher Jane who found this option for me,” says Sara.
She applied for the scheme and was accepted after finding, with Conway’s help, sources of funding to support her with bursaries to cover fees and living expenses. Hope was restored. All she needed now was for the Home Office to grant her a visa to take up the course in Glasgow. She thought that after everything she had been through this would be the easy bit. But three rejections citing contradictory reasons followed.
She was told in one rejection that the Home Office was satisfied she had appropriate funds in place to support her study in the UK although they deemed her not to be a genuine student. She cried and cried at that accusation, after all the years of doing everything possible to pursue her medical studies. “I would like to ask the home secretary what is her definition of a ‘genuine student?’ I wish I had the opportunity to visit her in person and ask her this question face to face, eye to eye.”
Then, in another refusal, they said she didn’t have suitable funds in place, but accepted she was a genuine student.
Sara underwent a phone interview with a Home Office official. “The interview was very tough. It lasted about an hour and a half and the man asked me lots of questions about my mother, my father, my background. After the interview he told me to keep checking my email and I was hopeful I was going to be granted a visa.”
But once again her hopes were dashed. She is now pursuing a degree in accounting and finance in another country, undisclosed for safety reasons, because it is more affordable than a medical course. “I don’t have any other option,” she says.
In London, Conway despairs about the inconsistent decision making by the Home Office. “Sara is a good and wonderful person who wants to do good in the world,” she says. “It would seem that the Home Office is so obsessive in its target seeking that it has become blinded to exceptional cases like Sara’s, denying the UK of the benefits that such motivated and talented people could bring.
“In spite of all the obstacles Sara encountered pursuing her dream to become a doctor, she never gave up. Then, when that wonderful new door of opportunity was opened up to her by the University of Glasgow, instead of walking through it with hope and excitement, it is our British Home Office that unequivocally slams the door shut in her path. I feel a deep shame that the government is cutting off a life-changing opportunity for a truly exceptional person, who has already been persecuted in her own country simply for being a woman.”
On 28 September, Mahmood delighted the audience at the Labour party conference by announcing she was reactivating a refugee resettlement route, albeit a small one, highlighting Afghan women and girls as one of the groups who would benefit. It later emerged that there will be significant restrictions to the scheme for some eligible nationalities (it is only open to Palestinian refugees who have already escaped Gaza and are registered as refugees with the UN, for instance), while the much larger refugee family reunion scheme remains suspended after more than a year.
Sara refuses to give up on her dream of qualifying to become a doctor. She tries to keep up with the latest scientific developments in medicine.
“In Afghanistan, so many people don’t have arms or legs because of all the fighting,” she says. “If I can qualify as a doctor I would like to help people in my country. My ambition is to become a cardiac surgeon because as far as I know there are no female cardiac surgeons in Afghanistan and I would like to be the first.” If she achieves this, she says, “my goal is to use my experiences to inspire other Afghan girls to pursue education and overcome the obstacles in their lives”.
If she can’t ever return to her country, she wants to work with Doctors Without Borders. “They work with people in difficult-to-reach places. I believe that people in those places deserve to have a good doctor to treat them. From my perspective, doctors are superheroes. They are the best for people. Whatever happens, I will always keep my white coat with me. It is the history of my struggle.”

More prisoners recalled to jail than released in England and Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:33 UTC
03:00:33 KST

More people were recalled to jails in England and Wales in the first half of this year than were released, despite government efforts to reduce the prison population, according to figures released on Thursday.
Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data shows that 12,338 people were recalled to custody between the beginning of April and the end of June, while 12,278 people were released. It continues a trend set between January and March, when 13,193 people were returned to prison and 12,977 released.
A total of 52,716 prisoners were put back behind bars in the year to June after breaching the terms of their licence – 27% up on the previous 12-month total.
The high recall rate is a key contributor to the prison capacity crisis and helped to prompt early release schemes earlier this month.
The MoJ figures also show 79,274 inmates were freed early from prison between September 2024 and June 2026 under emergency measures brought in by the government to try to tackle the overcrowding crisis.
The move, known as the SDS40 early release scheme, cut the proportion of sentences some prisoners must serve in England and Wales from 50% to 40%. It is one of several policy changes that are likely to have contributed to the rise in recalls, the MoJ said.
The emergency measures were replaced with a permanent scheme for early releases from 1 October under the Sentencing Act 2026.
The Howard League for Penal Reform said the “alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse”, as it called on the government to find a “lasting solution” to the overcrowding crisis.
Rob Preece, the head of communications at the Howard League, said: “The prison system is under enormous pressure, with chronic overcrowding, staff shortages and awful conditions that make it close to impossible to rehabilitate people effectively. Imposing ever longer sentences has led us to this crisis, but the alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse.”
Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said the number of recalls must be urgently addressed to avoid prison spaces being filled up again by people sent back to jail.
“A significant proportion of those released immediately go back to chaotic lives involving addiction, mental health problems and homelessness. Without adequate support and stable accommodation in place as soon as they step outside the gate, it is very difficult to break the revolving cycle of going back into prison too many are caught up in,” he said.
The MoJ said it was “vital those who break the rules can be hauled back to prison”. The department said the rise in recalls amid SDS40 releases was also likely to have been influenced by policy changes that result in most offenders being taken back into custody for 56 days before being released again – known as a fixed-term recall – instead of being held until the end of their sentence.
Incidents of self-harm and violence have remained high as pressure on the prison system has grown. Safety in custody statistics showed that 360 people in prison died in the 12 months to the end of September 2026, including 66 people who died in circumstances recorded as “self-inflicted”.
Prisons recorded 68,231 incidents of self-harm in the 12 months to the end of June 2026, at a rate of one every eight minutes. Self-harm incidents fell by 12% in men’s prisons and fell by 3.8% in women’s prisons.
A separate dataset showed that the number of serious offenders on probation who were charged with a serious further offence had increased for the third successive year, to a record number.
Of 281 serious offenders charged, 119 were registered sexual offenders, 128 were murderers, and four were terrorists or posed a terror risk, according to figures on multi-agency public protection arrangements.

Why jet lag throws even foraging seabirds off course
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:27 UTC
03:00:27 KST

Seabirds returning from foraging trips can be thrown hundreds of miles off course by a form of jet lag that arises when their body clocks get out of sync with local time, researchers say.
Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.
The impact was limited on adult shearwaters because the birds were able to correct their bearings in flight. At most, the birds veered off course by about 15 degrees. After correcting their course, this added only an estimated 3 miles to a 600-mile journey.
But less experienced birds were likely to have a tougher time, the study found, with first-time foragers at risk of flying off course by hundreds of miles.
Most studies on birds’ biological clocks have been conducted under laboratory conditions but Dr Patrick Lewin, a behavioural and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford, set out to investigate wild birds with the help of his colleagues.
Their analysis of 20 years of GPS tracking data revealed a clear effect when the Manx shearwaters flew east across lines of longitude as they returned home, leading their clocks to run up to an hour or so behind local time. “The bird’s internal clock can be subject to a jet lag phenomenon, manifesting as birds flying off course,” Lewin said.
Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky as the Earth rotates, reading its position correctly relies on the birds adjusting their heading relative to the sun, using their body clock to keep track of the time of day. Sunset and sunrise keep the bird’s body clock in sync, helping them adjust to changes in local time.
Writing in Science, Lewin said the mismatch between local time and the birds’ internal clocks could make them drift off course when the sun lay farther around the sky than expected. Surprisingly, the errors remained when birds followed the coastline, where landmarks could have guided them, further supporting the idea that the sun plays a central role in anchoring their sense of direction.
“For adult shearwaters, this lag has very limited impact on their overall journey, with errors adding a calculated 5km to a 1,000km journey,” Lewin said. “However, for first-time migrant birds, such orientation shifts due to sun compass errors could result in deviations of hundreds of kilometres as they lack a map sense to help reorient them when they lose their way.”
Prof Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved in the study, said it was a significant finding: “It seems to confirm in wild animals what more controlled experimental studies have shown: reliance on the sun compass for animals that move during the day, even when it is not accurate.”
Manx shearwaters spend most of their lives far out at sea. They cover enormous distances but return each year to islands off the west coast of the UK to breed in burrows.
“It’s not clear from the study what the consequences of these errors are, since the birds return to their colony and the errors are small,” Holland said. “Nonetheless, it highlights the importance of understanding the role of biological rhythms across multiple contexts in animal behaviour, as more and more we are starting to realise just how important these are for numerous biological functions.”

People in interracial relationships tend to be more politically liberal, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:02 UTC
03:00:02 KST

An analysis of data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health found that people with a romantic partner of a different race had 37% greater odds of holding more liberal political views than people with a same-race partner. However, the size of this difference varied depending on people’s race, sex, and marital status. The paper was published in The Journal of Race, Ethnicity, and Politics.
Romantic relationships and political beliefs may seem like separate aspects of life, but research suggests that they are closely connected. In the United States, people with conservative political views tend to place greater importance on traditional family structures and are more likely to prefer romantic partners of the same race. Those with liberal views, on the other hand, tend to be generally more accepting of interracial relationships.
Over the past several decades, interracial relationships have become increasingly common, reflecting broader changes in American society and attitudes toward racial diversity. Since the U.S. Supreme Court struck down laws prohibiting interracial marriage in 1967, public acceptance of such relationships has increased substantially. Recent estimates suggest that roughly one in five newlyweds and cohabiting adults in the United States has a partner from a different racial or ethnic background. However, relatively little is known about the political beliefs of people who are actually involved in such relationships.
One possibility is that people in interracial relationships are more politically liberal because they are generally more open to relationships across racial boundaries and may have greater awareness of racial discrimination. At the same time, political preferences differ considerably according to race, ethnicity, sex, and marital status, making the relationship between romantic partner choice and political ideology more complex than it might initially appear.
Study author Byron Miller and colleagues wanted to compare the political beliefs of people in interracial relationships with those of people in same-race relationships. They expected people in interracial relationships to be more liberal on average, but they also hypothesized that this association would depend on a person’s race, sex, and marital status.
They analyzed data from wave 4 of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health). This is a large-scale, longitudinal study in the United States that began in 1994–1995 with adolescents in grades 7–12 attending 80 high schools and 52 middle schools. Since then, researchers have followed participants into adulthood, collecting data on their physical and mental health, social relationships, behaviors, and socioeconomic circumstances. At the time of wave 4, in 2008, participants were approximately 24 to 32 years old.
The analysis included 12,603 participants. Their political beliefs were measured with a single question: “In terms of politics, do you consider yourself very conservative, conservative, middle-of-the-road, liberal, or very liberal?” The researchers classified participants as being in an interracial relationship if their current or most recent romantic partner’s race differed from their own, and they also took into account participants’ race/ethnicity (white, Black, Hispanic, or Asian), sex, marital status, age, and education.
About 15% of participants were in interracial relationships. People in interracial relationships were much less likely to be white than those in same-race relationships (34% versus 74%), and more likely to be Hispanic or Asian.
After accounting for demographic characteristics, people in interracial relationships had 37% greater odds of holding more liberal views than those in same-race relationships. But this association differed across groups. It was weaker among Asian and Hispanic participants than among white participants, and weaker among married participants than among those who were unmarried, while it was stronger among women than among men.
When the researchers looked at combinations of these factors, they found that among married participants, interracial relationships were more strongly linked to liberal views for Black and Asian adults than for white adults. Combinations of race and sex showed no statistically significant differences. The authors suggest that some Asian and Hispanic adults with conservative views may prefer partners from the white majority, while the pattern among married Black and Asian adults may reflect people choosing partners who share their political views.
“Interracial relationships are a catalyst for major changes in racial/ethnic relations and diversity in the United States, especially as children from these romantic relationships contribute to the biracial baby boom,” the study authors wrote. “[A]s this demographic continues to grow more prevalent as the United States becomes more racially/ethnically diverse, the political beliefs of biracial families are likely to have an increasingly greater influence on the policies, processes, and representatives that shape racial and ethnic politics.”
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the political views of people in interracial relationships. However, the design of this study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results. Because of this, it remains unknown whether liberal individuals are more likely to start a relationship with a person of a different race, whether a relationship with a person of a different race makes an individual more liberal, or whether other factors influence both political attitudes and relationship choices.
The data were also collected in 2008, before Donald Trump’s presidency, which some researchers argue has reshaped the political views of men and women, so the findings may not reflect current patterns. Political views were measured with a single question, and the study did not examine specific racial pairings within couples, such as Asian-white or Black-Hispanic partnerships.
The paper, “Biracial at the Ballot Box: Exploring the Association Between Interracial Relationships and Political Beliefs,” was authored by Byron Miller, Madelyn Chandler, and Nico Allen.

====================================================================================================

One Nation might not win Victoria, but NSW is where the real fight is
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Labor battles against One Nation insurgence while feeling inflation pain
New South Wales Premier Chris Minns delivered an attention-grabbing prediction this week.
"By any poll, by any measure, [One Nation leader] Mike Newman will either be the premier or the opposition leader after March 13," Minns said on Sydney radio.
While the immediate focus is on One Nation's performance at the Victorian election in late November, next year's NSW contest will be a more important test for the insurgent party.
On present indications, the best One Nation could do in Victoria would be to prop up a Coalition minority government, although there seems a fair prospect Opposition Leader Jess Wilson could get to a majority. There's no chance of One Nation Victorian leader Warren Pickering becoming opposition leader.
A good performance in Victoria obviously would be a fillip for One Nation, but the NSW election will be the big pointer for the future.
The latest Resolve Political Monitor NSW poll, published in September, has Labor on 29 per cent, One Nation 25 per cent and the Coalition 24 per cent.
The Minns government, although in minority, should be in a strong position to win a second term. A pragmatist from Labor's right, and a leader with a relatable style, Minns has distanced himself from the Albanese government, which is still bogged in the problems from its controversial budget, with a now deeply unpopular prime minister.
High inflation adds to the problem
The NSW opposition is weak. On current assessments, the Liberals are considered likely to lose metropolitan seats to Labor. The Nationals could face a near wipeout, with One Nation well placed to grab regional seats.
Newman, formerly a trade bureaucrat who spent many years working in Japan, is a more credible figure than Pickering.
If One Nation did become the official opposition in NSW, the most populous state, that would be a serious shock to, and realignment of, the political system in this country.
It would have sweeping implications federally, notably diminishing both the Liberals and Nationals. It would surely shake the leadership of Angus Taylor, who is from NSW.
One question, as NSW moves towards its election, is whether voters, who usually distinguish between state and federal issues, might, if the Albanese government is still in the doldrums, use the opportunity to give the feds a kick over the cost of living.
This week's high inflation figures — with the headline figure at 4.3 per cent in the year to September (up from 4 per cent in the year to August) and the underlying rate at 3.7 per cent — have homebuyers bracing, given the high market expectations of another interest rate rise on Tuesday. That would be the fifth rise this year.
The government is feeling ever more sharply the blow back from a disgruntled electorate to which it can't afford to give relief.
While it continues to reject the argument that its own spending has contributed significantly to the high inflation, it is also responding to that argument. Treasurer Jim Chalmers this week was at pains to emphasise the mid-year budget update due in December would contain a savings package.
But both he and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese refused to commit to these amounting to net savings.
"We'll continue to have those discussions … in the cabinet, in the ERC (Expenditure Review Committee). That's what we do," Albanese said.
Loading
Government still ahead on economic management
Reserve Bank officials, who have been out and about in recent days including at Senate estimates hearings, have been walking a delicate line.
They are trying to get across the message that spending needs to be contained, while keeping within their own lane, which requires they are not seen to be telling the government how it should act.
Of course, government spending (which also includes state spending) is not entirely responsible for the inflationary problem. Although there was an issue before the Middle East conflict, the war is a major factor in accelerating inflation.
The biggest increase in Wednesday's inflation figures was in the cost of fuel. More generally, a surge in private sector investment from the AI boom, combined with supply constraints, adds to inflation.
But spending is part of the problem. And for the government, it is the present actual and political pinch point.
In the latest Essential poll, released this week, when people were asked (from a list) what was most responsible for the rising cost of living, 32 per cent said government spending, while 24 per cent opted for global events, and 19 per cent for supermarket price gouging.
A frustrated Chalmers said early this week, in a podcast with Nine: "So for people who think we should cut much harder, they should nominate, I think, those areas that should be cut more substantially. But we have been finding savings, many more savings than our predecessors, and that's because we take the hard yards of budget sustainability seriously."
Meanwhile, responding to calls of "What would the Coalition do?", the opposition this week listed $31 billion worth of cuts and other savings, focused on the climate bureaucracy, "corporate welfare", the housing bureaucracy, and changes to the tobacco excise. It said these cuts would more than fund its promise to index income tax brackets.
The Essential poll showed the disquiet among voters continues to grow. More than six in 10 voters (61 per cent) said they thought the country was on the wrong track, compared with 54 per cent in January and 46 per cent in October 2025.
Despite this unease, the government was still ahead on economic management, with 32 per cent of voters selecting Labor when asked which party they would trust to "ensure the economy works in the interests of everyday Australians". But One Nation followed, on 29 per cent, with the Coalition, which sees the economy as its favoured ground, on just 18 per cent.
Albanese won't be on hand when the Reserve Bank delivers its decision on rates on Tuesday. He'll be at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda. It had been thought the PM might skip it, given how many international meetings he has to attend during summit season. But King Charles made it clear he hoped to see him there.
On Thursday, Albanese was asked if he could give people "a sense of when their lives are going to get easier and not harder".
"These challenges won't be solved overnight," he said. It was a grim message.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

Labor's student visa crackdown has created a problem it didn't intend

03:00:00 KST

Labor warns against 'overcorrection' on student visas as universities face $2b revenue hit
In short:
Labor has acknowledged fears that its tougher student visa rules are putting off genuine applicants and hurting Australia's universities.
The federal government says it will make the system easier to navigate without weakening its crackdown on student migration.
What's next?
Universities will be consulted on revised financial requirements and changes to how student visa applications are assessed.
Labor will recalibrate its international student crackdown with an overhaul of visa requirements to ensure the tough rules do not deter quality applicants from Australia.
The federal government will review financial requirements for international students from South Asia amid concerns that high refusal rates are dissuading genuine applicants and damaging Australia's education sector.
Visa rejections have soared in the two years since a ministerial direction was introduced to strengthen assessments of whether education is the primary purpose behind a student's application.
Assistant Minister for International Education Julian Hill will use a speech in Sydney today to defend Labor's reforms to the sector as necessary for restoring integrity but will warn against an "overcorrection".
New international student commencements at public universities are projected to fall about 18 per cent this year, wiping about $2 billion from revenues over three years.
Mr Hill will say tighter visa rules are only partly responsible for those losses, with competition from other countries and cost-of-living pressures among the other factors.
But he will acknowledge Labor's crackdown is having unintended consequences, with high refusal rates discouraging the very students Australia wants to attract.
"They are terrified of a visa refusal that hurts their chances of studying elsewhere," Mr Hill will say.
New financial guidance for students
Home affairs and education officials are developing new financial standards for South Asia and a replacement for Ministerial Direction 106, with universities and education agents to be consulted in November.
The direction was introduced in 2024 to help immigration officials assess whether student visa applicants genuinely intended to study in Australia, including scrutinise their financial circumstances.
Student visa rejections subsequently soared, with more than 24.2 per cent of applicants knocked back last financial year.
More than 51 per cent of all student visa applications from Nepal were rejected over that period, while than 40 per cent of Indian applicants were refused.
The changes now under consideration are designed to provide greater certainty for prospective students about their chances of securing a visa.
Mr Hill will flag the possibility of raising financial thresholds, arguing clearer requirements could improve visa approval rates even if fewer prospective students qualify.
"Even if this means raising the financial standards and a smaller pool of prospective students, I want grant rates to improve and greater certainty for everyone," he will say.
Labor does not want to 'tank' universities
The government is also considering a New Zealand-style system allowing students to deposit funds covering their tuition and living expenses to demonstrate their financial capacity, although Mr Hill will caution this would be a longer-term reform.
He will insist Labor has no intention of abandoning its efforts to rein in student migration, arguing the changes are necessary to protect the integrity of the system.
Mr Hill will say the government's intention is not to "tank" the international education sector as other nations, such as Canada, have done.
International education is Australia's fifth-largest export sector and supports about 250,000 jobs.
But Mr Hill will take aim at private education providers he says "harvest" profits, while public institutions reinvest surpluses into teaching, research and facilities.
"In a sector where overall customer numbers onshore have to be limited, then the highest value for Australia — as a nation and for taxpayers — comes from students at public institutions, studying with diverse cohorts of young Australians and international peers," he will say.

Economist delivers 'worst-case scenario' on interest rates as inflation fails to cool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Up to three interest rate hikes and a recession on the cards as inflation woes persist
Australia has a dirty little secret.
Despite four Reserve Bank interest rate hikes, supposed fiscal restraint, and a recent small improvement in productivity, inflation is rising.
At face value, it makes no sense. Millions of households continue to struggle to make ends meet.
Dig a little deeper, though, and the logic of why the country continues to struggle with inflation is painfully simple.
There's simply too much money chasing too few goods and services.
There appears to be only one solution: lower demand until the economy breaks.
Moving pieces of economic puzzle
To understand Australia's inflation problem, look no further than the Reserve Bank's commentary.
Following its most recent decision to raise the cash rate, the RBA's statement began by saying that inflation was already too high.
It went on to say "… and some of the upside risks flagged in August are materialising".
"The conflict in the Middle East has broadened, and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed in the August forecasts," it wrote.
"AI-related demand is driving rapid growth in global prices for technology-related goods.
"And there remains pressure on domestic capacity."
Put simply, the economy is struggling to supply the goods and services to meet current demand, and higher energy prices add to the cost-of-living pain.
The solution then is to boost the nation's ability to meet demand.
Failing that, demand needs to come down.
Inflation slipping away from us
Better news on the supply front came in the most recent national accounts, where GDP per hour worked (one measure of productivity) moved out of negative territory, albeit to zero.
But over the year, it sits at -0.2 per cent.
Lacklustre productivity means the only near-term option is for demand to fall.
Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers said on Wednesday the government was doing its bit.
"We've been able to manage the budget in a much more responsible way than it was being managed by our predecessors … we accept our part in the fight against inflation," he said.
And while private (or business) investment did not contribute to GDP in the June quarter, it was driven by household consumption (+0.2 percentage points).
It has put a target on the back of households as the ones to blame for the "excess" demand.
Iran war making inflation sticky
And this is the critical point. The Iran war is squeezing oil supplies and forcing fuel prices higher.
The Reserve Bank says its liaison program shows businesses are passing higher production costs on to customers.
Worse still, as RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser said this week, is that businesses don't really see an end in sight to elevated costs.
"There's just some sign that some companies might be thinking, you know what, maybe prices aren't going all the way back.
"And if they're not, we're going to have to take that into account with the pricing decisions."
This paves the way for his "nightmare" central banker scenario of unanchored inflation expectations.
Sledgehammer to demand
One way to reverse this vicious cycle is to ensure consumers don't have money in their pockets to spend, or at least not as much.
Hence, interest rate rises take money out of consumers' pockets.
So, rather than supply not meeting demand, demand can't meet supply.
Economic theory tells you prices then stop rising and actually fall.
Why? Because business owners are forced to lower prices to bring customers back into their stores.
To be fair, the Reserve Bank has tried to set this path in motion, but its "cautious" approach has proved too cautious.
But if households spend so little that the corner store doesn't replace a leaving staff member, the person who would otherwise have landed that job buys fewer items and saves more … and so on.
This environment could push the unemployment rate beyond 5 per cent, former NAB chief economist Alan Oster says.
But interest rates need to rise higher for this to occur.
"My worst-case scenario would be two or three further rate rises, which I think would clearly cause you recession,"
Mr Oster said.
"And I think you're probably going to struggle anyway.
"Certainly, I'd expect, I'll wait until they've actually done it before I review my forecast, but I would expect to see lower growth and higher levels of unemployment and probably unemployment with the five in front of it," he said.
So will rates keep rising?
Betashares chief economist David Bassanese does not think the RBA will need to hike interest rates beyond November, but concedes Australia would likely enter a recession if it did.
"All up, my base case is that RBA will raise rates next week but then leave rates on hold at the last meeting of the year in December — providing households at least a small pre-Xmas reprieve," he said.
Loading
"Given gathering signs of weakness in the economy, particularly the very weak outlook for house prices, my expectation is the RBA won't need to raise rates further in 2027, though the risk still lay firmly to the upside.
"Should rates need to rise even further next year, the risk of recession would no doubt intensify."
The number of interest rate hikes from here, says State Street Investment Management economist Ma Krishna Bhimavarapu, will depend on how much weaker the economy gets in coming months.
"We still expect the cash rate to ultimately have a 5-handle, but the path from here will depend on how quickly the economy slows," he said.
The nation faced two options 12 months ago: improve productivity or else.
The exogenous shock of an oil-sensitive war made improving productivity urgent, but we've missed the boat.
The Reserve Bank is now left with the unenviable task of taking a sledgehammer to demand for the greater good.
Let's be honest, it's positively sinister, as are most dirty little secrets.

Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.
Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.
For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.
But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.
Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.
Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.
“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.
The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.
This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.
“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

Any company or individual considering purchasing Russian diesel fuel should understand that they are committing a crime and that Congress is watching. In addition, they could be held accountable by a future administration, even if the current one is turning a blind eye
Blumenthal also called for the disclosure of information about the sellers, buyers, terminal operators, and insurers involved in the transaction, as well as any instructions from the Treasury Department.

Emergency stockpiles are a luxury that not everyone can afford | Letters

The Be Ready campaign may offer sensible advice in principle (Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises, 22 October), but as a midwife working in Tower Hamlets, one of the poorest boroughs in London, I can see first-hand that its practical recommendations risk excluding precisely those families who are already most vulnerable.
For families living in a single room in a shared house, storing nine litres of water per person alongside three days’ worth of essential supplies may simply be unrealistic. When families are already struggling with the cost of food, heating and everyday necessities, buying additional emergency provisions may also be financially impossible.
Perhaps local councils could create a stockpile hub where those in need could access the recommended supplies, free of charge. Being prepared should be a public health measure, not a privilege reserved for those who can afford it.
 
Keira Callaghan
 
London
While it flies in the face of just-in-time principles, I think the initiative to improve resilience is sensible in the current situation (Andy Burnham says he has emergency stockpile of beans, soup and Twiglets, 23 October). However, due to health issues, I rely on a monthly repeat prescription of several life-preserving medications. It used to be normal practice to request a new prescription when I opened the last box, but now the policy at my GP surgery appears to be that they will not issue a new prescription until a week before I need them.
The pharmacy then requires up to a week to process the prescription, meaning that my medications are always dispensed at the last minute. Localised shortages and periodic mistakes have caused me problems in the past, and I suffer from prescription anxiety every month. This policy is also incompatible with the latest government advice to stockpile essential medication. When the inevitable catastrophe strikes, I will find myself without my essential medication, and I doubt that 75 tins of beans and a packet of Twiglets will be much consolation.

So, just keep calm and carry on.

Save Hammersmith Bridge – but keep it free of cars | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:54:56 UTC
02:54:56 KST

Simon Jenkins is a great defender of our national heritage, having produced many books on the subject and frequently written in the Guardian against aggressive modern architectural horrors. How shocking, then, to find him arguing for the replacement of Hammersmith Bridge simply to provide for yet more cars on the roads (Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t, 23 October). He claims that the principal cause of congestion is “London’s epidemic of roadworks”, when actually it’s the fact that there are just too many cars trying to use a road network that isn’t designed for them.
Furthermore, he says that, in its present state, the bridge “merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross it” – and yet between 12,000 and 15,000 people use it every day. Reopening it to motor traffic (and increasingly heavy cars have massively contributed to the current state of degradation of the bridge) would bring little benefit. Well over half the households in Hammersmith and Fulham don’t have access to a car, and there are very good public transport links in the area; there is even a well-thought-out plan put forward by the Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit group to run driverless electric “pod” vehicles to provide for those who are unable to walk across Hammersmith Bridge.
And quite apart from the huge difficulty involved in enabling the tearing down of a Grade II* listed structure (where’s our doughty defender of national heritage now?), there is no effective business case for replacing it at enormous cost to provide for yet more cars, when for both environmental and health reasons (particularly because of the pollution they cause), the whole emphasis should be on reducing our reliance on cars. If only someone in authority would summon up the courage to tackle the motoring lobby.
 
Dr Richard Carter
 
Putney, London
Simon Jenkins is right to castigate the different London authorities that have failed to replace Hammersmith Bridge over a period of seven years. No other capital city in Europe would allow such a prolonged truncation of a major transport artery, preventing vehicles from crossing the river. London is not a unitary authority and its mayor does not have the powers of his peers in other capitals to raise the finance to pay for the cost of a new bridge. The lack of joined-up thinking appears to be baked in to the planning processes of the different relevant authorities.
This sorry state of affairs in south-west London has led to permanent traffic chaos along the Upper Richmond Road and the hell that is Putney High Street during rush hour. Were it not for the British obsession for so-called “heritage” projects, we could have had a temporary bridge capable of carrying traffic years ago. Instead citizens are obliged to walk or pedal their way across a wonky bridge in order to get to the other side for the sake of a misplaced nostalgia for Victorian engineering feats.
 
Julian Heddy
 
East Sheen, London
The outdated photograph published with Simon Jenkins’s off-beam article on Hammersmith Bridge suggests decrepitude, when the reality is quite different. Thanks to £55m of investment by Hammersmith and Fulham council, this iconic, Grade II* listed bridge has found a successful new purpose as an active travel crossing, with 15,000 people a day walking and wheeling across its reopened main carriageway.
I know of no “growing body of opinion” calling for its replacement. On the contrary, the settled local preference has moved to build on this success with a proposal to introduce a fleet of lightweight, autonomous electric shuttles to fill the public transport gap to ensure all residents can cross comfortably and safely. Community-led Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit is working with Ohmio UK and partners to deliver this vision.
Traffic on neighbouring bridges and the wider road network is down compared with before the bridge closed to motor vehicles, while Barnes’s local economy is booming, aided by the ebike revolution.
There is no credible business case for spending hundreds of millions bringing back polluting, dangerous and exclusionary through traffic. With the mayor targeting a 27% reduction in car traffic by 2030, the priority must be to build on this success, not undo it.
 
Charles Campion
 
Chair, Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit
Simon Jenkins is a respected commentator on London’s heritage and built environment, with a deep understanding of the costs of maintaining historic infrastructure. We share his commitment to London’s bridges, but not his views on how the City Bridge Foundation’s charitable funds should be used.
We maintain five Thames bridges: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium and Blackfriars, spanning centuries of engineering history. Their upkeep requires sustained investment and commitment, demonstrated by our current £15m Blackfriars Bridge refurbishment, repairing more than 2,000 cast-iron balusters and repainting the entire structure.
Our endowment exists to meet these responsibilities in perpetuity. It is not a general fund for London’s infrastructure, nor is its value a measure of money freely available to spend.
Alongside maintaining and supporting our bridges, where there are funds available, we make grants to charities tackling inequality and disadvantage across London. These funds are made for charitable purposes and governed by the legal and regulatory arrangements that apply to our work. They cannot simply be redirected to pay for the restoration or replacement of a bridge outside our remit.
We recognise the importance of London’s bridges to the people who rely on them every day, but other Thames crossings are the responsibility of other organisations. We share knowledge and experience with those responsible through industry groups.
For nearly 900 years, the legacy of Bridge House Estates has helped keep London’s bridges standing while supporting charitable work across the city. We are proud of this legacy and the charity partners working alongside us to build a fairer London.
 
Paul Martinelli
 
Chairman, City Bridge Foundation

8 of the most atmospheric Christmas markets worth visiting
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:54:43 EET
02:54:43 KST

8 of the most atmospheric Christmas markets worth visiting
Kyiv • UNN
Strasbourg, Dresden, Vienna and other cities preserve unique Christmas traditions. This selection tells about the markets and the main festive dishes.
European Christmas markets have long since evolved from simple winter markets into a large-scale cultural phenomenon, with each city preserving its own centuries-old secrets. Every market is special, with its own fairytale atmosphere and traditions. UNN has selected for you 8 of Europe's most spectacular winter destinations, their unique traditions, and the main gastronomic symbols that everyone should try.
Strasbourg
This French city is deservedly called the "capital of Christmas." The market was first established here in 1570 under the name "Christkindelsmärik." Before that, the city had hosted a Saint Nicholas market, but when Alsace became Protestant, Catholic holidays were abolished and the market was renamed in honor of the Christ Child. You should definitely try the local bredele cookies, which are baked exclusively for the holidays, and instead of ordinary mulled wine, try hot white Alsatian wine or spiced apple juice with cinnamon.
Interestingly, Strasbourg has an entire "Christmas tree guard service." The main tree in Place Kléber is selected for months in the surrounding forests: it must be perfectly symmetrical and taller than 30 meters.
Dresden
The local Striezelmarkt is Germany's oldest market; it has been officially mentioned in documents since 1434. At first, it was simply a single day of trading, when townspeople were allowed to buy meat after the strict Christmas fast. Be sure to try authentic Dresden stollen. Today, only a few dozen local bakeries have the right to place an official quality mark on it.
The market got its name from the word "Striezel"—the term once used for a festive cake. It is also here that the world's tallest wooden Christmas pyramid stands: a 14-meter structure from the Ore Mountains.
Nuremberg
The Christkindlesmarkt in Nuremberg is a place of strict traditions. You will not see plastic garlands or loud modern pop music here. The city council closely monitors that all stalls are made exclusively of natural wood and decorated with fresh fir branches. The market is famous for Nuremberg sausages. They are very small, about the length of a finger, and are traditionally served three at a time in a sliced, crispy roll. The market's main symbol is not Santa Claus, but the Christ Child. A girl is chosen for this role by the townspeople once every two years, and she opens the festival by delivering a speech from the balcony of the Frauenkirche.
Vienna
Vienna's markets are pure classic. The very first "December Market" here was authorized by Emperor Albert I as early as 1298. It is important to note that Vienna has not just one market, but more than a dozen different locations throughout the city. Every year, the markets issue signature cups shaped like boots or hearts, which you can keep as a souvenir after paying a deposit. They are used to serve the signature hot punch. It is here, near City Hall, that the most romantic market takes place: hundreds of illuminated figures are lit up on the trees in the park, while a huge ice rink is set up among the wooded paths.
Prague
The Czech winter fairytale is centered around Old Town Square. While steam rises from stalls serving grilled sausages, the Gothic Orloj clock counts down the hours to Christmas. Prague's markets are famous for trdelník—rolled dough with cinnamon and nuts—as well as fried hermelín cheese. Traditionally, a live nativity scene with real sheep, goats, and a donkey is installed in the center of the Prague market every year, and children are happily allowed to pet them.
Tallinn
The market on Tallinn's Town Hall Square is small but incredibly cozy. The northern winter atmosphere can be felt here like nowhere else—old stone buildings, snow, and lamplight. Tallinn will surprise you with blood sausage served with lingonberry jam, cinnamon-roasted almonds, and hot mulled wine with the famous Vana Tallinn liqueur added. According to local legend, it was in Tallinn, in 1441, that the Brotherhood of Blackheads erected Europe's first public Christmas tree, around which dances were held.
Wrocław
The Wrocław Christmas market on Market Square is now considered one of the largest in Central Europe. The historic center transforms into a real fairy-tale town with two-story wooden mills. Oscypek — smoked goat cheese from the mountains, grilled and served with cranberry sauce — is a delicacy no market is complete without. If you pay close attention, you may spot the famous local bronze dwarfs hiding throughout the Wrocław market. During the holiday season, some of them are even given tiny winter hats and scarves.
Zagreb
If you thought the best markets could only be found in the north, Zagreb easily disproves that. For several years in a row, the Croatian capital won the title of Europe’s best Christmas market. Here, you should try fritule — mini doughnuts with chocolate, cinnamon, or powdered sugar, served hot in cups. The market encompasses not just one square but literally the entire city: from Zrinjevac Park with its classical music pavilion to the historic underground Grič Tunnel, which is transformed into a light tunnel with musical accompaniment.

A delegation of Ukrainian, US and Russian representatives has arrived at the site from which humanitarian aid will be delivered to Russian-occupied Oleshky on Friday, Oct. 30.
Davyd Arakhamia, who leads President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Servant of the People party in parliament, said on Thursday, Oct. 29 that journalists from all three countries had also reached the location. Their presence, he said, is meant to make the next stage of the humanitarian mission as transparent as possible.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The truce, which marked a rare instance of de-escalation in Russia’s fifth year of war, initially began clouded by confusion as Chief of the Russian General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced a “silence regime” along the Kherson front beginning Oct. 27 – two days earlier than the Oct. 29 date set by the White House.
Despite fears of possible sabotage that Moscow’s unilateral announcement widely raised, the ceasefire is still holding as no incident has been reported for more than 64 hours.
Newsmax crew draws scrutiny
On Wednesday, Oct. 28 US First Lady Melania Trump, who mediated the agreement, announced that four journalists from the US conservative broadcaster Newsmax would be embedded with Ukrainian and Russian humanitarian officials in Oleshky.
She described them as “neutral observers” who would independently document the mission.
Shortly before, Kremlin’s economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev wrote on X that Russia was welcoming the Newsmax journalists to report firsthand on the mission; a post that Melania Trump shared.

Dmitriev’s growing role in Washington
Dmitriev heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), which the US Treasury sanctioned in 2022, under the previous Biden administration as it is closely connected to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Since US President Donald Trump struck a diesel arrangement with Putin on Oct. 9, Dmitriev has become not only Moscow’s main economic channel to the Trump administration, but possibly a key negotiator in the ceasefire.
The Trump administration is currently reviewing a request to lift sanctions on the fund, which helped arrange Russian diesel shipments to the US. Only a week prior, US special envoy Steve Witkoff confirmed that the US Treasury was working with Dmitriev directly.
Kyiv’s request for US journalists
Zelensky said that it was Ukraine’s idea to bring American journalists to the site, citing Kyiv’s distrust of the Russian side.
According to Ukrinform, he did not know which direction residents would choose when leaving. Moving deeper into Russian-occupied territory would be easier due to the routes available, he acknowledged, but many people in Oleshky want to reach Ukrainian-controlled areas.
“I know how technically the evacuation to Ukraine can take place, but I don’t know what will really happen,” Zelensky said.
Rights advocates warn of ‘human shield’
Ukrainian human rights advocates have warned that Moscow may try to keep part of the population in place.
Oleksandr Pavlichenko, executive director of the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union, told Ukrainian Radio that Russia sees civilians in frontline Oleshky as a human shield against Ukrainian fire, Ukrinform reported earlier on Thursday, Oct. 29.
According to Pavlichenko, there was no information available yet on whether Russian forces would subject evacuees to filtration, but warned that the risks existed. So far, he said, further details about international observers, including their number and access, remain unclear.
Saving the children from what Ukrainian senior authorities previously called a “death trap” remains a priority.
Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of Occupation, said Russian forces would almost certainly use the truce to move and rotate their units, adding that such activity could also take place on the Ukrainian side of the Dnipro River.
Human-made catastrophe
Oleshky, located on the left bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) southeast of Kherson city, has faced severe shortages of food, clean water and medicine for months, with the last food delivery reported on May 26.
According to Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha’s estimates, roughly 1,700 people remain in the city from a prewar population of 24,000, including 47 children.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets, who leads the humanitarian operation, earlier said that about 6,000 people, including some 200 children, remain across Oleshky and the surrounding settlements. In his view, up to 2,000 people could remain in Oleshky itself.
However, neither figure could be independently verified, particularly because Russian occupation authorities narrowly restrict access to information from the area.
Lubinets said on Sept. 16 that the residents had started escaping on foot independently across mined fields and under threat of constant Russian drone attacks, simply because they saw no other way out.
Before the truce was officially announced, Pope Leo XIV held a telephone discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 16, urging him to agree to an immediate ceasefire and allow the delivery of food and medical assistance to the city.
The pontiff then spoke to Zelensky on Monday, Oct. 19, reiterating his earlier request for a humanitarian ceasefire.
On Oct. 20, European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno declared a hunger strike in protest over the starvation of civilians in Oleshky.

Beskrestnov: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot interceptor missiles
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:54:24 EET
02:54:24 KST

Russia is producing ballistic missiles in volumes that exceed the global production capacity for Patriot interceptor missiles, stated Serhiy Beskrestnov (Flash), an advisor to the President of Ukraine on defense technologies.
"Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the number of Patriot interceptor missiles produced globally to counter them," he told reporters on Thursday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
According to Beskrestnov, Russia continues to manufacture Iskander and S-400 missiles, with production capacities in these segments exceeding current requirements. Furthermore, Russia has partially shifted production away from Kinzhal missiles toward ballistic missiles, Beskrestnov noted.
He emphasized that the increase in Russian ballistic missile production exacerbates the shortage of interceptors. He added that this imbalance is further compounded by the introduction of missiles from North Korea and Iran.
Beskrestnov noted that countering this threat requires an increase in the global production of PAC-3 interceptor missiles. At the same time, this process faces limitations, and scaling up production volumes takes time.

Six lanes and metro line under fire: Kyiv prepares about $22 million for backup river crossings after Russian strike on Southern Bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:52:25 UTC
02:52:25 KST

The Ukrainian government has instructed Kyiv to establish alternative routes after Russian attacks stopped traffic on one of the capital’s main bridges. The city authorities will bear the cost of the new crossings, with Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko saying the city needs an additional $22 million.
This year, Russia has launched tactics to spread panic among civilians and trigger more people to leave the country. In the latest attack, several Russia's ballistic missiles struck the Southern Bridge, used for vehicle and metro traffic, breaking a huge hole and paralyzing all the pathes. The bridge was closed. Now, there is a fear that more bridges can be targeted this way, dividing Kyiv in two parts.
The situation is urgent, as Ukrainian Transport Minister Mykola Kalashnyk says about 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro in Kyiv every day.
What is Kyiv’s response to the winter terror?
According to Klitschko, Kyiv convened the capital’s Defense Council on 28 October to find an answer to this difficult question.
The agenda included implementing a project to build combined water crossings over the Dnipro River and access roads to them.
“The military command will determine the locations, with approval to be granted, among others, by the Kyiv City Military Administration,” Klitschko said.
Under the government’s recommendations, the Kyiv city authorities must find $22 million for the project.
Klitschko had previously faced heavy criticism after it emerged that the city lacked sufficient shelters and last winter exposed serious shortcomings in preparing infrastructure for Russian attacks. These included a lack of alternative energy supply routes, poorly distributed energy, burst heating pipes that flooded apartments, and the inability of people with disabilities to reach shelters without elevators.
The mayor himself said the problems stemmed from the central government withholding funding, which had stalled numerous energy resilience projects and delayed their implementation.
The latest announcement also indicates that Kyiv has once again taken on the financial burden itself.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has been working with Japan on backup crossings. Tokyo has already delivered 720 meters of prefabricated bridge structures to Ukraine. The two sides are currently exploring how this equipment could be used to establish alternative crossings.
Step two: strengthening existing infrastructure
Another option is to reinforce existing bridges. City specialists are developing additional technical solutions to protect bridges across the Dnipro River, Klitschko said in his statement on 27 October, adding that proposals from the military had also been heard.
The issue of installing mobile shelters was also raised on the same day, the mayor of Kyiv said in a separate statement on his Telegram channel on 27 October. Despite intensifying Russian attacks and about, as Radio Svoboda reported in its article on 30 September, $11 million set aside in 2025, Kyiv still has only a handful of mobile shelters: LB reported in December 2025 that district tenders failed. Donors paid for the first one at a bus stop, the Kyiv City State Administration said on 15 October.
Klitschko raised the issue of shelters again after a court on 12 October ruled that local authorities must urgently install mobile shelters in public areas, including near public transport stops, parks, and squares, according to Kyiv’s Prosecutor’s Office.
Russia hits the Southern Bridge again
On 2 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times that Russian ruler Vladimir Putin had ordered the lifting of previous restrictions on airstrikes. Among new targets, according to him, were bridges, data centers, internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, and universities.
The night of 26–27 October showed what that looks like. Russia launched ballistic missile attacks in a few waves, and the second of them hit the Southern Bridge and the metro infrastructure on it, Klitschko said. The structure carries six lanes of road traffic and two metro tracks.
Zelenskyy put the night’s total at 16 ballistic missiles and blamed delays in deliveries of Patriot and NASAMS interceptors: “Every such delay is a new Russian hit on one target or another.”
