Israel election: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:32:00 UTC
02:32:00 KST

Israel election: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
October 29, 2026
Israel woke up on Thursday to allegations by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party that foreign actors may have sought to influence voter mobilization efforts in Arab communities during this week's legislative election.
No'am Sohlberg, the Supreme Court judge who heads Israel's Central Election Committee, sent a letter to Israel's internal security agency Shin Bet to look into the Likud's claims.
According to Likud's statement, Arab parties Ra'am and the Joint List — which received a record share of the vote, mostly due to unprecedented turnout in communities of Arab and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship — allegedly used "severe criminal offenses" to spur voters to go to the polls, including bribery, threats and other forms of election fraud.
"Severe suspicions were brought to my attention about improper intervention in the elections by foreign funding by outside actors that act against the Israeli interest," Sohlberg wrote in the letter, adding that he was "unable to testify" as to whether the allegations are true.
"The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party claimed in a statement. His own coalition lost seats, leaving both the prime minister and his opponents short of a majority — unless they were to work with one or both of the Arab parties.
Likud and other right-wing figures pointed to the unusually high turnout in Arab communities, reports of organized transportation to polling stations and concerns over foreign-funded voter mobilization campaigns as grounds for requesting an investigation. They argue that a formal review is necessary to maintain public confidence in the electoral process, regardless of whether wrongdoing is ultimately found.
Authorities refute allegations
Israel's elections are administered by the Central Election Committee, a body comprising representatives of parliamentary parties and chaired by a Supreme Court justice. Large-scale election fraud has historically been rare, although disputes over campaign conduct and voting procedures regularly arise.
Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”
"Election day went with a minority of irregular incidents in the area of election integrity, also compared to other elections," it said in a statement.
A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.
"We don't have any basis for claims of 'stolen elections,'" Dean Livne, the Committee's acting director general, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan 11, adding that the committee received "claims rather than evidence" from Likud and other parties.
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor and the head of the Yashar party, blamed the Israeli leader for leading an "improper influence operation" to cast doubt on the elections and create what he called "a fictive delegitimization" for the next parliament.
However, Eisenkot, also called for Likud's allegation of electoral fraud to be investigated.
The religious Muslim Ra'am party denied any involvement and said it would cooperate with any investigation.
Qatar released a statement denying any involvement in the Israeli elections, calling them "false propaganda aimed at dragging Qatar's name into Israel's political conflicts."
The controversy comes against the backdrop of growing polarization in Israeli politics and increasing public distrust between rival political camps.
Likud's motivation could be to decrease the Arab influence on Israeli politics, according to Amira Halperin, a senior fellow at the Palm Beach Center for Democracy and Policy Research. "The Arab votes were very, very important in this election," she said.
Such allegations could also hurt the public's trust in the election process Halperin argued: "We need to be cautious about predicting a failure of the democratic system."
Shin Bet head in focus
Israeli media reports have suggested that some of the concerns cited by Likud were based on intelligence assessments examined by the Shin Bet, though the agency has not publicly confirmed the details of any such findings.
Public broadcaster Kan reported the suspicions' extent as "relatively small," citing sources familiar with the Shin Bet investigation. Israeli daily Ha'aretz, too, quoted sources familiar with the allegations as saying the reports are "being blown out of proportion.”
David Zini, the head of the agency, said on election day that the elections in Israel are "safe, sound and supervised," adding that the Elections Committee and Israeli police are "successfully" preventing anyone from hurting it.
Zini's appointment earlier this year was criticized by opposition figures, who questioned both his qualifications for the role and Netanyahu's motives in selecting him. Supporters of the appointment rejected those criticisms, arguing that Zini's military experience and security background made him suitable for the position.
Separately, the Shin Bet, has been involved in investigating several of Netanyahu's closest aides on allegations of undisclosed ties to Qatar. Those investigations are unrelated to the current election allegations.
Pre-planned tactics?
Israeli outlet N12 has reported that in the weekend before the elections that Likud officials were discussing potential election-integrity complaints ahead of voting, although no evidence of actual irregularities had been presented at that stage, with a focus on Arab and Palestinian communities .
"They sat and brainstormed to find creative ideas of how to complain about this issue," said Daphna Liel, the reporter who broke the story.
Historic turnout
Arab and Palestinian participation in this week's election was unprecedented, with turnout jumping from around 50% in 2022 to about 80% in 2026, according to reports in Israel.
Arab voter participation has fluctuated significantly in recent decades. Turnout has often been influenced by debates within Arab society over whether participation in national elections can effectively advance the interests of Arab citizens, who comprise roughly 20% of Israel's population. The exceptionally high turnout in this election was widely seen as a sign of renewed political mobilization.
This resulted in huge success forthe Joint List and Ra'am, with 11 and eight parliament seats, respectively, in comparison to six and four in the 2022 election. Both parties have already voiced their willingness to cooperate with Israel's Zionist opposition to replace Netanyahu.
Most parties in Israel's Zionist opposition promised not to join a coalition with Arab parties ahead of the elections, with the exception of left-wing Zionist party "The Democrats” (HaDemocratim).
On election day, there were also allegations over "systematic delays" in voting in Arab and Palestinian polling stations, according to Adalah, an Israeli-Palestinian NGO for the legal rights of the Arab minority in Israel.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has dismissed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a senior military planner serving on the Pentagon's Joint Staff, following allegations that he disclosed classified information to the public, officials said Thursday.
Sylvia's firing is one of the highest-profile consequences to date from Hegseth's sweeping hunt for officials suspected of leaking information to the news media as the unpopular Iran war enters its ninth month.
Hegseth's effort includes a Pentagon task force to identify the source of leaks and the widespread use of polygraph exams on senior officials as part of these investigations.
Last year, he introduced a media policy that raised legal concerns among press organizations, and revoked the press credentials of journalists who refused to sign it.
A senior Pentagon official, speaking on condition of anonymity, accused Sylvia of failing three polygraphs questioning him about leaking classified information.
"The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second," the official said.
US President Donald Trump, who misidentified Sylvia as a woman, said the senior U.S. general has "got problems."
"We're very much looking for leakers, and she's going to have big problems, long-term problems," Trump told reporters.
Sylvia could not be immediately reached for comment.
Sylvia led the Directorate for Strategy, Plans, and Policy at the Joint Staff, known inside the military as the J5, a key position that helps advise the top U.S. military official, General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
He previously led the U.S. Army's 101st Airborne Division. His dismissal was first reported by The Atlantic magazine.
His removal comes as the U.S. military plans for a potential resumption of intensive bombings in Iran, something Trump has called "another little Epic Fury." The Pentagon has fumed about leaks during the Iran war, including about its planning and the expenditure of munitions.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that an internal U.S. military analysis estimates it would cost more than $29 billion in munitions alone to restock weapons used against Iran so far. That's the bulk of the more than $47 billion spent on operations in the war.
Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, said the decision followed an extensive investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
"This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action," Parnell said, without identifying other officials who may also be targeted.
Parnell added: "Our commitment was not an empty promise. We vowed to find you, and we meant it."
A spokesperson for the Joint Staff withdrew an initial statement expressing gratitude for Sylvia's 32 years of service, saying "we determined the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances."
"Out of respect for the service member and the ongoing personnel process, we will not comment further," the spokesperson said.

Senior US general fired, accused of leaking classified information
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 - Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired US Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, a senior military planner on the Pentagon's Joint Staff, over accusations he leaked classified information to the public, officials said on Thursday.
Sylvia's firing is one of the highest-profile consequences to date from Hegseth's sweeping hunt for officials suspected of leaking information to the news media as the unpopular Iran war enters its ninth month.
Hegseth's effort includes a Pentagon task force to identify the source of leaks and the widespread use of polygraph exams on senior officials as part of these investigations.
Last year, he introduced a media policy that raised legal concerns among press organizations, and revoked the press credentials of journalists who refused to sign it.
A senior Pentagon official, speaking on condition of anonymity, accused Sylvia of failing three polygraphs questioning him about leaking classified information.
"The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second," the official said.
US President Donald Trump, who misidentified Sylvia as a woman, said the senior US general has "got problems."
"We're very much looking for leakers, and she's going to have big problems, long-term problems," Trump told reporters.
Sylvia could not be immediately reached for comment.
KEY POSITION
Sylvia led the Directorate for Strategy, Plans, and Policy at the Joint Staff, known inside the military as the J5, a key position that helps advise the top US military official, General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
He previously led the US Army's 101st Airborne Division. His dismissal was first reported by The Atlantic magazine.
His removal comes as the US military plans for a potential resumption of intensive bombings in Iran, something Trump has called "another little Epic Fury." The Pentagon has fumed about leaks during the Iran war, including about its planning and the expenditure of munitions.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that an internal US military analysis estimates it would cost more than $29 billion in munitions alone to restock weapons used against Iran so far. That's the bulk of the more than $47 billion spent on operations in the war.
Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, said the decision followed an extensive investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
"This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action," Parnell said, without identifying other officials who may also be targeted.
Parnell added: "Our commitment was not an empty promise. We vowed to find you, and we meant it."
A spokesperson for the Joint Staff withdrew an initial statement expressing gratitude for Sylvia's 32 years of service, saying "we determined the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances."
"Out of respect for the service member and the ongoing personnel process, we will not comment further," the spokesperson said. REUTERS

The morning after: Israel’s election leaves more questions than answers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:30:13 UTC
02:30:13 KST

Israelis went to the polls expecting clarity. What they got instead was a political puzzle no one seems able to solve. On the latest episode of The Deep Dive, host Jacob Laznik and Knesset correspondent Keshet Neev unpack a whirlwind week in which months of polling were overturned almost overnight.
With more than 97% of votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud emerged as the largest party at around 27 seats, and his bloc leads the opposition 53 to 48, yet neither side has a path to 61.
Arab parties make the difference
The kingmakers in this deadlock are the Arab parties, which won a record 19 seats on the back of turnout above 80%, well past their previous high of 15. That surge also raised the electoral threshold and wiped out every small party that had dominated months of pre-election speculation.
The conversation moves quickly through the scenarios now being whispered in the Knesset corridors. Could a unity government bring together Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett? Laznik floats a provocative “200 IQ” scenario for how it might play out, and both hosts explain why the parties’ policy promises may make such a coalition unworkable, pointing to the Gantz precedent as a cautionary tale. They also examine the Arab parties’ unusual new posture, now focused less on longstanding red lines and more on ousting Netanyahu, alongside Avigdor Liberman’s role as the opposition’s wild card.
Then there is the story that broke publicly later: a Shin Bet investigation into possible foreign interference, with Qatar and Turkey reportedly under scrutiny. Qatar has denied involvement, and the Central Elections Committee says the integrity of the vote remains intact.
The hosts also look beyond Israel’s borders. They discuss how next week’s US midterms could reshape Washington’s approach to Iran, why reports of Donald Trump’s views on far-right ministers might push Netanyahu toward a broader coalition, and what it means that Netanyahu used election night to name toppling the Iranian regime as his first priority. They also reflect on what these first post–October 7 elections reveal: a Netanyahu bloc still in the lead, but noticeably weaker than before the war.
Neev offers viewers a practical guide for cutting through the deliberate noise of the coming weeks. As Laznik puts it, anyone claiming to know what happens next is lying.

Israel’s exit polls may have ‘fundamental problem’ after Netanyahu bloc surprise, pollster says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:29:56 UTC
02:29:56 KST

Israeli pollsters significantly underestimated Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political bloc in the latest election, Dr. Menachem Lazar, CEO of Lazar Research and Maariv's pollster, acknowledged in an interview with Nissim Mishal and Anat Davidov on 103FM, as he attempted to explain the discrepancies between the polls and the election results.
According to Lazar, there is no room for doubt.
"The pollsters were wrong, all of them. Some more than others, but there was a mistake. A serious mistake. I could argue that the last poll I conducted was on the Thursday before the election and that things happened between then and the election, but that is not really the reason. We were wrong. We saw a picture that ultimately turned out to be different. We gave the opposition a majority, and we saw that the Netanyahu coalition had a majority."
Lazar elaborated on the extent of the polling failure.
"We will have to conduct a full assessment of what happened once we see the final results. We need to wait another day. We underestimated the Netanyahu bloc, underestimated Benjamin Netanyahu's strength. We saw more or less the same thing in the 2015 election, how on the final day of the election he managed to increase Likud's strength."
He then explained how election polling is conducted and what the discrepancies might indicate about Israeli voters.
"There are two things that need to be done correctly with an exit poll: correctly distribute the polling stations, thoroughly examine how the exit poll polling stations were selected, look at the difference between the nationwide distribution and the distribution of those polling stations, and conduct another examination of the gap between the exit poll ballot box and the actual ballot box next to it.
"The exit poll ballot box is supposed to represent the actual ballot box beside it. This is not the first time. There may be a fundamental problem here, either with the polling stations and how the exit polls are positioned and constructed, or with how the Israeli public behaves ahead of elections."
'Neither side won'
Addressing accusations that the polls were intended to manipulate public opinion, Lazar said:
"Clearly, everything will head in that direction. There are more serious things we will need to examine. We examine ourselves after every election campaign. There is no election in which we produce results that match the parties' results exactly. Generally, we produce much better results when it comes to the blocs. There was the 2015 election, when there was also a similar discrepancy. We corrected ourselves in the election campaigns that followed. We will examine, correct, and hope that in the next rounds it will work better."
Lazar also addressed the issue of double-envelope ballots and the changes they could bring to the final distribution of Knesset seats.
"In my assessment, apart from the fact that the Arab parties have a smaller share of the overall vote, this should reflect what we are seeing in the Jewish sector. It could push the Reservists' Party and the Economic Party above the electoral threshold. They are short by around 40,000 votes, and they may reach that number.
"There is a certain chance that it could instead go to the Jewish Home party and Naftali Bennett, who were short by 1,400 votes, or Meretz, which was short by several thousand votes. Once again, a party could be on the threshold. We need to wait."
Lazar explained that the remaining ballots could also affect the balance between the political blocs, although he believes the overall election picture is relatively clear.
"The Arab parties could lose one or two seats, and there could be movement between the blocs. There are also the surplus-vote agreements. I think the overall picture looks fairly clear. Neither side won, and the entire argument is about who lost less. Now the question is how to form a government with this situation, or whether to go to new elections, where there are also assessments of what might happen."

Still, both blocs fell short of the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority without the support of the Arab parties, which won a record-breaking combined total of 19 seats.
The official vote count was announced amid a Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) investigation into suspicions that foreign entities, potentially including Qatar and Turkey, funneled money into Israel to influence voter turnout in the Arab sector.
CEC Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg directed Shin Bet head David Zini to investigate the suspected foreign funding and election interference.
The CEC later stated that the integrity of the vote at polling stations had been maintained.
The official vote count announced on Thursday included the remaining double-envelope ballots, which were the last to be counted.
How many seats does each party have?
Netanyahu's Likud is projected to enter with 27 seats, making it once again the largest party in the Knesset, according to the official vote count. United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit are expected to enter with seven seats, and the Religious Zionist Party and Shas are expected to enter with six seats.
Most TV channel polls before the elections showed Likud receiving significantly fewer seats, while the other parties in Netanyahu's bloc, such as Shas and Otzma Yehudit, were projected to gain more.
The opposition bloc, comprising Yashar, B’Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu, and the Democrats, is expected to enter the Knesset with 48 seats, according to data from the CEC.
Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar is projected to enter the Knesset with 21 seats. B'Yachad, led by Naftali Bennett, is expected to enter with 12 seats. Yair Golan's Democrats is expected to enter the Knesset with eight seats, and Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu is expected to enter with seven.
Most TV channel polling before the elections had shown the opposition bloc in the lead, and Yashar was projected to be the largest party in the Knesset.
The small right-wing parties hovering near the electoral threshold, Ofer Winter’s People of Israel and Yoaz Hendel’s The Reservists-Economic party, both fell short of the required 3.25% threshold.
The Joint List was projected to win 11 seats, while Ra’am was projected to secure eight seats in the next Knesset.
The prospect of a unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot remains possible, though Eisenkot had previously rejected serving under Netanyahu, including in a rotation government. Other opposition leaders have also ruled out joining a coalition led by the prime minister.
The political deadlock could also ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations.
By law, the president is required to consult the Knesset factions before deciding who receives the task of forming a government.
President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday called on political leaders to approach coalition negotiations with open minds, warning that Israel must do everything possible to avoid another round of elections.
He also called for a full investigation into the Qatari election interference allegations on Thursday amid the Shin Bet investigation, while warning against the threat of delegitimizing the voting process.

Belgium to vote on 'ICE-style' undocumented migrant home raids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:29:27 UTC
02:29:27 KST

Breadcrumb
Belgium to vote on 'ICE-style' home raids targeting undocumented migrants
Belgium’s parliament is set to vote on controversial legislation that would allow police to enter private homes to arrest undocumented migrants facing deportation, in a move campaigners have likened to tactics used by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The bill, due to be put to a vote on 5 November, would allow authorities to enter homes between 5am and 9pm with authorisation from an investigating judge. It would apply to foreign nationals who have received an enforceable order to leave Belgium. The measure could also include the homes of people suspected of accommodating undocumented migrants.
The proposal has faced widespread opposition from civil society organisations, lawyers, judges and local authorities, with critics warning that it threatens constitutional protections of the home, privacy and family life, while placing children and vulnerable households at risk.
They argue that the measure would allow authorities to enter private homes outside the framework of criminal investigations.
"The Belgian government may call them 'home visits', but that doesn’t change what they are: police forcibly entering private homes and traumatising families and children to arrest people who simply lack the right papers," Chiara Catelli, advocacy officer at the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants (PICUM), said in a statement.
"We've all seen the devastating consequences of home raids in the US, where they fuel fear and violence and tear families apart. It’s deeply alarming that an EU member state is now moving in the same direction," she said.
The legislation was introduced by Belgium’s Asylum and Migration Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt and Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden. It was approved by the Chamber of Representatives' Interior Committee in a second reading on 7 October and is now awaiting a vote in the full parliament.
PICUM has also raised concerns about the level of judicial oversight and the ability of those affected to challenge the legality of a raid before its consequences become irreversible.
Although an investigating judge would have to authorise entry, PICUM said the judge might not have access to the entire case file before making a decision. It also warned that people whose homes are searched could be left without an effective remedy to contest the authorisation.
Sotieta Ngo, executive director of the Coordination et Initiatives pour Réfugiés et Étrangers (CIRÉ), described the proposal as an attack on fundamental rights and solidarity.
"It's an attack against human dignity. It's an attack against solidarity. This proposal is a major violation of the constitutional principle of the inviolability of the home. From a democratic standpoint, there is nothing acceptable about this text," she said.
Under amendments approved by the parliamentary committee, an investigating judge would be able to determine how an operation is carried out and impose additional protections where children are present. However, opponents argue that these safeguards do not remove the risk of psychological harm to children and other household members.
Noor Ketels, policy officer at Vluchtelingenwerk Vlaanderen, said the consequences could extend well beyond the households directly targeted.
"The harm of this bill goes far beyond any single raid. Fear can stop undocumented people from seeking help and make those offering shelter afraid to open their doors. People already in precarious situations could be left with nowhere safe to turn," she said.
"Everyone’s fundamental rights must be protected, regardless of their residence status. We urge the Belgian Parliament to reject this bill."
More than 60 municipalities across Belgium have reportedly adopted motions opposing the proposal, while the Brussels regional parliament also passed a resolution against it on 2 October.
Protests against the legislation are expected across the country on 4 November, a day before the parliamentary vote.
The Belgian government has rejected comparisons between the proposal and ICE, arguing that the legislation is a narrowly defined measure intended to enforce existing deportation orders rather than target undocumented migrants generally.
Van Bossuyt has said the measure would apply to people who refuse to cooperate with their return and pose a threat to public order or national security, citing convicted sex offenders and people involved in terrorism as examples.
She has also stressed that police would need authorisation from an investigating judge before entering a private residence.
In the United States, ICE has faced heavy criticism over its conduct.
A tracker by US investigative outlet The Trace identified nine people killed in shootings involving federal immigration agents since President Donald Trump began deploying agents as part of his enforcement operations in June 2025. The figures include agents from ICE and other federal immigration agencies.

Pakistan rights activist Imaan Mazari and husband jailed for 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:28:18 UTC
02:28:18 KST

Pakistan rights activist Imaan Mazari and husband jailed for 10 years
Couple say they are ‘prisoners of conscience’ being made into an example by Pakistan’s military-backed authorities.
An antiterrorism court in Pakistan has sentenced prominent human rights lawyers Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, to 10 years in prison on terrorism-related charges.
Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra announced the verdict on Thursday, following their trial inside Adiala prison in the garrison city of Rawalpindi.
The couple were found guilty of putting “the security of [the England and Wales Cricket] team at risk”, the judge wrote, adding that it “clearly shows the intentions and objective of the accused to create a sense of terror”, according to a copy of the court judgement obtained by the AFP news agency.
At the same time, the ruling conceded that the security breach was “a very common nature ordinary type of incident apparently of removal of a barrier”.
The case relates to an October 2024 incident in which the couple removed road barriers in the capital, Islamabad, along a route designated for the touring England cricket team.
The couple were indicted on October 7, accused of obstructing police and inciting public interest, and pleaded not guilty.
In statements seen by the Reuters news agency, the couple denied the charges, while calling themselves “prisoners of conscience”, adding that they were being targeted for their human rights work.
In their defence document, the couple had earlier said they were “being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression and injustice”.
Relatives criticise judicial process
Shireen Mazari, who is Imaan Mazari’s mother and served as Pakistan’s human rights minister under incarcerated former Prime Minister Imran Khan, said it was a “sham trial without any due process”.
Mazari told the Reuters news agency the couple “were not permitted to defend themselves through their own lawyer, and were not provided with key legal documents”, adding that the defence would file a petition against the verdict in the Supreme Court.
Amnesty International called the convictions “an indictment of Pakistan’s justice system.”
“It was a test of the judiciary’s ability to uphold the principles of justice and the right to fair trial. It has failed that test miserably,” said Amnesty’s Yasmine Ahmend.
“It is clear that these ‘anti-terrorism’ charges are being used to punish Imaan and Hadi for their human rights advocacy,” she added.
Mazari and Chattha have been in custody since January 23, in a separate case over their social media posts.
A lower court sentenced them each to 17 years the next day under Pakistan’s Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, which critics have said is designed to quash antigovernment dissent online.
Although the Supreme Court later suspended those sentences, police re-arrested the couple the same day in the security breach case.
“Imaan and Hadi’s re-arrest dispels any pretence that the charges against them are anything other than a politically motivated attempt to punish them for their human rights work”, said Babu Ram Pant, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for South Asia, adding that the case demonstrates once again the authorities’ willingness to weaponise the legal system against critical voices.
Pakistan’s law minister, Azam Nazeer Tarar, has repeatedly said the country’s judiciary is independent.

Europe's total debt hits record high above $95T in H1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:26:29 UTC
02:26:29 KST

Sevgi Ceren Gökkoyun
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Total debt across 32 European nations topped $95 trillion in the first half of 2026 to reach a record high, the Institute of International Finance said on Thursday.  
Rising borrowing costs and political uncertainties are making it increasingly difficult to stabilize debt levels across the region, according to the institute's European edition of the Global Debt Monitor report.
Europe's debt pile accounted for approximately 25% of global debt during the six-month period, while the region's debt-to-gross domestic product ratio stood at around 325%.
The ratio remained more than 45 percentage points below levels seen at the onset of the eurozone debt crisis, the report noted.
France posted Europe's largest debt stock at $15.5 trillion, followed by the UK at $14.7 trillion, Germany at $13.5 trillion and Italy at $7.2 trillion.
Across economic sectors, financial institutions held the largest share of outstanding debt at $30.4 trillion, followed by non-financial corporations at $26.4 trillion, public debt at $22.5 trillion and household debt at $15.7 trillion.
France experienced the sharpest rise in borrowing costs among EU members this year, with its five-year credit default swap spread rising above 100 basis points to its highest level since late 2012, while Italy's spread stood near 75 basis points.
The report warned that persistent budget deficits, higher borrowing costs and shrinking fiscal buffers in a difficult political climate make stabilizing debt trajectories harder for European governments.
Heavy reliance on foreign investors to fund fiscal shortfalls leaves regional governments vulnerable to shifts in global risk sentiment and cross-border capital flows, the institute said.
Political gridlock could reignite market tensions as debt concerns increasingly concentrate in Europe's largest economies, raising the risk of broader financial spillovers, the report added.

02:26:06 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities in Israel, supposedly funded by foreign money.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.
“It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” Eisenkot said in a video message.
The prime minister’s allegations were quickly disowned by a range of government officials, including police officers and members of the election committee. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for “tarnishing an entire community”.
On Wednesday night, the prime minister posted a statement by Likud online, which described the claimed violations as “an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.
Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far-right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, holding the balance of power.
The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.
The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: “It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.”
Opposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.
Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.
Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.
The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.
The president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.
It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.
With almost all the votes counted, Netanyahu’s coalition has 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s bloc has 48, and the Joint List and Ra’am together have 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.
The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.
On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.
Voting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.
Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.
The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed the possibility of tactical voting in the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.
One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.
Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are being accused of taking Qatari money for promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.
“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.

Defendants handed life sentences amid tensions between Khartoum and Abu Dhabi over Sudan’s war and the RSF.
A court in the United Arab Emirates has sentenced eight people to life imprisonment over arms trafficking and money laundering to Sudan’s army, state media report.
The individuals supplied weapons and military equipment to the Sudanese army and were part of a money-laundering network connecting the two countries, the Emirati state-run news agency WAM said on Thursday.
It said the Abu Dhabi Federal Court of Appeal concluded on Thursday that the convicted individuals had participated in an integrated scheme for the illicit trafficking of weapons, ammunition and military equipment.
The accused were also found to have forged documents using companies and bank accounts in the UAE to channel funds relating to the arms deals and “conceal” their sources and destinations.
The court ordered the confiscation of ammunition and communications devices used in the crimes and the deportation of those convicted from the UAE after serving their sentences, WAM reported.

Ties between the UAE and Sudan have deteriorated as the Sudanese military has accused Abu Dhabi of supplying arms to its rival in Sudan’s civil war, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group, which it has been fighting since April 2023. The UAE has denied the allegation.
The war has displaced more than 14 million people and created severe poverty and food shortages.
This week, more than 100 people – mostly women and children – were killed when military drones hit a busy city market frequented by RSF fighters in the city of Nyala in the western region of Darfur.
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said a second attack hit a civilian neighbourhood. Rights groups petition Israeli court over expulsion of thousands of Palestinians from Hebron
Palestinian rights groups have filed an urgent petition with Israel's Supreme Court demanding the return of hundreds of families forcibly displaced from their homes in Hebron, as Israeli forces continue their military siege of the occupied West Bank city for a seventh consecutive day.
The petition calls for Palestinians expelled from the Al-Jalda, Ein Deir Bahha and Khallat Al-Maghariba neighbourhoods to be allowed to return to their homes, many of which have been seized by Israeli forces and converted into military barracks.
Lawyer Bassam Al-Qawasmi, founder of the All-Palestinian Gathering, said the court was awaiting responses from the Israeli military prosecution and army before proceeding with the case.
He explained that the legal action was launched after obtaining authorisation from Hebron Municipality and families affected by the forced displacement, with support from the city's newly established Relief and Support Committee.
The petition seeks to end the forced displacement, alleviate residents' suffering and secure their return to their homes.
Israeli forces have expelled thousands of Palestinians from neighbourhoods across Hebron since launching a major military operation last Friday after two Israeli soldiers were killed in an attack, imposing severe restrictions on movement and blocking access to residential areas.
More than 4,000 Palestinians have been displaced, while dozens of homes have been seized and converted into military outposts. The Israeli army has also demolished dozens of Palestinian buildings across the city.
Siege enters seventh day
Israeli forces continued raids and closures around Hebron's Old City on Thursday, continuing to occupy Palestinian homes in Al-Jalda and Ein Deir Bahha.
Troops also closed several iron gates surrounding the Old City, further restricting movement across the area.
The military operation has severely disrupted education, with dozens of schools suspending in-person classes and thousands of pupils forced to rely on remote learning and educational assignments.
According to Palestinian news agency Wafa, Israeli forces injured two Palestinians and detained seven others on Thursday, while settlers attacked Palestinian residents and vehicles in the Ras Al-Joura area near the city's northern entrance.
The Palestinian Prisoner's Society said on Wednesday that at least 110 Palestinians had been detained across the Hebron governorate since the operation began, including three women and seven children.
Israeli forces have also isolated 12 villages and communities in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, preventing residents from accessing markets, hospitals and essential services.
The offensive began after two Israeli soldiers were killed in a shooting near the illegal Israeli settlement of Telem last week. The Palestinian gunmen involved were subsequently killed by Israeli forces.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the closure of Hebron and instructed security forces to prepare for a wider lockdown across the occupied West Bank.
Extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich subsequently called for a military campaign in the territory similar to Israel's assault on Gaza.
UN warns of collective punishment
The United Nations and human rights organisations have condemned the operation, warning that mass displacement and sweeping restrictions on civilians could constitute serious violations of international law.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said collective punishment was a grave violation of international law, warning that threats to empty entire neighbourhoods raised serious concerns about ethnic cleansing.
Israeli human rights organisation B'Tselem described the operation as an act of collective punishment rather than a security measure.
Palestinian rights group Al-Haq also accused Israel of violating international law through its military siege.
Roland Friedrich, director of UNRWA Affairs in the occupied West Bank, warned that the displacement echoed Israeli operations in the northern West Bank in early 2025, where more than 34,000 Palestinian refugees remain forcibly displaced.

Meet the front-runners to replace Lagarde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:22:06 UTC
02:22:06 KST

A sign indicates the pedestrian way to the European Central Bank headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany on Oct. 23, 2026. | Kirill Kudyavtsev/AFP via Getty Images
FRANKFURT — The race to replace Christine Lagarde has reached fever pitch after she officially announced her intention to depart the European Central Bank in February next year.
The two leading contenders are familiar figures from the eurozone’s central banking circuit: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos, a measured economist with a reputation for quiet authority, and Dutchman Klaas Knot, a former hawk whose years on the ECB’s governing council left a more complicated legacy.
A recent Bloomberg survey of economists gives de Cos a slender lead: 12 respondents picked him, against nine for Knot. The survey offers a snapshot of expert preferences, not a forecast of the outcome. EU leaders will make the appointment, with national claims and other ECB vacancies likely to shape negotiations.
Advertisement
The choices will also be influenced by horse trading over what will likely be a package deal with the opportunity to fill the two executive board seats that will be vacant in January and May.
Softly spoken de Cos
An economist with a Ph.D. from the University of Madrid, de Cos joined the Bank of Spain in 1997, moved to Frankfurt in 2004 to be an adviser to the ECB’s executive board, before returning to the Spanish central bank. He rose through the ranks to become governor, serving from 2018 to 2024. In this role he restored the Bank of Spain’s reputation after a series of missteps before and during the financial crisis.
His achievement was implicitly acknowledged by his appointment to two terms as chair of the Basel Committee for Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for bank regulation. He now runs the Bank for International Settlements, the institution often described as the central bankers’ central bank.
His style is low-key: a modest dove, meaning that he is more attentive than hawks to growth and employment alongside inflation. Still, when inflation surged in 2022, de Cos backed the ECB’s shift toward higher rates. Equally, he has little time for governments that put off essential pension system reforms, having published a sharp critique of the Pedro Sanchez government while at the Bank of Spain.
His case
De Cos has long been groomed by Lagarde’s predecessor Mario Draghi, whose voice continues to carry a heavy weight in European economic debates and may influence the preference of some countries as they mull who to place at the top of the Frankfurt institution.
As France faces mounting debt pressures, de Cos’ experience as a senior Bank of Spain economist during the eurozone crisis could convince EU governments that he is the best fit. Galo Nuño, vice dean and professor of economics at IE University and a former alternate member of the ECB governing council, called it “a huge advantage.”
Advertisement
His challenges
The political arithmetic, however, could work against the Spaniard. France is keen to secure the role of the ECB chief economist, which becomes vacant in May 2027. Some officials may want to avoid pairing the ECB presidency and chief economist roles with candidates from highly indebted countries.
With inflation above target and the eurozone having lived through a severe inflation shock in 2022, some leaders may prefer a candidate with a more clearly hawkish record.
Enter: Klaas Knot.
Knot: Hawk turned pragmatist
Knot also has a strong economic background, boasting a Ph.D. from the University of Groningen. After early positions at the Dutch central bank, De Nederlandsche Bank, and the International Monetary Fund, he moved into senior roles at the Dutch Finance Ministry and returned to the DNB, which he led from 2011 to 2025. He has also chaired the Financial Stability Board, the global body tasked with monitoring risks to the financial system.
For much of Draghi’s presidency, Knot was a staunch hawk who publicly challenged the ECB’s stimulus measures. In September 2019, he called the package “disproportionate.”
His relationship with the ECB’s leadership was more harmonious under Lagarde. He supported both her pandemic crisis response package, PEPP, as well as the Transmission Protection Mechanism — a potentially more radical tool than any brought in under Draghi which allows the ECB to buy up unlimited debt of a single EU member country.
Advertisement
Knot remained an early advocate of raising rates when inflation took off but came to be described as a pragmatic hawk and team player.
His case
Supporters argue that a hawkish president could help the ECB support Southern European economies during a debt crisis while reassuring consumers and investors that the bank remains committed to price stability.
Knot’s former role as chair of the G20’s Financial Stability Board could also boost his case. Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding argued that “the question who may be best placed to deal with potential financial turbulences will likely play a key role in the choice of new ECB leaders.” This role was also Draghi’s springboard.
His challenges
Germany’s ambitions could be a stumbling block, as Northern European hawks will have had their turn with Knot. EFG Bank chief economist Stefan Gerlach said: “If Knot is appointed, then Germany can hardly argue that it is its turn to appoint the president after him.”
Some veteran governors still view Knot’s public break with Draghi as disloyal.
What happens now?
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said a decision would be taken by year-end, with eurozone ministers set to gather under the banner of the European Council in mid-December.
Advertisement
When it comes who will win the race, the history could cut both ways.
Nuño, who has seen both candidates in action, said each brings monetary-policy expertise and the political pragmatism needed to manage the challenges ahead.
The choice, then, will turn on which mix of policy temperament and political arithmetic EU leaders want at the top.

‘We make shit houses great again’: Visit Norway cleans up after Trump’s insult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:22:01 UTC
02:22:01 KST

Some might find it decidedly incommodious to be dumped on by Donald Trump as a “shithouse country”. Not the Norwegian tourist board, which chose instead to lift the lid on some of the nation’s loveliest lavatories.
“Are these the world’s best shit houses?” asked Visit Norway on its website, days after the US president vented his fury once more over failing to win the Nobel peace prize by describing Norway as a “shithouse country” at a rally on Sunday.
“Norway makes shit houses great again!” the agency continued above pictures of some of the country’s most striking public conveniences, adding: “These toilets are worth a visit, both when you really have to go – and when you don’t.”
Trump delivered his tirade at a rally in Michigan days before the US midterm elections. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually,” he declared, using a term he has previously applied to Haiti, Libya, Somalia and Yemen.
He added that he would welcome migrants from some countries but not Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize”. Earlier this month, Trump denounced the decision to award the prize to Navi Pillay, a former international criminal court judge.
“This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” he said. “I never heard of this person. The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited … And we will not forget, Norway.”
Along 18 designated scenic routes around Norway, Visit Norway said, leading architects had been tasked with transforming the humble wayside privy into an attraction in its own right. Several have since won international architecture awards.
The agency pictured a series of designer public conveniences, many of them architecturally striking and all offering breathtaking vistas overlooking fjords, beside rushing rivers and foaming waterfalls, and at stunning scenic viewpoints.
They “invite you to take your time and enjoy the scenery, even if you don’t have any business to take care of”, Visit Norway said, highlighting – among others – the restrooms at the Stegastein viewpoint in the Sognefjord region of western Norway.
This particular comfort station, the tourist board noted with uninhibited pride, had been ranked among the 10 best public toilets in the world by DesignCurial, the online architecture, design and interiors magazine.
Combining clean, minimalist lines with the fjord’s rugged and brooding landscape, the loos are famous for their large, black-tinted glass windows, which allow visitors a sweeping view from the throne while remaining invisible from the outside.
It also highlighted the unique, wave-shaped Ureddplassen loo on the wild coast of Helgeland, the southernmost district of northern Norway, hailed by several international publications as the most scenic restroom in the world.
Also featured are the solar-powered modernist bog at the Utsikten viewpoint, the “Instagram-worthy” Tungeneset loo (“looks pretty good underneath the northern lights”), and the world-famous triangular “golden toilet” on Senja island.
Jens Kjeldsen, a rhetoric professor at the University of Bergen, said that under the circumstances, Visit Norway’s response was well judged. “It’s like the bully in kindergarten,” he told NRK public television. “If you get too serious, the bully wins.”
Evgenia Egorova, a senior consultant at Visit Norway, told the broadcaster the response to its social media fightback had been immense. “The world needs a little laugh,” she said. “We thought: let’s meet them with kindness, and a little humour.”
Visit Norway said it had more stylish loos in the pipeline, including a forest-inspired latrine using dried wood from more than 60 trees. “Get ready for the pit stop of your life,” it urged, before signing off with a cheery: “Toodeloo!”
The Nobel peace prize is famously not awarded by the nation or even the government of Norway, but by the Nobel prize committee, which operates independently – something Trump “knows very well”, the foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said. “We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering.”

Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
Ukraine's Navy destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets in a strike against the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast, using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported on Oct. 29.
The aircraft were destroyed at the base of Russia's 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment near the settlement of Oktyabrsky, according to the Navy. The regiment belongs to the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of Russia's 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army. The Navy did not provide any visual confirmation of the strike. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
Later on Oct. 29, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the destruction of the two Su-34 jets, adding that Ukrainian forces had also hit a Russian Iskander missile launcher.
The Su-34 is one of Russia's main aircraft used to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, frontline settlements, and military positions. Strikes against these aircraft could weaken Russia's ability to carry out such attacks, while replacing the losses requires significant time and resources.
Russia had approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service as of Oct. 22, including the modernized Su-34M, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) reported on Oct. 29.
According to the agency, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed and another seven damaged since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Such losses are quite significant for the aggressor's aircraft fleet, whose restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation," HUR said.
The agency estimated that Russia can manufacture approximately 14 to 18 Su-34 aircraft annually, meaning the number of destroyed aircraft is equivalent to roughly 2.5–3 years of production.
Despite the losses, Russia continues to manufacture and modernize the aircraft to maintain its fleet and sustain aerial attacks against Ukraine.
The latest strike follows an Oct. 15 attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia's Voronezh Oblast that destroyed four Su-34M bomber-jets and damaged two more. The attack was also carried out using Neptune missiles.
The Ukrainian ground-launched Neptune cruise missile is best known for sinking Russia's Black Sea flagship, the Moskva, in 2022. Ukraine has since developed a longer-range version capable of striking targets up to 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) away.

Beskrestnov: Evacuating Kyiv is impossible; there is no precedent for this anywhere in the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:21:09 EET
02:21:09 KST

Evacuating Kyiv is not a viable solution; instead, every effort must be made to protect the city from potential Russian attacks on critical infrastructure—specifically water supply, sewage, and energy systems—says Serhiy (Flash) Beskrestnov, an advisor to the President of Ukraine on defense technologies.
"Evacuating Kyiv is nonsense—complete nonsense—because there is no precedent for this anywhere in the world. Even if we were talking about evacuating a thousand or ten thousand people, we simply lack the infrastructure to carry it out. Therefore, we must do everything possible to ensure Kyiv holds firm," he told reporters on Thursday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
According to Beskrestnov, Russia could target water supply and sewage systems, combined heat and power plants, electrical substations, and power generation facilities in an attempt to trigger a collapse in the capital.
He believes that preparations for potential attacks should have begun more actively back in the summer, specifically by installing protected generators, drilling additional artesian wells, and setting up stationary heating points.
Beskrestnov also pointed to the examples of Zaporizhia and Kharkiv, where, he noted, active work is underway to prepare for potential disruptions in heat and electricity supplies.
At the same time, he warned that deploying mobile boiler units will not, by itself, solve the problem, as their thermal emissions could make them visible to Russian drones equipped with thermal imaging cameras.
Beskrestnov urged Kyiv residents to prepare for potential disruptions to utility services, specifically, by stocking up on batteries and a small supply of fuel.

Meta discussed ‘whisper strategy’ against social media critic Jonathan Haidt, files show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:20:57 UTC
02:20:57 KST

Meta staff discussed deploying a “whisper strategy” to undermine the influential US academic whose work has inspired a global social media crackdown, according to court documents.
Employees at the parent group of Facebook and Instagram sought to discredit Jonathan Haidt, the social psychologist and author of The Anxious Generation, a book that helped tip the debate about online safety towards more stringent measures such as the under-16 ban in Australia.
Minutes of internal meetings contained in a recent legal filing in the US showed that staff discussed how to “get the academic community to disavow Haidt”.
They appear in a document titled “Well-being Meeting Sound-check Notes”, which refers to discussions of how Meta could “turn other academics against Haidt” and to a “whisper strategy” aimed at achieving that goal. It also mentions “debunking” his work.
Minutes from a meeting on 8 March 2023 mention “Curtiss”, an apparent reference to Meta’s then vice-president of research, Curtiss Cobb. It states: “Curtiss’s goal for this work: how do we get the academic community to disavow Haidt. Can’t co-opt them, so how do we enrage them … so the media finds him not credible.”
It then adds: “Not thinking about this as a loud strategy. A below-the-line campaign.”
It suggests getting someone called “Gellman” to write “a takedown piece”. The “Gellman” figure is not identified in the document but Andrew Gelman, a professor of statistics and political science at Columbia University who has been critical of Haidt’s work, wrote in a blogpost this week that he was “never hired by Facebook to do a hit job on Jonathan Haidt”.
Gelman said he had received money from Mark Zuckerberg’s company in the past on a “no-strings” basis but had never been asked by Meta to look at social media’s impact on teenagers’ health.
Haidt’s book The Anxious Generation argued that widespread use of smartphones has caused a mental health crisis for young people.
The academic has become a persuasive advocate for strict regulation of digital media and devices, including bans on social media for under-16s and on smartphones in schools. Early this year the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, asked Haidt to address officials on a possible social media ban for under-16s in the UK.
The minutes were produced before Haidt published his book in 2024 and discuss responding to a Substack post written by the academic in which he reviews “a bunch of articles”. It is not clear whether Meta acted on the ideas outlined in the minutes.
In statement to the tech news website The Verge, Haidt said he was “not surprised” by the discussions, which were revealed in a court filing as part of a litigation brought by school districts suing the company.
“When companies can’t dispute the evidence, they go after the messenger,” he said.
Meta has been approached for comment.

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Shahed Drone Infrastructure in Bryansk, Targeting Warehouses, Launch Sites and Radars
Ukrainian forces struck several Russian military facilities in the Bryansk region during operations carried out on October 28 and overnight into October 29, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. The targets included a Shahed-type drone storage facility, a drone launch site, and a fuel depot.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The strikes targeted three facilities supporting Russia’s attack drone operations near Navlya in the Bryansk region.
According to the General Staff, the targets included a warehouse storing Geran-type attack drones, a drone operating base, and a depot containing fuel and lubricants.
The Ukrainian military said the strikes were intended to reduce Russia’s ability to launch drone attacks against Ukraine, including its civilian infrastructure, using various types of unmanned aerial vehicles.
In addition to the drone-related facilities, Ukrainian forces targeted several other Russian military installations across the Bryansk region.
Two radar stations were struck near Starodub and the settlement of Medvedove, while drone command and control posts were targeted near Savlukove and Vitovka.
The General Staff noted that damaging Russian radar stations creates gaps in the country’s radar coverage, potentially weakening its ability to monitor aerial activity.
Beyond the Bryansk region, Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian command and observation post near Novohrodivka in Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
Separately, Ukraine’s 33rd Separate Mechanized Brigade reported on October 29 that Ukrainian forces had destroyed the command post of Russia’s 26th Tank Brigade using HIMARS following months of reconnaissance.
According to the brigade, Ukrainian reconnaissance units monitored the facility for several months, refining its coordinates and gathering intelligence to confirm the target’s location.
Once the command post had been positively identified, Ukrainian forces carried out the strike using HIMARS. The brigade said two munitions were sufficient to destroy the facility.

DoorDash to acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in $17B deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:20:06 UTC
02:20:06 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
US delivery firm DoorDash has agreed to acquire grocery delivery technology platform Instacart in a cash-and-stock deal valued at approximately $17 billion, the companies announced on Thursday. 
Under the definitive agreement unanimously approved by Instacart's board, DoorDash will pay $65 per Instacart share, representing a 26% premium over its closing price on Oct. 22.
The purchase price will be paid with at least 75% cash, with DoorDash stock capped at 25% of the total consideration.
Instacart shareholders may elect to receive all cash, DoorDash shares, or a combination of both, subject to proration.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online; someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," said Tony Xu, co-founder and chief executive of DoorDash.
"Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery," Xu added.
Chris Rogers, chief executive of Instacart, said joining forces with DoorDash allows the company to accelerate innovation and create new opportunities for retail and brand partners.
"When our purpose-built grocery technology and trusted retailer and brand relationships are combined with DoorDash's global consumer reach and logistics capabilities, we can create new opportunities for our retail and brand partners," Rogers said.
Following the acquisition, Instacart customers will gain access to more than 50,000 additional stores beyond the nearly 100,000 retail locations currently on its platform.
The merged company plans to integrate membership programs, allowing DashPass and Instacart+ subscribers to pay a single fee and saving users an estimated $100 million annually.
DoorDash committed to maintaining Instacart's brand, application and enterprise technology products, adding that local grocers will not face platform exclusivity rules.
DoorDash plans to fund the cash portion with cash on hand and proceeds from a 364-day senior unsecured bridge loan facility provided by JPMorgan Chase Bank.
The transaction is expected to close in late 2027 or the first half of 2028, subject to antitrust clearance in the US, regulatory approvals in Canada and Israel, and approval by Instacart stockholders.
Shareholders representing about 19% of Instacart's outstanding stock have agreed to vote in favor of the merger.

Unknown

2026-10-29

02:19:42 KST

On the ninth day, the Russian Knights aerobatic demonstration team acknowledged the deaths of two of its pilots: Colonel Oleg Yerofeyev, an honoured military pilot-sniper, and Lieutenant Colonel Vladimir Kochetov, a senior pilot.
The Russian Knights aerobatic demonstration team announced this on their Telegram channel.
The pilots died on October 21 during a training flight in a Su-30SM fighter jet.
Both pilots were experienced aviators with extensive flight hours.
Colonel Oleg Yerofeyev was deputy head of the 237-th Proskurov Guards Aircraft Demonstration Centre and had accumulated 3,300 flight hours.
Lieutenant Colonel Vladimir Kochetov was a flight safety inspector at the 237-th Proskurov Guards Aircraft Demonstration Centre and had accumulated 1,500 flight hours.
Both pilots were qualified to fly MiG-29, Su-27, Su-30SM and Su-35S fighter jets.
The Russian Knights aerobatic demonstration team was formed on April 5, 1991, based on the 1st Squadron of the 237-th Proskurov Guards Aircraft Demonstration Centre named after I. N. Kozhedub.
The team is permanently based at Kubinka Air Base in the Moscow region. Its fleet primarily consists of Su-35S fighter jets.
In peacetime, the team performs demonstration flights at ceremonial events and international gatherings.
However, during the full-scale war, the pilots are regularly assigned combat missions, usually flying in-service aircraft.
At the same time, there have been documented cases of aircraft from the aerobatic team being used directly in combat.

Ukraine’s central bank raised its key policy rate by 0.5 percentage points to 16.5% on Oct. 29, after sharply worsening its macroeconomic forecast. Ukraine’s economy is now expected to shrink this year, while inflation is set to finish 2026 far above earlier projections.
The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) downgrade confirms the gloomier outlooks other analysts published earlier, which already reflected the impact of recent Russian strikes on Ukraine’s largest businesses and the effect of the port blockade.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In the NBU’s updated forecast, the economy is expected to contract by 0.4% in 2026, against the 1.8% growth projected in the 2026 July Inflation report. Real GDP is expected to grow just 0.4% in 2027 (2.8% in the previous forecast) and 2.2% in 2028 (3.0% before).
This is also the second contraction of Ukraine’s economy since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The war caused a 28,8% drop in Ukraine’s GDP in 2022, while it grew by 5.5% in 2023, by 2.9% in 2024, and by 1.8% in 2025.
End-of-the-year inflation forecast is revised upwards to 12.5% in 2026 from 10.0% and 7.3% in 2027 from 6.9%, before returning to the 5.0% target in 2028. International reserves were cut in all three years, to $62.8 billion in 2026 ($69.7 billion before) and $57.0 billion in 2028 ($70 billion before). The current account deficit narrows to $3.6 billion in 2026 from the $16.1 billion projected in July, but widens to $49.5 billion by 2028.
NovaPay Invest to Buy 100% Stake in BTA Bank
Inflation was driven primarily by direct and second-round effects from the surge in fuel prices caused by the war in the Middle East, as well as the summer wave of Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s warehouses and logistics.
The NBU has also estimated the toll of Russian blockade of sea ports and attacks on production facilities and logistics, saying it subtracted 1.9 percentage points from this year’s GDP. In the third quarter this year, the NBU estimated that the real GDP decreased by 0.5% year-over-year.
“The NBU estimates that consequences of aerial attacks alone will add around 0.7 percentage points to annual inflation. Other important factors affecting the price dynamics will include effects of higher fuel prices and an expansion of fiscal stimulus,” NBU governor Andriy Pyshny said during the monetary press briefing on Thursday, where the NBU board presented the decision.
Metallurgical and ore mining enterprises suffered the greatest losses while performance also deteriorated in other industrial sectors, trade, and agriculture, he added. For 2027, the NBU assumes inflation will be restrained by the likely cooling of domestic demand and the labor market in the coming months after Russia’s attacks.
The central bank wrote that international aid in the third quarter fell short of expectations because Ukraine delayed reforms, although parliament adopted laws in October to unblock EU and IMF financing. Its forecast assumes about $50 billion in direct budget support and more than $32 billion under the defense component of the Ukraine Support Loan in 2026, and $52 billion and $37 billion respectively in 2027.
Lending growth remained strong despite tighter policy. In September, net hryvnia corporate loans grew more than 32% year on year and net retail loans more than 38%.
The war remains the primary risk to inflation and growth, per the central bank press release, as Russian strikes on production and infrastructure raise costs and cut supply, in addition to higher oil prices from the war in the Middle East.
The NBU’s forecast envisages keeping the key rate at 16.5% until the second quarter of 2027. The NBU expects a slow recovery in 2027-28, supported by investment in the defense industry, localization of weapon production financed by the Ukraine Support Loan, and reconstruction of critical infrastructure.

The interim report, Young People and Work, led by Alan Milburn, was published on May 28, 2026, with the final comprehensive recommendations report expected next month.
The Young People and Work report is an independent review of the increase in the number of young people who are not in education, employment or training.
Burnham added: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."

They have left everything behind to get away from US President Donald Trump's America. Entrepreneurs, academics, scientists and students: tens of thousands of US citizens have moved to Ireland in recent years. Last year alone, some 10,000 Americans settled there and nearly 100 even applied for asylum – citing political, racial or gender persecution.
For some US citizens, moving to Ireland feels like coming home. Around one in 10 Americans claims to have Irish roots, with ancestors who fled famine and hardship in the 19th century onwards, and applications for Irish passports have never been higher.
Emma Hensley is a postgraduate student at Trinity College Dublin. For her, Trump's America no longer guarantees women's rights. In County Cork, southern Ireland, Daniel Rothman has just arrived from Alaska, where he lost his job at NOAA, the US agency for oceans, fisheries and climate policies, after budget cuts imposed by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). Finally, Ophelia and her wife Zahra, a transgender couple, describe the increasingly dangerous discrimination faced by transgender people.
Ireland is welcoming these new arrivals from the US, but they could upset a fragile diplomatic balance. Dublin is a long-standing ally of Washington and one that relies on US investment to sustain its growth.
