Saudi Arabia needs a coalition against Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:21 UTC
01:42:21 KST

Saudi Arabia has a serious problem with Houthi insurgents in its large, mountainous and inhospitable neighbor to the south, Yemen. The Saudis have been fighting there in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government for more than a decade, but the stubborn Houthi rebels — with enormous support from Iran — continue to threaten Yemen’s stability and attack Saudi Arabia directly.
This vicious civil war has gone on for 12 years, starting with the rebel seizure of the capital, Sana’a, in 2014. Since then, nearly 400,000 people have died in the fighting, and the conflict has only intensified since the Israel-Hamas war began in 2023. The Houthis are now launching frequent long-range strikes on Saudi Arabia, including an attack earlier this month on the international airport in Riyadh that killed a dozen people, including an American, and wounded hundreds.
This is a major threat to the global economy. Yemen sits astride the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, through which 12 to 15 percent of the world’s shipping passes. Using alternative routes adds significant costs to seaborne goods.
The stakes are even higher for Saudi Arabia itself. With the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, the Red Sea port of Yanbu and the East-West pipeline that feeds it have become the main Saudi export lifeline, and the Houthis have already struck them.
So where should Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman turn for assistance? The most logical answer, of course, is the US — but US armed forces are heavily engaged in the war with Iran, and US President Donald Trump’s administration has so far held back from coming to the Saudis’ aid. Given that reality, Saudi Arabia would need to rely more heavily on other partners — starting with Turkey and Pakistan, but also potentially Europe and even Israel.
Fortunately for Riyadh, the kingdom concluded a smart regional defense pact in August with Turkey and Pakistan. These two fellow Sunni nations bring significant military capability to bear should they fulfill the Mecca Defense Pact’s pledge that “an attack on one is an attack on all,” much like NATO’s famous Article 5.
The problem for the Saudis is that the Houthis are dug into difficult terrain. Yemen’s mountains, in which the Houthi movement originated, are home to bases, caves and tunnels that support guerrilla fighters. The Saudis have struggled in mountain warfare against the Houthis — but the Pakistanis have deep experience in it.
During my time with NATO, I marveled at Pakistan’s Frontier Corps and other mountain troops. They have operated extensively in the mountains between Afghanistan and Pakistan, as well as at the “top of the world” in ongoing disputes with India, and have particular expertise in mountain counterinsurgency. Islamabad refused to join the Saudi-led coalition in 2015, when Pakistan’s parliament voted to stay neutral in Yemen, but the new pact should change that calculus. The crown prince would be wise to press the Pakistanis for help.
Another very different form of assistance could come from Turkey, the other member of the new pact. These would be naval forces to help keep the Red Sea open. The Turks operate new, sophisticated frigates and corvettes, and have plenty of experience in these waters. They were very capable members of the coalition NATO put together to combat Somali pirates. Asking Ankara to send a significant flotilla to the Red Sea, based out of Saudi ports on the kingdom’s west coast, would make sense.
The crown prince should also turn north to Europe. While the Europeans have so far stayed out of the war with Iran in the Strait of Hormuz, they have good reasons to support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis. The Suez Canal is a vital chokepoint for European economies, after all. And the EU could expand its existing Aspides naval mission in the Red Sea, now just a handful of ships with a defensive mandate, to help keep goods flowing and the Suez open.
The British are already helping defend Saudi airspace with Sky Sabre air defenses and an RAF tanker to refuel Saudi Typhoons. France is sending troops and air defenses to protect Yanbu, and Greek-operated Patriots have intercepted Iranian missiles over the kingdom. A larger EU naval or air mission could build on that foundation.
Finally, and most controversially, Saudi Arabia could look to Israel. There is already reportedly a level of quiet cooperation between Jerusalem and Riyadh on missile defense, cyber and special forces. This could be expanded to include naval cooperation coming from Israel’s naval base at Eilat on the Gulf of Aqaba.
The Saudis clearly have their hands full dealing with the Houthis and postponed until next year their important annual investment conference, the so-called “Davos in the Desert.” They need to get the Houthis back to the negotiating table. Part of doing so would be enlisting outside actors to present a capable front against the Yemeni rebels. The stronger that front turns out to be, the stronger Riyadh’s hand would be when talks resume.
James Stavridis is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist, a retired US Navy admiral, former supreme allied commander of NATO and vice chairman at Carlyle. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

US Army outlines Pacific deployments for possible 2027 China-Taiwan conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:19 UTC
01:42:19 KST

The US Army Pacific (USARPAC) is deploying forces and equipment across the region based on the assumption that Beijing could possess the military capability and the intent to invade Taiwan by next year, a top US commander said on Tuesday.
Speaking at the TechNet Indo-Pacific conference in Honolulu, US General Ronald Clark said that the threat posed by the so-called “Davidson window” is “still valid,” US military newspaper Stars and Stripes reported on Wednesday.
The term stems from a 2021 warning by Admiral Philip Davidson, then-head of the US Indo-Pacific Command, that the threat of Chinese military action against Taiwan could materialize within six years.
Photo: AP
The six-year timeframe has driven US defense budgeting and strategy in the Pacific with the goal of deterring or obstructing an invasion, Stars and Stripes reported.
Asked whether the Davidson window was still relevant, Clark said: “The answer for us at USARPAC is yes.”
The six-year window is “a period of time for which we’re snapping the chalk line to say we need to be ready by this date,” he said in the report. “So we’ve embarked upon a strategic approach to setting the theater that we refer to as Army Ready Forward.”
Under the Army Ready Forward initiative, USARPAC has placed equipment, materiel and personnel on a rotational basis west of the International Date Line on the island chains closest to China, Clark said.
The most pressing issue for the military is finding the right balance between “exquisite high-end systems and affordable, mass-producible alternatives,” particularly regarding autonomous systems, he said.
The 2027 timeline has been a focal point for US defense planning, although assessments of Beijing’s immediate intent vary.
In 2023, former CIA director William Burns said US intelligence indicated that Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) had instructed the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) to be ready by next year to conduct a successful invasion.
However, an annual threat assessment issued in March by the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence assessed that Chinese leaders did not currently plan to invade Taiwan in 2027.
“Chinese leaders do not currently plan to execute an invasion of Taiwan in 2027, nor do they have a fixed timeline for achieving unification,” it said. “Beijing almost certainly will consider a variety of factors in deciding whether and how to pursue military approaches to unification, including PLA readiness, the actions and politics of Taiwan, and whether or not the US will militarily intervene on Taiwan’s behalf.”

Following the scent to Singang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:16 UTC
01:42:16 KST

Several years ago, the Ministry of Economic Affairs began encouraging legacy manufacturing enterprises to reposition themselves as tourist factories. In these places — which draw busloads of Taiwanese tourists but few international travelers — visitors can learn about the history of particular industries, observe production, join DIY workshops and gain an appreciation of the unglamorous but valuable skills that underpin Taiwan’s economy.
Among the country’s most successful tourist factories are sites which make balloons, braised foods, cookies, fishing gear, ribbons and whisky. Few are so closely tied to local traditional culture, however, as Singang Incense Artistic Culture Garden (新港香藝文化園區) in Chiayi County.
The small town of Singang (新港) is best known for its principal place of worship, Fengtian Temple (奉天宮). Each year, the massive nine-day Mazu pilgrimage that starts in Taichung’s Dajia District (大甲) arrives at the temple, then turns around and resumes its homeward trek.
Photo by Steven Crook
Han Chinese have been burning incense made from agarwood, sandalwood and other fragrant ingredients since at least the Song dynasty (960–1279 AD), and incense has long held a central role in Taiwanese religion and temple culture. The burning of incense establishes a symbolic connection between the human and spiritual realms. Incense smoke is believed to carry the prayers and gratitude of the pious up to the deities they worship. Pioneers wishing to consecrate a new shrine carried with them ash taken from the censer of an established temple in their home region — a ritual known as fenxiang (分香, “dividing the incense”).
These traditions are familiar to anyone versed in Taiwanese popular religion, yet a visit to Singang Incense Artistic Culture Garden offers additional insights to those who can read Chinese or use their smartphone’s translation function.
Originally a thoroughly traditional incense making operation led by three brothers surnamed Chen (陳), the site became a tourism factory in 2008. It now includes an exhibition area, a demonstration workshop, a shop and a restaurant for visiting tour groups — as well as a large production area which is off-limits to the public.
Hoping to get some good photos of incense makers at work, I peered through the murky glass that separated me from two middle-aged men. They were busy dipping thin sticks in powder, shaking off the excess, then placing them in a machine that rolls the sticks to ensure they’re evenly coated.
To my surprise, neither man wore a respirator mask or eye protection. Even if the materials being used were 100-percent natural, the sifting and shaking generates plenty of dust. It can’t be healthy.
‘NINE SKILLS OF INCENSE MAKING’
I clambered around to the other side of the building, where a couple of doors had been left open, presumably to ventilate the workshop. Pictures taken, I headed for the air-conditioned comfort of the exhibition hall.
One display focuses on the “Nine Skills of Incense Making” that were essential before machines became available. The skills are, in order: dipping (in water, to moisten the bamboo splints); twisting (in natural gum, which ensures the incense powder stays on); resoaking (with water, to activate the adhesive); spreading (holding sticks in a fan-like shape, then tossing aromatic wood powder over them); twirling (rotating the sticks so the powder coating is even); tapping (to shake off excess powder); air drying (until they’re partly but not entirely dry); dyeing (each stick’s handle using red or pink pigment); and sun drying. Even then, the work isn’t done, as the finished sticks have to be inspected, bundled and packaged.
INCENSE MOTHER
One panel tells the story of Jiutian Xuannu (九天玄女), the putative inventor of incense sticks. Myth has it that her father was desperately ill and unable to swallow the bitter herbal medicines prescribed by traditional physicians. One day, she dried the medicinal herbs and ground them up into a powder. After adding a binding paste made from tree bark, she rolled the mixture onto narrow strips of bamboo. These she lit and placed in her father’s bedchamber, so he could breathe in the herbs.
The therapeutic aromas eventually cured him — and his daughter earned an additional name, Xiang Ma (香媽, “Incense Mother”). Over the past thousand years, beyond her role as the patron deity of incense, Jiutian Xuannu has also been worshipped as the goddess of warfare, longevity and sexuality.
Another part of the exhibition concedes that Taiwan’s incense-making industry has been in decline since the 1970s, yet it doesn’t offer any explanations. Rather than any decline in the amount of incense being burnt, I suspect it’s a consequence of cheap imports from China and Southeast Asia taking market share.
Several display cases contain exceptional woodcarvings and objects crafted from incense dough. Similar works of art can be purchased on site. They’re stunning but hardly cheap; I saw one carrying a price tag of NT$398,000. More affordable purchases come in the shape of aromatic sachets, essential oils, fragrant soaps, sandalwood shampoo and various types of incense. In addition to joss sticks of different calibers, there are incense coils, incense yuanbao (元寶, the shape gold and silver ingots used in the China of yore), incense powders and jingxiangfen powders (淨香粉) used in purification rites.
Returning to the car at the end of our visit, I poked my head into the company’s production area. Being a Sunday, the machines were quiet, but outside a pair of workers moved back and forth, turning over incense coils as they dried under the sun. If I learned one thing at Singang Incense Artistic Culture Garden, it’s that incense making — like many other traditional trades — brings its participants both daily tedium and economic stability.

Because of our position, we received extensive training in how to behave. This had special urgency for my group of volunteers: we had originally been slated for Nepal, but a US Peace Corps volunteer in another country had criticized that nation’s authoritarian president in public, and all of the Peace Corps volunteers were kicked out. As a result, the next group for that nation got sent to Nepal, and we got bumped to Kenya. The

Debate in Ivory Coast spills into concert halls

Ivorian reggae star Alpha Blondy abruptly interrupted his concert’s chilled-out vibes to wade into a far less laid-back subject — the coups in his country’s unrest-riven Sahel neighbors.
His comments swiftly went viral on social media, in a sign of how Ivory Coast’s poor relations with the military-led governments in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have spilled over into popular culture, with artists caught in the crossfire.
“To my Sahel brothers ... no more coups d’etat. That’s enough,” the singer, known for his political bent, told the crowd in Ivory Coast’s economic capital, Abidjan.
Photo: AFP
The past few years’ toppling of democratic governments in west Africa is “destabilizing the region,” Blondy said, leg propped up against a loudspeaker. “Africa has no time to waste.”
Since the coups, all three have turned their backs on France — and therefore on Ivory Coast, which the juntas consider far too close to their shared former colonial ruler for comfort.
Several Internet commentators from the Sahel countries accused Blondy of attacking their leaders while turning a blind eye to Ivory Coast President Alassane Ouattara’s largely uncontested election to a fourth term — a criticism echoed by some Ivorians.
With the climate tense, musicians and promoters have found themselves ensnared in controversies that have led to dozens of canceled concerts or boycott calls.
In the latest example, Burkinabe singer Issouf Manem-Yam was forced to apologize for remarks seen as insulting toward Ivorians after his Abidjan concert planned for the middle of this month was axed.
“He’s an artist; he shouldn’t take sides, even if his remarks were made out of patriotism,” a Burkinabe cultural figure told reporters.
The tipping point can be traced back to 2022 at least, when Mali detained 49 Ivorian soldiers for six months. With social media awash with calls to target the other country’s artists, Malian singer Mariam Ba had her Abidjan concert canceled, weeks before the same happened to Ivorian rapper Didi B’s planned gig in the Malian capital, Bamako.
The tit-for-tat cancelations have only become more frequent, with Malian artists targeted in Abidjan while Ivorian musicians have received at-times frosty welcomes in the Sahel capitals.
“We’ve documented a dozen cases of Malian artists who have fallen victim,” a Malian culture ministry official told reporters, adding that the subject was on the agenda when Ivory Coast’s security chief visited in the middle of this month.
Every political remark is under scrutiny.
For backing Ouattara during Ivory Coast’s presidential campaign last year, Malian artist Sidiki Diabate has been slated within his home country.
On the other side of the border, Ivorian diva Aicha Kone has frequently raised hackles in Abidjan for backing the Sahel juntas.
Blondy’s fellow Ivorian reggae singer Tiken Jah Fakoly also found himself mired in the squabble after criticizing clampdowns on free speech in Ivory Coast’s neighbors.
Under criticism by supporters of the three juntas, he replied in 2024 that the Sahel states “thought I was going to be their minstrel.”
Several months later, the affair took a bizarre turn after his beloved “Rasta Bambi,” a doe he had lovingly raised on his farm in Mali, went missing.
Supporters of the juntas on the Internet swiftly seized on Rasta Bambi’s disappearance to mock the singer, with one commenting ironically that the deer “is demanding democracy from you” and had “just broken the chains of slavery.”
Despite the tensions, Ivorian and Sahel artists have continued to criss-cross the border to play gigs in each other’s countries, with cultural ties proving stronger than diplomatic ones.
“Artists are truly above taking sides in politics,” the president of a cultural association in Abidjan said.
Instead of the Ivory Coast-Sahel row, the official blamed the political situation in the Sahel countries — which are all wracked by a long-running and bloody jihadist insurgency — for “reducing the mobility of artists”.
One Ivorian musician who has kept the music playing on in the junta-run nations is Serge Beynaud, who performed near the Burkinabe capital, Ouagadougou, at the end of last month.
Sole hitch of the evening: with the bouncers clearly intent on making sure no disorder disrupted the gig, one of his dancers was whipped by an over-zealous security guard.

Eight of England’s nine water companies still failing on environment, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:39:48 UTC
01:39:48 KST

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has summoned water industry bosses to Whitehall after a report found that the environmental performance of the big companies has worsened despite investment.
“People are sick of excuses,” Dame Angela said, after the Environment Agency joined the Drinking Water Inspectorate, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat for a joint report that rated eight of the nine water companies in England as “poor” or “requiring improvement”.
There were 74 serious pollution incidents, the category that causes significant harm to the environment, the report said. That was just one fewer than the previous year, despite billions of pounds of investment, bans on bosses’ bonuses and a public outcry. The watchdog’s environmental performance assessment ratings of water companies added up to 16 “stars” out of a possible 36, a fall from 19 the previous year, and the lowest score since the process began.
Changes could be imposed on the industry, Eagle warned: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and-branch reform cannot wait.”
The UK is one of only two countries in the world where the provision of water is fully privatised. The other is Chile, where water privatisation was imposed in the 1980s by a military dictatorship.
Overall, there were 2,666 pollution incidents in England in 2025 – a 40% increase on 2016, the EA said. Thames Water had the most, followed by Anglian Water, United Utilities, Yorkshire Water and Southern Water.
The Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Eagle was preparing to take “further action”, with “tougher consequences” for executives at failing companies.
Defra said it would “set out a clear set of improvement actions”, such as “tackling leakage”, “reductions in pollution incidents” and “improving customer satisfaction”. Rules that took effect last year would block bonuses for executives at companies receiving a one-star rating.
Environmental campaigners called for stronger action. “This is a system that rewards shareholders and creditors while our rivers, wildlife and bill payers lose out,” said James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action.
Thames Water, the worst offender, ought to go into special administration immediately, he said. “Ministers must end the failed privatisation experiment, review alternative models including public ownership, and give regulators the power to make polluters pay not the public.”
The four agencies have pooled their data in a joint report for the first time – a step towards combining currently fragmented regulatory responsibilities under a single watchdog. But Richard Benwell, the chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said a new regulator “must be more than a merger of existing institutions”.
“It needs a clear legal duty to restore nature, strong environmental targets and the powers and resources to enforce the law across the water industry, industrial agriculture, and chemical companies,” he said.
Water UK, the industry trade body, said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history, as well as other areas of good performance. However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough.
“While more than half of all pollution incidents last year were caused by blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies, there is clearly more work to do.
“It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth and end sewage entering rivers and seas.”

Russian rights group documents at least 69 deaths among victims of political persecution since 2022
At least 69 people subjected to politically motivated persecution by Russian authorities have died in Russia since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to a report published by Memorial’s Political Prisoner Support human rights project to mark the Day of Remembrance for Victims of Political Repression.
Illness and lack of medical care were the most common causes of death, accounting for 29 cases documented by the group. At least 20 people died from beatings, torture, or their aftereffects, and 10 died by suicide.
One person died as a result of a hunger strike, and another — Alexey Navalny — was deliberately killed in a penal colony. The causes of death of eight others remain unknown.
The group recorded the most deaths in 2024, when 26 people died. Another 13 died in 2025, and 16 died in the first 10 months of 2026, with October not yet over.
The average age of those who died was 51. The youngest on the list, Ukrainians Daniil Dakhov and Pavel Grimak, were both 18. The figures include people who died in pretrial detention centers and penal colonies, as well as during searches, under house arrest, and shortly after their release.
Memorial’s report recounts the stories of all 69 people who died. Meduza has reported in detail on some of them, including Ukrainian journalist Viktoria Roshchyna, pianist Pavel Kushnir, scientist Dmitry Kolker, Arctic researcher Valery Mitko, biker Kirill Buzmakov, and activist Anatoly Berezikov.

Egypt, US discuss Sudan crisis, efforts for political settlement

Şahin Demir
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Top officials from Egypt and the US discussed developments in Sudan and efforts to reach a comprehensive political settlement to end the country’s conflict, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry said Thursday.
The discussions between Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Massad Boulos, US President Donald Trump’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, took place during a call on Wednesday as part of consultations and coordination between Cairo and Washington on regional issues of mutual concern, it said in a statement.
Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s support for Sudan’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity, stressing the need to preserve its national institutions.
He also emphasized the need to intensify regional and international efforts to achieve a comprehensive political settlement that ends the crisis and meets the Sudanese people’s aspirations for security and stability.
Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have been at war since April 2023, stemming from disagreements about integrating the two forces. The fighting has killed tens of thousands and displaced 13 million, amid worsening famine and a humanitarian crisis.
The two officials also discussed developments in Libya and ways to advance the political process and end the country’s divisions.
Abdelatty stressed the importance of preserving Libya’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity, while supporting the unification of its national institutions.
He urged coordinated regional and international efforts to help Libyan parties reach a comprehensive and sustainable political settlement through a Libyan-led and Libyan-owned process.
The discussions also addressed maritime boundary delimitation under international law, particularly the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, according to the statement, without providing details.
Libya remains divided between two rival administrations: the internationally recognized Government of National Unity, led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh in Tripoli, which controls western Libya, and a government appointed by the House of Representatives in early 2022, headed by Osama Hammad in Benghazi, which controls eastern Libya and much of the south.
The UN has facilitated talks among Libyan parties to establish a consensual constitutional framework for simultaneous presidential and parliamentary elections, aimed at ending the transitional period and unifying state institutions.

Venezuela to offer state assets to private sector, President Rodriguez says
Oct 29 - Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez said on Thursday the government has made progress in identifying state assets to be offered to the private sector and former owners, a move that could reverse widespread nationalizations ordered by former President Hugo Chavez.
"I have instructed that non-essential assets held by the state be assessed to determine which can be offered to the private sector or returned to their former owners. This process is already well advanced," Rodriguez said in a televised address.
In April, Rodriguez appointed a government commission to audit and evaluate state-owned assets, including infrastructure in key industries such as energy, power and mining. They have been working on asset classification since, according to sources.
She did not provide further details on how the process may be carried out. Under Chavez, the nationalization of key projects and industries left over a dozen international arbitration claims, which mostly remain unsettled by the government.
In her speech, Rodriguez said that 44 energy contracts are currently being negotiated under the state's new oil law approved in January. The government has stated that 61 oil agreements have so far been signed, without providing details.
"Similarly, important negotiations are underway in the mining sector, specifically regarding gold, aluminum, and iron," she added.
The president also said that she has instructed law enforcement agencies not to arrest people without a warrant, and vowed to defend the right to "peaceful protest" in the country, which has a history of political repression and last week saw its first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years.
"The responsible exercise of political rights is guaranteed for everyone. Our doors are open," Rodriguez said.
In her address, Rodriguez also said that the government has planned four quarterly increases in the national minimum wage in 2027. REUTERS

Yemen's hospitals buckle as fighting escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:36:19 UTC
01:36:19 KST

Yemen's hospitals buckle as fighting escalates
TAIZ, Oct 29 - In a hospital in Yemen's Taiz, a 25-year-old pregnant mother of two lay immobilised after a bullet lodged in her spine while she was trapped inside her home without food or water for two days.
The UN and aid agencies say health needs in the besieged city of Taiz are critical, amid acute shortages of medicine, oxygen, surgical gloves, anesthetic and fuel. Hospitals near Yemen's front lines are facing large influxes of patients, treating up to 700 war wounded in a single week, according to the Red Cross.
Amal al-Sabri said she was injured by a sniper bullet in the village of al-Shaqb — perched on the slopes of Mount Sabir overlooking Taiz — as an escalation in fighting between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement takes a devastating toll on civilians.
Medics at Al-Thawra hospital in Taiz said they could not perform a scan because she was over four months pregnant.
"The bullet entered from the side and is now lodged near the spine. They (the doctors) couldn't remove it because of the fetus,” Sabri told Reuters. "Now I am giving up the fetus."
HEALTHCARE SYSTEM 'AT BREAKING POINT'
Taiz governorate, which hosts about half of the 281,000 people who have been newly displaced in Yemen since the start of August, has been largely isolated since October 3, with fighting preventing humanitarian supplies from entering and civilians from leaving.
Taiz, Marib and the Red Sea coast are seeing some of the highest casualties, with patients arriving at hospitals with gunshot wounds and complex blast injuries, according to the Red Cross.
“The healthcare system across Yemen is at a breaking point,” said Red Cross spokesperson Hachem Osseiran.
Even before the latest fighting, more than 40% of hospitals and healthcare facilities across the country were already either closed or partially functioning following years of protracted conflict, he said.
There are also concerns about the outbreak of disease as water runs short and rubbish accumulates on the street.
MEDICAL FACILITIES UNDER ATTACK
Throughout Yemen, primary care for pregnant women is disrupted. In some hospitals near the front lines, maternity wards are being converted into emergency rooms, Osseiran said.
“Some of them (doctors) have to make a very difficult and painful choice: Do I help this woman deliver her baby, or do I rush to a person who is bleeding out because of a gunshot wound?” he said.
In Taiz city, the UN says community midwives have stopped working due to restrictions on movement.
Not only are health services stretched, they are also under attack. A hospital in Taiz's Sabir Al-Mawadim district was hit by mortar fragments for the second time this month, while a strike on an ambulance killed its driver and a paramedic, according to the UN.
On Monday, another strike that hit near Mocha General Hospital — where medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières supports the maternity and pediatric wards — damaged the building and triggered panic among patients.
“Such incidents are preventing patients from coming to the hospital for fear of their lives,” MSF said. REUTERS

Five people, including four children, were killed and five others are missing after heavy rainfall and flash floods hit several Syrian provinces, the Emergency and Disaster Management Ministry said Thursday, Anadolu reports.
It said the deaths were recorded in the countryside of Raqqa and Deir ez-Zor, while five people were reported missing in the rural areas of Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and Aleppo, according to Syria’s SANA news agency.
Search operations for the missing are continuing in coordination with relevant authorities, it added.
Civil Defense teams rescued 25 people trapped by floodwaters or whose vehicles became stranded in Raqqa in northern Syria, Deir ez-Zor in the east and Homs in central Syria.
The ministry said emergency teams remain deployed in affected areas, responding to distress calls and assisting civilians.
In Deir ez-Zor, footage showed Syrian army helicopters taking part in operations to rescue those stranded by floodwaters and blocked roads.
Military helicopters rescued two people trapped by flooding along the Deir ez-Zor-Palmyra road, according to SANA.
– Hundreds of families evacuated
Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said earlier that all ministry teams were on alert in response to heavy rainfall and flooding.
The alert covered Aleppo, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, Hasakah, Hama, Homs and Latakia provinces, according to Alikhbariah TV.
The ministry said Civil Defense teams had carried out 165 field responses as of 11.30 pm (2030GMT) Wednesday, rescuing 15 civilians and evacuating 375 families from flood-hit camps.
The families were evacuated from the Sahlat al-Banat, Al-Younani and Al-Maqas camps in the Raqqa countryside after rainwater flooded the sites.
Emergency teams received more than 350 reports, while flooding put seven bridges, culverts and dirt roads out of service, according to the ministry.
More than 100 families were also trapped in the Kasrat Surur area in rural Raqqa after a dirt culvert collapsed, prompting an emergency response.
Teams pumped and drained water from more than 150 homes and public facilities, including two hospitals, schools and bakeries.
Large parts of Raqqa, Hasakah and Deir ez-Zor, as well as eastern Homs, Hama and Aleppo, have experienced heavy thunderstorms accompanied by hail and strong winds.
The rain triggered floods and overflowing waterways, cutting roads and damaging public facilities as rescue and emergency operations continued.

Alaska Governor Orders Probe Into Peltola Campaign Over Alleged Spoiler Scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:35:54 UTC
01:35:54 KST

Alaska’s Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign following a report that her team helped recruit candidates to draw votes from her Republican opponent, including a man with the same name.
The announcement, posted on social media overnight, followed President Donald Trump’s call for Peltola’s prosecution and escalated Republican efforts to challenge her candidacy just days before an election that could help determine control of the Senate.
On Thursday, Trump declined to say whether Peltola should be seated if she won. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” he told reporters before leaving for a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Peltola is challenging Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan in the Nov. 3 election. Another candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, has denied running at Democrats’ behest. Alaska’s Supreme Court upheld his eligibility for the ballot earlier this year.
The dispute intensified Wednesday after a New York Times report found that Peltola's team worked with people to recruit men named Dan Sullivan to run for Senate, as well as other candidates who could draw votes away from the incumbent.
Dunleavy said the reporting provided new evidence of an effort to mislead voters and supported state election officials’ earlier findings about Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy.
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” the governor wrote.
Peltola, a former congresswoman, dismissed the report, arguing that it diverted attention from issues including the incumbent Sullivan’s support for the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” she said during a campaign stop in Soldotna on Wednesday. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
A spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign, Alaskans for Mary, said in an email to TIME that it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” The campaign also said it had made no assertions in federal court about how Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy came about or who was involved in his decision to run. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), which was also reportedly involved in the plan, told TIME in a statement that it was “not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.”
Vice President JD Vance also backed an investigation Thursday, accusing Peltola of trying to mislead voters about her campaign’s involvement. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful,” he told reporters before a campaign trip to Texas.
Trump had accused Peltola and her campaign of voter fraud in a series of Truth Social posts Wednesday, calling for her removal from the ballot and prosecution.
“It was just determined that the Dumocrats in Alaska, despite their sworn statements to the contrary, put a man named Dan Sullivan on the Ballot in order to confuse the Public with respect to Highly Esteemed Senator Dan Sullivan,” Trump posted. “This is Voter Fraud at the Highest Level, and the Dumocrat Candidate, who was involved in the scheme, Mary Peltola, should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted—So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan. Nothing else will do!”
The Times noted that ballot-stacking tactics are generally considered legal and have been used by both parties.
At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department had already filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the election results under specific conditions if Senator Sullivan loses, citing the potential for “voter confusion.” The department wants the results recalculated as though votes for Daniel J. Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, and certification blocked if that would change the outcome.
TIME reached out to the Justice Department for comment on how the report affects its case. Attorney General Todd Blanche told Fox News on Wednesday that he expected to “hear more” from the department this week as officials receive new information.
“They are cheating,” Blanche said. “They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues, but by putting up a person with the same name, so that confuses Alaskans.”
What Peltola’s campaign reportedly did
According to the Times’ report, which was based on interviews, text messages, and documents prepared for a possible lawsuit, the Peltola campaign pursued a project known internally as “ballot composition,” which involved campaign lawyers and senior aides at the DSCC, which directs Democratic campaign strategy for Senate races nationwide.
One of the Times’ sources, Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who was fired during an August staff shake-up, said the operation to recruit potential spoiler candidates for the Alaska ballot began in the summer of 2025. The Times reported that Peltola’s campaign worked with a “veteran Democratic operative” named Jerid Kurtz, whom it described as having expertise in ballot maneuvering.
The Times reported that a Peltola staffer received instructions to “find as many people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska” as possible. Kurtz reportedly found a man in Petersburg named Dan Sullivan who was open to running for Senate.
Rios said Peltola wasn’t directly involved in the project but was “definitely aware.” The Times also reported that Rios later wanted to recant her statements but did not explain why.
Alaska has a nonpartisan primary system, in which voters may choose a candidate regardless of party affiliation, and the top four advance to the general election. Voters then rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins an initial majority, the lowest-ranking candidates are eliminated in successive rounds and their ballots transfer to voters’ next remaining choices.
The spoiler candidate tactic isn’t new
Alaska’s other Senator, Lisa Murkowski, who endorsed Sullivan but supported Peltola years ago, issued a statement Wednesday demanding that Peltola tell the “honest truth” about the apparent ballot-stacking effort.
“While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process,” Murkowski wrote. “Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments. By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong.”
Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sullivan’s campaign, also said in a statement that “not one player in this operation has acted in good faith with Alaska voters.”
Republicans have also used similar ballot-stacking tactics. In this year’s Alaska primary, a GOP-aligned political action committee reportedly spent money to boost left-leaning fringe candidates in an attempt to pull votes from Peltola.
When Peltola ran for re-election to the House in 2024, Alaska’s Republican Party supported an effort to help a federally imprisoned Democrat who had never lived in Alaska stay on the ballot.
A GOP-linked political action committee also spent over $1 million this election cycle to boost a third-party candidate in Ohio in a bid to undermine former Senator Sherrod Brown’s comeback bid.
In Minnesota in 2020, Legal Marijuana Now Party candidate Adam Weeks told a close friend before his death that he was recruited by unnamed Republicans to pull votes away from Democrats.

EU countries push back against Brussels plan to tax gas more than electricity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:35:22 UTC
01:35:22 KST

More than a dozen EU countries are challenging Brussels' plans to favour electricity over gas, warning that the proposals would undermine national control over energy taxation and grid charges.
More than a dozen EU countries have pushed back against European Commission plans to make electricity cheaper than gas through preferential taxation, warning that Brussels is overstepping its powers.
At a meeting of EU energy ministers in Luxembourg on Thursday, Germany, Italy, Malta, the Czech Republic, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Finland, Romania, Croatia, Poland, Latvia, Estonia and Hungary were among the countries calling for the controversial provision to be scrapped.
The proposal is part of the Commission's efforts to encourage households and businesses to switch from fossil fuels to electricity, as demand from industry, data centres, heat pumps and electric vehicles continues to grow.
But the rising cost of expanding and operating Europe's electricity grids is increasingly being passed on to consumers through higher bills.
The Commission proposal comes amid an energy crisis, exacerbated since the US-Israeli war against Iran which has sent prices soaring and intensified pressure on Brussels to ease the burden on households and industry.
Even before the Middle East conflict, European electricity prices were twice those in the US and China, prompting European manufacturers to demand "urgent and bold" action.
During an informal summit last February, EU leaders vowed to drop energy prices by making electricity taxation more favourable than natural gas in a bid to lower bills.
But several EU countries argue that tax policy should be dealt with in the ongoing revision of the Energy Taxation Directive, which requires unanimity, rather than being decided by a qualified majority vote, as the European Commission proposes.
Sweden's energy minister Ebba Busch called for better regulation instead of more bureaucracy.
“Given the very significant differences in grids and the grid characteristics across the Union, there is no one-size-fits-all solution for tariff design,” Busch said.
Spain, Denmark and Luxembourg have backed the Commission, though they called for some flexibility.
"The proposals should include flexibility for member states to set clear political priorities for ambitious electrification policies to ensure pace and scale of grid expansion," said the Danish permanent representative diplomat, Søren Jacobsen.
France sought a middle path, calling for the legal basis to be secured and suggesting the measure be tied to specific circumstances such as a gas crisis.
Luxembourg floated replacing the provision with a general obligation to promote electrification.
Brussels versus national control
The strongest opposition centred on the Commission’s plan to let it set common rules for how electricity grid charges are calculated across the EU, without having to seek fresh approval from member states and the European Parliament each time.
Italy, France, Germany, Slovakia, Poland, Spain, Finland and other countries argued that the plan would undermine the independence of national regulators and give Brussels too much power over decisions that they believe should be made at national level.
Finland noted that its parliament had formally concluded the proposal violates that principle.
"Member states must retain sufficient flexibility to reflect their national circumstances, investment needs and electricity systems. We are also concerned by the lack of comprehensive impact assessment," Finland's state representative Mika Nykänen said.
Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen held his ground in his closing remarks, saying the EU executive's proposal "makes a lot of sense".
The EU's top energy chief said that the legal services of both the Commission and the Council judged the proposal legally sound.
"It (the legal clause) could have both an immediate and a structural impact on reducing our electricity bills. We should not deprive our consumers and industries of the benefits of this proposal," Jørgensen told energy ministers.
The Irish Presidency, currently mediating EU negotiations, says it wants a compromise on network charges in December.

European Central Bank President Lagarde to step down early
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:34:55 UTC
01:34:55 KST

European Central Bank President Lagarde to step down early
Christine Lagarde will leave the post in February, nine months before the end of her eight-year term.
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde will step down months before her term ends, kicking off a race to succeed her against a turbulent backdrop in the eurozone.
Lagarde announced on Thursday that she will leave the post on February 7, about nine months before the scheduled end of her eight-year term. She said in a filmed statement posted on X that she was leaving “with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future”.
The move gives European Union leaders time to choose her successor before April’s French presidential election, which polls have suggested far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favoured to win.
The timing could allow current European Council members, including French President Emmanuel Macron, to take part in appointing Lagarde’s successor before France’s vote.
Macron, who is not allowed to run again, thanked Lagarde in a post on X for “the determined action she led at the head of the European Central Bank” during “a period marked by numerous crises”.
“The transition at the head of the ECB must now be prepared in an orderly and balanced manner with our European partners,” the leader of the eurozone’s second-largest economy added.
However, Markus Ferber, a German member of the European Parliament, warned: “If the impression arises that such a departure is timed around national elections, it damages trust in an institution that must stand above any domestic political calculation.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, leader of the eurozone’s largest economy, said Lagarde had led the bank “with great aplomb during challenging times”, and European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen thanked Lagarde “for everything you have done for Europe and the euro”.
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure praised her tenure. “Christine Lagarde has been an exceptional President of the ECB. As Europe navigated through crises and difficult times, she brilliantly modernised and strengthened the institution,” he posted on social media.
Marcel Fratzscher, president of the German Institute for Economic Research, told the Reuters news agency the early exit gives governments “an opportunity to appoint a successor who will safeguard European values and protect the ECB’s independence”.
Markets appeared unfazed. “Our view is that institutional behaviour is likely to outlast Lagarde and be quite similar, whoever takes over,” Simon Dangoor, head of fixed income macro investing at Goldman Sachs told Reuters.
Lagarde, appointed in October 2019, steered the bank through the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the United States-Israel war on Iran.
The ECB faced criticism for responding too slowly to the 2022 inflation surge, caused by post-pandemic supply chain bottlenecks and the war on Ukraine. Inflation is currently running at almost double the bank’s 2 percent target amid worries over France’s public finances.
A former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund, Lagarde arrived in Frankfurt in 2019 as the first ECB chief with no formal economics training or central banking experience, prompting some market participants to warn of a “credibility risk”.
In March 2020 as the pandemic shook sovereign debt markets, she said the bank was not there to narrow the gap between Italian and German borrowing costs. She went on to show that political diplomacy could steer a central bank through historic shocks.
Sources told the AFP news agency that leaving early would give Lagarde “greater freedom to express her views”. She has hinted she could campaign in the French presidential race, saying a European voice was needed in the debate.

Five people, including four children, were killed and five others are missing after heavy rainfall and flash floods hit several Syrian provinces, the Emergency and Disaster Management Ministry said Thursday.
It said the deaths were recorded in the countryside of Raqqa and Deir ez-Zor, while five people were reported missing in the rural areas of Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and Aleppo, according to Syria’s SANA news agency.
Search operations for the missing are continuing in coordination with relevant authorities, it added.
Civil Defense teams rescued 25 people trapped by floodwaters or whose vehicles became stranded in Raqqa in northern Syria, Deir ez-Zor in the east and Homs in central Syria.
The ministry said emergency teams remain deployed in affected areas, responding to distress calls and assisting civilians.
In Deir ez-Zor, footage showed Syrian army helicopters taking part in operations to rescue those stranded by floodwaters and blocked roads.
Military helicopters rescued two people trapped by flooding along the Deir ez-Zor-Palmyra road, according to SANA.

Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said earlier that all ministry teams were on alert in response to heavy rainfall and flooding.
The alert covered Aleppo, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, Hasakah, Hama, Homs and Latakia provinces, according to Alikhbariah TV.
The ministry said Civil Defense teams had carried out 165 field responses as of 11.30 pm (2030GMT) Wednesday, rescuing 15 civilians and evacuating 375 families from flood-hit camps.

Large parts of Raqqa, Hasakah and Deir ez-Zor, as well as eastern Homs, Hama and Aleppo, have experienced heavy thunderstorms accompanied by hail and strong winds.
The rain triggered floods and overflowing waterways, cutting roads and damaging public facilities as rescue and emergency operations continued.

Russian drone kills 14 at Ukraine train station, but local truce credited to Melania Trump brings some hope
Kherson, Ukraine — A jet-powered Russian drone hit two passenger trains stopped at a station in Dnipro in central Ukraine Thursday, killing at least 14 people and injuring 14 more, including a 40-year-old man whose legs were amputated, officials said.
A Russian cruise missile killed two 15-year-old girls in the northern city of Chernihiv, meanwhile, and three more civilians died when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in the central city of Kremenchuk, Ukrainian authorities said.
In all, 56 people were injured in the strikes, including 10 children, as Russia continued its deadly attacks on civilians even as a localized ceasefire credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump held in the stricken city of Oleshky.
Humanitarian aid was poised to roll into Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said Thursday, as the limited ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared away landmines.
Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, but the neighboring nations remain otherwise locked in the war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion more than 4 ½ years ago. Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.
Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv. Around half of the drones were heading to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.
Both sides thanked Melania Trump for what the White House said was her role in helping broker the temporary ceasefire so food and medical supplies can be delivered to some 2,000 desperate people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.
"The parties are fully adhering to the agreements, and no violations of the ceasefire have been reported," Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday, adding that aid deliveries were due to begin the following day.
His Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the truce was holding and that Russian engineers are working on demining Oleshky's roads.
"Both sides are fully honoring their commitments, and no violations have been recorded," she said. "This allows military personnel to continue clearing roads of mines and to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy."
Local people will also be able to evacuate, either into Russia or Ukraine, per their wishes, officials say. The mechanics of how that might work remained unclear.
Lantratova said she and her team were on their way to Oleshky for the aid delivery, adding that the operation was five months in the making.
Russian and Ukrainian representatives met in the Belarus city of Homel on Thursday to fly together to the Kherson region, Belarus state media reported.
A volunteer from Oleshky, Ksenia Arkhipova, told The Associated Press roughly 1,000 residents had told her they want to leave the city.
She said it was important that the Ukrainian delegation was present in Oleshky because many residents fear Russian authorities would identify individuals with pro-Ukrainian views or ties to Ukraine's military.
In the nearby city of Kherson, growing numbers of people were out on the streets as the truce held.
Nataliia Myronenko, 42, had a steady stream of customers at her coffee kiosk since early Thursday.
"Now, during the quiet, we have people at lunchtime and in the evening, which we didn't have under the attacks," she said. "For a while, people would race down this street because they were afraid to stop."
The pause has brought a sense of relief, she said. "It's a breath of freedom, when you don't look at the sky. You keep looking at your feet because of the mines, but you're not afraid of dying. It's so great," she said, adding: "It's such a privilege and a joy, but we understand it will end soon."
Moscow and Kyiv are keen to curry favor with Washington ahead of possible three-way talks next month.
American military support is vital for Ukraine, but President Trump has waived sanctions on Russia and publicly chided Zelenskyy, indicating he is disengaging with Kyiv.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel are sailing to the United States, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is expected to attend a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, starting Friday, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.
European leaders, on the other hand, have been trying to diplomatically isolate Russian President Vladimir Putin over Moscow's invasion and what they call a campaign of sabotage across the continent.
Ukraine earlier this month reported sudden and unexpected limits on Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communications.
Putin said Russia has been in contact with the American tech titan to coordinate their orbiting activities because it is building its own equivalent of Starlink.
"Elon Musk is a genius. Truly, a real genius," Putin said late Wednesday. "We and our American partners value this relationship, and despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely together."

Russian losses rise sharply in 2026

Russia now loses more soldiers than it recruits. But the war won’t end because of that.

Lithuania plans to introduce universal military conscription for men ages 18–22 starting in 2032
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:31:29 UTC
01:31:29 KST

Lithuania plans to introduce universal military conscription for men ages 18–22 starting in 2032
Lithuania’s State Defense Council has decided to introduce universal conscription in 2032, President Gitanas Nausėda said.
Universal conscription will apply to men ages 18 to 22, replacing the current selective draft. Women will still be able to volunteer for military service.
Lithuania currently drafts about 5,000 young people each year. Nausėda said the annual intake under universal conscription would be about 7,500 young men, based on demographic trends and the number of conscripts fit for service.
The 2032 start date was chosen to give the military time to prepare its infrastructure for the larger intake.
Lithuania abolished compulsory military service in 2008. It reinstated conscription in 2015 amid “increased threats” following Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Lithuania requires nine months of military service, or three months for those with specialized military qualifications.

German auto giant posts multi-billion-euro loss
German automotive giant Volkswagen has reported a €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) net loss for the third quarter of 2026, up from €1.1 billion a year earlier, as the country’s manufacturing sector faces growing economic pressure.
Europe’s largest carmaker announced the results on Thursday. Revenue fell 6.3% to €75.3 billion, and vehicle deliveries dropped 14.3%.
“US tariffs weigh on us, the Chinese market is shrinking, and competitive pressure in Europe is increasing significantly,” VW Group Chief Financial and Operating Officer Arno Antlitz said in a statement.
Volkswagen faces growing competition from cheaper Chinese vehicles in Europe, and its expanding electric car business remains less profitable than that of conventional models.
The results follow the auto giant’s announcement in September of sweeping restructuring plans that could eliminate up to 100,000 jobs and leave four German factories facing closure.
The pressures extend beyond the automotive sector. In an assessment on October 21, the German Economy Ministry acknowledged weakening economic momentum and sluggish manufacturing activity, particularly in energy-intensive industries.
German manufacturers have struggled with high energy costs since losing access to inexpensive Russian pipeline gas following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Germany is increasingly relying on defense spending to support economic growth. On October 8, the government raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.3%, acknowledging that public expenditure on defense and infrastructure is helping drive the recovery.
The shift toward military production is already visible in the automotive industry. In September, Volkswagen reached a preliminary agreement to sell its Osnabrueck factory for conversion to defense manufacturing, potentially preserving around 1,400 jobs. The project envisages cooperation with Israeli weapons producer Rafael on air-defense systems.
Weapons manufacturer Rheinmetall has also announced plans to expand production facilities, including armored vehicle manufacturing, potentially creating more than 1,000 jobs.
Germany’s expanding military industry has drawn criticism from Russia. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov questioned Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ambition to make Germany Europe’s leading military power, warning of the potential consequences and asking whether Berlin learned the lessons of World War II.
In June, Russian presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev accused European weapons manufacturers of profiting from the Ukraine conflict, arguing that they have a “serious financial interest” in prolonging the fighting. The EU maintains that its military support for Kiev is aimed at securing a lasting peace.

India increases growth forecast for fiscal year
October 29, 2026
India's Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review.
The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.
India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.
The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm."
The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter.
Inflation, fueled by El Nino and geopolitics, poses a threat
However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season.
It said that external factors like oil prices and "global uncertainties" — seemingly a reference at least in part to the instablity in the Middle East — continued to pressure the rupee's value and pose inflationary risks.
Consumer price inflation (CPI), the wholesale price index (WPI), food cost prices and fuel and power prices were all rising month for month, albeit at very different rates.
The CPI was up 5.54% year-on-year in September, but the WPI had risen more sharply at 11.39%. Food index inflation was up by 8% in rural areas, and a slightly more modest 7.18% in urban centers.
But, as in many other countries, fuel and power costs increases were in an entirely different league, at 25.85% inflation in September 2026 comapred to the same month a year earlier, prior to the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East.
Ministry says FX reserves ample, rupee's decline appears manageable
Although it has been a comparatively slow decline, the rupee has been consistently losing value against the US dollar over the past five years, threatening the country's relative purchasing power internationally. This slide has picked up pace in the last 15 months or so.
But the ministry pointed to foreign exchange reserves worth some $721 billion and said that India was "well-positioned" to weather such risks and sustain its expansionary trajectory..

China's Zhang wins 53kg total at weightlifting worlds

01:29:06 KST

NINGBO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's Zhang Haiqin won the women's 53kg title at the Weightlifting World Championships here on Thursday, holding off American Miranda Ulrey by one kilogram in the total standings.
Zhang lifted 98kg in the snatch and 123kg in the clean and jerk for a total of 221kg. Ulrey matched Zhang's 98kg in the snatch but managed 122kg in the clean and jerk for a 220kg total.
The two traded successful lifts throughout the snatch, both opening at 95kg before making 98kg. Both failed at 100kg on their third attempts, with Zhang taking snatch gold by virtue of her lighter body weight.
"I really wanted to make 100, that weight was over the record and I wanted it, but I rushed it a little," Zhang said. After the snatch, she initially thought she had finished second. "I didn't realize at the time, I thought I was second, and then my coach told me I was first."
Rosegie Ramos of the Philippines took snatch bronze with 97kg.
In the clean and jerk, Ulrey missed her first attempt at 119kg before making 120kg and 122kg. Zhang made 120kg and then 123kg on her second attempt, a lift she knew was crucial.
"The second lift is key. If you fall behind on the second lift it's very hard to come back," Zhang said.
Zhang then attempted 126kg on her final lift, which would have given her clean-and-jerk gold and broken the total world standard of 223kg, but she was unable to complete the lift.
"On the third lift I pulled too hard off the floor and my whole frame kind of collapsed, the weight just crushed me," Zhang told Xinhua. "I tried to stand up but I really gave it everything."
Clean-and-jerk gold instead went to Kim So Hyon of the DPR Korea, who lifted 123kg in the afternoon's Group B session before the Group A competition. Kim finished with a 214kg total, enough for bronze overall.
Because Kim reached 123kg first, she ranked ahead of Zhang in the clean and jerk. Zhang said she did not watch Kim's afternoon session.
"I was resting in the back, I didn't see it, it didn't affect my rhythm, I just focused on myself," Zhang said.
The world standards for the new 53kg category, which took effect Aug. 1 under the Los Angeles Olympic cycle, are 99kg in the snatch, 126kg in the clean and jerk and 223kg in total. Zhang lifted 101kg in the snatch and totaled 227kg at a national Grand Prix in August, but came up short of those marks on Thursday.
"Of course there's regret, the world record felt right there, but regret gives me even more motivation," Zhang said. "I just need to take it one competition at a time, make every lift, and go back and build a stronger, more solid base."
The men's 70kg Group A competition is scheduled for Friday. ■

Thand Ringqvist confirmed to Swedish Television (SVT) that she had accepted the nomination, saying the Center Party would "continue to take responsibility and contribute constructively to ensuring that Sweden gets a government."

The Social Democratic Party, Left Party, Green Party and Center Party together won 176 seats in the 349-member parliament in September's election, giving them a narrow majority but leaving them divided over the composition of a new government.
Under Sweden's constitution, a prime ministerial nominee is rejected if at least 175 members of parliament vote against the proposal. If four consecutive nominations are rejected, a new election must be held within three months. ■

Rwanda has participated in the CIIE since the first edition in 2018.

Muganza emphasized that the CIIE, an exhibition dedicated specifically to imports, "sends an important message that China is not only interested in exporting to the world, but is also actively creating opportunities" for companies from around the world to access the Chinese market.
Pointing to win-win cooperation, Muganza said the exhibition helps foreign companies gain access to the scale and opportunities of the Chinese market, while Chinese companies and consumers benefit from a wider range of international products.
On China's zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries, which came into force in May, Muganza said Rwanda considers the policy a very important development for Africa-China trade.
Muganza also noted that China's high-level opening up "sends an important and positive signal," creating opportunities not only for major multinational corporations, but also for producers and businesses from developing economies. ■

UN calls for faster ecosystem restoration
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:28:22 CST
01:28:22 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Around 252 million hectares of ecosystems worldwide are under restoration, but progress remains insufficient to reach the global target for 2030, according to a UN report published Thursday at the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital Yerevan.
Titled "Restoration progress report: Nature's comeback -- Scaling ecosystem restoration for people and planet," the report was jointly published by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the United Nations Environment Programme and the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity.
The report takes stock of global ecosystem restoration halfway through the United Nations Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, providing a comprehensive assessment of restoration efforts across terrestrial, freshwater, marine and coastal ecosystems.
It warns that the world remains off track to achieve Target 2 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which calls for at least 30 percent of degraded ecosystems to be under effective restoration by 2030. Countries have pledged to restore around 1 billion hectares, but the pace of restoration needs to triple to meet the 2030 target.
Terrestrial ecosystems make up approximately 92 percent of the total documented restoration area covered by the report. Meanwhile, recorded restoration efforts in freshwater, marine and coastal ecosystems remain limited, highlighting the need to strengthen monitoring and reporting in these areas.
Drawing on China's 7th National Report to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the report also examines the country's ecosystem restoration efforts. According to country-level data compiled in the assessment, China has the world's largest documented area of ecosystems under restoration.
Yelena Finegold, one of the report's authors, said accelerating global ecosystem restoration would require increased financing, stronger cross-sectoral planning and coordination, as well as greater capacity to implement restoration activities and monitor progress. ■

====================================================================================================

Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:28:22 UTC
01:28:22 KST

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.
With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.
The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).
“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.
To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.
Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.
“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.
As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.
The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.
“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

Media forum
The Russia-Africa media forum is taking place in Moscow on October 26-29, bringing together leading Russian and African media outlets.
