Qatar “categorically” denies Israeli election interference; says it will not be a “scapegoat” for Israeli politicians
Qatar denied allegations that it interfered in Israeli elections or funded activities intended to influence their outcome, in a statement posted on X by Majed Al Ansari, advisor to the Prime Minister and official spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry.
“We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections,” the statement said, rejecting accusations by “certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media” and adding: “If these claims were to be believed, Qatar would apparently own all of Israel.”
It called the accusations “ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure” and said, “Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians.”
The statement said Qatar has “no involvement in Israel’s political or electoral competition” and “will not remain silent while Qatar’s name is exploited to serve electoral agendas or narrow political interests.”
‘Ra’am has no connection to the matter, and we will cooperate fully,’ Party’s chairman Abbas reacts to investigation into foreign interference in elections
Ra’am Chairman Mansour Abbas said the party welcomes Justice Noam Sohlberg’s decision to investigate suspicions of an attempt to exert improper influence on the elections through foreign funding.
Abbas said upholding the integrity of the electoral process and the rule of law is a civic and democratic duty that Ra’am has made a core tenet of its mission.
He said Ra’am has “no connection whatsoever to the matter in question” or any other such affairs, and will cooperate fully with all law enforcement authorities to uncover the truth.
Responding to what he called a campaign of incitement and delegitimization against Arab citizens by Netanyahu, whom he referred to as “Abu Yair” and accused of employing Qatari agents in his own office, Abbas said: “Nothing will come of it, because there is nothing there.”
Herzog: allegations “must be fully investigated”; warns against tarnishing “an entire community” that voted

Balad chairman answers Likud election theft claims; says losing side “concocts a racist ‘blood libel’”

In Israel, the losing side concocts a racist ‘blood libel’ and calls upon the security establishment to use force to overturn the election results.”
The Arab party leader said what began with the unlawful disqualification of Arab electoral lists continued with incitement against Arab parties and the Arab public, and that on election day hundreds of armed far-right activists descended on polling stations in Arab localities in an attempt to suppress turnout.
Abu Shehadeh said Netanyahu and his associates are “dangerous individuals” building a narrative to reject the results of an election with “the most decisive outcome seen in Israel in decades.”
Golan says Netanyahu suffered “crushing democratic defeat”; accuses him of “ugly campaign of delegitimization”
In his own reaction to the news of investigations and the Likud Party accusing the Arab parties of fraud, Democrats Party leader Yair Golan said Netanyahu “has suffered a crushing democratic defeat” and “refuses to accept the voters’ verdict.”
Golan accused Netanyahu of trying to challenge the election results through “an ugly campaign of delegitimization,” directed against the will of the public and specifically against the Arab public.
He said any genuine suspicion regarding a compromise to the integrity of the elections “must be thoroughly investigated,” but that the “most grave instance of Qatari involvement” took place within Netanyahu’s own office, carried out by his closest aide.
Likud leads with 26 seats, Yashar 21, in unofficial count with 93.8% of votes tallied
The current coalition stands at 53 seats, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot stays at 48, and the Arab parties at 19.
The Joint List, currently at 11, was up one seat, competing over a single mandate with the other Arab party, Ra'am, which is back up to 8.
‘The "Ra'am-gate" affair is an earthquake. The elections have been stolen!’ Likud Party demands Shin Bet investigate Ra’am Party of fraud
Likud said the elections in Israel “have been stolen,” calling the “Ra’am-gate” affair “an earthquake” in a statement reacting to Justice Noam Sohlberg’s remarks about the involvement of foreign entities.
The party claimed that foreign entities intervened and bribed voters to benefit Arab parties, calling it an assault on democracy aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and the ousting of the right-wing government.
Likud said that no Zionist party may cooperate with Ra’am or the Joint List, replace the Speaker of the Knesset using votes purchased with cash, or form a government that poses a danger to Israel.
Despite these claims, the election committee explicitly stated that its investigation is not related to claims made by the Likud Party.
In an unusual move, the Israeli election committee chief orders Shin Bet to investigate foreign funding and election bribery amid ‘serious suspicions’
Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg instructed Shin Bet head David Zini to investigate suspected foreign funding and election bribery involving foreign entities.
Reports said the letter followed a briefing in which Zini presented Sohlberg with information described as “exceptionally grave.”
The allegations concern improper influence over the elections through foreign funding from outside actors working against Israeli interests, though Sohlberg wrote that he “cannot attest to the nature of the above suspicions.”
Sohlberg asked Zini to bring findings, if any, within the coming week, citing the legally established timelines for filing an election appeal.
Ra’am receives another mandate at the expense of the Joint List
Reports indicate that Ra’am has won an additional seat at the expense of the Joint List, with 91% of the votes counted.
The two parties signed a surplus-vote agreement that decides who gets their shared 19th seat. Under the latest official figures, Ra’am is about 1,200 votes short of claiming it.
Under the new tally, Ra’am holds 8 seats, up from 7, while the Joint List drops to 11 from 12. The two parties’ combined total remains at 19, and no other bloc has changed.
Israel election by the numbers: who might form the next government?
Israel has voted, and neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc is going to secure the 61 seats required to form government.
One of the two blocs will now need to begin the long and complicated task of negotiations between the smaller factional parties to form a government. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will decide who gets the first chance to do so.
This could involve the Arab parties, who may hold the balance of power. Whether either bloc would welcome an Arab-aligned party into their coalition, however, remains to be seen.

Netenyahu's Likud party alleges interference and fraud in Israel's election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:13:39 UTC
01:13:39 KST

Qatar has denied interfering in the election or funding efforts to influence the result, calling the accusations “ridiculous and dangerous”.
Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party are alleging election interference and fraud after Israel’s election results left his bloc short of a parliamentary majority.
The final count, expected on Thursday evening, is set to confirm that Netanyahu's bloc has fallen short of the 61 seats needed for a majority. With around 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 seats, the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot 48, and Arab-led parties 19.
The result represents major gains for the Arab-led parties, potentially giving them a decisive role in determining whether a government without Netanyahu can be formed.
The election saw record participation by Arab citizens of Israel, many of whom are descendants of Palestinians who remained after the country's creation in 1948. The campaign had seen Netanyahu and his far-right allies repeatedly portray Arab-led parties as a threat.
Netanyahu alleges interference
Netanyahu, who has served as Israel's prime minister on and off since 1996, has accused Arab parties of benefiting from foreign interference and funding. Neither he nor his allies have publicly provided evidence to substantiate those claims.
In a post on the social media platform X, Netanyahu quoted his Likud party, saying: "The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state through serious criminal offences of bribery, threats, violence, forgeries, and the use of prohibited software to mobilise voters."
In another post on Thursday morning, he wrote: "Why did Ahmad Tibi visit Qatar 4 days before the elections?" Ahmad Tibi is a Palestinian-Israeli politician and a senior figure in the Ta'al party.
Israel's Central Election Commission has asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate alleged foreign interference. However, the request itself reportedly did not specifically accuse Arab-led parties of wrongdoing. AP also reported that the commission said there was no basis, to its knowledge, for claims of systematic violations of election integrity.
The Arab-led Joint List rejected the accusations, saying Netanyahu’s camp was trying to delegitimise the Arab vote because of its increased political influence. It accused Netanyahu of "working to steal the election".
Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas said he welcomed an investigation into allegations of wrongdoing but said his party had "no connection" with them.
Netanyahu himself has previously faced scrutiny over alleged links between aides and Qatar, after two of his aides were arrested last year on suspicion of receiving payments from the Gulf state.
Qatar has categorically denied interfering in the election. Its Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed Al Ansari, said: "They accuse Qatar of buying off Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli political left and now, in this latest campaign, the Arab vote. These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure."
Israel's President Isaac Herzog has also called for a full investigation, while warning against stigmatising the country’s entire Arab community.
What happens next?
The full count is expected on Thursday evening, although the official election results are due to be certified by 4 November.
President Herzog will then decide whom to ask to try to form a government.
The next Knesset is due to be sworn in on 10 November.
If no coalition can be formed after several attempts, Israel could face another election early next year.
The political uncertainty is unfolding alongside the possibility of renewed Israeli or US strikes on Iran, which could further complicate coalition negotiations.

Data centres aren't necessarily the immediate cause, but they're a good proxy or target for that anxiety."

Bolsonaro leadership claim fails to win support from allies in Brazil
- Flavio Bolsonaro declared himself Brazil’s rightful “leader” after leaving for the US, but the claim won little support and left him more isolated in right-wing politics.
- Key allies, including Liberal Party chief Valdemar Costa Neto and São Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas, said Brazil’s election results must be respected and the country should move forward.
- Bolsonaro said he would lead the opposition from abroad, but party figures rejected fraud claims and backed Lula’s win, which was recognised by Brazil’s electoral authority and global leaders.
AI generated
SAO PAULO - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro’s decision to declare himself the country’s rightful “leader” has failed to garner support from key figures in his political camp, leaving the right-wing lawmaker increasingly isolated in Brazilian politics.
Bolsonaro made the claim in a letter he posted on social media after arriving in the United States on Oct 28, having left Brazil following his defeat to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes in the Oct 25 runoff.
Bolsonaro has cited the fact that a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice extended voting by two hours due to Lula campaign allegations of voter suppression in left-leaning northeastern states, though Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought a voting extension due to rain in conservative southern states.
He alleged he was a victim of an electoral coup, but did not provide evidence for electoral fraud.
Lula’s victory has been recognised by Brazil’s electoral authority, global leaders, international observers, and Bolsonaro’s own party.
“I did not like it,” the head of the senator’s Liberal Party, Valdemar Costa Neto, told reporters on Oct 29 when asked about the letter. “Flavio went through a difficult situation - we understand that - but we do not approve of it. We want to move the country forward,” he said later.
Sao Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas, a prominent Bolsonaro ally who campaigned vigorously for the lawmaker, told newspaper Estadao that Brazil’s election results must be respected and that it was time to move forward.
US President Donald Trump, who confirmed his administration had allowed Bolsonaro to enter the country, declined to comment on Oct 29 when asked who he thought was the legitimate winner.
“I watched the election. I didn’t take sides. I let it be. I was asked not to take sides by the president, the current president,” he said.
Parties recognise Lula’s win
Aecio Neves, head of the centre-right Brazilian Social Democracy Party and a vocal critic of Lula’s Workers’ Party, described Bolsonaro’s behaviour as “incomprehensible” in a statement, adding that opposition politics must be conducted from within the country.
Centre-right party Uniao Brasil, which backed Bolsonaro in the second round, said it was essential that institutions “remain greater than any individual.” The election was conducted with integrity and its results must be respected, it added.
The centrist Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB) party, which also supported Bolsonaro in the runoff, struck a similar tone.
“The MDB reaffirms its total confidence in the Brazilian electoral system and, therefore, in the legitimacy of the result of the election last Sunday,” it said.
‘Flavio is venting’
In his letter, Bolsonaro pledged to lead the opposition from abroad and “assume the risks” that local politicians could not, adding he would support a potential bid by Senator Rogerio Marinho for Senate president in 2027.
Marinho, who served as Bolsonaro’s campaign manager, told reporters that Bolsonaro remains “a leader” and “the most prominent figure on the right” in Brazil, given the support he received from nearly 60 million voters.
But Marinho also rejected allegations of electoral fraud.
“The Liberal Party cannot make that claim, nor can I make that claim, because there is no evidence to support it,” he said.
“Flavio is venting in response to the second-round election results, which were unexpected for all of us.” REUTERS

The ‘breathing space budget’ – breathing space for the government, that is | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:11:11 UTC
01:11:11 KST

Maybe it had been one of the greatest acts of political genius after all. The day after the budget is usually the moment when things start to fall apart. When clued-up journalists and economists have had a chance to go through all the fine points the chancellor would rather everyone had missed. The forecasts that suggest everything is predicated on a wing and a prayer. The hidden unfunded tax cuts. The greater-than-expected spending commitments.
But on Thursday morning Andy Burnham and John Healey could afford themselves a sigh of relief. All had gone about as well as they could have hoped. It turns out that when you don’t make any massive tax or spending commitments, there isn’t a great deal to unravel. All there had been was a raft of small-scale interventions designed to help people with their personal finances. Call it the Martin Lewis budget. In fact, Healey and Lewis now seem unable to get through the day without spending some time with each other. They certainly can’t stop talking about one another. It’s becoming unhealthily co-dependent. The gods of small things.
It had been billed as the “breathing space” budget. A budget to help get everyone through the coming year more or less alive. No hiding under tables or breaking open the emergency supplies of baked beans. Apocalypse averted. But the breathing space might just as well have been for the government. Difficult decisions delayed. Hope that we all wake up in 52 weeks’ time and the world looks like a less frightening place. And even if it doesn’t, it will always have had a year’s grace. A chance for the Tories and Reform to implode. You can always hope.
Come the traditional morning-after interview with the chancellor on the Today programme, the presenter Nick Robinson seemed uncharacteristically subdued. Normally he’s a terrier on occasions like these. There’s never been a budget that Nick wouldn’t have been able to do far better himself. But this one? This one was something you might find on the consumer affairs programme, You and Yours. And the BBC was in the process of axing that.
So the 20 minutes passed with little fuss. More a softball back and forth. Healey started with his usual infectious brand of pessimism. He was born to be the bearer of bad news. The poster boy for assisted dying. Everything was absolutely terrible. He wasn’t quite sure why anyone was still bothering with anything. If it had been up to him he would have ended the interview before it had started. There was nothing to say. Other than that, given the chance, he wouldn’t have started from here. Brexit, the pandemic, Ukraine, Iran, energy prices. The world was screwed. Britain was screwed. Lie back and prepare for the worst 10 years of your already miserable life.
Nick tried to find a reason to believe. Couldn’t the chancellor have made just a little more effort? Having a plan to have a plan wasn’t the usual budget fare. Healey, AKA Dr Death, shrugged. It was one up on having a plan to not have a plan. By now Robbo was audibly struggling. How could he put it politely? In the third year of a government with a 160-seat majority, surely Healey could have been a little more ambitious. This wasn’t exactly the big transformation that had been promised.
Could he even say if he would bring down the benefits bill? Apparently he could. “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Dr Death. Cue panic stations in the Treasury. Within seconds of Healey opening his mouth, dozens of government spinners were on the phones to every journalist to tell them they hadn’t heard what they had just heard. There had been collective false consciousness. When Healey had said that he would be bringing down a benefits bill that everyone agreed was too high and that the country could not afford, what he had really meant to say was that he would not be bringing down the benefits bill that he had no idea how to pay for. Fag packets gratefully received. That was about as close to news as we got.
Maybe it was just that while Healey was having one of his better days, Robinson was having one of his worse ones. Because he had also sounded uninterested in his interview with Andrew Griffith an hour earlier. An exercise in box-ticking rather than revelation because the shadow chancellor never has anything useful to add on the day after. Sure enough, Griffith insisted that he would have done everything differently while never going into the details of how. At which point, Robbo opened half an eye and observed that if it was really that easy, how come the Tories hadn’t fixed it when in office?
Indeed, Nick continued, it could be argued that Labour had been left to clear up the mess the Tories created. “I’ve never shied away from saying that the Tories have a chequered record,” Griffith said defensively. Er, I’m not sure that’s entirely true, Andrew. Your usual line is that history started in 2024 and that everything is the Labour government’s fault.
That just left time for Robinson to remind the shadow chancellor that he had been part of the Treasury team that had defended the Liz Truss mini-budget even as it was being shredded. “I will never publish plans without saying where the money is coming from,” said Griffith, before announcing £30bn of planned tax cuts without specifying which benefits he would cut to pay for them. Fair to say, he’s not a man who seems to learn from experience. Once in the Truss image, always in the Truss image.
The final piece of the Thursday jigsaw was the verdict from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. In the past this has been enough to completely destroy the reputation of some chancellors. I could never look at George Osborne in quite the same way after the IFS had rubbished one of his budgets. It’s one thing to be thought of as an economic quarter-wit. What’s really devastating is to have it proved.
Helen Miller, the IFS director, looked a bit knackered. She and her team had been up most of the night, going through both the budget and the OBR figures line by line, searching for the fatal flaw. And she was gutted to announce that there actually wasn’t one. There was as little in the budget as had first appeared. She announced that she was grumpy about some measures. Disappointed in others. Another was cack-handed. The tax system had been made more complicated, not less. Yet, all in all, these were minor gripes.
“This chancellor is hoping that things get better without actually needing to do anything,” Miller said in conclusion. I don’t think that’s right. Healey never travels in hope. Like the rest of us, he’s pretty confident everything is going to be worse in a year’s time. But he had got himself some breathing space.

‘If this works, it will be the first real ceasefire across a large stretch of the front’: Russia and Ukraine maintain truce in occupied Oleshky for more than two days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:05:56 UTC
01:05:56 KST

‘If this works, it will be the first real ceasefire across a large stretch of the front’: Russia and Ukraine maintain truce in occupied Oleshky for more than two days
Russia and Ukraine have halted hostilities around the occupied city of Oleshky since October 27. The Verkhovna Rada’s human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed on the morning of October 29 that the ceasefire had held for more than two days. Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, said humanitarian aid — “food, fuel, medicine, and hygiene products” — had been sent to Oleshky.
Lubinets and Lantratova set out for Oleshky on the afternoon of October 29. Lubinets will be the first Ukrainian official of such rank to visit Russian-occupied territories. Both commissioners said their main task is to deliver humanitarian aid to residents and ensure the safe evacuation of those who want to leave.
Sources who spoke to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda and were involved in organizing the ceasefire said the ceasefire around Oleshky is meant to test whether Ukrainian and Russian military commanders can carry out political agreements to end hostilities.
Organizing a halt to the fighting turned out to be “an extremely difficult task,” according to the outlet’s sources. A political order to cease fire does not by itself guarantee automatic compliance on the front line, a source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s administration told Ukrainska Pravda. Even Ukrainian troops demanded guarantees several times that if they stopped, “nothing bad would happen afterward,” the source said. The source explained:
We want to get the military — both our General Staff and the Russian one — used to the idea that if the political leadership has decided that in a given sector of the front we stop, freeze in place, and no one opens fire, the military can make that happen. They can guarantee it. Not a situation where the political leadership has reached an agreement and the military says, “Sorry, we can’t stop, we’ve got something going on.”
It is easier for the Russian side than for the Ukrainian side to organize and maintain a ceasefire, according to Ukrainska Pravda’s sources. “They [the Russians] have a rigid military vertical. We have a decentralized army. And someone — some well-known military blogger — could stir up the mood on air so much that everything falls apart afterward,” a source said.
If the ceasefire in Oleshky can be maintained, as planned, until the evening of November 1, the Ukrainian side expects to repeat this kind of local ceasefire later along other parts of the front. “That’s precisely so the military can learn how to do this: stop, ensure safe passage, and so on. So that later, if there’s some major agreement, we could implement it right away,” a source who spoke to Ukrainska Pravda said.
If this works, this will be the first example of a real ceasefire across a fairly large stretch of the front. It’s come at such a cost — the military, Russia’s Federal Security Service, and everyone else are doing nothing but trying to sabotage it. But we believe it will work out and that this will set a precedent.
The war in photographs
Russia’s Defense Ministry announced that it had begun clearing mines from roads leading into Oleshky and published photos and video of sappers at work. Russian President Vladimir Putin, speaking at a plenary session of the Russia–Africa summit underway in Moscow, claimed it was Ukraine that had mined the approaches to Oleshky, creating “practically a humanitarian catastrophe.”

In addition, the department noted that the quantitative growth in Hainan’s international services trade came with structural optimization, driven by both traditional and new factors. According to the published data, the Chinese special administrative region of Hong Kong, the United States, Russia, Ireland and Singapore are Hainan’s top five partners in this field. According to estimates, they accounted for more than 57% of total commercial activity in this segment of the island’s economy in the first three quarters of 2026.
The department also stated that the Hainan Free Trade Port would continue to use institutional and other advantages to strengthen the regional transport sector and inbound tourism and to introduce new types of services trade. At the same time, the province’s authorities plan to diversify the entry of local companies into foreign markets and ensure the high quality of their economic interaction with partners from other countries and regions.

Hidden ADHD common in women seeking treatment for depression and anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:00:01 UTC
01:00:01 KST

A recent study reveals that nearly one in five women seeking treatment for anxiety or depression also have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, with nearly half of those cases having never been previously diagnosed. The research highlights how overlapping symptoms can obscure the underlying attention condition in adult women. These findings were published in The International Journal of Psychiatry in Medicine.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition involving inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. During childhood development, hyperactive traits often fade, while inattentive traits tend to persist. Medical professionals historically diagnosed the condition much more frequently in males, and in clinical settings, the ratio of diagnosed males to females is roughly ten to one.
Population surveys show a much narrower gap, suggesting the condition often goes unrecognized in female populations. Women frequently display more subtle, internalizing symptoms like emotional sensitivity or internal restlessness. These internal struggles are easily mistaken for mood or anxiety disorders. Because conditions like major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder share traits with ADHD, such as difficulty concentrating, the underlying attention disorder is frequently missed.
An additional feature commonly reported by people with ADHD is hyperfocus. This phenomenon involves episodes of intense, prolonged concentration on specific tasks, often to the exclusion of everything else going on around the person. Though not an official diagnostic criterion, hyperfocus is well-documented and can substantially affect daily functioning.
Psychiatrists Hazal Yavuzlar Civan and Tonguc Demir Berkol from the Bakirkoy Prof. Dr. Mazhar Osman Training and Research Hospital for Psychiatry, Neurology and Neurosurgery in Istanbul, Turkey, conducted the research. They wanted to understand how ADHD manifests in women already seeking help for mood problems. They also examined hyperfocus to see if it could help clinicians distinguish these conditions.
The researchers recruited 170 female patients at outpatient psychiatric clinics. The participants first completed the Beck Depression Inventory and the Beck Anxiety Inventory, which are standard questionnaires that measure the severity of depressive and anxious symptoms. Women scoring above the threshold for clinical depression or anxiety then took additional surveys.
These follow-up surveys included the Wender Utah Rating Scale to measure childhood ADHD traits, a separate screening tool for adult ADHD symptoms, and the Hyperfocus Scale. Following the questionnaires, a trained psychiatrist conducted a structured clinical interview with each participant. The final diagnoses were based on standard psychiatric guidelines.
The clinical interviews revealed that 33 of the 170 women met the criteria for ADHD. Within this group, 15 patients had no prior ADHD diagnosis. ADHD was especially prevalent among women experiencing social anxiety disorder and a condition called double depression. Double depression occurs when a patient experiences a severe depressive episode on top of a chronic, long-term baseline of low mood.
The women with ADHD reported distinct life experiences compared to the participants who only had mood or anxiety disorders. They had more disciplinary issues in school, more frequent job changes, and a higher rate of family members with ADHD. The rates of past suicide attempts did not differ in a statistically significant way between the two groups, but the women with ADHD reported higher levels of current suicidal thoughts and feelings of failure.
When looking at specific depressive symptoms, the two groups diverged. The group without ADHD reported more concerns about physical health and changes in sleeping habits. The authors suggest this health-related worry reflects a somatic focus, which is a heightened awareness of bodily sensations commonly seen in anxiety and depression.
Conversely, individuals with ADHD often experience impaired interoception, meaning they have a harder time recognizing internal physical states. This altered awareness might reduce how often they notice or report physical symptoms like poor sleep.
ADHD was highly prevalent among women experiencing social anxiety disorder. The researchers suggest social anxiety in these patients may be driven by ADHD-related executive dysfunction, which impairs the brain’s ability to plan, organize, and interpret social cues. Difficulties in self-regulation often lead to repeated interpersonal failures, which can eventually create lasting feelings of shame and a fear of social evaluation.
The researchers also identified distinct patterns regarding symptom overlap. In the group without ADHD, higher attention deficit scores correlated with worse depression. Higher hyperactivity scores correlated with worse anxiety. Hyperfocus scores also rose alongside general ADHD-like symptoms in these women.
The women diagnosed with ADHD did not show these same statistical correlations. While their overall hyperfocus scores were substantially higher than the group without ADHD, the severity of their hyperfocus did not track directly with the severity of their mood or anxiety symptoms. The findings suggest hyperfocus may serve different roles depending on the diagnosis, acting as a coping mechanism in ADHD but manifesting as a maladaptive trait in mood disorders.
The study details how similar symptoms stem from different root causes. Both ADHD and anxiety can involve restlessness, distractibility, and tension. In anxiety, inattention usually stems from excessive worry, with mental energy consumed by ruminating or anticipating threats, and this type of distractibility often improves in relaxed environments.
In contrast, inattention related to ADHD is consistent across different settings and typically appears early in life. It is usually associated with poor task initiation, organizational difficulties, and mind-wandering that is completely unrelated to specific fears. The authors note that thorough developmental histories are required to distinguish primary ADHD from secondary attention problems caused by mood disorders.
The research relied on a cross-sectional design, meaning the assessments occurred at a single point in time. The methodology cannot determine the sequence of symptom onset. It remains unclear whether ADHD symptoms preceded the depressive and anxious symptoms, or vice versa.
The sample focused entirely on women seeking outpatient psychiatric care. The prevalence rates and symptom patterns might look different in men, people not seeking psychiatric help, or individuals treated in inpatient hospital settings. The group of women diagnosed with ADHD was also much smaller than the group without the condition, which limits the statistical power of certain comparisons.
Future research should follow patients over extended periods to track how these overlapping conditions develop over a lifespan. Incorporating biological markers or tracking symptoms in broader populations could further clarify how hyperfocus operates across different mental health diagnoses.
The study, “ADHD Comorbidity in Women With Depression and Anxiety: Prevalence, Clinical Features and Hyperfocus Dynamics,” was authored by Hazal Yavuzlar Civan and Tonguc Demir Berkol.

Moldovan President Calls Security Meeting After Massive Data Breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:55:21 UTC
00:55:21 KST

Moldovan President Maia Sandu has called a meeting of the country's National Security Council (CNS) days after a large-scale cyberattack on government information systems.
The attack, most likely carried out with the help of artificial intelligence, resulted in the extraction of personal data belonging to approximately 750,000 Moldovans.
On October 29, Sandu's office announced that the meeting would take place in "the coming days to assess the attack and determine appropriate response measures."
The head of the country's Cybersecurity Agency, Mihai Lupascu, told RFE/RL that "without a doubt, this is the most impactful...largest cyberattack recorded so far," adding that the operation was "highly sophisticated," "well-prepared," and involved "several waves."
"We are dealing with a situation in which a highly skilled cyberactor carried out these activities with the clear objective of compromising information systems and exfiltrating data," Lupascu said.
Previously, Prime Minister Vasile Tofan told cabinet ministers that there were "indications of a broader campaign involving foreign state actors" and that investigators were looking into "their involvement in the recent incident."
He did not specify which countries were suspected of being involved.
Officials from several European nations have been warning for months of an expanding campaign of hybrid activity -- hostile actions short of open warfare, including cyberattacks, sabotage, and the weaponization of migration -- by Russia amid its war on Ukraine.
Lupascu said that while it was "premature" to definitively attribute the cyberattack to a specific actor, its complexity offered clues about who might be responsible. "At the very least, those behind it have the technical capabilities and infrastructure needed to orchestrate and carry out such attacks."
Wedged between NATO member Romania -- with which it shares close linguistic and cultural ties -- to the west and war-ravaged Ukraine to the east, Moldova has struggled to shield itself from the fallout of Moscow's full-scale invasion.
According to Moldova's Electronic Government Agency (AGE), the attack targeted about one million people, almost half of the country's population, with attempts to extract data associated with personal identification numbers (IDNPs) taking place between October 19 and October 23.
Authorities have preventively suspended 82 digital public services and disconnected over 30 information systems to limit unauthorized access, it added.
The compromised data could include identification details, such as names and dates and places of birth; information about immediate family members; health insurance status and family doctors; social benefits, pensions, and disability status; driver's license details and photographs; vehicles and companies owned or managed; and financial information, including International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs), tax debts, and payment histories.
AGE said bank card data was not affected and that no unauthorized changes were identified in state registers.
The attackers allegedly exploited vulnerabilities in services accessible without authentication, subsequently using the information obtained to attempt additional data extraction.
Authorities said security problems had been addressed in most affected services, while the remaining ones would be gradually restored once security measures had been verified. A broader review of government systems was also under way to identify and fix vulnerabilities.
AGE warned that cyberattacks pose a growing threat to public institutions, with advances in artificial intelligence making it easier to automate attacks and identify security weaknesses.
Lupascu told RFE/RL that he believed artificial intelligence was used in the latest cyberattack on Moldova, "including [capabilities] that allow the identification of vulnerabilities." He added that such tools can identify vulnerabilities "that humans cannot."
"We must be aware that artificial intelligence tools will continue to generate cyberincidents in the next few years," he warned.

ECB’s Lagarde resigns early so she can speak freely on topics beyond monetary policy
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:53:05 CET
00:53:05 KST

FRANKFURT, Oct 29 (Reuters) - European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said on Thursday she had decided to step down eight months before her term was due to expire so that she can speak more freely on issues beyond monetary policy.
Lagarde, 70, has led the ECB since November 2019 and previously headed the International Monetary Fund. Her term would otherwise have run until October 2027.
“There is never a good time to leave,” Lagarde told a press conference. “But it’s embedded in the governance of the ECB that presidents, board members have to leave because they cannot be up for renewal.”
Lagarde said the decision to leave early was driven by a wish to engage on issues outside the ECB’s mandate.
“I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters,” she said.
She noted that ECB officials are bound by strict rules of neutrality: “We have an obligation of neutrality, we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy,” Lagarde said, adding that the mandate is “the price we pay for being independent.”
Lagarde said she no longer felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. “I’m interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation,” she said, without elaborating.
Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, Lagarde said she believed she had something to contribute beyond central banking. “There are things that I can say — whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I should say those things and I cannot do so in my current position,” she said.
Lagarde sought to reassure markets and staff that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank’s operations. “A process has already started to identify my successor,” she said, adding there were “plenty of excellent candidates — much better than me, actually.”
She dismissed concerns about continuity. “Don’t worry about decision making in limbo — no, absolutely not,” Lagarde said. “The institution is solid, strong, like a rock, and it will continue being so.”
(Reporting by Balasz Koranyi; Writing by Hugh Lawson; Editing by Catherine Evans)

There has been "a profound
transformation" in the phenomenon of human trafficking, Istat
said in a new report Thursday.
                                    
In recent years, it said, the incidence of labour exploitation
involving adult men has surpassed that of sexual exploitation
involving women—which had historically been the most prevalent
form.
                                    
This is according to a report by Istat (the Italian National
Institute of Statistics) titled "Human Trafficking in Italy:
2021-2025."
In 2025, there were 1,964 individuals formally identified as
victims of trafficking, consisting of 966 men and 915 women.
                                    
For the first time, the number of male victims has exceeded that
of female victims; the male share rose from 33% in 2022 to 49.2%
in 2025.
                                    
Minors identified as victims in 2025 totaled 53, accounting for
2.7%.
                                    
There were 1,088 victims of labor exploitation and 696 victims
of sexual exploitation.
                                    
Among the former, 883 out of 1,088 were men; among the latter,
597 out of 696 were women.
                                    
Istat notes that, over time, the capacity to identify potential
victims of trafficking has improved.
                                    
In 2025, Italy's protection system recorded 3,520 individuals,
up from 2,398 in 2021—an increase of 46.8%.
                                    
The number of people undergoing assessment rose by 58.1%, while
the number of victims taken into care increased by 19.3%.
                                    
Over five years, the proportion of men reached by the protection
system has risen from 26.1% in 2021 to 52.5% in 2025.
                                    
In absolute terms, the number of men has nearly tripled—from 625
to 1,848—while the number of women has decreased from 1,697 to
1,564.

Russia to extend diesel export ban, use quotas to fulfil US deal, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:51:16 UTC
00:51:16 KST

Russia to extend diesel export ban, use quotas to fulfil US deal, sources say
Oct 29 - Russia will extend its diesel export ban until the end of the year while allowing some companies to ship fuel under a quota system to meet its new export commitment to the US, two people familiar with the discussions told Reuters.
Moscow and Washington agreed a diesel supply deal after Presidents Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump spoke by phone earlier this month. The energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine announced alongside the agreement has allowed Moscow to increase fuel production. At the same time, fuel shortages earlier this year have prompted the government to maintain tight controls on oil product exports.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Tuesday that three tankers carrying Russian diesel to export markets were already under way and that a fourth would sail on October 28.
Novak also said Russian refineries were recovering quickly from repairs. The sources said refinery utilisation had risen 25% at the end of October from the start of the month after drone attacks on facilities subsided.
Under the current diesel export ban, the government permits limited exports through a quota system. Those quotas will quadruple from October levels to 2 million metric tons, or about 0.5 million barrels per day, in November, the sources said. Shipments under existing intergovernmental agreements will also continue.
The Energy Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The current ban on diesel exports is due to expire on October 31.
In October, the government exempted several refiners from the ban and granted them export quotas totalling 0.5 million tons, the sources said. A new government order expected in early November would expand the list of exempt refiners and set new export limits. If the quotas are used up quickly, the government could consider increasing them further, the sources added.
Nominal diesel production in Russia exceeds domestic consumption by about 40%. As refineries return to normal operating rates, they will need export outlets to prevent a domestic glut. REUTERS

Germany and Netherlands raise Schakal order to 291 fighting vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:47:21 UTC
00:47:21 KST

- OCCAR ordered 69 more Schakal wheeled infantry fighting vehicles, 35 for Germany and 34 for the Netherlands, raising the total on order to 291.
- Rheinmetall’s share is worth a medium three-digit million-euro sum, with deliveries planned between May 2032 and November 2033.
Rheinmetall has booked an order worth a medium three-digit million-euro sum for its share of 69 more Schakal wheeled infantry fighting vehicles for Germany and the Netherlands, the company announced, after the European procurement agency OCCAR exercised the first option under the program’s 2025 contract.
OCCAR placed the order with ARTEC, the Rheinmetall and KNDS Deutschland joint venture that builds the Boxer, for 35 vehicles for the Bundeswehr and 34 for the Royal Netherlands Army. Germany’s Bundestag budget committee approved the call-off on June 24, and the two countries announced the extra 69 vehicles in August, when Germany’s planned Schakal fleet grew to about 185 vehicles and the Dutch fleet to 106. Rheinmetall has now disclosed the value of its part of the work, without giving a precise figure, and said the vehicles are scheduled for delivery between May 2032 and November 2033.
“The activation of additional options for the Schakal confirms our customers’ confidence in this state-of-the-art system,” said Dr. Björn Bernhard, head of Rheinmetall’s Vehicle Systems Division.
The option call-off raises the total number of Schakals on order to 291. The main contract, signed at OCCAR’s headquarters in Bonn in October 2025, covered 222 vehicles, 150 for Germany and 72 for the Netherlands, with an order value of €4.7 billion (about $5.24 billion), of which Rheinmetall’s share was almost €3.4 billion (about $3.79 billion). Rheinmetall said that contract includes an option for up to 200 additional vehicles, so Germany and the Netherlands can still order more.
The Schakal, also known as the Boxer RCT30, mounts the unmanned turret of the tracked Puma infantry fighting vehicle on the Boxer’s eight-wheeled armored chassis. The turret carries Rheinmetall’s 30 mm MK 30-2/ABM automatic cannon, which can fire programmable airburst rounds that explode near a target, along with a launcher for MELLS anti-tank guided missiles, the German designation for the Spike LR. The vehicle carries a three-person crew and can transport up to six dismounted soldiers, so it can move an infantry squad and support it with fire once troops dismount.
Germany is buying the Schakal as the main vehicle for the infantry of its new “medium forces,” brigades built around wheeled vehicles that can cover long distances quickly on roads, a role between heavy tank and tracked infantry fighting vehicle units and light infantry. Because it shares its chassis with the Boxers already in German and Dutch service, the two armies can use common training, spare parts and maintenance. Germany originally planned the purchase in its 2025 draft budget, and the Schakal will be the first Bundeswehr Boxer built on the newer Future Common Drive Module. KNDS has said the first vehicles will be delivered starting in late 2027.
Key components are made at German sites run by Rheinmetall, KNDS Deutschland, MTU, Hensoldt and smaller suppliers. Rheinmetall also said German industry has guaranteed significantly faster delivery of the option vehicles if the Bundeswehr goes ahead with Arminius, a large planned Boxer program.

Pakistan: Terrorism conviction of human rights lawyers an indictment of justice system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:46:56 UTC
00:46:56 KST

Responding to the conviction and ten-year imprisonment of Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha today by the Anti-Terrorism Court in Islamabad, Yasmine Ahmed, Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact at Amnesty International, said:
“These convictions are an indictment of Pakistan’s justice system. This was not just Imaan and Hadi on trial, it was a test of the judiciary’s ability to uphold the principles of justice and the right to fair trial. It has failed that test miserably. It is clear that these ‘anti-terrorism’ charges are being used to punish Imaan and Hadi for their human rights advocacy.
“Imaan and Hadi have been consistently denied the right to an open and fair trial, which they were initially barred from attending in person. The trial was later shifted inside the prison premises where they were kept behind a cage-like structure during the hearings.
these ‘anti-terrorism’ charges are being used to punish Imaan and Hadi for their human rights advocacy
Yasmine Ahmed, Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact
“Imaan and Hadi are being targeted solely because of their refusal to stop their fearless human rights work and for exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. The weaponization of anti-terror laws to target dissent has become a norm in Pakistan. This injustice must not continue – we urge the authorities to immediately release Imaan and Hadi and drop all charges against them.”
Background
Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha are human rights lawyers who represent activists and marginalized communities subjected to enforced disappearances, unjust charges by the state and Pakistan’s blasphemy laws. They were sentenced to ten to 17 years’ imprisonment under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) on 24 January 2026 for social media posts criticizing the military and expressing solidarity with Baloch and Pashtun activists. The Supreme Court of Pakistan suspended their sentences and granted bail on 17 September, but they were re-arrested under anti-terrorism charges on the same day before they could be released. They were accused of chanting “anti-government slogans” and allegedly “blocking roads” during a peaceful protest by Baloch activists in March 2025. Their bail applications under the protest case are still pending, however, a separate trial under the Anti-Terrorism Act was initiated for a case relating to the alleged removal of security barriers in connection to a cricket match in 2024.
Civil society, lawyers and international organizations have raised concerns regarding the independence of Pakistan’s judiciary, especially in light of the recent twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh constitutional amendments. A year ago, two supreme court justices and one high court judge resigned in protest following the twenty-seventh amendment, and yesterday, a judge of the Lahore high court resigned citing executive interference in judicial functions.

Vance outreach to Iran related to medical supplies, says Trump
Oct 29 - US President Donald Trump said that Vice President JD Vance's outreach to Iran was about helping the country get medical supplies, after US media reported Vance had written to Tehran's top security official to revive peace talks.
Tehran has received a letter from Vance but it has not responded to it yet, Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported on Thursday.
Vance sent the letter to Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei in a bid to revive peace negotiations, the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times reported on Wednesday, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter. Reuters could not immediately verify the reports.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance sent the letter at Trump's direction. When asked by reporters later on Wednesday if he directed Vance to reach out to Iran to restart peace negotiations, Trump said: "No."
"What that is is they need help with medical supplies and various things. He (Vance) asked me what I thought. I said, if you want to do that, that's okay. Basically, it's getting supplies in to help people that are not well," Trump told reporters.
Iran's mission to the United Nations in New York did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the letter and Trump's remark. Vance's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran at the end of February. The US has also since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and escalated efforts to economically isolate Iran.
Iran has long blamed US sanctions for hindering civilian access to medical supplies.
In an August letter to the UN Security Council, Iran accused the US of intentionally depriving civilians "of access to food, medicines, medical equipment, energy and other necessities, with grave consequences for their rights to life, health, food and a decent standard of living."
Qatari mediators presented Iran with a new draft deal on Sunday to end the war, but a senior Iranian official said Doha had only put forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.
The war's impact on global energy costs has also weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt Trump's approval ratings ahead of the US midterm elections that decide control of Congress. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. REUTERS

Russian Banderol Missile Kills Two 15-Year-Old Girls, Injures 15 in Chernihiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:39:47 UTC
00:39:47 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Banderol Missile Kills Two 15-Year-Old Girls, Injures 15 in Chernihiv
A Russian missile strike on central Chernihiv killed two 15-year-old girls and injured at least 15 people, including three children, on October 29, according to regional authorities.
Viacheslav Chaus, head of the Chernihiv regional military administration, identified the weapon as Russia's S8000 Banderol cruise missile in a statement published on the administration's official Telegram channel.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Russia killed two 15-year-old girls with its Banderol in central Chernihiv," Chaus wrote.
The missile struck during the day, when the city center was crowded with pedestrians. Eleven injured people were hospitalized, while medical personnel treated the other injured people at the scene. Businesses, residential buildings, and vehicles sustained extensive damage.
Emergency services continued working at the impact site as authorities assessed the destruction and casualties.
The S8000 Banderol is a Russian jet-powered cruise missile developed by the sanctioned defense manufacturer Kronstadt. Designed primarily for launch from Orion reconnaissance drones, the missile has a reported range of approximately 500 kilometers and carries a warhead weighing up to 150 kilograms.
According to Ukraine's Defense Intelligence, it can perform sharp maneuvers during flight while maintaining the trajectory of a conventional cruise missile.
Russia has been expanding production of Banderol missiles despite international sanctions targeting its defense industry. In August, Ukraine's military intelligence reported that Russian manufacturers were capable of producing up to 80 missiles per month. Intelligence officials also identified foreign-made electronics and components used in the weapon, including parts supplied through intermediaries despite restrictions on Russia's military-industrial sector.
The flow of Western technology into Russia's weapons factories has become a growing focus for Kyiv, which earlier in October appealed to employees of manufacturing, logistics, and trading companies for tips on illicit procurement networks.
To circumvent sanctions, Russian firms have reportedly relied on shell companies and complex supply routes through third countries to obtain microelectronics and dual-use goods.
The appeal came during a week when Russian strikes killed more than 100 Ukrainian civilians and injured over 400 others, including children, hitting residential buildings, passenger buses, shopping centers, and schools.

US bans Chinese labs from testing electronics ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
The FCC measure targets testing facilities with alleged PLA ties, giving US labs until December 2028 to expand capacity
The United States on Thursday banned all Chinese laboratories from testing electronic devices destined for the US market, just weeks before US President Donald Trump is due to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) voted to bar testing laboratories and certification bodies in China and other economies that lack a “mutual recognition agreement” or reciprocal trade agreement with the US.
“This is consistent with President Trump’s broader effort to restore balance and fairness with respect to America’s dealings with foreign nations,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.

Nearly 80% of Captured Foreign Fighters Want to Return to Russia—Moscow Won't Take Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:39:20 UTC
00:39:20 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Nearly 80% of Captured Foreign Fighters Want to Return to Russia—Moscow Won't Take Them
Nearly 80% of foreign nationals captured by Ukrainian forces while fighting for Russia want to return to the country, although Moscow is largely unwilling to take them back, hromadske reported on October 29.
Andrii Yusov, deputy head of Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, revealed the figure during an October 20 discussion of the documentary "Predatory Recruitment: Evans's Story."
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"They do not take into account that the Russian Federation and Putin mostly do not want to take them back and will not," Yusov noted, referring to the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin.
According to Yusov, some foreign prisoners claimed they had been unaware they would be sent to fight against Ukraine. Several maintained that they had traveled to Russia for civilian work, such as "painting fences," or to attend a "cultural festival."
However, a survey conducted by the Coordination Headquarters found that nearly 50% of captured foreign nationals acknowledged knowing they were joining the Russian military to fight against Ukrainians. The findings indicate that a substantial share of those surveyed understood the nature of their recruitment before arriving on the battlefield.
Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals has drawn increasing attention amid reports of misleading employment offers and promises of high salaries. The hromadske documentary examines the case of Evans, a Kenyan citizen who signed a contract with the Russian military after accepting its promises of lucrative employment.
He subsequently ended up in Ukrainian captivity, with his experience illustrating how Russia recruits foreigners for its war against Ukraine.
The scale of that recruitment has grown sharply since the full-scale invasion, with Russia's Defense Ministry signing contracts with nearly 46,000 foreign nationals from 151 countries, up from just 94 contracts recorded in 2022.
Of the 18,500 foreigners Moscow aimed to recruit in 2026, 16,168 had already signed by October. Roughly 47% of captured foreign fighters joined hoping to obtain Russian citizenship, and some sought to return to Russia to collect promised contract payments and benefits.
Moscow has also used legal and administrative restrictions against migrants living in Russia without citizenship, presenting military service as one of the few routes to legal residency and a Russian passport.

Cabinet gathers to weigh right-wing bloc’s new joint demands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:36:19 UTC
00:36:19 KST

Cabinet gathers to weigh right-wing bloc’s new joint demands
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Top members of the Dutch cabinet have gathered to discuss demands made on Thursday by a newly formed alliance of right-wing parties that could determine the future of the government’s tax plan.
On Thursday morning, leaders of the far-right JA21, orthodox Protestant party SGP, and farmer-citizen movement BBB announced they are banding together to force concessions in the tax plan negotiations.
They set out their demands – mainly concerning asylum, nitrogen and abortion – in a letter to the cabinet on Wednesday evening.
If their demands are met, the group says, it will support the cabinet on the rest of the tax plan and take a “constructive” approach to the budget.
The parties want to scrap plans to raise taxes to fund defence spending for NATO, as well as a planned VAT rise on flowers, and they want profit exemptions for small businesses raised.
Adjustments to the nitrogen plans demanded by BBB, harsher measures against asylum by JA21, and a pause on late-term abortions, home abortions and surrogacy demanded by the SGP are now joint demands by all three parties.
The move makes prime minister Jetten’s plans for broad support in which parties across the political spectrum back his plans, even more unlikely.
So far, opposition parties on the left and the right have said the coalition must choose a direction: side with left-wing parties like PRO and Volt, or with the right wing. Within the coalition, D66 and CDA prefer the former option, but the VVD has been leaning rightwards.
The letter contains a number of potentially intractable policies. Ending an obligation to the so-called “spreading law”, which requires all councils to house a fair share of asylum seekers, is something asylum minister Bart van den Brink (CDA) has said he cannot commit to.
Dropping the defence tax is particularly sensitive for the CDA. The SGP’s demands on abortion and surrogacy will clash with D66’s stances, broadcaster NOS reported.
The nitrogen proposals also conflict with agreements the cabinet has said are needed to get permits issued again, and PRO has said it will withdraw its support if the nitrogen plans are substantially changed.

Russia, Ukraine launch humanitarian missions to frontline town of Oleshky
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:35:48 CST
00:35:48 KST

MOSCOW/KIEV, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Russia and Ukraine on Thursday dispatched representatives on humanitarian missions to Oleshky, a frontline town in Ukraine's Kherson region, to deliver aid to residents and help civilians leave safely amid a worsening humanitarian situation.
Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that the operation had begun, telling the Zvezda television channel that a flight had departed from Moscow and that demining was underway as part of a complex operation.
Russia's Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said she had set off for Oleshky on Thursday to carry out the mission.
"Our main task is to deliver humanitarian aid to the people remaining in the city. We will also ensure the possibility of a safe exit for those who wish to leave Oleshky," she said.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian delegation led by Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets also departed for the town on Thursday.
David Arakhamia, chairman of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, said on Telegram that the delegation would "monitor the situation and provide updates on the operation as soon as communication becomes available."
Lubinets said on Facebook that the mission's priorities were to deliver humanitarian aid and help ensure the safe evacuation of residents, adding that an agreement with Lantratova, with the support and coordination of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, made the mission possible.
With about 2,000 people remaining at present, Oleshky lies on the left bank of the Dnieper River, opposite the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson. The town has been under Russian control since February 2022 and is facing a humanitarian crisis, with shortages of food, medicine and other essential supplies amid continued fighting, according to officials.
The humanitarian mission followed an agreement on a temporary ceasefire in the area to facilitate aid deliveries and civilian evacuations. The ceasefire is scheduled to remain in effect until 10:59 p.m. Moscow time (1959 GMT) on Nov. 1, according to the Russian side. ■

ANKARA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A fairy chimney collapsed Thursday in Cappadocia, a tourist hub in central Türkiye, killing two people and injuring another, Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok told private broadcaster NTV.
The incident occurred near the entrance to the Goreme Open-Air Museum and was caused by heavy rainfall in recent days, Kok said.
Health and rescue teams were dispatched to the scene.
Cappadocia is renowned for its fairy chimneys, which are tall, thin rock spires shaped like mushrooms, cones or towers formed over millions of years by wind and water eroding volcanic rock.
The region's landscape features valleys, rock-hewn churches, cave dwellings, and underground cities, reflecting its rich geological and cultural history, and attracting tens of thousands of foreign visitors each year. ■

Letter from Mideast: At 16, I carry a rifle and dream of home
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:35:30 CST
00:35:30 KST

by Ali Ahmed
ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- I once imagined myself in a doctor's white coat. Poverty and war put a rifle in my hands instead.
My name is Ali Ahmed. I am 16 years old. Since June 2026, I have been a soldier in a Yemeni pro-government force.
My first monthly salary -- 265 U.S. dollars -- seemed to prove that I had made the right decision.
As the eldest of seven children, I felt useful for the first time in a long while. I sent money home to cover my father's medical bills and help feed my younger siblings.
My mother was relieved, but frightened, too. She understood before I did that the salary came at a price. I knew how to pull a trigger, but little about fighting a war.
About a month after enlisting, I was sent to the front in Hays district, Hodeidah governorate. One night, Houthi fighters surrounded our position, and gunfire tore through the darkness. I could barely see where the shooting was coming from. I aimed at the flashes and fired in panic.
My hands shook. My legs shook. My heart felt as though it were trying to escape my chest.
Two young men from southern Yemen, like me, were killed that night.
I could not stop picturing my mother. For the first time, I truly understood that I might return home not as a son, but as a body.
The war soon taught me another lesson. Four of my friends were killed in a drone strike, and we had to gather what remained of them.
Until then, danger had meant noise: gunfire, explosions, and shouting. After that day, I learned to fear silence, too. Death can arrive without warning.
The life at home I had once hated became the life I longed for. I would gladly have spent all day delivering orders on my motorbike under the scorching sun, earning almost nothing, if it meant coming home alive.
The war followed me into my sleep. Even on quiet nights, I lay waiting for something to happen. Eventually, I saw a doctor because I could no longer sleep properly. The medication helped me sleep, but it could not give me back the peace I had known before the war.
I also began to see the war differently.
Before enlisting, I had never met a Houthi fighter. Then I saw Houthi prisoners. Some were young; others looked exhausted or frightened. But they looked familiar. They looked Yemeni.
I could not help wondering: Did they have sick fathers, too? Younger brothers waiting for food? Had they once imagined another future, as I had?
When you see the other side from a few steps away rather than across a battlefield, war stops looking as simple as it once did.
If the fighting ended tomorrow, I could sit with a Houthi fighter and drink tea. Without rifles between us, we might discover how much our families had in common, and how little we had known about the people we feared.
At the front, we talked more about home than politics. We talked about mothers, wives, children, and food. Sometimes, we asked one another for a final favor: if we were killed, find a way to break the news gently to our mothers.
I do not know when the fighting will end. But I know what I want if I ever make it home for good.
I want to sit with my family by the sea, with a plate of white rice and fish and a glass of red tea. Nothing more. Just all of us, together and safe.
Editor's note: Ali Ahmed is from Yemen's southern port city of Aden. He joined the Giants Brigades in 2026.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Xinhua News Agency.

Putin hails Russia-Africa partnership as natural alliance for multipolar world
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:35:29 CST
00:35:29 KST

MOSCOW, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday described Russia and Africa as "natural allies" in building a multipolar world order, saying the ruble already accounted for up to 85 percent of trade settlements between Russia and African countries.
"Russia and Africa are united by truly strong bonds of friendship and close partnership," Putin said, speaking at the plenary session of the third Russia-Africa Summit at the Kremlin. "We are natural allies in building a multipolar, genuinely democratic world order, a world order free from dictate and double standards, based on respect for the norms of international law and the basic principles of the UN Charter," he said.
Putin reaffirmed Russia's support for strengthening Africa's role in key multilateral institutions, including the UN Security Council and international financial institutions.
"We supported the resolution adopted by the UN General Assembly last December establishing the International Day Against Colonialism, December 14. And of course, we welcome the UN decision in March this year to recognize the transatlantic slave trade as the gravest crime against humanity," he said.
Putin added that Russia had opened eight new embassies in Africa since the previous summit in 2023, bringing the total to 48. Russia is also developing a network of trade missions, which currently covers 16 African countries, he said.
"All this allows us to protect our economic exchanges from external influence and makes them more resilient to fluctuations in the global economic and political environment," he said.
Putin added that closer alignment between the Eurasian Economic Union and the African Continental Free Trade Area could create additional opportunities to expand trade and capital flows.
The participants are expected to adopt a final declaration, an action plan for the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum for 2027-2029, and a declaration on cooperation for the peaceful use of artificial intelligence. ■

China Focus: China expands, diversifies launch infrastructure to meet rising space industry demand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:35:21 CST
00:35:21 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China is expanding and diversifying its launch infrastructure to meet the growing demand from the commercial space industry, with its offshore launch platforms, commercial spaceports and dedicated launch pads opening up new avenues for private rocket makers to send spacecraft into orbit.
A typical example is a commercial rocket carrying nine satellites that lifted off from a ship in the East China Sea near Shanghai in September this year. Although the densely populated economic hub has no traditional rocket launch site, sea-based launches are able to connect Shanghai to the country's growing space industry.
China's first sea launch took place in 2019, off the coast of Haiyang in east China's Shandong Province. The coastal city has since built a spaceport for rocket assembly, testing and launch operations. Teng Yao, chief engineer of the spaceport, said sea launches offer greater flexibility in choosing launch locations and trajectories, and allow rocket debris to fall into waters that are unpopulated.
Wenchang in south China's Hainan Province, which hosts a launch site tasked with missions of launching space station modules and lunar probes, has added facilities specifically for commercial rocket and satellite launches since 2024.
Meanwhile, the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone near the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China has developed launch pads tailored to private rocket makers.
Access to launch pads has been a challenge for China's commercial space sector. Wang Lifeng, a professor at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, cited limited launch capacity, tight schedules and long distances between launch sites and rocket assembly facilities as constraints on growth.
Large satellite networks like Qianfan (or Spacesail) and GW constellations, which each have more than 10,000 satellites, further increase the need for a steady flow of launches.
Diversified facilities not only boost launch numbers but also make launch operations more efficient.
Wenchang's commercial spacecraft launch site has put its first two pads into regular service. The second pad alone can accommodate more than 20 rocket types and can be prepared for another launch in 66 hours. The third and fourth pads in the second phase are scheduled to be operational by the end of the year. Upon full commissioning, the site is able to handle about 60 launches annually.
Haiyang offers another route to greater efficiency. Peng Haomin, co-founder of Orienspace, said the private company's facilities are clustered in Haiyang's spaceport, allowing rockets to be assembled, tested and loaded onto a launch ship within 5 km.
"This has replaced usual transportation over more than 1,000 km, drastically cutting logistics time and cost," Peng said.
Dedicated facilities can also streamline rocket operations. Meng Xiangfu, deputy chief commander of Lijian-1 rocket of commercial spaceflight company CAS Space, said that with its tailored launch pad and technical facilities at the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone, the company can complete the testing and preparation of a rocket in 10 days.
The expansion of launch infrastructure not only benefits the space industry, but also helps boost local economy through investment.
With more than 30 aerospace projects landed, Haiyang has attracted 33.5 billion yuan (around 5 billion U.S. dollars) in related investment. Wenchang's space industry park hosts over 700 companies, while Shanghai is developing a commercial spaceport-related terminal to link rocket assembly with port logistics and sea launch services.
These developments fit into a broader global trend of investing in space capabilities to support the sector's growth, as the United States aims at expanding its space transportation capabilities and Russia calls for efforts to upgrade its industrial and ground-based space infrastructure.
A 2025-2027 action plan issued by the China National Space Administration calls for coordinated development of commercial space launch sites and supports new types of commercial launch systems, including sea-based launch and recovery facilities.
At the same time, China is pressing ahead with the development of heavy-lift and reusable launch vehicles to further expand launch capacity and improve cost efficiency.
Analysts note that efficient operation of these facilities could equip China's commercial space sector with the launch capacity and operational flexibility it needs. ■

VIENNA, October 29. /TASS/. NATO is becoming an official arms store for Kiev despite insisting it is not a party to the Ukraine conflict, said Dmitry Polyansky, Russia’s permanent representative to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
He was commenting on the alliance’s plans to allow Kiev to purchase weapons directly through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA).
"The alliance, which insists at every opportunity that it is not a party to the conflict, is becoming an official arms store for Kiev," he told a regular meeting of the OSCE Permanent Council. TASS has obtained the text of his remarks.

The UK has also announced a 10-billion-pound aid package (around $13.3 billion) for Ukraine.

FM Sybiha: Russia’s deliberate attacks on civilians are Putin’s real response to easing sanctions
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha made this statement on the social media platform X, according to Ukrinform.
The head of the Foreign Ministry noted that Russia committed yet another horrific act of terror against Ukrainian civilians in Dnipro, striking a train platform and killing at least 14 people, while another 14 were injured.
In addition, Russian troops also struck a passenger bus in Zaporizhzhia, wounding at least one person; the center of Chernihiv, killing two 15-year-old girls and wounding 23 others; and a residential apartment building in Kremenchuk, killing at least three people and wounding 19, including five children.
“These were deliberate attacks on civilians,” Sybiha emphasized.
He stressed that Putin’s Russia continues to kill Ukrainians in broad daylight, demonstrating complete disregard for human life and international law.
“This is Putin’s real response to every sign of Western weakness and every misguided decision to ease sanctions, delist oligarchs, or grant exemptions. Such missteps must stop,” the minister stressed.
In his view, every Russian attack must be met with a response that weakens Russia’s ability to wage war. Specifically, this involves strengthening Ukraine’s air defense, increasing pressure on Moscow, and taking measures to disrupt Russian drone and missile production.
As reported by Ukrinform, at around 11:00 a.m. today, the enemy launched four jet-powered strike UAVs toward the Dnipropetrovsk region. Three of them were shot down by air defense systems, while one struck the platform of the Dnipro railway station. As of midday, the strike had reportedly left 14 people dead and 14 wounded.

attentions.
