We must implement the Party's organizational line for the new era and apply stringent standards to the education, cultivation, selection, appointment, management, and oversight of officials. On this basis, we will build up the ranks of high-caliber officials with firm political commitment, outstanding professional competence, excellent work conduct, and strict discipline. Following sound guidelines in appointing officials, we should take targeted, well-designed measures to select and appoint officials, inspire officials to foster and act on the correct view of performance, enhance officials' competence in fulfilling their duties and breaking new ground, improve the training and selection of outstanding young officials, and strengthen management and oversight of officials, with a view to promoting the training, recruitment, and utilization of talented people across the board.
It was stated that Party organizations at all levels play the principal role in exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance. It is therefore essential to systematically advance the development of Party organizations at all levels and in all sectors to strengthen their political and organizational functions. This will help ensure that the Party's lines, principles, and policies, as well as the Party Central Committee's decisions and plans are implemented through well-coordinated, targeted, and effective efforts. More specifically, we should give play to the exemplary role of Party organizations of central Party and state organs, bolster the functions of local Party committees, take coordinated steps to improve primary-level Party organizations across all sectors, promote Party building in emerging sectors, build a strong contingent of Party members, and refine mechanisms to ensure alignment across different levels of Party organizations.
It was pointed out that improving conduct and tightening discipline are effective measures to advance full and rigorous Party self-governance. We must work in concert to enhance Party spirit, improve Party conduct, and tighten Party discipline, and integrate conduct improvement and discipline enforcement with anti-corruption measures. Drawing on the experience gained in advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance through conduct improvement efforts, we will ensure steady improvements in our conduct, supervise and govern the Party with strict discipline, and pool support and strength with a positive image. In practice, we will follow the Party's mass line in the new era, steadfastly implement the central Party leadership's eight-point decision on improving work conduct, put in consistent and sustained efforts to improve conduct, ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive.
It was noted that taking integrated steps to ensure that officials do not have the audacity, opportunity, or desire to commit corruption is both an important strategy for full and rigorous Party self-governance and a fundamental guideline for our fight against corruption. The Party tolerates no corruption, as it has no special interests of its own besides the interests of the working class and the greatest possible majority of the people. Keeping this firmly in mind, we must steadfastly follow a distinctive Chinese path of anti-corruption and strengthen the Party Central Committee's centralized, unified leadership over anti-corruption work. We must take systematic steps to address both symptoms and root causes of corruption and adopt a holistic approach that combines severe punishment, targeted remedy, and effective prevention, carrying this fight through to the end. While maintaining a tough stance against corruption, we should also strengthen checks on and oversight over the exercise of power, fortify the cultural-ethical foundations for championing integrity and disdaining corruption, and enhance coordinated efforts to prevent corruption by rooting out audacity, opportunity, and desire.
It was noted that strengthening Party regulations and institutions represents a long-term, fundamental strategy for ensuring full and rigorous Party self-governance. We must uphold the Party Constitution as the fundamental code of conduct for all Party members, deepen institutional reforms related to Party building, and integrate law-based governance of the country and regulation-based self-governance of the Party, thus providing strong institutional support for persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance. For this purpose, stronger measures will be taken to improve the framework of Party regulations and institutions, ensure the enforcement of institutions, and eliminate hidden rules.
It was stated that persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance entails further improvement to Party and state oversight systems. With this in mind, we should ensure that Party committees (leading Party members groups) exercise general oversight, improve the dual leadership system for discipline inspection and supervision, pursue greater integration and efficient collaboration between intraparty oversight and other avenues of oversight, and give play to the role of inspections as a powerful tool of comprehensive oversight.
It was stressed that persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance is the common political responsibility of all Party members. Attaching crucial importance to the responsibility system for Party self-supervision and self-governance, we will establish a robust, unified system where all sides perform their respective responsibilities in close collaboration. Furthermore, relevant performance assessment mechanisms will be improved, so that those who have failed to effectively carry out Party self-supervision and self-governance and caused serious problems in this regard are strictly held to account.
It was pointed out that studying and implementing the guiding principles from this plenary session represent a major political task for the entire Party both at present and in the period to come. With this in mind, we should fully grasp the guiding principles from the session, strengthen organization and leadership, and make tenacious efforts to solve prominent problems, seeing that all arrangements of the Resolution are implemented to the letter.
It was stressed that all aspects of our work agenda should be steadily advanced at the turn of the year. To fulfill this year's main goals and tasks for economic and social development and secure a good start for the 15th Five-Year Plan period, we will adhere to the general principle of pursuing progress while ensuring stability; fully and faithfully apply the new development philosophy on all fronts; move faster to foster a new pattern of development; make full and proper use of macro policies; tap deeper into the potential of domestic demand; further deepen reform and opening up; and pursue sustained and high-quality economic growth driven by innovation. In an effort to ensure security while pursuing development, we will press ahead with initiatives to see that public services are inclusive, meet essential needs, and provide a cushion for the people most in need, and deliver better results in our work related to workplace safety, disaster prevention, mitigation, and relief, food and drug safety, as well as social stability. As part of our endeavors to consolidate and expand the progress made in the study campaign on establishing and practicing the correct view of performance, we will, in the midst of a new round of elections at all levels, step up training for new members of leadership teams, particularly their heads, on the view of performance to inspire and guide them to deliver for the people through hard work in line with the requirements of serving the public good, benefiting the people, making sound decisions, and taking solid, down-to-earth actions.

TEHRAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The navy of Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) announced on Thursday that three "violating" oil tankers that sought to cross the Strait of Hormuz through the "unauthorized" route south of the waterway exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines over the past 24 hours.
In a statement on the IRGC's official news outlet Sepah News, the navy said the vessels were abandoned off the strait's southern coasts.

Iran tightened its grip on the strait on Feb. 28, barring safe passage of vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States following their joint strikes on Iranian territory.
In a separate statement on Thursday, the IRGC Navy said its electronic warfare unit managed within the preceding hours to take control of the guidance and navigation systems of a U.S. Army MQM-170 Outlaw "espionage and decoy" drone west of the strait and land it safely.
It added that the drone had been tasked with identifying Iran's air defense systems along the southern coasts, and data recovery showed it had taken off from the coast of a regional country.
In another statement on Thursday, the IRGC said its aerospace division's air defense systems shot down an MQ-1 Predator drone east of the strait within the preceding hour. It was the 14th MQ-1 intercepted by its air defense forces in recent months. ■

Feature: Myanmar's Thadingyut Festival blends faith, family, grassroots commerce
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:06:06 CST
21:06:06 KST

YANGON, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Sunlight glints off the gilded spires of the Botahtaung Pagoda against a clear, pale blue sky in downtown Yangon. Tens of thousands of devotees have gathered here to pay homage to the Buddha during the Thadingyut Festival, one of Myanmar's most cherished occasions for family reunions and religious devotion.
On the full moon day of the festival, which marks the Buddha's descent from heaven, the pagoda compound hums with the footsteps of pilgrims and visitors.
"Since the Full Moon Day of Thadingyut coincides with my daughter's birthday, our family comes to the pagoda to perform meritorious deeds," said Ei Phyu, a local resident from Yangon.
During the three-day festival, which ran from Oct. 25 to 27 this year, her family lights oil lamps at home, makes donations, and prepares rice, meals and curries to offer to Buddhist monks and share with neighbours, she said on the sidelines of a candle-lighting event held by the pagoda's Board of Trustees on the evening of the full moon day.
Devotees like Ei Phyu are part of a vast wave of worshippers gathering at sacred landmarks across Myanmar. While Botahtaung Pagoda typically welcomes 4,000 to 5,000 visitors on a standard day, daily attendance leaps to between 30,000 and 70,000 during major religious holidays, according to U Aung Myat, a member of the pagoda's Board of Trustees.
The festive spirit extends far beyond Yangon, lighting up regions like Bagan and Kyaukse with hot-air balloon releases, live music concerts, and traditional contests.
In Kyaukse Town, located in the Mandalay Region, the famed Kyaukse Elephant Dance Competition stood out as a highlight of the weekend festivities.
U Tin Aung, who has served as a judge for the competition for over two decades, emphasized the heritage behind the spectacle. He noted that the 75-year-old tradition plays a vital role in preserving local cultural identity.
The Thadingyut Festival is a time for paying respect to elders and reuniting with family members who work in different places, he said, noting that the Kyaukse elephant dance festival also reflects these values, bringing people from towns and villages together in celebration.
Beyond offering ordinary citizens a welcome respite from daily hardships, the festival serves as a vital economic engine for local governments aiming to stimulate grassroots commerce and support small entrepreneurs.
In the ancient city of Bagan, market fairs showcasing traditional foods and products from micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) were held alongside traditional balloon releases in the pagoda-dense archaeological zone, according to U Myo Min Aung, deputy director of the Hotels and Tourism Development Implementation and Training Department in Bagan.
At People's Square in Yangon, Khin Thida Tun, owner of Pyae Thanakha, sold various value-added products made from thanakha, a natural cosmetic paste made from the ground bark, wood or roots of the thanakha tree, on the sidelines of a four-day Thadingyut fair featuring live performances and an MSME market fair.
"I'm thrilled to participate as an MSME owner because it gives us a chance to promote our brand locally and network with other businesses," she said, adding that her booth welcomed roughly 100 regular customers and new visitors in a single day. ■

CANBERRA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Australia's physical energy exports, including coal, liquefied natural gas (LNG), uranium and crude oil, fell to their lowest level in 10 years in 2024-25, declining 3.1 percent overall, official data showed on Thursday.
Black coal remained Australia's largest energy export, falling 1.1 percent, while LNG exports declined 2.2 percent, according to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
Renewable energy production continued to grow, up almost 10 percent in 2024-25, following a 5-percent rise in 2023-24. Solar remained Australia's largest renewable energy source, up 11 percent, while wind production increased 15 percent, the ABS said in its latest Energy Account report.
Total household energy use increased by 0.3 percent in 2024-25, with petrol, electricity and natural gas remaining the main energy products used by Australian households, according to the ABS. ■

China Focus: AI drives digital transformation in China's primary care
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:05:51 CST
21:05:51 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China is introducing AI-powered tools in community health centers to speed up the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare, improve primary care, expand equitable access and enhance public well-being.
Artificial intelligence (AI) assistants that support voice-based consultations, automated medical records, medication-risk screening, follow-up reminders and health education are appearing in community health centers. They are becoming a key part of the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare.
The push comes as family doctors in China take on a wide range of duties, from resident registration and chronic-disease follow-up to initial screening and public-health record keeping, often burdened by heavy paperwork and limited staffing.
AI-assisted family-doctor services have been introduced in many cities and provinces this year.
In May, the Longgang District of Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province launched the "Ant Afu" app, allowing residents to check medical reports, obtain AI-assisted interpretations, sign up for family-doctor services and link family members' health information.
In Beijing's Fengtai District, the Majiapu Community Health Service Center has deployed an AI family doctor and an AI health steward. Built on large models and AI-agent technologies, the system supports chronic-disease management, wearable-device monitoring and automatic risk alerts, with high-risk cases forwarded to contracted family doctors.
In Wuxi, east China's Jiangsu Province, AI was used in a citywide cancer screening campaign. Residents completed risk self-assessments through a mobile app or an AI-powered voice questionnaire, and big-data models identified high-risk groups for follow-up screening at 49 institutions equipped with AI-assisted imaging, ultrasound and endoscopy systems.
According to the Wuxi Municipal Health Commission, the AI-enabled screening significantly improved cancer detection among high-risk groups, with liver and lung cancers detected at markedly higher rates than in the general population.
Industry insiders say the most significant shift is that AI is moving from isolated add-on tools into routine clinical workflows in some community health centers. Earlier systems often required doctors to open separate applications for image reading or diagnostic support. The newer AI systems are being integrated with hospital information systems and health-checkup platforms, so that AI prompts appear within the interfaces doctors already use.
"AI used to seem lofty and unrelated to primary care," said Nie Chunlei, vice president of the Community Health Association of China. "But now we can see it has taken root at the grassroots level."
With growing demand and expanding real-world deployments, more tech companies are entering the sector, further driving the digital upgrade of grassroots healthcare services.
Ant Group's Ant Afu health app has rolled out its "AI agent plus human doctor" model in more than 40 cities. Tens of thousands of grassroots doctors use the platform, and it had served more than 5 million residents by mid-August this year.
The push is not limited to Ant Group. JD Health, Runda Medical and others are also ramping up investment in primary-care AI, each drawing on its own strengths.
Policy support has become more explicit. In October 2025, five national agencies issued guidance identifying intelligent clinical decision support, AI-enabled family-doctor services and coordinated chronic-disease management as priority areas. The guidance sets a goal of basically achieving full coverage of AI-assisted diagnosis and treatment in primary care institutions by 2030.
Still, industry insiders caution that scaling AI across primary care requires careful adaptation. AI cannot simply be transplanted into primary care; it must be tailored to frontline needs, embedded in daily workflows and built into applications that are replicable, scalable and can be regulated -- challenges that will take time to resolve.
Sun Dehui, R&D director at the Beijing Medical Robotics Industry Innovation Center, said primary-care AI is a clear long-term direction for public health. With policy support increasingly focused on the grassroots level, the sector is poised for rapid growth in the coming years, offering significant market potential while continuing to ease the burden on frontline clinicians and benefiting residents with chronic conditions. ■

21:05:50 KST

ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's government said Thursday that Aden International Airport had resumed normal operations after a temporary suspension triggered by a Houthi attack that damaged its runway a day earlier.
Transport Minister Mohsen Haidara announced the resumption during an inspection of the airport, saying technical teams had carried out urgent repairs to the section of the runway hit in the Wednesday's attack, according to a statement from the Ministry of Transport posted on social media platform X.
Haidara said flights to and from Aden were being rescheduled and airlines had been notified to resume services.
He condemned the attack on what he described as a "civilian facility" serving passengers from across Yemen.
The reopening came a day after explosions were heard near the airport in two rounds of attacks that halted operations and prompted hundreds of passengers, including patients, to leave.
Shortly before the blasts, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea issued what he called a "final" warning urging people at the airport to evacuate immediately.
Sarea claimed that a Saudi military cargo aircraft was at the airport transporting weapons, without providing evidence. The Yemeni government did not immediately respond.
The attack came amid an escalating confrontation between the Houthis and government forces supported by the Saudi-led coalition, with missile, drone and air attacks intensifying in recent days.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting the coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government. ■

Alyoshki ceasefire, humanitarian convoy: statements by ombudswoman, Defense Ministry

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The compliance of Russia and Ukraine with the ceasefire, which has been in effect around the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region for 54 hours now, is allowing the servicemen to clear roads of mines and prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova reported.
Russia’s battlegroup Dnepr is clearing roads of mines and explosives to ensure the safety of the routes to Alyoshki. According to the Russian Defense Ministry, servicemen are clearing the area of unexploded ordnance to facilitate aid delivery and resident evacuations.
TASS has compiled the key information known at this time.
Compliance with ceasefire
According to Lantratova, the ceasefire declared in connection with the humanitarian mission in the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region is being fully observed, with no incidents: "The ceasefire has been in effect for 54 hours: since 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27. The parties are fully complying with their commitments, and no violations have been recorded."
The human rights commissioner noted that she is in constant contact with her Ukrainian counterpart Dmitry Lubinets, and that they are coordinating the implementation of the agreements together.
Lantratova emphasized the importance of continued compliance, as the safety of the town's residents and everyone involved in the mission depends on it.
Humanitarian aid
Lantratova reported that a large humanitarian convoy with food, medicine, and all the essentials for the residents of Alyoshki has been put together: "We have gathered all the items that the people need into this convoy, which will be delivered to those in need in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region."
The ombudswoman clarified that the list of items needed by the people in Alyoshki was compiled at the request of the residents themselves. First and foremost, the list includes food, medicine, hygiene products, fuel, and heating supplies.
She noted that preparations are underway to deliver essential supplies to those remaining in the town and to ensure a safe exit for those who wish to leave.
Ensuring safe passage for humanitarian convoy
The Russian human rights commissioner emphasized that the parties’ adherence to the ceasefire allows the servicemen to "continue clearing roads of mines and prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy."
She added that the Russian army is carrying out all the necessary engineering and technical work and that mine clearance operations are underway.
Defense Ministry’s statement
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr is clearing roads to ensure the safety of routes to Alyoshki, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
According to its statement, sections of road adjacent to the city are being cleared of explosive devices and unexploded ordnance to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians.
The ministry emphasized that servicemen from the battlegroup Dnepr discovered NATO ammunition near the bypass road leading to the town of Alyoshki.
According to the Russian army, most of the Ukrainian armed forces' mines found near Alyoshki were scattered by drones and are predominantly of Western manufacture.
The ministry noted that unexploded NATO-standard munitions pose a "particular danger" to Alyoshki residents because they "can detonate from the slightest mechanical impact."
To ensure the safety of Alyoshki’s civilians, sappers from the battlegroup Dnepr are destroying the mines on site "using a shaped charge," the Russian Defense Ministry stated.
On situation in Alyoshki
At 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27, the Russian Armed Forces declared a ceasefire in the Kherson area of the line of engagement in preparation for a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region.
Earlier, with the assistance of US First Lady Melania Trump, Russia and Ukraine agreed to a ceasefire in Alyoshki to ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid and prepare for the evacuation of the civilian population through a special safe corridor.
An independent US media organization will accompany and document the actions of Russian and Ukrainian groups throughout the process.
On September 21, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki as critical.
Ukrainian shelling and drone attacks have made it impossible to deliver food or medicine to the city.

Shadow fleet sanctions: Can the EU act if the US pulls back?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:01:00 UTC
21:01:00 KST

Russia shadow fleet sanctions: Can the EU act if the US pulls back?
October 29, 2026
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has increasingly relied on a so-called shadow fleet to bypass Western sanctions and transport its oil around the world.
Other heavily sanctioned countries, including Iran and Venezuela, have also been accused of using such vessels to export petroleum products.
These tankers often rely on deceptive practices like turning off their location transponders to evade detection and conceal the cargo's true origins or destinations.
The fleet, which consists largely of aging, uninsured and poorly maintained tankers, has raised widespread concern across the shipping industry. Yet it has expanded rapidly in recent years and now accounts for nearly 19% of global oil tanker capacity, according to estimates by financial intelligence firm S&P Global.
"The shadow fleet is a scourge," Elisabeth Braw, senior fellow at the think tank Atlantic Council, said, adding that "it is in nobody's interest" to have these ships sailing around in the world's oceans.
She pointed out that these tankers undermine the maritime order and increase the risk of accidents and environmental damage.
"Every country should use its leverage with Russia to ask it not to use the fleet," she told DW, noting that ultimately all countries suffer the consequences.
Easing sanctions to reduce freight rates?
To clamp down on the fleet and curb Russia's oil export revenues, the United States and European countries have stepped up efforts to intercept tankers accused of violating sanctions.
The Trump administration, however, is reportedly considering lifting sanctions on some shadow fleet vessels and allowing them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.
A US official told Reuters earlier this month that the move was intended to ease record-high global freight rates.
Lifting sanctions on the shadow fleet "would decrease the effectiveness of the sanctions regime overall," said Michael Carpenter, senior fellow for Transatlantic Affairs at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS). Such a move "rewards the aggressor and helps Moscow gain revenues to continue attacking Ukraine," he told DW.
"This is the exact opposite of what the US should be doing if it wants to end the war."
Carpenter, who previously served as US ambassador to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said any sanctions relief would also put the US and the EU "strategically at odds with each other, with the EU clearly backing Ukraine and the US increasingly supporting Russia's financial goals."
This view is shared by Ben Harris, vice president and director of Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution.
Lifting sanctions on shadow fleet tankers would "make it substantially easier for Russia to trade its oil at market rates," he said, pointing out that it would "improve its government finances since so much revenue is tied to energy markets."
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, however, rejected suggestions that the US was removing sanctions from shadow fleet tankers.
"We are converting dark tankers to legitimate tankers," Bloomberg quoted Wright as saying last week. "There is no removing of sanctions," he stressed, adding that the US government was working with investors who buy idle sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.
"We're going to move some of the ships from what I call the 'bad-guy fleet' to the 'good-guy fleet,'" Wright said. "They will not carry sanctioned oil anymore."
The US government has yet to unveil a detailed plan for shadow fleet tankers.
Trump's deal with Putin raises concerns
The proposal follows a deal that US President Donald Trump struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin this month to allow sales of Russian diesel onto global markets.
The agreement was seen as part of Trump's efforts to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
The US president also waived broad new sanctions on Russia authorized by a recent legislation, which targeted Moscow's energy revenues and threatened tariffs against the world's largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas.
The decision was sharply criticized by Ukraine and its European allies over concerns that it could undermine the credibility of sanctions and weaken Western economic pressure on Moscow.
Harris said that "the US sanctions carry outsized weight because of the threat [for countries and businesses] of being cut off from the US financial system."
What can the EU do?
If the US steps away from its sanctions on the shadow fleet, he argued, "the responsibility shifts to European policymakers." But they have "less effective options because of the diminished threat of severing financial ties."
Still, the expert stressed that Europe has some tools, pointing to the continent's key role in global shipping and insurance services.
"They can implement measures demanding that tankers carry legitimate and established insurance when traveling through their waters," he said, noting that it "would mean that many shadow fleet tankers could not in practice legally transport Russian oil."
Harris added that European policymakers could also pressure countries worldwide to better regulate the tankers flying their flags.
Carpenter said even if US eases some restrictions, the EU will have no choice but to continue enforcing its sanctions on these vessels.
"The vast majority of the shadow fleet traverses the Baltic Sea and exits it via the Danish Strait," he noted, adding that the EU is "uniquely positioned to board and inspect vessels moving through this key chokepoint."
But Russia has threatened to seize ships belonging to European countries in retaliation for interdicting and seizing Russian vessels suspected of being part of the shadow fleet.
And without US backing, Carpenter said, "it will be harder for EU countries to take on the burdens and risks of sanctions enforcement."
Braw echoed this view, saying that Ukraine's European allies will have to remain united and continue working closely with partners such as Japan, Australia and Canada. Nevertheless, she stressed that what they can achieve on their own "is far less than what they can achieve if the US is part of the team."

Ketamine and MDMA treatments are linked to epigenetic changes in genes tied to brain plasticity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:00:38 UTC
21:00:38 KST

Ketamine and MDMA treatment were associated with changes in DNA methylation, a chemical modification that can influence gene activity, at genes linked to neuroplasticity and immune processes, according to a study published in Translational Psychiatry. The changes were measured in blood and saliva samples from people treated for depression or post-traumatic stress disorder.
DNA methylation is a chemical mark that can influence how easily a cell reads certain genes. It does not alter the DNA code itself. Researchers often measure methylation in blood or saliva because those samples are easier to collect than brain tissue. However, a change in blood or saliva does not necessarily mean the same change has occurred in the brain.
Ketamine and MDMA are being studied for mental health conditions, including depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Both are sometimes called psychoplastogens, compounds thought to promote neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to form and reorganize connections. They act through different mechanisms, and researchers do not yet fully understand how their effects may last beyond the treatment sessions.
Led by Moira G. Semple of Arizona State University, the researchers investigated whether either treatment was associated with methylation changes in genes considered relevant to brain health. Rather than examining the entire genome, they focused on about 2,900 genes that are particularly active in the brain or involved in signaling between nerve cells, an approach intended to make the analysis more manageable in small samples.
The researchers analyzed samples from two separate studies. The ketamine group included 20 people (average age about 40; 15 women) with moderate-to-severe depression, PTSD, or both. They received six ketamine infusions over two to three weeks, with blood samples collected before treatment and 10 days after it ended.
The MDMA group included 16 people (average age about 43; seven women) with severe PTSD who took part in a Phase 3 clinical trial of MDMA-assisted therapy. They received three MDMA doses about four weeks apart alongside psychotherapy, with saliva collected before treatment and six to eight weeks after the final session. Neither analysis included a comparison group that did not receive the drug.
In each group, no individual methylation site changed enough to remain statistically significant after correcting for the large number of sites tested. When the researchers combined results across all the sites within each gene, they identified 405 genes with statistically significant methylation changes after ketamine and 346 after MDMA.
In both groups, the changes clustered in biological pathways related to neuroplasticity, such as the structure and organization of synapses, the points where nerve cells communicate. Some pathways related to immune and stress-response signaling also emerged. Ketamine was associated with changes in genes involved in glutamate signaling, while MDMA was associated with changes in genes such as BDNF, which supports the growth and survival of nerve cells, and a dopamine transporter gene.
The two treatments overlapped only partly at the level of individual genes. Forty-seven genes changed in both groups, but only about a quarter changed in the same direction, and the sizes of the changes were not correlated. The overlap was greater at the level of broader biological pathways, and both treatments were associated with increased methylation of EFNA5, a gene that has been linked to PTSD in large genetic studies.
Some of the patterns also differed. Ketamine changes were more strongly linked to synapse-related pathways, while MDMA changes were associated with a wider range of processes, including the movement of substances across cell membranes and electrical signaling. The authors noted that these differences could reflect the treatments’ distinct effects, but could also be due to differences between the studies, such as the use of psychotherapy with MDMA, the mix of diagnoses in the ketamine group, and the different sample types and collection times.
The authors summarized the shared pattern: “Across both compounds, altered loci [locations in the genome] converged on pathways related to neuroplasticity and neuroimmune regulation.” This is evidence of treatment-associated molecular changes, not proof that these changes explain why either treatment may help patients.
Some limitations should be noted. The groups were small, neither included a comparison group, and the study did not examine whether the methylation changes were related to symptom improvement. The ketamine and MDMA participants were not compared within one trial and differed in diagnosis, treatment context, and whether blood or saliva was tested.
The study also could not show whether the methylation changes affected gene activity, and participants receiving ketamine were allowed to continue most of their medications. Smoking and ethnicity, both of which can affect methylation, were not included in the analysis. Two of the authors are employees of TruDiagnostic, an epigenetic testing company, and nonprofits led by two other authors helped fund the MDMA analyses.
The study, “Brain-targeted epigenetic effects of two emerging psychoplastogens: ketamine & MDMA,” was authored by Moira G. Semple, Sarah E. Mennenga, Ryan Smith, Varun B. Dwaraka, Baruch Rael Cahn, Joseph Tafur, David M. Rabin, Berra Yazar-Klosinski and Candace R. Lewis.

A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics
The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation
One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.
The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.
Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.
The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.
There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.
Nailing a Mars cloud’s features
Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.
The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.
The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.
While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.
The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.
“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.
Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

Russia drone strike on Ukrainian railway station kills 13
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Russia drone strike on Ukrainian railway station kills 13
The UN’s top humanitarian official in Ukraine on Thursday condemned a Russian drone attack on the city of Dnipro that killed at least 13 civilians and injured 10 others at its main railway station.
“Civilians preparing for a trip, welcoming or bidding farewell to loved ones faced death and devastation,” said Matthias Schmale, the Humanitarian Coordinator for Ukraine, adding that displaced people and humanitarian workers at a transit centre at the station were left in shock by the nearby explosions.
Media outlets reported that a jet-powered drone hit the station as a train due to travel to Zaporizhzhia stood at a platform. An 11-year-old boy was among the injured, according to regional officials cited in the reports.
Rising risks for rail passengers
Mr. Schmale expressed condolences to the families of those killed on behalf of the UN, noting that train travel is a key means of transportation in Ukraine.
Since the start of the year, he said, travellers and railway workers have faced increased risks on every journey due to Russian military strikes and air alerts affecting the safety and reliability of trains.
According to figures from Ukraine’s railway operator cited by media outlets, attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
Recent months have seen repeated attacks across the country on civilian infrastructure critical to daily life, including bridges, hospitals, schools, shopping centres and railway stations, Mr. Schmale said.
Inured to violence
“The images from Dnipro cannot become another story that fades from attention. Behind every casualty is a person, a family and a future changed forever,” he said.
“It cannot be repeated often enough that civilians and civilian infrastructure are protected under international humanitarian law.”
Aid convoys head for Oleshky
Mr. Schmale told UN News in an interview on Thursday that preparations to get aid into Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Kherson region, were “accelerating” while a local ceasefire held, and that deliveries could arrive as early as Friday.
The ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump and announced by the White House on 23 October, is due to end on the evening of 1 November.
Ukraine’s Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets, has said he is on his way to the town and will accompany residents out.
Mr. Schmale said mined roads were a key reason residents had been trapped. He pointed to images of a stretch known locally as the “road of death”.
“It’s clear any safe passage both in and out has to have mine clearance preceding it,” he said, adding that reports reaching him confirmed demining was under way.
Offer of support ‘not taken up’
The UN has no direct role in the evacuation. “We have offered support, but it’s not been taken up,” Mr. Schmale said, adding that none of its partners were involved either.
Under established procedure, evacuees will get help once they reach Government-controlled areas.
That includes food and other material assistance, and possibly help finding housing. “There’s a high likelihood that we will get involved the minute they are here,” he said.
More than 1,000 likely to remain
Mr. Schmale said estimates varied, but he had heard that 200 to 300 people might leave, “which would leave more than 1,000 there, and they would need support”.
He cited accounts from UN human rights monitors, civil society groups and the Ukrainian authorities.
The town’s remaining health facility was “barely functional” and short of medicine, he said, and keeping warm through winter amid energy disruption would be a growing challenge. Safe water and public infrastructure were also pressing needs.
“Because they’ve been trapped in that place for so long under heavy bombardment, mental health issues should never be overlooked,” he said.

Nature is making a comeback – now restoration funding must quadruple
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Nature is making a comeback – now restoration funding must quadruple
From salmon spawning grounds in Canada to coral reefs in Indonesia, ecosystems around the world are being restored at an unprecedented rate.
Some 252 million hectares across 149 countries – an area of land and sea roughly the size of Kazakhstan – are currently under restoration, making this the largest documented effort of its kind to date. More than one million green jobs have also been created in the process.
“Today, we are witnessing the makings of one of the largest movements for nature in recorded history,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
Stepping it up
However, more action is needed to meet global restoration targets, UNEP and sister agencies said in a report launched on Thursday at the COP17 biodiversity conference in Yerevan, Armenia.
Nature’s comeback - Scaling ecosystem restoration for people and planet comes at the halfway point for the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, which runs through 2030.
The report assesses progress on a global commitment to restore around one billion hectares of land – roughly the size of China – by the end of this period and ensure that 30 per cent of the world’s ecosystems are under conservation, in line with a 2022 agreement known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
For this to happen there must be rapid acceleration, particularly in freshwater, marine and coastal ecosystems. Annual funding for restoration also needs to increase more than fourfold from $64 billion to $296 billion – an investment that could create up to 32 million jobs worldwide by 2030.
‘Restoration works’
“Five years into the UN Decade, the message is clear: restoration works,” said Dongyu Qu, Director-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), which co-published the report alongside UNEP and the UN biodiversity secretariat.
“The challenges are to make restoration an integral part of the sustainable management of land, water and natural resources, and to have a coherent transformation of agrifood systems.”
Natural bounce
Helping nature to bounce back is essential for food and water security, climate resilience, jobs and wellbeing.
Research suggests that restoring just 15 per cent of global priority areas could prevent 60 per cent of projected species extinctions while 30 per cent of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions could also be sequestered.
Yet progress is variable across ecosystems and countries. For example, restoration of terrestrial ecosystems has reached nearly half the 30 per cent target, but marine and coastal restoration has been far more limited.
The report said restoration must be sustained long enough to both enable ecosystem and biodiversity recovery while delivering lasting benefits for communities.
“We cannot expect to fix nature with one hand while we destroy it with the other one,” said Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) Secretariat.
“Governments must address the drivers of ecosystem degradation and invest in monitoring mechanisms to ensure the durability of the restoration movement to date.”

Lithuania to introduce universal military conscription in 2032, president says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:55:00 UTC
20:55:00 KST

Lithuania plans to introduce universal military conscription in 2032, requiring a larger number of young people to serve in the armed forces amid security concerns, President Gitanas Nausėda said Thursday.
The State Defence Council, which comprises the country’s political and military leadership, agreed on the timeline at a meeting, Nausėda told reporters afterward.
Women would continue to be able to perform military service on a voluntary basis, he said.
Lithuania currently drafts more than 5,000 young people into the armed forces each year. Under universal conscription, the annual number would rise to about 7,500, accounting for demographic trends and the fact that some young people are deemed medically unfit for service, the president said.
Nausėda said the 2032 target would give the country time to invest in adequate accommodation for the larger number of conscripts and train enough instructors.
The authorities also need to balance conscript training with refresher training for reserve personnel to ensure both are carried out effectively, he said.
“I think implementing conscription from 2032 is optimal,” Nausėda said.
According to Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, the government wanted a quicker transition to universal conscription, but were convinced by the military to push back the date to 2032.
“You could say there is political will, but at the same time, there is the question of the military’s readiness. The military has clearly stated that they would be ready by 2032,” Sinkevičius told reporters after Thursday’s State Defence Council meeting.
The date for introducing universal conscription was discussed “at length and in detail, with lively debates” at the council, the PM said.
“Everyone agreed that this isn’t a race, nor is it a matter of setting a specific date in stone – that we must move toward universal conscription and that it is inevitable, but needs to be done when you’re prepared,” he said.
The preparations would include training some 300 instructors and building suitable facilities to house the young draftees, he added.
The council also agreed to expand the range of service options available to conscripts. These could include training as drone operators or assisting the State Border Guard Service and firefighting and rescue services, the president said.
After trying to switch to fully professional armed forces, Lithuania restored partial conscription in 2015, citing increased security threats following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014.

'Feels like being hit by a bus': Rib remodelling beauty surgery on the rise

PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, October 29: Spanish papers discuss Wednesday's deadly train collision. The New York Times investigates whether a "safest seat" in the event of a train crash exists. Next, we look at a report about "the shocking rise of rib remodelling". We end with some photos from the Arctic and Antarctica.
Spanish papers are reacting to the devastating train crash that killed dozens of people on Wednesday. Both El Mundo and El País emphasise that it's not the first time this has happened – the last train accident in Spain was only nine months ago. El País also has a first-person story: "I travelled on this train", writes a journalist who works for the paper. He happened to be there during the crash. He already covered the Adamuz disaster in January and now he writes: "I had that feeling again of living through a nightmare". He also describes the strange calm and how he and other passengers managed to free themselves from the last carriage.
The New York Times asks the question "Is there a safest seat in a train crash?" The answer is not so simple. There's a rough consensus that it's best to sit in the middle of the train, in case of a hit from the front or the back. Some experts are even more precise, saying the best bet is sitting in the middle, in an aisle seat facing backward – that's because if the train suddenly stops, the whiplash would be less brutal and there's a smaller chance of being hit by flying objects. But experts told the paper that there are too many variables in train crashes to say for certain. This time in Spain, for example, the hit was from the back, so the safest place to sit would have been in the front of the train. But of course passengers couldn't have known in advance of the nature of the crash.
The tragedy is still very recent, but it could already have political repercussions. According to Democrata, it could harm Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's reputation before snap elections that are happening in only a month's time. The weak link among his ministers is Oscar Puente, the transport minister, who was already in post in January during the first train crash. According to the paper, he has three options: "continuity, resignation or dismissal". Puente is under fire, and not only because of the actual crashes. Some time after the previous rail disaster, he appeared in a comedy video in which he imitated a derailing train.
Next, The Guardian reports that rib remodelling surgery is on the rise. First, the patient's ribs are fractured, and then the person has to stay in a corset for three months, almost 24/7. The idea is to give the person a wasp-like waist. The Guardian spoke to people who went through it, who say it's extremely painful and feels like "being hit by a bus". One lady who did it couldn't sleep comfortably for more than a week because she was in constant pain. Although the procedure remains rare, more and more people are deciding to do it. Between 2018 and 2024, there were more than 2,300 patients, with an overall complication rate of 3.7 percent, which remains quite high for beauty procedures.
Finally, a new photography book by polar specialists Sue Flood and Ian Dawson captures the Arctic and Antarctica. The Times shows its favourite photographs that "document life at the frozen edges of the world".

ASTANA, October 29. /TASS/. Kazakhstan imported 6.4 bln cubic meters of gas in January-September 2026, compared with 4.7 bln cubic meters for the whole of 2025, with Russia among its suppliers, BES.media reported, citing a response from the country’s Energy Ministry to an inquiry.

Hackers expose US immigration surveillance network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:53:26 UTC
20:53:26 KST

Hackers expose US immigration surveillance network
Personal and operational details of more than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors, including undercover immigration agents, have been leaked online, reportedly exposing the department’s internal structure and surveillance operations.
The disclosure comes amid growing public anger over President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign, with the department’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facing growing criticism over aggressive raids, detention conditions, and the use of force against migrants and protesters.
Released on Wednesday by transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), the files contain names, contact details, job titles, and internal system access groups across ICE, Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and other DHS agencies.
DHS confirmed to the media that it is “aware of a potential breach” and is working to address it, adding that it will protect employees and update the public “when more information is available.”
What’s in the files?
Dubbed ‘Icepick’, the archive was supplied to DDoSecrets by a hacktivist group called ‘Department of Peace’. It contains around 21,300 CBP records, 6,600 linked to ICE, and 3,400 to Homeland Security Investigations, along with records from immigration services, cybersecurity, and other DHS divisions. Some records match employees’ social media profiles, but others exposed internal organizational charts and previously undisclosed programs and operations.
According to Wired, the files reference undercover investigations, wiretapping, and immigration databases, with internal access groups linked to surveillance tools including Palantir’s Falcon software and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition system used by immigration agents. Other groups reference AI services including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Elon Musk’s xAI chatbot Grok. Access groups are lists of employees authorized to use particular systems, which means the records could help identify which employees have access to surveillance tools and how DHS operations are organized.
“This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” investigative journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew, who developed a searchable version of the archive, said in a statement accompanying the release. She called it “a complete game changer for anyone investigating DHS,” arguing that it could help identify agents and their chains of command.
DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said the files go beyond an ordinary employee directory.
“Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations,” she said, pointing to officials overseeing covert investigations, efforts to identify government leakers, and deportation programs.
The hackers claim to have obtained the records through DHS’s Okta employee login system, though Okta denied that its systems were compromised.
Why now?
The hackers linked the leak to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s pledge to intensify immigration enforcement. Speaking after two fatal ICE shootings in Texas and Maine, Mullin said federal agents are “turning up the heat on the streets,” despite growing criticism of their tactics. “On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ‘turning up the heat.’ This is what happens to ICE when you do that,” a Department of Peace spokesperson said in a statement published by DDoSecrets.
The disclosure comes amid growing backlash over Trump’s immigration crackdown, a central priority since his return to the White House in January 2025. His push for mass deportations, expanded detention, and tighter border controls has sparked protests over aggressive raids, masked agents, and alleged racial profiling.
Anger intensified after federal agents fatally shot US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota in January, followed by other violent incidents involving ICE officers. Just this month, federal agents shot and wounded a Dominican migrant during an arrest in New York, prompting further demonstrations.
ICE has also faced scrutiny over detention conditions, with at least 52 deaths in its custody during Trump’s first 500 days back in office, according to Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights.
The administration maintains that its operations are necessary to enforce immigration law and remove dangerous criminals. The Icepick publishers say the records can help journalists, lawmakers, and civil liberties groups investigate DHS activities. Emma Best argued that the disclosure can enable investigations, congressional inquiries, and legal challenges by replacing the administration’s “anonymity with accountability.”
Yet another breach
The disclosure adds to a series of US government data security incidents.
In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed that it stole personal data on nearly all FBI agents and their spouses, including sensitive job details and medical information. The group said the attack was “not financially motivated” and demanded that the FBI withdraw a cybersecurity advisory published in May that it claimed contained false allegations about it.
Separately, a Pentagon personnel system breach reportedly exposed Social Security numbers, personal details, and military job records belonging to more than 3 million people, including service members and their families. The incident prompted a class-action lawsuit last week.

Ukraine has a national typeface called Zakon — what makes it distinctive
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:51:52 EET
20:51:52 KST

Ukraine has a national typeface called Zakon — what makes it distinctive
Kyiv • UNN
The Zakon typeface was created based on Ukraine’s artistic tradition for documents and the visual identity of government institutions. It will be introduced gradually.
Ukraine has unveiled the national typeface Zakon. It was created based on the Ukrainian artistic tradition. The Ministry of Culture of Ukraine reported this on October 29, UNN writes.
Details
"The new national typeface Zakon was presented publicly for the first time in Kyiv. It was developed by Ukrainian designers based on the historical heritage of the country's lettering tradition. The new typeface is intended to establish Ukrainian identity in the state's visual space and gradually replace typefaces of Russian origin in official documents," the Ministry of Culture noted.
The development of a national typeface is provided for by Resolution No. 4764-IX of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine dated January 2026, "On Strengthening the Role of the Ukrainian Language in Establishing the Ukrainian State."
"We continue to establish Ukrainian identity in the visual space. The creation of a national typeface is an important step toward ensuring that state institutions represent Ukraine through our artistic tradition and contemporary Ukrainian design. A typeface is part of a state's recognizable image. Through the form of its letters, it conveys the character of our culture and makes it present in everyday life. We seek to ensure that Ukrainian design shapes the image of our state and that cultural heritage becomes a source of new solutions," said Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy — Minister of Culture of Ukraine Tetiana Berezhna.
What the typeface is for
The initiative, the Ministry of Culture noted, is aimed at creating the state institutions' own visual language. After all, certificates, letters of appreciation, diplomas, awards, and plaques are still designed using typefaces of Russian origin, including Izhitsa and Petersburg, as well as typefaces Cyrillicized by the Russian studio ParaType.
The Ukrainian typeface tradition in contemporary design
Zakon is a classic Ukrainian antiqua that combines national graphic traditions with modern requirements for document design.
The development was based on the legacy of six outstanding masters of Ukrainian lettering. Heorhii Narbut was the author of the first Ukrainian banknotes and the coat of arms of the Ukrainian State under Hetman Skoropadskyi, and one of the founders of the Ukrainian Academy of Arts. Many of his typographic solutions remain part of Ukrainian identity to this day.
Vasyl Krychevskyi was the author of the coat of arms of the Ukrainian People's Republic and left a significant typographic legacy.
Yakiv Hnizdovskyi lived in emigration but sought to bring the Ukrainian alphabet closer to the Western typographic tradition. His work also helped contemporary masters.
Robert Lisovskyi was a graphic artist, a master of Ukrainian book type, and a follower of Mykhailo Boichuk and Heorhii Narbut.
During the Soviet era, Vasyl Khomenko created a Ukrainian typeface that was used virtually until the end of the Soviet Union.
Vasyl Chebanyk is a luminary of contemporary calligraphy who designed the ceremonial copy of the Constitution of Ukraine and left a rich typographic legacy.
The typeface incorporates characteristic features of Ukrainian graphics: asymmetrical serifs, diamond-shaped dots above the letters "і" and "ї," and the distinctive mark above "й" in the tradition of Heorhii Narbut. Its proportions also draw on the European tradition of classical antiqua typefaces.
Four Ukrainian type designers worked on the creation of Zakon:
-  Oleksii Chekal is a calligrapher, a research fellow at the Museum of Books and Printing of Ukraine, and the author of typefaces for the Orthodox Church of Ukraine; 
-  Hennadii Zarechniuk is a researcher of Ukraine's typographic heritage and a co-author of the Kobzar KS, Zahar, and Dnipro typefaces; 
-  Dmytro Rastvortsev is the author of the e-Ukraine typeface and a co-author of UAF Sans for the Armed Forces of Ukraine; 
-  Andrii Shevchenko is the author of the Arsenal typeface, which won a competition for a contemporary Ukrainian typeface for official business use. 
The project manager is Taras Ishchyk, a serviceman and the author of the graphic style of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Three typefaces for the state's different needs
The Zakon typeface family consists of three typefaces:
-  Zakon Text is intended for office work, official documents, and everyday text work. It is freely available for use; 
-  Zakon Decor was created for designing ceremonial documents, awards, and inscriptions; 
-  Zakon Letterpress is intended for printing original copies of regulatory and legal acts of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. 
The two latest typefaces are available under a closed license to a limited number of users. The font includes four styles: Regular, Italic, Bold, and Bold Italic.
How the national font will be implemented
The transition to Zakon will take place gradually, without additional costs for the mass replacement of existing signs, forms, and other materials.
After the presentation, the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine will provide government institutions with the font and instructions for installing it. At the first stage, Zakon Text will be tested during the preparation of letters, orders, forms, and other documents. The feedback received will help the developers improve the font.
At the same time, the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine is working to make Zakon the font used for the official publication of regulatory legal acts.
You can learn more about the national font, download it, and leave feedback on the website of the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine.

these glowing amber sculptures begin with a natural polymer produced by tiny insects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:50:05 UTC
20:50:05 KST

these glowing amber sculptures begin with a natural polymer produced by tiny insects
ori orisun merhav explores a future of multispecies design, where biological processes inform how we manufacture and inhabit the world.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
insects make the material for ori orisun merhav’s sculptures
Brussels-based designer Ori Orisun Merhav is experimenting with a natural polymer produced by tiny lac insects, transforming their resinous secretions into glowing sculptures and sculptural furniture. Through her research practice Made by Insects, she heats and blows the amber-colored material into clusters of translucent bubbles, some perched on branching steel structures, others suspended as elaborate chandeliers.
The material is known commercially as shellac, a substance typically used as a protective coating. Here in Merhav’s hands, it takes on a completely different spirit.
Her latest works extend the research into 3D printing and large-scale installations, imagining how an insect-produced material might become part of our built environment. After years of research into the insects themselves, the designer has received a 2026 Dutch Design Award for her experimental approach to material production.
the tiny insects behind an unlikely design material
The insects that produce this shellac are known scientifically as Kerria lacca, and are roughly the size of a grain of sand. They attach themselves to the branches of host trees and feed on their sap, converting sugars into a natural resin that hardens around their bodies. This protective enclosure allows the insects to develop and reproduce. The hardened resin can then be collected from the branches, washed and processed into shellac, a material humans have used for centuries in furniture finishing and other applications.
Designer Ori Orisun Merhav first encountered the insects while researching ecological relationships during her studies at Design Academy Eindhoven. She was fascinated by their ability to manufacture a polymer through their own biological processes, and she traveled to Thailand to study lac cultivation and meet the communities who harvest it. There, she learned about the insects’ life cycles and the agricultural practices surrounding their production.
The research became her 2022 graduation project, The Lac Lab Open Source, an evolving archive of material experiments that eventually grew into Made by Insects. It also introduced her to the economic realities of shellac production, as synthetic alternatives have steadily reduced demand for the natural resin.
learning to build from the insects themselves
Back in her studio, Merhav began testing what the material could do beyond its traditional applications. Shellac softens when heated and hardens again as it cools, allowing her to stretch it into thin membranes and blow it into hollow forms using techniques borrowed from glassmaking.
Her earliest experiments produced large, individual bubbles, but their delicate walls made them brittle and difficult to transport. Looking more closely at the insects’ protective structures, she discovered that their enclosures comprised many smaller, interconnected cells.
The observation changed her approach. Merhav began blowing smaller volumes and joining them into larger structures, developing a new language of clustered forms that draws directly from the insects’ construction methods. In works such as Branching Insects Chandelier and Meet Me Under the Insects Tree, the amber bubbles grow along slender metal supports, casting warm light through their uneven surfaces.
The finished pieces have an almost botanical appearance, although their structural logic comes from the resinous shelters of insects.
3D printing a polymer made by another species
Merhav’s experiments have since expanded into digital fabrication. Working with Ginger Additive, Reflexlab and Aeditto, she produced her first 3D-printed shellac objects in 2023, later continuing the research with material engineer Tom Samson and the Bio-Polymer Lab at Avans University of Applied Sciences in the Netherlands.
The process explores how a naturally occurring polymer can move through a printer without chemical modification. Temperature and the material’s behavior during extrusion influence the forms as they take shape, leaving behind uneven surfaces and visible layers of hardened resin.
Her Morphopoiesis vessels offer a closer look at this emerging technique. The objects rise in irregular, cellular walls, with ridges of deposited material forming dense networks around their hollow interiors.
a woven insect canopy takes shape in london
At Sarah Myerscough Gallery, Merhav’s ongoing research has grown into an environment visitors can move through. Portal Into The Multi-Species, on view from October 14th to November 7th, 2026, occupies the gallery’s entrance corridor with delicate shellac bubbles attached to steel branches. Further inside, the forms become larger and more textured.
In The Woven Insect Canopy, palm sheaths coated in insect-produced resin are held within sculptural steel supports, their fibrous surfaces illuminated from within by LEDs.
The series includes Awakening, Regeneration and Bifurcation, the latter reaching 140 centimeters in height. Light passes through the shellac-coated fibers to reveal their interwoven structure beneath the amber surface. The works point to an interior shaped by biological processes. A material originally created as a protective shelter has become part of an imagined architecture.
who makes the materials we live with?
Merhav’s interest in mutualism runs through the project, beginning with the relationship between lac insects and the trees that sustain them. The insects depend on their hosts for nourishment, while cultivation involves managing the trees’ health and the insects’ reproductive cycles.
Human participation adds another layer, through the farmers who maintain these environments and the makers who work with the harvested resin. The ecological relationship itself is complex, yet the research draws attention to the many participants involved in producing a single material.
These sculptures, for Merhav, are part of a much longer exploration of how these relationships might inform design. The work remains experimental, with the material’s fragility and the demands of fabrication continuing to shape its possibilities. Still, her lamps and vessels offer a tangible glimpse of an unusual manufacturing future. An insect produces a polymer to protect itself on a tree branch. Generations later, a designer studies that structure and finds a way to build with it.
project info:
designer: Ori Orisun Merhav | @ori_orisun
research practice: Made by Insects

How two high-speed trains collided in central Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:50:00 UTC
20:50:00 KST

Two high-speed trains collided just before 9 am on Oct 28 in Spain, killing at least 68 people and leaving more than 50 injured. Rail services between Madrid and the southern Andalusia region have been suspended. It is Spain’s deadliest train crash since 2013.
An Iryo express train had stopped at a red signal when it was struck by a Renfe high-speed train between the towns of Los Yebenes and Urda, near Toledo, about 118km south of Madrid by rail. The trains were both heading south from Madrid to Seville.
The crash is the second collision between high-speed trains on the same line in nine months. An accident between trains operated by the same two companies killed 46 people in January. Iryo is a private high-speed rail operator, while Renfe is owned by the Spanish government.
Addressing reporters in Madrid, Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said a computer malfunction had automatically stopped all traffic on part of the line. Puente said the fatal train crash occurred after the central command centre erroneously told the Renfe train to restart, without any speed restrictions.
Authorities said there were 147 passengers on the Iryo train, and 397 were on the Renfe train.
Prior to the crashes in 2026, Spain’s last major rail disaster occurred in 2013, when 80 people were killed and 145 injured after a high-speed train veered off the track on a sharp bend as it approached the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

McDonald’s China is giving its fries a place beside the keyboard. Developed with Lenovo, the brand’s French fry-shaped wireless mouse translates its familiar red carton and yellow contents into a computer accessory, incorporating plastic recovered from old Happy Meal toys. The collaboration brings together two recognizable features of the fast-food experience: the packaging that holds lunch and the small plastic object that tends to outlast it. This time, the latter gets something useful to do.
The design keeps the visual shorthand intact. A red lower shell carries the Golden Arches, while molded yellow fries rise across the top, giving the mouse an uneven silhouette that departs from the anonymous curves of conventional office hardware. The food reference determines the object’s shape as well as its colors, turning a piece of takeaway packaging into something intended to stay on the desk.
RECYCLED HAPPY MEAL TOYS FORM THE MOUSE’S PLASTIC SHELL
According to the product information, more than 60% of the exterior casing is made from recycled plastic sourced from collected Happy Meal toys. Lenovo describes a process involving sorting, shredding, purification, and material modification to produce recycled ABS suitable for manufacturing. The toys lose their original forms along the way: their material returns to production, eventually taking on another distinctly McDonald’s identity.
The collaboration sits within McDonald’s China’s Reimagine Good Things initiative, launched in 2021 to explore new uses for recovered materials. Previous products have included trays and flowerpots, extending the program into everyday objects. Here, the shift from toy to computer accessory also changes the intended user and setting. Something once handed out with a children’s meal reappears among the equipment of adult working life, retaining a little of its former playfulness.
WIRELESS CONNECTIVITY HIDES BENEATH THE FRENCH FRY SHAPE
Behind the sculpted fries, the mouse offers Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless connectivity, quiet-click buttons, and three adjustable sensitivity settings. A 380mAh rechargeable battery powers the device. Its accompanying carrying pouch unfolds into a mouse pad, allowing the accessory’s protective cover to become part of the desktop setup. The specifications give the novelty object a practical role, although its distinctive outline alone says little about comfort over a full working day.
This limited release places the mouse between functional equipment and branded collectible, with its appeal resting on an immediately legible transformation. A carton normally associated with a brief stop for food becomes an object designed for repeated use. Whether that makes answering emails more appetizing is another matter.
