India’s refining boom finds an opportunity in the global diesel crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:46:54 UTC
20:46:54 KST

India’s refining boom finds an opportunity in the global diesel crunch
India’s long-planned refinery expansions could make it an even bigger diesel supplier in 2027, just as disruptions to Russian and Middle Eastern shipments have created an unexpected export opportunity for Indian refiners.
State-owned refiners plan to add 16.5 million tons of annual diesel production capacity next year, executives said at an industry conference in Goa on Tuesday. The projects were originally intended to meet India’s growing domestic fuel requirements, not the current global diesel shortage.
“The expansion is driven by a portfolio, but the opportunity is in diesel,” XAnalysts founder and chief oil analyst Mukesh Sahdev told RT.
Why are global diesel supplies tight even as oil demand is falling?
The US-Iran war has disrupted Middle Eastern fuel shipments, while attacks on Russian refineries and export restrictions have reduced supplies from another major producer. Diesel powers transportation, factories, and farms, and the shortages are largely driving the current price inflation and affordability crisis.
Global diesel and gas oil availability fell by 1.7 million barrels per day – equivalent to roughly two-and-a-half times Japan’s daily diesel consumption last year – in the third quarter, compared with a year earlier, according to figures from the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the Energy Institute.
Wholesale diesel prices surpassed $200 per barrel in September, nearly double their prewar levels, and reached around $220 in Europe and the US, the IEA said.
The shortage persists despite weakening overall oil demand, as diesel consumption has remained comparatively resilient and inventories have fallen, the agency said. On October 15, IEA members agreed to accelerate emergency stock releases, including over 20 million barrels of diesel.
How are Indian refiners positioned to benefit?
Indian Oil Corporation, the country’s largest refiner, expects expansions to add around 8 million tons of diesel a year. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation’s new Rajasthan refinery is expected to produce 3 million tons next year, while the expanded Numaligarh refinery in Assam state will add another 3 million tons, Reuters reported.
Bharat Petroleum Corporation plans another 1.5 million tons of annual output. In all, India’s plans will expand overall refining capacity from 267 million tons annually to 300 million by 2030.
The country already produces more diesel than it consumes.
Refiners produced around 59 million tons from April to September, against domestic consumption of around 46 million, according to Oil Ministry data cited by Bloomberg.
The additional volumes are coming onstream amid a global shortage, creating a commercial opportunity for projects originally designed around Indian fuel demand, ICRA senior vice president Prashant Vasisht told RT.
Russian crude ‘a natural fit’
New refining capacity alone does not guarantee more diesel. Refineries need suitable crude oil, while equipment limits how much of it they can turn into diesel, Vasisht explained.
“Indian refineries are also getting the right quality of crude oil,” Sahdev said, noting Russian, Iraqi, and heavier Venezuelan grades as suitable feedstocks for diesel production.
Russian crude is “a natural fit for the Indian system,” he added. The new Rajasthan refinery can process Russian Urals and Iraqi Basrah grades, S&P Global reported in July.
Sahdev said India’s reliance on Russian barrels has also grown as production from traditional suppliers in Malaysia and West Africa declined.
Can India fill the global supply gap?
India is already the world’s second-largest seaborne diesel exporter after the US, according to data analysis firm Kpler. Exports reached 596,000 barrels per day in September, compared with the year-to-date average of 482,000 barrels per day, the data shows.
Additional Indian production could make a meaningful difference to global supplies, but it cannot replace all the diesel lost because of disruptions affecting Russia and the Middle East, the analysts cautioned.
“We are providing very large quantities to Europe and some of the other regions, but these are still not enough,” Vasisht said.
Not all the additional diesel will be available for export. India’s growing domestic demand, refinery operations, and freight costs will determine how much reaches overseas buyers.
The IEA expects global refinery output to recover in 2027, but warns that depleted inventories could keep diesel markets tight well into next year.
But expanding production alone is not enough, Sahdev cautioned. India also needs stronger commodity-trading networks and financial mechanisms to capture the full value of its growing refining capacity.
“If India does not do this, then somebody else will make money on Indian capacity,” he said.

High-speed rail use, which had broken records in 2024 and 2025, fell 15% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, data from Spain’s competition authority showed.

Possible dwarf planet discovered beyond Pluto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:40:07 UTC
20:40:07 KST

Possible dwarf planet discovered beyond Pluto
Astronomers have discovered a large icy object beyond Pluto that could qualify as a dwarf planet, potentially adding a new member to the solar system’s officially recognized group.
The discovery was announced on Thursday by the US-funded Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which houses the world’s largest 3.2-gigapixel digital camera, built specifically for astronomy.
Researchers estimate that the object, provisionally named 2026 ED138, is between 600 and 1,500 km in diameter and may be one of the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found. It currently sits roughly 46 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Pluto’s average distance, for comparison, is about 40 times Earth’s.
The object likely escaped detection until now because it appeared against a crowded backdrop of millions of stars near the plane of the Milky Way. However, Rubin’s repeated images and tracking software has now allowed scientists to pick out its movement.
#ICYMI: our Solar System has a newly-discovered dwarf planet candidate! Meet 2026 ED138, recently revealed by NSF–DOE Rubin Observatory ☄ Let's get to know this new world a little bit, shall we? https://t.co/wTOg898zBu https://t.co/RC0HP5rZiL
— NSF-DOE Rubin Observatory (@VRubinObs) October 28, 2026
If confirmed, ED138 would join five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union, which include Eris, Haumea, Makemake, Ceres, and Pluto, which was considered the solar system’s ninth planet until it was reclassified in 2006. Dwarf planets orbit the Sun and have enough gravity to become roughly round, but share their orbital neighborhoods with other bodies.
ED138 may be large enough to meet the roundness requirement, but astronomers still need more research and better measurements before determining its status.
“The main thing we need to do is to establish the physical size of 2026 ED138,” discoverer Matt Holman, an astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard and Smithsonian, told Reuters. He explained that ED138’s size is currently estimated from the sunlight it reflects. However, a small shiny object can appear just as bright as a large, dark one, Holman said.
To narrow down the true size of the object, researchers could use Chile’s ALMA telescope which can detect radiation emitted by ED138 itself, helping get a more accurate measurement.
The last dwarf planet officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union was Haumea in 2008. Other candidates have since emerged, including 2017 OF201, whose discovery was announced in May 2025, but none have yet been formally added to the list.

New restrictions for anglers starting November 1: where fishing will be banned and what fines will be imposed
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:39:50 EET
20:39:50 KST

New restrictions for anglers starting November 1: where fishing will be banned and what fines will be imposed
Kyiv • UNN
The ban will be in effect from November 1, 2026, until the beginning of the 2027 spawning season. Violations will incur fines, confiscation, and compensation for damages.
From November 1, 2026, a seasonal ban on catching fish and other aquatic biological resources in wintering pits will come into effect in Ukraine. It will remain in force until the beginning of the spring-summer spawning period of 2027. UNN reports this, citing the State Environmental Inspectorate and the State Fisheries Agency.
Why a ban on catching fish is being introduced
Wintering pits are deep sections of rivers, lakes, and reservoirs where fish gather as the weather turns colder. In cold water, their activity decreases, metabolic processes slow down, and their need for food diminishes. Mass fishing in wintering areas can cause significant damage to populations, so these areas are protected until the beginning of spawning.
This is an annual seasonal restriction provided for by the Recreational Fishing Rules, approved by Order No. 700 of the Ministry of Agrarian Policy dated September 19, 2022. The exact date when the ban ends will be determined depending on the start of the spawning period in the respective water bodies.
Where fishing will be prohibited
The ban does not apply to all water bodies or every deep-water area, but only to officially designated wintering pits. Their lists and boundaries are approved by the territorial bodies of the State Fisheries Agency in separate orders.
In particular, 78 wintering pits have been designated in Rivne region. They are located in separate sections of the Horyn, Sluch, Styr, Ikva, Liiva, Pripyat, and Putilivka rivers, as well as in the Basivkut Reservoir and Lakes Nobel and Ostrivske.
In Zhytomyr region, the restrictions will apply to designated sections of the Sluch, Teteriv, Irsha, Irpin, Uzh, Ubort, Khomora, Hnylopiat, Zdvyzh, and other rivers. Environmental protection authorities in Volyn also announced the start of the ban.
It is important to understand that fishing within a wintering pit is prohibited even from the shore. Before traveling to a body of water, anglers are advised to check the map or description of the boundaries of prohibited areas in the orders of the relevant territorial office of the State Fisheries Agency.
What fishing gear is permitted outside wintering pits
Outside designated wintering pits, recreational fishing is permitted by law unless other local or seasonal restrictions apply to the water body.
If a body of water is covered with ice, ice-fishing rods and tip-ups may be used. If there is no ice cover, fishing is permitted with float and bottom rods, spinning rods, and fly-fishing gear using natural or artificial bait. The total number of hooks on all of one angler’s gear must not exceed seven.
From freeze-up until the ice breaks up, fishing gear with hooks in which the distance from the shank to the tip of the point exceeds 10 millimeters is also prohibited. The use of poaching gear and other prohibited fishing methods is not allowed regardless of the time of year.
How much fish may be caught
On waters of general use, the daily limit for most fish species is three kilograms and one additional fish of any weight that meets the minimum permitted size. For certain species, including bleak, Amur sleeper, and pumpkinseed, no weight limit has been established. However, these limits apply only where fishing is permitted. They do not grant the right to fish in wintering pits. Restrictions on catching certain species and rules introduced for the period of martial law in specific regions must also be observed. Current restrictions should be checked before every trip.
What fines are предусмотрed for violations
For violating fishing rules, citizens face a warning or a fine of between 34 and 170 hryvnias. A serious violation, including the use of prohibited gear, carries a fine of between 340 and 680 hryvnias, with possible confiscation of the gear and catch. If illegal fishing causes substantial damage, criminal liability may arise under Article 249 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The sanction provides, in particular, for a fine of between 17,000 and 51,000 hryvnias or other types of punishment stipulated by law.
In addition to fines, violators must compensate for damages for each fish caught illegally. For example, the charge is 5,117 hryvnias for one catfish, 3,706 for a common carp, 3,587 for a pike-perch, 3,468 for a pike, 3,162 for a perch, and 1,649 hryvnias for a bream.
The amount of compensation is determined according to government rates, regardless of the weight of the individual caught. That is precisely why fishing in a prohibited area can cost significantly more than an administrative fine. To avoid trouble, environmental inspectors urge people to check the official lists of wintering pits in advance and comply with seasonal restrictions.

Ukraine's vast train network is a vital form of transport in the country, where journeys between east and west can take 24 hours.

Zelensky slams sanctions relief
Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three jet-powered drones in a daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.
The head of Ukraine Railways, Oleksandr Pertsovsky, said an elevated threat level had been announced.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform," he said on Facebook.
In the aftermath of the attack, Zelensky refreshed his criticism of a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to ease some sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel onto global markets.
"How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating," he asked.
At least five others were killed across Ukraine in separate Russian attacks, according to local officials.
Two teenagers killed
A strike on the city centre of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded more than a dozen, the head of the city's military administration, Dmytro Bryzhynsky, said.
A drone also slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing two and wounding several – including a six-year-old – the local governor said.
Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.
The Kremlin earlier this week vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under US mediation.
Zelensky said on Wednesday it would be a "huge success" if the local ceasefire in Oleshky – brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump – allowed for the evacuation of stranded citizens.

Locals caught there have resorted to hunting and eating pigeons in recent months, former residents in touch with those in the city told AFP.
Russia and Ukraine are to meet next month with US envoys to discuss ways to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II, with no firm dates set for the talks yet.
Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.
Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.
Ukraine and its allies say ceding ground to Moscow would be tantamount to a capitulation and leave Kyiv vulnerable to future Russian attacks.

Four women on trial after séance at Dutch cemetery

Unknown Publisher

Four women on trial after séance at Dutch cemetery
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Four women went on trial in a Utrecht court earlier this week for desecrating children’s graves during a séance they held at Amersfoort’s Rusthof Cemetery five years ago.
Prosecutors have demanded community service sentences of up to 200 hours for the women, who were trying to contact the dead after hours during a paranormal gathering. Two others with them, who are said only to have observed the ritual, are not being charged.
The cemetery’s director at the time was fired for giving the women permission to conduct research into the “so-called energies of the deceased” after closing time. The parents of children buried there had not been notified of the gathering.
Desecration?
The case has been before courts before, but the legal question now is whether the women’s activities constitute desecration.
The participants, who were found out after the father of a buried child discovered a camera at the grave site, allegedly used cat toys with lights to help them communicate with the dead children.
“It is terrible to be confronted with this kind of fact after the loss of a loved one,” prosecutors said. “The way the suspects have dealt with the graves goes against any sense of respect.”
At least 10 relatives have reburied their loved ones in other graves as a result.
Distraught parents
“When people ask me how it feels, I say it feels like rape,” Radia Drost-Laabidi told RTV Utrecht. She and her husband buried two of their daughters at Rusthof. She’s suffered from insomnia ever since and barely visits her daughters’ graves. Now she’s looking for answers. “Why?” she says. “That is my question.”
Only one defendant turned up in court this week, 81-year-old Irene B. Lawyers for the defendants argued that since nothing was damaged or destroyed, there is no desecration.
The court is expected to deliver its verdict next month.

Ukraine: 14 killed in Russian drone strike on crowded Dnipro train station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:33:00 UTC

Ukraine: 14 killed in Russian drone strike on train station
October 29, 2026
The death toll from a Russian drone attack on a passenger train which was stopped at a station in Dnipro in eastern Ukraine on Thursday morning has risen to 14, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed.
According to Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia, a jet-powered drone struck a crowded platform on which people were waiting to board a regional train to Zaporizhzhia, about a two-hour journey to the south.
"Despite an increased threat warning, people were on the platform," the company said.
Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three drones in the daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.
In images circulating on social media, bodies could be seen strewn across a train station platform, with police officers kneeling beside them.
"Russia is deliberately hunting civilians: on trains, at stations, in residential buildings," Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said. "There is no justification for this terror, and there never can be."
Dnipro city mayor Borys Filatov also confirmed the incident, which he called a "tragedy."
Zelenskyy issues veiled Trump criticism after 'horrific' attack
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack "horrific" and demanded international action from Kyiv's allies.
"Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues," he said.
"How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating?" he asked, referring to a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin which saw some sanctions on Russia eased and the release of Russian diesel stocks onto global markets.
French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his "deep concern" that Russia continues to "opt for escalation" by targeting civilians.
"In this context, we must aim for much more than a localized ceasefire — such as the one recently negotiated for Oleshky," the French president said on social media, describing Moscow’s rejection of "all proposals to that end" as "intolerable."
"Together, we must redouble our efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace and bring Russia to the negotiating table," he said.
"These are deliberate strikes against civilians, brazen in their cruelty, and the Russians are carrying them out right as the humanitarian operation in Oleshky is unfolding," continued Zelenskyy.
"Russia's signals are clear – they want the war to continue, and everyone around the world must still work very hard to achieve major de-escalation through strong steps and appropriate pressure on the aggressor."
How Russia targets Ukrainian trains
Russia has been targeting Ukrainian trains and stations since day one of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing railway workers and passengers.
Faced with an increasing number of Russian drone attacks, Ukrainian trains began large-scale passenger evacuations this year — often while trains are already mid-journey.
In September alone, more than 5,800 trains had to be evacuated due to the threat of strikes, Ukrzaliznytsia told the AFP news agency.
Most evacuations take place in regions near the front line, in the south and east of the country: in Odesa, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia.
When a potential Russian strike is detected, the train comes to a halt and passengers are required to leave their carriages and wait at a safe distance until the danger has passed.
With commercial air travel in Ukraine shut down due to the war, the country's vast railway network has become essential for transporting people and goods, as well as for entering and leaving Ukraine.
Ukraine: More Russian attacks
Also on Thursday, authorities reported at least five other fatalities resulting from other Russian attacks across Ukraine.
A strike on the city center of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded more than a dozen, according to the head of the city's military administration.
Elsewhere, a drone slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing two and wounding several — including a six-year-old.

Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:30:32 UTC
20:30:32 KST

Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- Wiley
- Summary:
- Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.
- Share:
Could the amount of daylight you get each day offer clues about your risk of developing dementia? A large new study suggests that exposure to brighter daytime light is associated with a lower likelihood of developing the condition.
The findings, published in General Psychiatry, point to daytime light exposure as a potentially overlooked factor in brain health.
Brighter Daylight Linked to Lower Dementia Risk
To investigate the connection, researchers analyzed data from 87,577 adults who wore wrist devices equipped with accelerometers. The devices allowed scientists to measure participants' exposure to light during both the day and night. Over a median follow-up period of 8.1 years, 741 participants developed dementia.
The results revealed a notable pattern. People exposed to average daytime light levels exceeding 1,000 lux (a moderately bright light level equivalent to an overcast day outdoors) had a 16% lower risk of developing dementia. Spending longer periods in even brighter daytime light (at least 5,000 lux) was associated with further reductions in risk.
Too Little Daylight Emerges as a Surprising Dementia Risk Indicator
One of the most striking findings involved people who received very little bright light during the day. Getting less than 0.7 hours, or 42 minutes, of bright daytime light daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than 6 established dementia risk factors.
Interestingly, researchers found no statistically significant connection between nighttime light exposure and dementia risk. This suggests that daytime brightness, rather than light exposure at night, may be particularly relevant to the relationship identified in the study.
"Daytime light exposure may serve as a novel indicator of dementia risk," said corresponding author Hongliang Feng, PhD, of Guangzhou Medical University, in China.
Although the findings reveal an association, they do not establish that getting more daylight directly prevents dementia. Instead, the research highlights daytime light exposure as a potentially valuable indicator of dementia risk that deserves further investigation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Wiley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Nana Zheng, Wei Wang, Biao Li, Xionge Mei, Yue Liu, Jing Du, Ngan Yin Chan, Joey W. Y. Chan, Xiaoman Xing, Xiao Tan, Christian Benedict, Yun Kwok Wing, Jihui Zhang, Hongliang Feng. Associations between wearable‐device‐measured daytime and nighttime light exposures and dementia risk: A prospective cohort study. General Psychiatry, 2026; 39 (3) DOI: 10.1002/gps3.70039

Poland to Send Ukraine 2 More Soviet-Designed MiG-29s—Only One Is Airworthy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:30:31 UTC
20:30:31 KST

- Category
- World
Poland to Send Ukraine 2 More Soviet-Designed MiG-29s—Only One Is Airworthy
Poland will transfer two Soviet-designed MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine in the near future, along with ammunition and other military equipment as part of a new aid package worth roughly $55.7 million, according to Rzeczpospolita on October 29.
Dariusz Łukowski, director of the Strategy and Defense Planning Department at Poland’s Ministry of National Defense, confirmed that.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“In the near future. The decision has been made, and these two MiG-29s will be transferred,” Łukowski said when asked when Ukraine would receive the fighters.
According to information obtained by the Polish outlet, one of the two aircraft has already reached the end of its service life, while the second remains airworthy.
The fighters will form part of a broader Polish military assistance package valued at about $55.7 million.
The package is also expected to include 155mm and 152mm artillery ammunition, ammunition for the six-barrel cannons used by F-16 fighters, and missiles for Poland’s Piorun man-portable air-defense systems.
Poland’s Defense Ministry has officially confirmed that Warsaw is preparing another military aid package for Ukraine, although it has declined to disclose the complete list of weapons and equipment for security reasons.
The ministry said the final scale of the package will depend on Poland’s own national security requirements and the capabilities of the Polish Armed Forces, as determined by the chief of the General Staff.
Some of the equipment being transferred is expected to come from systems Poland is withdrawing from active service as they reach the end of their planned operational life.
Warsaw stressed, however, that equipment no longer required by the Polish military may still provide significant value to Ukraine, which continues to operate Soviet-designed aircraft and weapons alongside its growing fleet of Western systems.
The additional MiG-29s would add to Poland’s previous transfers of the fighter type to Ukraine and could provide Kyiv with another airworthy aircraft as well as a valuable source of spare parts and components for keeping the remaining fleet operational.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine is restructuring its combat aviation around Western-style fighter wings, has already established the 107th F-16 Aviation Wing, and is preparing airbases capable of supporting multiple aircraft types—including Sweden’s Gripen—as part of a long-term Air Force transformation through 2035.

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The United Nations Security Council is a universal instrument within the international community; humanity has no other such tool at its disposal, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the plenary session of the Russia-Africa summit.

Minimalist House in Japan by FORM/Kouichi Kimura is "reduced to the essentials"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Minimalist House in Japan by FORM/Kouichi Kimura is “reduced to the essentials”
A monochrome palette and pared-back, open interiors define the aptly named Minimalist House, a home in Japan designed by local studio FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects.
Located in Shiga prefecture, the 73-square-metre home is formed of cubic volumes clad in corrugated metal and black render, perched on a hill overlooking the nearby Lake Biwa.
Minimalist House was designed for a single occupant, but FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects wanted to challenge the assumption that this would mean small-feeling interiors.
This led the studio to create a series of voids and long sightlines that it said help to “liberate space”.
“When hearing ‘a home for a single occupant’, people typically imagine a compact house,” founder Kouichi Kimura told Dezeen.
“Here, living alone is regarded not as a spatial constraint, but as a condition that liberates space,” he added.
“Starting from the individual as the base unit, the house explores a new way of single-person living through the minimal composition reduced to the essentials, with the space that invites in the surrounding view, light, wind, and sound.”
The plan of Minimalist House revolves around a tall void cut through its centre, which extends upwards into a skinny, double-height volume projecting from its roof with a large window.
Finished with grey-plastered walls and dark stone floors, a kitchen, dining space and study occupy the ground floor, with metal and concrete steps leading up to a living space and bedroom above.
Facing the road, the front of the home has been left almost entirely blank. Instead, the interiors open up on the opposite side towards views of the lake in the distance, with the dining table, study and bed pushed up against large, deep-set windows.
“Each floor is designed as a single open layout,” explained Kimura. “The double-height space vertically connects the upper and lower levels. Manipulating floor and ceiling levels gently articulates each space without clearly dividing them.”
“The living space on the upper level is designed not only for daily life, but also for enjoying music. Within the double-height volume, sound resonates off the walls and ceiling, filling the entire space,” he added.
A glass corridor with sliding doors separates the main home from a single-storey washroom, which the studio introduced to ensure that this everyday passage would capture views out over the lake.
“Placing these wet areas away from the main structure creates a natural flow of movement in daily life,” Kimura explained.
“Walking through the glazed corridor in between allows one to touch the landscape, light, and breeze, offering a gentle transition in the everyday time,” he added.
Minimalist forms and interiors often feature in the work of FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects, with the studio’s previous projects in Shiga including a blocky hair salon and home and a skinny home with carefully-placed windows to avoid overlooking.

Estonia's volunteer rescuers send 146th aid shipment to Ukraine
The Estonian Rescue Association (Päästeliit) has sent aid to Ukrainian rescuers, funded by donations and the Foreign Ministry, providing shelter, power and heating for over 30,000 people this winter.
The Kyiv consignment has included a minibus, two high-pressure tents with trailers, diesel heaters, power stations, lighting towers and heated blankets, enough to set up two emergency centers, Estonia's Embassy to Ukraine announced.
"This was our 146th shipment to Ukraine. Every time we hand over new equipment, we hope the situation will improve. Unfortunately, the head of Kyiv's rescue service confirmed that the situation is already worse than ever, and that the coming winter will put civilians — especially children — in an even more difficult position than last year," said Piia Kallas, head of the Estonian Rescue Association, a volunteer organization which complements the Rescue Board (Päästeamet).
Estonian Rescue Association delivered emergency tents and equipment to Ukraine's rescue services @SESU_UA. The aid will provide temporary shelter, electricity and heating for more than 30,000 people during the winter. The package was funded by @MFAestonia and donations. https://t.co/fOGAZI2tOy
— Estonia in Ukraine (@EE_Ukraine) October 28, 2026
The shipment delivered to Kyiv included a minibus, two high-pressure tents with trailers, diesel heaters, battery power stations, battery-powered lamps, lighting towers, heated blankets, folding tables and chairs, fast chargers, thermos flasks, changing mats, children's toys and play mats. With this equipment, rescuers can set up two emergency centers where residents can find temporary shelter and warmth, charge their devices and receive psychological first aid.
A second delivery reached rescuers in Rivne oblast in southeastern Ukraine, including an off-road vehicle, a generator, battery power stations, lighting towers and heaters. The generator was donated by a private donor who decided to give their equipment to those who need it most.
Since the start of the invasion in February 2022, with support from donors and partners, the Rescue Association has delivered nearly €7 million worth of rescue equipment and vehicles to Ukrainian rescuers.

Firehawk raises $150M at $1.4B valuation to build more rocket motors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:26:16 UTC
20:26:16 KST

- Firehawk raised more than $150 million in a Series D led by Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, valuing the company above $1.4 billion.
- The funds will expand its Oklahoma propellant plant and Mississippi missile integration site to scale rocket and artillery motor production.
Dallas-based rocket propulsion firm Firehawk has raised more than $150 million in a Series D round that values the company at more than $1.4 billion, money it will use to scale up U.S. production of rocket propellant, solid rocket motors and artillery motors, the company said on social media on Oct. 28.
Private equity firm Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, co-founded by Dallas investor Kyle Bass, led the round, with new and existing investors and strategic partners also taking part. Firehawk said the round was upsized and oversubscribed, and the Dallas Morning News reported its original target was $100 million. The company did not disclose how much each investor put in.
The money will fund the build-out of Firehawk’s propellant and rocket motor plant in Lawton, Oklahoma, and its missile integration facility in Crawford, Mississippi, along with new research and development sites and more hiring, the company said in its funding announcement. Firehawk plans to produce more than 100,000 artillery motors in 2027 under a commercial agreement with General Dynamics, and its Oklahoma plant is expected to start low-rate production by mid-2027.
Firehawk was founded in 2019 by CEO Will Edwards to make hybrid rocket engines powered by 3D-printed fuel, and it now describes itself as covering the whole chain from propellant to motors to complete rounds. Its pitch is volume: the U.S. military’s appetite for rockets and missiles has outrun the small number of established solid rocket motor suppliers, and Firehawk says its patented manufacturing process can produce propellant faster and at larger scale for smaller tactical weapons.
The company broke ground on its Great Plains Arsenal rocket motor and propellant plant in Lawton in April. Its Crawford site can integrate 40,000 tactical rockets a year, and Firehawk says it plans to raise that to about 120,000 at full-rate production.
Much of that work centers on the Hydra-70, the 70 mm unguided rocket fired from U.S. Army attack helicopters and other aircraft. This summer the U.S. Army picked Firehawk as one of four new companies to build Hydra-70 rockets, alongside iRocket, Nammo Perry and Albers, with each required to deliver 24 prototype M151 rockets within 18 months. In August, Firehawk fired six Hydra-70 rockets at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, all of which worked as intended.
The Series D follows a $60 million Series C that closed in September 2025 and a strategic investment in November 2025 aimed at speeding up solid rocket motor production and integration.
Firehawk has not said how many Hydra-70 rockets or rocket motors it has delivered to the U.S. military so far, or when its Oklahoma plant will reach full-rate production.

Mathematicians find an infinite number of Ramanujan equations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:19:15 UTC
20:19:15 KST

The legendary mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan and Yifeng Huang, a postdoctoral researcher at Emory University, have something in common: they will not be ignored. In 1912 Ramanujan, a 24-year-old clerk at what was then the Madras Port Trust in India, began mailing pages of new, unproven formulas to mathematicians across England. One of his letters eventually reached British mathematician G. H. Hardy at the University of Cambridge, who recognized Ramanujan as a visionary, invited him to visit and helped launch his groundbreaking career.
More than a century later, Huang, while a graduate student at the University of Michigan, began e-mailing mathematicians letter after letter—more than 40 in total. He scarcely heard back.
Huang’s ideas concerned two formulas that appeared in Ramanujan’s letters and are now known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. In September 2026 Huang and a few collaborators uploaded a proof that the historic equations represent a single case of a much grander geometrical theory. In particular, the work showed that the Roger-Ramanujan identities correspond to a trefoil knot in a certain space. The trefoil, known as the shape of the familiar Celtic knot, is one of the simplest mathematical knots. And related knots, they found, reveal an infinite number of previously unknown identities.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Everything about this subject, even the original discovery, is a surprise,” says George Andrews, a mathematician at Pennsylvania State University and an expert on Ramanujan’s math. Ramanujan, Hardy and their collaborators “were all unable to prove this,” he adds. “So the things that have cropped up from knot theory were a total surprise to me.”
The Roger-Ramanujan Identities
Hardy was responsible for shaping much of early 20th century number theory. Initially skeptical when he received a letter from Ramanujan, Hardy later wrote that he recognized the letter’s author as “a mathematician of the highest quality, a man of altogether exceptional originality and power.” It was a pivotal moment.
Two of Ramanujan’s formulas were startling: they represented an infinite series of sums on one side and an infinite series of products on the other, with no visible reason for the two to agree. By 1916 British mathematician Percy MacMahon had found a way to read them. These two equations were similar to ones studied two centuries earlier by mathematician Leonhard Euler. Euler had a neat trick for sidestepping such complexity: he connected the equations to a type of counting problem known as a “partition.” A partition of a number is a way of writing it as a sum. MacMahon transformed Ramanujan’s formulas into two kinds of partitions that looked nothing alike, but whose counts always came out identical.
Here’s how one side of a Ramanujan equation was partitioned: count the number of ways to sum up to a certain value using numbers that are at least two whole numbers apart. For instance, 6 can be written as 1 + 5, 2 + 4 and 6. So there are three partitions.
On the other side, sum using only numbers that end in 1, 4, 6 or 9. For 6, the answer is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 4 and 6, which also gives three partitions.
The formulas say these two very different counts agree for every number. Before Ramanujan could prove them, he came across an obscure proof by English mathematician Leonard James Rogers in an old math journal. Thus, the equations became known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities.
“It was regarded, for most of the 20th century, as an isolated gem,” Andrews says. No one suspected it lay at the heart of a much larger theory.
In the early 1970s Andrews uncovered an infinite family of the identities. “I discovered them only to learn that [mathematician] Basil Gordon had done them first,” Andrews says, “which was a huge disappointment for me.”
The new family came to be known as the Andrews-Gordon identities.
Since then the identities have turned up in strange places: in representation theory, in the study of symmetric functions, even in physics via the “hard hexagon model,” which describes how gas atoms can settle onto a surface in a triangular pattern.
“Who would have thought that the Rogers-Ramanujan identities were related to how liquid helium behaves when poured onto a graphite plate?” Andrews says.
A Pinch to Build a Conjecture
Yifeng Huang had a hunch.
Matrices—little spreadsheets of numbers—can undergo operations such as flips and transpositions, which must be done in a certain order to get the correct result. But if the values of the matrices are chosen such that the order of operations doesn’t matter (meaning they “commute”), then the matrices behave like coordinates and can be used to describe curves. Take any smooth curve, such as the parabola y = x2, and replace y and x with pairs of matrices. A textbook-level problem might ask: How many pairs of matrices make the equation true? A math student can find the answer.
But what happens if you use a curve that isn’t so smooth—one that has a “pinch” in it, also known as a singularity? Now textbook theory breaks down. These matrix counts had neverbeen studied.
While he was still a Ph.D. student at the University of Michigan, Huang started counting matrices on pinched curves such as y2 = x3, which comes to a sharp tip when x and y equal 0. Before long, his counts reproduced a familiar formula: one side of the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. “Already this discovery is fascinating,” Huang says. “I’m wondering what is going on. It can’t be a coincidence.”
From that single example, Huang made a bold, vague guess: What if every pinched curve hid a new identity, with its matrix count collapsing into a neat formula? Hoping to discuss the idea further, Huang wrote letters to a small group of mathematicians—around five to 10 people.
University of Virginia mathematician Ken Ono received one of those letters. But thinking Huang’s idea was “crazy,” Ono dismissed it.
Another letter recipient was Alexei Oblomkov, a mathematician at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, whose work connects algebraic geometry and knot theory. “I thought it was kind of a great idea, and later we met at one of the conferences, and I liked the idea even more,” Oblomkov says.
By then, Huang and Ruofan Jiang, now a mathematician at the University of California, Berkeley, had devised a systematic way to count how many matrices make the formulas for pinched curves true.
Oblomkov brought geometry to the table. Zoom in on the pinch in y2 = x3, he advised, and surround it with a tiny sphere in four dimensions, where mathematicians say such curves naturally live. The curve pierces the sphere along a closed loop in a “trefoil” knot. Both counts lead to the classic Rogers-Ramanujan identities. What about another curve? It also led to another knot, which was hiding another family of identities. And another curve led to yet more.
The team’s ideas crystalized into the Huang-Jiang-Oblomkov (HJO) conjecture. Simply stated, pick any two numbers a and b that are greater than 1, with no common factor. The conjecture predicts that for the curve xa = yb, a count of the matrix solutions will always collapse into a Rogers-Ramanujan-type identity. This translates into infinitely many families of identities, one for every value of a. The case a = 2 is the family Andrews and Gordon found. Every larger value of a was uncharted. And each curve comes with its own knot: the trefoil for a = 2 and b = 3 and more intricately wound torus knots for the rest.
The Proof
Again, Huang began sending out e-mails—more than 40 in 2023—and gave a circuit of seminar talks.
This time, when Ono received one of Huang’s letters, he found the idea “mind-blowing,” he says. “That’s when I joined this chase.”
By then Ono had signed on to the artificial intelligence company Axiom Math as its founding mathematician. He, Huang and another Axiom mathematician, Kenny Lau, worked for seven months in tandem with AxiomProver, the company’s math-focused AI system.
Because the ideas were so new, Ono says, they couldn’t simply ask an AI model to solve the problem—there was no literature for it to learn from. Instead AxiomProver worked like a research assistant, testing a far more expansive space of ideas than would be humanly possible. It also translated the proof into Lean, a machine-friendly language for automated proof checking. In the end, the quartet made of humans and AI stitched together ideas from five different areas of math to prove the conjecture.
Ono’s take on AI in math is more hopeful than many in his field. “Everyone talks about the end of math,” he says. “But someone had to invent this structure. This is what we should be doing.”
The team members posted their HJO conjecture to the preprint server arXiv.org in August 2026. And in September, the three followed up with the conjecture’s proof.
Recast as geometry, the old identities now point toward unmapped territory, raising questions that mathematicians are eager to explore.
“We found something exciting,” Oblomkov says, “a way to extend the geometry in the case when it’s not a trefoil knot, but a so-called Hopf link—basically you have two circles tied together. So that will be the next paper.”
Oblomkov also says Fields Medalist Peter Scholze has published a few papers that take some of Huang’s ideas even further. The pinched curves xa = yb are only the beginning. The equation is, Huang says, “only the first example of a singularity I would write down.” Oblomkov agrees: “It’s just the first case, and there will be many more.”

Five things you need to know about the Trump administration’s rollback of methane regulations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:19:02 UTC
20:19:02 KST

The Trump administration has taken an axe to environmental regulations—and this week the target became methane gas emissions.
The White House plans to slash laws governing how much methane is emitted from oil and gas wells. This includes relaxing rules around flaring—or burning off excess natural gas at well sites—as well as doing away with a program that requires speedy fixes for large methane leaks. The move also lowers standards for marginal wells, which produce little oil and gas but are responsible for about half of the industry’s methane emissions.
It’s the latest bump in a regulator roller coaster for methane. Attempts to regulate emissions on a federal level began in 2015, when the Obama administration sought to bring methane under the Clean Air Act. The first Trump administration rolled back that rule change. Then, during the Biden administration, the then Democratic-controlled Congress reinstated the methane regulations and cleared the way for the Environmental Protection Agency to apply the new standards to older equipment. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act also included provisions for charges for heavy emitters and allocated money for both industry and research to help them comply with the rules.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
All of that again went out the window with the second Trump administration. As the latest changes start to take effect, here are five things you need to know about methane and the ways that these moves will affect you.
Methane is a major driver of climate change
Carbon dioxide may be more prevalent in the atmosphere, but methane is a heavy hitter, climate-wise. The gas has been responsible for about 30 percent of the rise in global temperatures since the start of the industrial revolution, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). A methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for about 12 years, while an excess carbon dioxide molecule can persist for centuries. But methane traps heat about 80 times more effectively than carbon over 20 years and about 28 times more effectively over the course of a century. In other words, it may be shorter lived, but the damage methane does while it’s in the atmosphere is greater.
Oil and gas leaks are a major source of methane
Each year, according to the IEA, about 580 million metric tons of methane enter the atmosphere. About 40 percent of this comes from natural sources such as swamp gas and volcanic emissions. The other 60 percent comes from human sources.
Agriculture is the biggest contributor to this anthropogenic portion of methane emissions, but the combination of natural gas and petroleum production, processing and transportation comes in second. These processes are responsible for 28 percent of all U.S. methane emissions, according to the EPA.
Methane regulations have done little to move the needle
With all the regulatory back-and-forth, it’s perhaps unsurprising that research into methane emissions finds little evidence that federal rules make a difference. In a recent paper in Communications Earth & Environment, Johns Hopkins University associate professor of environmental health and engineering Scot Miller and his colleagues used satellite data to track emissions independently.
“Overall,” Miller says, “you see this landscape across the U.S. where methane leaks from oil and gas facilities are declining, but it’s not necessarily due to any kind of concerted federal action.”
Methane emissions declined by about 11 percent between 2019 and 2024, but the decline was caused by technological changes in the industry and the establishment of new natural gas pipelines that can carry methane to market—without this transport system, operators often burn off natural gas at well sites.
“If [natural gas is] actually a valuable markable product, there is evidence to show that leak rates tend to go down,” Miller explains.
The new rules would loosen restrictions on the most common oil wells in the U.S.
The new changes are twofold. First, the EPA plans to eliminate the Super Emitter Program, which would have allowed third parties to monitor oil and gas operations for leaks, via satellite, for example, and alert the EPA to leaks of 100 kilograms of methane or more per hour. Operators notified by the EPA of such large leaks would then have to investigate the leaks within days.
The Super Emitter Program has actually never been in effect, so this will make little immediate difference. “This is like the nail in the coffin,” Miller says. “These rules are already not being implemented.”
The other change would affect marginal oil and gas wells. These are wells that produce 15 barrels (2,384 liters) or less of oil per day or 90,000 cubic feet (2,549 cubic meters) or less of natural gas per day over a yearlong period. These wells accounted for 7 percent of U.S. oil and gas production as of 2021, according to the EPA, but produce about 50 percent of the industry’s methane emissions. They’re also plentiful, accounting for more than 70 percent of onshore oil and gas wells.
Each marginal well produces only a little profit, so operators may not have much incentive to invest in repairs and upgrades, Miller says.
“Methane leaks from the oil and gas industry have been declining over time, but these marginal wells are arguably a stubborn outlier,” Miller says. “The regulations proposed during the Biden administration would have helped address this issue.” But they may never come to pass now.
There is broad pushback against regulating methane
Biden administration rules to regulate methane, enacted in 2023, were expected to keep 58 million tons (52.6 million metric tons) of the gas out of the atmosphere between 2024 and 2038. Their rollback is part of a broad push against methane mitigation, however. “I think, potentially, this move would make it more difficult for a future administration to reimplement emissions regulations,” Miller says.
In the European Union, a 2024 regulation would have required methane monitoring and reporting on any imported oil, natural gas and coal. But this month, the European Parliament voted to approve a three-year delay on that regulation.
In another possible blow for methane reduction, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which the Senate plans to take up in November, would bar agencies from revoking permits issued during the Trump administration to drill on public land and would make it harder for future administrations to require methane leak monitoring or limits on flaring on public land.
“It’s difficult to have an effective or a consistent federal regulatory policy if those regulations are constantly seesawing up and down,” Miller says.
Disclosure: The reporter’s spouse is employed in the oil and gas industry and owns interests in wells.

Gaza protesters shout down ex-German FM (VIDEO)
Former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock was shouted down by pro-Palestinian activists during a speech at a Swedish university, Berliner Zeitung has reported.
The heated confrontation happened earlier this week at Uppsala University, where Baerbock was delivering a lecture on international cooperation and multilateral leadership, the outlet said on Wednesday.
Activists repeatedly interrupted her speech, accusing her of defending Israeli attacks on civilian infrastructure.
“You justified the bombing of hospitals and schools in Gaza, and now you come here to talk about peace!” one protester shouted.
Another challenged Baerbock over her talk of democracy and freedom, demanding: “Whose democracy are you defending? Whose freedom do you actually stand for – only that of Israelis?”
Baerbock initially attempted to deflect the accusations, suggesting that protesters raise their concerns during a question-and-answer session after the lecture. However, as the interruptions continued, she snapped: “Now I’m speaking!” The promised discussion reportedly never took place.
Baerbock headed Germany’s Foreign Ministry from 2021 to 2025 and staunchly defended Israel’s military campaign in Gaza following the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023. Berlin continued approving weapons supplies to Israel despite mounting international criticism, authorizing around €161 million ($168 million) in military exports in 2024.
The former minister herself sparked controversy in October 2024 when she argued in the German parliament that civilian sites in Gaza could lose their protected status under international humanitarian law if Hamas used them for military purposes. Her remarks drew criticism from those who accused Berlin of providing political cover for Israeli strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Beyond her stance on Israel, Baerbock’s tenure as Germany’s top diplomat drew criticism over a lack of diplomatic pragmatism, inconsistent foreign policy positions, and a string of high-profile verbal blunders. She also called for the protection of Palestinian civilians and stressed that Israel’s military operations were bound by international humanitarian law.
Israel launched its Gaza offensive following the October 2023 Hamas-led attack, which killed around 1,200 people and saw some 250 taken hostage. More than 75,000 Palestinians have since been killed across the occupied territories, including at least 21,500 children, according to a UN Commission of Inquiry.
In a report released on Monday, the commission concluded that Israel had continued committing “genocide” in Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire, with Israeli strikes reportedly killing another 1,431 Palestinians as of September 30. Japan's ruling bloc, DPFP agree to cut 31 lower house seats as opposition raises doubts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:16:03 CST
20:16:03 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Japan's ruling coalition and the opposition Democratic Party for the People (DPFP) on Thursday agreed on a plan to cut 31 proportional representation seats in the House of Representatives, Kyodo News reported.
The move has drawn criticism from opposition lawmakers, with some saying it would weaken parliament's oversight of the government and is meant to pave the way for revising Japan's pacifist constitution.
According to the report, the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), its junior coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party (JIP), and the DPFP will jointly draft a bill and seek its passage during the current parliamentary session, which runs through mid-December.
Because the three parties together hold a majority in both houses of the Diet, Japan's parliament, the bill is likely to pass.
Six other opposition parties oppose the plan, saying it lacks justification and that cutting proportional representation seats would favor larger parties, Kyodo News said.
A rally against the seat cuts was held in front of the National Diet in Tokyo on Wednesday evening.
Mizuho Fukushima, leader of the Social Democratic Party, suggested the move is intended to sideline forces cautious about constitutional revision and pave the way for amending the pacifist constitution.
Tetsuya Shiokawa, chair of the Japanese Communist Party's Diet affairs committee, noted that according to estimates by the LDP, the plan would increase the LDP and the JIP's combined share of lower house seats by several percentage points.
He said the move would make parliament less representative of public opinion, weaken oversight of the government, and embolden Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration to push through its policies on the strength of its seat advantage.
Japan's House of Representatives is elected through a mixed electoral system that combines both single-seat districts and proportional representation.
Of the current 465 seats in the lower house, 289 are elected from single-seat constituencies and 176 through proportional representation.
In single-seat districts, the candidate with the most votes wins. For proportional representation, voters select a party or political group, and seats are allocated according to vote share across 11 regional blocs nationwide.
The three parties' plan would cut only proportional representation seats. It also includes changes to how proportional representation seats are allocated and would allow multiple parties to compile a joint list of proportional representation candidates. ■

Ukraine’s Linza bomber drone clears path for UGV in German exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:13:13 UTC
20:13:13 KST

- Frontline Robotics’ Linza drone took part in Quantum Systems’ Forward Edge 26 exercise in Germany, working with other unmanned systems through MOSAIC UXS.
- In one scenario, a Vector drone spotted simulated enemy drones on a ground vehicle’s route and Linza struck them with payload drops.
Ukrainian drone maker Frontline Robotics flew its Linza bomber drone alongside German, Ukrainian and other unmanned air, ground and sea systems during Forward Edge 26, a two-week exercise in Germany hosted by Quantum Systems, the company said on social media.
In one deployment, Quantum Systems’ Vector reconnaissance drone spotted simulated enemy drones along the route of an unmanned ground vehicle, and Linza then attacked the targets by dropping payloads, clearing the way for the ground vehicle, Frontline Robotics said. The company said the drone completed its missions in heavy rain and dense fog, but it did not say how many sorties it flew or how many targets it hit.
All of the systems in the exercise were connected through MOSAIC UXS, Quantum Systems’ software for controlling and coordinating unmanned platforms from different manufacturers in a single operational picture. Quantum Systems said it ran Forward Edge 26 at a military training area in central Germany and wrapped it up on Oct. 22, with no crewed vehicles in the scenarios. Systems located in Ukraine, the United States and Australia were also flown remotely during the event.
The exercise was built around four scenarios: defense against an attacking force, convoy and force protection, coastal and port surveillance, and minelaying and route clearance. In the convoy scenario, laser-based counter-drone systems protected an unmanned convoy, while the maritime scenario linked aerial and sea-based systems for coastal monitoring. Industry participants included Daimler Truck, Volkswagen, XTEND, Planet and Quantum Systems’ German-Ukrainian joint ventures, Quantum Frontline Industries and Quantum Tencore Industries.
Linza, which means “lens” in Ukrainian, is a quadcopter that can drop munitions on targets, lay mines, carry a radio relay, scout and deliver small loads of supplies to frontline positions. Frontline Robotics first introduced it in 2024 and unveiled the Linza 3.0 version in February, which the company says carries up to 4 kg (8.8 pounds) over a tactical range of 15 km (9 miles), with AI-assisted visual navigation that lets it hold position over a target without relying on satellite signals. Frontline Robotics says more than 80 units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces now use the drone.
Quantum Systems and Frontline Robotics build Linza together through Quantum Frontline Industries, a joint venture whose factory outside Munich opened in February in the presence of German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and is meant to eventually produce more than 10,000 drones a year. Germany has funded joint production of the Linza under the Build with Ukraine program, and earlier this month the joint venture signed a contract to supply Linza and Zoom reconnaissance drones to Ukraine’s National Guard in 2027.
Quantum Systems’ own Vector, the reconnaissance drone that cued Linza’s strike in the exercise, has flown extensively in Ukraine, including a mission in which one aircraft survived 11 hits and kept flying. Frontline Robotics also builds the Burya remote weapon turret, which Danish company Dropla has agreed to integrate on its unmanned ground vehicles.

German industry groups urge Berlin to join defence bank initiative
BERLIN, Oct 29 - German business and industry associations on Thursday urged the government to join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), saying membership was needed to close financing gaps for companies in the defence sector and protect their access to future projects.
The joint statement was signed by groups including the German Security and Defence Industry Association (BDSV), aerospace association BDLI, the chamber of commerce DIHK, engineering association VDMA, savings banks group DSGV and the Startup Association.
The proposed multilateral institution, backed by Canada, seven other NATO countries and Ukraine, would provide long-term, low-cost financing for defence, security and resilience projects.
"The geostrategic threat situation urgently requires new answers and approaches: financing for the defence sector must be secured sustainably over the long term," said Elisabeth Hauschild, managing director of BDSV.
The associations said the bank could offer guarantees for commercial loans to small and medium-sized companies, including startups, as well as long-term loans, venture capital and equity financing for capacity expansion, innovation and critical raw materials.
"As a multilateral development bank, it provides the decisive risk buffer through guarantees and long-term financing instruments—particularly where established banks have so far been reluctant to support long-term contracts for the Mittelstand," Hauschild said.
The DSRB, which will be based in Canada, has faced challenges securing support from larger European nations. Reuters was first to report in September last year that Britain had declined to join the project.
A spokesperson for the German finance ministry told Reuters on Monday that Germany was an observer in the negotiations on DSRB's charter and was reviewing open questions.
Germany should participate in the bank's founding process and join the group of founding states as soon as possible, the business associations said.
The groups warned that companies from member countries could receive preferential access to procurement projects financed by the DSRB under its planned charter rules. If Germany stayed outside the institution, its companies could be excluded from market opportunities or face a competitive disadvantage against rivals from member states, they added. REUTERS

Christine Lagarde: The outsider who led the ECB her way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:11:13 UTC
20:11:13 KST

Christine Lagarde: The outsider who led the ECB her way
FRANKFURT, Oct 29 - Christine Lagarde's decision to step down early as European Central Bank president ends an eventful seven years at an institution she was never expected to lead.
The former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund arrived in Frankfurt in 2019 as the first ECB chief with no formal economics training or central banking experience — prompting some market participants to label her a "credibility risk."
In fact, she knew so little about the institution that Lagarde, 70, later said she had accepted the job thinking the presidency was a five-year mandate, rather than eight.
Yet after a tenure dominated by a pandemic, two energy shocks and the worst inflation spike in the euro zone's history, Lagarde leaves with a record that defied the sceptics.
"Her seven years at the ECB have been, on the whole, pretty good," said Willem Buiter, an economist and former Bank of England official, noting that the ECB managed to bring inflation back down faster than peers in Britain and the United States.
Her exit, however, threatens to be as political as her arrival.
By walking away before her eight-year term ends, Lagarde gives European Union leaders a chance to pick her successor before a French election next spring that opinion polls suggest far-right candidate Marine Le Pen will win, replacing President Emmanuel Macron.
For an institution that fiercely guards its independence from political meddling, the timing has drawn sharp criticism from central bank watchers.
"This is debasing the institution and just following the purely political calculus of the French president," said Paul De Grauwe, a professor at the London School of Economics.
Lagarde and Macron have not addressed such criticism directly. Lagarde has said she would not be a candidate for the French presidency but would advocate for pro-European values in her home country "in whichever capacity" she deemed most efficient.
'BETTER WITH BUTTER'
Throughout her career, Lagarde has stood apart from more technocratic colleagues through a mix of charm, consensus-building and folksy pragmatism.
Favouring plain-speaking homilies over dense economic theory, the then-IMF chief famously declared that "everything is better with butter" when discussing growth and told governments to "fix the roof while the sun is shining".
Unorthodoxy was a hallmark of Lagarde's career, and the subject of her upcoming autobiography "Lady First".
A former corporate lawyer who spent years in Chicago, she entered French politics in 2005 as an outsider. Early missteps earned her the domestic moniker "Madame Lagaffe," but she soon became one of then-President Nicolas Sarkozy's sharpest operators, steering French banks through the 2008 crash.
She led the IMF through Europe's debt crisis, navigating a messy Greek rescue that imposed harsh austerity, and sparked outrage in Athens when she bluntly urged suffering citizens to "pay their taxes".
Her appetite for high-stakes bets showed again in 2018 with a record $57-billion lifeline for Argentina to back then-President Mauricio Macri. The gamble unravelled, failing to halt a currency collapse or avert a deep recession, and left the IMF bound to its most troubled debtor.
THE SPREADS CRISIS AND THE TRIBAL CLIQUE
Her occasional unfamiliarity with the nuances of central banking still peeked through.
In March 2020, as the pandemic rattled sovereign debt markets, Lagarde told a press conference the ECB was "not here to close spreads" between Italian and German borrowing costs.
The comment triggered an immediate selloff in bond markets and forced her to swiftly walk it back.
Under Lagarde's watch, the ECB swiftly rolled out emergency bond-buying that stabilised markets as COVID-19 spread. It launched its fastest series of interest-rate hikes to bring inflation under control following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, although it later acknowledged it had been slow to recognise the full impact of spiking energy prices.
As ECB president, she once described economists as a "tribal clique" — a provocative jab at the profession's establishment, though she later softened the blow by saying she hoped to join the tribe.
A 'MORE POLITICAL' ECB PRESIDENT
Lagarde used her political skills to repair rifts. Unlike her predecessor Mario Draghi, whose top-down style embittered some hawkish northern European peers, she worked to build consensus among the euro zone's 21 national central bank chiefs.
Her willingness to wade into politics remained evident: in January, Lagarde walked out of a World Economic Forum dinner in Davos during a speech by US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that criticised Europe, an episode that underscored fraught transatlantic relations.
Whoever succeeds her when she leaves the ECB on February 7 will face fresh challenges including strains in French bond markets ahead of next year's election and a Middle East conflict that threatens a new bout of inflation.
Ultimately, Lagarde's legacy may be a paradox: an outsider who showed that political diplomacy could steer a central bank through historic shocks, but whose early departure served as a final reminder of her political instincts.
"She was put there for a reason: being more political than her predecessor and, on that mission, I think she largely succeeded," Frederik Ducrozet, head of strategy and macro research at Pictet Wealth Management, said. REUTERS
