Four more arrested in election bribery probe as Likud seeks revotes at Arab polling stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:09:20 UTC
20:09:20 KST

Police arrested four more suspects Thursday in an investigation into alleged vote-buying on behalf of the Arab Ra'am party, including three school principals from Bedouin communities in southern Israel, as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party prepared to challenge election results at polling stations where it alleges bribery and other violations occurred.
Three of the four newly arrested suspects were subsequently released to house arrest.
The arrests bring the number of people detained in the investigation to seven since Tuesday's parliamentary election. The case centers on allegations that money and other benefits were offered to voters in exchange for supporting Ra'am, an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas.
The developments come amid a separate investigation into suspected foreign interference in the election, possibly involving tens of millions of shekels from Qatar. That inquiry is being conducted by the Shin Bet domestic security agency at the request of Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, chairman of the Central Elections Committee.
The two investigations are distinct, and no connection between the suspected Qatari funding and the alleged vote-buying involving Ra'am has been established.
Likud, meanwhile, is escalating its challenge to the election results as part of a broader political campaign against cooperation with Arab parties following an inconclusive vote that left neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition with a clear parliamentary majority.
The party is preparing to seek the annulment of results at polling stations where it claims voters were bribed or prohibited methods were used to influence the vote, ynet has learned.
Cash payments, fuel vouchers and allegations of vote-buying
A Bedouin source from the Negev, familiar with political activity in the region, described what he alleged was a system used by Arab parties, particularly Ra'am, in the days leading up to the election.
According to the source, political activists visit the homes of low-income residents and offer financial assistance ranging from 200 to 300 shekels ($65 to $95), including to families affected by home demolitions and residents of unrecognized Bedouin villages.
He alleged that the payments are presented as assistance to needy families, while recipients are asked in return to support a particular party at the ballot box.
In other cases, he claimed, fuel vouchers worth 100 shekels ($32) are distributed to people who transport residents to polling stations.
The amounts can vary depending on family size, he said, with payments allegedly distributed one or two days before the election and sometimes on Election Day itself.
The source argued that some residents do not view such payments as election bribery but rather as financial assistance, particularly given the poverty and lack of basic services affecting disadvantaged Bedouin communities.
"I don't understand what all the fuss is about," he said. "We learned this from Shas, which has been doing it for years and even distributes money in synagogues."
Shas is an ultra-Orthodox Jewish political party that has long been part of Netanyahu's governing alliances.
"So why all the fuss now? Just because we're Arabs? Because we turned out to vote and became a powerful political force?" the source asked.
His allegations against Shas were not substantiated in the account.
Likud prepares legal challenge to election results
Senior Likud officials said the party intends to petition election authorities in the coming hours over polling stations where it suspects bribery or the use of prohibited methods.
"New elections must be held at these polling stations," senior party officials said.
Attorney Ilan Bombach, Likud's legal adviser and a deputy chairman of the Central Elections Committee, is preparing the petition based on material the party previously submitted to the committee.
Likud alleges that the material documents election bribery and the use of prohibited methods, including applications that tracked the identities of voters at polling stations.
The planned challenge is separate from the Shin Bet investigation into suspected foreign financing.
Likud maintains that the evidence it has already submitted is sufficient to invalidate results at certain polling stations and require voting to be repeated there.
Bombach is not alleging that ballot papers were forged or that vote totals were falsified. Instead, the petition focuses on alleged bribery, the use of prohibited election methods and the distribution of money or other benefits to voters in exchange for their support.
The party's allegations have not been established in court.
Under Israeli election law, election results can be challenged through a separate legal process. Courts may order voting to be repeated at specific polling stations if violations are established and could have affected the results.
The planned petition comes as Arab parties have emerged with potentially decisive parliamentary influence following Tuesday's election, intensifying political disputes over whether the opposition could form a government with their support.
Seven suspects detained, including three school principals
The latest arrests follow the detention of three suspects on Election Day by investigators from Lahav, the Israel Police's national investigations unit, on suspicion of election bribery and conspiracy to commit a crime.
The original suspects were identified as Ibrahim al-Gharibi, 42, from the Al-Azazmeh community; Hussein Masaudin, 63, from Segev Shalom; and Saif Abu Riaash, 38, a physician from the Al-Sana tribe.
A magistrate's court initially extended the detention of al-Gharibi and Masaudin until Sunday while ordering Abu Riaash released to house arrest.
Police appealed the physician's release, however, and his detention was subsequently extended as well.
During court proceedings, a Lahav representative said Abu Riaash had organized gatherings at private homes to encourage residents to vote for Ra'am.
"He holds meetings in people's homes to get them to vote for Ra'am, even though he is a doctor, and that is problematic," the police representative said.
Al-Gharibi is suspected of violating election law after investigators searching his home discovered cash. A search of his vehicle also uncovered envelopes bearing Arabic writing, green shirts and flags, and Ra'am ballot slips.
Masaudin, meanwhile, accused authorities of politically motivated persecution.
His defense attorney said envelopes discovered at his home bore the name of the Islamic Movement, the religious and political movement associated with Ra'am, and that each contained 1,000 shekels ($320) intended as charitable donations to low-income families.
Investigators also seized another envelope containing 12,000 shekels ($3,840). Masaudin said that money belonged to his son.
The suspects have denied wrongdoing, and the allegations remain under investigation.
'The Bedouins came out to vote because they feared for their lives'
A relative of Abu Riaash rejected suggestions that the surge in Bedouin voter turnout resulted from improper financial inducements.
Instead, he attributed the increase to anger over National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose policies toward Bedouin communities in the Negev have drawn criticism.
"The increase in voter turnout in this election is because of one thing: the failed minister who caused damage in the Negev, Ben-Gvir," the relative said.
"Of course the Bedouins came out to vote. They feared for their lives. There's also no sense of security."
The relative said his own experiences during the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack had strengthened his determination to influence the country's political direction.
"I was at the gas station in Kfar Aza on Oct. 7. I am officially recognized as a victim of a terrorist attack, so of course I want to influence this government and change it," he said. "That's how everyone is thinking."
Separate Shin Bet investigation examines suspected Qatari funding
In a parallel development, Sohlberg, who also serves as deputy chief justice of the Supreme Court, sent an unusual letter to Shin Bet Director David Zini calling for an investigation into suspected foreign funding and election bribery involving foreign actors.
The letter followed a meeting between Sohlberg and Zini on Wednesday.
The suspected interference reportedly involves an attempt by Qatar to influence Israel's election through transfers estimated at tens of millions of shekels.
The intelligence underlying the suspicions has been described as "solid," although the precise nature of the alleged payments, their intended recipients and whether any election bribery actually occurred remain unclear.
According to information obtained by ynet, the Shin Bet had possessed the intelligence for several days but waited to determine whether the suspected bribery would take place.
The agency declined to comment on the investigation.

Teledyne FLIR wins $48M to turn 10 Bulgarian Strykers into CBRN scouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:06:36 UTC
20:06:36 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Teledyne FLIR Defense a $48 million contract to equip 10 Bulgarian Strykers with upgraded CBRN reconnaissance sensor suites.
- The work runs through 2028, with the sensor suites integrated in Bulgaria after the vehicles are delivered.
Teledyne FLIR Defense has won a $48 million U.S. Army contract to fit Bulgaria’s new Stryker fleet with the same upgraded chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear reconnaissance sensor suite now going to U.S. Army units, the company announced on Oct. 26.
U.S. Army Contracting Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, awarded the contract under a Foreign Military Sales agreement, the government-to-government route through which allies buy U.S. defense equipment. Bulgaria will equip 10 of the nearly 200 Strykers it is buying with the Nuclear, Biological and Chemical Reconnaissance Vehicle (NBCRV) Sensor Suite Upgrade, turning them into dedicated vehicles for detecting contamination ahead of other troops. Work will run through 2028 at several Teledyne FLIR sites in the United States, and the sensor suites will be fitted in Bulgaria after the vehicles arrive.
The NBCRV is the CBRN reconnaissance version of the Stryker. Its crew drives into or near a suspected contaminated area, detects and identifies hazards from a distance, collects samples and reports what it finds so commanders can decide where units can safely move. Teledyne FLIR is the lead integrator for the U.S. Army’s upgrade of that system, which adds more automated sensors and an unmanned aircraft, and the company began delivering the new suites to U.S. Army units in 2025.
Among the third-party sensors in the package, the upgraded vehicle carries Teledyne FLIR’s R80D SkyRaider drone fitted with the company’s MUVE B330 biological detector, which lets the crew sample the air for biological agents away from the vehicle. The U.S. Army tested a Stryker launching the SkyRaider with the MUVE B330 during development. A Teledyne FLIR command and control system ties all the sensors and platforms together and automates part of the analysis to reduce the workload on the crew.
“The upgraded Stryker vehicles will provide Bulgaria with the most advanced mounted CBRN reconnaissance capabilities in Europe,” said Dr. JihFen Lei, President of Teledyne Defense and Aerospace Group and Senior Vice President of Teledyne Technologies.
“Together, our two Stryker modernization efforts highlight the breadth of sensor solutions Teledyne FLIR can deliver to NATO allies and partners, helping warfighters detect, identify and respond effectively to an array of battlefield threats,” Lei said.
The new award is Teledyne FLIR’s second Bulgarian Stryker contract this year. In January, the company won a contract worth up to $32 million to supply thermal sights and radars for Bulgaria’s Stryker fleet, giving crews 360-degree visibility and long-range threat detection.
Bulgaria is buying the Strykers to replace its Soviet-era tactical vehicles and to operate equipment compatible with other NATO forces. The first five combat vehicles arrived at the Black Sea port of Burgas on Feb. 14, along with eight more provided free of charge through a U.S. assistance program, and the fleet is going to the 61st Mechanized Brigade.
Teledyne FLIR said it has received contract vehicles worth more than $240 million for the NBCRV Sensor Suite Upgrade program since 2024. In June, it also won an $11.2 million U.S. Army contract for more than 45 SkyRaider-based CBRN sensor drone kits for dismounted units operating away from the reconnaissance vehicles.

As criminal networks spread in Latin America, Quito is new battleground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:06:32 UTC
20:06:32 KST

As criminal networks spread in Latin America, Quito is new battleground
QUITO, Oct 29 - For years, the neighborhood watch group in the working-class area of Solanda in Ecuadorean capital Quito had patrolled their nighttime streets armed with little more than whistles and sticks, on the lookout for cellphone snatching and other petty crimes.
But then they realized the criminals were changing. Members of notorious national gangs began to move into the area, and shootings, contract killings and extortion took hold. The watch suspended the patrols, fearful they might be targeted themselves. Their place was taken by heavily armed troops, sent by the national government.
Ecuador's importance as a transit point for cocaine exports from Colombia and Peru has spiked over the last half-decade, stoking an explosion in violence and crime in the once tranquil South American country that has caught up everyone from Pacific fishermen to politicians, journalists and grandmothers forced from their homes.
President Daniel Noboa, an ally of the administration of US President Donald Trump, has responded with a widespread military, police and legislative crackdown on crime, sending soldiers into the streets and hardening sentences, among other measures. The government has notched several major captures or killings of gang leaders, but that has led to fragmentation, creating vicious internecine violence and splinter groups seeking new territory.
That now includes Quito. This historic Andean city, with its whitewashed colonial buildings, cobbled streets, and backdrop of cloudcapped volcanoes, has long been a draw for tourists and digital nomads. But it is becoming an increasing focus of criminal activity, residents, police and analysts say. Gangs are using local drug sales to gain a foothold in neighborhoods, taking advantage of the capital’s strategic location to distribute drugs to the country’s ports, from where cocaine destined mostly for Europe and the US is shipped.
“Criminal organizations have tried to establish themselves in certain neighborhoods through small-scale drug trafficking," police Lieutenant Colonel Juan Chacon told Reuters as his team conducted a raid on an alleged drug distribution site in central Quito. "That connects them to a range of other crimes."
Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones, all gangs which the US has designated as foreign terrorist organizations, are present in Quito, according to police.
Solanda, built as a public housing project in the 1980s, with a busy commercial district and narrow streets of modest houses, appears on a national government list of high-risk Quito areas. Residents have installed a surveillance camera system on every street corner and metal gates at entrances to side streets to prevent unknown people from entering.
“With the cameras, you can identify the criminal and avoid exposing yourself,” said Maria Eugenia Alban, a community leader in Solanda. “Now criminals are no longer acting alone, and they are armed.”
GANGS 'TRYING TO ESTABLISH A FOOTHOLD'
The pushback from authorities has had some success. An increased security response in Solanda lowered violent death figures to just two between January and September of this year, down from 13 in the same period of 2025, according to government records.
Violent death figures in Quito overall fell in 2024 and 2025 from a high of 294 in 2023, according to Interior Ministry data, as Noboa sent soldiers onto the streets. And violence still remains below that of Ecuador's port cities like Guayaquil and Duran.
But, the armed forces say, it is a constant battle.
“Organized crime groups are trying to establish a foothold in Quito,” Lieutenant Colonel Miguel Saavedra, head of a tactical army brigade which is responsible for controlling guns, ammunition and explosives in the capital, told Reuters at a checkpoint where his unit was checking cars for weapons. His troops were seeking to "safeguard and restore security" in the city, he added.
About 4,000 police and military personnel were deployed at entry points and along strategic corridors in Quito as part of a security plan announced by Noboa in August. The city has been under a 60-day state of emergency since September.
During the first six weeks of the plan, police arrested more than 300 people, according to national police figures. The military joined police operations to check for weapons at entrances to high-risk neighborhoods and conducted targeted patrols.
Drug seizures in Quito were up nearly 500% between January and September, compared with the same period a year before, according to police figures.
Military and police operations across Ecuador cost gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining and fuel and arms trafficking nearly $20 billion in losses between January and July, according to the Defense Ministry.
However, crackdowns in one place can prompt criminal groups to seek out more favorable territory where residents are less wary of crime, said Colonel Mario Pazmino, a former head of army intelligence and current security analyst.
He said Quito is part of the “cocaine triangle," serving as a transit and temporary storage point for drugs coming from the Colombian coastal city of Tumaco and Putumayo province, before being transported across Ecuador along Pacific and Amazon road corridors.
The capital’s strategic position has been exploited by a growing number of criminal groups over the past year, said Tiziano Breda, an analyst at conflict-monitoring organization ACLED, although its status as a "transit point" lowers the risk of it being the focus of the sort of violent disputes between groups seen elsewhere.
“In Quito’s case, international cartels and national gangs are beginning to converge and establish themselves,” Pazmino said. “Quito is a hub city. The gangs come to protect the merchandise and look for other activities.” REUTERS

In Lebanese village near Israeli troops, farmers brave danger to harvest their olives

Unknown Publisher

In Lebanese village near Israeli troops, farmers brave danger to harvest their olives
ZIBQIN, Lebanon Oct 29 - In a field overlooking a lush valley in southern Lebanon, residents of the village of Zibqin balanced on branches picking their olives while Lebanese Army soldiers stood nearby.
Zibqin is adjacent to Israel’s self-declared “security zone” in southern Lebanon, where Israeli troops have demolished dozens of villages, saying armed group Hezbollah had embedded itself in civilian infrastructure — a claim the group denies. Israeli shelling frequently strikes the valley below the olive groves despite a June ceasefire between the two sides.
As Palestinians, Israeli rights groups and the UN report increased violence and olive thefts by Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Lebanese farmers also fear for their safety, illustrating how conflict is again upending the annual harvest.
Despite the danger, Lebanese farmers are returning to fields they have tended for generations, determined to harvest a crop that is one of their main sources of income and nutrition.
Ali Bzieh, a 65-year-old farmer from Zibqin, said he had no choice but to come to the fields. “This is my land, this is my livelihood, this is a harvest we wait for from one year to the next,” he said, sitting under the branches of an olive tree. “We have an attachment to this land, to the plants, and to the crops — we don't leave them.”
LIMITED PROTECTION
Many families came back to Zibqin after the ceasefire between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah. But the situation remains unstable, Raef Bzieh, a local official, said. “The ongoing bombing and the aggressions taking place on the outskirts of the village have of course caused worry and panic among the people.”
The danger prompted residents to ask the Lebanese Army to accompany them to their fields. But Mustafa Barakat, a 50-year-old carpenter, said that even with the army, the villagers did not feel safe. “But if the Israelis decide to cause harm, they can harm us, and the army,” he said. “They have struck the Lebanese Army more than once.”
Israeli attacks have killed 26 Lebanese soldiers in 2026, according to statements posted by the Lebanese Army on X. The Lebanese Army is not party to the conflict between Hezbollah and Israel.
In response to questions from Reuters, the Israeli military said its strikes in Lebanon are against Hezbollah and its infrastructure and are not directed at the Lebanese Army or civilians. It also said it is working to "enable the olive harvest and assist residents in carrying it out".
Thirty-eight Israeli soldiers have been killed in southern Lebanon in 2026, according to posts on the Israeli military's website.
WAR CHANGES HARVEST’S RHYTHMS
Barakat's days in the olive grove used to start in the early morning and stretch until sunset. Now, he limits his time in the field to when the Lebanese Army is present.
The danger has reshaped what was once an occasion for families to gather and share the hard work of harvesting olives.
“In the past, we used to treat this (harvest) season like an outing," he said. He used to come with his family to the fields and prepare food together. "Now, you can’t bring children… bombing could occur, and they could get hurt," he said.
The conflict has affected the harvest in other ways too: “We weren't able to tend to our olive trees, so our olive trees did not yield as they usually do,” said Ali, who was displaced for several months. He said the harvest was half what it normally was.
Ali said that he hoped the situation wouldn't escalate further and force his family to flee again. But many in Zibqin were bracing for that possibility: some residents continue to pay rent for apartments in areas further north. Others have already reserved a place to stay in the event of further escalation.
Yet as war casts its shadow over the harvest for the fourth consecutive year, the farmers refuse to abandon their fields.
“This land is our identity, it is the passport we carry," said Barakat. "If we abandon it, we are truly left without an identity." REUTERS

Estonian unicorn Pipedrive announces 'major' restructuring, office closures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:05:00 UTC
20:05:00 KST

Estonian unicorn Pipedrive announces 'major' restructuring, office closures
Estonian-founded customer relationship management (CRM) software firm Pipedrive is to significantly downsize, the company announced Thursday.
ERR has obtained a letter to employees from Pipedrive CEO Paulo Cunha , in which he writes that the company is significantly reducing its size in all its locations — which means fewer teams, management layers and locations. Cunha said the changes affect most of Pipedrive's current jobs and roles, adding the company will be speaking to every employee individually over the next two days, to explain whether their job is at risk and what will happen next.
Äripäev also reported Pipedrive is to make structural changes which will significantly reduce its size both in Estonia and in other countries it has a presence in.
Pipedrive marketing chief Mariliis Beger would not confirm to Äripäev whether the Tallinn and Tartu offices will remain open, stating: "We can't say at the moment, because different employment laws apply in different countries."
The group currently employs nearly 800 people, around half of them in Estonia.
In his letter, Cunha said the aim is to turn into a company which brings new solutions to market faster, understands its customers more deeply and succeeds through product strength. He said the goal is more time for work requiring depth and fewer obstacles to doing it — "in many ways a company that operates like the startup we started out as."
Pipedrive says it intends to remain product-focused and continue investing in its core CRM aspects, with a sharper focus on quality and reliability. Alongside that, it says it is building an AI-driven sales system for teams which records sales conversations, keeps data current, recommends next steps and handles routine tasks so salespeople can spend more time selling.
The company states it also wants to reduce its dependence on paid search advertising, cut management layers and meeting frequencies, and consolidate into fewer locations, so that most core teams are located in the same office.
"Small businesses' habits and expectations around buying software are evolving quickly," Cunha continued, adding that continuing to deliver value to customers requires changing how software is built and sold, and how the company operates.
He said more small businesses are asking artificial intelligence (AI) for software recommendations, that free web traffic driving the company's growth has fallen sharply, and that paid traffic to replace it costs more.
Cunha wrote that recent product updates had taught the company it needs to move faster: "We invested more in product and marketing, reorganized product development, changed our ways of working and significantly reduced operating costs." But he said those steps alone were not enough: "To build a company that matches our vision, we need a smaller and simpler organisation, focused on fewer priorities and more strongly product-centered."
He added that the layoffs do not mean AI is being used to cut costs or to replace people — AI has simply changed what customers want and how they find the product.
According to Äripäev, Pipedrive is closing its Portuguese office. It still operates in Tallinn, Tartu, New York, Prague, Florida, London, Berlin and Dublin.
Founded in 2010 by Ragnar Sass, Timo Rein, Martin Henk, Urmas Purde and Martin Tajur, Pipedrive became one of Estonia's 10 unicorn firms (a privately held startup valued at US$1 billion or more) around a decade later.

KOBLENZ, Germany – A German probe into a 300 million euro (S$428 million) global payment-fraud has been dealt a blow after a court cast doubt on the investigation by prosecutors who say millions of credit card holders were duped in a scam that enlisted the help of payment-company executives.
The court in Koblenz, where the first charges in the Operation Chargeback case were filed, has now told prosecutors more investigations are needed as a “central hypothesis” may no longer be valid.
The judges are considering releasing the accused who are in pre-trial detention, prosecutors told Bloomberg in a statement.
The court’s move came after it reviewed results of interviews prosecutors did in October with suspects held in the United States.
No decision has yet been taken on the detained but it may come as early as Oct 29, a spokesman for the prosecutors said.
Among the people indicted are Mirko Hullemann, former founder of payment company Unzer, ex-Wirecard manager Brigitte Hauser-Axtner and Ruben Weigand.
Hullemann, Weigand and others have been in detention for more than a year now. They have denied the allegation.
The Koblenz court didn’t immediately reply to an e-mail seeking comment.
In 2025, prosecutors disclosed a global probe when they raided more than 60 locations and arrested some 20 individuals as part of the investigation.
They allege that networks of criminals defrauded people across the globe of more than 300 million euros by obtaining their credit card data and signing them up for fake porn, dating or other sites, with four German payment firms handling the illicit transactions.
In total, German authorities have said they identified 44 suspects in their probe. BLOOMBERG

Switzerland narrows second air defense choice to Israel or France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:02:10 UTC
20:02:10 KST

- Switzerland shortlisted Israel’s Barak MX and the French-Italian SAMP/T NG for a second long-range air defense system on Oct. 28.
- The Swiss government kept its delayed Patriot order and will decide in early 2027 on further steps and funding.
Switzerland has narrowed its search for a second long-range air defense system to Israel’s Barak MX and the French-Italian SAMP/T NG, and will keep its delayed order for U.S. Patriot systems, the Swiss government decided on Oct. 28, Switzerland’s defense procurement agency armasuisse said.
The Federal Council, Switzerland’s seven-member government, picked the two finalists after evaluating offers from four manufacturers in France, Israel and South Korea, citing technical, military, arms policy and security policy factors. It told the defense department to continue assessing both systems and to weigh foreign policy and economic considerations as well before a final choice, without saying how many fire units it wants or when a contract could be signed.
The Swiss government said it needs long-range ground-based air defense, with an adequate stock of interceptor missiles, to counter long-distance attacks including ballistic missiles, working alongside short- and medium-range systems and fighter jets.
A second system alongside Patriot would let Switzerland protect a wider area and reduce its dependence on a single supplier and a single logistics chain, it said.
Switzerland ordered five Patriot systems in 2022, with deliveries due to begin in 2026 and finish in 2028, but in July 2025 the U.S. Department of War told the Swiss defense department that it would reprioritize Patriot deliveries to support Ukraine, pushing Switzerland to later production lots. In May, the Swiss defense department said Washington now expects the delay to run five to seven years because of the war in the Middle East, up from an earlier estimate of four to five years, and that Switzerland is withholding payments to the U.S. government while delivery dates and costs remain open. The Swiss government said the United States has decided to put countries that gave Ukraine their own Patriot systems first in line, but concluded that dropping Patriot without a replacement is not an option in the current situation.
Barak MX, built by Israel Aerospace Industries, is a modular system that can fire interceptors of different ranges from the same launchers and is part of the air and missile defense network Israel has agreed to build for Greece. SAMP/T NG, made by the French-Italian Eurosam consortium of MBDA and Thales, is the latest version of the system France and Italy already operate, and Switzerland passed over an earlier SAMP/T offer when it chose Patriot in 2022.
French defense site Opex360 reported that armasuisse approached five manufacturers in May, including South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace with its L-SAM, Israel’s Rafael with David’s Sling and Germany’s Diehl Defence with the IRIS-T SLX, alongside the two systems that made the shortlist.
The long-range purchase sits on top of other Swiss air defense programs. Switzerland is buying Diehl’s IRIS-T SLM for the medium-range role after it was left as the sole bidder in that competition, and it plans to buy Rheinmetall’s Skyranger short-range air defense to counter drones, while rising costs have led the government to cut its planned F-35A fleet from 36 aircraft to about 30.
Parliament is due to debate an extra 24 billion Swiss francs for the armed forces during its winter 2026 session, including 6 billion francs for the second long-range system and at least part of Patriot’s higher costs. Once the evaluation is complete and Parliament has decided on that funding, expected in early 2027, the Federal Council will rule on a possible additional credit for Patriot and on how to proceed with the second system.

Hungary to stick with Orban-era nuclear cooperation deal with US
BUDAPEST, Oct 29 - Hungary's government has asked parliament to make legally binding a nuclear cooperation agreement with the United States that the previous government of Viktor Orban signed in February.
The move shows that under Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who ousted Orban in an election earlier this year, Hungary will stick to the nuclear deal even though Washington had openly backed his predecessor before the April vote.
The Hungarian government submitted the bill the day before Foreign Minister Anita Orban, who is not related to the previous prime minister, met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and signed memorandums of understanding on energy and law enforcement cooperation in Washington on Thursday.
"The MOUs are key milestones, but they are part of the process. We are driven to take actions, to take action plans, and to have agreements," Anita Orban said after the signing ceremony and before starting her meeting with Rubio.
According to the bill, the agreement on civilian nuclear cooperation, signed during Rubio's February 16 visit, would become legally binding. The deal covers civilian nuclear energy including small modular reactors (SMRs), and it encourages Hungary to select US nuclear technology and companies as its main suppliers for new projects.
Parliament is likely to approve the bill as Magyar's government holds a two-thirds majority there.
Rubio visited Hungary two months before the April election and offered a robust endorsement of nationalist Viktor Orban, who ended up losing power after 16 years.
Last year, Hungary took a key step towards importing SMR technology by partnering with Poland's Synthos Green Energy, which holds the rights to GE Vernova Hitachi's technology in Central Europe.
In November 2025 Hungary signed an agreement to buy American nuclear fuel and US technology to store spent fuel at a Russian-built nuclear power plant.
Hungary is also considering replacing Russia's Rosatom as the main contractor in the expansion of its Paks nuclear power plant and has started sounding out alternative suppliers as part of a review of the project. Magyar's government is expected to decide on the Paks expansion later this year or early in 2027. REUTERS

Childhood abuse is linked to distinct brain differences depending on age, sex, and type of maltreatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:00:37 UTC
20:00:37 KST

Experiences of abuse and neglect during childhood are linked to distinct differences in brain structure among young adults, depending on their age, biological sex, and the specific type of adversity they faced. A new neuroimaging study published in European Neuropsychopharmacology indicates that physical abuse and the tendency to downplay childhood hardship are associated with a thinner outer layer of the brain, whereas a pattern combining emotional abuse and female sex is tied to a smaller left amygdala, a region involved in processing emotions.
Childhood maltreatment encompasses physical, emotional, and sexual abuse, as well as physical and emotional neglect during a person’s formative years. Individuals who experience early maltreatment are more likely to develop mood and anxiety conditions at a younger age and often experience more severe symptoms than peers with the same psychiatric diagnosis who were not mistreated.
To understand why, scientists examine how early stress relates to the physical structure of the cerebral cortex, the folded outer layer of neural tissue that covers the brain and handles complex thought and sensory processing, and the amygdala, an almond-shaped cluster of neurons deep inside the brain’s temporal lobes that detects threats and regulates emotions.
Pinpointing consistent brain changes linked to early adversity has proven difficult when studies treat trauma as a single summary score or look at individual brain regions in isolation. For instance, a 2025 analysis of over 3,200 adults, which included several authors of the new study, found that links between childhood maltreatment and brain gray matter volume did not replicate from one group of participants to the next.
Some researchers argue that more consistent patterns emerge when studies account for biological sex and zoom in on smaller anatomical compartments. Along these lines, a 2020 study of youth at risk for mental illness indicated that dividing the amygdala into its individual subregions helped link childhood physical and sexual abuse to smaller volumes in specific compartments tied to anxiety and depressive symptoms.
How people answer trauma questionnaires also complicates neuroimaging research, as some individuals minimize or deny painful childhood memories, possibly as a way of coping with past distress. Earlier work, including a 2016 study of nearly 20,000 people, showed that this tendency to idealize one’s upbringing on surveys is common and can blur the distinction between psychiatric patients and healthy volunteers.
Building on these insights, Fabian Huth of the Carl Gustav Carus University Hospital at Technische Universität Dresden, David Popovic of the Max Planck Institute for Psychiatry and Ludwig-Maximilian-University in Munich, and their colleagues used machine learning to test how specific abuse items, trauma denial, age, and sex together relate to brain structure in young adults at the earliest stages of mental health difficulties.
The researchers analyzed data from 251 help-seeking adolescents and young adults aged 17 to 35, with an average age of about 25 and a nearly even split between 130 males and 121 females. Participants were recruited across six university hospitals and early detection centers in Germany as part of a larger project tracking individuals with early mood or anxiety symptoms, ADHD, or other risk factors for bipolar disorder. The authors focused on young people early in the course of their mental health challenges to reduce the influence of chronic illness and long-term treatment, although a majority of participants with medication data were already taking antidepressants.
Each participant completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire, a 28-item survey that measures emotional, physical, and sexual abuse alongside emotional and physical neglect. The questionnaire also includes three items designed to detect minimization or denial of hardship, such as strongly agreeing with the statement, “I had the best family in the world.” Participants underwent structural MRI scans to measure the thickness and surface area of the cerebral cortex across dozens of regions, as well as the volumes of nine subregions within the amygdala and multiple subregions of the hippocampus, a neighboring seahorse-shaped structure involved in memory and stress regulation.
Clinicians rated each participant’s depressive symptoms and overall psychological, social, and occupational functioning on a 1 to 100 scale, and participants completed a questionnaire about subclinical psychotic experiences. Functioning was rated again one year and two years later. Rather than averaging the trauma items together or statistically removing the effects of age and biological sex, the authors fed all 28 questionnaire items, age, sex, and 182 brain measurements into a pattern-finding algorithm known as sparse partial least squares. This mathematical technique identifies clusters of life experiences and demographic traits that vary together with distributed networks of brain structure, while controlling for overall head size and scanning site.
To check that the patterns would generalize, the team repeatedly tested them on portions of the data held out from model building. The analysis uncovered two distinct brain-behavior profiles across the sample. The first profile linked older age, severe physical abuse, and extreme trauma denial to a thinner cerebral cortex across both halves of the brain (a difference between participants, not a measured loss of tissue over time), which the researchers refer to as cortical thinning. This pattern accounted for 18 percent of the shared variance between the participants’ questionnaire profiles and their brain measurements, with cortical thickness making up over 86 percent of the brain pattern while cortical surface area and deep brain volumes contributed very little.
Follow-up statistical checks showed that the physical abuse item, which asked whether the person had been hit so badly that a teacher, neighbor, or doctor noticed, and the denial item, which claimed having the “best family in the world,” each independently predicted this cortical thinning pattern. None of the 22 participants who strongly endorsed the denial statement reported more than minimal physical abuse, yet denial was linked to the same pattern of thinner cortex. However, this cortical thinning profile was not statistically significant as a predictor of how well participants functioned in their daily lives one or two years later.
The second profile identified a female-specific pattern that accounted for 32 percent of the shared variance between the behavioral and brain data. The pattern linked female sex, which carried the most weight, and higher levels of emotional abuse, with smaller contributions from physical abuse, emotional neglect, and sexual abuse, to smaller volumes in the left amygdala. Specifically, this reduction was concentrated in the total left amygdala and three of its internal compartments: the basal, paralaminar, and accessory basal nuclei, while hippocampal subregions did not contribute to the pattern.
Unlike the cortical thinning pattern, the female-specific emotional trauma profile was linked to later daily functioning. Across all female participants with follow-up data, average daily functioning scores improved from 62.6 at the start of the study to 69.6 after one year and 72.0 after two years, but women who scored higher on the emotional abuse profile had worse functioning at both the one-year and two-year marks, an association that held at two years even after accounting for baseline functioning. Paradoxically, having smaller left amygdala subregions alongside emotional trauma initially predicted better functioning at the two-year mark, though this brain-outcome link was no longer statistically significant after accounting for baseline functioning.
To better understand this amygdala pattern, the researchers divided participants with high emotional trauma scores into subgroups with smaller versus larger left amygdala volumes and trained a classification algorithm on 17 clinical and diagnostic measures. Among the most extreme third of the female group, comprising 26 women per subgroup, the algorithm distinguished those with larger versus smaller amygdala volumes with 69.2 percent balanced accuracy, whereas models for male participants performed no better than a coin toss.
Descriptively, women in this extreme subgroup who reported high emotional trauma and had larger left amygdala volumes showed somewhat poorer daily functioning than those with smaller volumes, although direct statistical comparisons between the groups were not significant. The classification result was also modest: it did not hold when the groups were split at the median, and its accuracy was not statistically better than the male model’s.
“What interests me most is the attempt to understand how different experiences of maltreatment relate to brain structure across the early stages of mental health difficulties,” Zai-Fu Yao, an associate professor in the College of Education and director of the Research Center for Education and Mind Sciences at National Tsing Hua University in Taiwan, who was not involved in the research, told PsyPost. “Understanding someone’s developmental history may tell us something that their current diagnosis alone cannot capture. One finding deserves particular attention: the cortical-thickness pattern was not associated with functioning at follow-up. Identifying a brain difference and explaining a person’s everyday difficulties are separate scientific tasks.”
“The clinical meaning of an imaging finding still has to be demonstrated,” Yao added. “For me, this makes the study valuable as a starting point for asking more precise questions about individual differences. We need to understand what these patterns mean in people’s lives before assigning them a label such as vulnerability or resilience.”
These observations align with research covered by PsyPost earlier in 2026, which examined a broader international cohort spanning healthy individuals and patients across the lifespan rather than young adults with early affective or anxiety syndromes, and similarly found that childhood trauma is linked to age- and sex-specific differences in brain structure.
At the same time, the cortical thinning results stand in tension with a study, which evaluated brain structural changes linked to childhood trauma using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire in healthy adults rather than young adults with early affective and anxiety disorders, and found that moderate to severe childhood trauma was associated with larger gray matter volume in parts of the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes.
Beyond structural brain scans that measure physical volume, other studies have used functional brain imaging to observe how strongly the amygdala reacts during emotional tasks. “Broadly, it extends evidence linking childhood maltreatment with differences in brain systems involved in emotional processing,” Yao said. “In our 2025 meta-analysis, which included 30 studies involving 2,474 participants, we identified convergent evidence of increased right-amygdala activation during emotional tasks among people with maltreatment histories.”
“The present study examines a different aspect of the picture: structural variation, particularly in the left amygdala, and how it relates to maltreatment profiles, age, and sex,” Yao explained. “These findings address different measurements and different sides of the amygdala. A smaller volume does not, by itself, tell us whether a region responds more strongly or weakly.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because brain scans were only collected once at the start of the study, the findings cannot establish whether smaller amygdala subregions or a thinner cortex were caused by childhood maltreatment, existed prior to the trauma, or emerged as temporary adjustments during the early stages of a mood disorder.
“The word ‘thinning’ can sound as though the researchers watched people’s brains lose tissue over time,” Yao noted. “They did not: the imaging analysis used a single assessment. Similarly, ‘smaller’ and ‘thinner’ have no universal psychological meaning. These measurements alone cannot tell us someone’s intelligence, capacity to learn, or potential for recovery.”
Additionally, when the researchers tested emotional abuse and left amygdala size directly, the link was not statistically significant. Biological sex was by far the strongest predictor of amygdala size, and the authors acknowledge that the multivariate pattern needs to be confirmed in larger, independent samples.
“I would describe this as promising exploratory evidence,” Yao said. “The multisite sample of 251 participants, follow-up assessments of functioning, and analytical safeguards against overfitting are meaningful strengths. However, internal cross-validation cannot replace replication in an independent sample. I am more confident in the broader association between maltreatment and variation in emotional-processing systems than in the precise age- and sex-specific interpretation proposed here.”
“The direct trauma-by-sex interaction for left-amygdala volume was not statistically significant, so I would treat the female-specific interpretation as provisional,” he added. “These qualifications leave the findings worth investigating, while limiting how confidently we can describe them as sex-specific mechanisms or predictors of recovery.”
The study also relied on young adults recalling their childhood experiences on a questionnaire, a method that is vulnerable to memory inaccuracies and the influence of current emotional distress. In the case of the “best family” denial item, which only 22 participants strongly endorsed, the authors note that it remains uncertain whether those who claimed to have a perfect family were actively suppressing memories of unacknowledged abuse or simply displaying a defensive response tendency. Future studies that track young people’s brain development over several years and combine self-reports with objective records of childhood adversity and cognitive testing could help determine how these brain patterns evolve and whether they can guide personalized mental health care.
“I would be especially careful with the questionnaire findings described as denial or minimization,” Yao cautioned. “Those responses cannot establish that someone experienced undisclosed abuse, and the imaging findings cannot resolve the truth of an individual’s childhood history. There is also a human point that matters to me: people should never have to produce an abnormal brain scan for their suffering to be taken seriously.”
“The question I find particularly compelling is: what helps a person update their expectations of danger when their circumstances become safer?” Yao continued. “That would require measuring learning directly, alongside actual changes in safety, social support, and treatment. The brain keeps learning from experience. An important next step is to discover which experiences help that learning become less constrained by past danger.”
The study, “Childhood maltreatment is linked to transdiagnostic age- and sex-specific cortical thinning and reduced amygdalar volume in young adults,” was authored by Fabian Huth, Clara Vetter, Clara Weyer, Kyra Bröckel-Bundt, Christina Berndt, Julia Martini, Birgit Maicher, Falk Gerrik Verhees, Paula M. Henneberg, Leonardo Tozzi, Andreas Jansen, Tilo Kircher, Irina Falkenberg, Florian Thomas-Odenthal, Martin Lambert, Vivien Kraft, Gregor Leicht, Christoph Mulert, Andreas J. Fallgatter, Thomas Ethofer, Anne Rau, Karolina Leopold, Andreas Bechdolf, Andreas Reif, Silke Matura, Felix Bermpohl, Jana Fiebig, Stefanie Schreiter, Thomas Stamm, Christoph U. Correll, Georg Juckel, Vera Flasbeck, Udo Dannlowski, Eva Mennigen, Philipp Ritter, Paris Alexandros Lalousis, Peter Falkai, Nikolaos Koutsouleris, Michael Bauer, Andrea Pfennig, David Popovic, and Pavol Mikolas.

It only takes one rumour: How a small trigger can lead to a deadly stampede
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:00:28 UTC
20:00:28 KST

Stampede at Kolkata pandal during Durga Puja claimed 19 lives.
NEW DELHI: It begins with a rumour, feeds on panic and ends in tragedy. A stampede can turn a celebration into chaos within minutes, leaving thousands gathered in joy struggling to find a way out. In a tightly packed crowd, even a small disturbance can have deadly consequences.A similar script played out in Kolkata on October 17. On the night of Maha Saptami during Durga Puja, pandal-hoppers gathered in large numbers at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin pandal. The crowd swelled further after a sudden spell of rain prompted people waiting outside to seek shelter, while visitors near the exit stopped moving.An announcement over the public address system warning that the pandal was about to collapse added to the panic. Investigators believe several factors contributed to the stampede, including overcrowding, narrow entry and exit points, inadequate crowd management and the misleading announcement.
The crowd crush, which police said lasted around three minutes, claimed 19 lives and left at least 25 people injured.India is a country of festivals, and its massive religious gatherings also make it prone to stampedes. This year, it was Kolkata.
Last year, it was Karur in Tamil Nadu and the Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj. The locations change, the crowds differ, but the tragedy keeps repeating itself.This raises an important question: despite elaborate planning and dedicated crowd management teams, why do stampedes keep happening? And what can authorities do to prevent a small disturbance from turning into a disaster?
The anatomy of a stampede
Public excitement soars during religious gatherings. Actual turnout often exceeds what authorities anticipate, resulting in more people entering an area than it can safely accommodate.As the crowd swells, even a small disturbance, a rumour, someone tripping and falling, a sudden power outage or even a broken barricade can lead to a situation in which people lose control of their movement.According to a 2014 report by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), titled Managing Crowd at Events and Venues of Mass Gathering: A Guide for State Government, Local Authorities, Administrators and Organizers, crowd disasters can be triggered by several factors.Structural problems such as weak temporary structures, collapsed barricades, poorly lit stairways, slippery roads and narrow entrances and exits can lead to a crowd crush.
Fires, electrical failures and security scares can also turn an otherwise manageable gathering into a dangerous crush.The report explains the causes of stampedes through the "FIST" model which is an acronym for Force, Information, Space and Time. According to the model, the four factors that can contribute to a crowd disaster are the force exerted by the crowd, the information that triggers its reaction, the physical space available and the duration of the incident."The FIST circumstances namely crowd force, the information upon which the crowd acts, the physical space involved, and the time duration of the incident play a very important role resulting in either overcrowding or high desired velocity," the report says.In simple terms, when too many people are packed into a limited space, pressure builds as those behind continue moving forward while those in front are unable to move. At extreme crowd densities, people can be pushed against one another with such force that they lose control of their movements. Even those who remain standing can struggle to breathe.Deaths in such situations do not necessarily occur because someone has literally been "trampled" under the feet of others. The NDMA says compressive asphyxia, which occurs when pressure on the chest prevents a person from breathing, has historically been the most common cause of death in crowd disasters."On occasions, this has led to deaths because of crushing, suffocation, and trampling. Historically, compressive asphyxia has been the most common reason for deaths in crowd disasters," the report says.
Psychology of the crowd
Crowd psychology is also a factor that can contribute to a stampede-like situation. According to the NDMA report, individuals often conform their thoughts and behaviour to those of a larger group rather than acting independently."Individual behaviour in a crowd is sometimes influenced by the behaviour of others. The individuals within a crowd may act differently than if they were on their own," it says."The unlawful actions of a few people can result in larger numbers following them. Research has shown that understanding of crowd behaviour has led to community based approach to crowd control instead of force based control," the report adds.For instance, long queues at places of worship may lead some devotees to climb over fences, prompting others to follow and causing overcrowding in another area.However, crowd behaviour is not always irrational. People react to incomplete information, the movement of others and the fear of danger. In dense crowds, they may also lose the ability to control their own movement.This is why rumours and misleading announcements can be particularly dangerous. People may begin moving towards an exit without knowing what is happening elsewhere in the venue. If the exit is already congested, the sudden movement can increase pressure on those trapped in the crowd.
How should police act and react?
Talking to The Times of India, former Bihar director general of police Abhayanand, who handled several such gatherings during his long service, said police should refrain from using force when a crowd is already panicked during a stampede-like situation."There is always a trigger, however small. It is followed immediately thereafter by a rumour which spreads like wildfire," Abhayanand said."I haven't followed any SOP in my days. I followed two basics: The crowd has panicked. Don't increase the panic by lathi charge. If there is an individual in whom the crowd has trust and if he can be made to communicate with the crowd, its effect is magical," he added.
"Crowds where there is some common binding force experience stampede. Such stampedes are easier to manage," he further said.Abhayanand also recalled handling a similar situation during the funeral procession of Ranvir Sena chief Brahmeshwar Mukhiya in Patna in 2012. He said police refrained from using force against a particularly unruly gathering of supporters."The crowd was itching for a trigger, and a police lathi charge could have set things off. We restrained ourselves because the repercussions would not have been limited to the capital but could have spread across the entire state," he told TOI."Those indulging in arson wanted the police to react and resort to a lathi charge. That was precisely what they were trying to provoke, but we did not allow that trigger to be pulled," he added.His account points to the importance of police response when a crowd is already on edge. An attempt to disperse people by force can worsen the situation if it causes them to rush towards a narrow exit or move against an incoming crowd.
Preparing for the unexpected
The NDMA has also laid down guidelines on how authorities should manage crowds and respond when a stampede-like situation develops.According to the agency, the guiding principle should be to bridge the gap between demand and supply. This requires controlling the number of people entering a venue, regulating the crowd within it and managing the outflow when necessary.The NDMA recommends designated staging points through which visitors should pass, along with effective systems to count and monitor people moving through them. Multiple routes should be encouraged to prevent bottlenecks and facilitate the movement of vulnerable groups.Crowd management also requires authorities to anticipate disturbances without allowing their response to trigger a larger crisis."Such miscreants should be immediately quarantined and removed. Action should be taken immediately with tact and firmness, without inviting undue attention from the general public, which may be there if force is used," it says."Inappropriate or poorly managed control procedures may precipitate crowd incidents rather than preventing them. For example, police reacting to a group of unruly people may chase them in a direction opposite to the incoming crowd, which may create a collision, and hence a disaster. Special attention should also be given to the border of the venue and the floating crowd moving there because the mischief is usually caused at such places," it adds.
The agency also recommends "input control" by restricting or staggering entry to prevent overcrowding. Authorities must be able to regulate, slow or temporarily stop the inflow when a venue reaches its safe capacity.This also means keeping entry and exit routes clear, ensuring that people leaving a venue do not collide with those entering, and monitoring areas where crowds tend to gather or stop moving.Communication is another important part of crowd management. The NDMA says a lack of reliable information can cause people to panic or change direction, leading to dangerous crowd movements."Communicating with visitors and providing them with the correct information is a very critical factor in all situations," the report says, stressing that communication is essential during normal operations, emergencies and recovery.
The Kolkata tragedy showed how quickly things can go wrong when these safeguards fail. Police said the crowd had become congested near the exit during the rain, even as the entry point remained open. The misleading announcement about the pandal collapsing is believed to have added to the pressure, although investigators are still examining the exact sequence of events.Ultimately, effective crowd management lies in anticipating pressure, regulating movement and ensuring that a small trigger does not turn into an uncontrollable chain of events. The challenge is not just to prepare for the thousands expected to attend an event, but also to recognise when a gathering is becoming unsafe and act before it is too late.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Ohio’s Data-Center Revolt Is Upending the Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:00:11 UTC
20:00:11 KST

Patty Spillman and Jen Belt drive through the outskirts of Grove City, Ohio, mapping the battle lines of a war they’ve waged for months. Pointing out the window of Belt’s blue Chrysler mini-van, Spillman notes the precise borders of a proposed 310-acre data-center campus. She singles out the electrical substation and towering power lines, and recounts the personal histories of neighbors who got offers to sell their land to Headwaters Site Development, the Texas-based company proposing to construct a cloud-computing storage facility on this patch of rural farmland about 10 miles outside Columbus. In between fields of drying corn-stalks and short rows of soybeans, some farmers have planted “no data center” signs on their lawns.
Spillman’s 165-year-old farm sits across the street from the proposed complex. A soft-spoken retired bus driver, Spillman, 63, is a Republican who voted for President Donald Trump three times. Belt, a 51-year-old artist and marketing contractor, is a Democrat. For months, they’ve co-led a group called Protect Grove City, which mobilized a community effort to thwart the proposed data center. The residents’ concerns are legion: water usage, noise and environmental concerns, energy costs, the cloak of secrecy hanging over the project. “This is our community. What if we don’t want you here?” says Spillman, whose mother-in-law turned down an above-market offer from Headwaters of around $1.5 million for 30 acres of land.
Community pushback prompted the Grove City council to pass a yearlong moratorium on data-center construction. In November, Grove City residents will vote on a proposal to go even further, making all large developments subject to voter approval. The issue has upended the intimate politics of this conservative community of 45,180. Community Facebook groups are filled with bickering, angry residents have filled council meetings, and activists filed freedom-of-information requests seeking answers about city officials’ communications about the referendum. Grove City’s longtime mayor, Richard “Ike” Stage, and other local leaders have fought against their efforts, saying the ballot initiative to restrict development would hurt economic growth.
The fervor against data centers is spreading across the state. Ohio has some 200 data centers, making it one of the biggest hubs in the country. In a former swing state that went red in the Trump era, Republicans admit the groundswell of political opposition to data centers has created a political opening for Ohio Democrats in the upcoming midterm elections.
“I’m as Republican as they get, but it’s going to be a tough year for Republicans in the state of Ohio,” says Nick Owens, a former county GOP chair and Trump delegate at the 2024 Republican National Convention. Owens is now working with the anti-data-center group Conserve Ohio. “I can get on my phone right now and text or call 10 or 12 people from 10 different corners of the state, from all different political backgrounds, from all different socio-economic backgrounds,” Owens says, “because we’re all united about this.”
A national Gallup poll published in May found that more than 70% of voters oppose building an AI data center in their area. In Ohio, where the average household’s electric bill climbed some 15% in the past year and more than 66% over the past decade, the sentiment is even more negative. A September survey by Bowling Green State University found that nearly 80% of Ohioans support a moratorium on data centers. More than 100 local governments in Ohio have reportedly enacted data-center moratoriums; in November, at least 10 will vote on adding a data-center ban to their charters, while two others will decide whether to recall mayors who cut data-center deals. In the eyes of opponents, the facilities—and the powerful AI industry that backs them—have come to represent an attack on their safety, jobs, pocketbooks, and quality of life.
It’s not clear just how potent the issue will be at the polls in November. By themselves, data centers don’t rank as a top-tier national campaign issue, according to voters—in a recent Pew Research Center survey, the economy, the future of democracy, health care, education, and immigration made up the top five. But Democratic candidates have sought to connect data centers to many of those themes. They’re promising to ease affordability concerns by cracking down on high electricity bills through data-center restrictions, pledging to strengthen democracy by fighting Silicon Valley’s opaque deals to get facilities built, casting AI companies as puppet masters in an unequal economy, and painting their political rivals as corrupt leaders seeking to curry favor from powerful companies. This election cycle, $137.6 million has been spent on broadcast ads about data centers, with Democrats making up 77% of that estimated spending, according to the analytics firm AdImpact.
Some Democrats believe data centers could be a decisive issue in tight races, especially in red states like Texas, Iowa, and Ohio. In those states and others, voters have told pollsters they trust Democrats more on the issue. President Donald Trump has positioned himself as one of the industry’s biggest champions, deriding opponents of data centers as “backwards and poor.” The wave of populist anger has “become the one thing that unites Americans right now,” says Megan Mullin, a UCLA political-science professor. “They connect to bigger themes that are becoming really important in American politics—around affordability, around energy affordability, around suspicion and discomfort about AI, about populist resistance to the accumulation of wealth and tech titans.”
In early October, Don Leonard, the Democratic candidate in Ohio’s 15th Congressional District, arrives at the Schmidlapp Free School Library in Piqua. The space is decorated for fall with artificial flowers, and filled with activists and community leaders ready to detail the latest data-center controversy.
Meta, which has been rapidly building out its data-center infrastructure to fuel its AI push, made plans to erect a $1 billion campus in the area. The company hashed out the deal in secret last year, according to city documents and news reports, using a private LLC and nondisclosure agreements with local officials. After Meta was outed as the company behind the data center, the social media giant and Piqua government officials said the project would bring economic investment to the region. In a statement, Meta told TIME the company is reviewing its use of nondisclosure agreements.
Leonard heard from Alisha Lange, 42, who worried about contamination of her well water. Lange, a registered Republican, was among those angered by the secrecy surrounding the project and revelations that several city officials had been awarded $3,000 bonuses by the city after winning Meta’s business. In response, outraged residents successfully petitioned to add a measure to the November ballot designed to recall Piqua’s mayor and other elected officials.
A former city and regional planning professor at The Ohio State University, Leonard, 48, sports a stubbly beard and speaks with a deliberate unpretentiousness. Normally, a progressive candidate wouldn’t stand much of a shot in a congressional district that’s been represented by Republicans for the past 15 years. The incumbent, former coal-industry lobbyist Mike Carey, won by 13 points two years ago. But by the time Leonard won the primary in May, residents in the district, which includes Grove City, were aflame over data centers. Leonard pushed his team to add a data-center question to their polling. They found more than 70% of likely voters in the 15th District wanted greater say over where data centers are located and how they operate. “If we were going to message on it, we had to confirm quantitatively what we knew from listening to the constituents,” Leonard explains in an interview at a modern co-working space in Columbus. “Which is that data centers are one of the most bipartisan issues in Central Ohio right now.”
Leonard sees data centers as “the mascot for predatory capitalism,” forcing communities to absorb increased electricity costs and environmental threats as their local landscapes are remade by huge companies based far away. He says the developments have exacerbated the anxieties of residents who watched neighbors lose solid factory jobs to outsourcing and suspect they’ll once again be the losers in an AI-driven economy. “There’s a feeling like we didn’t even govern the last revolution—globalization—and now they’re hoisting another one on us,” Leonard says. “They’re doing it in our backyard. They’re attacking our way of life.”
It’s not clear whether the backlash will be enough to catapult Leonard into contention in a solidly Republican district. There has been no non-partisan polling in the race, nor any public debates, and Carey holds a clear fundraising advantage, raking in $4 million to Leonard’s $1.2 million, according to campaign filings, though a recent influx of spending against Leonard is a sign Republicans may be a little nervous.
But in other races in Ohio, Democrats spy a clear opportunity.
On a crisp fall day, Sherrod Brown takes the microphone during a small rally outside a Franklin County strip mall. He begins with talking points about economic inequality that he could have fed this crowd of Democratic organizers and voters at any point during his 18 years representing the state in the Senate. But then Brown pivots to an attack line that might have landed with a thud even a year ago. “These data centers are in Ohio now thanks to Jon Husted,” Brown says of his Republican opponent. “They come into communities. They gulp up the land. They swallow the water. Then they get these huge tax breaks.”
After three terms in Washington, Brown was defeated in 2024, when Trump won Ohio for the third straight time. The cornerstone of his comeback bid this year has been the data-center issue. In stump speeches, social media posts, and advertisements blaring across television, Brown blames Husted for the role he played as lieutenant governor in fostering data-center growth in the state, which gave data centers an estimated $2.5 billion in incentives, including breaks on sales and property taxes, from 2017 to 2024, according to a report by the Ohio Chamber of Commerce. (The report also estimates that the centers brought in twice as much in revenue to the state’s coffers.)
Back then, Husted, like other political leaders in both parties, often celebrated tech companies like Google and Amazon, which built the sprawling campuses, as a boost to Ohio’s economy. Husted campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce called Brown’s critiques hypocritical, noting that in 2015 the former Senator himself praised an Amazon Web Services data-center project in Ohio, calling it “great news.”
Now Husted is playing defense on the issue, sponsoring a Senate bill designed to get data centers to pay for electrical-system upgrades that was ultimately blocked by Democrats. Data centers should be a local decision, he says. Polls show the race as a toss-up. But a recent New York Times/Siena poll found that Ohio was one of five right-leaning states—Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, and Texas are the others—where Democrats are outperforming expectations in Senate races, in part because voters said they thought the Democratic candidate would do a better job on data centers.
The party is eager to press that advantage. Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, has called for a conditional moratorium on data centers until they meet certain requirements, such as covering the cost of their own electricity, meeting environmental standards, and participating in community-benefit agreements. Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee, wants to force hyperscale data centers to cover electricity costs and abide by air- and water-quality standards. Acton has assailed Ramaswamy for not committing to selling off his investments in tech and AI stocks, calling these holdings a conflict of interest.
A similar pattern is playing out in other states. In Texas, both Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico and his Republican opponent Ken Paxton have proposed tighter restrictions on data centers and accused each other of being supported by tech-aligned donors. The state’s Republican governor Greg Abbott, who is locked in a surprisingly tight race of his own, has imposed a temporary moratorium on new data centers until an audit is complete. In Iowa, data centers have been a flash point in the race between Democratic Senate nominee Josh Turek and Republican nominee Ashley Hinson, with Turek proposing restrictions and Hinson emphasizing the need for local control.
Ike Stage first became the mayor of Grove City in 1988. A retired banker who helped set up the local chamber of commerce, he credits cheapish land, a convenient location, and a business-friendly climate for the steady stream of calls he’s fielded from developers over the years. Companies like medical manufacturer American Nitrile have moved in, along with three hospitals and two scientific-research facilities. “Not many cities can say that,” Stage says in an interview at city hall, where brightly colored maps of the area adorn the walls.
Stage has aspirations for Grove City to grow further. In 2018, it adopted a vision that included better transportation options, more parks, and mixed-use developments. Officials also eyed more than 9,000 acres of agricultural and vacant land they thought could be turned into “light industrial-style development.”
Seven years later, Headwaters Site Development, founded by former Google data-center infrastructure leader Michael Lebow, had a similar thought. It contacted property owners in a rural area just south of Grove City’s limits. One of the homesteads belonged to Patty Spillman’s family, which rejected the deal. “Most of us turned them down,” Spillman says. But not all. By this spring, Headwaters had found enough homeowners willing to sell to cobble together the necessary land.
During two information sessions at a local food bank in April, Headwaters representatives pitched locals on what they called Project Maple. Headwaters says it plans to sell the $6.9 billion project to an unidentified tech company, and pledged to support community-friendly zoning requirements that would be assumed by the buyer, such as a 100-ft. height limit, concealing landscaping, and noise levels that aren’t louder than a dishwasher. Headwaters says the project would bring 250 permanent jobs, pay for its own energy costs, and take precautions to keep water usage low. But according to advocates, Head-waters’ refusal to say which tech company would ultimately buy the facility was unnerving. “They just skirted around giving us straight answers about anything,” Jen Belt recalls. “A lot of people left mad.”
The anger emboldened the activists. Belt circulated a petition calling for the city council to reject any upcoming data-center applications. The group posted negative information about the facilities on their personal social media pages, as well as in popular Facebook groups, and put up no data centers signs near the proposed site.
The following month, Grove City councilman Mohamed Omar, 26, announced he was working on legislation to impose a 12-month moratorium on local data centers. Headwaters responded by sending a letter to city council members, arguing that such a moratorium could violate its due process rights. (Lebow says the company has no plans to sue.)
Yet the implied legal threat intensified the community pushback against the project on the eve of the moratorium vote. In June, the moratorium passed 6-1. Emboldened, the anti-data-center advocates with Protect Grove City decided the one-year moratorium wasn’t enough, and wrote a proposed amendment to the city’s charter, which functions like a governing constitution. It would prohibit the city from approving zoning applications for developments that occupy at least 50 acres, use more than 20 megawatts of power at peak capacity, or consume more than 500,000 gallons of water per day unless a majority of voters have backed the project in a public referendum. To drum up support, they canvassed local farmers’ markets, parks, and sporting events to ask people to sign a petition to put the measure on the ballot in November. Within a few weeks, they secured enough signatures.
City officials nervously tracked news coverage of the data-center backlash across Ohio and beyond, according to emails obtained by TIME. The charter amendment wouldn’t just inhibit the Headwaters project, they warned. It would fundamentally change how any future development deals are approved, and perhaps inhibit existing organizations, including churches, a hospital, and schools, from expanding by imposing overly burdensome processes. Critics contend residents already have opportunities to weigh in on upcoming developments through the normal city approval process. “It’s going to affect business. It’s going to affect our schools. It’s going to affect our taxes,” says Steve Funk, 70, who runs a car dealership in Grove City.
The city has been sending mailers to residents explaining the amendment’s potential effects. Residents have gotten into bitter personal disputes over the amendment in Facebook groups. “It’s bad,” says Omar. “It almost feels like the city is torn.”
To Stage, tech companies have done a poor job trumpeting the benefits the facilities bring to local communities, allowing residents’ anxieties about the industry to flourish. He likens the backlash to the fears Americans had about railroad expansion during the 19th century, when rural farmers worried about the effect the technology might have on their livestock. Americans eventually got used to trains. But Stage also recognizes that he’s on the short side of public opinion. Stage is up for re-election next year. “I’ve won most elections pretty handily, and I’ve been through 11 of them,” he says. “But you never, never make that assumption.” —With reporting by Leslie Dickstein
