Trump’s Approval Is at a New Low. Here’s Where Other Presidents’ Stood Before the Midterms—and How Their Parties Fared
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:00:10 UTC
20:00:10 KST

With the pivotal November elections looming, President Donald Trump’s approval rating earlier this month dropped to the lowest point of his second term—and the lowest level any President’s has reached heading into the midterms in decades.
Trump’s approval rating fell to 30% in early October, according to polling from the Pew Research Center. The last time an American President’s approval rating was at a comparable low this close to the midterms was Harry Truman in 1946.
“This is historically low approval ratings for a President,” says Peter Enns, a professor in the department of government at Cornell University and co-founder of the survey research company Verasight.
Data indicates that much of Americans’ dissatisfaction with the Trump Administration is being driven by the economy; according to polling from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, released earlier this month, only 26% of U.S. adults express support for how Trump is tackling it.
Similarly, just 17% of adults in the country say they approve of how the President is addressing the cost of living, according to the AP-NORC poll. Many adults also disagree with the Trump Administration’s war in Iran: the same AP-NORC poll found that only 28% expressed support for how Trump is handling the issue.
“Part of the reason Trump’s approval ratings are so low is he’s pushing policies and pushing positions that are very unpopular, and so the conflict in Iran is a great example; the public understands that this was Trump’s decision, and they understand this connects to extremely high gas prices,” Enns says. “It’s very unusual for a President to position himself on the side of so many unpopular positions.”
Those issues could be critical ones for voters as they go to the polls. The Pew Research Center found that the vast majority of registered voters—84%—say that the economy is a “very important issue” for them heading into the midterms. A smaller majority of 57% also deemed foreign policy “very important” to their vote in the upcoming elections.
Even without a historically low approval rating, midterm elections are a challenging environment for the sitting President’s party. And political experts say that this year’s election looks like a difficult one for Republicans.
How does the President’s party typically fare in midterm elections?
Typically, the party in the White House loses congressional seats in the midterms. Enns says this is a “well-known phenomenon” that is likely a result of frustration from both a President’s supporters, who may feel that there hasn’t been enough progress on the policies they wanted to see coming out of the Administration, and those who didn’t vote for the President, who may be even more frustrated because they disagree with the Administration’s actions.
“That doesn’t mean everybody’s changing their vote,” Enns points out. “It just means the backlash, the tides, are working against the incumbent President.”
Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, says that a possible explanation for this historical trend is that voters may be seeking “partisan balance in Washington.” When voters aren’t satisfied by policies coming out of the Administration, they may try supporting the opposition party in the midterms—particularly when one party controls the White House and both chambers of Congress, as is the case with Republicans right now, Panagopoulos says.
“There’s simply nobody else to blame for government actions and current policies if voters are unhappy with those besides the Republican Party [right now],” he continues. “It’s very easy for [voters] to point the finger to the Republicans if they’re not happy with what they’re seeing.”
There are, though, exceptions to this trend. In 2002, then-President George W. Bush’s Republican Party actually gained seats in both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections.
“It bucked the historical trend,” Panagopoulos says. “It’s one of the rare examples [of that].”
Political experts like Panagopoulos largely attribute the GOP’s success in the 2002 midterms to Bush’s high approval rating—63% heading into the midterms, according to Gallup data—in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
There have also been some instances when the opposition party was expected to win big in the midterms but fell short of those predictions. Going into the 2022 midterms, for instance, then-President Joe Biden’s approval rating sat at 40%, according to Gallup polling, and Republicans were widely expected to see major victories in the election. And while the GOP gained nine seats in the House, that wasn’t as substantial a win as many had predicted—and Democrats actually gained a seat in the Senate.
Panagopoulos suggests that part of the reason for that could be because Biden’s approval rating wasn’t at a historic low. He also points out that 2022 was the first election cycle with newly drawn district lines, which also could have affected the results.
Michele Swers, a professor of American government at Georgetown University, puts forth another explanation: the 2022 midterms took place just a few months after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, which may have harmed Republicans' advantage in the election.
“Sometimes, the political environment can intervene,” Swers says.
How can a President’s approval rating affect the midterm elections?
Swers likens the midterm elections to “a referendum on how things are going with the presidency.”
“The President is the one figure that everybody in the nation knows,” she says. While the President himself isn’t on the ballot in the midterms, “in general, the President loses seats because people are angry with the President, and they take that out on the President’s party because the President is also the leader of their party.”
Panagopoulos says that a President’s approval rating is “among the best predictors of outcomes in midterm election cycles” because it encapsulates “a wide range of sentiments about how voters perceive the performance of the incumbent party or president.” And Panagopoulos adds that the lower the President’s approval rating is, the greater the likelihood that his party will lose more congressional seats in the midterms.
What does Trump’s low approval rating mean for Republicans’ chances in the midterms?
Political experts agree that Republicans are grappling with a difficult political climate right now.
The vast majority of generic ballot polls—surveys that ask respondents which party they would back in the midterms or which party they would like to hold the majority in Congress after Election Day—show that Democrats are outpacing Republicans. Polling also indicates that Democratic voters are more enthusiastic about this midterm election than Republicans are; about 91% of Democrats compared to 86% of Republicans, according to a recent PBS News/NPR/Marist poll.
Republicans are even struggling to maintain their usual advantage in staunchly red states, including in Texas, where Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico holds a small lead in the polls over his Republican opponent Ken Paxton.
“I think we can expect Republicans to be facing an uphill battle at the polls,” Panagopoulos says. “We can expect that they will likely lose seats in the House and also the Senate. And the question is will they lose enough seats to lose the majority in either or both those chambers. That is entirely within the realm of possibility. And that has to do both with Trump’s relatively low approval rating, historically speaking, but also the constellation of candidates in the mix.”
Panagopoulos points out that, while the party in the White House typically loses seats in the midterms, that doesn’t necessarily mean that the opposition party gains enough seats to win the majority in the House or the Senate; flipping the majority in both chambers can be challenging to do.
Enns also notes that polling—both presidential approval ratings and vote intentions—is “a snapshot in time” and is “a representative sample” of likely or registered voters.
“We don’t know until Election Day who is for sure going to vote,” Enns says. “The election outcome may not map onto exactly what we’d expect from the polls because who votes, we don’t know until Election Day.”

Proteus demonstrator to get American autonomy software
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:00:05 GMT
20:00:05 KST

Leonardo will use Shield AI’s Hivemind software to develop autonomy for Proteus, the uncrewed rotorcraft it built with the Royal Navy and UK Defence Innovation, under an agreement that gives the company’s engineers the tools to write their own mission autonomy, according to the companies.
The two firms will work together through the Hivemind software development kit so that Leonardo engineers can build new autonomy capabilities for rotary-wing operations, including anti-submarine warfare, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, and contested logistics helicopter operations.
Tom Schaefer, vice president of Hivemind engineering at Shield AI, said: “Leonardo builds some of the most widely flown rotorcraft in the world, and Hivemind gives its engineers new tools to add autonomy to them. Autonomy software is never finished. It changes with the mission, the threat, and the sensors on the aircraft. Leonardo’s engineers can therefore tailor Hivemind software to their mission sets, and the work stays with them.”
Adam Wardrope, vice president for market development in helicopters at Leonardo in Britain, said: “As we look to the demands of our customers and the reality of military and security operations in both wartime and in peacetime, there is a need for autonomy powered by AI. The ability to develop and integrate mission autonomy using Hivemind onto Proteus will support the implementation of autonomous capabilities.
“When combined with our long-standing design, development, and manufacturing expertise in crewed and uncrewed rotorcraft, we believe we will be able to benefit from Shield AI’s software to support the development and delivery of autonomous solutions, potentially also extending it through other programmes within our rotary-wing portfolio.”
Proteus is a vertical take-off and landing technology demonstrator developed with the Royal Navy and UK Defence Innovation under the Rotary Wing Uncrewed Air System programme, designed around a modular payload bay that can take about a tonne of equipment or two standard NATO pallets. That bay is what makes the aircraft interesting, because the same airframe can carry sonobuoys, a radar, or stores for resupply depending on what is bolted into it. The aircraft made its first flight early this year after demonstrations in synthetic scenarios, with Leonardo-designed autonomy already on board.
The Royal Navy’s Maritime Aviation Transformation strategy, which Proteus informs, sets out how maritime aviation develops to 2040, and the Strategic Defence Review’s hybrid navy depends on uncrewed aircraft taking on tasks that currently consume Merlin and Wildcat flying hours. Anti-submarine warfare is the task where the pressure is greatest, with the Defence Committee reporting this month that it is not persuaded British attack submarines are putting to sea as often as they should and that the department has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap.
Shield AI’s Hivemind is the autonomy software behind the company’s V-BAT and X-BAT aircraft, and the arrangement here supplies the toolkit instead of the finished product, so Leonardo owns and sustains what it builds. Keeping that work in house matters for a British programme, because autonomy that cannot be modified without going back to a foreign supplier is autonomy that cannot be adapted at the speed operations demand.
Leonardo employs around 8,000 people in Britain, with its helicopter business based at Yeovil in Somerset, where the Merlin and Wildcat fleets are supported.

"If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

“If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly”
Architects are increasingly, and existentially, anxious about AI. It can already produce images, generate endless options, manipulate form, draft text, analyse information and take on increasing amounts of technical production. The predictable professional response is to become defensive: to identify the bits of architectural work that machines cannot yet do, protect them, regulate them and insist ever more loudly on the special status of the architect.
This is absolutely the wrong response. Architecture has always had a tendency to retreat when it feels threatened: as its actual control over the production of buildings has diminished, it has clung ever more tightly to authorship, professional territory and the idea that certain activities somehow belong uniquely to architects. AI merely makes the weakness of that position more visible.
If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly. If producing drawings, images, options and information constitutes our entire claim to value, we are defining our value in far too limited terms.
We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers
The profession has spent decades confusing the production of architectural artefacts with architectural intelligence, and we have run out of road. We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers. If we design a back extension, give it a sufficiently enigmatic name, photograph it carefully, attach enough rhetoric, we somehow persuade ourselves that we have made Ronchamp.
Architectural culture has encouraged this inflation for decades, in that every modest building becomes a manifesto, every detail becomes a proposition and every project arrives with the expectation that it should reveal something profound about architecture itself.
But the age of the hero is exhausted. The profession no longer has the cultural authority, the economic power or, frankly, the public attention to sustain this fantasy, however enthusiastically we continue to perform it for one another. AI may simply accelerate the reckoning: if machines can generate endless formal novelty and beautiful images, the architect’s claim to importance can’t continue to rest on being the singular creative intelligence who produces the special object.
The economic model that supported this fantasy is broken too. Architecture remains notoriously poorly paid relative to the length and cost of its education, the responsibility it carries and the hours it routinely demands. Yet architects have tolerated this for decades because the profession offered another form of compensation – the most important thing of all for architects: recognition, via awards, publications, photographs, lectures, the approval of our peers and the possibility that one small project might provide a tiny share of architectural glory.
We have accepted low pay, long hours, insecure employment and unpaid competitions partly because we have been sold the idea that authorship itself is a reward. If the work is meaningful enough, beautiful enough or visible enough, perhaps the sacrifice will somehow be justified.
That bargain has always been dubious, but it now looks increasingly absurd. Most architects will never become Corbusier, however many evenings they work, and most projects will never become Ronchamp, however much rhetoric is wrapped around them. Architectural status – irrelevant to most outside a handful of people in the profession – has nevertheless become a kind of substitute currency, and architecture has been remarkably successful at persuading people to accept less of the real kind in return.
We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do
AI makes the bargain even harder to sustain. If the production work on which fees have traditionally depended becomes faster and cheaper, defending the same exhausted model will simply drive fees and salaries down further.
The answer cannot be to produce the same things more efficiently for less money. We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do.
The more interesting response to AI is not to ask how architects protect what they currently do, but what architects might become capable of doing if some of that work no longer defines them.
With this, architectural intelligence becomes most useful where there is no simple answer. The most interesting projects rarely arrive as neatly defined problems awaiting visually arresting solutions. Instead, they involve conflicting needs, uncertain briefs, difficult sites, volatile markets, limited resources, political constraints and people who want different things. They involve other consultants who know things the architect does not, clients who change their minds, communities whose needs cannot be compressed into a consultation report and materials that stubbornly refuse to behave predictably like lines on a drawing.
This mess is the essence of architecture. The most useful architect is not simply the person who generates a solution, they are someone able to enter an unresolved situation, figure out what the problem actually is, connect different forms of knowledge, make spatial judgements and establish enough structure for something useful to emerge via collective endeavour rather than their own brilliance.
This demands a radically different model of authorship, which is less author and more host. That doesn’t mean becoming a passive facilitator, it means knowing how to bring people together, anticipating problems, establish frameworks within which others can work, exercising judgement, knowing when to intervene, and knowing when to shut up and not be the hero.
It also changes what architects might reasonably be paid for. At present, architecture fees are overwhelmingly organised around a relatively linear journey from brief, to concept, to information, to construction and eventually completion, but much of the work that might make architecture genuinely valuable sits awkwardly around the edges of that process.
Understanding a problem before a brief becomes fixed is often unpaid. Working seriously with communities gets compressed into consultation. Engaging directly with materials and makers is treated as secondary to design. Returning after occupation to understand what worked and what failed is rarely properly funded. Helping a building adapt over years barely appears in conventional fee structures at all.
There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like
But architects should be paid for diagnosis and briefing, for bringing different forms of knowledge together, for testing possibilities at full scale, negotiating spatial conflicts, post-occupancy work, adaptation and long-term stewardship. Practices should be able to maintain relationships with buildings and communities rather than disappearing at practical completion. Architecture fees might begin to pay for judgement over time, rather than simply production on the way towards an object.
This is not some romantic idea of architects becoming artists, activists or community workers instead of running viable businesses (which contemporary practice is not). Quite the opposite: it is about identifying forms of architectural value that are difficult to automate and, more importantly, are actually useful.
For the past 20 years, our educational initiative Studio in the Woods (pictured top and left) has accidentally provided a small laboratory for some of this. Its significance has never really been the timber structures that emerge over several days of co-production. Instead, the interesting aspect of Studio in the Woods is what happens when people design and make together under conditions in which the answer is not known beforehand, where ideas encounter the friction of weight, resistance, gravity, tools and materials. Where experts and non-experts work together as equals, and leadership moves according to what needs to happen next.
The skill of the architect in these situations is not to surrender judgement, but to exercise it differently. What should be negotiated? What can remain unresolved? Where is precision necessary? Where might uncertainty be productive? Who knows something that I do not? These are much more interesting questions for the future of the profession than whether AI can draw a convincing building.
There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like: eliminating uncertainty, standardising processes, increasing predictability, producing ever-more information and pretending that buildings can be completely resolved before anybody actually makes them. Now, machines are becoming extremely capable at exactly those things and we are surprised to find ourselves threatened, and we should stop trying to beat them at their own game.
Human architectural intelligence is at its richest when it is situated, relational and embodied. It involves judgement without complete information and responsibility for consequences that cannot be fully predicted. It means understanding materials as part of landscapes and economies, buildings as things that change through occupation, and design as something produced between many people rather than delivered by one.
None of this means drawings, technical knowledge, form or aesthetic judgement cease to matter. They matter enormously, but they are merely parts of architectural intelligence, not its definition.
The architect of the future does not need to be the person with the most original idea and the most charisma. They might instead be the person who can understand an uncertain situation, recognise what matters, establish a framework for action and create the conditions in which something richer than their own initial idea can emerge. AI may make the old version of the architect less necessary, but I’m not sure that is something we should mourn.
Piers Taylor is the founder of architecture practice Invisible Studio and the convenor of Studio in the Woods. He is professor of knowledge exchange in architecture at the University of the West of England and an external examiner at the Arts University Bournemouth, having previously held positions with the Architectural Association and the University of Cambridge. He holds a PhD from the University of Reading. He has presented several architecture shows on television including BBC programmes The House that £100k Built and The World’s Most Extraordinary Homes. His first book, Learning from the Local, was published in 2025.

Estonia's Ukraine recovery conference shifts focus to resilience
An international conference hosted by Tallinn in January, aimed at raising support for Ukraine's post-war reconstruction, will change its theme to "resilience" as Russia's daily attacks continue.
The Ukraine Recovery Conference is set to be held in the Estonian capital on January 28-29 and was initially planned to focus on the defense sector and postwar plans.
However, on Wednesday, a joint statement issued by the governments of Estonia and Ukraine said the tone had shifted.
Russia is trying to undermine Ukraine's resilience as winter looms with daily attacks on the country's "economy, energy sector, communications networks, and critical infrastructure," the statement said.
The conference's main aim will now be to "serve as a platform for mobilizing international support for Ukraine at a time when it is needed most."
"Given the current circumstances, the conference will shift its primary focus from recovery to resilience," the statement said.
"The key objective is to mobilise the resources Ukraine urgently needs. We expect URC to deliver tangible results: concrete decisions, specific financial commitments, and assistance mechanisms that can be put into operation as early as this winter," it explained.
The statement added that Ukraine needs "the strongest possible support from its international partners, coordinated efforts, and swift decisions" at this time.
As Russia continues its daily attacks on Ukraine's economy, energy and critical infrastructure, the Ukraine Recovery Conference #URC2027 in Tallinn on 28–29 January will shift its focus from recovery to resilience. The goal is to mobilise urgent international support, secure concrete financial commitments and deliver practical solutions to help Ukraine withstand this winter. A joint statement by the governments of Estonia and Ukraine ⤵️ https://t.co/pWiZQW1Cnr

Russian attacks cause new power outages in three Ukrainian oblasts

Due to grid restrictions caused by Russian attacks, some regions are also experiencing scheduled hourly power cuts, while industrial and business consumers face power capacity restrictions.

And a lot of the time it's quite smooth, I say. I've said that now. But yeah, it's been quite good this year from an engineering perspective. But we do get different issues each year, and that's for me to analyze and collect that data and then feed it back in. But yeah, engineering's definitely the fun side of it.
AS1 Chris Keen: So as you say, it is down to the teams which you oversee. Tell us about those teams.
Sergeant Polly: So there's lots of teams involved. I have three engineering teams. So my engineering team's names got changed after our 20th display season. So we changed them to the names of previous paint schemes, the names that the public gave them.
So I have Team Gina, Team Moggy, and Team Blackjack Those teams consist of five individuals that are picked from 29 Squadron. Between them I have to have at least a sergeant, and then between that mix there has to be an avionics and a mech supervisor and operator of each trade. So that's four of them, and then we have an armorer.
And then when we go overseas, I have to take additional engineers with me. So as I previously said, sometimes we have to put extra tanks on. So overseas we take a tank team, so that's an additional two armorers go to remove those tanks, 'cause we're only allowed to display with a center line fitted. So with that we also take a squipper.
So that's our survival equipment. That's just the RAF nickname for them, and they're there just to check over the pilot's kit after each display. And that's the engineering teams.
AS1 Chris Keen: And it is quite an honor, isn't it, being part of the display team? I've loved every second of it. So in terms of the engineering teams, how do you select who gets to be on them?
Sergeant Polly: So the selection process actually starts pretty much after the season ends. So normally around November time we advertise. So for the engineering teams, they can purely come from 29 Squadron. That goes out in the squadron and via other media devices. And people can put their name down. They put which authorizations they have to working on Typhoon, if they've been on the team before, how long they've been on Typhoon.
And then come January, we have a large management meeting run by myself, and we go down and select the teams. So we start with the sergeants, then to the corporal to make sure that we've got a mech and an AV. And then we fill the, the free junior slots with an operator from being a mech, an AV, and a armorer.
And then that's the team. And then we'll, once I've got the names and I know which team's who, I will then go back and sit and work out which displays they can do to make it fair. So we try and give each team one of the big displays, and then some of the ones that are, like, based away from Coningsby, and then the ones that are based from Coningsby to make it even between the teams, rather than just going one, two, three, one, two, three, one, two, three, where the likelihood is one of the teams would get all of the overseas and the other teams would just get all of the Coningsby ones, what wouldn't be fair.
So it does take a little bit of planning to try and work it out. And for 15 slots last year, we had 54 people volunteer. So again, it was very hard to narrow it down to those 15 engineers, and then we have six on reserve. So there's 21 people that have the opportunity to go away. However, with 54, there's a lot of disappointed people on the squadron, but we encourage them to put their names down for PR or aircraft guard so they at least get to go away with a team and start to understand how we work, and then we always encourage them to put their names down the following year, and hopefully their experience levels are a bit higher and they get selected for Eng.
AS1 Chris Keen: Brilliant. So the big one then, which I've asked Tom and Aidan, I asked them what their highlights were for this season, but let's slightly change it for you because you've been around a lot longer, 10 years. So what highlights have you had over that time?
Sergeant Polly: Oh, that's a really difficult question Oh, there's just been so many highlights over the time.
Being part of the team that went to Canada, so the first time the Typhoon display team had been to North America was so much fun. The Canadians were lovely, and really strangely, so normally when we go away, the jets are there straight away. But we actually had a day before the jets arrived, so we got to actually go round and see a little bit of Canada, what was nice, what we don't normally get to do.
Another cool place that I've been was Turkey. Again, we had a bit of downtime in the middle, so we got to go and watch all of the hot air balloons take off at Cappadocia. So that was a really fun thing to do with the team, something nice. Air shows, RIAT is fantastic. So many of our corporate sponsors are there, and we just get hosted so well, and you get to see the other side of the RAF that you don't normally get to see when you're on the flight line.
So that's a true highlight. I think just the people as well. So from being on the engineering team, the camaraderie that you build with those other four individuals is fantastic. You have little in-jokes and, 'cause you just go away with them constantly for five months. It's just fantastic. So I do miss that.
But then we kinda have our own type of that in the office, so that's really good fun. Another highlight was I've been lucky enough to work on most of the paint schemes, but I was the engineering manager for Moggy, so Moggy does always have a place in my heart. Having to go over and keep her a secret in the paint shop, to having to tow her across at midnight, or as we called it Operation Midnight Moggy, getting all the pan lights turned off so that we could get her over to the haz so that no one could see her.
And then just how much everyone loved her it was just such a cool thing to be a part of for D-Day 80 as well. Yeah, that was definitely a highlight for me.
AS1 Chris Keen: So sadly, your time is up and you're moving on. What is next for you?
Sergeant Polly: I'm going over to a new section in cyberspace. I'm really looking forward to that, managing a different team in an area that I have a, an understanding of but not a complete understanding of, 'cause they're a different trade from me.
But hopefully I'll be able to bring the understanding of airworthiness and other aspects that I've learnt from all my time on the squadron. So I'm super excited for that, 'cause that's something different that I haven't done before, and I'm just really looking forward to that opportunity.
AS1 Chris Keen: And finally then, Polly, I've gotta finish with this.
Are you gonna miss it?
Sergeant Polly: Yes. I'm 100% gonna miss display. It's been such a big part of my life for so long, but all good things have to come to an end, and I have to give other people the opportunity. I've already done four seasons, what's way more than anyone else has ever done. So it's not fair for me just To hog it from everyone else.
So I will miss it, but it's definitely a good time for me to move. I'm promoted to chief technician, so it's a fantastic way to leave the job, and last week I got awarded the Mark Long Trust Most Outstanding Contribution to UK Display Flying. So both super positive things to be leaving the display world with.
So yeah, I will miss it though.
AS1 Chris Keen: Now, I've been lucky enough this season to go to quite a few air shows, which has been incredible because I do love air shows. And whilst at those air shows, I've been talking to quite a few people. And without sounding biased, I have to say that seeing the Typhoon is a huge highlight, if not the main highlight of the show.
And the man behind the stick this year is Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation, AKA Dragon 01. He takes us right back to the start of where his love of aviation first began.
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: I've been involved in aviation from a very young age. I grew up in South Wales and my family are all kind of aviation geeks, so I went to air shows from the age of two And that's what kinda sparked the interest for me.
From there, I joined the air cadets at age 13, learned to fly with them, and became a gliding instructor. I then went to university, joined the University of Wales Air Squadron flying the Grob Tutor, and from there went on to join the RAF on my fourth attempt as well. So it took me four goes to get in the RAF, but got there eventually.
Then went through flying training, flew the Tucano, the Hawk, and then eventually ended up on Typhoon, and did my first operational tour up at RAF Lossiemouth with 6 Squadron, and did operations in the Middle East, some Baltic air policing, and did exercises in places like Australia, Germany. So had a great time when I was up in 6.
From there, came back down to 29 Squadron, the Operational Conversion Unit, as an instructor, and was lucky enough to be selected for the 2026 display.
AS1 Chris Keen: So the Typhoon Display Team, very front-facing. A big part of it is to get people to want to join the Royal Air Force. Just talk us through the process of your training and how long it took to get where you are.
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: Yeah. So the training process all started for me at RAF Cranwell, where you do initial officer training. For me at the time, it was 32 weeks. I think it's a little bit shorter now. But that's where essentially you learn how to be in the military. The first part is all of the stuff that you see on films where you do drill, you iron your kit a lot, you're up early in the morning making sure your room's tidy.
And then you learn more about the air warfare kind of stuff and how to conduct yourself in the RAF. And yeah, that lasted for 32 weeks. From there, I went on to elementary flying training. So that was on the Grob Tutor again. I was a little bit lucky that I'd already flown the Grob at university.
But there you're just learning the basics of how to fly an aircraft really. It's a small prop airplane. And you develop some of the skill sets like formation flying, aerobatic flying, and things like that. And by the end of EFT, you're then streamed. So you can either be streamed rotary, so you'll go on and fly in helicopters, or multi-engine, where you'll fly a transport aircraft or ISTAR aircraft, or fast jet.
And fast jet is what I was gunning for, and I was lucky enough that I got selected for fast jet training. So the next stage of training for me was basic fast jet training, which was done at RAF Linton-on-Ouse on the Tucano. It's now done at Valley on the Texan. And it's essentially a, a, a faster, slightly more complex airplane, and you learn more of the skill sets that are applicable to flying a fast jet And that was awesome fun, and that lasted for about a year at RAF Linton-on-Ouse.
Post that, you then go onto your advanced flying training, which is done on the Hawk, and that's your first jet, so learning how to handle a jet aircraft. The first half of the course is done on 25 Squadron, and that's where you're basically learning how to just fly a jet. You're not learning how to fight in it or anything like that.
But once you've completed that section of the training and you're comfortable with flying the Hawk, you can then go on to the second half of the course, which is where you're learning tactics and weapons, so how to actually fight in an aircraft, which is the job that you go on to do And once you've completed that, you then are streamed to your final frontline type.
So it's either F-35 or Typhoon. I was lucky enough to get Typhoon. And then you go on to operational conversion unit where you're taught how to fly the Typhoon and how to do all the stuff you've done on the Hawk, but on a slightly faster, pointier aeroplane. So all in all, it took me about five years from start to finish.
The timelines vary. You can get it done in as little as three, three to four years. But yeah, five years worth of training before I got to Typhoon.
AS1 Chris Keen: And then so when you become, let's say, operational then, have you had any highlights or favorite moments during that time?
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: Yeah, so probably one of the coolest things I got to do was an exercise, it was called Gun Heroes, and it was out of Ramstein Air Base in Germany.
And it was essentially all the NATO partners in Europe, and the Americans as well, took aircraft into Ramstein, all the fighters, and it was a, a BFM exercise, so basic fighter maneuvers, but dog fighting to all intents and purposes. So you all got sat down in a hangar. There was a guy at the start who gave out a little brown envelope to each of the pilots, and in that brown envelope you had a time and a bit of airspace to go to and a radio frequency.
And you would get airborne on your time slot, go to the bit of airspace, dial in the radio frequency, and there'd be somebody else in another jet on the same radio frequency. You'd call that you're both ready to have a fight, and then you would tune in, and the first time you knew what you were gonna fight was when you saw it at the merge, and that was epic.
It was really good fun. And the Typhoon is the jet to do that in as well. It's a pretty potent air combat fighter, so we had a good time.
AS1 Chris Keen: Amazing. Yeah, I've heard you quite a few times during my tour here say just how good the Typhoon is.
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: Yeah, it's designed to get up close and in your face, and there's not many things that can surprise a Typhoon.
Typhoon's got all of the thrust available. It's very agile, so in air combat it's pretty epic.
AS1 Chris Keen: So let's talk about the display team then. How do you go from being a, can't really say normal because you're all pretty amazing- ... but how do you go from being a normal Typhoon pilot to becoming the Typhoon display team pilot?
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: Yeah, so the first step is you have to be an instructor on 29 Squadron. That makes you eligible to put your application in to be the display pilot, and it's something that I wanted to do since I was little, so I, as soon as I could, I put my application in. And then there's a selection process. So you're interviewed, and you do a flying skills test where essentially you go in the simulator and you're given one of the previous year's sequences to learn, and you just have a go and see how you do.
At the end of that, you're either told that you got the job or y- you haven't. I was lucky enough to get the job But the display flying is really different from what we n- do day to day, 'cause you don't learn aerobatics in the Typhoon. You learn how to do air combat, but you don't learn how to fly eye-pleasing maneuvers close to the ground.
So there's an entire workup process to get you to the point where you're able to then perform in front of the crowd, and you're given something called PDA, public display authority. But the truth of it is that, the standard of people that we get coming through the Typhoon Force is that anyone could do it if they were given the right training.
You couldn't just jump out of your frontline role and go and fly a display, but if you had the same workup that I've had, any of the, the pilots on the frontline or on 29 Squadron could fly a display. But it takes a good sort of six months to get to that point where you're ready to do it.
AS1 Chris Keen: When you get selected and then you have to go through the workup, what does that entail?
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: So the first thing that happens, I was selected a year in advance so I could shadow my predecessor, Nathan Shoyer. So I shadowed him for his season, where you just go along to a few of the air shows and kinda see what it's all about. Then you kinda pick up, like learning through osmosis really, what being a display pilot involves.
And then when it comes to, your time in the seat, the first thing you have to do is come up with your routine your sequence, and there's a list of approved manoeuvres that you can fly in the Typhoon, and it's up to you how you sequence them, orientate them to the crowd, and, you can put slight variations on the manoeuvres and things like that.
And that all starts in the simulator, and it's just a case of Going into the simulator, having an idea of what you think might look cool, and practicing it and seeing whether you can actually fly the manoeuvre. And then I think about the sort of December time was when I had my sequence, like I first wrote it out in full as to what I thought would work.
And then you go into your formal workup at the start of the year. So January 2026, that's when you do assessed simulators. So you have a number of supervisors, generally previous display pilots, who will go into the simulator with you. You'll fly a sequence, and they'll critique it, give you tips, and whip you into shape.
You have to do about sort of 10 simulator trips before you're then cleared to do it airborne. But the first time you do it airborne as well is up at 5,000 feet. You don't do it straightaway down at low level, and that's just so you can get a feel for what the G-forces and that are like because in the simulator, you're pulling full back stick, but you- you've not got any of the physical sensation that you'd actually have in the jet.
So it's best to do that for the first time up at height just to give yourself a bit of a buffer. Then once you've done that, you work down the heights. So you do another sort of 10 trips at 1,500 feet over the airfield, and that's where you're getting more of a feel for how the aircraft's gonna handle at lower level.
But again, you've got that safety buffer being a bit higher in case you do mess up any of the maneuvers 'cause doing it close to the ground, you've got half a second or so before you- you're in trouble. Then once you're deemed safe and competent at that height, you can then come down to your sort of final display heights, which is 500 feet for aerobatics and then 100 feet for like the high-speed passes.
And you do a few practices at those heights before you're ready for your public display authority, and then that's when AOC One Group comes and gives you the seal of approval and says you're good to go.
AS1 Chris Keen: Amazing. I think it's really cool that you get to come up with your own routine.
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: Yeah. It was good fun.
It was good fun 'cause you can be as creative as you like with it, and having been to lots of air shows as a kid, I had an idea of what I wanted to do. I think with Typhoon, one of the, one of the highlights of Typhoon is the noise, so this year I've tried to make sure that I've got the engines pointing in people's faces as much as possible in full reheat to really blast the noise over the crowd 'cause I think that's one of the things people consistently say they take away from air shows is just how loud it is.
AS1 Chris Keen: Yeah.
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: So that was part of the, the design sequence.
AS1 Chris Keen: Do you have a favorite and a least favorite part of the routine?
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: I think my favorite maneuver is one that I've called the Reuben Maneuver 'Cause my six-year-old stepson helped me come up with it. It's a tricky maneuver to fly. It's an aileron roll into a hesitation roll into a Derry turn, so it's quite a precise maneuver.
You have to be on it to fly it crisply, and it's one of those w- when you get it right, it's pretty satisfying to do, but it's quite easy to get it wrong as well. So I'd say that's my favorite. My least favorite maneuver, physically, yeah, the outside turn. So outside turn is where essentially you turn the wrong way, so you're not pulling positive G, you're pushing negative G, and the Typhoon can go to minus three G and that's what I do in that maneuver, and it is...
It's not pleasant. So if you've ever hung upside down on the monkey bars as a kid and you get that feeling of all the blood being pushed into your face, it's like that but obviously three times the force, so you feel like your eyes are gonna pop out. So it's pretty painful, that one. I don't know why I put it in there.
I suppose it looks cool
AS1 Chris Keen: And obviously it's been an incredible season this year. So many people online telling us just how in awe they are of seeing you, and just how amazed they are. What does it feel like for you being in the cockpit?
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: It's awesome. It's one of those where when you're actually flying the display, you're kinda locked in, so you have to be completely focused on what you're doing.
So whilst it's enjoyable, it's almost like it's that feeling of enjoyment comes once you've finished the display- ... 'cause you, you don't really have ... I certainly don't have the brain capacity to enjoy it at the time. I am enjoying it, but I don't have the capacity to think, "Oh, this is cool."
But yeah, it's incredible. You get to do things in the jet that you otherwise wouldn't get to do. Flying upside down at 500 feet and 600 miles an hour is pretty epic.
AS1 Chris Keen: Do you ever get nervous before a display?
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: Yeah. Yeah, you always get butterflies in your stomach, and I think that's, I think that's important in a way, 'cause it keeps you on your toes.
One thing that can be dangerous in this world is complacency. So I think if I ever got into the cockpit to do a display and I wasn't feeling some form of butterflies, then it's probably time to get out of the cockpit, to be honest, 'cause you need that, that healthy respect for the fact that what you're doing is pretty dangerous if you get it wrong, to keep you focused and make sure you stay safe.
AS1 Chris Keen: And obviously I've been lucky enough to see you before a few of your displays this season. You take yourself off, don't you?
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: Yeah. It's just to refresh what you're about to go and do. So generally I'll take myself away and just mentally go through the whole sequence as ... and how I'm gonna fly it, and adapt it for the specific display venue that I'm at, or what the weather conditions are gonna be like on the day.
'Cause there's always subtle changes that you have to make in the routine depending on where you are, and it's good to mentally rehearse those beforehand because you don't wanna be thinking about it for the first time when you're actually in the moment, 'cause you just don't have time to.
So yeah, I generally try and take myself away for a little bit to go and do that. But then also I quite I've been pretty fortunate this year that all the engineering teams, they're a really sociable people And they allow me to just relax before I go in as well, 'cause you could get yourself too worked up.
But it's nice having a team of people that you can have good banter with, so- Yeah ... so that's quite nice.
AS1 Chris Keen: Yeah, I was gonna say that. You've got quite a large team around you, haven't you?
Flight Lieutenant Tom Nation: Yes. Yeah, there's a huge team of people that make this work. So we have, upwards of 70-odd people that are involved in the display.

It's a huge team of people that work behind the scenes to get the jet airborne in the first place. I'm just the, essentially just the driver at the end that does that bit, so I'm the lucky one, but there's a lot of people that do a lot of hard work behind the scenes.

Youth 'tram surfing' in Tallinn prompts safety warning from TLT
A photo has gone viral on social media which appears to show a boy riding on the front of a moving tram in Tallinn, prompting authorities to issue a warning.
Tallinn's public transport operator, TLT, says minors, or anyone, playing dangerous games on trams risk serious injury or death.
The photo shows what appears to be a minor sitting on an external part of a tram which had halted at the Volta stop in North Tallinn.
Apparently sitting on the tram's front buffer, the youth would have likely not been visible to the driver.
Tarmo Lai, head of TLT's service division, told ERR incidents of this kind happen from time to time, spiking during the school vacations – this week is the half-term break for most schools.
"There is a period when these incidents don't happen at all, and a period when something is happening every day," he said, adding that cases tend to when children have too much free time on their hands.
Lai said TLT works with the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) and Tallinn's Municipal Police (Mupo) to address the issue; officers have visited schools in the Kopli area where the recent incident took place, to stress to schoolchildren the inherent danger in such acts.
While there have been no fatal accidents in the course of risk-taking acts involving public transport, Lai noted with a tram weighing 45-60 tonnes, the potential consequences of a slip are obvious.
"If you fall under there, the consequences will most likely resemble a genuinely horrifying horror film," Lai put it, noting the outcome would likely be far more severe than those from pranks or other misuse of e-scooters, another known area of concern.
A tram driver braking hard to avoid an incident could also put passengers at risk of injury, while the rapidly darkening mornings and afternoons at this time of year only serve to exacerbate the risk.
There have been several other reported incidents and one fatality involving Tallinn trams in recent months.

The Danish Security and Intelligence Service, known as PET, is warning Ukrainians in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them to carry out sabotage, potentially without their knowledge.
PET said in a press release that it is issuing information material in Ukrainian. The service has previously warned the wider Danish public about the threat.
Emil Græsholm, PET’s head of counterintelligence, said the warning also needs to be available in Ukrainian because Russian intelligence services may attempt to recruit Ukrainians living in Denmark.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making it appear that they are participating in Russian sabotage.
Russian intelligence services can hide their identities and recruit through intermediaries, leaving those carrying out assignments unaware of who they are working for.
Tasks may be presented as journalism, market research or general documentation, making them appear harmless, PET said.

PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.

Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.

The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.

Travelers heading to western Greenland will no longer need to change planes in Nuuk after aviation authorities approved the opening of Ilulissat’s expanded airport on Thursday.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority granted final safety approval overnight, following inspections and a test flight.
“Following a long series of inspections and a test flight, we have approved that the airport meets the necessary level of safety required to operate a modern, international airport,” said deputy director Lars Korsholm.
The approval comes with temporary restrictions during the airport’s initial operating period. These will gradually be eased as the airport gains experience.
Korsholm said the restrictions were unlikely to affect scheduled flights, particularly outside the tourist season.
The airport’s runway has been extended from 845 meters to 2,200 meters, allowing larger aircraft to land in Ilulissat, a town on Greenland’s western coast near Disko Bay.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen had to connect through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.
Initially, Air Greenland will generally operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday, with additional weekly departures during busy periods, including Christmas and New Year.
Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.
The expansion forms part of a multibillion-krone investment in Greenland’s airports, which also includes improvements in Nuuk and a new airport near Qaqortoq in southern Greenland.
The projects aim to improve transport connections and support economic development, particularly through increased tourism.

Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.

Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.

The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.
Electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex recalled over electric shock risk
Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.
According to Epiq ApS, the affected products lack child safety protection covering the socket openings, creating a potential electric shock hazard.
The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.

The recall covers the following four products:
Scoop ledningssæt med tre stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with three sockets. EAN code: 5713359129661.
Basis ledningssæt med fire stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with four sockets. EAN code: 5713359131749.
Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.
Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.
The company has instructed customers to return affected products to their original Bilka or Føtex store for a refund without requiring proof of purchase.

Preben Bang Henriksen has been expelled from Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, after refusing to promise that he would follow the party’s position in future parliamentary votes.
The lawmaker confirmed his expulsion Tuesday following a meeting at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing.
“The conclusion of a vote was that I am expelled,” he said.
Henriksen will continue as an independent member of parliament but said he had hoped to remain in Venstre.
The dispute followed a September vote on legislation concerning fertilizer use, when five Venstre lawmakers opposed the party’s position over concerns about its impact on agriculture.
Venstre chairman Troels Lund Poulsen subsequently sought stronger party discipline, receiving support from the party’s national executive committee Sunday.
“Once the debate has taken place, and a majority has decided on a direction, the expectation is that the majority backs it, even if one wished for a different result,” Poulsen said Tuesday.
Henriksen refused to make that commitment, arguing that lawmakers should retain their independence.
Under Denmark’s Constitution, members of parliament are bound only by their own convictions.
However, Venstre’s internal rules prevent lawmakers expelled from its parliamentary group from remaining party members.
Henriksen, a former lawyer from Aalborg, entered parliament in 2011 at age 57.
He has served as the party’s justice spokesperson and chaired parliamentary committees overseeing legal affairs and intelligence services.
Known for following his own conviction, he has previously gone against the party line. In 2021, he voted with eight members against launching an impeachment trial against Inger Støjberg, who ended up being convicted. The members were granted a free vote when they voted.
In the 2024 book “Ærlig talt – Borgen indefra”, he described that he was close to leaving Venstre because of Lars Løkke Rasmussen’s purchase of clothes with party money. The book also contains criticism of political conformism and the workflows at Christiansborg.

Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

Norwegian will lay off 123 employees at Copenhagen Airport, including 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew members, as it reduces the number of aircraft based in the Danish capital.
The decision follows talks with Flyvebranchens Personale Union, or FPU, the union representing the employees, according to Danish business outlet Finans.
Most affected staff will leave at the end of January next year, with the remaining departures planned 10 months later.
“It is a sad day for Norwegian, and I am incredibly affected on behalf of the affected employees,” Sara Neergaard, the airline’s country manager in Denmark, told Finans.
“But there is no other way. The redundancies are happening out of necessity.”
Norwegian plans to reduce its Copenhagen-based fleet during the summer season from 16 aircraft to 14. The airline says demand varies considerably between seasons, requiring 16 aircraft during the summer peak but only 10 in winter.
The change will not reduce the number of summer departures from Copenhagen. Some summer routes will instead be operated by aircraft based in Spain.
Union challenges the decision
FPU Chair Thilde Waast described the layoffs as an attempt to “undermine Danish working conditions.” In a written response, she accused Norwegian of seeking to replace Danish employees with “cheaper Spanish labor.”
Neergaard said the union had rejected options that could have reduced the number of layoffs, including seasonal contracts under which staff would work more in summer and less in winter, as well as voluntary leave.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline by passenger share last year, according to the airport’s latest financial report. It carried 15% of passengers, behind SAS at 38% and ahead of Ryanair at 9%.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest base after Oslo. The airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen last year.
EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news
A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.
Editor-in-chief Michael Dyrby describes the content as AI-assisted rather than fully automated.
Human editors select stories, determine their angles, review AI-generated drafts, make revisions and choose images before publication.
“We could have made it so that AI did everything. But it doesn’t,” Dyrby said.
AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.
The aim is to produce more journalism with fewer resources while maintaining editorial control.
“We will find out,” Dyrby said, describing Projekt Y as an experiment in journalism’s future.
Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.
Its target audience is primarily adults aged 28 to around 60.
Dyrby, who graduated from the Danish School of Journalism in 1989, previously helped launch TV 2 News in the mid-2000s.
Projekt Y has received media subsidies and will also generate revenue through advertising.
Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.
“The ambition is to create a technology that is so simple that everyone can use it and create their own media outlet, and in that way help democratize the use of media,” Dyrby said.
Additional publications are planned throughout the remainder of this year and into 2027.
Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

Denmark issues safety guidance for vulnerable people after CPR data leak
The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.
The agency also recommends considering contact with police, a crisis center, the Danish Stalking Center or another specialized counseling service.
People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.

Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.
The practice occurs on a limited basis at a slaughterhouse in Tarnow in southeastern Poland, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.
The method is legal in Poland but has been prohibited in Denmark since 2014, when prior stunning became mandatory.
Danish Crown said the Polish facility slaughtered 69,000 cattle in 2025. The company said only “a minority” were slaughtered using the kosher method but declined to provide a specific number.

Sokolow chief executive Przemyslaw Gostkiewicz said Poland has a particular tradition of kosher slaughter that allows Jewish people to follow their dietary rules.
“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.
Danish Crown did not say whether it would continue permitting the practice.

Danish authorities will cull 27,000 turkeys Monday after highly pathogenic avian influenza was detected in a flock in Stokkemarke on the island of Lolland.

The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.
