The physics of getting fired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
21 minute listen
The senior partner didn’t waste any time. ‘I’m sorry, Zahaan,’ he said, ‘your services are no longer required at the firm.’ We sometimes called him the Burger King behind his back, because he ate a Whopper Meal at his desk every day. I’d never spoken to him before, and now I never would again.
It was the summer of 2001. I was fresh out of university and nine months into my first job as a management consultant in London. My parents had allowed me to move back into my old room, where I routinely collapsed after getting home from the office well after midnight. Professional life was punishing, but I gave it my all. For a brief time, I felt like I was flying: at my first performance review, I was told I had ‘partner potential’.
But then I got a phone call, telling me that one of the senior American partners wanted to meet me. That was unusual; but then again, I’d been working so hard and getting such good feedback, I figured it couldn’t be anything too bad. I was directed to an office on the first floor, several levels below where I usually sat.
After he fired me, my ears buzzed and my chest tightened; I don’t remember much else, except being told that I shouldn’t even return to my desk. It became apparent that the location of the meeting had been chosen because it would allow me to take a single flight of stairs down to the ground floor. No one would need to see me, and I wouldn’t need to speak to anyone.
The decision felt cruel and unfair. But more than anything, it seemed to violate the laws that for many years had been my way of making sense of the world: the laws of physics. Cause and effect, action and reaction. What followed was an unlikely journey – one in which the equations I thought I’d left behind at university became, unexpectedly, a companion through the messiest parts of life.
Before work, before university, I attended a competitive and prestigious all-boys school in London. While I’ll be forever grateful for the opportunities my education afforded me, life still felt tough for me as a lonely and anxious teenager. The school’s social currency was confidence, quick comebacks, and an effortless cool I never quite mastered. I often felt like I was watching from the edges, trying to decode the rules of a game that everyone else grasped intuitively.
The only thing that got me through was physics. The most fundamental of the sciences, physics represented a world that was perfectly ordered. It offered structure, rules and predictability. There was no social speculation; I could just work hard and try to figure things out. Problems and solutions, equations and outcomes. It didn’t matter how popular I was – what mattered was whether I understood the system. Slowly, the chaos of the world developed a sense of form and structure.
That clarity stayed with me, through school and into university. I read physics at Oxford, convinced for a long time that I wanted to become a scientist. It wasn’t always easy; there were late nights, bitter struggles with problem sets, moments I wondered if I’d ever get it. But when it clicked, it was wonderful: entropy, quantum mechanics, cosmology, all those deep, strange laws that govern the Universe. Physics seemed like it had a purpose, and I thought we’d go the distance.
But at some point in my final year at university, things started to change. Physics still fascinated me, but I found myself drawn to other subjects too – politics, economics, business. I wanted to understand not just how the Universe worked, but how people did. So after graduating, I decided to leave physics behind and see where those other interests would take me.
For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist
As it turns out, when I stepped away from physics, many others did too. In the years after I left university at the turn of the millennium, physics began to fade from view in the English classroom. In 2006, physics A-level entries (post-16 qualifications in the UK) were down 37 per cent from where they were in 1991. The absolute numbers have since rebounded – but not for everyone. Today, the gender gap remains stark: only 23 per cent of A-level physics entries in 2026 came from girls, a figure that hasn’t budged much in decades. And more than half of GCSE physics classes in England (taken by 14- to 16-year-olds) are taught by a non-specialist, with a shortage of some 3,500 physics teachers nationally.
Research looking at why students choose or reject physics has found that it’s seen as abstract, difficult, and disconnected from real life – a perception that’s remained steady, even as enrolment has recovered. Meanwhile, newer fields – computer science, behavioural economics, even data journalism – have felt more immediate, more applicable. They speak the language of now.
What’s strange is that this perception problem has happened at the same historical moment in which physics has begun popping up in other surprising places.
Dominic Cummings, the strategist behind Brexit and later Boris Johnson’s chief adviser, gave physics a fair share of the credit for the success of his campaigns. In one of his highly popular newsletters, he paraphrased the theoretical physicist Richard Feynman: ‘The most important thing is not to fool yourself and you are the easiest person to fool.’ Then there’s Elon Musk, who credits the success of his many business ventures to physics and ‘first-principles thinking’: discard convention, start from fundamental truths. And for decades, the legendary investor Charlie Munger made the same case in finance, saying that the ‘logic and power’ of physics had helped him enormously.
For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist, praised by public figures whose decisions affect millions of lives. But look closer, and the picture is more complicated.
In the first instance, billionaires and political operatives make for awkward ambassadors; Cummings, Musk and Munger might be brilliant, but they’re also extremely divisive. But more than who they are, what interests me is how they’re putting physics to work – whether they’re truly thinking with the discipline, or just brandishing it for rhetorical effect. Is ‘physics’ simply a shorthand for cutting through complexity, for stripping down problems to their most basic parts? Or does it genuinely offer something distinctive that other sciences and ways of thinking cannot?
Philosophers call the first approach ‘reductionism’: the idea that if you break any system into small enough components and trace them far enough, you eventually arrive at physics. That view can be powerful, and explains why so many people find it attractive.
It’s also been spectacularly successful. When 19th-century physicists showed that heat was simply the motion of atoms – that temperature, seemingly its own phenomenon, was actually just particles bouncing faster – an entire science collapsed into physics. Years later, that same approach helped particle physicists break matter into smaller and smaller pieces until arriving at something apparently irreducible. From the reductionist instinct came quarks, leptons and the Higgs boson. Their catalogue blueprint, the Standard Model, remains one of the greatest intellectual achievements in human history.
But reductionism has its limits. Take politics: a radical reductionist might say that this too comes down to physics, because politics is about the behaviour of groups of people; groups are made of individual people; people are made of atoms; atoms are governed by physics. But does this mean that we could predict the outcome of, say, a national election by studying the behaviour of individual atoms inside the brains of every registered voter? Unlikely. Putting aside issues of practicality, what would be the point? Economists already have economics. Psychologists already have psychology. Politicians have political theory. Physics has value only if it’s additive and illuminating.
For me, the real value of physics had never been as a cudgel for smashing things up into their smallest bits, but as a framework for navigating systems – for recognising patterns, probing assumptions, and testing whether the models we rely on actually work as they’re meant to. We see this way of thinking throughout the history of science. When cholera swept through Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow didn’t know its cause. But he mapped the cases, identified the pattern, and traced the outbreak to a single water pump on Broad Street. The founder of what we now know as epidemiology, Snow worked by constructing and interrogating mental models of the world, probing their assumptions, and following the data wherever they led.
The question, then, is not simply whether physics can be borrowed as rhetoric, but whether it really helps us to see the world more clearly, in ways that complement and benefit other disciplines. That, at least, was what stayed with me after I stopped studying it formally. Not equations or textbooks, but a way of thinking that I found myself reaching for when my world was falling apart.
Getting fired was one of those moments. I had worked so hard, yet somehow I’d still failed. Everything I understood about cause and effect told me this shouldn’t have happened. But here I was, after months of working flat out, with nothing to show for it.
An infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance
While some might have turned to therapy or career counselling, I turned back to physics to try to move on. The immediate cause was clear enough. The dot-com bubble had burst, sending ripples across the global economy that eventually reached my desk. Belts tightened, and the harsh rule in such circumstances tends to be last in, first out.
The dot-com bust was not the first nor last time something like this would happen. In 2008 came the subprime mortgage crisis; in 2011, the eurozone crashed; in 2013, the rupee tanked; in 2015, there was turbulence on the Chinese stock market; and in 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic. All these crises had two things in common. First, almost no one saw them coming – at least not precisely when or where or how. Second, they weren’t triggered by some enormous dramatic collapse, but by small, seemingly innocuous failures that cascaded into something far larger. For example, it just took a few small incidents that might otherwise have passed unnoticed – like the failure of a local mortgage lender in Southern California – to precipitate the subprime mortgage crisis.
All these events are examples of what physicists might call chaotic systems – deterministic in theory, but in practice so sensitive to initial conditions that tiny variations can spiral into radically different outcomes. A well-known example is the ‘three-body problem’, popularised by Liu Cixin’s 2008 novel of the same name and a 2024 Netflix adaptation. If you have two planets orbiting each other, you can write down neat equations to predict their paths forever. But add a third planet, and suddenly the maths explodes into unpredictability. The three bodies are still governed by clear laws, but an infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance.
The mathematician Edward Lorenz discovered something similar in 1961 when running weather simulations. His first attempt entered starting values rounded to six decimal places. His second try was rounded only to three. Yet the results diverged so dramatically that he initially suspected it was a computer fault. In fact, tiny differences in initial conditions had cascaded into entirely different weather systems. The atmosphere, like the economy, like a career, was deterministic in principle and unpredictable in practice.
As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do
Understanding the crash was one thing, but physics also helped me think about what came next. I had believed that inputs led to proportional outcomes; logically, in that world, the way to get ahead was to work as hard as possible. But physics teaches that chaotic systems play by different rules. They call instead for surge capacity, an extra buffer that allows them to absorb shocks. Without it, even small failures can lead to total collapse.
Think of a power grid. Most of the time it hums along without problem. But during an unexpected surge, such as a heatwave when millions of air conditioners are switched on at once, the system can overload and shut down. To prevent this, engineers design grids with slack in the system and extra capacity to handle unexpected spikes. Without it, a minor disruption can cascade into a blackout.
That was my mistake. As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do. We optimise everything from our schedules to our to-do lists – convinced that if we just push a bit harder, we’ll be fine. But the more we operate at our limits, the more fragile we become.
Physics provides a different lesson. Rather than relentlessly maximising, resilience is about building the capacity to withstand outlier events when they come. That might mean time slack, leaving space in our lives to recover rather than scheduling every minute. It might mean career slack, developing new skills, side projects and networks, rather than relying on a single path. Surge capacity might not prevent a crisis, but it sure helps survive one.
After my brief and bruising spell in consulting, I joined the civil service and spent most of the rest of my 20s working in government. I loved the sense of purpose, the colleagues and the privilege of shaping policy. Yet, if I’m honest, I still carried a small canker of resentment and jealousy towards my former consulting colleagues.
Compared with the UK national average, I know I was paid well as a civil servant. But with friends on six-figure salaries, it felt like I was failing at something. They could afford nicer clothes, cars and apartments. And then there was the magic trick of turning money into more money by buying assets, further widening the gap between their bank balances and mine. What stung wasn’t the inequality itself, but the perceived unfairness of the circumstances. I felt like I’d worked just as hard and still fallen behind. That distinction between inequality and unfairness became important to me.
Psychologists have shown that we’re wired to make this distinction from a very young age. In one Yale study, children were asked to split 10 coins between two people based on their performance on a task. When the two people performed equally, the children split the coins five-five – equal and fair. When one person did better, the children split the coins six-four – unequal but still fair. The interesting result happened when the children were told that both people had performed equally, but they now had to split 11 coins. With no way to maintain fairness, what could the children do? They decided to simply throw away one coin. Time and again, the children prioritised fairness.
People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged
This distinction is also evident in physics. Inequality, in the literal sense of unevenness, is built into the fabric of the Universe. In the very beginning, the cosmos was smooth and equal, a uniform fog. Only when tiny imperfections appeared – quantum fluctuations that allowed matter to clump in some places more than others – did galaxies, stars and planets emerge. Without that inequality, there would have been no structure, no possibility of life. In that sense, inequality is not always a flaw. Sometimes it is the condition for growth and diversity.
We see the same principle in natural systems. Rivers branch into unequal tributaries. Lungs and blood vessels evolve into networks with a few large arteries feeding many smaller ones. That inequality of size isn’t corruption or greed, but a kind of efficiency. It allows flow. Yet when the flow is blocked, like when a river silts up or a vessel clogs, the system fails. The problem, in other words, is not inequality itself, but unfairness: the obstruction of flow, the stacking of rules, the blocking of opportunity.
I think this is true in human systems, too. A society where some are richer than others may be tolerable, even healthy, so long as opportunities and resources can still move freely. But a society where opportunity is blocked, where the rules are stacked, where unfairness rules – people reject that instinctively. Just as I did when I looked at my friends’ consulting careers and wondered why I’d been cast out. Physics, then, suggests that a lack of justice is the real problem, rather than inequality per se. People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged.
Suddenly I saw this dynamic about fairness everywhere I looked. The financial crisis of 2007-08 wasn’t just about banks making risky bets, but about the perception that ordinary people paid the price while bankers walked away with bonuses intact. The eurozone crisis wasn’t just about debt, but about southern European countries being squeezed by rules they hadn’t set. The Occupy protests, the Arab Spring, Brexit, Donald Trump – all, in their different ways, were rebellions against unfairness.
Looking at the world through a physicist’s lens, these moments resemble phase transitions. You can heat water gradually and nothing seems to change – until you reach a critical threshold, a boiling point, and suddenly the whole system transforms from liquid to gas. Human societies, too, can bear strain for a while. But once unfairness feels systemic, the pressure builds until the system flips.
Small wonder, then, that in an age of tumult and transition, physics has found new admirers – especially among those who want to catalyse radical change, for better or worse. Musk speaks of first principles, Cummings of complexity. Their examples show how the tools of physics can shape thinking far beyond the laboratory. But in their hands, physics can feel more like a weapon than a framework, a way of bulldozing nuance in the name of clarity. For the rest of us, the challenge is not simply to borrow the garb and glamour of physics, but to carry forward its mindset – one that values humility as much as boldness, and curiosity as much as certainty.
That, I think, is where physics can still make its greatest contribution. Not by giving us ready-made answers or comforting illusions of inevitability, but by training us to question ourselves and live with the resulting uncertainty. Public discourse is saturated with physics, yet we need a deeper grounding in what it really teaches us about how to ask better questions, to test our own blind spots, and to admit what we don’t know. That need feels more urgent as new technologies only increase the temptation to reach for shortcuts.
We need artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both
So what would it take to embed this shift? My journey with physics began when I was a teenager, and that’s where I believe we need to start now. Too often, we present physics to young people as dry and technical. We teach them equations but not frameworks, facts without wonder. We rarely tell them that physics can help with the messiest parts of life, bound up as they are with uncertainty, resilience, decision-making.
In the UK, we make things worse by forcing students to choose just three or four subjects to study for the final two years of school. In practice, this often forces a split between being on the ‘science’ track or the ‘arts’ track. That false binary deprives us of exactly the kind of multidisciplinary thinkers we need: artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both.
When I visit schools now, I try to show physics as a kind of superpower. I want young people to feel that physics is something they can use, not something that excludes them. More than anything, I want them to feel it’s theirs.
I started this essay as a young man being shown the door by a superior. I ended it somewhere else entirely, with physics as a way of making sense of the messiest parts of life. But, really, what I’ve been edging up to is a story about how certain hardwon habits of mind can help us find meaning in the messiness and unpredictability of reality. For those of us who are not professional scientists, maybe the real task isn’t to love physics uncritically, or wield it carelessly, but to use it wisely. Physics shouldn’t be a shortcut to rock-solid certainty, so much as a way to live more humanely without it.

Norway raises cyber risk level to 'high' as attacks increase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:59:28 UTC
18:59:28 KST

Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) has raised the country’s cyber risk level to “high”, the second-highest on its scale, citing a deteriorating security situation and events in recent months.
Announcing the decision at a news conference on Tuesday, NSM Director Arne Christian Haugstoyl urged Norwegian businesses to strengthen their digital defences and immediately address known software vulnerabilities.
The authority warned that rapid advances in artificial intelligence are enabling threat actors to identify and exploit security weaknesses more efficiently.
“Businesses therefore have hours, not days or weeks, to close known vulnerabilities,” Haugstoyl said.
In a press release, NSM called on Norwegian companies to implement preventive security measures without delay and published 21 recommended actions for businesses across the country.
Justice and Emergency Preparedness Minister Astri Aas-Hansen also urged companies to assess their IT security and rapidly address vulnerabilities, broadcaster NRK reported.
Stolen data sold on dark web
According to Haugstoyl, successful cyber operations targeting Norwegian businesses have tripled over the past year, with several incidents causing serious consequences.
One publicly known case involved the municipality of Lorenskog, where a large amount of data was stolen in a breach.
The stolen information was later sold on the dark web.
The elevated risk assessment highlights growing concerns over cyber threat actors’ ability to exploit digital vulnerabilities, particularly as artificial intelligence accelerates their capabilities.

From Hitler’s rise to farmers’ misery in India: How the Great Depression changed lives far beyond America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:59:22 UTC
18:59:22 KST

In October 1929, billions of dollars in wealth evaporated from the American stock market, setting off an economic catastrophe that would reach far beyond Wall Street.Years of speculative buying, easy credit and inflated share prices had created a market built on the expectation that stocks would keep rising. When confidence collapsed, investors rushed to sell. The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged nearly 13 per cent on October 28 and another 12 per cent the following day, in what became known as Black Monday and Black Tuesday.But the crash was only the beginning. Bank failures, collapsing demand and business closures deepened the American downturn, while the withdrawal of US loans, falling international trade and the constraints of the gold standard carried the crisis across borders.
The result was the Great Depression, a global disaster that would help propel Adolf Hitler towards power in Germany, devastate farmers in colonial India, push millions of Britons into unemployment, and expose the fragility of economies around the world.What followed was not merely a financial collapse, but a decade of economic hardship and political upheaval that changed the course of the twentieth century.Germany’s economic collapse turned Hitler into a political forceThe Great Depression hit Germany at a time when its economy was already vulnerable, turning a global financial crisis into a national catastrophe.
The country was still struggling with the consequences of the First World War, including reparations, political instability and the devastating hyperinflation of 1923.Its recovery during the second half of the 1920s depended heavily on foreign credit, particularly loans from the United States.
Under the Dawes Plan of 1924, American lending helped stabilise German finances and supported economic recovery. But this dependence became a major weakness when the Wall Street crash struck in October 1929.As American banks and investors came under pressure, new lending dried up and foreign creditors recalled short-term loans. German banks and businesses struggled to obtain credit, investment declined and companies began cutting production and jobs.The consequences were severe. Industrial output contracted, businesses failed and unemployment soared. By 1932, around 5.6 million Germans were registered as unemployed, while industrial production had fallen by approximately 40 per cent from its 1928 level.The crisis also paralysed political decision-making. Chancellor Hermann Müller’s coalition government collapsed in March 1930 amid disagreements over unemployment insurance, paving the way for increasingly unstable governments that relied on presidential emergency powers.This economic desperation created an opening for Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party. They portrayed the Weimar Republic as weak and incapable of protecting ordinary Germans, promising jobs, national revival and decisive leadership. Their message appealed to sections of the middle class, struggling farmers, small business owners and workers disillusioned with the political establishment.The electoral shift was dramatic. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Nazis won just 2.6 per cent of the vote in the 1928 parliamentary election. Their share rose to 18 per cent in September 1930 and 37 per cent in July 1932, making them the largest party in the Reichstag.Nazi campaigning deliberately exploited the hardship. A 1932 election poster preserved by the US Holocaust Memorial Museum carried the slogan “Our Last Hope - Hitler”, presenting the Nazi leader as an answer to national despair.The party used mass rallies, newspapers, posters and speeches to promise economic recovery and political order. At the same time, it spread antisemitic conspiracy theories, blamed Jews and communists for Germany’s problems, and attacked democratic institutions.Hitler did not win an outright majority in a free national election. On January 30, 1933, President Paul von Hindenburg appointed him chancellor following negotiations with conservative political leaders who believed they could control him. The Nazis subsequently dismantled democracy and established a dictatorship.The Great Depression did not, by itself, cause Hitler’s rise. But the collapse of American lending, mass unemployment and the failure of Germany’s political leadership to restore confidence created conditions that the Nazis exploited with devastating consequences.India’s farmers were crushed as crop prices collapsedIn British-ruled India, the Great Depression turned a global economic crisis into a rural emergency, exposing the financial vulnerability of millions of cultivators and deepening resentment against colonial rule.As international demand weakened and agricultural prices plunged, farmers earned less from their crops but continued to face debts, rent and land revenue obligations. For many, the crisis meant selling produce at a loss, struggling to repay moneylenders and risking the loss of their land.
A 2022 research paper by historian Alok Oak, published in Studies in Indian Politics, documents the scale of the collapse. India’s agricultural price index fell from 203 in 1929 to 127 in 1931, using 1873 as the base year. The price index for raw cotton dropped from 133 to 70 over the same period. The decline was particularly damaging for cultivators who depended on commercial crops to generate cash for household expenses, rent and taxes.The crisis was compounded by the structure of the colonial economy. According to Oak, the British government refused to devalue the rupee amid concerns about meeting its foreign financial obligations. Meanwhile, Britain’s exports to India fell from £90.6 million in 1924 to £52.9 million in 1930, a decline of about 41 per cent. Falling trade and agricultural prices squeezed rural incomes and weakened economic activity.The timing was significant for India’s independence movement. At its Lahore session in December 1929, the Indian National Congress declared Purna Swaraj, or complete independence, as its goal. On January 26, 1930, Congress observed Independence Day, building momentum for a new phase of resistance.The Depression did not create the struggle against British rule, which had much deeper roots, but worsening economic conditions made questions of taxation, rural livelihoods and control over India’s economy more urgent.Mahatma Gandhi launched the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930, beginning with the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi. By challenging the British monopoly on salt and the tax imposed on a basic necessity, Gandhi chose an issue that affected Indians across social and economic divisions. The campaign transformed an everyday grievance into an act of mass resistance and helped bring the nationalist movement into the lives of ordinary people.Gandhi also urged Indians to boycott foreign goods, particularly British-made cloth, and promoted khadi and domestic production. These campaigns had a political and economic purpose. Reducing dependence on imported goods could challenge British commercial interests while encouraging Indians to support local producers. At a time when the global crisis had exposed the vulnerability of export-dependent economies, the message of economic self-reliance gained added significanceResearch by Stanford University political scientists Rikhil Bhavnani and Saumitra Jha has also identified a link between economic shocks and nationalist mobilisation. Their working paper found that districts producing export crops and affected by interwar trade shocks, including the Depression, were more likely to support the independence movement in the 1937 and 1946 elections.The researchers argue that these shocks helped bring agricultural exporters into a broader coalition demanding political change. The findings suggest that the Depression’s political consequences extended beyond immediate protests and influenced support for nationalism in subsequent years.The crisis also reinforced Gandhi’s emphasis on village industries and economic self-reliance. He argued that political freedom would mean little if rural India remained trapped in poverty and dependent on external markets. Gandhi promoted khadi and cottage industries as ways to create employment, strengthen village economies and reduce dependence on imported goods.In 1934, the All-India Village Industries Association was established to advance this wider effort. Historian Alok Oak argues that the Depression and the limits of colonial economic policy helped strengthen Gandhi’s focus on rural production and economic autonomy.Britain’s industrial decline pushed millions out of workBritain entered the Great Depression with its traditional industries already struggling to compete in international markets. Coal mining, shipbuilding, iron and textiles faced declining demand and growing competition, leaving industrial communities vulnerable when the Wall Street crash of 1929 further restricted global trade.As exports weakened and businesses cut production, unemployment soared. According to the UK National Archives, the number of unemployed people climbed to almost 3.5 million by 1932, with the North East of England, Scotland’s industrial lowlands and the mining valleys of Wales among the hardest-hit regions.
Families faced prolonged hardship, while the government’s introduction of a means test in 1931 intensified resentment among people seeking unemployment assistance.The crisis also exposed the limits of Britain’s monetary policy. The country had returned to the gold standard in 1925, tying sterling to a fixed gold value. As economic activity contracted, deflation deepened and unemployment rose, the government faced growing pressure to defend the pound while supporting the domestic economy.The situation became critical in 1931 as investors withdrew funds from London and the Bank of England lost gold reserves. The National Archives’ record of the government’s September 20 announcement says more than £200 million had been withdrawn from the London market since mid-July. Britain suspended the gold standard the following day.The political consequences were immediate. The Labour government under Ramsay MacDonald split over how to address the financial emergency and public spending. MacDonald subsequently formed a National Government with Conservative and Liberal support, while Labour suffered a major defeat in the October 1931 election.The departure from gold eventually gave Britain greater freedom to lower interest rates and allowed sterling to depreciate, helping exporters and supporting the early stages of recovery.A research paper by economists Jason Lennard and Meredith M Paker found that leaving the gold standard reduced unemployment by 2.7 percentage points in export-intensive industries relative to less export-dependent industries.Yet recovery was uneven. Traditional industrial regions continued to experience hardship, and hunger marches brought the plight of unemployed workers into public view.Britain’s experience demonstrated how the Great Depression could undermine established industries, destabilise governments and force a major economic power to abandon a monetary system it had once considered essential to financial stability.From Wall Street to the WorldThe Great Depression proved that an economic crisis does not stop at a country’s borders. A stock market collapse in America helped fuel the rise of Hitler in Germany, deepened the misery of farmers in colonial India, pushed millions of Britons out of work, and devastated economies around the world.
Yet the damage went far beyond lost jobs, failed banks and falling crop prices. Across continents, the Depression changed not only how people earned a living, but also how they viewed their governments and their future.Its legacy helped reshape the global economic order. The failure of protectionism, the instability of international finance and the inability of countries to contain the crisis through isolated national responses influenced the push for greater economic cooperation after the Second World War, including the Bretton Woods system.But the Depression’s most enduring warning is political as much as economic: when livelihoods collapse and governments appear powerless, public anger can become an opening for extremism.The crash began on Wall Street in 1929; its consequences reached farms, factories, homes and parliaments around the world, changing the course of the twentieth century.

Pentagon fires top military planner
The Pentagon has fired its top military strategist as Washington draws up contingency plans for a possible escalation of hostilities with Iran.
Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia has been removed from his position as director for strategy, plans, and policy (J5) on the Joint Staff, a spokesman confirmed late Wednesday, following media reports of his dismissal.
His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced into retirement a year ago amid reported friction with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine. Sylvia previously served as vice director of the J5.
The Pentagon did not explain Sylvia’s departure. His responsibilities included developing military strategies and plans to advise the chairman and the US president. He joins nearly two dozen senior military and civilian officials removed during Hegseth’s tenure.
The secretary has portrayed the dismissals as part of an effort to reduce the military’s bloated ranks of generals and make the armed forces more efficient and lethal. Critics, however, have characterized the shake-up as an ideological “purge.”
President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of renewing large-scale hostilities with Iran, including resuming the intensive bombing campaign conducted during the first 40 days of the conflict, which the US and Israel launched in late February. A potential escalation could be timed around the November midterm elections.
Military experts have widely expressed concern that another bombing campaign would fail to “finish the job,” as Trump has put it, while further increasing the conflict’s economic toll worldwide. Tehran has repeatedly warned that it is prepared to retaliate against US allies in the Gulf region if it faces renewed attacks.
Conversely, speculation has emerged that Trump could dismiss Hegseth after the midterms, when the opposition Democratic Party is expected to make gains in both chambers of Congress. Critics of the Iran war, including Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, have argued that firing the secretary could help Trump avoid a potential impeachment battle if Democrats take control of the House.
Trump’s public rhetoric remains supportive of Hegseth and his policies.

BJP's big win in MLC elections comes with setbacks in Nagpur and Varanasi
The MLC elections across four states brought both shock and cheer for the BJP and Congress. While the Congress suffered a humiliating defeat in Karnataka, where it is in power but failed to win a single seat, the BJP faltered in two constituencies which mattered the most. The alliance swept all four seats in Karnataka, won six of the 11 seats in Uttar Pradesh and secured four of the eight seats in Bihar. In Maharashtra, the ruling Mahayuti won two of the five seats, while the opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi secured three.The Congress's only victory came from Nagpur, a political stronghold of Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis and Union minister Nitin Gadkari. In Uttar Pradesh, the Samajwadi Party retained the Varanasi Teachers' constituency and was heading towards victory in the Graduates' seat, both of which it had won in 2020.
BJP-led NDA secured 16 of the 28 MLC seats across four states, while the SP won five seats in Uttar Pradesh and Congress retained Nagpur in Maharashtra.
What began as celebrations and sharp jibes at the Congress on Wednesday turned into a war of words on Thursday, as the results in Nagpur and Varanasi gave the opposition grounds to question the BJP's claims of electoral dominance.
BJP mocks Congress over 'zero' seats
As the early results came in on Wednesday, BJP leaders targeted the Congress over its poor performance, particularly in Karnataka, where the party is in power but failed to win a single seat.PM Modi took a swipe at the opposition party on X, pointing out that voting in the four states had taken place using ballot papers."Guess how many seats Congress won?" he asked.
The remark came amid the Congress's repeated allegations over electronic voting machines and its demand for a return to ballot-paper voting.BJP president Nitin Nabin also targeted the Congress, saying the party had failed to win public support despite voting being conducted using ballot papers."The people are repeatedly rejecting Congress' anarchist politics," Nabin said, adding that public trust remained with PM Modi irrespective of whether elections were conducted using EVMs or ballot papers.
BJP president Nitin Nabin targeted Congress over its poor performance in the MLC elections, pointing out that voting had taken place using ballot papers.
BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi also attacked Rahul Gandhi over his allegations of vote theft"Kamchori ki aadat chhodiye. Vote chori ka shabd apke muh se khud chhoot jayega," he said, asking the Congress leader to give up what he described as a habit of avoiding hard work.
Nagpur win gives Congress a chance to respond
Congress candidate and sitting MLC Abhijeet Wanjari defeated BJP's Sudhakar Kohale to retain the Nagpur Division Graduates' constituency after more than 40 hours of counting.Kohale had initially taken the lead before Wanjari overtook him through preferential votes.Nagpur is important for the BJP. Besides housing the RSS headquarters, it is associated with Fadnavis and Gadkari, both of whom campaigned for Kohale.The Congress had wrested the seat from the BJP in 2020, when Wanjari defeated Sandip Joshi. By retaining it in 2026, the party prevented the BJP from reclaiming a constituency it had dominated for decades.The Maharashtra Congress also targeted Fadnavis over a social media post in which he had claimed that the party had failed to win a single seat.

Sharing a screenshot of what it said was a deleted post by Fadnavis, the party accused him of celebrating before counting was complete. The post had described the Congress's performance as a "big fat zero".The Congress said Fadnavis had been forced to delete the post after the Nagpur result and warned that the outcome was only a trailer of future political battles.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh also responded to PM Modi's remarks, questioning the BJP's losses in Nagpur and Varanasi."The Prime Minister needs to introspect, but instead, he's lecturing others! Before counting Congress's seats, I wish he'd also reflect on why the BJP lost both seats in his own parliamentary constituency of Varanasi, and how Congress managed to defeat the BJP in RSS's stronghold of Nagpur?" Ramesh said."Mr. Modi, stop the trolling," he added, accusing the government of failing to address inflation, unemployment and weak private investment.Ramesh claimed that voters in Varanasi, Nagpur, Lucknow, Prayagraj and Patna had expressed dissatisfaction with the Centre's policies.
Varanasi setback gives SP a boost ahead of 2027
The BJP's biggest setback in Uttar Pradesh came from Varanasi, where the Samajwadi Party retained the Teachers' seat and established an unassailable lead in the Graduates' constituency.The BJP retained six of the 11 seats contested in the state, while the SP won four and was heading towards a fifth.The SP had won both Varanasi seats in 2020 as well. Six years later, the BJP has failed to dislodge the party from either constituency despite its strong presence in the region.Although the two MLC constituencies cover a wider geographical area than PM Modi's Lok Sabha seat, the results carry political significance given Varanasi's association with the Prime Minister since 2014.They also come after PM Modi's victory margin in Varanasi declined from nearly 4.8 lakh votes in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections to around 1.5 lakh in 2024.Across Uttar Pradesh, the SP's tally is set to rise from three seats in 2020 to five, while the BJP has retained its tally of six.The SP had also emerged as the largest party in Uttar Pradesh in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, winning 37 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats against the BJP's 33.BJP deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya acknowledged that the party had expected a better performance."These elections are decided by highly educated and qualified voters. The BJP has repeated its previous performance, but we expected to win more seats. We will examine why we fell short," Maurya said.The SP, meanwhile, has repeatedly accused the BJP of electoral irregularities, allegations the ruling party has rejected.On polling day, Akhilesh Yadav had claimed that the BJP was attempting to influence even the MLC elections, which have a limited electorate."If the BJP can do this in MLC polls for teachers and graduate constituencies where a limited number of people cast votes, one can imagine their preparation for the assembly polls," he had said.
What do the results mean for 2027?
The NDA's overall tally shows that the BJP and its allies remain ahead in these Legislative Council contests. But the results in Nagpur and Varanasi also show that the party has struggled to regain certain seats despite its strong presence in both regions.In Uttar Pradesh, the SP and Congress are preparing to contest the 2027 assembly elections together, hoping to build on their performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls.
The alliance won 43 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats in 2024, reducing the BJP's tally from 62 in 2019 to 33. Akhilesh Yadav has said the alliance will continue in 2027, although the two parties still need to settle their seat-sharing arrangement.The MLC results, however, cannot be treated as an indication of how the state will vote in the assembly elections. These contests involve a limited electorate of registered graduates and teachers, unlike assembly polls, which are decided by a much wider voter base.For the BJP, which is seeking a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh, the challenge will be to counter the opposition's gains. For the SP-Congress alliance, the question is whether it can repeat its 2024 Lok Sabha performance when the state's 403 assembly seats go to the polls in 2027.

Video receivers for UAVs virtually immune to EW deployed to special op zone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:50:31 UTC
18:50:31 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) units in the special military operation zone in Ukraine have received Spektr-K video receivers designed to operate at frequencies above 12 GHz, the press service of the developer, Sector JSC, reported.
It said that the device operates at frequencies that are beyond the reach of electronic warfare systems.
"Spektr-K video receivers designed to operate on ‘invincible’ frequencies have begun arriving in the special military operation zone, enabling stable signal reception in areas where electronic warfare systems are currently absent. The device consists of a proven Spektr receiver paired with an analog converter. The converter handles the lower range; together, they provide reception from 1,000 to 12,000+ MHz. It is precisely this expanded range that allows operation in areas where jammers (devices that create radio interference to block wireless communications) simply do not exist and are not currently expected to appear," the statement reads.
According to the developers, the upper limit of the reception frequency range is considerably broader than the officially stated range; however, "the exact values are being deliberately withheld." Sector also noted that before being deployed to the special military operation zone, Spektr-K was tested at the Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies.
"The device can be tuned to any arbitrary frequency, without being tied to ‘frequency grids’ or ‘standard channels.’ If a signal exists in principle, the receiver will work with it. A full scan of the band with RSSI display takes less than 12 seconds, which gives the operator a comprehensive picture of the airwaves," the press service noted. The device features a superheterodyne circuit with double conversion (splitting the signal into two intermediate frequencies), which "ensures stable operation amid interference and minimizes the impact of mirror channels."
"The receiver is versatile: it captures video signals from any analog drone - whether friendly or enemy - which also makes it an effective tool for intercepting video imagery as part of electronic intelligence systems. In addition, the device can be easily integrated into virtually any ground control station in place of the standard video receiver," Sector added.
Sector JSC is a developer and manufacturer of Russian specialized equipment for drones and unmanned aerial vehicles. The company’s products are used by both military and civilian UAV operators.

Ukraine will drive European security even without near-term NATO membership – Chentsov
Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration, Vsevolod Chentsov, made the statement in Brussels at the "Support Ukraine, Defend Europe" event organized by the Kyiv Security Forum's EU Office, an Ukrinform correspondent reports.
"We probably had to reconsider our attitude to NATO. Yeah, we've been looking to NATO direction as a security umbrella, but now I think it's a different story. "And it doesn't matter in that regard whether Ukraine immediately becomes a NATO member. Ukraine is and will be a factor of European security, an important partner for NATO, and hopefully soon member of the EU," Chentsov said.
He focused on Ukraine's accession to the EU as a security factor. Chentsov acknowledged that Kyiv had long viewed EU membership as an alternative "security umbrella" for Ukraine.
"We are changing this perception right now. Again, Ukraine is a factor for EU security in the broader sense, right? It's not only about the Ukrainian Armed Forces, probably one of the most capable armed forces on the continent, but we are also talking about Ukrainian experience in the broader domain of resilience. We are talking about democratic resilience and relevant instruments," he said.
He warned that Russia had now dared to threaten European countries directly and had begun sending "messages," such as the drone incident in Leipzig. Russia is resorting to blackmail and threats, but this is only the beginning.
"It's time for member states, for NATO to join forces with Ukraine and to learn how it is to live under constant threat. In our case, unfortunately, this is a physical kinetic threat, and in your cases, it is still a hybrid threat. So this is a change of the situation we are living through, and also a change of roles that we have to play, to perform," Chentsov said.

A man arrested after a gun attack in the Paris suburbs, killing one person and wounding seven including a child, has admitted to "targeting individuals who appeared to be Muslim, African, or North African", prosecutors said Thursday.
Last Friday, the 39-year-old, identified as Kevin T., opened fire with a submachine gun from a moving vehicle as he drove through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière, west of Paris. He was arrested later that day. Most of the victims were of foreign origin.
The attack came in an increasingly tense political climate, with presidential elections just six months away and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leading opinion polls.

Russia Reopens Azov Sea Passage for Grain Ships Following Months of Maritime Stagnation
Russia has allowed grain vessels to exit the Sea of Azov for the first time since July, granting temporary departure clearance to ships operating out of the commercial ports of Temryuk and Kavkaz.
According to three sources familiar with the matter, permission for departure was granted on October 26 with at least one vessel already passing through the Kerch Strait into the Black Sea, Bloomberg reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ships that are fully crewed and prepared for transit are currently permitted to submit applications to secure official clearance to leave harbor.
Despite the granted clearances, commercial vessels navigating across the Black Sea remain exposed to security risks and potential strikes while en route.
However, without a formal ceasefire, granting ships permission to depart the Azov Sea provides only a partial solution to the export bottleneck. Vessels navigating across the Black Sea remain highly vulnerable to drone attacks.
“Initial market reaction was brisk to the downside,” said Bertrand Oesterle, a commodity broker and vice president with StoneX. “Few believe a reopening of ports will significantly alter the risk outlook,” Bloomberg reported.
Over the course of a week from July 6 to July 12, 2026, Ukrainian unmanned systems carried out a systematic campaign in the Sea of Azov, striking 90 Russian vessels—including tankers, tugboats, ferries, and cargo ships—before reaching a total of 105 vessels targeted within eight days.
In response to the continuous drone attacks, Russia temporarily suspended navigation through the Don–Azov Canal and stopped processing applications for passage through the Kerch Strait to protect its fleet.
The operation targeted river-sea class tankers and support ships used to deliver fuel to Crimea, transfer crude oil into the Black Sea, and sustain Russian military logistics along the occupied coastline.
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said on July 10 that they had struck 13 Russian shadow fleet vessels in a single operation. Combined with an earlier FPV drone attack conducted by the Kairos unit, Ukrainian officials say 48 Russian vessels were hit over a five-day period.

Beijing has promoted General Zhang Shengmin, the key player in the anti-corruption campaign that has cut deep into the military’s top leadership, to its top decision-making body, the Politburo.
Zhang, who was last year promoted to vice-chair of the Central Military Commission (CMC), the top command body, was the military’s anti-corruption chief from 2018 until July this year, and is the top enforcer in Beijing’s fight against corruption in the People’s Liberation Army (PLA).
That drive left the seven-member commission with only two members – top commander President Xi Jinping and Zhang himself.

Two German citizens arrested over suspected Starlink equipment arson attempt in Vilnius
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:48:00 UTC
18:48:00 KST

Lithuanian authorities have identified two men suspected of attempting to set fire to Starlink equipment in Vilnius earlier this month. Both men, who live in Germany, have been arrested there at Bulgaria’s request, Lithuanian law enforcement officials said Thursday.
The suspects are foreign nationals in their 20s, one holding German and Turkish citizenship and the other German and Serbian citizenship, Saulius Briginas, deputy head of the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau, told reporters.
Investigators believe the men arrived in Lithuania on the eve of the incident and left immediately after the attempted arson.
“They have no ties to Lithuania and came here to commit this crime,” Briginas said. “This was not a spontaneous crime. They knew exactly where they were going and what they intended to do, and they prepared for it in advance.”
Nėrijus Puškorius, chief prosecutor in the Organised Crime and Corruption Investigation Division of the Vilnius Regional Prosecutor’s Office, said the men face suspicions of forming an organised terrorist group to commit terrorist crimes, participating in a terrorist group, travelling for terrorist purposes and committing a terrorist act that could have had serious consequences.
The most severe penalty for forming or participating in a terrorist group is 10 to 15 years in prison, Puškorius said.
The suspects had been placed on a wanted list, and Lithuanian authorities are cooperating with law enforcement partners in Bulgaria, Poland and Germany.
“The two individuals have been detained in Germany,” Puškorius said, adding that a decision on whether they will be transferred to Lithuania would be made later.
Briginas said the suspects were also linked to arson attacks targeting Starlink equipment in Poland and Bulgaria. More people have been detained in Poland in connection with the incidents, he said.
The two men arrested in Germany are not believed to have personally set fire to Starlink equipment in Poland, but investigators suspect they were involved in that crime as well.
The attempted arson in Vilnius took place several weeks ago at premises belonging to Lithuanian company Delska, where the US company SpaceX operates and stores Starlink equipment. Lithuanian politicians have linked the incident to Russia.
Similar incidents have been investigated in Bulgaria, where several antennas used to connect to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire, and in Poland, where a fire broke out at a Starlink satellite communications station in the country’s central region in September.

What are Southeast Asian nations doing to help the United States tackle its challenges? A reporter with the American right-wing organisation Turning Point USA put the question bluntly to US President Donald Trump’s defence chief this week in the Philippines.
As US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth pitched closer naval ties and maritime security cooperation at a gathering of defence ministers from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) and other regional powers, the question injected transactional politics into what is usually the realm of diplomatic niceties.
Analysts say the Pentagon chief’s proposal is unlikely to produce a substantial Asean-wide framework, given the bloc’s long-standing refusal to choose sides and the limits of its consensus-based system.

Israelis await final election results as Netanyahu faces uncertain path to power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:45:25 UTC
18:45:25 KST

Israelis on Thursday waited for final election results to confirm what they see taking shape: No majority of parliament seats for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies, or for the array of parties seeking to unseat him.
Difficult decisions lie in the weeks ahead, including whether some Jewish and Arab parties will team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu will toss that aside and join forces with the deeply divisive prime minister. While this plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
Final results could come as early as Thursday evening after about a half-million absentee ballots are counted from military personnel, diplomats, people in prisons and hospitals, and others. They are not expected to sway the results dramatically.
The chief rival to Netanyahu, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, in his first public statement since an address to supporters early on Wednesday, spoke of a government in service to all and reflecting the will of the people.
He did not mention the prospect of joining forces with the Arab-led parties that had a strong showing as some Palestinian citizens of Israel broke longstanding vows never to vote in a country in which they have long been subject to discrimination.
One of those Arab parties, the Joint List, late on Wednesday noted the “unprecedented show of strength" and the Jewish voters "willing to swim against the tide of racism." It said it was open to political cooperation.
Netanyahu's Likud party, despite receiving the most votes, has accused the Arab-led parties of stealing the election and asked the election committee to investigate. It did not provide specific evidence to support its claims. The election committee has said the number of reported irregularities in the relatively calm election was low.

Law Firm Linked to Elon Musk Started an ‘Election Integrity’ Organization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

The law firm that helped set up Elon Musk’s America PAC has created a new, nationwide “election integrity” organization aligned with Donald Trump’s false claims of election fraud, WIRED has learned.
The organization, a nonprofit called the Association of State and Local Election Officials, was established by a lawyer then at Lex Politica, the Musk-linked law firm founded by Chris Gober, who was chief counsel for America PAC in 2024 and is now running in Texas for a spot in the House of Representatives.
The board of directors, according to the nonprofit’s registration filing in Texas, boasts Florida secretary of state Cord Byrd, current and former state election officials in Georgia, a Michigan state representative, and the president of Cleta Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, a Trump administration-aligned election denial group. Byrd announced his involvement with the group—which he said won’t begin until after the election—alongside Florida governor Ron DeSantis in September, as the pair touted its mission, which aims to bring what they call “election integrity” policies down to the state and local level nationwide.
It’s not clear if Musk is involved in the organization. Until now, Musk has simply been a funder of Republican candidates and causes, and a benefactor of government contracts. Musk’s financial involvement in the midterm elections has been extensive: Musk’s America PAC is financing a sprawling canvassing operation aimed at helping Republican candidates get out the vote in November, and Musk is the single largest donor to Republican candidates this election cycle, spending more than $445 million, targeting Senate races key to maintaining a Republican majority. Since July, Musk has spent nearly as much money—$276 million—to boost Republican candidates as he did during the entire 2024 presidential election cycle. These elections are crucial for Musk. If Democrats win majorities in the House and Senate, Musk and his companies could be the subject of congressional investigations.
The link between a law firm that has worked with Musk and officials involved in purported “election integrity” activities is not surprising. For years, Musk has pushed the racist great replacement theory, which posits that minorities are systematically replacing white people in the US and in Western countries around the world. Election denialism—rooted in the unfounded theory of widespread voting by undocumented immigrants—is part of that racist theory of demographic societal change.
Musk has continually pushed election conspiracies that align with Trump’s false claims of election fraud, and this year, he’s doubled down. Musk has been a major disseminator of election misinformation this cycle, and recently boosted the false story that Texas US senate candidate James Talarico had been committed to a psychiatric facility in Ohio. America PAC has also spread inaccurate information about mail-in ballots.
The Association of State and Local Election Officials was first registered on June 17 by Michael Garcar as a nonprofit in Texas. At the time, Garcar was an attorney at Lex Politica, which was expanded after its lead lawyer, Gober, helped launch Musk’s America PAC. Gober has represented Musk’s and America PAC’s political interests in court cases in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.
On July 20, the Association of State and Local Election Officials was granted tax-exempt status by the IRS, according to an agency letter addressed to the organization at its Washington, DC, address. That address—a box in a UPS Store on Pennsylvania Avenue—is the same as the one Garcar listed on the organization’s Texas filing and belongs to Lex Politica, according to a US Supreme Court filing from one of the firm’s attorneys, Erin Hawley, wife of Senator Josh Hawley. The nonprofit’s Texas registration was first unearthed by True North Research, a progressive research group.
Garcar has since left Lex Politica and now works for Five Rings Law Group. The firm lists just two partners—both Lex Politica alums—and former Koch Industries lawyer Jenny Kim. Before launching Five Rings, Kim worked for Gober.
Garcar, Kim, and Gober did not respond to questions about Lex Politica’s ties to the Association of State and Local Election Officials.
At a September 24 press conference about the organization, Byrd and DeSantis announced their partnership with the nonprofit and said the Association of State and Local Election Officials will use Florida’s hard-line voting and election rules as a “blueprint” to enact similar policies across the country.
Byrd said the organization would “have state chapters to support, educate, and train local and state election officials on election integrity, because that’s something that the other side has been very good at.”
“They’re the ones going in and certifying and training people who run our elections, and not doing it in a way that we think comports with the law and voter trust,” Byrd said. The association “will be a national organization to promote election integrity, principles, and federal law and policy,” he added.
Under Byrd and DeSantis’ leadership, Florida has enacted rules and laws that voting rights advocates have criticized, including passing a state version of the federal SAVE Act that requires proof of citizenship at polling locations and prohibits the use of student IDs to vote beginning in 2027. “I’m very excited to head up that initiative and take what we’ve done in Florida as the blueprint, as the model for the nation, take it nationwide,” Byrd said in September.
The offices of Byrd and DeSantis did not respond to questions about their involvement with the organization.
The organization’s board is also staffed by Sharon Bemis, the president of Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, the country’s most prominent election denial organization; Julie Adams, an election denier who is both a member of the Fulton County Board of Elections in Georgia and a regional coordinator for the Election Integrity Network; Janice Johnston, who recently left the MAGA-dominated Georgia State Election Board; and Michigan state house representative Ann Bollin, who has coordinated with the Election Integrity Network.
The organization’s board members did not respond to questions for this story, though Johnston and Bollin have both previously denied being election deniers. The organization’s Texas registration contains no information about its work, and the group does not appear to have a web presence.
But the presence of Johnston and Adams on the board is telling.
In Georgia, Adams has made a name for herself by pushing Trump’s conspiracies about widespread election fraud and has sued multiple times for access to voting records with the help of the Republican National Committee. She has refused to certify results without being allowed to inspect voting records.
Johnston recently left Georgia’s State Election Board for what she said were “family and personal responsibility” reasons, and her time there was marked by turmoil, partisanship, and legal battles based on false fraud claims. Under her direction, the election board pursued specious investigations of Fulton County, supported mass voter purges championed by election denial activists, and worked to effectively eliminate voting machines.
Adams and Johnston have long targeted Fulton County for supposed fraud, and gleefully celebrated when, in January, the FBI raided an elections warehouse there, seizing tens of thousands of ballots from the 2020 election. Johnston was one of the unnamed witnesses in the FBI affidavit that preceded the raid, providing information about alleged double-counted ballots to the agency that had already been investigated and proven to have had no effect on the outcome of the 2020 election.
The Justice Department briefly fought in court to keep her name hidden from public view, but described a witness in the affidavit as “a Republican-appointed member” of the State Election Board who previously “was an obstetrician,” which identified Johnston. As the raid was being carried out, Johnston went live on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast from an SUV parked nearby.
When asked about Johnston’s presence on the board of the new Musk-linked election denial organization, Sara Tindall Ghazal, the lone Democrat on the Georgia State Election Board and Johnston’s former colleague, replied, “lol.”
“I mean this quite seriously, ‘lol.’ That’s my comment,” she tells WIRED.
And while Musk has quietly increased his political funding of Republicans, he has taken a bit of a step back from publicly discussing or posting about US politics and elections—with the exception of Talarico. His most recent post about voting is from September, when he responded to a question from Senator Mike Lee, a Republican from Utah. “Who benefits from noncitizen voting?” Lee asked on X.
“Democrats, which is why they push for open borders and noncitizen voting!” Musk responded. “Incentives explain behavior.”
Update: 10/29/2026, 12:20 PM EDT: WIRED updated the article to clarify True North Research is not linked to the Democratic Party.

Events in Macedonia for Italian Language Week
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:42:49 CET
18:42:49 KST

Italian Language Week in the World made a stop in Štip, at the Training Center of “Goce Delčev” University, with the interdisciplinary event “Italy—Genius and Style: Italian Cuisine and Fashion Between Tradition, Creativity, and Innovation.” On this occasion, the Italian Ambassador to Skopje, Paolo Palminteri, presented Jovana Karanikikj Josimovska, a professor of Italian Language and Literature at the same university, the insignia of Knight of the Order of the Star of Italy, in recognition of her many years of commitment to strengthening cultural relations between Italy and North Macedonia.
                                    
The ambassador also congratulated her on two recent major awards: the Flaiano Prize for her co-authored book on Italian literature and culture spanning the Baroque, the Enlightenment, and Neoclassicism, and the Ministry of Culture’s National Translation Award for her Macedonian translation of Pellegrino Artusi’s *Science in the Kitchen and the Art of Eating Well*, the first such translation into a South Slavic language.
                                    
Cuisine, along with fashion, took center stage at an event featuring Dusica Saneva Popova, a professor in the Department of Tourism, and Sanja Risteski, from the Department of Textile and Apparel Design, who explored the excellence of “Made in Italy” in gastronomy and design.
                                    
The Language Week program then continued in Strumica with the culinary workshop “Hands-On! Let’s Learn, Knead, and Create,” an opportunity to learn, experiment, and give shape to creativity through cooking. Finally, at the North Macedonia Film Archive in Skopje, there will be a screening of the film *Cercatori d’angeli* (2026) by Leopoldo Pescatore, organized in collaboration with the Swiss Embassy.

Moscow says 1,214 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:42:12 UTC
18:42:12 KST

The Russian Defence Ministry reported on Thursday that 1,214 Ukrainian drones targeted 20 Russian regions overnight.
This figure exceeded the previous largest-ever attack reported by Russia on September 20, when 1,110 drones were launched from Ukraine.
"During the past night, air defence duty forces intercepted and destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said 613 drones targeted the capital region overnight.
"Most of them were neutralised by Defence Ministry air defences on distant approaches," he said on the Russian social media platform Max.
Sobyanin noted that 231 drones were destroyed on the approach to Moscow during that period.
Russia’s civil aviation authority, Rosaviatsia, said temporary restrictions on arrivals and departures were imposed at Moscow’s Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports “to ensure flight safety.” They were later lifted.
Two planes flying from Istanbul to Moscow turned back in mid-air and returned to Istanbul because of the restrictions at Vnukovo, a source in air traffic control services told the TASS news agency.
Restrictions were also imposed at airports in 18 other Russian cities, according to the report.
Ukraine has yet to release a statement regarding the claims, which could not be independently verified due to the ongoing conflict.

Early warning radar flown on Protector type airframe
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:40:23 GMT
18:40:23 KST

General Atomics and Saab have flown an airborne early warning radar on an uncrewed MQ-9B, the same aircraft the Royal Air Force operates as Protector, tracking fighter jets and commercial aircraft along with maritime targets at long range during months of testing, according to the companies.
The flights used a Saab LoyalEye radar carried in payload pods on a General Atomics MQ-9B operating from the company’s Desert Horizon facility in southern California, and demonstrated simultaneous tracking of several airborne and maritime targets, including multiple instrumented fighter jets acting as targets.
David Alexander, president of General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, said: “This has been one of the most highly anticipated flight tests we have performed. The level of customer interest in AEW capability on MQ-9B throughout the world is extremely high. It just makes sense.”
Carl-Johan Bergholm, head of Saab’s surveillance business area, said: “This flight test underscores Saab’s commitment to evolving airborne early warning capabilities to meet future operational needs. LoyalEye complements existing capabilities by adding flexibility, extending reach, and enabling a more efficient use of resources in demanding environments.”
Airborne early warning has always meant a large crewed aircraft, because the radar, the operators and the fuel to stay up all demanded size, and the number any air force can afford has fallen with every generation. Britain is buying three Wedgetail aircraft to replace a Sentry fleet that once numbered seven. The Royal Air Force will hold one of the smallest early warning forces of any major air arm.
Putting the radar on an uncrewed aircraft changes the arithmetic of that problem, because an MQ-9B can stay airborne far longer than a crewed jet, costs a fraction as much to buy and operate, and risks nobody if it is lost. What it cannot do is carry the battle management staff who make a Wedgetail more than a big flying radar, so the companies describe the command and control function being performed elsewhere, on the ground, on a ship or aboard an existing crewed aircraft, etc.
Protector entered Royal Air Force service at RAF Waddington this year, replacing Reaper, and ministers confirmed this month that eleven of the sixteen aircraft on order have been delivered. The type is certified to fly in civil airspace. Earlier armed drones were not, and that certification is why Protector can fly over Britain.
General Atomics is also developing a short take-off and landing version of the MQ-9B intended to operate from aircraft carriers, a configuration the Royal Navy has watched closely as it works out what flies from HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Queen Elizabeth alongside the F-35B.
Saab’s existing airborne early warning radars fly on the GlobalEye, based on the Bombardier Global 6000 business jet, which Sweden operates and which has been sold to the United Arab Emirates and ordered by Denmark.

Trump-Putin diesel deal has not lowered US fuel prices – WSJ
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:40:00 EET
18:40:00 KST

Trump-Putin diesel deal has not lowered US fuel prices – WSJ
Average US diesel prices have risen by 7 cents since US President Donald Trump reached a deal with Russia on diesel supplies.
Source: The Wall Street Journal
Details: According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average price of a gallon of diesel in the US reached US$6.35 on Wednesday 28 October (about US$1.68 per litre), up from US$6.28 per gallon when Trump announced the deal.
On 9 October, Trump wrote that Russia was expected to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to US and global markets in October, a further 500,000 tonnes in November, and another 1 million tonnes immediately afterwards.
However, the newspaper reported that analysts remain sceptical that the deal will help bring down high diesel prices in the US and worldwide.
Experts also say Russia may be unable to export the promised volumes of diesel because of the poor condition of its oil refineries and export restrictions.
Even if Russia manages to do so, the promised volumes would cover only a fraction of the global shortfall. They amount to just over 100,000 barrels per day in October and around 125,000 barrels per day in November. In 2025, Russia was able to ship around 800,000 barrels per day.
Background:
- On 22 October, the first tanker carrying 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel set sail for New York. The vessel is expected to arrive in the US on 7 November. Two more tankers were subsequently added.
- One of the three tankers is under sanctions imposed by the EU, the UK and Canada.

Jetten backpedals on plans to tax the royals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:38:45 UTC
18:38:45 KST

Jetten backpedals on plans to tax the royals
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Prime minister Rob Jetten is refusing to act on calls for the royal family to pay taxes, despite his party D66 having actively backed the idea for years.
The Dutch royals receive personal salaries, which is only a fraction of their overall wealth, and plans to tax them on their incomes have been debated by parliament for more than a decade.
The king, for example, will receive roughly €7.5 million from the state next year, of which €1.2 million is personal income and the rest covers staff and running costs. He pays no tax on it. In January 2024 D66 tabled a motion calling on the government to change the constitution so that the royals would pay income tax.
For the first time in history, the motion got two-thirds parliamentary support, with over 100 MPs backing it. But the successive prime ministers Mark Rutte and Dick Schoof both refused to push the plan forward.
Last December D66 also voted for a similar motion by GroenLinks-PvdA (Pro) MP Laura Bromet, asking that royals who receive an allowance pay the same taxes as everyone else.
Now Jetten appears to be doing the same. He told MPs on Wednesday that the yearly debate had become an “unproductive dynamic” and that he wants a broader review of a “future-proof monarchy” instead.
He promised the Christian Democrats (CDA) that it would not lead to a ceremonial monarchy. Ending the exemption would also require a change to the constitution, which exempts the king from tax on his allowance.
Opposition parties are furious at his backpedalling on the issue. “D66 was angry every year that the motions were not implemented. Now the party has a unique opportunity to reflect on the future of the monarchy,” Socialist (SP) MP Sandra Beckerman told NOS. “You would think that you would seize that opportunity.”
Dutch republican group Republiek, which campaigns for the abolition of the monarchy, wrote an open letter to Jetten saying “a large majority of the population indicates time and again in polls that they are in favour of the king paying taxes.”
“For twelve years now, there has been a majority in the House of Representatives in favour of abolishing the tax exemption for the royal family. Time and again, the plans failed during the implementation by the prime ministers. But now you are our prime minister.”
The letter is signed off using the campaign slogan D66 used to come to power in the current coalition: “In your own words: het kan wel” (it’s possible).
MPs will soon vote on a motion from Bromet backing Jetten’s review, and one from Beckerman telling the cabinet to act on the royal tax motions parliament has already passed.
