Taiwan semiconductor output forecast to top NT$9.1 trillion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:36:46 UTC
18:36:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The nation's semiconductor industry output is forecast to exceed NT$9.1 trillion (US$279.6 billion) this year, Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association Chair Hou Yung-ching (侯永清) said Thursday.
The figure would represent a 40.9% increase from last year, when industry output was NT$6.5 trillion. Thirty years ago, output stood at NT$180 billion, according to CTEE and Tai Sounds.
Hou said Taiwan ranks first globally in wafer manufacturing and semiconductor packaging and testing, and second in chip design. Its comprehensive industry structure and close cooperation across the supply chain have supported growth.
Rapid AI development is driving demand for related equipment, materials, and chemicals, prompting suppliers to expand production capacity. Securing land for new facilities has been a particular hurdle, Hou said.
With government assistance, the association has helped suppliers identify suitable sites for expansion. Four materials suppliers are expected to begin construction in April next year, while another seven are still completing the necessary procedures.
The association has also worked with the Industrial Technology Research Institute and chipmaker TSMC to establish a platform for equipment suppliers to test their products and better understand manufacturers' requirements. The initiative aims to help suppliers address technical gaps and develop products that meet industry needs.
Hou said the country's semiconductor industry has significant room to grow, although energy supply and other external factors remain challenges. As the sector expands, the association has added 18 international corporate members since 2023, bringing its total membership to 220, up from 57 founding members.

Taiwan's Wan Hai Lines expands Indian market presence with new route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:36:26 UTC
18:36:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wan Hai Lines Ltd. is expanding its presence in the Indian market with the launch of a new shipping service in late November.
The new service will connect markets in Vietnam, southern China, Malaysia, and western India. Container ships with capacities of 2,800 to 3,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) will operate on a 35-day rotation, according to CTEE.
Wan Hai expects the new route to complement its existing network and strengthen shipping connections across the region. The port rotation will cover Haiphong, Qinzhou, Nansha, Shekou, Port Klang, Mundra, Nhava Sheva, and Port Klang before returning to Haiphong.
The company reported consolidated revenue of NT$21.8 billion (US$669 million) in September, up 97.63% from a year earlier. Revenue for the first nine months reached NT$136.2 billion, an annual increase of 27.28%, according to UDN Money.
Wan Hai said shipping demand has recovered more strongly than in previous years following China's National Day holiday in early October, as manufacturing and shipping activities gradually resume. Cargo owners are arranging shipments earlier than usual to reduce supply chain uncertainty caused by port congestion, shipping delays, and fluctuating fuel costs.
The fourth quarter is traditionally a peak season for intra-Asia short-sea shipping. With cargo volumes continuing to grow and freight rates remaining at relatively favorable levels, Wan Hai expects its operating momentum to remain stable.

Brussels rejects Baltic states’ €500 million anti-drone request, suggests borrowing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:34:00 UTC
18:34:00 KST

The European Commission has responded to a request by Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia for 500 million euros to develop anti-drone defences, but has offered no new funding on the scale sought by the three Baltic states.
Defence ministers from the three countries sent a letter to the European Commission in late September requesting urgent financial support to strengthen defences against drones.
Several stray drones have entered the Baltic airspaces this year amid air attacks between Ukraine and Russia.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, Estonian Defence Minister Martin Herem and Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis sought the funding to develop an anti-drone system that could also serve as a model for other European Union countries.
The letter was classified, but Kaunas told LRT that the Baltic states wanted to combine drone detection, artificial intelligence and interception technology into an integrated air defence system.
“Air defence and anti-drone solutions are important not only for our region but for all of Europe. Lithuania has taken the lead in developing an anti-drone air defence system,” Kaunas said.
The Baltic states had hoped the European Commission would approve additional funding for regional anti-drone defences before the end of this year. The commission previously told LRT.lt that it was carefully assessing the request and took member states’ concerns very seriously.
However, Andrius Kubilius, the European commissioner for defence and space, told LRT on Wednesday that the commission had sent its response but could not offer the additional funding the Baltic states had sought.
“One possibility now is to make use of additional funding under the SAFE instrument. We will announce a new call in the near future, because 21 billion euros remained after the first call,” Kubilius said.
He added that there were few other substantial funding opportunities available through EU budget programs because the current budget period was nearing its end.
Funding for anti-drone measures may also be available through the Integrated Border Management Fund, LRT understands, although the sums involved would be far below the 500 million euros requested by the Baltic states.
SAFE loans offer an alternative
The Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, instrument, launched last year, provides 150 billion euros in favourable loans for defence procurement across the EU.
The scheme offers loans with repayment periods of up to 45 years and advance payments of up to 15%. The loans are financed through EU-level borrowing, benefiting from the bloc’s AAA credit rating.
Lithuania has been allocated access to up to 6.375 billion euros in SAFE loans. The government plans to use the funds to establish a land forces division, develop the Baltic Defence Line, strengthen air defence, purchase ammunition and military equipment, and finance other military modernisation projects.
In October, Lithuania’s Finance Ministry submitted its first request to the European Commission for a 1.06-billion-euro loan under the scheme.
If approved, the request would bring Lithuania’s total SAFE funding, including a 800-million-euro advance received in June, to 1.86 billion euros, about 29% of the country’s total allocation.

Explainer-How could Israel break the election deadlock?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:32:03 UTC
18:32:03 KST

Explainer-How could Israel break the election deadlock?
JERUSALEM, Oct 29 - Israel's election this week was indecisive and there is no clear winner poised to form a government. Benjamin Netanyahu remains in office as caretaker prime minister, but faces a parliament stacked with an opposition majority vying to oust him.
Here are some scenarios that could follow:
ANOTHER ELECTION
After the formal final election results are published next week, Israel's President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with party representatives and then taps the candidate whom he deems to have the best chance to form a government.
If the candidate fails, another can try and if that candidate fails, the Knesset can nominate another. There is a deadline for the process of around 100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is held.
Herzog said on Wednesday that everything must be done to avoid another election and urged the parties to come with an open mind to the consultations with him.
UNITY GOVERNMENT
Netanyahu's Likud party, emerging as the largest in the Knesset, forms a coalition that would likely include centrist and right-wing opposition parties such as Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, the second-largest party, Avigdor Lieberman's Israel Our Home and Naftali Bennett's Together faction.
That grouping would secure 66 seats, a majority in the 120-seat parliament.
However, this option appears remote at this point because it would mean Netanyahu would likely have to abandon his natural political allies, the far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties. Further, the opposition parties would have to break their main election pledge to their voters: unseating Netanyahu.
Still, if neither camp is able to form a government at the end of weeks of protracted negotiations, a unity government may emerge as a last option.
Renewed fighting with Iran, or other players, could also push the sides together.
EISENKOT MINORITY GOVERNMENT
If Herzog taps Eisenkot first, he could try to form a government with Yashar's natural allies — Together, The Democrats and Israel Our Home — propped up by Israel's two Arab parties, even if they are not members of this government: Ra'am and the Joint List.
Eisenkot's camp would number 48 seats, according to the latest vote tally, with the Arab parties numbering 19 seats that together reach a 67-seat majority.
But even if Eisenkot reverses his campaign pledge not to have Arab parties in government and accepts their support, it would be a hard sell to many Israelis whose attitudes toward Israel's Arab minority have hardened further since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack.
Netanyahu has focused his campaign on delegitimizing support from Arab parties, who surged to record heights in Tuesday's election, and for now, only The Democrats, a centre-left party, has come out publicly calling for their inclusion.
Both Arab parties have signalled that they are prepared to cooperate with Eisenkot's camp.
Ra'am joined Bennett's government in 2021, the first time an independent Arab party entered an Israeli coalition. That government collapsed after 18 months.
NETANYAHU FINDS A MAJORITY FOR A RIGHT-WING GOVERNMENT
Netanyahu's coalition has fallen from its original 64 seats to 53, according to the latest election results. But Israel's longest-serving leader is viewed as one of its most skilled politicians and he could split the opposition by peeling away members of its parties and bringing them over to his side.
He has managed to do this before, including as opposition head in the run-up to the 2022 election, which he won. But the coalition he was battling at the time had a far narrower lead and he did not need too many defectors to destabilize his political rivals. REUTERS

Germany news: Merz says North Korea threatening Europe's freedom

- VW has been struggling to keep pace with competition from China and to transition to electric vehicles
- Berlin's mayoral candidate Elif Eralp is under fire over her interview with Der Spiegel
Here are the main headlines from and about Germany on Thursday, October 29, 2026:
Elif Eralp: Berlin's potential next mayor caught in dispute over private interview remarks
A German news magazine's decision to publish private interview notes has sparked a controversy surrounding Berlin's potential next mayor.
On Thursday, Der Spiegel published internal comments on an interview by Elif Eralp, who led the socialist Left Party (Die Linke) to victory in September's state election. Her office had accidentally included the remarks while approving an interview for publication.
In the notes, Eralp expressed fears for her family's safety if she publicly named Ibrahim Ibrahim, a pro-Palestinian activist who is reported to have links to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which the EU designates a terrorist organization. Ibrahim had attended the Left Party's election-night celebrations and was photographed with prominent Left Party Bundestag member Ferat Koçak.
Eralp also cited advice she received from Berlin police against publicly naming individuals linked to organized crime, though that advice was reportedly related to a separate case. Der Spiegel questioned whether her fears could affect her independence as mayor. Eralp rejected suggestions that she could be intimidated and pledged firm action against terrorism and organized crime.
She is reportedly considering legal action against the magazine and a complaint to Germany's Press Council. The magazine has also faced criticism for publishing remarks intended for internal use, raising questions about the balance between public interest, privacy, and journalistic ethics.
The timing is significant. Eralp, the daughter of Turkish immigrants, could become Berlin's first Left Party mayor and the first woman of Turkish descent to hold the office. Her party won 25.7% of the vote in September's election and hopes to form a government with the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens. Both prospective partners have approved formal coalition negotiations.
The Left must decide whether to follow suit at a party conference this Saturday, October 31. The far-left party is also facing accusations of antisemitism involving some of its members. Newly elected lawmaker Vanessa Emde faces possible exclusion from the Left's parliamentary group following comments questioning whether states, including Israel, have an inherent right to exist. The Left has been part of Berlin coalition governments before but has never led one. The controversy comes at a pivotal moment in its effort to do so.
German diplomacy: From Asia to Latin America
Germany's leaders are on a foreign relations push, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz on a trip to South Korea, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul in Panama and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier in China.
Merz spoke of the threat North Korea posed to Europe's freedom by supplying troops to fight in Russia's invasion of Ukraine. He wraps up his visit with a trip to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, meanwhile, is in Panama where he is visiting ahead of traveling to Atlanta for the G20 meeting.
Wadephul is there to promote free trade and also handed over humanitarian supplies to his Panamanian counterpart Javier Martinez-Acha Vasquez.
And then German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities in China and picked up a ping-pong paddle for a game with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll, who is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.
Wadephul visits Panama ahead of traveling to the G20 meeting in Atlanta
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul landed in Panama on Wednesday evening for a visit.
After his arrival at Panama City airport, Wadephul handed over humanitarian supplies to his Panamanian counterpart Javier Martinez-Acha Vasquez.
The aid shipment is made up of about 20 tons of supplies. Panama was hit by a powerful earthquake earlier this month.
The supplies include water filters, blankets, tarpaulins, cots and kitchen sets worth over €150,000 ($167,000).
More than 5,000 people are still being housed in emergency shelters, weeks after the magnitude-7.7 quake on October 9, which resulted in injuries and damaged hundreds of buildings.
Wadephul also thanked the Central American country for maintaining the Panama Canal "so responsibly and ensuring it is fit for the future, as well as more generally focusing on preserving balance in the region."
Restrictions on other sea routes due to the conflict in the Middle East has meant that the Panama Canal is more important to global trade than ever.
Wadephul is due to hold talks on Thursday with Martinez-Acha Vasquez and President Jose Raul Mulino.
Wadephul will travel to the US state of Georgia for the G20 summit in Atlanta on Friday and Saturday.
IN DEPTH: The search for President Steinmeier's successor
Several names are being floated to replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's ceremonial head of state — including some that could be the first woman to hold the post.
Read our full report here.
Ping-pong vs. politics: Steinmeier takes on German Olympian Boll
After delivering his speech at Peking University, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities to play ping-pong with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll.
In the university sports hall, the two faced each other, accompanied by two Chinese participants — a referee and the university president. Right from the start, Steinmeier downplayed his chances, and subsequently lost 1–7.
Boll, who won silver at the Beijing Olympics in 2008, is the most successful German table tennis player of all time.
He won several Olympic medals, as well as titles in World Cups and World Championships during his storied career, which saw him ranked as the number 1 player in the world in 2003, 2011 and 2018.
To this day, Boll remains one of the best-known Germans in China, where ping-pong is unofficially considered the national sport.
Boll is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.
Steinmeier calls for fair trade in China during Bejiing visit
Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Thursday called on China to reduce economic imbalances between the two countries, as well as between China and Europe.
Steinmeier, who was speaking at the renowned Peking University, also urged China to work with Germany and other European nations to strengthen the international, rules-based order and "to advocate for peace and free global trade."
The German president, who holds a largely ceremonial role, spoke of his respect for China's rapid development in its economy, technology and politics, calling China a "defining world power."
But Steinmeier added, "With greatness and power comes great responsibility."
"We are not concerned about China's rise. We are watching how China rises," he said.
"We do not want to decouple from China; on the contrary, we want to structure trade in such a way that it continues to benefit both sides." This, he said, requires fair and uniform rules.
Steinmeier was referring to the high barriers European companies face when trying to operate in the Chinese market. Since China heavily subsidizes its exports to Europe, the European market comes under pressure too quickly.
This poses "the danger of one-sided vulnerability," Steinmeier said. Europeans cannot want this for their economy, just as "China does not want it for its economy."
What did Steinmeier say about China and the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East?
He also called on China to exert more influence on Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.
According to Steinmeier, China's interests are also at stake in this war, just as they are in the Middle East. As a major trading power, China also needs free sea lanes, intact supply chains, and a secure energy supply.
"The longer these conflicts persist, the weaker the global economy as a whole becomes — and with it, one of its largest economies: China," the president said.
Steinmeier addressed future issues in which China should take a particular interest: climate change and artificial intelligence. He appealed to his hosts, saying that when it comes to AI, "we should jointly establish international guidelines so that the technology remains under human control," he said.
On the final day of his state visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership and hold talks with, among others, President Xi Jinping.
Steinmeier is making his first visit to China in eight years, as he seeks to boost bilateral ties.
Friedrich Merz accuses North Korea of threatening Europe's freedom
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday said North Korea was threatening "freedom throughout Europe" by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Merz highlighted that Russia was supplying weapons to North Korea.
The chancellor said this arrangement therefore shows how "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects Korea's security."
North Korea has boosted its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pyongyang has provided Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. It has also, according to South Korean intelligence services, sent about 15,000 soldiers to fight alongside Russian forces.
In exchange, Russia provides financial backing, military technology and security guarantees to North Korea.
Before Merz's arrival on Thursday, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, according to the South Korean military.
At the start of his visit, Merz said he hoped that Korea would eventually be unified. The peninsula has been split along the 38th parallel since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953.
Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen their two nations' strategic and security ties, which includes joint military exercises and exchange of intelligence.
The chancellor is expected to conclude his trip to South Korea with a visit to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.
WATCH: Can Germany's pivot to Asia end its reliance on China?
Germany is looking for new partners in Asia. As Chancellor Friedrich Merz travels to Singapore, Japan and South Korea, Berlin is trying to reduce its economic dependence on China while adapting to a changing global order. But can countries in the Indo-Pacific, besides China, help Germany diversify its trade and security partnerships?
This week on Berlin Briefing, DW's Giulia Saudelli speaks with DW Business Reporter Steven Beardsley and DW Chief Political Correspondent Nina Haase, who is traveling with the chancellor.
They discuss Germany's push to "de-risk" from China, growing security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, and whether middle powers can work together to shape the future global order.
Germany, South Korea upgrade ties to 'enhanced strategic partnership'
Germany and South Korea on Thursday pledged to work together on the economy, energy and security and high-tech industries, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said.
The South Korean leader made the announcement after a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Seoul.
At a joint press conference, Lee told reporters that he had asked Merz for Germany's backing in securing favorable treatment for South Korea as part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act.
The two leaders also agreed to improve bilateral ties to an "enhanced strategic partnership," Lee said.
8-year-old girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German zoo
An eight-year-old girl sustained serious injuries after she was attacked by at least one wolf at a wildlife park in Brandenburg in east Germany.
The child was brought to hospital by a rescue helicopter on Wednesday.
Local officials said a zookeeper had helped prevent other children from being attacked.
Police are investigating how and why the attack occurred, which took place during a special program for children.
Police on Thursday said their investigation was centered on a staff member who was in the enclosure with the children, a spokeswoman said.
The Teltow-Fläming district administration said the incident happened before the wildlife park's regular opening hours as part of an "Animal Keeper Day" for children.
The administration also said the attack had taken place in the polar wolf enclosure.
"While the animals in the wildlife enclosure were being watered, the wolves kept there attacked a girl and seriously injured her," the district administration said.
The zookeeper's quick action prevented "further harm to two other girls" who were also at the scene, the district added.
The park will remain closed for the time being, officials said, as authorities launch a safety review at the wildlife park, which is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin.
Police are still probing the circumstances that led to the children being inside the enclosure.
The Johannismühle Wildlife Park said it was cooperating with authorities but could not provide further details due to the open investigation.
"We deeply regret the incident, and the affected family has our full support," the park said.
The wildlife park was closed until further notice "due to technical reasons," a sign at the entrance said on Thursday.
A wolf bit a woman in a busy shopping area in Hamburg this year, in what is thought to be the first such attack since wolves were reintroduced to the country in 1998.
German Chancellor Merz says he hopes for Korean reunification
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is visiting Seoul, said at the start of his visit that he hopes North and South Korea will eventually be reunited.
The Korean Peninsula has been divided into two states since the Korean War ended in 1953.
Merz pointed to his own country's division between West and East Germany for much of the second half of the 20th century.
"Korea and Germany are united by the painful experience of division," he wrote in the guest book during his meeting with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
"I also wish for the people of Korea what we are fortunate to experience in Germany: unity in freedom."
North Korea is a largely isolated dictatorship ruled by Kim Jong Un, while the South is a democracy that has close ties with the West.
The two Koreas technically remain at war since a truce ended hostilities.
Merz is set to visit the demilitarized zone (DMZ), which divides the two countries, on Friday.
The German chancellor's visit to South Korea is the last stop on his tour of Asia this week, which has also seen him visit Japan and Singapore.
IN DEPTH: Bayern Munich coach's hospital stay highlights need for better support
Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany has just returned home from the hospital, admitting that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"

WATCH: Why big automakers are losing China
They were once top sellers in China. Now the likes of Volkswagen, Toyota and Honda are losing ground to a new generation of Chinese carmakers. What happened?
VW reports 3rd quarter losses of €5.8 billion
Volkswagen (VW) reported third quarter losses of €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) on Thursday, as it faces rising competition from China.
Germany's biggest car maker had reported a loss of just over €1.07 billion in the same period last year.
Volkswagen, like other car makers, has struggled to keep pace with fierce competition from China, the world's biggest car market. VW has also struggled with the transition to electric vehicles and with declining demand.
Volkswagen last month warned that its 10-brand group, which includes makers such as Audi, Seat and Skoda, was facing a 10-billion-euro hit to its annual profits.
The most significant hit came from Porsche, Volkswagen's luxury sports car and SUV subsidiary. Porsche, which was once a major driver of profits for the VW group, was also one of the main factors behind VW's quarterly losses in 2025.
The luxury brand has been hit by a sales slump in China, US tariff policy and its electric vehicle strategy.
VW announced this year that it plans to cut over 100,000 jobs across the group by the end of the decade as it tries to reduce costs. It announced on Thursday that its restructuring would cost the company 31 billion euros.
The company is considering or has decided to shut down multiple German factories — including plants in Zwickau, Emden, Hanover, and Neckarsulm.
"What matters now is swift and consistent implementation," Arno Antlitz, VW's chief financial officer said in a statement. "We cannot lose any time and need to act quickly and decisively."
For more on this story, read our full report by DW's Mark Hallam.

All children evacuated from Sumy Oblast's border areas, but 34,000 civilians remain
All children have been evacuated from border areas in Sumy Oblast where mandatory evacuation has been ordered, but around 34,000 civilians still remain there.
Source: Oleh Hryhorov, Head of Sumy Oblast Military Administration, in an interview with Ukrinform
Quote from Hryhorov: "Around 34,000 civilians still remain there. They are all different people, and we are constantly explaining the situation to them. We regularly have two or three people refusing evacuation."
Details: Hryhorov recalled that residents of 213 settlements in the oblast are subject to evacuation. More than 57,000 people, including 8,000 children, have already been evacuated from these areas.
He also said that the regional administration is not currently planning to announce a mass evacuation for the winter from the oblast's major cities, including Sumy and Shostka.
Background: In June 2025, Hryhorov reported that more than 60% of residents had left border areas in the oblast. All residents had been evacuated from 60 settlements.

Spanish Transport Minister Blames Train Crash That Killed 69 on ‘Inexplicable’ Error
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Spain's Transport Ministry has increased the provisional death toll from Wednesday's high-speed train collision to 69. The number of people injured is pending confirmation.
Police have appealed to family members of the crash victims to provide DNA sampling to help with the identification process.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Thursday said that authorities are "working day and night, not only to provide a response to the victims and their families, but to clarify every last detail of this tragedy and to strengthen security so that it never happens again."
As the country's top institutions continue investigating the cause behind the collision, Transport Minister Óscar Puente has suggested that a combination of “inexplicable” human error and a computer failure was likely behind the tragedy, which occurred near Urda, Toledo, more than 80 miles south of Madrid.
Puente said in a press conference that the state-operated Renfe train slamming into the rear of a stationary private train operated by Iryo was due to an “inexplicable” order from a command center for Spain’s trains. Puente noted that the center had a computer malfunction before the order.
“It was the control center, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” Puente said. He added later: “Clearly, it was a wrong decision.”
Puente said that they have identified the person who decided to let the Renfe train continue moving even though the Iryo one had already stopped, but he has not spoken to the control center operator. “This person is subject to whatever the investigation determines,” Puente said in the press conference.
Renfe said train services between Madrid, Ciudad Real, and Andalusia have been suspended.
The Wednesday collision is now the deadliest train crash in the country since a 2013 incident in Santiago de Compostela that killed 80 people. But the latest collision follows a similarly deadly train crash in January, which involved high-speed trains operated by the same two companies. In that crash, which occurred in Adamuz, Córdoba, 46 people died and 122 sustained injuries.
Sánchez, who visited the crash site, said his government would declare three days of mourning in response.
Despite the accident, Puente insisted that the Spanish rail system is “safe and comparable to that of other countries in our region.” However, while there are “very clear” regulations and protocols in place, he admitted, “failures can obviously occur.”
What happened?
The crashes involved a Renfe high-speed train bound for Seville with 393 people on board, and an Iryo train carrying 151 passengers. The Renfe train departed Madrid at 8:00 a.m. local time, while the Iryo train left a little earlier at 7:54 a.m., plying the same route.
Spain’s rail infrastructure uses the German LZB (Linienzugbeeinflussung) system, a railway safety technology that monitors train speeds and sends traffic instructions to the driver’s cab. Operations are meant to revert to manual control when the automated safety system fails.
Puente, in the press conference, said that at around 8:30 a.m., three computers on the railway network experienced a communication failure, taking the LZB control system offline along a 63 km (39 mi) stretch of the track. This automatically stopped about six trains traveling on that section, Puente said. The central command center would assume manual management of rail traffic.
By 8:36 a.m., the command center authorized the Renfe train to continue its journey “normally,” even though Puente says internal protocols dictate otherwise and that a “red signal” should have prevented the journey from resuming. The Renfe train had 25 km (15.5 mi) to travel before it struck the Iryo train, roughly 17 minutes later, at 8:53 a.m. The speed it reached before the impact is still unknown, but it could reach up to 200 km/h (124 mph) for that stretch of track.
What to know about Spanish high-speed rail
Spain is among the world leaders in investing in domestic high-speed rail infrastructure—defined as rails for trains that can travel 250 km/h (155 mph) and over, according to the European Commission’s Ninth Rail Market Monitoring report last year. The report shows that of European Union countries, Spain allocated the most to high-speed rail between 2018 and 2022, averaging €1.5 billion (around $1.67 billion) per year.
Latest data from the International Union of Railways shows that Spain has laid nearly 4,000 km (2,400 mi) of high-speed track, second only to China, which has laid more than 47,000 km (28,000 mi).
The European country only legally opened its domestic commercial high-speed passenger rail market to private competitors in December 2020, and Iryo became one of the commercial high-speed operators in Spain in 2022.
Spanish news outlet El Debate reported, citing data from the State Railway Safety Agency, that the number of “significant accidents” on the country’s rail network has increased over the years.

Liquid Glass Finally Makes Sense on the iPhone Duo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Apple rarely admits a mistake. But when it unveiled new versions of its operating systems this summer, it came close.
“With all major design updates, there’s a natural process where we take a bold leap forward, and then we continue to iterate,” said Apple's human interface designer, Shubham Kedia, during a predictably sleek keynote video. “Our team really appreciates your feedback, and we considered it deeply as we refined the new design.”
Not quite “Sorry, everyone, we messed up,” but for Apple, practically an apology tour. The subject was Liquid Glass, Apple’s most divisive interface design since at least iOS 7. Apple's Vision Pro mixed-reality headset (which itself flopped) inspired the translucent design language, and the company brought it to millions of other Apple devices.
The result was a mess—at odds with Steve Jobs’ famous line, “Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.” Liquid Glass started obsessed with gloss and effects, despite promises it would bring your content to the foreground. Yet Apple’s own press release showed interfaces with illegible text. Worse, users found constant reflections and flickering color shifts distracting, and a lack of clarity across devices hurt accessibility.
But iOS 27, alongside updates to Apple's other software platforms, signaled a shift in priorities after Kedia’s mea culpa. Kedia spoke of reincorporating design cornerstones in what was, if not quite a U-turn, then at least a rediscovery of a core principle: how it works. Instantly, interface elements across Apple devices gained greater clarity and structure, making it easier to tell apps' components from content. The most obvious change, though, was a slider.
Thinking Differently
Apple said it tuned Liquid Glass to diffuse complex content more effectively, keeping elements legible when above imagery and text. But it also acknowledged that not everyone wants the same thing—some users might prefer a more tinted look, and others “would like Liquid Glass to be even more clear.” You can now decide for yourself with the Liquid Design slider in Settings. For a company known for being opinionated, such bet-hedging was surprising but not unwelcome. Choice isn’t a bad thing, and now users had more of it.
“I immediately pushed that slider all the way to the most tinted setting, and pretty much all the legibility issues vanished,” Ben Rice McCarthy, an indie developer behind popular apps like Obscura and Indigo, tells WIRED. McCarthy has long criticized Liquid Glass. Now? Not so much.
“Liquid Glass introduced a lot of issues without adequate solutions, but this year’s operating systems solved or improved a lot of them,” McCarthy says. “There’s the adaptiveness of the interface. Buttons can grow into menus. Controls merge and divide like cells as you transition between views. Toolbars can expand and contract smoothly as the view changes size.”
Flexibility matters when resizing windows across any device. But while announcing its updates, Apple also dropped major hints that all but confirmed new hardware—it showed iPhone apps running on an iPad or a Mac could resize to a suspiciously specific shape that matched the rumored inner display dimensions of Apple’s upcoming folding phone.
Designed to Flow
When Apple showed off the iPhone Duo, everything clicked. Its passport-shaped display bucks the trend of iPhones and their rivals growing taller over the years. The Duo is wider and almost squat, and when opened, it naturally defaults to landscape, echoing the iPad Mini display.
Apple being Apple, it wanted to avoid the jarring jolt between displays that’s often evident on rival foldables, so it made content appear to move seamlessly from one screen to the other. That begins with the hardware. As Molly Anderson, Apple's vice president of Industrial Design, said at the September keynote: “To achieve this continuity, we designed iPhone Duo around a consistent aspect ratio that is the same across both displays.” But it’s the software—rooted in Liquid Glass—that sells the illusion.
The most arresting element is a fancy animation, which various folks in the Android space are now busy being “inspired” by. It reinforces the idea of a flowing interface. Meanwhile, Liquid Glass freed Apple from being prescriptive about where essential controls live. On the Duo, they sit at the side. When the phone’s closed, that frees up space for content. When it’s open, the controls stay in a consistent spot, so you never have to hunt for them. Reorient the device, and everything settles into the most appropriate place.
That’s form following function, not function being subservient to form. This device and its flexible interface don’t strictly need the Liquid Glass design language, but the two feel made for each other. Liquid Glass finally makes sense on the iPhone Duo—and with Apple’s other refinements, it’s starting to make sense elsewhere, too.
Clarity of Purpose
How much of this is happenstance is hard to say. Given Apple’s lead times, pure coincidence seems unlikely. And even if Liquid Glass wasn’t made with the Duo in mind, it adapts to it.
Liquid Glass feels more considered. It’s increasingly tuned for individual devices rather than governed by a “universal” aesthetic forced onto them all. The result is operating systems that feel solid rather than fragile, with interfaces less likely to fight content for your attention. On Macs and iPads, the Liquid Glass revamp now looks more like a love letter to Aqua—Apple's water-themed interface introduced in 2000. On the iPhone, it’s usable again. On the Duo, it’s a delight.
That’s not to say it’s perfect. “There’s some weirdness that hasn’t been fully resolved, and there needs to be a consistency to all these materials or the metaphors break down,” McCarthy says. “But overall, Liquid Glass is vastly improved.”
And it’s worth remembering that while the Duo is new, Liquid Glass is relatively young, too. As developer Steve Troughton-Smith wrote, “For some iPhone apps, even with keen developers, it will take six months to a year of work to properly support iPhone Duo. A lot of developers are still trying to finish the Liquid Glass transition they started last year.”
A useful reminder that transitions take time. But at least now, Apple’s vision looks clear.

Büro Ole Scheeren designs winding concrete gallery in South Korea "without traditional thresholds"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Büro Ole Scheeren designs winding concrete gallery in South Korea “without traditional thresholds”
Architecture studio Büro Ole Scheeren has revealed designs for the Suseong Continuum, a snaking, concrete art gallery in Daegu, South Korea.
Set to be built within the city’s Yeonhwaji park, the 364-square-metre gallery was designed specifically for showcasing digital art.
Berlin-based Büro Ole Scheeren designed the gallery as a continuous space, without any enclosed rooms and or doorways, in a bid to reflect the “flows” of digital art.
“We wanted to build a gallery without traditional thresholds: a gradient of realities that morph into one another as you gradually move through the space,” studio founder Ole Scheeren said.
“The substance of digital art is not rooted in the physical domain of distinct objects and isolated experiences… it exists in a world of overlaps and connections, where one condition potentially flows into the next.”
“Landscape, circulation and exhibition become a continuous experience,” the studio added.
The Suseong Continuum gallery was unveiled as part of this year’s Suseong International Biennale, which invites architects to realise permanent public works across Daegu.
Commissioned by the Suseong District Government, the design by Büro Ole Scheeren is expected to open for the biennale’s 2028 edition.
Once complete, visitors will access the space via a winding path, from which the gallery was designed to emerge as an extrusion.
Conceived as a “continuation of the landscape”, the gallery’s twisting volume will be partially embedded into the park’s topography and oriented toward a nearby lotus pond.
Its structure will be built using board-marked concrete to create a rough exterior texture. Inside, this textured surface will transition to smooth concrete walls for projecting media onto.
According to Büro Ole Scheeren, the gallery’s layout and materiality were designed to reflect the transition from the park’s natural landscape to the digital interiors.
“Technology is often seen as an opposite to nature,” Scheeren said. “With Suseong Continuum we wanted to explore how we can create a way of extending the way we perceive the relationship between both domains – a journey that starts in the park and that seamlessly carries you into the digital realm.”
“There is no single moment where one world ends and the other begins, it is a continuous transformation.”
“What begins as natural landscape gradually transforms into digital media,” the studio added.
Renders of the gallery’s stripped-back interior reveal its immersive exhibition spaces framed by curving walls.
A layered ceiling will run the building’s full length to conceal all lighting and technical infrastructure, which was developed by the studio in collaboration with the Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe.
“The interior unfolds as a spatial gradient in which light, sound, enclosure and immersion shift gradually along the visitor’s route,” the studio said.
“Curving walls widen into open spaces and tighten into passages; atmospheres transform rather than switch,” it added.
The design will remain on show at the Suseong International Biennale until 22 November.
In Shenzhen, China, the studio has revealed plans for skyscrapers with “waterfall” facades and its design for the Róng Museum of Arts is currently under construction.
Images by Büro Ole Scheeren

Navantia UK raises apprentice target by half
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:25:48 GMT
18:25:48 KST

Navantia UK is increasing its commitment to recruit apprentices across its British yards from 500 to 750 by 2030, an announcement made as the Scottish Secretary and the defence industry minister visited the company’s yard at Methil in Fife, according to the company.
The apprentices will work on building three Fleet Solid Support ships for the Royal Fleet Auxiliary and will be ready to take on further projects for the Ministry of Defence.
Donato Martinez, chief executive of Navantia UK, said: “There is real momentum at Methil. We are investing in the yard, bringing in new work and recruiting more people. We also need to build the skills that will support the yard and our wider business in the years ahead.
“That is why we are increasing our nationwide commitment from 500 apprentices by 2030 to 750. It will give more young people the chance to build skilled careers in our industry and help us develop the workforce we need as the business grows.
“Methil has an important role to play in the future of UK shipbuilding. The investment being made here, the skills in the workforce and the opportunities ahead, including Programme Euston, give us a strong base to keep building from.”
Investment at Methil has reached £26.7 million since Navantia UK acquired the yard in January 2025, including a further £12 million announced this year for training facilities, machinery, infrastructure and new technology. The workforce has grown from 180 to 275 and 75 apprentices are now training at the site, including 21 who arrived this year, part of a company-wide intake of 121 joining 222 already employed across the four British yards at Methil, Arnish, Belfast and Appledore.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “The UK Government worked hard to secure the future of yards such as Methil as part of our commitment to Scotland’s industrial heartlands, and today with Navantia I’ve seen the difference that commitment has made. A busier order book, a growing workforce and a large increase in apprenticeships – this is what’s possible when government and industry work together.
“There are huge opportunities with the defence dividend that come from being part of the United Kingdom. I’m proud that the UK Government’s support for the sector is delivering skilled jobs and growth for communities right across Scotland. This is a new age of industrialisation for the UK, with Scotland at its heart.”
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Apprentices are at the heart of defence’s industrial base that keeps this country safe. These opportunities pave the way for the next generation, providing essential skills, training and experience while contributing to the security of the UK.”
Programme Euston, referred to by Martinez, is the Ministry of Defence programme for new floating docks at His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde, and the Chancellor confirmed that those docks will be built and delivered in British shipyards. The GMB union has argued that Methil should get the work.

Estonia to call all women aged 40 for breast cancer risk analysis screening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

Estonia to call all women aged 40 for breast cancer risk analysis screening
Estonia is set to become the first country in the world where people are invited to screening programs based on genetic data. Next week, all 40-year-old women will receive an invitation for genetic testing to determine their individual breast cancer risk, regardless of whether or not they have health insurance.
Until now, women have been invited to breast cancer screening after their 50th birthday, but starting next week, all 40-year-old women will receive an invitation so that each woman's risk of developing breast cancer can be calculated based on genetic data.
"If this risk is higher than usual – if the risk for these 40-year-old women is the same as it is for other women at the age of 50 – then including these women in screening earlier is justified. Starting mammography already at the age of 40," said Steven Smit, head of the biobank laboratory at the Estonian Genome Center.
Around 3,000 genetic variants are taken into account when calculating the risk. However, the study does not include BRCA gene mutations, which led actress Angelina Jolie to decide to have her breasts removed 13 years ago to prevent developing the disease.
"These are hereditary forms of cancer, which are assessed through separate tests as needed if there has been breast cancer in the family," Smit said.
There are almost 10,000 40-year-old women in Estonia, and invitations will be sent both to those who have already donated their genes to the Estonian Genome Center and to those who have not.
"The gene donors' data will not be checked automatically. The first step is still to go to the Health Portal and submit a declaration of consent there so that the data can be used in the healthcare system," said Krista Kruuv-Käo, head of preventive services at the Estonian Health Insurance Fund.
The same declaration of consent must also be completed by women whose data is not in the Estonian Genome Center. They will receive a referral to a laboratory to provide a blood sample.
It is also possible to put this service in place for other serious diseases, but the Health Insurance Fund does not consider this reasonable, as the state would not have the capacity to follow up on them.
"We are also analyzing how we could use genetic risk in the case of cardiovascular diseases to more precisely involve those people whose risks are higher in preventive measures," Kruuv-Käo said.
Currently, the Estonian Genome Center holds data on approximately one-fifth of Estonia's population, and no new gene donors are being accepted.
"The Genome Center would certainly be fully prepared for this, but at the moment there is simply no funding available for it. The Genome Center's general funding has also been reduced in recent years," Smit said.

China Focus: China expands foreign business access at world's largest free trade port

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:23:45 CST
18:23:45 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China has unveiled 16 measures to make it easier for foreign businesses and professionals to operate in the Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP), the world's largest FTP by area, with new policies covering energy trade, medical services and bonded business operations, according to a government circular made public Thursday.
Under the measures, foreign physicians legally licensed to practice medicine overseas may obtain permits to provide clinical diagnosis and treatment services in Hainan for up to three years, with extensions available in accordance with relevant regulations.
More convenient policies regarding work permits and stay and residence will also be introduced for foreign nationals.
The Hainan FTP, located in China's southernmost island province, launched island-wide special customs operations in December 2025, allowing freer entry of overseas goods, expanded zero-tariff coverage and more business-friendly measures as part of China's efforts to promote high-standard opening-up.
Overseas companies will be allowed to use bonded facilities at Hainan's liquefied natural gas (LNG) receiving terminals, while the FTP will be supported in conducting LNG futures delivery warehouse operations after LNG futures contracts are launched.
Other measures include promoting offshore trade, expanding the range of products eligible for bonded maintenance, facilitating the entry of eligible bonded remanufactured products into pilot free trade zones on the Chinese mainland, encouraging the use of the yuan in new forms of barter trade, and deepening the FTP's economic and trade cooperation with China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Bonded remanufactured products entering mainland pilot free trade zones will be subject to applicable import tariffs, import-related value-added tax and consumption tax. They must also meet all applicable technical requirements for equivalent new products and relevant regulations on remanufactured products, and be clearly labeled as such.
The circular also calls for improved insurance products and services in areas such as international transportation and bonded maintenance.
The latest measures come amid robust growth in Hainan's foreign trade. In the first three quarters of 2026, the province's goods imports and exports reached 285.44 billion yuan (about 42.5 billion U.S. dollars), up 49.8 percent year on year, while trade in services rose 11.7 percent to 56.95 billion yuan, according to data from Hainan's provincial commerce authorities.
Trade in maintenance and repair services more than doubled year on year to 3.31 billion yuan during the same period, according to the provincial commerce department. The trade mainly came from imports of aircraft materials and components and revenues from aircraft maintenance services.
The number of newly established foreign-invested enterprises in Hainan rose 38.6 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, according to the State Administration for Market Regulation.
The FTP measures are part of China's broader efforts to promote high-standard opening-up. The country has announced plans to further expand pilot opening-up programs in sectors such as value-added telecommunications, biotechnology and wholly foreign-owned hospitals, while taking steps to facilitate cross-border trade and investment.
The circular was jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and the General Administration of Customs. ■

SYDNEY, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have mapped genetic links to 16 diseases, identifying nearly 1,500 genes that may contribute to conditions ranging from cancer to immune and neurological disorders.
The team, from the Garvan Institute of Medical Research in collaboration with the Murdoch Children's Research Institute and the University of New South Wales in Australia, and other partners, analyzed the gene sequence and activity of more than 9 million individual immune cells from nearly 2,000 people, the largest dataset of its kind, according to a statement released Thursday by the Garvan Institute.

The research could help accelerate drug development and precision medicine by identifying the genetic mechanisms underlying disease and the patients likely to respond to particular treatments. ■

China's longest metro loop line enters full operation in Wuhan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:23:06 CST
18:23:06 KST

A train runs on the Wuhan Metro Line 12 in Wuhan, central China's Hubei Province, Oct. 29, 2026. China's longest subway loop line, the Wuhan Metro Line 12, started full line operation on Thursday. The 59.9-km line has 37 stations and stretches across seven administrative districts of the city. By far, the total mileage of Wuhan Metro in operation has exceeded 581 kilometers. (Xinhua/Xiao Yijiu)
WUHAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Metro Line 12 in Wuhan, the capital of central China's Hubei Province, became fully operational on Thursday, making it China's longest metro loop line, according to the China Association of Metros.
Stretching 59.9 kilometers and serving 37 underground stations across seven urban districts of Wuhan, the line connects the Wuchang and Hankou railway hubs and offers transfers to 18 existing and planned lines. A full loop takes about 96 minutes.
The line opened in two phases. The first phase, 35.3 kilometers long, entered service on May 1 this year. With the second phase now operational, Wuhan Metro's operational length exceeds 581 kilometers, roughly the driving distance between Berlin and Munich or between Rome and Milan.
Wuhan, known as the "river city," has complex geological and hydrological conditions, which posed multiple challenges during construction. The line passes under the Yangtze River twice and the Hanjiang River once. Construction teams overcame a series of technical difficulties, including high water pressure and composite strata.
One cross-river tunnel, in particular, is approximately 4 kilometers long, with its lowest point 71.4 meters below the Yangtze River surface. The project has provided valuable experience for building super-large-diameter cross-river tunnels in China.
Wuhan, home to over 13.86 million permanent residents, is a key transport hub in China and a core city of the Yangtze River Economic Belt. The opening of Metro Line 12 is expected to further facilitate cross-river commuting.
China has issued a plan to comprehensively advance the high-quality development of integrated transport services during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the Ministry of Transport announced in July this year. The plan aims to basically establish a modern integrated transport service system by 2030.
Under the plan, China will improve connections among different modes of transport, make passenger transfers more convenient and enhance freight logistics services. ■

Army standing up a Deep Recce Strike Brigade
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:21:11 GMT
18:21:11 KST

The Army has approved and is implementing a Deep Recce Strike Brigade to pull intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and precision strike together at corps level, including what the department calls novel one-way effectors, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Stuart Anderson, the Conservative member for South Shropshire, asked what progress had been made on accelerating the development and deployment of the new Recce-Strike approach set out on page 111 of the Strategic Defence Review.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Army has approved and is implementing a Deep Recce Strike Brigade to provide Corps-level (HQ ARRC) integration of intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and precision strike capabilities, including novel one-way effectors. The 5th Generation Land Force programme will increase human-machine teaming, autonomy and decision advantage, further accelerating recce-strike capability across the force.”
A one-way effector is a munition that does not come back, in practice a loitering munition or an attack drone, and the phrase has become the department’s preferred term for a class of weapon that Ukraine has turned into the dominant means of killing vehicles and artillery well behind the line of contact.
The headquarters named is the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks in Gloucester, a NATO corps headquarters Britain provides and commands. The brigade’s output therefore arrives at the level where a corps commander shapes a battle, above divisional and brigade level.
The Strategic Defence Review published in June 2025 set out recce-strike as the organising idea for the future Army, describing a mix of sensors, long-range fires and autonomous systems connected by a digital targeting network. The Defence Investment Plan put £1.8 billion into that targeting web, and the Army has separately acknowledged that its existing drones cannot talk to each other, creating the Uncrewed Systems Centre to deal with that.
The 5th Generation Land Force programme covers the Army’s wider modernisation, including human-machine teaming and the mix of crewed and uncrewed platforms the service expects to field through the next decade.

====================================================================================================

New evidence links Singapore palm oil giant to Indonesian deforesters, despite denials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:20:14 UTC
18:20:14 KST

DEFORESTATION INC
New evidence links Singapore palm oil giant to Indonesian deforesters, despite denials
Two environmental groups have uncovered operational, commercial, personnel and logistical links between First Resources and Indonesian suppliers accused of forest destruction. It’s not the first time the company has obscured its supply chain.
One of the world’s largest palm oil producers allegedly misled investors and corporate customers when it denied links to Indonesian suppliers accused of deforestation, a group of environmental organizations found.
The Singapore-based First Resources group, owned by the billionaire Fangiono family, oversees more than 270,000 hectares of oil palm plantations and is currently under scrutiny as Indonesia and neighboring nations battle a toxic haze caused by illegal fires used to clear land for agriculture.
In 2024, First Resources rejected allegations by the Gecko Project, a partner of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, which had linked the conglomerate to a company now known as Kalimantan Agro Sejahtera (KAS) and palm oil firms allegedly responsible for deforestation on the island of Borneo. The findings were part of Deforestation Inc., a cross-border investigation led by ICIJ that exposed how a lightly regulated sustainability industry overlooks forest destruction and human rights violations when granting environmental certifications.
The Rainforest Action Network and the Environmental Investigation Agency have now uncovered new evidence showing that First Resources, KAS and another company appear to be part of the same corporate group, and have operational, commercial, personnel and logistical connections.
Confidential financial information and court records reveal that, despite marketing its operations as sustainable, First Resources “laundered” into its supply chain palm oil sourced from the suppliers linked to forest loss, according to the reports published today. The company sells its products to Cargill and other major food processing and trading firms.
The researchers also followed trucks and barges and found that a Fangiono-controlled bulking facility was used to offload and transport crude palm oil sourced from mills belonging to First Resources, KAS Group and FAP Agri — indicating close trade relationships. Companies’ employees interviewed by the researchers also confirmed that the firms were linked to each other, the RAN report said.
Alex Helan, a senior researcher at RAN, said the new revelations show how major players in the forestry sector use “tactics of hide and seek through corporate structures” that weaken authorities’ fight against forest destruction.
“Deforestation in Indonesia has been declining over the last decade, influenced by market expectations for deforestation-free products, together with stronger government enforcement,” Helan told ICIJ. “However, this progress is being undermined by companies using complex corporate structures to hide their continued links to deforestation.”
First Resources denied the allegations, saying it operates according to the law and “does not have coordinated, integrated, and co-mingled Crude Palm Oil (CPO) supply chains” with the Indonesian suppliers mentioned in the report.
‘Related parties’ undercut sustainability claims
First Resources first pledged to end deforestation in its supply chain in 2015. Since then, more than half of its plantations have been certified as sustainable by the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, a voluntary certification organization, according to corporate records.
Companies often use their green certification status to attract lenders, investors and clients committed to “environmental, social and governance” guidelines.
As a publicly listed company on the Singapore Stock Exchange, First Resources is also required to submit a sustainability report, in which it routinely touts its commitment to transparency and environmental standards. The report is not reviewed by an independent third-party — a loophole identified by ICIJ’s Deforestation Inc., which showed how forestry companies use certifications based on flawed audits to advertise products and operations as compliant with environmental standards, labor laws and human rights, misinforming shareholders as well as customers.
The new findings by RAN, EIA and Kaom Telepak raise questions about the company’s sustainability claims — and the RSPO’s and the Stock Exchange’s ability to hold it accountable.
According to the environmental groups, over the last decade, large-scale deforestation has continued in a number of palm oil concessions surrounding First Resources facilities operating under the name KAS Group. The company is controlled on paper by a businessman with a very limited public profile who has been described by researchers as a close associate of the Fangionos’.
The KAS Group operates across several Indonesian provinces with about 15,000 employees, 70,000 hectares of land and six palm oil mills, according to job and training adverts uncovered by the researchers. Information about its ownership is hidden behind shell companies incorporated in the British Virgin Islands, a secrecy jurisdiction.
Satellite images analyzed for the report reveal that KAS Group and FAP Agri, another palm oil producer allegedly linked to First Resources, were responsible for clearing more than 9,300 hectares of forest between 2021 to 2026, including areas inhabited by the endangered Eastern Grey Gibbons.
Last year, the RSPO found its member, First Resources, in breach of the organization’s transparency rules and suspended it temporarily. It did not, however, require the company to treat the suspect suppliers as part of the same group, and First Resources has continued to deny links to the Indonesian firms.
“The RSPO complaints panel got it wrong,” RAN’s Helan said, “and has thereby allowed apparent laundering of deforestation palm oil to take place.”
Newly uncovered records from a lawsuit filed by KAS Group in 2022 includes employees’ statements describing regular transport of KAS palm oil to First Resource operations, RAN’s report said. Internal accounting files obtained by the researchers and dated April 2024 also appear to identify the three companies – First Resources, KAS Group and FAP Agri – as “related parties” and show close trading links, the report said.
FAP Agri denied any wrongdoing in a statement to RAN. KAS Group did not reply to requests for comment.
The EIA investigation also found that South Sorong concessions sold by First Resources in 2025 and a First Resources-linked shipping company have the same ultimate owner: an entity registered in the British Virgin Islands. This raises “significant questions about whether the divestment resulted in complete separation from the assets,” EIA’s analyst Ben Melling told ICIJ.
Taken together, Melling said, the findings show that “buyers, investors and certification bodies need to step up their due diligence.”

3 in 4 pilots report dozing off or fighting sleep while flying planes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:20:00 UTC
18:20:00 KST

3 in 4 pilots report dozing off or fighting sleep while flying planes
- A European Cockpit Association (ECA) survey found 76.8% of 7,200 pilots across 32 countries had at least one cockpit “microsleep” in four weeks, raising fears about fatigue and safety.
- Only 37.2% usually report when they are too tired to fly, while 24.2% do not report it and fly anyway.
- Microsleeps are involuntary episodes of sleep lasting a few seconds. People experiencing them may appear awake, even with their eyes open, but fail to process information.
AI generated
Three in four pilots have admitted to briefly dozing off or struggling to stay awake while inside the cockpit, a European survey has found.
The report, released on Oct 26 by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), has renewed concerns about overworked and exhausted flight crews that, in turn, present an unseen risk to flying.
The ECA drew on responses from about 7,200 pilots across 32 countries.
Some 76.8% of those surveyed reported at least one cockpit “microsleep” in the previous four weeks, while 38.8% said they usually do not get enough rest to prevent fatigue from accumulating.
They cited brief and uncontrolled sleep, head nodding and fighting to keep their eyes open.
Microsleeps are involuntary episodes of sleep lasting a few seconds. People experiencing them may appear awake, even with their eyes open, but fail to process information, according to the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health.
The survey was voluntary and conducted online from Aug 4 to Sept 7.
Reporting fatigue is itself a problem, the ECA said.
Only 37.2% said they usually report themselves unfit when they are too tired to fly, while 24.2% said they do not report it and fly anyway.
“When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit,” Captain Coen George, an ECA board director, said in a statement.
‘Alarming number’
Incidents of pilots falling asleep while helming a flight have been reported in Asia.
On Jan 25, 2024, both pilots aboard a Batik Air flight from Kendari to Jakarta fell asleep during the flight, according to Indonesia’s National Transportation Safety Committee. The Airbus A320 was carrying 153 passengers and six crew members.
The captain had been resting when the first officer inadvertently fell asleep. The captain woke up about 28 minutes after the first officer’s last radio transmission, found the aircraft off its intended flight path and woke his colleague.
The plane landed safely, with no injuries or damage.
Investigators found that the first officer’s sleep before duty had been interrupted while helping care for his month-old twins.
In a statement to People magazine, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency said flight-time limits provide a safety baseline, while airlines must actively manage fatigue through reporting systems, operational measures and a culture that allows crews to raise concerns without fear of consequences.
The cockpit association’s president, Captain Tanja Harter, called for stronger oversight and protections for pilots reporting fatigue, saying the lack of meaningful progress since 2023 required action from airlines and regulators.
“Having more than three in four pilots say they reported dozing off while at work is definitely an alarming number, and the industry does need to take note of this,” Bobby Laurie, a Pennsylvania-based travel expert and former flight attendant, told Fox News Digital.
“But it’s not necessarily a warning sign that the flight that you’ve been on had a pilot or both pilots asleep,” he said.

US First Lady praised for Oleshky relief truce as Moscow strikes Ukrainian commuters
Oct 29 - Russia and Ukraine both praised US first lady Melania Trump on Thursday for helping to broker a truce around the acutely deprived Russian-held Ukrainian town of Oleshky, as efforts began to bring in food and medicines and enable hundreds to leave.
Yet any sense of wider relief in a war that began with a Russian invasion almost five years ago was rapidly dispelled by a drone strike that killed 13 people crowding onto a commuter train at the main station in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, according to local officials, where no ceasefire was in place.
The Oleshky operation aims to address a growing crisis in a town marooned inside a war zone since 2022 - but is also part of a diplomatic dance where both sides want to show US President Donald Trump that they back his peace efforts, albeit for different reasons.
Yana Lantratova, Russia's human rights commissioner, said she was taking four journalists from the conservative US outlet Newsmax to the area as her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets, also headed for Oleshky.
PUTIN SAYS MOSCOW IS MAKING PEACE EFFORTS
President Vladimir Putin told a summit in Moscow that relief supplies would begin reaching civilians on Thursday and Friday, "with the support, incidentally, of the First Lady of the United States".
Lubinets, for his part, extended Kyiv's "special thanks" to someone who was "personally devoting her time and attention to the humanitarian mission and assistance to civilians in Oleshky".
Trump has cast Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy as an obstacle to peace while praising Putin, who emphasised on Thursday that Russia was "working on issues relating to a possible peaceful resolution of the Ukrainian crisis itself".
Although Russia, like Ukraine, denies targeting civilians, strikes on trains and other civilian infrastructure have become increasingly common as Ukraine's stocks of air defence missiles have dwindled. Civilian deaths have also increased inside Russia.
On Thursday, the state rail company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a jet-powered drone had hit a platform in the Ukrainian industrial hub of Dnipro where a commuter train was preparing to depart for nearby Zaporizhzhia.
Although US-mediated peace talks are due to resume next month in Abu Dhabi after a long pause, the two sides are far apart when it comes to terms for ending the war.
But both recognise the power of Trump, who has another two years in power left regardless of the outcome of US midterm legislative elections next month, to affect the course of the conflict.
Russia still hopes that Trump can pressure Kyiv into agreeing a deal that meets many of its conditions - such as full Russian control of Ukraine's Donbas region and a bar on Ukraine joining the transatlantic defence alliance, NATO.
Kyiv, meanwhile, wants to ensure that US intelligence sharing continues along with full access to Elon Musk's recently disrupted battlefield communications system, Starshield, and that European-bought US military hardware, including Patriot interceptor missiles, continues to flow.
KHERSON CEASEFIRE DUE TO CONTINUE UNTIL SUNDAY
The truce applies only to Oleshky and the wider Kherson region, which has suffered years of near-daily drone and artillery attacks. Some 1,500 of the prewar population of 24,000 people are believed to live among the ruins, under regular shellfire amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Ukraine has long accused Russia of refusing to let aid in or people out. Russia says it is Ukrainian mines on the approach roads and Ukrainian shelling that have prevented the delivery of aid or the safe evacuation of residents.
By the middle of Thursday, neither Ukraine nor Russia had reported any violations of the ceasefire, which was due to last until Sunday.
"Demining is under way there, and we hope that today or tomorrow residents will be able to receive humanitarian aid safely and without obstruction, and that those wishing to leave will be able to do so,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was cited as saying by the Interfax news agency.
Residents wishing to leave and return to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government are expected to exit via Russia-controlled Crimea before crossing into southern Russia and being flown to Belarus from where they will be able to cross the border into Ukraine. REUTERS

No reason was given for Sylvia’s departure and no replacement has been named, The Atlantic said.
AFP has contacted the Pentagon for comment.
The reported sacking comes as Trump is widely considered to be weighing fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on Nov 3.
“We may do another little Epic Fury,” Trump said last week, referring to US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war.
He did not give any indication on timing.
Neither the United States nor Iran has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, settling instead into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships.
Sylvia’s previous roles included leading the 101st Airborne Division – the US army’s air assault division – and heading a unit in Iraq. AFP
