Promises and Perils of Nepal’s India Pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:11:00 UTC
18:11:00 KST

After months of keeping New Delhi at arm’s length, Nepal’s Balendra Shah government is discovering both the appeal and the political risks of drawing it closer.
Formed after the March 2026 elections, the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) government did not start on the right foot with the southern neighbor. First, new Prime Minister Balendra Shah declined a one-on-one meeting with then-Indian Ambassador Naveen Shrivastava, in keeping with his policy of not meeting any foreign officials.
What rankled more with the Indians was his subsequent refusal to meet India’s Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, who was coming to Kathmandu carrying Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s formal invitation for Shah to visit India. Misri’s trip was called off. India — which continues to emphasize its “unique” relations with Nepal that are unlike its ties with any other country — saw this as a snub, and a breach of trust.
Those were not the only irritants in bilateral ties. The new government in Kathmandu started taxing goods bought by Nepali nationals in Indian border towns, hampering the business of these hubs that rely on Nepali buyers. Entry of Indian vehicles into Nepal was also restricted.
That was the state of affairs for the first five or six months of the Shah government.
But the tide seems to have turned and the government now appears keen to woo the Indians. At the forefront of this effort is Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle.
Even before the March elections, as a top RSP leader, Wagle had repeatedly visited New Delhi with a message that should his party come to power, it would go the extra mile to protect Indian interests.
Of late, Wagle seems to have gotten the government’s green light to boldly assert that the era of “anti-India nationalism” in Nepal is over and his government is ready to turn over a new leaf with the southern neighbor.
Curiously, he and his government also sound accommodative of India’s self-declared red lines. In a recent interview with The Hindu, the Nepali minister said that Nepal now accepts that India’s refusal to buy hydropower from Nepali projects with Chinese investment is a “new geopolitical reality.”
Yet the finance minister is only laying the ground for Shah’s much-awaited India visit in the third week of November. Home Minister Sudan Gurung has also contributed to this effort, outlining potential areas of bilateral cooperation in a recent op-ed. Big deals are being planned during Shah’s visit.
But for any government in Kathmandu, close relations with India come with both costs and benefits. The obvious benefit is that New Delhi pulls many strings in Kathmandu, and it can make life difficult for a Nepali prime minister it does not like. The latest overtures of his government toward India suggest Shah does not want to be one of them.
If Shah can convince New Delhi to, say, secure an additional air route for Nepal during his India trip, it will be a new feather in his bhadgaule cap — and a tangible achievement for his nationalist base back home.
Yet there are also costs of closer ties with India. Whatever Wagle says, the days of anti-India nationalism in Nepal are far from over — as is also evident in the fierce criticism of his remarks in Nepali intellectual circles. Nepalis continue to be suspicious of the oft-meddling regional hegemon that has thrice imposed crippling blockades on the landlocked country.
Shah got an overwhelming mandate, and he can afford to use some of his political capital to push through vital projects with India. But irrespective of how well Shah’s India trip goes, there will still be irritants in bilateral ties.
For instance, a major disagreement remains between Kathmandu and New Delhi on an old border dispute. After India and China unilaterally opened the Lipulekh pass — a trijunction point between the three countries — for trade earlier this year, Kathmandu swiftly dispatched diplomatic notes to New Delhi and Beijing. This issue could again flare up as both New Delhi and Beijing seem to be in a mood to overrule Nepal’s objections and give continuity to their trade through the pass.
It will be hard for the Shah government to stand firm on Lipulekh — something that is in keeping with the Nepali public sentiment — while also pursuing closer cooperation with India. If it does not handle the issue well, a “compromise” on territorial integrity to secure favorable trade terms could even be portrayed domestically as a surrender to the regional hegemon.
Then there is China. The government has signaled that closer ties with India are worth paying the price of narrowing the space for Chinese investment in Nepali hydropower.
Yet if the government pushes Beijing too far through such gestures, it will violate a central tenet of Nepali foreign policy: maintenance of a delicate balance between Beijing and New Delhi. There will thus be a strong opposition to an overt India tilt.
In the end, Shah and his ministers would do well to avoid making sweeping claims that old constraints in India-Nepal ties have disappeared or that the anti-India nationalism in Nepal has run its course. Nurturing this complicated relationship requires sustained diplomacy and setting of realistic expectations. Only then can Nepal protect its interests.

Hello Kitty firm apologises, cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China backlash
Sanrio, the company behind the hugely successful Hello Kitty franchise, has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media accused the show of "smearing China", sparking a social media backlash.
Sanrio, the Japanese company behind the popular character Hello Kitty, apologised on Thursday over its tie-up with a TV spy drama criticised as being anti-China, which had prompted the cancellation of a merchandise collaboration with the show.
It comes days after Chinese sponsors dropped football superstar Kylian Mbappé over comments calling communist leader Mao Zedong a "dictator", for which the Real Madrid forward later apologised.
Read moreReal Madrid apologises to China over Mbappé's Mao Zedong comments
In one episode of "Vivant", a drama with a wide audience in Japan, a Chinese-affiliated organisation had been depicted torturing a member of the Japanese military's unofficial spy unit.
"We have recently received feedback from various quarters regarding the collaborative merchandise with the Japanese television drama VIVANT," Sanrio said in a statement.
"We sincerely apologise for any concern this may have caused."
The project "contains expressions that are inconsistent with the Sanrio Group's corporate philosophy", it said.
Sanrio said it had "decided to cease this collaboration, as well as all subsequent projects and promotional campaigns".
Hello Kitty and other cute Sanrio characters had been depicted as characters from "Vivant" – currently in its second season – in a range of novelty merchandise items.
Read moreFrench-Saudi ‘Dragon Ball’ theme park puzzles Japanese manga fans
Before the apology, Chinese state media outlet the Global Times had accused the show of "smearing China", saying it had "sparked shock and fierce backlash on social media".
The series reflects the "anti-China narrative of the current conservative Japanese right-wing administration, catering to the trend of right-wing extremism in Japanese society", it said.
Long-frosty ties between the countries have worsened since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested last year that Japan could intervene militarily in any conflict over Taiwan.
Beijing claims self-ruled Taiwan as its territory and has vowed to bring it under control one day.
'Beauty and goodness'
The drama "is a completely fictional entertainment work", private broadcaster TBS, which created "Vivant", said in a statement to AFP.
"There is absolutely no intention to deliver messages that disparage any particular nation or hurt public sentiment," it said.
The network's president told Japanese media that TBS "does not in any way take a position that foments conflict between nations or condones the use of force or violence".
Comments posted on Chinese social media platform Weibo before Sanrio's announcement had angrily criticised the merchandise tie-up.
"Sanrio, you are a brand for conveying a message of beauty and goodness, why have you got involved with this?" one post said.
"It's disappointing," read another. "The founder has long taken part in various anti-war activities, and Sanrio was originally founded on the ideals of stopping war and cherishing peace."
Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun echoed the complaints at a regular news briefing on Thursday, following Sanrio's statement.
"This television drama once again reveals the persistent existence inside Japan of a force that seeks to use cultural products to vilify and smear China and spread anti-Chinese sentiment," he said.
"This should raise alarm amongst the international community and enlightened individuals within Japan."
The furore follows similar ire from the country over Mbappé's comments.

Restricted airspace now covers fifty defence sites
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:00:09 GMT
18:00:09 KST

Restricted airspace has been applied over fifty defence sites and a further one hundred and seventy are expected to follow in December, part of a wider effort to harden British military bases against drones, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Mark Pritchard, the Conservative member for The Wrekin, asked what additional support is being given to Guardian, the protective security element of Standing Joint Command, in light of increased threats to British military bases.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Defence Investment Plan provides an additional £470 million over four years for security technology and infrastructure. Restricted Airspace has been applied to 50 Defence sites, with a further 170 expected in December 2026, while £15 million has been invested in remotely piloted and counter-uncrewed aerial systems and training over the past 18 months.”
Restricted airspace makes flying a drone over a site unlawful without permission. That does not stop anyone flying, but it gives the police and the Ministry of Defence Police an offence to act on, and it removes the argument that an operator did not know where they were.
The department has set out £240 million for Project PRESAGIUM, an enhanced counter-drone system intended to detect and defeat emerging threats, and the Army is running Project Halo Shield to examine what commercially available counter-drone technology could do for site protection. The £15 million figure for remotely piloted and counter-drone systems and training over the past eighteen months is small compared with those programmes and covers work done while they are being stood up.

Astronomers Discover a Possible New Dwarf Planet in Our Solar System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Scientists are on the verge of confirming the discovery of another member of the solar system, a potential dwarf planet. Astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile located the object, provisionally named 2026 ED138.
The prospective planet measures somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers in diameter and is located about 46 astronomical units from the sun (an astronomical unit being Earth’s approximate distance from the sun). For comparison, Pluto—which is also now considered a dwarf planet—orbits at an average distance of 40 astronomical units. Based on its location, ED138 belongs to the population of trans-Neptunian objects. According to its discoverers, it could be one of the brightest known objects of this type and also among the largest.
The difference between a planet and a dwarf planet is largely their environment. While both orbit the sun and have sufficient gravity to assume a nearly spherical shape, a planet has cleared its orbit of other bodies of comparable size. Dwarf planets, on the other hand, coexist with other objects in the region of the solar system they traverse. This is the main reason why Pluto ceased to be considered a planet in 2006 and was reclassified as a dwarf planet.
Matthew Holman, a researcher at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and a member of the observatory’s operations team, identified the object on October 13 while analyzing data collected by Rubin in 2026. A more thorough search allowed the team to locate additional observations in archived records dating back to 2016. Thanks to this set of images, the team was able to reconstruct more than a decade of the object’s trajectory.
Astronomers explain that ED138 had managed to “hide” from us because its position in the night sky is against the disk of the Milky Way, which we usually see as a thick band of millions of stars. This concentrated brightness makes it difficult to distinguish fainter objects, but the Rubin Observatory’s enormous amounts of data made it possible to identify the object amid that sea of light.
Though ED138 appears to have the right characteristics, astronomers have yet to confirm whether it is a dwarf planet. For now, astronomers know it is a trans-Neptunian object, but they need to determine its size more precisely to establish whether its own gravity is sufficient to give it a nearly spherical shape. If it meets the requirements, ED138 would join the group of five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris.
It is also not the only celestial body awaiting possible classification as a dwarf planet. Astronomers have identified dozens of objects in the outer solar system that, based on their size and other characteristics, could meet the criteria. Among the best-known candidates are Gonggong, Quaoar, Sedna, and Orcus. Experts acknowledge that the list could be even longer.
Confirming them as dwarf planets is no easy task. The enormous distance at which they lie makes it difficult to directly measure their size and mass and, above all, to determine whether their own gravity has given them a nearly spherical shape. To obtain high-resolution images of Pluto, for example, the New Horizons probe had to be sent to its vicinity—a journey that took nearly nine and a half years from its launch in 2006 to its flyby in 2015. Three years later, it reached the object Arrokoth, a small planetesimal even farther away.
The solar system is often depicted as a star surrounded by eight planets, but in reality it is a much more extensive and populous structure. In addition to planets and moons, it contains dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, and a vast number of small bodies that extend far beyond Neptune. The Kuiper Belt extends to approximately 50 astronomical units, while the scattered disk reaches nearly 1,000. Much farther out lies the Oort Cloud, a region we have never directly observed and that could extend up to about 100,000 astronomical units from the sun.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:59:56 UTC
17:59:56 KST

As Latvia's 14th Saeima concluded its work on Thursday, Speaker of Parliament Daiga Mieriņa of the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) called on lawmakers to maintain respect for the Saeima and democratic values, stressing that the country is always greater than any political party, parliamentary group or parliamentary term.
In her final address to the outgoing parliament, Mieriņa acknowledged that the past four years had not been easy and had required considerable work, patience and compromise. Nevertheless, lawmakers had managed to maintain dialogue even when their opinions differed.
The Speaker recalled that during the 14th Saeima's term, parliament held 219 sittings, conducted 7,911 votes, adopted 1,060 laws and held 3,555 committee meetings.
She emphasised that the Saeima is a mirror of society, reflecting what Latvia has been and what it is today.
Mieriņa thanked lawmakers for their contributions to strengthening parliamentarism, democracy and the Latvian state, noting that every member of parliament had left their mark over the four years, whether through adopted legislation, initiatives or parliamentary debates.
She stressed that in a democracy, there are no small or large mandates, only the trust of voters granted for a limited period.
Addressing lawmakers who will continue serving in the next parliament, Mieriņa encouraged them to retain the ability to listen not only to their own voters but also to those who hold different views.
She also urged them to respect parliamentary traditions and the people on whose behalf decisions are made.
At the same time, Mieriņa noted that society is changing and a new generation is knocking on parliament's doors, bringing its own perspectives and expectations of politics.
She stressed that politicians must be willing to listen to this generation and make room for new representatives.
Mieriņa emphasised that no politician is irreplaceable, as members of parliament serve for a limited time, while Latvia, democracy and the people they serve remain.
Concluding her address, the Speaker wished lawmakers success in both their political careers and personal challenges.
She also quoted author and speaker Neale Donald Walsch, saying that a true leader is not someone who has the most followers, but someone who creates the most leaders.
Mieriņa ended her speech with the traditional Latvian wish: "May Latvia live as long as the sun!"

US reporters to monitor Russia-Ukraine truce in frontline town – Melania Trump

US reporters to monitor Russia-Ukraine truce in frontline town – Melania Trump
American journalists will observe a humanitarian mission under a Russia-Ukraine truce in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Kherson Region, Russia, US First Lady Melania Trump has said. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has confirmed that the reporters are expected there, and that demining operations are already underway.
Alyoshki, located on the left bank of the Dnieper River, was largely cut off from essential supplies and basic services for months under a Ukrainian siege, with drone attacks and remotely laid mines hampering aid deliveries and evacuation efforts from a town where an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 civilians remained.
Russian Foreign Ministry envoy Rodion Miroshnik described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods,” accusing Ukraine of obstructing humanitarian efforts.
However, after US mediation spearheaded by the Slovenian-born US first lady, Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the area starting October 27 to allow humanitarian assistance to flow in and evacuations to proceed. As of Thursday, both Russian and Ukrainian officials reported no truce violations. The pause is scheduled to last until Sunday.
Writing on X on Wednesday, Trump said four American journalists from conservative US outlet Newsmax will arrive in Alyoshki and accompany Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian leaders. “Serving as neutral observers, they will independently record and permanently document this historic humanitarian mission,” she said.
Dmitriev confirmed that Newsmax reporters will be there, adding: “Humanity and peace must prevail.”
Speaking to reporters before departing to Alyoshki, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said other foreign journalists are also expected to arrive, without providing further details.
Both Trump and Lantratova confirmed that Russia and Ukraine have begun clearing mines to secure aid routes. “It is now crucial to make the roads safe so that people can leave the town,” Lantratova said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said on Thursday that most Ukrainian mines found near Alyoshki were scattered by drones, and that they are predominantly Western-made. It also released a video showing a large-scale demining effort involving remotely-controlled robots.
The Alyoshki crisis was discussed during an October 9 phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, the leaders agreed that Russia’s human rights commissioner would maintain direct contact with Melania Trump’s office. US envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently met with Putin in St. Petersburg last week to discuss proposals for ending the Ukraine conflict.

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The authorities in Spain and Portugal, together with Kiev, are working to develop weapons for strikes against Russia, while their own citizens are grappling with a housing and economic crisis, Viktor Medvedchuk, head of the Other Ukraine movement and former leader of the Opposition Platform - For Life party banned in Ukraine, said.

"As a result, the political choices made by Madrid and Lisbon seem highly contradictory. On the one hand, there is condemnation of military actions in the Persian Gulf. On the other hand, these countries are being drawn into the war in Ukraine, which requires funding and cuts to social service budgets. While Spaniards are being forced to live in tents due to the housing crisis, and Portuguese authorities acknowledge the lack of affordable housing as one of the most pressing social problems, the governments of both countries are at the same time allocating state resources, industrial capacity, and technological expertise toward expanding arms production for Ukraine," he concluded.

====================================================================================================

Delhi’s De-Hyphenation Policy is Taking Shape in the South Caucasus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:52:00 UTC
17:52:00 KST

Few would have pictured Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar sharing a stage with his Azerbaijani counterpart, Jeyhun Bayramov, after Baku’s public backing of Islamabad during the India-Pakistan crisis of 2025.
Following the terrorist attack at Pahalgam on April 22, 2025, Azerbaijan was one of the few countries that did not publicly condemn the attack. After a telephone conversation with the Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on April 26, Baku issued a statement, expressing concern over the “recent tensions between India and Pakistan” and stressed the need to “refrain from unilateral actions in such a volatile situation.” Then, after India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, Azerbaijan explicitly condemned the Indian military strikes, saying they harmed civilians. It expressed solidarity with the people of Pakistan.
Against this backdrop, Jaishankar’s visit to Baku on October 23 – the first standalone visit by an Indian external affairs minister since 2018 – when he held talks with Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev and Foreign Minister Bayramov, marks an important step toward repairing strained bilateral ties.
At the joint press conference, Bayramov acknowledged that India and Azerbaijan “had different viewpoints on different issues,” before going on to describe discussions with Jaishankar as “very long and positive and fruitful.” Jaishankar echoed this sentiment, describing the discussions as “focused and forward looking” with both sides exchanging views on “various aspects” of the bilateral relationship and discussing important “regional and global developments from a strategic perspective.”
While no agreements were signed, both sides agreed to deepen cooperation in the oil and energy sector, expand trade and investment, and exchange commercial and business delegations. They also agreed to strengthen regular political consultations and exchange high-level visits. During the visit, Jaishankar reportedly raised the issue of cross-border terrorism, security, and common threats. Notably, including “cross-border terrorism” brought New Delhi’s primary security friction with Pakistan directly into the bilateral conversation, despite Islamabad’s close ties with Baku.
Jaishankar’s visit was not an isolated diplomatic gesture, but rather the latest in a series of moves to accelerate a thaw in India’s ties with Azerbaijan. Jaishankar’s visit to Baku was a follow-up to the meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Aliyev on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit at Bishkek in August-September this year.
Jaishankar’s visit was immediately preceded by a visit by the Indian Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh to Baku, where he led the Indian delegation for the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) held on October 15.
High-level diplomatic contact between New Delhi and Baku was restored in April this year, when India’s Secretary (West) Sibi George visited Baku for the 6th round of the India-Azerbaijan Foreign Office Consultations. The visit came less than a year after Baku condemned India’s military strikes on Pakistan. According to an Indian Ministry of External Affairs media release, the issues discussed included “trade, technology, tourism, pharmaceuticals, energy, culture, people to people exchanges and [the] fight against cross border terrorism.” The previous foreign office consultations were held in 2022.
According to an Indian media report, Azerbaijan resumed crude oil exports to India in September 2025, after a 10-month break caused by pricing issues that led to a halt in supplies. India-Azerbaijan bilateral trade has steadily dropped from $1,882 million in 2022 to $1,435 million in 2023, $958 million in 2024 and just $400 million in 2025. In the first 9 months of 2026, bilateral trade has already reached $600 million, Bayramov said.
It is important to understand the regional geopolitical context in which the thaw in New Delhi-Baku ties is playing out. India’s engagement in the South Caucasus has historically been weighted towards Armenia, Azerbaijan’s adversary in the decades-long Nagorno-Karabakh conflict. This has been a persistent irritant in India-Azerbaijan ties.
Meanwhile, Armenia has emerged as India’s strongest partner in the region – especially through defense cooperation – in recent years, driven largely by mutual concerns over an Azerbaijan-Pakistan-Türkiye nexus. The signing of the U.S. brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict in August 2025 paved the way for New Delhi to separate its relations with Baku from its position on the conflict, without risking derailing ties with Yerevan.
The evolving regional landscape has further accelerated this alignment. Nascent signs of rapprochement between Azerbaijan and Türkiye are evident, with the recent bilateral agreement to promote cooperation in academic engagements.
In September 2025, Armenia and Pakistan also established diplomatic relations after over 30 years of non-recognition by Islamabad. As more extra-regional actors come to play an active role in shaping the South Caucasus’ future, New Delhi is fast realizing it has more to lose by not engaging in multi-directional diplomacy with all actors.
Interestingly, Jaishankar’s visit comes at a time when Azerbaijan’s school hijab ban has strained Baku’s ties with one of its closest partners, Türkiye. After Baku announced a headscarf ban on September 21, Türkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan implicitly criticized the move at the U.N. General Assembly, calling it an assault on fundamental freedoms. The resulting criticism from Erdogan and other Türkish officials prompted a sharp response from Baku, triggering a rare diplomatic showdown between partners who describe themselves as “One Nation, Two States.”
Although Jaishankar’s visit was likely planned well in advance and unrelated to this sudden friction, the trip coincided perfectly with these shifting regional dynamics. It opens a valuable window for rapprochement, granting both nations greater geopolitical maneuvering space in light of New Delhi’s fraught relations with Ankara.
Another reason why New Delhi is looking to revive ties with Azerbaijan is to accelerate work on the International North South Transport Corridor (INSTC). Originally proposed in 2000, the project sat dormant for years until New Delhi recently signaled interest in reviving it, as an alternative to the conventional Suez Canal route amid growing vulnerability in global maritime chokepoints. Azerbaijan, which serves as the land bridge for the Western Route of the INSTC, will play a crucial role if New Delhi wants this route to become a dependable commercial artery. In this context, Baku agreeing to “closer coordination” on INSTC is a welcome development for New Delhi.
Yet, India’s ‘”de-hyphenation” policy may not automatically translate to a reset in ties. Because a formal peace treaty remains absent, the agreement between Azerbaijan and Armenia amounts to little more than a fragile truce. If the conflict persists or reignites, New Delhi will find itself increasingly intertwined in turbulent regional security dynamics.
Moreover, whether this relationship broadens or stagnates will also depend to a large extent on Baku’s willingness to accommodate New Delhi’s concerns regarding Pakistan and Kashmir.
Azerbaijan has been a consistent and vocal supporter of Pakistan’s position on the Kashmir issue, most notably at multilateral forums such as the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). Azerbaijan has consistently backed statements and communiques within the OIC and its contact group on Jammu and Kashmir, which condemned India’s actions in Kashmir.
Azerbaijan will be hosting the 2027 OIC Summit, and New Delhi will closely scrutinize how it frames the Kashmir issue in the grouping. Any overtly provocative framing is likely to adversely impact the future trajectory of India-Azerbaijan diplomatic and economic ties.
The trust deficit between the two sides is deep-rooted, and the recent rapprochement seems unlikely to bridge the big ideological differences between the two nations.
Nevertheless, engagement is a positive step, and a practical reflection of New Delhi’s ‘multi-alignment’ approach towards foreign policy.

Fundraiser for soldier killed during operations to recover missing Italians in the Maldives
Italy
Unknown Publisher

India objects to US upgrade of Pakistani F-16s
India has raised objections to a $686 million US package to upgrade Pakistan’s F-16 fighter jets and extend their service life, Indian media have reported.
Washington has gone ahead with the upgrade even as India and the US continue to deepen defense cooperation under a ten-year partnership framework signed last year. India and Pakistan, both nuclear-armed, clashed briefly last year with drones and missiles following a terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 26 civilians.
Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, in his talks with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Wednesday, also raised the possibility of sensitive American military technology supplied to Pakistan reaching third countries, the Economic Times reported, citing officials familiar with the discussions. The two officials met on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus in Cebu, Philippines.
The proposed package, notified to the US Congress in December, is intended to modernize Pakistan’s aging F-16 fleet and extend their operational life through 2040.
It includes 92 Link-16 tactical communication systems, avionics upgrades, secure communications, navigation equipment, spare parts, and training, according to a US Defense Security Cooperation Agency notification published last month. The package does not involve the sale of new fighter jets, and the US agency said it would not alter the basic military balance in the region.

He also offered to share that experience with ASEAN partners through joint drills and intelligence sharing.

Washington has maintained that the upgrades would support cooperation with Pakistan in counterterrorism operations, improve coordination between the two countries’ air forces, and address aircraft safety concerns.
India has previously objected to American support for Pakistan’s F-16 fleet, including in 2022 when Washington approved a $450 million maintenance package. Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar also questioned Washington’s justification that the aircraft were needed for counterterrorism operations.
During Wednesday’s meeting, the two sides reviewed progress on military coordination, technology sharing, and defense production, according to India’s Defense Ministry. Its public statement did not mention the F-16 objection.

Investing in conventional weapons better than developing nuclear program of one's own – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

Investing in conventional weapons better than developing nuclear program of one's own – expert
Jim Stokes, a GLOBSEC expert and former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy (2023-2025), expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Ukraine joining NATO. That is the most credible option. NATO's deterrence has worked for more than 77 years because no state has ever attacked the Alliance. I do not usually use the word 'guarantee,' but there are benefits to being covered by extended nuclear deterrence from the United States, the United Kingdom and France," the expert said.
At the same time, he cautioned against expecting a nuclear program of one's own to provide absolute protection. Stokes, who headed the Staff Group of NATO's Nuclear Planning Group, outlined his arguments.
According to him, the decision to develop an independent nuclear capability cannot be taken lightly, as no one wants further proliferation of nuclear weapons, which are currently possessed by only a limited number of states. Political commitments, financial costs, the technical expertise and technology required, and the time and money needed to produce a certain number of nuclear weapons must all be taken into account. In addition, a country would need delivery systems, a doctrine, command-and-control procedures, and many other supporting capabilities.
"All of this requires a great deal of effort. I say this as someone who worked for a long time on countering the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction," Stokes said.
He also cited North Korea as an example of a country that has become a nuclear power. However, the expert noted, North Korea is a pariah state. Ukraine, or any other country, therefore needs to consider whether it wants to become a pariah and potentially face sanctions by withdrawing from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. "Would that really provide the security they seek?" he said.
At the same time, Stokes acknowledged that he understood those who argue that, from a national security perspective, nuclear weapons offer the ultimate guarantee of national security and sovereignty.
The expert therefore believes it would be better to devote time, money and effort to conventional defense.
"Whether you can be part of a nuclear alliance and reinforce that arrangement, as in NATO or another alliance, or whether there are other ways to obtain some form of security guarantee. There seem to be better options that would be available rather than pursuing a national nuclear weapons program," Stokes concluded.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that in exchange for giving up its nuclear weapons, Ukraine should have received a "security umbrella." He described the guarantees the country received at the time as "an unfair game and a major mistake."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The National Institutes of Applied Research said Tuesday that it worked with Material Science Service Company to use a special coating to stabilize wafers for material analysis.
Shrinking semiconductor processes are prompting manufacturers to develop high-numerical-aperture extreme ultraviolet lithography. The process uses metal oxide photoresists to produce finer circuit patterns on chip wafers.
NIAR said in a press release that the process is still under development and has high structural requirements. Wafers also need to be dissected to check for possible post-processing defects.
NIAR also said that cutting a wafer open may ruin its nanostructure and material interfaces. The team applied a thin coating before cutting for structural stability.
NIAR President Tsai Hung-yin (蔡宏營) said etching is one thing, but quality checking is just as important. The institute noted that material analysis is crucial to ensuring the wafers meet standards.
The institution said the National Center for Instrumentation Research uses atomic layer deposition (ALD) to form the coating. MSS used the center’s custom-built ALD equipment to test different materials.
MSS also announced that it will partner with NIAR on production verification. MSS Chair Liu Chi-lun (柳紀綸) said he is optimistic, as the firm has received requests from the world’s leading semiconductor equipment makers.

Taiwan warns of forest fire risks as dry season begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:49:58 UTC
17:49:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency warned Thursday that the public should take extra care with fire as the dry season increases the risk of forest fires, particularly in central and southern Taiwan.
The agency said 390 forest fires, or 89% of the total recorded over the past decade, occurred between October and May, before the arrival of the plum rain season. Careless use of fire caused 97% of forest fires, underscoring the importance of prevention, per a press release.
The agency launched a public awareness campaign, “A Single Spark Destroys a Forest,” urging people visiting forests to avoid careless use of fire. To help the public assess local conditions, the agency operates the Forest Fire Risk Assessment System, which provides local fire risk forecasts for the next seven days.
When prolonged drought leaves forest-floor vegetation and other combustible material exceptionally dry, the agency may activate disaster-prevention cell broadcast alerts to warn people in affected areas. The agency urged the public to follow three rules: do not burn weeds, do not discard cigarette butts, and do not burn garbage.
Under Article 34 of the Forest Act, starting a fire in a forest area or forest protection zone without permission is prohibited. Violators can face fines of up to NT$600,000 (US$18,000).
Anyone who deliberately sets fire to another person’s forest faces three to 10 years in prison and may also be liable for civil damages, per the press release.
The agency offers a reward of NT$100,000 for reports of suspected criminal acts involving the burning of national or public forests that lead to the perpetrator being caught. A separate NT$5,000 reward may be given to the first person to report a forest fire, subject to applicable requirements.
Anyone who discovers a forest fire should immediately call the toll-free forest protection hotline at 0800-000930 or the fire department at 119. The agency urged the public to treat forest fire prevention as a shared responsibility and avoid leaving any potential ignition sources behind when visiting the mountains.

Storms Austen and Boelo leave cliffs up to 1.2 metres high on the Flemish coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:47:00 UTC
17:47:00 KST

Following autumn storms Austen and Boelo, cliffs have formed along the coast. On the beaches of the resorts of Blankenberge and Middelkerke, these cliffs are up to 1.2 metres high. The Maritime and Coastal Services Agency (MDK) is pulling them down using machinery. In Knokke-Heist, its was local council workers that levelled the cliffs.
Storms Austen and Boelo leave cliffs up to 1.2 metres high on the Flemish coast
The first autumn storm, Austen, swept across Belgium on Friday 23 October. The Royal Meteorological Institute (RMI) issued a code orange warning for gusts of up to 100 kilometres per hour. A day later, storm Boelo also swept across Belgium. A code yellow warning for wind was issued for the coast.
The effects of the storms are particularly clear on the beaches of Blankenberge and Middelkerke. There, experts identified cliffs up to 1.2 metres high, stretching over hundreds of metres. These are steep, almost vertical walls of sand. They form when waves wash away sand at the high-water mark during a storm.
Higher than 1 metre
The cliffs can be dangerous. They are not always clearly visible, meaning walkers could easily experience a nasty fall. “Sometimes the beach recovers naturally, thanks to the tides. If the cliffs are higher than 1 metre, we have to level them out with a machine,” explains Dries Derudder of the Maritime Services and Coast Agency(MDK). “That is now only the case in Blankenberge and Middelkerke.”
‘The cliffs will be levelled on Thursday or Friday at the latest, so that everything is safe in the run-up to the autumn half-term.’
Cliffs had also formed on the beach in Knokke-Heist. The largest were up to 2 metres high. There local council workers demolished the cliffs. “We’ve created a sort of passageway from the soft sand to the wet sand,” explains Bert De Brabandere, the alderman responsible for beaches. “People can walk there safely. In time, the water will wash away the cliffs.”

URDA, Spain – Rescuers picked through mangled carriages on Oct 29 in a grim search for victims of Spain’s second fatal high-speed train crash in 2026, as the death toll rose to 69 and hopes of finding further survivors faded.
After cranes were used through the night to lift parts of the wreckage of the Oct 28 crash, emergency workers were seen carrying what appeared to be a body wrapped in a blanket from one of the trains in the central Spanish province of Toledo.
Regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said the death toll had risen to 69 people and that human remains had been found during overnight rescue efforts. Work now involved crane operations, particularly on a carriage that was still overturned.
“We do not believe there could be any more fatalities beneath that one, but I say this with caution,” he said.
Unions blame lack of funding
Meanwhile, train drivers in Spain went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety after what is Europe’s deadliest train accident since a 2013 derailment in Spain’s Santiago de Compostela.
“We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again... It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had,” said Diego Martin of the train drivers’ union SEMAF.
“We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again. Everyone should be able to travel without the risk of suffering this kind of accident,” he added at Madrid’s Atocha railway station.
The crash, which followed another fatal accident in January involving the same rail companies on the same line, has also upended campaigning for a Nov 29 snap election, with the leaders of Spain’s two main parties suspending campaign events.
Spain’s government has declared three days of national mourning for those killed in the crash, which Transport Minister Oscar Puente said happened after several trains stopped due to a signal failure.
A state-run Renfe train was then authorised to proceed at normal speed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, Puente said on Oct 28.
Unions have already blamed a lack of funding and will to improve safety, saying that talks after the accident in January were abandoned in April.
Meanwhile, the government has said that the decision to authorise the Renfe train to continue its journey was “inexplicable”.
Pope sends condolences
Pope Leo sent his condolences to the families of those killed, wished a speedy recovery to the injured and conveyed his support and comfort to all affected, the Vatican said, adding he had also encouraged rescue workers to continue their efforts.
Of those injured, 57 remained in hospital, said the authorities.
The crash prompted a major operation, which Spain’s Interior Ministry said involved the deployment of more than 800 military and police personnel, over 200 vehicles, three helicopters, a mobile command post, drones, mounted units and search dogs.
As investigations began, a judge in Toledo barred anyone not involved in emergency, security, healthcare or judicial work from the crash site with a 2km exclusion zone in both directions along the Madrid-Seville high-speed rail line.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who travelled to Toledo to take part in a meeting to monitor and coordinate the emergency response, said the authorities were working “day and night” to support the victims and their families and to “get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy”.
Meanwhile, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the centre-right People’s Party, which is currently leading in polls, was due to visit the town of Urda, where local people rushed to help with rescue efforts in the aftermath of the crash.
Foreign nationals among casualties
Spain’s Foreign Ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, information available so far showed. One of them was killed and at least seven were injured.
The Oct 28 accident has added urgency to a debate about safety on Spain’s railways, Europe’s longest network and until recently a source of pride in the country.
Train drivers would go ahead with their strike to press for structural changes in railway safety, SEMAF said, adding that it was studying further action.
Renfe said the strike caused significant disruption to rail services, adding that passengers could change or cancel tickets free of charge and would be notified of affected services. REUTERS

28 October 2026, The Hague – Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Mihai Popșoi held a meeting with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Tom Berendsen.
The discussions focused on Moldova–Netherlands relations and cooperation priorities for the period ahead, with an emphasis on expanding cooperation in various sectors, including support for the Republic of Moldova’s European integration process.
Deputy Prime Minister Mihai Popșoi expressed appreciation for the Netherlands’ support, reflected in initiatives aimed at reforming the justice system, strengthening the rule of law and enhancing the Republic of Moldova’s resilience against hybrid threats, information manipulation and cyberattacks. He also expressed Moldova’s interest in continued Dutch assistance in these areas, including cybersecurity.
The Moldovan Foreign Minister stressed that support from the Netherlands and other partners is essential for strengthening the country’s capacity to ensure the security of its citizens, advance reforms and align with European standards. Mihai Popșoi thanked the Dutch authorities for their support and emphasised that the Republic of Moldova is ready to open the remaining two negotiating clusters: Cluster 4, “Green Agenda and Sustainable Connectivity”, and Cluster 5, “Resources, Agriculture and Cohesion”.
“Despite the challenges, the Republic of Moldova continues its path towards the European Union with determination. We know that this is a complex process that requires hard work and sustained efforts. We bear an enormous responsibility, but we are confident that, together with reliable partners such as the Kingdom of the Netherlands, we will succeed in completing the transformations our country needs to become an EU Member State,” Mihai Popșoi said.
For his part, Minister Tom Berendsen reaffirmed the Netherlands’ support for the Republic of Moldova’s accession to the European Union and expressed readiness to deepen cooperation in areas of mutual interest.
The two ministers reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the partnership between the Republic of Moldova and the Kingdom of the Netherlands and agreed to maintain dialogue to identify new opportunities for cooperation for the benefit of citizens of both countries. South Korean prosecutor seeks death penalty for Yoon over martial law
The prosecution argues only the death penalty could hold the ex-president fully accountable for a crime as serious as planning a rebellion
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
A South Korean special prosecutor on Thursday demanded the death penalty for ousted president Yoon Suk-yeol, ahead of an appeal court verdict on rebellion charges over his brief imposition of martial law in December 2024.
The Seoul High Court has yet to set a date for a verdict on Yoon’s appeal of a life sentence handed down in February by the Seoul Central District Court. The court found that he illegally mobilised troops and police to seize the legislature, arrest political opponents and establish unchecked rule for a “considerable time”.
Investigators led by special prosecutor Cho Eun-suk also appealed the ruling, arguing Yoon deserved the death penalty because his actions posed a grave threat to the country’s democracy. An execution would be unlikely. South Korea has not executed anyone since 1997, effectively maintaining a moratorium on capital punishment following calls for its abolition.

Unknown

08:43:25 UTC
17:43:25 KST

26 October 2026, Nicosia – Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Mihai Popșoi held a meeting with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Cyprus, Constantinos Kombos, during an official visit at the invitation of his Cypriot counterpart.
The discussions focused on the priorities of Moldova–Cyprus relations, Cyprus’s support for advancing the Republic of Moldova’s European path, expanding cooperation in areas of mutual interest, and regional security developments.
The two ministers welcomed the strong cooperation between their countries and reviewed the progress made by the Republic of Moldova in its accession process to the European Union. Deputy Prime Minister Mihai Popșoi thanked the Cypriot authorities for their support, including during the Cypriot Presidency of the Council of the EU, which contributed to the official opening of negotiations on the first cluster, “Fundamentals”, in June this year.
“Accession to the European Union is the Republic of Moldova’s most important national project since gaining independence. The reforms we are implementing contribute to the country’s development and improve conditions for both citizens and businesses by bringing us closer to European standards. We want a stronger and more resilient Republic of Moldova that, in turn, contributes to Europe’s security and prosperity. To advance on this path, we need the support of all EU Member States,” Mihai Popșoi said.
“Cyprus has supported the Republic of Moldova’s European aspirations and will continue to advocate for its accession to the European Union. You have made remarkable progress so far, and we encourage you to maintain this momentum. We also want to deepen bilateral cooperation in areas of mutual interest and strengthen institutional ties between the Republic of Moldova and the Republic of Cyprus,” Minister Constantinos Kombos stated.
The officials discussed opportunities to increase bilateral trade and attract investment to the Republic of Moldova. Mihai Popșoi encouraged Cypriot companies to take advantage of the opportunities offered by Moldova and noted that flights between Chișinău and Larnaca provide direct air connectivity between the two countries.
Another topic of the meeting was the protection of citizens’ rights and the facilitation of their mobility. Mihai Popșoi and Constantinos Kombos discussed the possibility of negotiating agreements on social security, the mutual recognition of driving licences, and the recognition of academic qualifications.
To continue the bilateral dialogue, the Moldovan Foreign Minister invited his Cypriot counterpart, Constantinos Kombos, to pay a visit to the Republic of Moldova.

Purges at the Pentagon: Hegseth fires top military planner

Purges at the Pentagon: Hegseth fires top military planner
Kyiv • UNN
Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed from his position as director of J5 without an immediate replacement. The dismissal came amid possible U.S. strikes on Iran.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired the Pentagon’s top military planner. A Pentagon representative said this on October 28, UNN reports, citing AP.
Details
This is the latest in a series of generals being dismissed, and it comes even as U.S. President Donald Trump is considering resuming strikes on Iran in the eight-month war.
U.S. Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed as head of the Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff. He became the second general dismissed from the position, known in military circles as "J5," under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee, was forced to retire in October last year.
A Pentagon representative said there was no immediate replacement for Sylvia and that no reason for his dismissal had been provided.
A representative of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff said: "The Chairman, Joint Staff and Joint Force express their deep gratitude to Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia and his family for 32 years of distinguished service to our country" and "wish him and his family all the best."
Typically, the J5 director and his staff are responsible for developing and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the U.S. president. Sylvia’s dismissal came amid Trump’s repeated statements about launching new military operations against Iran.
Trump vowed to "finish what was started" in Iran after the war with Israel began eight months ago and said new strikes could take place after next week’s midterm elections.
According to two diplomats familiar with the situation, U.S. officials warned a number of Middle Eastern countries and regional allies that they needed to be prepared for the possible resumption of hostilities after Tuesday’s election, as well as possible retaliatory measures by Iran. They said Trump had not yet made a final decision on new strikes.
A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are heading to the region.
War with Iran has already cost the United States $47.1 billion - NYT28.10.26, 09:38 • 6580 views
Last month, Hegseth said he had ordered the reduction in the total number of senior officer positions to be doubled to 20%, to be completed by January 1, 2027. There are currently about 800 admiral and general positions.
Some members of Congress have criticized the reduction in the number of general officers as a "purge" that will take years to recover from.
"He has some deeply rooted resentment toward the leadership in the Army. He is getting rid of an entire generation of great Army leaders, and it will take a whole generation to recover from this," Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, a former U.S. Navy combat pilot who has criticized Hegseth, said last month.

Türkiye hosts 13th OTS summit to advance Turkic unity and cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:33:53 UTC
17:33:53 KST

Türkiye is hosting the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara to further “unity in language, thought, and deed” among its member states.
The summit kicked off on Thursday with the Meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the OTS.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hosted the meeting, according to diplomatic sources.
Foreign ministers of the OTS posed for a family photo ahead of the meeting.
The two-day summit is hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan under the theme Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.
Established in 2009, the OTS, formerly known as the Turkic Council, adopted its current name during its eighth summit held in the Turkish metropolis Istanbul in 2021.
While Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are members, Turkmenistan, Hungary, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, and the Economic Cooperation Organization hold observer status.
The organisation said on October 24 that the summit will bring together the heads of state of its member states, as well as high-level representatives from observer states and its secretary general, to “discuss the current state and future prospects of cooperation within the Organization,” among other issues.
It said in a statement that the heads of state are expected to review the progress achieved across the OTS’ priority areas, and that particular emphasis will be placed on “further strengthening unity and solidarity” among the Turkic states and advancing cooperation under the Turkic World Vision 2040.
It added that the summit will also mark Türkiye’s assumption of the OTS’ chairmanship from Azerbaijan, and is expected to address the appointment of a new secretary general and the organisation’s strategic priorities “for the forthcoming period.”
“The Heads of State are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, together with a number of decisions and documents aimed at deepening cooperation and further strengthening the institutional framework of the OTS,” it added.
The leaders’ summit will be held on Friday.
‘Unity in deed’
Turan Gafarli, a non-resident fellow at the Baku-based Topchubashov Center, defined support among Turkic states and bolstering their political solidarity as the significant aspect of the Ankara summit.
Noting that they are living through a period in which the world faces “increasing uncertainty,” Gafarli told Anadolu that the Turkic world is evolving into a political structure that is “developing the capacity to act in unison in the face of international developments.”
“Naturally, this is a long-term process. Yet, the true meaning of brotherhood is not just coming together during good times, but standing by one another during difficult ones,” he said, noting his belief that the summit in Türkiye will further solidify the “atmosphere of trust built to date.”
Gafarli highlighted the term of unity used in the summit’s theme as “highly significant,” as well as expressed belief that the summit will give momentum to developments particularly in the realms of economic relations, transport corridors, and political coordination.
He stated the growing strategic importance of the Middle Corridor presented a “historic opportunity” for the Turkic states to become more closely interconnected economically, but that this requires a number of steps, including bolstering trade between member states.
“Furthermore, it is essential that the Turkic states engage in closer consultation on international issues and advocate more robustly for their shared interests,” he said, adding he believes Türkiye’s chairmanship could bring fresh dynamism in this context.
Meanwhile, Shairbek Dzhuraev, the president of the Crossroads Central Asia research institute based in Bishkek, shared the belief that tangible progress has been observed most evidently in the economic sphere, underlining transport and transit in particular.
“The development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route depends on the harmonisation of tariffs and the simplification of customs procedures. In this context, results can be measured by the time and cost involved in transporting goods,” Dzhuraev said.
Dzhuraev further underlined digitalisation as a second promising area, which he defined as the focus of the organisation’s informal summit held in Turkistan in southern Kazakhstan in May.
“The most substantial outcome of the Ankara summit would be the establishment of concrete timelines and mechanisms for implementing decisions already reached – particularly those concerning transport and trade,” he stated.
As part of the OTS Ankara summit, sports is also an area where unity is expected to be shown “in deed.”
During a news conference in Ankara ahead of the summit, Kursad Zorlu, the ruling Justice and Development (AK) Party's deputy chair in charge of relations with Turkic states, said the event includes plans for players from Turkic states to be classified as domestic rather than foreign in one another’s leagues, saying the initiative would foster a football ecosystem across the Turkic world.

Unknown Publisher

Drones target one of Russia’s largest chemical complexes in Bashkortostan, media report
This was reported by The Moscow Times, according to Ukrinform.
It is noted that the drones targeted the Bashkir Soda Company (BSC) plant. Smoke began to rise above the plant following the attack.
BSC is one of Russia’s largest chemical complexes and ranks first in the country in the production of soda ash and baking soda.
According to the publication, the enterprise is part of the Roskhim holding company, which holds a controlling stake (57.43%). At the same time, the complex is included in the Russian Ministry of Industry and Trade’s closed registry of defense enterprises.
BSC supplies military plants with hydrochloric acid and dichloroethane, and is also the only Russian producer of terephthaloyl chloride.
This is a critically important compound for the production of synthetic ballistic fibers, high-strength polymers, and aramid materials, according to the report.
It is used to manufacture body armor, helmets, and armor components for military equipment and aircraft.
Prior to this, drones had already attacked the BSC on August 27. Smoke was also seen rising above the facility at that time. Authorities did not comment on the attack.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Russian city of Lipetsk was attacked by missile strikes; according to preliminary information, a fire broke out in the area of the Novolipetsk Metallurgical Plant.

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China strongly condemns and firmly opposes the United States' decision to add three Chinese entities to the so-called "Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List," a spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce said Thursday.
There is no forced labor in China, and people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang enjoy freedom and equality in employment, with their labor rights and interests effectively protected by law, the spokesperson said in response to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's announcement that it had added three Chinese entities to the list.
The U.S. measures have no factual basis, the spokesperson said, accusing the U.S. side of persistently manipulating human rights issues to pursue unilateral protectionism and bullying under the guise of human rights protection.
The spokesperson noted that the United States had recently added a large number of Chinese entities to the same list. China had lodged solemn representations with the U.S. side and taken resolute countermeasures.
Disregarding China's firm opposition, the United States has continued to impose new sanctions, this time targeting Chinese biomedical technology companies, the spokesperson said.
Such actions run counter to the consensus reached by the two heads of state, seriously undermine the stability of China-U.S. economic and trade relations, and are contrary to humanitarian principles, the spokesperson added.
The spokesperson urged the United States to immediately stop its political manipulation and smear campaigns, and cease its unjustified suppression of Chinese companies, adding that China will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its own interests. ■

Debris from the UAVs fell on the grounds of a factory in Sterlitamak, Bashkortostan. Minor damage was reported, and the plant is operating normally.

Scale
- Alert air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions last night, according to the Defense Ministry.
- The ministry reported that enemy UAVs were shot down over the Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Kaluga, Tula, Smolensk, Lipetsk, Voronezh, Tver, Oryol, Ryazan, Vladimir, Samara, Saratov, Penza, and Rostov Regions, the Moscow Region, the Republic of Bashkortostan, and the Republic of Udmurtia.
- An attempted drone attack on Moscow by the Ukrainian armed forces, carried out on Wednesday evening and overnight, was one of the largest of the year so far, according to TASS estimates based on data published by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin on his Max channel.
- According to the mayor, between 8:30 p.m. Moscow time (5:30 p.m. GMT) on October 28 and 7:00 a.m. Moscow time (4:00 a.m. GMT) on October 29, a total of 613 enemy UAVs were heading toward the Moscow Region.
- Most were neutralized by the Defense Ministry’s air defense forces at a distance, while 231 drones were destroyed on approach to Moscow, he specified.
- Air defense forces destroyed 170 Ukrainian drones over the Kaluga Region, Governor Vladislav Shapsha reported on Max.
- Air defenses destroyed 42 Ukrainian drones over the Tula Region overnight, Governor Dmitry Milyayev wrote on his Max channel.
- A drone attack was thwarted in Sterlitamak, Bashkortostan. Eight drones were shot down, Mayor Emil Shaimardanov reported on Telegram.
- Air defense forces destroyed four drones over the Ulyanovsk Region, Governor Alexey Russkikh wrote on his Max channel.
Consequences
- Debris from the UAVs fell on the grounds of a facility in Sterlitamak, Bashkortostan, according to a report by Mayor Emil Shaimardanov on Telegram.
- Minor damage was reported.
- The plant is operating normally.
Airport operations
- Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) reported that temporary restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures - necessary to ensure flight safety - had been imposed at Moscow’s Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports.
- These restrictions have now been lifted.
- Two planes flying from Istanbul to Moscow turned back in mid-flight and returned due to safety restrictions at Vnukovo Airport in Moscow, a source in air traffic control services told TASS.
- In addition, restrictions were imposed at airports in Bugulma, Izhevsk, Kazan, Kaluga, Kirov, Nizhnekamsk, Orenburg, Penza, Perm, Samara, Saransk, Saratov, Ulyanovsk, Ufa, Cheboksary, Chelyabinsk, Cherepovets, and Yaroslavl.

American weightlifter Morris proud of bronze in Chinese debut, eyes bigger prize
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:30:21 CST
17:30:21 KST

NINGBO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- American weightlifter Hampton Morris said he was proud of his bronze medal at the IWF World Championships despite narrowly missing out on gold after failing his final clean-and-jerk attempt.
Morris, 22, lifted 143 kilograms in the snatch and 185kg in the clean and jerk for a total of 328kg, finishing third in the men's 65kg category behind DPR Korea's Pak Myong-jin, who set two world records with a 187kg clean and jerk and a 331kg total, and Türkiye's Muhammed Furkan Ozbek, who took silver with 330kg on Wednesday.
"I'm very, very proud of what I was able to accomplish today. I had some very, very tough competitors," Morris told Xinhua.
There were nevertheless positives for the American, whose 143kg snatch was a personal best, improving on the 142kg he lifted at a domestic competition six weeks earlier.
However, Morris welcomed the challenge posed by his Asian rivals, who had swept the podium at last month's Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.
"Not nervous, but more excited. It's a really incredible opportunity to be able to compete here," he said. "I'm grateful that they're able to push me as much as they have."
The American's respect for his competitors was evident throughout the competition. During his interview with Xinhua, Morris briefly excused himself to greet Chinese lifters Ding Hongjie and He Yueji, shaking hands with both before returning to answer questions.
Competing in China for the first time, Morris has also embraced his experience away from the platform. He shared his amusement at encountering a food-delivery robot at his hotel in Ningbo in a post on Instagram.
"It's amazing. I've really, really enjoyed being here," he said.
Morris is already a familiar figure among Chinese weightlifting fans, having attracted attention for his cheerful demeanor at the 2024 Paris Olympics, where he won bronze in the men's 61kg category.
His clean-and-jerk lift of 172kg set an Olympic record and helped him become the first American man to win an Olympic weightlifting medal since 1984.
The lifter from Marietta, Georgia, had previously won clean-and-jerk gold at the 2023 world championships in Riyadh, becoming the first American man to claim a world weightlifting title since 1984.
With a 190kg clean and jerk already achieved in training, Morris believes he has the strength to challenge for further records and titles, with the Los Angeles Games his next major target. ■

Unknown Publisher

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia has called for stronger international cooperation to ensure stable global gas markets and reliable energy supplies, emphasizing that energy security is fundamental to industrial competitiveness, investment confidence and sustainable economic growth, the Ministry of Economy said on Thursday.
As renewable energy deployment accelerates, natural gas will continue to provide the reliability and flexibility needed to support electricity systems and industrial activities, particularly amid rising energy demand across Asia and the ASEAN region, the ministry said in a statement.
Against the backdrop of geopolitical uncertainty, supply disruptions and price volatility, Malaysia emphasized the importance of market transparency, predictable policy frameworks and sustained investment across the natural gas value chain. Greater cooperation between producers and consumers is essential to strengthening supply resilience and maintaining confidence in long-term energy investment, it said.
Malaysia reaffirmed the importance of deepening cooperation through the Gas Exporting Countries Forum and observer countries in market intelligence, liquefied natural gas trade, infrastructure development and technology exchange, the statement said. ■

Spain mourns 68 killed in second deadly high-speed train crash this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:27:33 UTC
17:27:33 KST

Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday after its second high-speed rail collision this year killed 68 people and injured over 100, as relatives sought news of missing loved ones.
The crash occurred on Wednesday morning in Castilla-La Mancha when a state-run Renfe train struck the back of a stationary train operated by private company Iryo.
Emergency crews searched the wreckage overnight near the village of Urda, using cranes to lift mangled metal. Police drones resumed flights over the site at daybreak.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said an automatic control system had failed along 69 kilometres of track, stopping trains. The control centre later resumed traffic in what he called “inexplicable circumstances”, despite having time to identify and correct the error.
The disaster has raised fresh safety concerns after a January collision in Andalusia killed 46 people when a derailed train crossed onto an adjacent track. That investigation remains ongoing.
Relatives seek answers
A school in Urda, about 130 kilometres south of Madrid, was opened to relatives seeking information about loved ones.
Red Cross workers and psychologists provided support to families, while the Civil Guard established offices in Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to collect DNA samples and help identify victims.
Survivors described the force of the collision and the chaos inside the trains.
Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian holidaying in Spain, said he had been asleep when he woke up “in the air”.
Pablo Mejia, 42, said a last-minute seat change had saved his life. He described a powerful impact, passengers piled on top of one another and seats ripped out.
“I think I've been born again,” he told AFP.
Flags flew at half-mast as official ceremonies and public events were cancelled or scaled back.

Türkiye marks 103rd Republic Day with ceremonies, nationwide celebrations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:26:37 UTC
17:26:37 KST

Türkiye is marking the 103rd anniversary of the founding of its Republic with ceremonies in the capital and festivities across the country.
Celebrations in Ankara were set to begin with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and senior state officials visiting Anitkabir, the mausoleum of founder Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. Erdogan will lay a wreath, observe a moment of silence and sign the memorial book, then receive congratulations at the Presidential Complex.
In a video message, Erdogan said Türkiye is stronger today than yesterday and will be more powerful, prestigious and effective in every field tomorrow. He pointed to progress over the past 24 years in defence, energy, transport and diplomacy.
The Republic was declared on October 29 1923, with all 158 lawmakers present in Parliament voting in favour. Ataturk was subsequently elected the country’s first president with all 158 votes.
On Thursday, Türkiye’s senior officials also marked the anniversary.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said the government is working towards the 2053 and 2071 visions under Erdogan’s leadership, aiming to carry its gains further, while Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahceli said his party was determined to carry the Republic’s legacy into the “Century of Türkiye”.
National Intelligence Organization (MIT) chief Ibrahim Kalin said the Republic embodied Türkiye’s independence, unity and shared future, adding that MIT would continue working to protect national security and sovereignty.
Turkic leaders in Ankara
This year’s anniversary coincides with the 13th Organization of Turkic States (OTS) summit, which brings the leaders of the five member states to Ankara on October 29-30.
Erdogan will open the Bestepe National Garden with an equestrian show, then host an official dinner for visiting leaders.
Guests will be welcomed by the Mehter band and by soldiers and flags representing 16 historic Turkic states. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov will receive a state medal, and the president will present this year’s Ali Sir Nevai International Award.
The programme will also feature a concert by Türkiye’s Presidential Symphony Orchestra, a traditional dance performance organised by TURKSOY, an international organisation promoting Turkic culture, and live music by Turkish singer Kirac and Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen.
Celebrations across the country
Republic Day events are taking place across Türkiye.
The “Türkiye Pedals” initiative will bring together cyclists across all 81 provinces from October 29 to November 1, ahead of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya on November 9-20. Open to licensed athletes, cycling clubs, students, families and cycling enthusiasts, the events aim to promote cycling as a sustainable transport option and raise public awareness of the climate change.
The historic Istiklal Road is being crossed on horseback to mark the Republic’s 103rd year. Organised for the third time by the Equestrian and Culture Association, the ride follows the 95-kilometre route along which weapons and ammunition arriving at Inebolu Port were sent on to Anatolia during the War of Independence. Forty-five riders from across Türkiye are taking part in the two-day journey.
The Osmangazi-Türkiye Century Run on the Osmangazi Bridge is expected to draw around 6,000 participants, with nearly 8,000 applications received and athletes from 19 countries signed up. The event, held for the first time on October 29, features a 10-kilometre race for elite runners and a 5-kilometre public run. Kocaeli Metropolitan Municipality Mayor Tahir Buyukakin said organisers aim to make it a traditional annual event, bringing together people of different generations to mark the Republic Day.
In Corum, residents marked the day with a march carrying a 103-metre Turkish flag.
In Diyarbakir, students unfurled a 54-square-metre Turkish flag at the historic Ickale in the Sur district, in the shadow of the city’s thousands-of-years-old walls and stone structures. The event was led by the provincial education directorate, and the choreography was filmed from the air by drone.

New apps challenge Tallinn's official public transport website
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:24:00 UTC
17:24:00 KST

New apps challenge Tallinn's official public transport website
Public transport apps enterprising developers have come up with are growing in popularity and offer an alternative to Tallinn's official public transport website.
Unlike many European capitals, Tallinn still has no official public transport mobile app, while critics say the official site at transport.tallinn.ee is getting outdated and is not very user-friendly.
"The people who should know how best to do these things haven't done anything. This is the kind of thing that was being done in 2010, and in 2026 we really shouldn't still be dealing with something like this," said Kaspar Sanglepp, creator of the Go Now app, one of the competing products.
"To quickly see bus times, you have to go to different websites and click through a lot of things. I wanted to be able to get that information with one click," Sanglepp said.
"The visual design is 10–15 or more years old. It takes so much time just to get to the route planner," said Sander Pukk, creator of another app, called Mis? Kuhu? ("What? Where to?").
All public transport vehicles in Tallinn and Tartu send their location to the system every 10 seconds. Using this publicly available data, developers have created three different free apps. Despite not being advertised, between them they have amassed over 2,000 daily users.
The newest app on the scene, Tallinn Live, garnered 4,000 views in four days.
"Tallinn Live project, it's very simple: you just are going to the app, you are just using it. That's why it's basic, and that's why people love it," Taha Yasin Erel, creator of Tallinn Live, told "Aktuaalne kaamera".
"I got lots of, hundreds of comments, hundreds of new ideas, and I started with these ideas, and people started to like it more," Erel went on.
Most public transport stops in Tallinn are still old school in that they lack display boards and have only printed timetables. At peak times and with all the ongoing roadworks in Tallinn, there is often a difference between when a bus, trolleybus or tram is scheduled and when it actually arrives, something which apps can help with.
"Real-time information has definitely been the main thing. Many stops still don't have those display boards, so being able to see whether a bus is running late or not has been the subject of the most positive feedback," Pukk went on.
According to Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse, however, surveys show that people are satisfied with Tallinn Transport's website. The city nevertheless plans to update it.
"The Transport Department (TLT) is currently carrying out the relevant analyses, and we certainly plan to update it in the coming years to make it more user-friendly, with an app or a mobile view," Jesse said.

Norwegian PM denies claims about conversation with Putin
