'We must learn so that it doesn't happen again': Oct. 7 veterans prepare soldiers for the next war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:39:37 UTC
15:39:37 KST

On Oct. 7, 2023, as Israel awoke to an unprecedented nightmare, these four company commanders were still serving in more junior positions. They rushed from the officer training school, private trips and weekend leave straight into the chaos in communities near the Gaza border, including Be'eri, Kissufim, Nir Oz and the Re'im junction.
They rescued civilians under heavy fire, witnessed scenes they had previously thought existed only in movies and, in some cases, suffered serious injuries. Now, after three consecutive years of intense fighting in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank, they command companies at the Givati Brigade's training base, the Nahal Brigade's training base, the Paratroopers' training program and the squad commanders' course.
The officers are bringing hard-earned operational lessons and insights gained at great personal cost to the training grounds, where they are responsible for educating and shaping the next generation of combat soldiers.
"On Oct. 7, I was a team commander in the Gefen Battalion at Bahad 1," recalled Capt. Y., now a company commander overseeing recruits in the Givati Reconnaissance Unit, referring to the IDF's officer training school.
"We started that morning at 7 a.m., and I drove south with my father to reach the assembly point. I spent my first hours of fighting with two officer cadets, and from there we drove to the Re'im junction area, near the site of the music festival, and then to Nir Oz.
"I separated from the cadets to join my team because I understood that I was responsible for my unit and couldn't let my soldiers fight without me. We brought combat equipment from Bahad 1 and then headed into fighting in Sufa, Nir Yitzhak and the Yesha junction. We spent three or four days restoring control."
One moment from those first days remains particularly vivid.
"There was a moment when we stopped the Humvees, quickly prepared ourselves and the company commander told us to forget what we knew and understand that we were entering a combat zone," Capt. Y. recalled.
"When you're in the Gaza or Lebanon sector and someone tells you that, you understand. But I looked around and saw kibbutzim and Israeli communities. That really struck me. It was a period of tremendous shock and disbelief."
A generation that did not experience Oct. 7
Serious injuries and prolonged combat have become inseparable parts of the commanders' stories.
Capt. N., now a company commander in the Paratroopers' 890th Battalion training program who is set to be promoted to major, fought in Be'eri during the first days of the attack as part of a force known as "Ben-Mosh."
"We ran through Be'eri for two consecutive nights, going from house to house, rescuing residents and fighting in firefights until the community was declared clear," Capt. N. said.
"From there, we moved on to preparations for entering Gaza. A week after the ground offensive began, I was seriously wounded by friendly fire. Shrapnel cut into my windpipe, I was sedated and placed on a ventilator, and I underwent two months of rehabilitation. As soon as I could, I went straight back to my company."
Three years later, the new generation of soldiers is one that did not experience Oct. 7 firsthand as combat troops.
"Today, apart from my deputy company commander, no one serving under me was there on Oct. 7 or at the beginning of the ground offensive," Capt. N. said.
"My job is to help the soldiers imagine what it looked like. We were there, and we remember the initial shock. Our responsibility is to make sure that shock doesn't happen again next time."
Capt. A., a company commander in the IDF's squad commanders' course, puts the cultural and disciplinary lessons in stark terms.
"When I apply Oct. 7 to the training of commanders, I tell my trainees one thing: We must never forget. We must not forget what happened to us and what was done to us, and we must not forget that we failed in our mission," Capt. A. said.
"Alongside heroic battles, there were quite a few professional lessons we must learn so that it doesn't happen again. And it could happen tomorrow morning.
"My trainees were schoolchildren on Oct. 7, and now the responsibility rests on their shoulders. If they forget, we'll fall back into the same assumptions that made us less effective.
"At the tactical level, when I say there could be a war tomorrow morning, it's not a cliché. It's a belief I translate into daily preparations: maintaining constant readiness with ammunition, drills, defensive procedures and readiness at dawn.
"In my view, operational culture is the greatest lesson. Where that culture was lacking, that's where we failed."
'We failed in our mission to defend'
These lessons are shaping the next generation of soldiers from the ground up.
Capt. Y., a company commander at the Nahal Brigade's training base who is currently leading recruits through a week of field training, recalled the moment everything changed for him.
"We entered Kissufim into a full-scale battlefield, with gunfire coming from every direction and rockets in the air," he said.
"As we were driving, a friend who was in the vehicle with me was speaking on the phone with his family in Be'eri, explaining how to tie a shirt into a tourniquet to save their younger brother, who had been shot.
"We went from house to house under fire to rescue families and act as human shields for them. Our mission was to make sure no civilian was harmed, and we failed in that mission."
Capt. Y. of the Nahal training base said today's recruits arrive with a profound sense of responsibility. They understand that they are the country's protective vest, he said, and are eager to learn from the combat experience their commanders have accumulated.
Capt. Y. of the Givati Reconnaissance Unit described his company as part of a "generation of victory," a generation that has fought continuously for three years across multiple fronts, including Gaza and Lebanon, and demonstrated levels of resilience and capability rarely seen among soldiers performing mandatory military service.
All four commanders agree that the operational experience gained at such a heavy cost will, in their view, leave the next generation of combat soldiers better prepared to face the most demanding challenges.

They tried to persuade some leaders not to come, citing various difficult conditions in Russia,” Ushakov told RT. - 19:17 GMT Russia and African countries have adopted a joint declaration at the conclusion of the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, setting out priorities for cooperation on security, international affairs and economic development. 
Key points of the declaration:
· Maritime security: Oppose the unjustified detention, seizure or arrest of civilian vessels, including African-flagged ships, in violation of international law.
· Sanctions: Oppose unilateral coercive measures that violate international law, including sanctions imposed outside the UN Security Council, and work to reduce their economic impact.
· Sovereign assets: Oppose the freezing and attempted confiscation of sovereign assets, as well as political and economic coercion against sovereign states.
· Colonial reparations: Pursue legal mechanisms to assess and compensate for damage inflicted on African countries during the colonial era.
· International justice: Counter the politicization and misuse of international criminal justice mechanisms, including their use to exert neocolonial pressure on African states.
· UN reform: Work toward reforming the Security Council to increase African representation.
· Counterterrorism: Strengthen cooperation against terrorists’ use of drones, encrypted platforms and digital finance.
· Arms control: Oppose the politicization of international arms control, disarmament and nuclear nonproliferation mechanisms.
· IMF and World Bank: Push for reforms to give African countries greater representation and influence in decision-making.
· G20: Call for South Africa’s full and active participation in the group to be restored as soon as possible.
· Cultural heritage: Support the return of cultural objects and historical artifacts taken from African countries during colonial rule.
· Space cooperation: Expand peaceful space exploration, satellite technologies and joint research.
· Trade and infrastructure: Develop cooperation in precious metals and expand maritime, river, road, rail and aviation infrastructure.
· Climate policy: Oppose discriminatory protectionist measures introduced under the pretext of combating climate change.
· Sovereignty: Counter neocolonial practices that undermine states’ independence, restrict their decision-making or facilitate the exploitation of their natural resources.

- "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity," The Times of Israel quoted acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne as having written in a letter.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end
With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.
That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.
The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.
Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.
The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.
Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.
Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.
According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.
This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.
The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.
UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law.
"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.
"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."
Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.
He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW
Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.
"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."
Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.
"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.
Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.
WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock
Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.

Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.

Ousted defense ministry chief to run for Parempoolsed at Riigikogu election

Ousted defense ministry chief to run for Parempoolsed at Riigikogu election
Kaimo Kuusk, former Defense Ministry permanent secretary and former ambassador to Ukraine, is joining Parempoolsed and running for the Riigikogu next spring.
Parempoolsed are seeking to win their first ever Riigikogu seats at the March 2027 election.
Kuusk said via a party press release that he decided to run because he wants to see real impact from his work for Estonia's benefit: "I want my experience, skills and values to serve Estonia's security and defense capability."
He also hit out at what he called undemocratic approaches taken by some of the major parties.
"I can't stand by and watch Estonian democracy being eroded. It's very important to me that Estonia be a state governed by law. I won't accept it if Reform runs the same kind of politics in the country as Center does in Tallinn, where positions aren't allocated via competitions but in the party office," Kuusk said.
Kuusk also criticized the government's decision to hold a planned Ukraine aid conference in late January, which he said, given the situation there in winter, is the least suitable time for Ukraine yet convenient for campaign point-scoring for some of the political parties.
"We're setting the Ukraine reconstruction conference at the least suitable time for the Ukrainians, as Reform and Eesti 200 politicians want to tie it to the front of their election cart. Aid to Ukraine like this is of no benefit to Ukraine," Kuusk added. He noted a worrying trend which he says has emerged in Estonian politics whereby aid to Ukraine is seen primarily as having election propaganda value, at the cost of the state's functioning. "Various state institutions have consequently fallen out with each other. Something has gone wrong when, during a war, the most important question becomes who gets to open a kindergarten in Ukraine."
Kuusk stressed he joined Parempoolsed, founded shortly before the last Riigikogu elections in 2023, as he believes in the party's team and clear plans. "Parempoolsed offer values-based politics that will make Estonia's future better. I like that Parempoolsed dare to decide," he explained.
Parempoolsed chair Lavly Perling said she values Kuusk as a team player. "In addition, Kaimo hasn't worked on aiding Ukraine only on paper, but has been physically on the ground in Ukraine. I also know that as ambassador Kaimo was very active in economic diplomacy, opening doors in Ukraine for Estonian companies," said Perling, a former prosecutor general who has worked in Ukraine.
"Kaimo joining the team makes us even stronger and shows that people believe in Parempoolsed. For the voter who wants a better future for Estonia, the only alternative to the populists in spring 2027 is Parempoolsed," Perling added.
Kuusk, 50, was Estonia's ambassador to Ukraine from 2019 to 2023, ambassador to Lithuania from 2023 to 2024, and Defense Ministry permanent secretary from 2024 until September. Before entering the foreign service he worked for several decades at the Foreign Intelligence Service (Välisluureamet).
Kuusk was dismissed as Defense Ministry permanent secretary in September, weeks after incoming Defense Minister Martin Herem (Reform) made Kuusk's departure a condition of taking up the ministerial spot.
Kuusk's last working day at the ministry was September 15. The government justified his dismissal on the basis of failed cooperation. SDE chair Lauri Läänemets asked the Chancellor of Justice to review the legality of that dismissal. Hanno Pevkur, who resigned as defense minister at the start of September following a defense procurement scandal, said national defense leadership could not be left the victim of mutual distrust.

Antalya Prepares to Host COP31 and Foster + Partners Unveils World Trade Center Yerevan: This Week’s Review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

This week's architecture news covers a range of projects addressing the changing needs of cities, from the adaptation of existing sites to the development of new cultural and public spaces. As Antalya prepares to host COP31, projects in Rotterdam and Pittsburgh focus on the renovation of established cultural institutions, while developments in Copenhagen, Chicago, and Tbilisi explore new approaches to recreation, public access, and urban regeneration. Elsewhere, Foster + Partners has revealed plans for a mixed-use development in Yerevan, VG13 Architects has won the competition for a new stadium and sports district in Zagreb, and Aria Property Group has unveiled a residential and public precinct in Brisbane ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
Climate Action and the Adaptation of Existing Sites
As Antalya prepares to host COP31 from November 9 to 20, 2026, the conference also brings attention to how existing sites can accommodate large-scale international events. SP Architects is adapting the former EXPO 2016 grounds to host the summit, combining existing infrastructure with new permanent and temporary structures. The venue will include a Blue Zone for formal UN climate negotiations and a Green Zone for public events, while the site is intended to remain in use for fairs, concerts, and other activities after the conference. The adaptation of existing infrastructure also features in recent developments involving cultural institutions. In Rotterdam, Mecanoo has released new images of the renovation of Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, which has been closed since 2019 due to maintenance issues, water-related problems, and fire risks. The project brings together the restoration of three historic buildings with changes to circulation, exhibition spaces, and visitor facilities. In Pittsburgh, AD—WO has been selected to renovate the Heinz Architectural Center at Carnegie Museum of Art, rethinking its galleries and introducing spaces for collection study, research, and public learning. While differing in scale and purpose, the three projects address how existing buildings and sites can be adapted to meet changing institutional and public needs.
New Cultural Destinations and Public Spaces
New projects in Copenhagen, Chicago, and Tbilisi explore how architecture can support public access, cultural activity, and shared urban life. In Copenhagen, Kengo Kuma & Associates' KAI Water Culture House is scheduled to open on December 5, 2026, on Paper Island. The 5,800-square-meter complex will include ten indoor and outdoor pools, wellness facilities, and cultural spaces, extending the island's waterfront activities; dedicated harbour swimming areas are expected to follow in early 2027. In Chicago, RAMSA has unveiled plans for a new Welcome Hall at the Kenneth C. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry. The project will reopen the museum's historic North Portico as a year-round entrance and introduce a glazed volume connecting it to the exhibition spaces, replacing a lengthy subterranean arrival route with a shorter, accessible connection. Meanwhile, Stefano Boeri Architetti has been selected to develop the masterplan for Loco Park, transforming a former electric locomotive factory in Tbilisi into a mixed-use neighbourhood. The proposal combines housing, shops, cafés, workshops, parks, and shared gardens across a network of buildings and open spaces.
On the Radar
Foster + Partners Reveals Design for World Trade Center Yerevan in Armenia
Foster + Partners has revealed the design for World Trade Center Yerevan, a mixed-use development in Armenia's capital combining offices, a hotel, residences, retail, and cultural venues. The project comprises two towers connected at three levels, with shared amenities and landscaped terraces. The buildings rise above a low-rise podium, freeing up approximately 50 percent of the site for public space. The masterplan extends the green axis of nearby Diana Abgar Park and introduces plazas, pedestrian routes, and event spaces while preserving historic Frik Street. Located within the area shaped by Alexander Tamanian's 1924 masterplan for Yerevan, the development seeks to connect the city's architectural heritage with new urban uses. Designed for the city's seismically active conditions, the project is also targeting LEED and WELL Gold certifications and is planned to be net-zero-ready.
VG13 Architects Wins Competition for New Maksimir Stadium in Zagreb
Italian practice VG13 Architects has won the international competition to design a new 35,000-seat Maksimir Stadium and the adjacent Svetice Sports and Recreation Centre in Zagreb, Croatia. The proposal combines the UEFA Category 4 stadium with a wider sports district on the edge of Maksimir Park. The masterplan connects the park to the Borongaj transit hub through a diagonal pedestrian route, with landscaped public spaces, rain gardens, and sports facilities distributed across the site. The design also draws on the original stadium, designed by Vladimir Turina in 1946, reinterpreting its open form and cantilevered stands. The existing stadium, which was damaged in the 2020 earthquake, is scheduled for demolition from 2027. Construction of the new complex is expected to begin in 2029, with completion planned for 2030.
Aria Property Group Reveals Sanctuary Precinct in Brisbane Ahead of the 2032 Olympic Games
Aria Property Group has unveiled the design of Sanctuary, a mixed-use precinct in South Brisbane, Australia, scheduled for completion ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Designed by Richards + Spence and Bates Smart, the project combines five laneways, two restored heritage buildings, twelve retail and dining spaces, and a public urban meadow. The ground-level layout prioritizes pedestrian connections, linking the site's three active frontages through landscaped courtyards and public spaces. Above the public realm, Sanctuary Residences comprises 231 apartments across 43 levels, with naturally ventilated corridors, shaded balconies, and all-electric systems. Completion is expected in mid-to-late 2029.

Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, elder statesman of Mexican left, dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:26:14 UTC
15:26:14 KST

Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, elder statesman of Mexican left, dies at 92
MEXICO CITY, Oct 28 - Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, an icon of the Mexican left who took up the banner of the disenfranchised in the 1980s to force changes in the political system despite never winning the presidency himself, has died at 92, the government said on Wednesday.
The first elected mayor of Mexico City, and the son of President Lazaro Cardenas, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas shook Mexico's ruling establishment to its foundations when he ran for the top job in 1988 before losing a hotly disputed election.
That election pitted Cardenas against young technocrat Carlos Salinas, candidate of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, which had dominated Mexico since 1929.
With the two running neck-and-neck on election night, the government suddenly announced the system counting the votes had crashed.
After it came back online, Salinas was declared the winner, although many analysts and Cardenas himself believed the PRI had rigged the vote to retain its hold on power.
The contest was a watershed in Mexico, leading to political reform that strengthened the opposition. Two presidential elections later, in 2000, the PRI was finally ousted.
"His role in Mexico's contemporary history is fundamental," said President Claudia Sheinbaum, hailing Cardenas' impact on Mexican politics.
"In 1988, he led a peaceful democratic movement that channeled the desire for change of millions of Mexicans," she said on social media, alluding to his supporters' belief that he was the rightful winner of the disputed presidential election.
"That historic election, in which he should have been recognized as president, marked the beginning of the democratic transformation."
Cardenas ran unsuccessfully for president twice more, fronting a leftist ticket for the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), which he helped found after breaking with the PRI in 1987. He finished third in 1994 and 2000.
Between those bids, the tall, soft-spoken Cardenas became mayor of Mexico City in 1997, beginning a long run for the PRD at the helm of the capital.
The PRD’s power waned after Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who followed in Cardenas’ footsteps as Mexico City mayor, split from it to found his own Morena party, which became the main force of the Mexican left and propelled him to the presidency.
But Cardenas' early backing of the PRD marked a turning point in Mexican politics following decades of PRI domination.
It was Cardenas who finally galvanised leftist opposition to the PRI, said historian Lorenzo Meyer, adding, "And he had the capacity to mobilise."
Cardenas paved the way for subsequent leftist challenges to the highest office, campaigning in remote villages never before visited by presidential candidates.
In later years, he emerged as an occasional critic of Lopez Obrador, a polarizing, often abrasive figure who succeeded him as the standard-bearer of the left and captured the top job in 2018.
Lopez Obrador raised huge protests when he too was denied victory in a bitterly contested presidential election in 2006, and again cried foul six years later. But the dignified Cardenas remained the left's spiritual leader for many Mexicans.
Cardenas believed free market economics would not save Mexico from economic malaise, favoring a more state-centric model, similar to that later embraced by Lopez Obrador.
COALITION BUILDER
Cardenas was born in Mexico City on May 1, 1934, the first year of his father's six-year term. A champion of land reform who nationalized the oil industry in 1938, Lazaro Cardenas was one of the most popular presidents in Mexican history.
Ironically, the late president's success helped fortify the PRI, whose legitimacy his son later challenged.
Cardenas earned an engineering degree in 1957, then spent two years in France, West Germany and Italy on a fellowship.
After returning to Mexico, he began a career as a planner and hydraulic engineer, and entered politics in 1976 as a senator for his home state of Michoacan.
As PRI governor for Michoacan from 1980 to 1986, Cardenas was seen by some as too aloof to be a compelling administrator, but his reputation for honesty stood apart from the party’s growing association with graft in the minds of many Mexicans.
Michoacan became a bastion of the PRD, and Cardenas' son, called Lazaro like his grandfather, also served as governor.
The younger Lazaro later took up senior roles under Lopez Obrador and Sheinbaum, preserving the Mexican left’s historic ties with the family.
The challenge to the PRI by Cardenas began in late 1986 when he helped form the Democratic Current within the party.
The Current led calls for the PRI to adopt a more democratic means of selecting its presidential candidate, but these were ignored and leading members left the party in 1987.
"The PRI leadership has stopped our campaign for more open procedures within the party, but we will continue the struggle for true democracy in Mexico," Cardenas said at the time.
Impressed by his coalition-building skills, newspaper El Financiero once described Cardenas as the sole candidate "who can gather leftist militants, neoliberals, and even ecologists." REUTERS

'Desolation, despair': Spain begins three days of mourning after deadly train crash
Spain entered three days of mourning on Thursday after a high-speed train collision killed 69 people and injured scores more. The incident has prompted fresh questions about rail safety and management.

Spain began demanding answers on Thursday after the toll from the country's second high-speed train collision this year rose to 69 people, with scores injured and distraught relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
One of Europe's deadliest rail disasters this century struck south of Madrid on Wednesday morning when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.
Manuel San Emeterio, whose 54-year-old brother Pepe is missing, came to the central city of Toledo to provide DNA samples to the Civil Guard after finding out about the accident through a smartwatch notification.
"The uncertainty is the worst thing that you deal with, everyone is dealing with it," he said. "But I think there's something that counters it, which is hope ... we must never lose it."
Toledo has received 52 of the corpses, overwhelming its morgue's capacity of 30 and forcing the army to set up an improvised facility, an AFP journalist saw.
Forensics experts in green jackets, a black funeral car and army vehicles moved in and out of the site, equipped with red marquees and refrigerated containers.
Read moreRail safety questioned after Spain suffers second fatal high-speed train crash in a year
Sniffer dogs and thermal drones searched for bodies at the crash site outside the central village of Urda, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid.
Among the victims was Fatima Banez, a former labour minister for the main conservative Popular Party (PP), Spain's CEOE business association confirmed on Thursday.
'Nervous and desperate' relatives
Jose Miguel Fernandez, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to families still waiting to learn the fate of their loved ones.
"Many of them were calm, others were nervous and desperate. They wanted to know straight away and get news" of their loved ones, he told AFP.
Flags flew at half-mast on public buildings with official ceremonies and public events cancelled or scaled back on the first of three days of national mourning.
A minute of silence was observed up and down the country, including at Spain's busiest train station Atocha in Madrid, where some mourners shed tears.
Wednesday's accident happened on a key line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville, which was also the scene of a collision in January that killed 46 people.
It has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain's high-speed rail network, the second-largest in the world after China's.

Russia attacked Ukraine with 112 drones; 75% of the jet-powered drones destroyed
Kyiv • UNN
Overnight, Russia launched 112 drones at Ukraine, including 40 jet-powered ones. Air defenses shot down or suppressed 97 unmanned aerial vehicles; hits were recorded at seven locations.
On the night of October 29, Russia attacked Ukraine with 112 drones, more than a third of them jet-powered. A total of 97 unmanned aerial vehicles were shot down or suppressed, including 75% of the jet-powered drones. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia attacked with and where the attacks came from
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, on the night of October 29 (starting at 18:00 on October 28), the enemy attacked with 112 Shahed-type attack UAVs (40 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones launched from the following directions: Oryol, Millerovo — Russia, and the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk.
How the air defense performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 97 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (30 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and drones of other types; approximately 7 attack UAVs remain in the air, and combat operations are ongoing.
Hits by the enemy’s means of air attack were recorded at 7 locations, as well as the fall of downed targets (debris) at 5 locations.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed Army Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a senior military strategist at the Pentagon, from his post on the Joint Staff, The Hill reported on Wednesday.
Hegseth fired Sylvia, who headed the Joint Staff's Directorate for Strategy, Plans and Policy, known as the J-5, this week, the news outlet reported, citing two US officials familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues.

Sylvia’s removal marks another senior military personnel change under Hegseth, who took over as defence secretary in January 2025.

Norway’s Kongsberg doubles new orders in the third quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:07:53 UTC
15:07:53 KST

- Kongsberg’s order backlog reached a record NOK 174.2 billion, about $18.8 billion, after NOK 23.3 billion in third-quarter orders.
- Third-quarter revenue rose 50% to NOK 11.3 billion, helped by missile, NASAMS air defense and remote weapon station demand.
Norway’s Kongsberg ended the third quarter of 2026 with a record order backlog of NOK 174.2 billion (about $18.8 billion), after taking in NOK 23.3 billion (about $2.5 billion) in new orders, more than double the NOK 9.5 billion it booked in the same quarter last year.
The defense group reported on Oct. 29 that third-quarter revenue rose 50% to NOK 11.3 billion (about $1.2 billion), while operating profit, or EBIT, climbed 66% to NOK 1.9 billion (about $205 million). The backlog grew by NOK 16.7 billion during the quarter, and orders so far this year total NOK 67 billion (about $7.2 billion). Its book-to-bill ratio, which compares new orders with revenue in the same period, was 2.06, meaning Kongsberg booked about twice as much new work as it delivered.
The figures cover the defense and Discovery businesses Kongsberg kept after splitting off Kongsberg Maritime as a separate listed company, so they are not directly comparable with group results reported before the split. At the end of the second quarter, the company’s backlog stood at about NOK 157.5 billion and quarterly revenue at NOK 10.4 billion.
“At a time when European security is being challenged, our task is to strengthen defence capabilities through technology, capacity and delivery performance. We are expanding our capacity, including in Poland, to meet growing demand. Our focus now is on executing on our strong order backlog, which provides a solid foundation for continued growth,” said Eirik Lie, President and CEO of KONGSBERG.
Missiles, air defense and remote weapon stations drove most of the demand. In July, the U.S. Air Force ordered more Joint Strike Missiles, the air-launched version of Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile designed to be carried inside the F-35’s weapons bay, and later in the quarter the U.S. Marine Corps signed a framework agreement with the company covering production and sustainment of the Naval Strike Missile. In October, Denmark became the seventh country to announce plans to buy the Joint Strike Missile for its F-35s.
The largest single deal was in air defense. In September, Kongsberg signed a NOK 10 billion (about $1.08 billion) contract to supply the NASAMS medium-range air defense system to Belgium, which became the 18th country to order it, after Belgium agreed in July to buy 10 NASAMS systems through the Netherlands. The Dutch procurement agency signed the contract on Belgium’s behalf, building on the Netherlands’ own record NASAMS and NOMADS order with Kongsberg in 2024.
Kongsberg also won a contract to supply remote weapon stations, gun mounts operated by a crew member from inside the vehicle, for the Canadian Army’s Armoured Combat Support Vehicle program. The company counts those stations as part of its counter-drone offering, which also includes the CROWS C-UAS kit it has fitted to a donor-funded drone hunter vehicle for Ukraine.
The company is also building up its underwater and U.S. business. During the quarter, the U.S. government awarded Kongsberg a $54 million contract related to autonomous underwater capabilities, and U.S. authorities approved its purchase of Sonatech, a maker of underwater acoustic equipment. Zone 5 Technologies, the California missile maker Kongsberg bought in the second quarter to add low-cost weapons that can be built in large numbers, was selected for a $65 million U.S. Navy program during the quarter.
Kongsberg has said it aims to grow annual revenue to NOK 100 billion (about $10.8 billion) by 2029, and it is expanding production capacity, including in Poland, to work through the backlog. The company did not say how much of the NOK 174.2 billion it expects to deliver in the fourth quarter.

Albanese has a sewerage problem and the Coalition loves the stench
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:06:04 UTC
15:06:04 KST

analysis
Albanese has a sewerage problem and the Coalition loves the stench
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Anthony Albanese seems to have a bad habit of turning what should've been a one day, or one week, story into a month-long affair.
What is the source of the clog this time? The curious case of a $6m "invitation-only" grant to the Marrickville Golf Club.
When the ABC first published the story last month, the prime minister chided the public broadcaster for it. He declared the funding was to fix the issue of raw sewage flowing into the local river when the plain floods.
He repeated that defence in the House of Representatives. As did Infrastructure Minister Catherine King, as recently as Sunday. But as we learnt this week, that wasn't exactly the case.
Under questioning on Monday, infrastructure department officials confirmed that sewerage works were not part of the project. To make matters worse, that brief was shared with the prime minister's office before the ABC first raised questions about the grant last month.
Albanese was in classic politician form as he got out the mop to clean up the mess the next day. He didn't say he was wrong, but rather "it was not correct" for him to defend the funding with links to sewerage. It was the NSW government that had "stepped in" to tackle the problem.
For the Coalition, his answers stunk. And it's no surprise they've used it as an easy win. The way the story has dragged out over the past month was likened to the never-ending story that was Albanese's ill-fated "melons" remark on the Bush Deep podcast.
It's the same character-chipping exercise Labor ran on an unpopular Scott Morrison over his final term in parliament. The opposition were gleeful at times as they questioned Albanese, pointing to everything from denying he fell off stage during the last election campaign to this grant to paint him as a "serial liar".
Albanese may have been able to shrug off claims he misled the parliament, but the perception that he's not upfront with the public will be harder to flush away.
Taxes, cuts and 'savings'
Of course, every question the Coalition dedicates to the golf club grant is one less on the economy — yet another source of pain for the government.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers isn't having the best of times at the moment. The latest monthly inflation figures, up from 4 per cent to 4.3 per cent in the year to September, have all but locked in a Melbourne Cup Day rate rise.
This would take rates to an 18-year high, and another Reserve Bank board meeting is scheduled for December. Essentially, as Tom Crowley wrote this morning, the worst is still yet to come.
The treasurer maintains that government spending is not to blame, pointing the finger at the war in the Middle East and the AI data centre boom for driving up prices. Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson backed Chalmers up in estimates: "We can only control what we can control."
Nevertheless, Chalmers and Albanese are looking for savings ahead of December's mid-year update. The prime minister says he hasn't directed his ministers to find cuts (sorry, savings), but rather they're all just collectively working together to spend less.
Loading...
Basically, don't expect there to be a pre-Christmas cash splash. Longer term, Chalmers also flagged it could complicate Labor's plan to deliver a larger round of tax cuts in the lead up to the next election.
But speaking of tax cuts, David Shoebridge made his first National Press Club appearance as leader where he again declared his party could take Labor's place.
He came armed with a tax plan that, due to the electoral reality, will never see the light of day and faced questions about internal culture in the party and his opposition to providing military aid to Ukraine.
Loading
'Leave the politics of MAGA in the US'
Angus Taylor released his own costings for a handful of the Coalition's proposed spending cuts. In short, several of Labor's climate and housing initiatives would be scrapped in favour of the opposition's own spending promises such as indexing income tax brackets to inflation.
The Coalition decided to unveil the numbers on Monday; the same day parliament had set aside for reflection and messages of support for independent MP Helen Haines.
Haines remains in a serious but stable condition after an alleged attack outside of her electorate office last week. Her first words afterwards, as shared in the chamber by Allegra Spender, were of concern for staff and gratitude for first responders and bystanders.
For most of the day, you could hear a pin drop in the chamber. MPs of all stripes shed tears as they spoke about Haines and the impact she's had on the parliament.
Among the tributes, another message was braided through.
After months of calling for the temperature to be turned down, Albanese said there was no way to shrug off the "very real rise in anger that distorts and corrodes our public discourse".
"We cannot allow disagreement to become a full stop," he said.
Taylor was unconvinced by that argument and rejected that there was a link between robust parliamentary debate and political violence. Crossbenchers Zali Steggall and Monique Ryan, who are close to Haines, called his speech tone deaf.
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie's tone differed to his leader's, calling for Australia to "leave the nasty personal politics of MAGA in the United States".
With Haines front of mind, politicians were on their best behaviour during Question Time — only a glass breaking punctured the silence around the speaker.
However as the days went on, things returned to somewhat regular programming. By Wednesday, Speaker Milton Dick was growing tired of MPs trying to up the ante. Nationals MP Llew O'Brien was ejected for swearing.
Watching over it all was the cardboard cockatoo sitting in Haines's vacant seat. A second was also placed at Aussies, the cafe and general store in Parliament House, serving as a gentle reminder of the promises they made on Monday.

‘There’s nothing scary about it’: Life goes on in Lithuania s troops patrol Russia border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Life in Lithuania’s southwestern town of Vištytis remains undisturbed. Local residents are not troubled either by the threat posed by Russia or by the Lithuanian troops deployed along the border with the Kaliningrad region, who are helping border guards patrol the area.
The military has been assisting the border guards since early October. Around 100 troops are expected to continue doing so until mid-November.
Government officials describe the decision as a precautionary measure in response to the possibility of a new wave of mobilisation in Russia. However, the authorities stress that the threat level along the border has not increased.
“[Potential deserters] will try to cross the state border illegally, both on land and on water. That is why we have stepped up surveillance on land, on water and in the air. As we say here, along the green border, the blue border and in the air,” Rimantas Kundreckis, commander of the Vištytis border guard post, told BNS.
The deployment of troops is estimated to have almost doubled the frequency of patrols along the border with the Kaliningrad region.
The Lithuanian-Russian state border, including the boundary of territorial waters, stretches for almost 300km. It runs through plains, forests and bodies of water.
“There’s nothing particularly scary about it, despite what I read in so many places these days,” Sandra told BNS as she hurried home carrying an armful of groceries.
She is one of just a few hundred residents of Vištytis, in the Vilkaviškis district. Most locals spend the gloomier days of autumn indoors, leaving the town’s central square looking almost deserted, with only the occasional person hurrying toward a nearby shop.
“Nothing has really changed here. You can just see that there are more patrols, but nothing else is happening. The only difference is that the military has arrived, and we see the occasional military vehicle,” the 31-year-old woman said.
She said she was not afraid of the worsening security situation in the region. Nor was her daily life being disrupted by the soldiers recently seen alongside the border guards.
“Life is normal. Everything is just as it was before. There’s no special preparation going on, with people stocking up on supplies or preparing shelters. We’re just living our lives, like everyone else in Lithuania,” Sandra said.
The state border runs through a lake
In Vištytis, a lake separates Lithuania from the Kaliningrad region.
Bright red posts protruding from the water mark the point up to which people who have provided their details to border guards are permitted to sail. Another line of yellow posts, 50 metres beyond them, marks the end of Lithuanian territory.
From the pier where border guard patrol boats moor, you can see a Russian flag flying high just a few hundred metres away.
The lake is monitored by cameras and patrolled by a border guard boat. According to Kundreckis, enhanced surveillance of the lake has helped reduce the number of accidental border crossings.
Previously, people who went out on the water to fish or relax sometimes failed to notice that they were approaching Russian territory. Border guards can now warn them of a potential violation in advance, either by calling them using the contact details they have provided or by approaching them in an official patrol boat.
Accompanying officers on a patrol of Lake Vištytis offers a practical demonstration of how border controls work. When the patrol boat spots another boat, it slows down. Officers observe the person on board and assess the distance from the marked boundary before continuing on their way without making contact.
Such checks are part of the officers’ daily duties.
The most recent border violation recorded by the Vištytis post occurred at the beginning of the year, when two Russian citizens entered Lithuania by walking across the frozen lake. Around 10 similar violations are typically recorded each year.
‘Invaluable experience’
Among those contributing to the border protection mission are troops from the Second Territorial Unit of the Darius and Girėnas National Defence Volunteer Forces (KASP).
Company commander Leonas Ruzgas sees the deployment as an opportunity not only to contribute to the country’s security but also to help soldiers develop their skills.
He was among the first to arrive at the border.
“Border guards have quite a few technological innovations and systems that we do not use, [...] because our work does not require them. So it is good to see how much our border protection has improved, share experience and learn from them,” Ruzgas said.
The commander of the Vištytis border guard post agreed. He said the deployment offered opportunities for professional development not only for officers and soldiers serving on the ground, but also for their commanders.
“The practical experience is truly invaluable. You cannot get it anywhere else, really,” Kundreckis said. “If Day X [war] were to come and the military had to take up a position here, both ordinary soldiers and commanders would already be familiar with the specifics of the area.”
Troops are rotated along the border approximately every four to five days. Different soldiers are usually sent each time, although those who wish to return can do so.
According to Ruzgas, incoming troops adapt to the duty schedules of State Border Guard Service (VSAT) officers, and their powers are largely the same.
Kundreckis said the soldiers assisting the border guards had also brought equipment that was “being successfully used to monitor both land areas and airspace”.
The post commander said he had not noticed any signs of a potential threat, describing activity on the other side of the border as routine daily operations.
“Whether it is a coincidence or not, there has been an increase in military fighter jet flights near the state border. Explosions could be heard somewhere at the training ground towards Kudirkos Naumiestis, and their helicopters have also been flying near the state border more frequently,” the commander said.
‘I was born with the Russians’
Virginijus Dapkus, who owns a farm near Vištytis, told BNS that the authorities’ heightened attention to security made him laugh.
“I was born with the Russians, grew up with the Russians and have dealings with the Russians. I know them very well, and what our authorities, our government, are saying makes me laugh. It is just scaremongering, and they have their own objectives,” Dapkus said as he prepared to go fishing.
He said he felt perfectly comfortable in Vištytis, although he was saddened by the fact that fishing was no longer permitted on the other side of the lake. According to him, the catch now is “like night and day” compared with what it used to be.
“When we were together with the Russians, we used to fish only on the Russian side. Now we fish in a swamp on the Lithuanian side. That is what we call it – the swamp,” he said.
Pranas Stankevičius, a 93-year-old former deportee, also used to fish in Lake Vištytis.
“I used to fish on the lake, but now we are no longer allowed to. You cannot put out a fishing net; they can see everything now. Everything is very restricted,” the pensioner complained.
The elderly man, who was repairing his car in the street, said he had previously enjoyed travelling to Kaliningrad, where he traded goods with others. Nevertheless, he said he understood the current border controls.
“It is not that bad. A border is a border. What can you do? We belong to Lithuania, so let them guard the border,” he said.

2026-10-29
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Life in Lithuania’s southwestern town of Vištytis remains undisturbed. Local residents are not troubled either by the threat posed by Russia or by the Lithuanian troops deployed along the border with the Kaliningrad region, who are helping border guards patrol the area.
The military has been assisting the border guards since early October. Around 100 troops are expected to continue doing so until mid-November.
Government officials describe the decision as a precautionary measure in response to the possibility of a new wave of mobilisation in Russia. However, the authorities stress that the threat level along the border has not increased.
“[Potential deserters] will try to cross the state border illegally, both on land and on water. That is why we have stepped up surveillance on land, on water and in the air. As we say here, along the green border, the blue border and in the air,” Rimantas Kundreckis, commander of the Vištytis border guard post, told BNS.
The deployment of troops is estimated to have almost doubled the frequency of patrols along the border with the Kaliningrad region.
The Lithuanian-Russian state border, including the boundary of territorial waters, stretches for almost 300km. It runs through plains, forests and bodies of water.
“There’s nothing particularly scary about it, despite what I read in so many places these days,” Sandra told BNS as she hurried home carrying an armful of groceries.
She is one of just a few hundred residents of Vištytis, in the Vilkaviškis district. Most locals spend the gloomier days of autumn indoors, leaving the town’s central square looking almost deserted, with only the occasional person hurrying toward a nearby shop.
“Nothing has really changed here. You can just see that there are more patrols, but nothing else is happening. The only difference is that the military has arrived, and we see the occasional military vehicle,” the 31-year-old woman said.
She said she was not afraid of the worsening security situation in the region. Nor was her daily life being disrupted by the soldiers recently seen alongside the border guards.
“Life is normal. Everything is just as it was before. There’s no special preparation going on, with people stocking up on supplies or preparing shelters. We’re just living our lives, like everyone else in Lithuania,” Sandra said.
The state border runs through a lake
In Vištytis, a lake separates Lithuania from the Kaliningrad region.
Bright red posts protruding from the water mark the point up to which people who have provided their details to border guards are permitted to sail. Another line of yellow posts, 50 metres beyond them, marks the end of Lithuanian territory.
From the pier where border guard patrol boats moor, you can see a Russian flag flying high just a few hundred metres away.
The lake is monitored by cameras and patrolled by a border guard boat. According to Kundreckis, enhanced surveillance of the lake has helped reduce the number of accidental border crossings.
Previously, people who went out on the water to fish or relax sometimes failed to notice that they were approaching Russian territory. Border guards can now warn them of a potential violation in advance, either by calling them using the contact details they have provided or by approaching them in an official patrol boat.
Accompanying officers on a patrol of Lake Vištytis offers a practical demonstration of how border controls work. When the patrol boat spots another boat, it slows down. Officers observe the person on board and assess the distance from the marked boundary before continuing on their way without making contact.
Such checks are part of the officers’ daily duties.
The most recent border violation recorded by the Vištytis post occurred at the beginning of the year, when two Russian citizens entered Lithuania by walking across the frozen lake. Around 10 similar violations are typically recorded each year.
‘Invaluable experience’
Among those contributing to the border protection mission are troops from the Second Territorial Unit of the Darius and Girėnas National Defence Volunteer Forces (KASP).
Company commander Leonas Ruzgas sees the deployment as an opportunity not only to contribute to the country’s security but also to help soldiers develop their skills.
He was among the first to arrive at the border.
“Border guards have quite a few technological innovations and systems that we do not use, [...] because our work does not require them. So it is good to see how much our border protection has improved, share experience and learn from them,” Ruzgas said.
The commander of the Vištytis border guard post agreed. He said the deployment offered opportunities for professional development not only for officers and soldiers serving on the ground, but also for their commanders.
“The practical experience is truly invaluable. You cannot get it anywhere else, really,” Kundreckis said. “If Day X [war] were to come and the military had to take up a position here, both ordinary soldiers and commanders would already be familiar with the specifics of the area.”
Troops are rotated along the border approximately every four to five days. Different soldiers are usually sent each time, although those who wish to return can do so.
According to Ruzgas, incoming troops adapt to the duty schedules of State Border Guard Service (VSAT) officers, and their powers are largely the same.
Kundreckis said the soldiers assisting the border guards had also brought equipment that was “being successfully used to monitor both land areas and airspace”.
The post commander said he had not noticed any signs of a potential threat, describing activity on the other side of the border as routine daily operations.
“Whether it is a coincidence or not, there has been an increase in military fighter jet flights near the state border. Explosions could be heard somewhere at the training ground towards Kudirkos Naumiestis, and their helicopters have also been flying near the state border more frequently,” the commander said.
‘I was born with the Russians’
Virginijus Dapkus, who owns a farm near Vištytis, told BNS that the authorities’ heightened attention to security made him laugh.
“I was born with the Russians, grew up with the Russians and have dealings with the Russians. I know them very well, and what our authorities, our government, are saying makes me laugh. It is just scaremongering, and they have their own objectives,” Dapkus said as he prepared to go fishing.
He said he felt perfectly comfortable in Vištytis, although he was saddened by the fact that fishing was no longer permitted on the other side of the lake. According to him, the catch now is “like night and day” compared with what it used to be.
“When we were together with the Russians, we used to fish only on the Russian side. Now we fish in a swamp on the Lithuanian side. That is what we call it – the swamp,” he said.
Pranas Stankevičius, a 93-year-old former deportee, also used to fish in Lake Vištytis.
“I used to fish on the lake, but now we are no longer allowed to. You cannot put out a fishing net; they can see everything now. Everything is very restricted,” the pensioner complained.
The elderly man, who was repairing his car in the street, said he had previously enjoyed travelling to Kaliningrad, where he traded goods with others. Nevertheless, he said he understood the current border controls.
“It is not that bad. A border is a border. What can you do? We belong to Lithuania, so let them guard the border,” he said.

Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
Custom-designed furniture by Derya Arpac, Lærke Ryom, Kasper Kyster and Daniel Schofield sets the scene for this unconventional bookstore in the Danish capital.
Simone Book Services is a Copenhagen shop specialising in rare and independent books and magazines, but it can also be an exhibition gallery, a listening space, or a venue for book launches and other informal gatherings.
Turkish-born architect Arpac oversaw the intentionally “un-Scandinavian” interior, which includes modular shelves made from aluminium and cherry wood, mobile book trolleys and a counter dressed in leather.
The concept for the store was born out of conversations between Arpac, who works for furniture brand &Tradition, and founders Tugce Kayar Subay and Ibo Subay, a married couple with backgrounds in fashion media and marketing.
The Subays had amassed such an impressive collection of art, design and fashion literature that they launched a “literary branding” business in February 2026, curating libraries for exhibitions, offices and brand spaces.
Simone gives the couple a physical platform for this business and allows it to evolve further. It showcases their curation of books and magazines, but also furniture and objects related to reading culture.
“Tugce is the book nerd, and I’m the design nerd; we came up with this idea of combining our passions,” Arpac told Dezeen.
“We wanted to create a space where people would come and be inspired.”
Arpac’s own contribution to the space is a system of wall-mounted shelves crafted from cherry, a red-hued hardwood that offers a different aesthetic to traditional Scandinavian timbers like oak, ash or pine.
“The shelving appears to extend and climb through the space, almost like scaffolding or the structural skeleton of a building,” she said.
The leather-wrapped counter was designed by Ryom, who specialises in alternative methods of upholstery. Similar to the Garments chairs she developed for The Mindcraft Project, the bar’s edges feature zippers that open up to reveal storage areas.
Kyster developed a shelving system made from folded sheets of unpolished aluminium, intended for displaying magazines. The system is modular, so more panels could be added in future.
For seating, Schofield crafted a bench out of sheets of black-pigmented MDF that slots neatly into the store’s corner. It’s joined by mobile book trolleys made from the same material, encouraging visitors to move books around the space.
In addition to the four designers, artist Staffan Sundström was invited to create paintings for the bookstore. He contributed three pieces for the store opening, although the display will change as works are sold.
The store also includes an area dubbed “the red room”, a David Lynch-inspired space featuring red walls and matching floor-to-ceiling curtains. This 20-square-metre space offers scope for small-scale events and exhibitions.
Since opening, Simone has hosted various events, including a book launch for photographer Lasse Dearman, a curated library for sports brand ASICS and a pop-up for fashion label Bonnetje Recut.
Future ambitions include the launch of “reading objects”, including everything from bookmarks and paperweights to lighting and shelving.
Photography by Armin Tehran and Hampus Berndtson

====================================================================================================

Cambodia: Politically connected security companies enabled slavery and rape in scamming compounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:58:00 UTC
14:58:00 KST

- Five private security companies identified where guards committed or facilitated abuses
- Members of political elite, military and police linked to security companies at multiple scam compounds
- Accountability lacking despite government crackdown
Cambodian private security companies connected to the country’s military, police and powerful business networks have helped sustain a scamming industry built on trafficking, forced labour, torture and slavery, Amnesty International said in a new report published today.
Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia identifies five private security companies that provided services at scamming compounds – and details their links to members of Cambodia’s military, police and business elites. Amnesty also identified multiple members of the military and police who worked as security guards, trained or supervised guards at more than 20 compounds.
“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“This report demonstrates Cambodian corporate actors’ direct involvement in scamming compounds. Our findings also begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny.
“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”
Guards central to confinement and abuse
Building on its previous investigations that exposed slavery, human trafficking, rape, forced labour and torture inside Cambodia’s scamming compounds, and documented the failures of the government’s subsequent crackdown, Amnesty’s latest investigation examines the security infrastructure that allowed the compounds to confine and control trafficked people and forced them to scam people globally.
Between January 2023 and September 2026, Amnesty International interviewed 151 scamming compound survivors and reviewed records concerning more than 400 additional victims. Researchers identified 86 compounds, visiting 82 of them, and found security guards at every compound.
In this latest report, Amnesty identifies the private business companies responsible for guarding the compounds and abusing the victims. We also geolocated videos from more than 200 security guards’ TikTok accounts to 23 compounds across Cambodia until August 2026. The new evidence collected by Amnesty links more than 20 members of the military and police to the private security companies that guard scamming compounds and to at least 22 of the 86 compounds.
When guards escort trafficked people to punishment rooms or stand watch during rape and torture, they are enabling abuses
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
Amnesty’s report also connects various prominent business and political figures to these security companies – including a former bank CEO, a property developer and the son of a former deputy prime minister.
Survivors consistently described guards as responsible for preventing escape, while many reported guards beating people who attempted to flee. Survivors also described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.
At the compound Park 8, also known as PV01, “Maia”, a woman from Cameroon, said guards restrained her on arrival and later took her to a dark room where managers raped her while guards stood outside. “Gabe”, a Ugandan survivor at the same compound, described being chained above basins of water, beaten for hours and shocked with an electric baton.
Most of the 151 survivors interviewed said guards carried or had immediate access to electric shock batons. Several reported seeing guards or other people carrying firearms.
“When guards escort trafficked people to punishment rooms or stand watch during rape and torture, they are enabling these abuses – and so too are the supposedly legitimate corporate actors who employ them,” Agnès Callamard said.
“Investigations must assess and follow responsibility from the lowest ranks all the way upwards to the companies, including the managers and owners who recruited, deployed and controlled security guards at scamming compounds.”
Five companies linked to at least 23 compounds
Amnesty International identified five private companies that guarded compounds where serious human rights abuses were documented. Three had links to Cambodian authorities.
Leap Somnang had the largest footprint of the companies identified and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo. All said its guards stopped them leaving compounds under threat of violence, while several described guards participating in beatings, electric shocks and keeping the victims in prolonged isolation.
Security Response, a company with close links to the Panda Bank and Huione corporate network, was linked to five compounds, including Park 8 (PV01).
ZD Security, formerly BIC Security, was linked to two compounds in Botum Sakor, including Long Bay (BS04), where survivors described torture and other ill-treatment, forced labour, unlawful confinement and violence against people trying to leave.
Dara Security was linked to two compounds in Sihanoukville, while Best Security was linked to a Bavet compound where Amnesty documented human trafficking, forced labour and child labour.
Amnesty’s report finds that at least three high-ranking military and police officers had links to compounds, strongly indicating involvement with the industry:
- The company Leap Somnang is controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chairman while also being a Colonel in the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces.
- Amnesty’s analysis showed phone numbers for Deputy Police Chief Lay Channy listed on an advertisement for Best Security. Channy was involved in the crackdown in Bavet, where Best Security guarded a compound.
- Brigadier General Tek Bunthoeun has a direct, and potentially controlling, interest in the property development comprising the BM02 compound, where Amnesty documented torture, confinement and forced labour.
Amnesty also identified multiple prominent figures with apparent business connections to compounds, without making any finding as to their personal responsibility for the abuses documented in the report. Amnesty International wrote to each corporate actor and individual identified in this report, and the full responses received are included in the report.
Links to military and police demand investigation
Amnesty International analysed official uniforms, insignia, identification numbers, public records and social-media timelines to help pinpoint precisely where and when military and police personnel were present at compounds.
In three compounds, apparent active military personnel were seen training, leading or supervising guards. In other cases, Amnesty identified apparent state personnel carrying firearms or occupying guard positions.
“The evidence suggests military and police involvement in a number of scamming compounds that helps explain how abuses at these sites persisted despite years of public reporting and repeated law-enforcement operations,” Agnès Callamard said.
Closure without accountability
Following a government crackdown launched in July 2025, large-scale scamming compound operations currently appear to be dormant. However, Amnesty International is unaware of investigations into the five security companies profiled in the report, their owners and managers or the wider commercial and state connections documented.
Prior to the publication of Amnesty’s report, Cambodian authorities responded on 15 October noting that 77 police officers had been disciplined in connection with scamming compounds.
Meanwhile, in response to Amnesty’s findings, Sophat Ban denied holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an advisor to the company owner”.
Best Security denied Lay Channy had any control over the company despite acknowledging that his phone number appeared on a company sign. Security Response denied all allegations made in Amnesty’s report, and Best Security responded that it “has no history of providing services at location BA06” and said would consider “legal action if someone has stolen (the) company’s uniform.”
Amnesty International is calling on the Cambodian authorities to establish prompt, independent and adequately resourced investigations into private security companies connected to compounds; investigate apparent serving military and police personnel involved in compound security; suspend company licences while credible allegations of serious abuse are investigated; and ensure victims have access to effective remedies and reparations.
Many of the abuses documented could constitute serious crimes under international law and Cambodian law. This includes by security guards who participated in abuses, as well as managers, executives and directors of the security companies who were aware of them.
“Even if scamming compounds are dormant at the time of publishing this report, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Agnès Callamard said.
“Largely in response to international outcry over the scamming compounds, the Cambodian authorities have announced a range of crackdown measures. But a crackdown measured only in raids, arrests and deportations risks leaving the architects and enablers untouched. Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”

China expands foreign business access at world's largest free trade port
