‘Show courage, Eisenkot’: Arab parties offer support but face silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
00:22:45 UTC
09:22:45 KST

Israel's Arab parties, projected to win a combined 19 seats in the next Knesset, have offered to help replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government, even without joining a new coalition. But despite their potentially decisive role in breaking the political deadlock, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and key parties in his bloc have so far shown little willingness to embrace their support.
The Joint List formally declared Wednesday evening that it was prepared to cooperate with the opposition to establish an alternative government, following an election in which an unusually high turnout among Arab voters significantly strengthened their parliamentary representation.
The offer comes as Netanyahu and his Likud party challenge the legitimacy of votes cast for Arab parties, citing alleged election irregularities, while Eisenkot's opposition bloc remains divided over whether it should rely on Arab lawmakers to form a government.
Neither of the two main political blocs is projected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-member parliament, leaving the Arab parties in a potentially pivotal position. Yet their electoral success does not necessarily mean they will be included in the negotiations that determine the next government.
Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen described the election results as a "historic day," saying they demonstrated the growing political influence of Israel's Arab citizens. "We have proven that we are a political force that cannot be ignored, and that no future can be built here without our voice," Jabareen said.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, he made clear that removing Netanyahu from office was the Joint List's immediate priority.
"The public that placed its trust in us wants to change the current reality and bring down the Netanyahu government. The first step is removing Netanyahu and the Knesset speaker," he said.
Jabareen also strongly rejected Likud's allegations of election irregularities, accusing Netanyahu's party of trying to undermine the legitimacy of Arab voters.
"There are people in Israel who want to deny the legitimacy of votes for Arab parties. There were no violations in the election, and Likud's accusations are the words of sore losers," he said.
Jabareen further claimed that Netanyahu wanted to remain in office as caretaker prime minister and drag Israel into another election as early as next March.
Asked about potential cooperation with Eisenkot, Jabareen said the Joint List had not yet examined the opposition leader's plans for forming a government. However, he emphasized that his party wanted to see the current coalition removed from power.
"Ben-Gvir is responsible for the escalation in murders in Arab communities. Bringing down the government means bringing down Smotrich and Ben-Gvir and the government that incites against us," he said. "We need a change in policy and a government without racists."
In a formal statement issued Wednesday evening, the Joint List went further, explicitly declaring its willingness to cooperate politically with Eisenkot's bloc to replace Netanyahu.
"The Joint List will do everything in its power to bring an end to Netanyahu's rule. We are prepared for political cooperation to establish an alternative government that will present a genuine alternative and commit to a fundamental change in the racist policies of the current government," the statement said.
The party also demanded that any future government recognize the rights of Israel's Arab citizens and end what it described as the exclusion of Arab representatives from the country's political institutions.
The Joint List attributed its electoral gains to an unusually high turnout in Arab communities, which it described as a response to the outgoing government's policies.
"Our public understood the significance of this moment and flocked to the polls, from the Galilee and the Triangle to the Negev," the party said, referring to major regions with significant Arab populations.
"Faced with incitement, intimidation and racism, they turned Election Day into an unprecedented show of strength against the Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich government."
The party also said thousands of Jewish Israelis had voted for the Joint List, arguing that the support reflected a broader constituency committed to peace, equality and Jewish-Arab partnership.
It pledged to continue working toward a future based on full equality and genuine political partnership.
Ra'am chairman Mansour Abbas, whose Islamist party is running separately from the Joint List, also addressed the strong performance of Arab parties, offering an ironic expression of gratitude to members of the outgoing government.
In an interview with i24NEWS, Abbas credited the electoral surge to the very politicians who had been among the Arab parties' fiercest critics. "The unprecedented electoral achievement is entirely thanks to Ben-Gvir, Smotrich and the entire government, which neglected Arab society in Israel," he said.
His remarks reflected a broader argument among Arab political leaders that frustration with the Netanyahu government's policies, particularly its handling of crime and violence in Arab communities, helped mobilize voters.
Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi delivered an even more explicit message to Eisenkot, saying his party was willing to help establish a minority government that would remove Netanyahu from office.
Crucially, Tibi stressed that the Joint List was not seeking ministerial positions or demanding to become a formal member of the coalition. Instead, it was prepared to consider supporting such a government from outside, provided it received commitments on issues important to Arab citizens.
Among those conditions would be a serious government effort to tackle crime and violence in Arab communities, alongside a halt to home demolitions in Bedouin towns and villages. Tibi said the demolitions had intensified during Netanyahu's tenure.
Such an arrangement could allow Eisenkot to establish a minority government supported by Arab lawmakers in parliamentary votes without formally including their parties in the coalition.
Tibi said he had received hundreds of calls and messages since the first exit polls were published Tuesday night, including an approach from what he described as a "significant figure" within the opposition bloc. He acknowledged, however, that Eisenkot himself had not contacted him.
Tibi said he had conveyed a clear message that the Joint List was both "ready" and "willing" to help pave the way for a different government. But for that to happen, he said, Eisenkot and his political partners would have to "show courage."
The appeal comes despite opposition from several prominent parties in Eisenkot's bloc to forming a government that would depend on Arab political support.
Although the Arab parties' projected 19 seats could prove crucial in preventing Netanyahu from securing another term, cooperation with them remains politically contentious among Eisenkot's potential coalition partners.
The 19-seat dilemma facing Eisenkot
The strong showing by the Joint List and Ra'am followed an exceptionally high turnout among Arab voters, approaching 80%, according to election figures cited in the report.
The mobilization helped increase Arab representation in the Knesset and may have prevented Netanyahu's bloc from reaching the parliamentary majority needed to form a government independently.
But it has also created a difficult political question for Eisenkot: How can he replace Netanyahu without relying on the parliamentary strength of the Arab parties?
The dilemma is particularly complicated by the conditions Eisenkot has set for parties seeking to join his government. Those include recognizing Israel as a Jewish state and acknowledging Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be dismantled.
Those requirements could make formal cooperation with Arab parties difficult, even if their support from outside a coalition would not necessarily require them to become government partners.
The Joint List's willingness to consider external parliamentary support offers Eisenkot a potential alternative to a traditional coalition agreement. But it remains unclear whether such an arrangement could overcome the objections of his other political partners or satisfy his own conditions.
For now, the Arab parties are openly signaling their willingness to help bring about a change in government, while Eisenkot has yet to present a framework for cooperation with them.
On Wednesday evening, he reiterated that his priority was establishing what he called a "Zionist government committed to military conscription."
The contrast leaves Israel's opposition facing a central question in the aftermath of the election: whether it is prepared to rely on the Arab lawmakers whose votes could be essential to ending Netanyahu's rule.

Flavio Bolsonaro’s escape to the US: How it happened

Flavio Bolsonaro’s escape to the US: How it happened
- Flavio Bolsonaro defied a court order to surrender his passports after his election defeat and ongoing investigations, sparking confusion and a search for his whereabouts.
- He denied plans to leave Brazil, but later crossed into Argentina with valid travel documents, while Brazilian police said there was no official record of his departure.
- He then flew via Ecuador to Miami, arriving in Florida with his family and a cancelled diplomatic passport, according to US border records.
AI generated
SAO PAULO - Flavio Bolsonaro’s clandestine escape to the United States bewildered Brazil and triggered a frantic search for his whereabouts.
The Supreme Court had ordered the son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro to forfeit his passports after his electoral loss on Oct 25, amid fears he would leave the country due to ongoing investigations against him.
But the defeated right-wing presidential candidate failed to hand them in, choosing instead to flee to the US via Argentina and Ecuador.
AFP takes a look at the frenzied 24-hours that left the world scratching its head as Bolsonaro went off the grid.
Refuses to concede
Bolsonaro makes a brief, stone-faced speech from Brasilia on the night of Oct 25 following his electoral defeat to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
He refuses to recognise the result and promises to seek an annulment of the election.
Exit blocked
The next day, the 45-year-old posts a video on Instagram, speaking outdoors in front of a bare wall.
He tells his followers that the Supreme Court has banned him from leaving the country in “a clear attempt to intimidate me.”
“I never had any intention of leaving the country. I will surrender my passports and defend myself against this travesty,” he said.
The ban on his travel is linked to one of several ongoing investigations against him.
Vacant vehicle
On Oct 27, the Argentine outlet Infobae reports that Bolsonaro plans to board a flight in the north-eastern city of Puerto Iguazu.
Journalists including AFP witness Bolsonaro’s official motorcade leaving his Brasilia residence.
It is initially impossible to know whether one of the three black cars is carrying him.
Local media reports the dispersal of the motorcade soon afterward, while the driver of the middle vehicle – usually transporting the politician – rolls down the window and shows that no one is on board.
Going dark
As speculation runs rampant, a police source confirms the cancellation of Bolsonaro’s Brazilian and diplomatic passports to AFP.
American media meanwhile reports that the defeated candidate is en route to the US.
Back in Brazil, confusion reigns, and Bolsonaro’s campaign manager says he has no idea where his boss is.
“I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it,” a dumbfounded Rogerio Marinho tells the press in Brasilia.
Hopping borders
It turns out that while the world had been speculating on his whereabouts, Bolsonaro is still in Brazil.
He only crosses the border into Argentina at 0150 GMT on Oct 28, the neighbouring country’s immigration authorities announce – over 12 hours after the first reports emerge that he has left.
The senator enters Argentina “with valid travel documents and no legal impediment” via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge linking the Brazilian city of Foz do Iguacu with Puerto Iguazu, Argentine authorities say.
Flavio also holds an Italian passport.
It remains unknown how he got to Argentina from Brasilia, more than 1,500km away.
Brazilian police say there is no official record of his departure from the country.
They say they are investigating his failure to hand over his passports, but this does not classify him as a fugitive.
Flight
A private jet then whisks Bolsonaro and his family to Ecuador’s port city of Guayaquil, Argentine immigration authorities say.
The plane makes a brief refuelling stop at the virtually empty airport.
AFP reporters witness the aircraft taking off again, and the FlightAware website shows that it is heading to Miami.
Some 927,000 people track its course via the website Flightradar.
Arrival
Around 12 hours after their departure from Argentina, the Bolsonaro family hits the tarmac at Florida’s Opa-Locka airport.
He enters the United States with his cancelled diplomatic passport, according to the Department of Homeland Security website that tracks border controls.
Flavio Bolsonaro wears a black shirt and shoulders a backpack as he disembarks the plane alongside his wife and two daughters, AFP observes.
Minutes later, a vehicle drives away from the airport. AFP

Leak website releases data on tens of thousands of US govt employees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Leak website releases data on tens of thousands of US govt employees
- Distributed Denial of Secrets said it released data on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security staff, including names, contacts and sensitive job details.
- The leak appears to come from a group called “Department of Peace”, which said it wanted to “limit further harm by the DHS” and support oversight.
- Reuters verified some details and said the files exposed nonpublic information on internal charts and operations, raising privacy and security risks.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets said on Oct 28 it has released data on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including details about officials working in sensitive fields such as surveillance and human intelligence.
DHS said in a statement it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively”.
The agency said it was working to ensure its employees were properly protected and would update the public “when more information is available”.
The disclosure – which the non-profit data transparency group says draws on information obtained by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” – is the third major government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.
In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees.
In October, the Defence Department was hit with a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.
The DHS data includes names, phone numbers and e-mail addresses of employees from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and other DHS component agencies.
Also included in the data were job titles and e-mail groups, which, among other details, showed which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work.
In a statement, Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the hacktivist and journalist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it.
Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight.
Crimew said her tool would provide “FOIA material for years to come!”
The Department of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”.
The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.
Best’s statement said the Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim.
Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”
Reuters could not immediately verify the authenticity of the entire data trove, but it was able to match personal information about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs.
Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.
In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organisation charts or previously undisclosed programmes or operations. REUTERS

From Human Proxies to Autonomous Adaptation: The Next Phase of Russia's Hybrid Activity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

From Human Proxies to Autonomous Adaptation: The Next Phase of Russia's Hybrid Activity
Russia’s disposable sabotage networks already give Moscow room to manoeuvre. AI agents that adapt autonomously could make that strategy of optionality cheaper and more persistent.
In the aftermath of the failed early August sabotage operation at Germany’s Leipzig airport, The Insider (an online publication specialising in investigative journalism) published an investigation alleging some of the actors in a wider network of operatives behind the GRU-linked attack: Oleg Levushkin as organiser, Andrei Karshakov as the hand behind the ‘dud drone’, and Roman Kovalevsky as an associate whose role remains unclear. Leipzig is one of an increasing number of incidents through which Russia-linked operations make two emerging features in so-called ‘hybrid activity’ explicit.
Disposable Agents and Disruption
First, as Julianne Smith, the former US ambassador to NATO, has argued, Russia appears increasingly willing to conduct operations in which its involvement is difficult to deny. The old proxy model preserved plausible deniability, which, now, while useful, is no longer a prerequisite. A new organisational model reflects a wider category of inexperienced and untrained operatives whose significance is structural. Disposability allows for replacement and a preservation of capacity. The model also has a potential strategic benefit. Establishing state responsibility does not necessarily settle what response is warranted. Russia appears willing to tolerate some level of exposure so long as the model itself can shift uncertainty about an operation’s attribution to its place in a wider campaign and probe NATO’s response threshold.
Second, disruption offers Russia another vector through which it can impose costs when its efforts to deter European support for Ukraine through other means – such as repeated threats of targeted nuclear retaliation – no longer appear credible. Imposing costs through disruption is not a direct substitute for deterrence; instead of changing foreign policy, disruption redirects resources and increases the costs of an ally’s infrastructure resilience. This risks compounding the political cost of sustained support. The strategic payoff from this type of disruption and sabotage across domains lies in the accumulated costs imposed on NATO Allies, rather than the success of any particular operation.
Anthropic identified Russia-based actors using Claude Code to develop and test software for an autonomous drone swarm, including target-selection and engagement functions
Together, this organisational model and the use of disruption preserve Russia’s optionality: Moscow can vary its threshold-probing disruption operations, and impose costs without committing to a single course of action or risking direct confrontation, while exploiting differences among NATO Allies’ perception over the significance of its activity and the response it warrants. This is where a fourth member in the wider operational network holds promise for extending such a strategy: Claude.
An Adaptive Loop
Anthropic’s September 2026 threat-intelligence report describes a Russian-linked espionage actor using Claude in AI-driven workflows to conduct intrusions against Ukrainian and European government, diplomatic and defence targets. Agents monitored whether deployed malware was being detected and, when security products identified it, autonomously modified and rebuilt the tools before redeploying them. This was not a fully autonomous campaign: human operators retained direction over the operation, including important decisions about targeting. Separately, Anthropic identified Russia-based actors using Claude Code to develop and test software for an autonomous drone swarm, including target-selection and engagement functions. Together, the instances demonstrate an adaptive loop in which a defensive response no longer necessarily forces an attacker to stop and devise a new approach manually.
This changes the cost of sustaining probing activities in efforts to disrupt and sabotage. Under a more human-dependent model, each new attempt requires time, technical expertise and operator attention. An agent pursuing a human-supplied objective could instead test alternative approaches, assess the results and adjust its behaviour continuously. Applied across multiple target environments, discovering and maintaining pressure points could become cheaper, continuous and adaptive, even when individual attempts are detected or disrupted.
On 13 October, MI5 chief, Ken McCallum, alluded to these risks separately: on the one hand, Russia is turning to criminal and volunteer intermediaries as its traditional covert network has degraded. On the other hand, terrorists were caught seeking to use AI to develop reconnaissance and attack methods. There is no evidence that Russia is already using autonomous agents to manage a coordinated campaign designed to manipulate NATO’s response thresholds. But the operational conditions for such a strategy are emerging. Autonomy could extend Russia’s existing optionality from the choice of actor and operation to the execution of the operation itself. An agent need not understand the political significance of its actions, or act out grievance. It would be enough for it to adapt technically, generating different effects across systems while leaving the state to decide how to exploit the resulting uncertainty.
Implications for NATO
For Russia, autonomous systems would not merely be a cheaper or faster assistant in its disruption effort. Continuous operational adaptation will change the strategic value of optionality itself. For NATO, this reinforces the need to assess persistent patterns of activity rather than treating every incident as a discrete technical problem. Disruption can remove access and force an adversary to expend resources rebuilding its capabilities, but it may not deter further activity if adaptation becomes cheaper. Responses need to connect technical disruption with intelligence cooperation, law enforcement, financial measures and other instruments that impose costs on the networks enabling these operations. Many of these measures are captured in RUSI’s new deterrence framework. It is up to NATO Allies to solve the underlying technical, strategic and political differences in perception. Even when attributions have been made, an operation may produce different effects across Allied networks, vary in severity and interpretation, and be attributed to the same wider campaign only over time.
Moscow has not adopted the use of autonomous systems as a deliberate strategy yet. Greater autonomy need not necessarily produce more effective coercion. Agents can fail, behave unpredictably or generate activity that has little strategic value. Nor does autonomy remove the need for human decisions about objectives, target selection and acceptable risk. But by lowering the cost of technical adaptation, autonomous systems could make it easier to sustain the kind of varied, persistent pressure from which Russia already derives strategic value. Claude will not take Oleg, Andrei or Roman’s jobs, but it could change what the network around them is able to do and when. NATO Allies must pre-empt this challenge, and prevent the capability of continuous adaptation from becoming a challenge of enduring advantage.

U.S. stocks close higher as Fed holds rates steady
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:56:20 CST
08:56:20 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks ended higher on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve opted to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged, as investors weighed persistent inflation concerns and the prospect of further rate hikes.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 97.53 points, or 0.19 percent, to 52,475.1. The benchmark S&P 500 added 21.38 points, or 0.28 percent, to 7,743.98, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index gained 72.04 points, or 0.27 percent, to close at 26,549.85.
Eight of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors closed in positive territory, with technology and energy leading the market higher by advancing 0.48 percent and 0.41 percent, respectively. Bucking the upward momentum, utilities and real estate paced the decliners, sliding 0.88 percent and 0.65 percent, respectively.
Following a two-day policy meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee voted in a split decision to hold the federal funds target range steady at 3.75 percent to 4 percent, after raising rates by a quarter percentage point in September. The decision revealed divisions within the committee, with Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Fed Governor Lisa Cook dissenting in favor of an immediate 25-basis-point rate hike.
In its policy statement, the U.S. central bank emphasized that incoming economic data will guide the timing and scale of future moves, noting that "the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee's 2 percent goal."
"Ensuring price stability and watching inflation is not about some fixed date on a calendar or some isolated data point," Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said. "It's about ensuring we have clear objectives and it's about monetary policy strategy," he added.
Financial analysts widely noted that the October pause sets the stage for a potential year-end rate increase. In a written note, ING Bank observed that policymakers will assess two employment reports and one inflation print before their next gathering in December. They pointed out that because the November consumer price index will be released the day after that meeting, officials will have access to internal figures beforehand.
In corporate developments, shares of enterprise software and cloud infrastructure provider Oracle jumped 10.73 percent after management issued an ambitious fiscal 2030 revenue target of 225 billion U.S. dollars, representing an annualized growth rate of 35 percent.
Market participants are now turning their attention to after-the-bell quarterly results from mega-cap cloud and AI companies Microsoft and Alphabet. ■

Alphabet reports rising Q3 revenue, falling net income
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:56:13 CST
08:56:13 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Alphabet, the parent company of Google, reported Wednesday that its third-quarter revenue rose 25 percent year on year to 127.58 billion U.S. dollars, driven by strong growth in its search and cloud computing businesses, while net income declined 24 percent.
According to the company's earnings report, operating income increased 30 percent to 40.58 billion dollars in the quarter ended Sept. 30, while net income fell to 26.47 billion dollars from 34.98 billion dollars a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share dropped to 2.12 dollars from 2.87 dollars. Net income available to common stockholders dropped 25 percent to 26.17 billion dollars.
The decline in net income was largely attributable to a swing from investment gains to losses. Alphabet reported a net loss of 8.66 billion dollars on equity securities, compared with a net gain of 10.73 billion dollars a year earlier.
Google Cloud revenue surged 103 percent to 30.71 billion dollars, driven by strong demand for enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and solutions. The segment's operating income jumped to 11.12 billion dollars from 3.59 billion dollars a year earlier.
Google Services revenue grew 11 percent to 96.3 billion dollars, including a 12-percent increase in Google Search and other revenue to 63.35 billion dollars.
Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said the company's AI investments were driving search query growth, with the year-on-year growth rate reaching its highest level in five years. He also said the Gemini AI app had reached 1 billion users. ■

Fort of San Diego in Acapulco bears witness to Manila Galleon trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:56:08 CST
08:56:08 KST

This aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 27, 2026 shows the Fort of San Diego and Acapulco Bay in Acapulco, Guerrero state, Mexico. First built in the 17th century, the fort once served to defend the port against pirate attacks and protect trading vessels arriving from Manila, the Philippines. It now houses the Historical Museum of Acapulco Fort of San Diego. The port city of Acapulco on Mexico's Pacific coast was once a major hub for trade between Asia and the Americas. In 1565, a Spanish galleon sailing from the Philippines reached Acapulco, helping establish a trans-Pacific maritime route. For approximately 250 years, the Manila Galleon trade connected Manila in the Philippines with Acapulco in Mexico, carrying Chinese silk, porcelain, and other Asian goods to the Americas and transporting silver from the Americas to Asia. Traces of this historic maritime trade can still be found in Acapulco today, from the centuries-old Fort of San Diego and Chinese porcelain displayed in its museum to models of sailing ships and a monument commemorating the Manila Galleon. (Xinhua/Li Muzi)

Microsoft's quarterly revenue rises 19 pct, net income up 32 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:56:05 CST
08:56:05 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- U.S. technology giant Microsoft reported Wednesday that its revenue rose 19 percent year on year to 92.28 billion U.S. dollars in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.
According to the company's earnings report, net income for the quarter ended Sept. 30 increased 32 percent to 36.63 billion dollars from 27.75 billion dollars a year earlier.
Operating income climbed 21 percent to 45.92 billion dollars from 37.96 billion dollars in the same period last year, while diluted earnings per share rose to 4.92 dollars from 3.72 dollars.
The company said its reported net income was affected by gains and losses associated with its investments in artificial intelligence company OpenAI. The investments generated a net gain of 207 million dollars in the quarter, compared with a net loss of 3.09 billion dollars a year earlier.
Excluding the impact of those investments, Microsoft's adjusted net income increased 18 percent to 36.42 billion dollars year on year. Adjusted diluted earnings per share rose 18 percent to 4.89 dollars.
Cloud computing remained a major growth driver. Microsoft Cloud revenue increased 30 percent year on year to 63.9 billion dollars, while revenue from its Azure cloud platform surged 48 percent to 33.17 billion dollars.
Under the company's revised business reporting structure, revenue from its Agents and Infra segment increased 25 percent to 76.8 billion dollars, while revenue from its Devices and Consumer segment declined 3 percent to 15.48 billion dollars.
Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue grew 17 percent on a reported basis, while Microsoft 365 consumer cloud revenue also increased 17 percent. Search and advertising revenue, excluding traffic acquisition costs, rose 12 percent.
Meanwhile, Xbox content and services revenue declined 2 percent, while Windows OEM and devices revenue fell 22 percent.
Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said the company made a strong start to its new fiscal year, with Microsoft Cloud revenue growth accelerating to 30 percent. She said the company's revenue, operating income and earnings per share all exceeded expectations.
The company also reported that its commercial remaining performance obligation increased 73 percent year on year to 677 billion dollars.
Microsoft returned 10.2 billion dollars to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases during the quarter. ■

Fox News viewer dip pre-US midterm election suggests Republican unease

Fox News viewer dip pre-US midterm election suggests Republican unease
- Fox News prime-time viewers fell 28% in four weeks before the US midterm elections, suggesting weaker Republican and MAGA enthusiasm, with Trump’s approval also down to 32%.
- MS NOW and CNN both gained viewers, while Fox still led cable news overall and said it remained number one across cable, digital, social and streaming.
- Experts said political conflict drives ratings, but cable TV is declining as people move to YouTube, and Nielsen’s 2026 measurement changes may affect audience numbers.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Fox News, the most-watched cable news network, saw a 28% prime-time viewer decline over the past four weeks leading up to the midterm elections, a sign the network’s traditionally conservative audience may be less enthused about the Nov 3 contest.
The Fox Corp network averaged 2 million evening viewers from Sept 28 to Oct 25, according to Nielsen data.
Versant Media Group’s MS NOW experienced a 15% increase to 1.16 million viewers, while Skydance Corp’s CNN averaged 644,000 viewers, a 16% increase over the same period.
Recent troubles for US President Donald Trump and the Republican Party may have cut into viewership.
The Democrats are currently favoured by both traditional polls and prediction market odds to win the House of Representatives and Senate, as voters grapple with issues around affordability, a controversial war in Iran and tariffs.
Trump’s approval rating dropped to a low for him of 32% last week, according to a poll from Reuters and Ipsos.
That’s bad news for Fox, said Hang Media Inc chief executive officer Jon Klein, a former executive at CBS News and CNN.
“They live or die based on the president’s poll approval ratings and in general, the popularity of MAGA,” Klein said.
Some support for Trump’s Make America Great Again movement may have shrunk during his second term.
Podcaster Joe Rogan, for example, has tamped down his once-vocal backing of the president.
These changes have likely contributed to Fox’s viewership decline, according to Reece Peck, an associate professor at the College of Staten Island and author of the book Fox Populism: Branding Conservatism as Working Class.
While Fox still has a “diehard boomer demographic” committed to tuning in, the current election cycle “just does not inspire the urge to watch your favourite show,” Peck said.
Trump has also signalled his displeasure with Fox News, saying in an Oct 25 social media post that the network was giving excessive air time to opponents of the Republicans.
The president joined the network for a telephone interview that morning.
Fox News commanded more than half of the cable news audience in total day viewership, beating combined viewership for CNN and MS NOW, the network said in a release on Oct 28.
“Fox News has been the number one network in cable news for nearly a quarter century, through every administration since 2001,” the network said.
“As we’ve grown our business across platforms, we’ve expanded our dominance to digital, social and streaming, currently not only ranking as number one in cable, but also leading YouTube with nearly 4 billion video views this year, one billion more than the competition.”
In October 2025, Fox garnered viewership boosts from covering topics like the Gaza ceasefire and continued coverage on right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated the month before.
In 2026, Nielsen also introduced changes to its methods for measuring viewership.
The National Football League, which dominates TV viewership, voiced concerns in August that the changes would negatively impact audience numbers.
Overall, the cable industry continues to see declines in viewership as consumers turn to platforms like YouTube for content, according to Paul Hardart, director of the entertainment, media & technology programme at NYU’s Stern School of Business.
He said that for Fox specifically, the network did better when Joe Biden, a Democrat, was in office prior to Trump because political news networks thrive off of conflict.
“Fox News did really well when Biden was the president because it’s adversarial, and I think you may have the inverted effect happening with CNN and MS NOW,” he said.
The newsletter Status reported earlier on the Fox News ratings decline. BLOOMBERG

HAVANA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Cuba on Wednesday celebrated the overwhelming approval by the UN General Assembly of a resolution to lift the U.S. embargo, calling it a "victory" in the face of unprecedented pressure from Washington to defeat the initiative.
In a post on X, Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel described the resolution's broad backing as a "victory for the heroic Cuban people," who have not surrendered despite the "economic suffocation, threats and abuse by the U.S. government."
UN member nations debated the resolution, titled "Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed by the United States of America against Cuba," between Tuesday and Wednesday before approving it by 130 votes in favor, 17 against and 25 abstentions.
Diaz-Canel underscored the overwhelming international opposition to the embargo, "even in the face of the crudest pressure and blackmail" from Washington to alter the outcome of the vote.
The outcome "is a triumph of the truth over those who rely on lies and blackmail to subject an entire nation to collective punishment," he said.
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez, who led the Cuban delegation to the UN General Assembly, also called the vote a "new victory" against the U.S. sanctions and further proof that "Cuba is not a threat, the embargo is."
This marks the 34th time the international community has voted to end the embargo, which official figures show has caused nearly 179 billion U.S. dollars in economic losses to the Caribbean island.
In 2025, countries voted to condemn the embargo with 165 votes in favor, seven against and 12 abstentions.
For more than six decades, Washington has imposed stiff economic, commercial, and financial sanctions on Cuba, a policy intensified by the Trump administration. ■

Designing Engagement for Multilingual Learners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:42:05 UTC
08:42:05 KST

Douglas Fisher and Nancy Frey create conditions where all students can progress from participation to ownership
Walk into a busy classroom and you may see students participating in very different ways. One student eagerly contributes to a discussion. Another listens carefully but says little. A third speaks animatedly with a classmate but becomes quiet when asked to share with the whole class. Still another completes every assignment without ever volunteering an idea.
Which students are engaged?
The answer is more complicated than it first appears.
We often judge engagement by what we can see. A student who raises a hand, looks at the teacher, completes an assignment, and participates in discussion appears engaged. Yet visible participation tells us only part of the story. Behavioral engagement matters, but it does not necessarily reveal how deeply students are thinking, how connected they feel to the classroom community, or whether they see themselves as capable learners.
For Multilingual Learners, this distinction is especially important. A student may be deeply engaged cognitively while still developing the language needed to express complex thinking publicly. Another may understand a concept but hesitate because producing an answer in an additional language requires extra processing. Silence, therefore, should not automatically be interpreted as disengagement.
Instead of asking “Why aren’t these students engaging?” educators can ask a more productive question: “What conditions are we designing that make engagement more, or less, likely?”
That shift matters because engagement does not happen by chance. It is designed. When classrooms are intentionally designed around invitation, relationships, clarity, productive challenge, and agency, Multilingual Learners are more likely to participate, persist, take intellectual risks, and ultimately take greater ownership of their learning.
Begin with Invitation
Every classroom sends messages. Some are obvious: Welcome. Work with a partner. Share your thinking.
Others are communicated through everyday instructional decisions: Whose ideas receive attention, and whose names and experiences appear in examples? How much time do students have to formulate responses, and are multiple ways of communicating accepted? What happens when someone makes a mistake?
Together, these signals answer an important question for MLs: “Is my thinking wanted here?”
An invitational classroom communicates that students’ contributions matter before their English is polished or perfect (Purkey & Novak, 1996). That distinction is significant. If participation requires MLs to produce immediate, public, grammatically accurate English, the classroom may unintentionally communicate that language performance is valued more than thinking. Students quickly learn the safest response: remain quiet until they are certain.
Invitation changes the equation. Teachers can invite MLs into academic conversations by giving them opportunities to rehearse ideas with partners before speaking publicly, use visuals or other representations to support communication, connect concepts to prior experiences, and collaboratively construct ideas with peers. Instead of treating language development as a prerequisite for meaningful participation, teachers make meaningful participation part of language development.
The goal is not simply to get MLs to talk more. It is to create conditions in which they recognize that what they have to say is worth hearing.
Make Belonging Visible
Engagement is social. Students continually notice who gets heard, who receives support, whose ideas are taken seriously, and who seems to matter (Smith et al., 2026). When patterns of classroom interaction consistently communicate fairness, respect, and advocacy, students receive a powerful message: You belong here and your participation is genuinely welcomed.
For MLs, belonging cannot be separated from language. Language is more than a tool for completing assignments. It is connected to family, culture, experience, knowledge, and identity. When students’ linguistic resources are treated primarily as obstacles to overcome, students may understandably conclude that parts of themselves should remain outside the classroom.
An engagement-focused classroom takes a different stance. Teachers learn to pronounce students’ names correctly. They learn about the languages students speak and the knowledge they bring. They create opportunities for students to draw on their full linguistic repertoires when appropriate. They select examples and texts that broaden whose experiences and perspectives are represented. Most importantly, they monitor everyday interaction patterns.
- Who gets called on?
- Whose response gets expanded?
- Who receives follow-up questions?
- Whose ideas become part of the lesson?
- Who is interrupted?
- Who rarely speaks?
Belonging is not established by a multicultural poster or a single celebration. It emerges through repeated experiences demonstrating that students are respected, known, and intellectually valued. Belonging is built through patterns students experience repeatedly and collectively, rather than through isolated acts of care.
Make Learning Clear Without Making It Easy
MLs are simultaneously navigating content and language. Unclear instruction therefore creates an especially significant barrier to engagement. Students need to understand more than what they are supposed to do. They need to understand what they are supposed to learn.
Consider the difference between these two questions:
“What are you doing?”
and
“What are you learning?”
They sound similar, but they reveal very different classroom experiences. Students can successfully complete a worksheet, copy notes, highlight a passage, or construct a poster without necessarily understanding the learning those activities are intended to produce. Clarity redirects attention from task completion to learning.
For MLs, teachers can make learning more navigable by communicating learning intentions in accessible language, unpacking important vocabulary, modeling processes, providing examples and nonexamples, using visuals and demonstrations, checking understanding frequently, and making success criteria visible.
Importantly, clarity does not mean simplifying the intellectual work. In a study focused on seven to 17-year-olds, Markant and Amso (2015) found that when learners don’t know where to direct their attention, IQ becomes a determining factor in learning. But when learning goals are made explicit for students, the direction of attention becomes a mediator and IQ is no longer the predictor.
Protect the Challenge, Provide the Support
Good teaching for MLs sometimes gets confused with making learning easier. That is a mistake.
MLs need access to the same rich thinking, complex texts, interesting problems, academic conversations, and intellectually demanding experiences as their peers. The challenge is not something from which students should be protected. It is something they should be supported in navigating.
Productive challenge becomes possible when students have a foundation of belonging and clarity. When students feel safe and understand what they are working toward, difficulty can function as an invitation rather than a threat.
The teacher’s task, then, is not to remove struggle but to distinguish between productive struggle and unnecessary barriers. Suppose MLs are analyzing a complex scientific phenomenon. The intellectual challenge might involve identifying patterns, evaluating evidence, and developing an explanation. Those demands should remain.
But unfamiliar vocabulary, dense directions, or an expectation that students formulate an immediate whole-class response in English may introduce barriers unrelated to the intended learning.
Teachers can reduce those barriers while preserving the thinking. Students might examine a diagram before reading, discuss observations with a partner, annotate a text, use sentence frames when helpful, sketch their thinking, or rehearse an explanation before sharing it publicly.
The principle is simple: Scaffold access, not thinking.
Expand What Counts as Participation
A classroom can look wonderfully engaged while providing surprisingly little opportunity for students to think. This matters for MLs because teachers can easily mistake quiet compliance for success or silence for disengagement.
Engagement includes behavioral participation, but it also includes cognitive and emotional dimensions. Cognitively engaged students analyze, connect, monitor, revise, and make meaning. Emotionally engaged students feel safe enough to participate, take intellectual risks, and persist when learning becomes difficult.
We therefore need to expand the evidence we use when determining whether MLs are engaged.
Ask yourself: Are students making meaning? Are they interacting with ideas? Are they explaining their thinking to someone? Are they asking questions? Are they revising their thinking? Are they using feedback? Are they connecting new learning to what they already know?
A Multilingual Learner discussing an idea with a partner, drawing a representation, annotating a text, or listening closely before contributing may be deeply engaged even when that engagement does not resemble traditional whole-class participation.
Move from Voice to Agency
Ultimately, the goal is not simply to help MLs participate in classrooms designed entirely by adults.
It is to help them influence their learning. This is where engagement becomes agency.
Agentic engagement occurs when students move from responding to instruction to helping shape it. They ask questions, request clarification, seek feedback, express preferences, monitor their progress, adjust strategies, and contribute ideas about how learning unfolds.
For MLs, this may be one of the most consequential shifts we can make.
Too often, students who are still developing English are positioned primarily as recipients of support. Adults select the scaffold, determine the grouping, simplify the language, provide the sentence frame, and decide when the student is ready to participate.
Support is necessary. But support without agency can unintentionally teach dependence. Imagine instead asking students:
- Which resource would help you understand this?
- Would you like time to rehearse before sharing?
- How could you show what you understand?
- What part is confusing?
- What feedback would help you next?
- Who could you work with to move your thinking forward?
These are small changes, but they reposition MLs from people for whom instruction is designed to people who participate in designing their own learning.
Change the Question
When a Multilingual Learner does not participate, hesitates to speak, stops working, or withdraws from a challenging task, it is tempting to locate the problem within the student.
She lacks confidence.
He isn’t motivated.
They don’t know enough English yet.
Sometimes those explanations may contain part of the story. But they should not be our starting point.
Engagement by design asks us to become curious about the learning environment.
- Was the learner genuinely invited?
- Does the learner experience belonging?
- Is the learning clear?
- Is the challenge productive and supported?
- Does the learner have meaningful opportunities for voice and agency?
These questions move us away from trying to make MLs conform to a predetermined image of an “engaged student.” They ask us instead to examine the conditions we have created.
The most powerful shift may be from asking “How do I get my Multilingual Learners to engage?” to asking “What am I designing that makes it possible for Multilingual Learners to engage?” That question reflects a central premise: engagement grows when invitation, relationships, clarity, challenge, and agency work together (Fisher et al., 2026).
And when those conditions are intentionally designed, Multilingual Learners are no longer merely completing assignments or participating when called upon. They begin asking questions, contributing ideas, taking intellectual risks, monitoring their progress, supporting peers, and making decisions about their learning.
They move from participation to ownership. And that is engagement worth designing.
References
Fisher, D., Frey, N., Smith, D., & Marshall, J. (2026). The Engagement by Design Playbook: Creating Environments Where Students Thrive. Corwin.
Markant, J., & Amso, D. (2015). “Leveling the Playing Field: Attention mitigates the effects of intelligence on memory.” Cognition, 131(2), 195–204. doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2014.01.006.
Purkey, W. W., & Novak, J. M. (1996). Inviting School Success: A Self-Concept Approach to Teaching, Learning, and Democratic Practice (3rd ed.). Wadsworth.
Smith, D., Fisher, D., & Frey, N. (2026). Belonging in School: Creating a Place Where Kids Want to Learn and Teachers Want to Stay—An Illustrated Playbook (2nd ed). Corwin.
Douglas Fisher is professor and chair of educational leadership at San Diego State University and a leader at Health Sciences High and Middle College. Previously, Doug was an early intervention teacher and elementary school educator. He is a credentialed teacher and leader in California. In 2022, he was inducted into the Reading Hall of Fame by the Literacy Research Association. He has published widely on literacy, quality instruction, and assessment, as well as books such as Welcome to Teaching, PLC+, Teaching Students to Drive Their Learning, and Student Assessment: Better Evidence, Better Decisions, Better Learning.
Nancy Frey is professor of educational leadership at San Diego State University and a leader at Health Sciences High and Middle College. Previously, Nancy was a teacher, academic coach, and central office resource coordinator in Florida. She is a credentialed special educator, reading specialist, and administrator in California. She is a member of the International Literacy Association’s Literacy Research Panel and has published widely, including books such as Welcome to Teaching, PLC+, Teaching Students to Drive Their Learning, and Student Assessment: Better Evidence, Better Decisions, Better Learning.

What we know about the deadly train crash in Spain

What we know about the deadly train crash in Spain
Jonathan Wolfe
- A high-speed train crash near Toledo killed at least 68 people and injured dozens. A Renfe train hit a stopped Iryo train on the Madrid-Seville route.
- Spain’s transport minister called the traffic control decision “inexplicable”. Audio suggests operators let the Iryo train resume “normal speed” and did not warn the Renfe driver.
- Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Spain must reinforce rail safety. The crash may affect the election campaign after two other fatal train accidents this year.
AI generated
TOLEDO, Spain – A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another on Oct 28 near Toledo, Spain, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens of others, according to local emergency officials.
It was one of the deadliest train crashes in the country’s history.
The crash comes months after another deadly train crash in southern Spain that involved the same carriers, killing 46 people in January.
The accident on Oct 28 was the third fatal train crash in Spain in 2026, adding to deep concern about the safety of the country’s extensive rail system.
What happened?
Around 9am (4pm Singapore time), a train belonging to the private rail operator Iryo was stopped on the tracks near Toledo when a train operated by Spain’s national rail company, Renfe, barrelled into it.
Both trains were covering the route between Madrid, the capital, and the southern city of Seville.
Oscar Puente, Spain’s transportation minister, said in a news conference that the crash appeared to result from what he called an “inexplicable” decision by traffic control operators to tell the Renfe train to continue its journey when the other train was stopped farther along the tracks.
Spanish newspaper El Pais in the evening on Oct 28 obtained audio of exchanges between the conductors and the operators in Madrid, in which the operator authorised the driver of the Iryo train to resume “normal speed”.
But seven minutes later, the Iryo driver reported she could not restart the train. The Madrid operators apparently did not tell the driver of the Renfe train that it needed to brake.
Passengers involved in the crash told local news outlets that the impact tossed people around cabins. Some crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them.
Video filmed inside one of the train cars and verified by The New York Times showed smoke rising from a charred, mangled carriage on the slope by the rail line.
In the afternoon on Oct 28, the trains were surrounded by ambulances, police cars and fire trucks, with helicopters flying low overhead. Dozens of Civil Guard officers, some wearing white protective suits, were inspecting the scene.
Both trains appeared to have sustained substantial damage, according to images from the scene. The nose of the Renfe train, which was travelling to Seville, appeared destroyed. Three rear carriages of the Iryo train appeared to have been derailed, two of them overturned.
More than 50 people were injured in the crash, according to local officials. Some 397 passengers were aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train, local news outlets reported.
How are officials responding?
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez travelled to the scene of the crash on Oct 28.
“It’s not possible for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in one year,” he said, adding that while the Oct 28 accident and a fatal January crash on the same line seemed unrelated, Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced.
With national elections set for the end of November, the crash has the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign, in which opponents have attacked the competence of the left-wing government of Sanchez.
“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” conservative opposition leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo wrote on social media.
“The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.”
What is Spain’s history with train collisions?
The collision on Oct 28 came months after a deadly collision involving the same carriers that killed 46 people.
In that accident, in January, a train belonging to Iryo derailed near the town of Adamuz as it travelled north toward Madrid from Malaga. Two of its rear cars fell onto the opposite track and were struck by a south-bound train operated by Renfe.
An official report on what caused that accident is not yet completed, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.
In 2013, 80 people were killed when a high-speed train carrying more than 200 passengers derailed near Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain and slammed into a concrete wall.
The driver of the train admitted to speeding before the accident and was also on a call with a railway official before the crash.
The accident on Oct 28 was the third fatal crash in Spain in 2026. Days after the accident in January, a commuter train near Barcelona struck a collapsed retaining wall and derailed, killing one person. NYTIMES

She described the revised document as "lacking both originality and fresh thinking," adding: "In effect, this cements the EU's politicised approach to the high latitudes – a region that Brussels now views primarily through the lens of escalation and, as stated, the containment of Russia."
Derailing diplomatic efforts
Turning to Ukraine, Zakharova accused Kiev of trying to derail diplomatic efforts by Moscow and Washington to resume consultations on a settlement for the over four-year war, accusing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being "literally obsessed" with continuing the conflict.
She also said that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will attend the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta, Georgia on October 30-31.
In this context, she said that most of the organisational issues for the Russian delegation's participation in the meeting have been resolved.
"I should mention, however, that given that the departure is scheduled for within the next 24 hours, most issues were successfully resolved at the last minute. So, the delegation has been formed, all formalities are complete, and it is ready to get to work," she said.

But as the election results began to take shape, the tone from Shas and United Torah Judaism shifted somewhat. Knesset member Yitzhak Goldknopf, for example, said he would not rule out talks with other parties and that any decision would be referred to the rabbis, leaving the door open to negotiations with both political blocs.
Yet despite the focus on the possible makeup of the next coalition, discussions within the ultra-Orthodox community on Wednesday centered largely on another set of figures, which in some circles attracted even more attention than the seat totals of Shas and United Torah Judaism. Two new parties had challenged the established ultra-Orthodox factions: "Black Color," a party representing draft evaders, and "The Haredi Public," representing working ultra-Orthodox Jews and those interested in military service and greater integration into state institutions. Both managed to challenge the established parties in the public debate, but all eyes were on Election Day, when they faced their real test. It is difficult to say they succeeded.
The questions they raised for veteran lawmakers did, however, pose a significant challenge. At the time of writing, "Black Color" had received 9,500 votes, while "The Haredi Public" had received 9,029.
Both parties' campaign headquarters reported harassment, intimidation, vandalism of signs and equipment, and ballot slips disappearing from polling stations. In numerical terms, the results were deeply disappointing, particularly for Moti Leitner, chairman of "The Haredi Public," who had sought to protest the established ultra-Orthodox parties' failure to address the needs of Haredim interested in state-run education, pre-military preparatory programs and other options.
Indeed, this has become a major topic of conversation in Bnei Brak. Yeshiva students have been constantly checking the vote counts of the two new parties. Officials from "Black Color," headed by Yaakov Chaim Miller, insisted after the election that the outcome did not constitute a crushing defeat.
"'Black Color' is not measured solely by the number of votes it received, but by its impact on the public and the message it brought to the forefront," the party said. "We spoke of three to four seats' worth of voters who would not vote for the ultra-Orthodox parties, and that is exactly what happened. Hundreds of thousands of votes did not come home, and the demand to formally settle the status of yeshiva students has become an issue that can no longer be pushed aside."
"We are proud to have given this community a voice and placed the need to enshrine the 'Torato Umanuto' status, under which Torah study is recognized as a full-time occupation, at the top of the agenda once and for all. (And if you had only allowed them to vote for 'Black Color,' we would be in the Knesset today, but you preferred that they stay home.) As long as there is no comprehensive arrangement and clear decision, we will continue to lead the struggle boldly and without fear until we achieve our goal. The ultra-Orthodox public demands a genuine, comprehensive and unequivocal arrangement," the party concluded.
The extremely low vote totals also came as a bitter surprise to supporters of "The Haredi Public." On Tuesday night, before the final results were known, Leitner said: "The barrier of fear has been broken. A spark of hope has been ignited. Tonight marks the beginning of a long journey. Tonight is our victory in the face of threats, fraud, curses and insults. We stood our ground and did not break. This election campaign will be remembered as historic for us, the ultra-Orthodox. We stand like a fortified wall, defending what is ours for the sake of our children. The eternal nation does not fear a long road."
It appears that even ultra-Orthodox society, where changes are taking place on the margins in state-run Haredi education, employment opportunities and even military enlistment, is not yet ready for a political movement that challenges its established representation.

Fury erupts outside Spanish Transport Ministry after train disaster (VIDEOS)
Protesters clashed with police outside the Transport Ministry in Madrid as they demanded accountability for a high-speed train collision that killed at least 68 people near Toledo.
Wednesday’s crash near Urda in Toledo province was Spain’s second major railway disaster in less than ten months. On January 18, a train derailed near Adamuz, Cordoba province, and collided with another train traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people.
According to elDiario.es, the demonstration, organized by far-right groups Falange and Revuelta, demanded the resignations of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and Transport Minister Oscar Puente. “How many more people have to die before we throw these murderers and traitors out of our institutions?” Falange spokesman Federico Campanero said in a speech.

RFK Jr. under fire for claiming Arabs ‘don't produce science’ or literature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
23:28:26 UTC
08:28:26 KST

Doctors, vaccine researchers and health policy organizations have sharply criticized U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over his claim that Arabs around the world make no contributions to science, literature or research.
Criticism has focused not only on what opponents describe as the racist nature of his remarks, but also on the fact that the official overseeing America's health care system and medical research made assertions contradicted by a long list of Nobel laureates and recipients of other prestigious scientific awards.
Kennedy made the comments Monday at a campaign rally in Michigan, where he appeared alongside Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who is running against Abdul El-Sayed, an Egyptian American Muslim, physician and former public health director in Detroit.
During his speech, Kennedy sought to warn against the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood, describing what he claimed was the decline of the Arab world since the movement was founded in Egypt in 1928. "There are 500 million Arabs in the world, and they don't produce science. They don't win Nobel Prizes, Fields Medals [the most prestigious award in mathematics] or Wolf Prizes [an international scientific award established in Israel]. They don't produce literature," Kennedy declared.
He argued that the Muslim world had once been a global center of art, literature, science and engineering, but that the Muslim Brotherhood had destroyed that tradition, turning the societies in which it operated into stagnant communities preoccupied with hatred, war and victimhood.
Among the first to respond were members of Kennedy's own family.
His sister, human rights activist Kerry Kennedy, shared remarks her brother had previously made condemning politicians who incite hatred against minority groups. "There was a time when I agreed wholeheartedly with my brother. Today, I am deeply ashamed of him," she wrote.
She said a person's ethnicity or religion does not determine their scientific or intellectual abilities, describing her brother's statements as "false, cruel and derogatory."
The scientist Kennedy forgot
El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate targeted by the political attacks, also responded. "It's ironic to hear someone who uses the language of eugenics and completely rejects science come to Michigan to lecture an Arab American scientist with two doctorates who believes in science, including vaccines," he said.
El-Sayed called Kennedy "the most unqualified health secretary we've ever had" and added that, if elected to the Senate, he would seek to investigate his performance in office.
Professor Peter Hotez, one of America's leading vaccine and tropical medicine researchers and founding dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor College of Medicine in Texas, reminded Kennedy of his late colleague Ahmed Zewail, the Egyptian American scientist who won the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 1999. Hotez and Zewail previously served as U.S. science envoys during the Obama administration.
"The brilliant Nobel laureate Ahmed Zewail would disagree," Hotez wrote on X. "May he rest in peace. At least he didn't have to hear this." Hotez added that Kennedy had also "forgotten that medieval Arab scientists played a central role in preserving and transmitting the knowledge of Aristotle, Hippocrates and Galen, which eventually reached scholars of the European Renaissance."
Dr. David Gorski, a surgical oncologist and professor of surgery at Wayne State University in Detroit, linked Kennedy's statements to his history in the anti-vaccine movement. "I've been saying for years that racism and antivax go together like the white sheets of the Ku Klux Klan," he wrote on X, referring to the white supremacist organization. "And here's another example."
Dr. Alastair McAlpine, a pediatrician and vaccine researcher at British Columbia Children's Hospital in Canada, also criticized Kennedy. "Aside from being an unimaginably racist statement, it's also completely false," he wrote. McAlpine listed Arab scientists, writers and human rights activists who have received Nobel Prizes and Wolf Prizes, concluding: "Kennedy is a disgrace."
The video Kennedy denied
The U.S. advocacy group Protect Our Care, which promotes access to health care and has criticized the Trump administration's policies, joined the condemnation. The organization described Kennedy's speech as an "outright racist tirade," adding that while this was not the first time he had made remarks it considered racist, it might be the ugliest incident yet.
In its statement, the group also recalled comments Kennedy made in 2024, when he claimed that Black children were routinely given psychiatric medications that caused violent behavior and suggested placing them on rehabilitation farms where they could undergo "reparenting."
When confronted with those statements during congressional proceedings this year, Kennedy denied making them, despite the existence of video footage documenting his remarks. 
The facts themselves contradict the health secretary's assertions. Just last year, Palestinian American chemist Omar Yaghi, who was born in Jordan, won the Nobel Prize in chemistry, having previously received the Wolf Prize in 2018. Egyptian scientist Ahmed Zewail won the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 1999, while Egyptian author Naguib Mahfouz received the Nobel Prize in literature in 1988. British mathematician Michael Atiyah, who was of Lebanese descent, won the Fields Medal in 1966.
Kennedy also conflated Arabs, an ethnic and linguistic group, with Muslims, followers of a religion whose adherents are predominantly non-Arab.
Muslim Brotherhood allegations enter Michigan Senate race
Kennedy's remarks come amid the heated Senate campaign in Michigan ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
President Donald Trump and other senior Republicans have alleged that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, claims the Democratic candidate categorically denies. His half-sister, Iman Abdelhadi, wrote in 2012 that their shared mother had been active in the Islamist movement in Egypt during the 1970s. "My family has long been in the Muslim Brotherhood," she wrote.
El-Sayed, who initially also denied family connections to the movement, later said he had been raised by his father and stepmother and had no firsthand knowledge of his biological mother's activities.
Kennedy has declined to address the controversy surrounding his remarks. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services also did not respond to media requests for comment.

Ukrainian military personnel received six-seat ATC BOLT 1000 buggies worth 625,000 hryvnias — what their advantage is

Ukrainian military personnel received six-seat ATC BOLT 1000 buggies worth 625,000 hryvnias — what their advantage is
Kyiv • UNN
The buggy transports up to six military personnel, equipment, and the wounded. It is cheaper than a pickup truck, but has no armor protection and does not replace armored vehicles.
Ukrainian servicemen use domestically produced six-seat ATC BOLT 1000 buggies designed to transport personnel and equipment and evacuate the wounded near the front line. The cost of one such vehicle is UAH 625,000, which is significantly cheaper than a new pickup truck. Defense Express reports this, writes UNN.
Details
The buggy was developed by the Ukrainian company Ground Force. The vehicle is designed to carry six people and has a stated payload capacity of 550 kg, including the passengers' weight.
A cargo compartment for equipment, ammunition, and other property is provided behind the seats. Its design also allows the wounded to be transported in a sitting or lying position.
How the Ukrainian buggy differs from pickups and quad bikes
The ATC BOLT 1000 is equipped with an 85-horsepower gasoline engine, 4×4 all-wheel drive, and 350 mm of ground clearance. The vehicle also has a winch with a pulling force of 2,040 kg and a device for towing a trailer.
According to Defense Express, the first operational results demonstrated the buggy's advantages when performing certain logistical tasks, particularly due to its off-road capability, maneuverability, and ability to transport a group of servicemen.
The ATC BOLT 1000 costs UAH 625,000. For comparison, a new Toyota Hilux in Ukraine costs from UAH 1.96 million, although these vehicles belong to different classes.
At the same time, the buggy has no armored protection, and its off-road capability depends on the nature of the terrain. Therefore, it cannot fully replace pickups or armored vehicles.
The manufacturer provides warranty service, repairs, and the supply of spare parts. The first batch of mass-produced ATC BOLT 1000 vehicles was delivered to one of the Ukrainian Armed Forces' units in spring 2026.
