Beautiful landscapes may briefly put the brakes on the brain’s movement system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:00:53 UTC
07:00:53 KST

People tend to react slightly more slowly after viewing landscape photographs they find appealing, and their brains show weaker signs of getting ready to move, according to new research published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience. By recording electrical signals from the scalp while volunteers viewed nature scenes, the researchers found that images people liked more were linked to dampened movement-preparation signals alongside brain rhythms associated with heightened visual engagement. These findings suggest that experiencing beauty may prompt the brain to temporarily shift its resources away from physical action so it can focus more fully on taking in sensory details.
When people encounter an arresting view, such as a mountain range or a striking painting, they often feel momentarily transfixed. Psychologists refer to the mental and emotional evaluation of such sensory experiences as aesthetic appreciation. A central question in neuroscience is how this state of appreciation interacts with motor inhibition, which is the process the brain uses to suppress or hold back physical movement and the preparation to act.
Early brain-scanning research into how people respond to visual art pointed to an intriguing relationship between beauty and the brain regions that control body movement. For instance, a 2004 brain-imaging study found that looking at paintings rated as ugly triggered stronger activity in the motor cortex than looking at paintings rated as beautiful, which some researchers have interpreted as an urge to move away from unpleasant images. A few years later, the authors of a 2007 theoretical paper argued from a different angle that appreciating art actively engages the brain’s movement circuits, proposing that viewers mentally simulate the physical actions, gestures, or brushstrokes depicted in an artwork.
More recent neuroscientific frameworks have sought to reconcile how beauty affects the balance between perceiving the world and acting within it. In a 2020 review, researchers advanced what they call the “Stopping for Knowledge” hypothesis, arguing that the sense of beauty acts as a signal for the brain to temporarily halt physical action so it can redirect its limited processing power toward absorbing new information from the environment. Although earlier experiments using musical chords hinted that pleasant sounds can slow down button presses, researchers had not yet directly tested whether viewing preferred images suppresses the brain’s step-by-step preparation for physical movement.
To examine how visual appreciation affects physical readiness and brain activity, Paolo Barbieri and Irene Ronga of the BraIn Plasticity and behaviour changes Group in the Department of Psychology at the University of Turin and their colleagues, two of whom proposed the “Stopping for Knowledge” hypothesis, conducted two laboratory experiments to test it. The researchers examined whether looking at subjectively appealing photographs would slow down a person’s subsequent physical reactions and dampen the electrical brain signals that build up right before a movement takes place.
“The study was motivated by a theoretical hypothesis about motor inhibition that has received relatively little empirical attention, particularly in the visual domain,” study author Paolo Barbieri told PsyPost. “The idea is that temporarily inhibiting our tendency to act may allow us to focus more fully on a stimulus, giving us the time and resources needed to extract information and process it more thoroughly. We wanted to investigate whether aesthetic appreciation might be associated with this kind of temporary decoupling between perception and action.”
For their experiments, the researchers assembled a collection of 180 black-and-white photographs of natural landscapes, including mountains and seashores. They standardized all the photographs for brightness, contrast, resolution, dimensions, and color spectrum so that basic visual differences would not skew how participants reacted. In the first experiment, 30 right-handed young adults (17 women, with an average age of about 25) sat 80 centimeters from a computer monitor and viewed a random selection of 100 landscape photos one at a time.
Each trial in the first experiment began with a small cross in the center of the screen for 1.5 to 2.5 seconds, followed by a landscape photograph displayed for a random duration between 5 and 6 seconds. Varying the display time prevented participants from predicting the exact moment the image would vanish. Participants were instructed to look at the landscape and press the spacebar as fast as possible the instant the photograph disappeared, and then they had up to 3 seconds to rate how much they liked the image on a scale from 1 (least appreciated) to 9 (most appreciated). On 5 percent of the trials, a static white-noise image appeared instead of a landscape, serving as a check to ensure participants were paying attention and withholding their button presses when instructed.
Before analyzing reaction times, the researchers filtered out trials where participants failed to respond, pressed the key in less than 100 milliseconds, or reacted unusually slowly (removing about 8 percent of trials overall). For each participant, they compared reaction times following the roughly 25 highest-rated landscapes, which received an average score of 7.76 out of 9, against the 25 lowest-rated landscapes, which averaged a score of 3.06.
The results showed that participants reacted more slowly after viewing photographs they found appealing, taking an average of 297 milliseconds to press the spacebar after preferred images compared to 288 milliseconds after non-preferred images. This 9-millisecond slowdown represents roughly a 3.1 percent increase in reaction time, corresponding to a medium-sized statistical effect within participants.
To understand what happens in the brain during this brief delay, the researchers recruited a separate group of 20 right-handed young adults (10 women, with an average age of 25) for a second experiment using electroencephalography (EEG). This technique uses a cap fitted with small sensors on the scalp to measure electrical activity generated by the brain down to the millisecond. Participants completed four blocks of 80 trials, viewing the same set of 80 landscape images four times across the session, with each photo displayed for a fixed duration of 5 seconds.
Instead of reacting to the disappearance of the photograph, participants in the second experiment waited for a colored circle, acting like a traffic light, to appear on the screen right after the landscape vanished. When a green circle appeared, which happened on 75 percent of the trials (240 target trials per person), participants had to press the spacebar as quickly as possible and then rate the photograph on the 1-to-9 scale. When a red circle appeared on the remaining 25 percent of trials, they had to hold back their button press. Keeping the viewing time fixed at 5 seconds before the traffic light cue appeared allowed the scientists to track how the brain prepared to make a movement while the participant was still looking at the landscape.
The behavioral results of the second experiment echoed those of the first. Participants rated their top cluster of roughly 80 preferred trials at an average of 7.56 and their bottom cluster of 80 non-preferred trials at 3.54, and they were once again slower to press the spacebar after looking at preferred landscapes. Average reaction times were 504 milliseconds following preferred images compared to 497 milliseconds following non-preferred images, a 7-millisecond delay (or about 1.4 percent slower) that reflected a medium statistical effect. Overall reaction times were about 200 milliseconds longer in the second experiment than in the first, likely because participants had to identify the color of the traffic light before deciding whether to respond.
When the researchers examined the EEG recordings, they focused first on the readiness potential, a slow buildup of negative electrical voltage across the front and central areas of the scalp that naturally begins one to two seconds before a person performs a physical action. Larger readiness potentials generally indicate stronger preparation to move and tend to accompany faster reaction times. During the final moments of viewing preferred landscapes, specifically between 73 and 14 milliseconds before the traffic light cue appeared, this electrical buildup was noticeably smaller than when participants viewed non-preferred landscapes.
This dampening of movement-related brain activity continued even after the green traffic light appeared on the screen. Electrical brain responses linked to evaluating the green cue (occurring between 290 and 470 milliseconds after the light appeared) and physically executing the key press (between 660 and 1,010 milliseconds) were also reduced following preferred photographs. When the authors analyzed all trials individually without grouping them into categories, they found a consistent relationship across the entire rating scale: the higher a participant rated a specific landscape, the weaker their brain’s movement-preparation and execution signals tended to be.
“One of the reviewers suggested an additional analysis examining the relationship between aesthetic appreciation and neural responses on a trial-by-trial basis,” Barbieri explained. “Initially, I thought the effect might be driven mainly by the contrast between highly appreciated and poorly appreciated images, with intermediate ratings potentially obscuring the relationship. I was genuinely surprised to find that our brain responses were modulated so precisely and parametrically by our subjective preferences.”
In a final step, the team analyzed how the power of rhythmic brain waves, measured in cycles per second (hertz), shifted over time. They looked closely at alpha waves (8 to 12 hertz), which typically drop in power when the visual areas of the brain are actively focused on processing sights, and beta waves (roughly 20 to 33 hertz), which tend to surge in power when the brain is actively holding back physical movement. About two seconds before the traffic light cue appeared, viewing preferred landscapes produced both a steeper drop in alpha wave power and a stronger surge in beta wave power compared to viewing non-preferred landscapes, followed by another beta wave increase roughly 410 to 460 milliseconds after the cue. The authors interpret these rhythmic patterns as a sign that appealing images heighten visual attention while putting the brakes on motor planning.
“I think our findings offer an interesting perspective on how perception and the motor system bidirectionally interact,” Barbieri said. “They suggest that when we engage with something we appreciate, our tendency to act immediately may slow down, allowing us to focus on and explore what is in front of us. More broadly, this raises the possibility that a mindset oriented toward learning, exploration, and change may benefit from temporarily stepping away from more immediate, pragmatic goals.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. First, the reaction time delays observed after viewing preferred images were only 7 to 9 milliseconds on average. The effect is subtle, and the motor system is not shut off during aesthetic experiences. As the authors point out, holding back outward movement can happen at the same time that a viewer mentally simulates actions on the inside, and dynamic art forms like dance performances or energetic paintings may engage the motor system differently than calm black-and-white nature photographs.
“The differences in reaction times were small, amounting to fractions of a second,” Barbieri noted. “At first glance, this might seem to have little practical significance. However, perception–action cycles occur continuously throughout our daily lives, second after second. Even small shifts in how these cycles unfold may accumulate over time and reflect qualitatively different ways of engaging with the world.”
The laboratory setup also differs from how people usually experience art and nature in the real world. Viewing standardized grayscale photographs on a computer screen for five seconds at a time, and seeing the same images repeated four times across the second experiment, does not capture the complexity or emotional depth of walking through an art gallery or standing in front of a real landscape. In addition, the experiments tested relatively small groups of 30 and 20 young adults, so future studies with larger and more diverse samples will be helpful to confirm how broadly these patterns apply.
Because preference was based on participants’ own ratings rather than assigned by the researchers, the comparisons show how reactions varied alongside liking rather than proving that liking itself caused the slowdown. Other qualities of the favored images could also have played a role, despite the researchers’ efforts to standardize basic visual features.
“An important point is that aesthetic appreciation was measured through subjective ratings, independently of the images’ features,” Barbieri added. “In other words, we were interested in how much participants personally appreciated each image, rather than assuming that certain visual properties are inherently more beautiful than others. Our findings therefore concern the relationship between individual aesthetic preferences and motor responses, rather than a universal response to objectively beautiful images.”
Finally, although the brain wave recordings suggest that participants paid closer visual attention to preferred images while suppressing movement preparation, the experiments did not directly measure whether participants actually learned or remembered more information from those scenes. Alpha and beta brain waves are broad signals that can reflect several overlapping mental processes during a task, and future work will also need to explore how split-second, automatic impressions of beauty compare to deliberate ratings over longer periods of time.
“My next goal is to bring together different aspects of this framework within a single experiment,” Barbieri said. “In particular, I would like to investigate whether the decoupling between perception and action is accompanied by a greater predisposition to learn from and attend to the surrounding environment. This would help us understand whether motor inhibition is part of a broader state that facilitates exploration and information gathering.”
“More broadly, this study is part of a research program that views aesthetic experience as a possible way of navigating sensory uncertainty through curiosity rather than anxiety,” Barbieri concluded. “When we encounter something unfamiliar or unpredictable, we may experience uncertainty as a source of discomfort, or we may become curious and motivated to explore it. We are interested in understanding how aesthetic experiences might facilitate the latter response, fostering an openness to new information and learning. This perspective is also explored in our previous work.”
The study, “The gentle grip of beauty: Neural bases of motor inhibition during aesthetic appreciation,” was authored by Paolo Barbieri, Jacopo Frascaroli, Greta Varesio, Francesca Piovesan, Ludovico Bechis, Pietro Sarasso, and Irene Ronga.

Due to the massive drone attack, flights have been restricted at Moscow's airports. Two planes from Turkey returned to their departure airports.
On the evening of October 28, Moscow and the Moscow region came under a massive drone attack. Due to the threat of strikes, the Russian authorities imposed restrictions on the operation of the capital’s airports, while two passenger planes traveling from Turkey to Moscow were forced to turn back. This was reported by Russian media outlets, including TASS and ASTRA, UNN writes.
Details

Amid the attack, two passenger planes operating flights from Turkey to Moscow changed course and returned to their departure airports because of restrictions at Vnukovo.
There is currently no information about possible strikes, damage, or casualties. The Russian authorities’ statements regarding the number of drones shot down have not been independently confirmed.

Ukraine seeks European partners’ help with buses and generators, Bezgin says
Vitalii Bezgin, Ukraine’s Minister for Communities, Territories and Internally Displaced Persons, told an Ukrinform correspondent on the sidelines of the 51st session of the Council of Europe’s Congress of Local and Regional Authorities in Strasbourg.
“Representatives of Spain have already expressed their readiness to help under existing interregional agreements. We discussed buses, and they are ready to provide them. We also discussed generator deliveries. The basis for such assistance could be the agreements Catalonia signed with three Ukrainian regions earlier this autumn. These are memorandums with Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, and Lviv regions,” Bezgin said.
According to him, regional transport needs are growing because of continued Russian attacks. “In Kherson alone, losses of municipal vehicles amount to two per day,” he said.
The ministry also aims to expand direct partnerships between Ukrainian regions and regions in Council of Europe member states.
Bezgin identified French regions as active partners, highlighting their cooperation with Kharkiv region. In particular, the Kharkiv Regional Council has a partnership with France’s Grand Est region, through which communities receive generators among other assistance.
At the same time, Bezgin said eastern regions have fewer partnerships because of more complicated logistics.
“Our communities and regions have established the most ties with Poland, while cooperation with Czechia, Slovakia, and Austria needs to be intensified. Another effective mechanism we are proposing here is for partner countries to take responsibility for supporting the recovery of specific regions. There are already examples: Estonia’s support for Zhytomyr region, Denmark’s for Mykolaiv region, and Belgium’s for Chernihiv region,” he said.
In return, Ukraine offers partners its own expertise, particularly in defense technologies and the management of territories during combat operations.
According to Bezgin, European representatives are interested in meeting directly with Ukrainian manufacturers to discuss investment opportunities and business development.
There is also demand for practical experience in local self-government during wartime. Bezgin said a delegation of 16 Lithuanian mayors had recently sought information on legislative preparations, reserve formation, and the organization of community governance in the event of military threats. Other Baltic states, Finland, Poland, and Norway have shown similar interest, he added.
“We also plan to present a dedicated section on managing territories in active combat zones at the next Ukraine Recovery Conference, URC 2027, in Tallinn,” Bezgin said.
As Ukrinform previously reported, following the publication of Unbreakable Kherson, the Kherson Regional Military Administration plans to publish three more thematic guides compiling the experience of Ukraine’s regions and relevant ministries in keeping communities functioning during the war.

Speaking minutes before Bayern’s last-32 German Cup tie with Magdeburg, Eberl told ARD the doctors had determined the cause of the illness and had discharged the 40-year-old Kompany.

Russia is building a new drone launch facility near the Millerovo military airfield in the Rostov region, capable of supporting up to 100 attack drone launches per day, the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense (HUR) reported on October 28.
The facility's construction was confirmed through satellite imagery, according to Oboronka, citing an official statement by HUR. The site is located near Russia's border with Ukraine's temporarily occupied Luhansk region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The facility's configuration indicates that it is designed to prepare and launch jet-powered attack drones, likely Geran-4 and Geran-5, as well as their modifications. Preliminary estimates suggest that once construction is complete, the site will be capable of supporting up to 100 launches per day," HUR stated.
According to the intelligence directorate, satellite imagery showed no visible signs of active construction at the site in late August 2026. By mid-October, Russian forces had established launch positions and supporting infrastructure.
HUR noted that the rapid construction could be explained by the use of standardized technical solutions and the concentration of resources on relatively simple launch infrastructure.
"The construction of a new UAV launch facility just 3.5 kilometers from Millerovo airfield means that the Russians intend to use the same air defense systems protecting the airfield to defend it," HUR explained.
The facility could also benefit from existing roads, communications networks, logistics infrastructure, and technical support systems associated with the military airfield.
However, HUR emphasized that the actual launch rate would depend on the availability of drones, fuel, warheads, trained crews, operational equipment, and assigned missions.
Meanwhile, Russia is modernizing its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered attack drones, the intelligence directorate reported. The Geran-4 has a range of up to 770 kilometers and has received additional autonomous navigation capabilities, including an optical terrain-matching system.
HUR also reported that Russia has equipped the Geran-4 with a domestically produced jet engine and a new warhead designed to strike bridges and power transmission line supports.
The Geran-5 has a reported range of up to 950 kilometers. Its K5 modification is being fitted with a similar optical navigation system, potentially improving its ability to navigate without relying exclusively on satellite signals.
According to HUR, Russia currently operates at least 12 permanent attack drone launch facilities. The Millerovo site would expand this network and could form part of preparations to intensify drone strikes against Ukraine, particularly during the winter.
The Millerovo site is not an isolated expansion: the Tsymbulova drone base in the Oryol region has also been adding shelters and launchers for jet-powered drones as Russia ramps up output of the Gerans themselves.
As of early October, Russia was producing around 2,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month, though further growth hinges on turbojet engines largely supplied by China. Russian forces have also amassed roughly 10,000 piston-engine strike drones and launch both types together in successive waves to exhaust Ukrainian air defenses.
Ukraine has been developing interceptor drones in response, with a domestically produced P1-SUN JetKiller downing a Geran-5 on September 30.

F-22s, F-15s Rotate in at Kadena to Bolster Pacific Airpower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:37:22 UTC
06:37:22 KST

Squadrons of F-22 Raptors and F-15C Eagles have arrived at Kadena Air Base, Japan, for temporary deployments as the critical Pacific base awaits its permanent F-15EX fighters.
Stars & Stripes reported Oct. 27 that a squadron of F-22s from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, finished arriving Sept. 30. Another squadron of F-15s, from Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base New Orleans, La., also recently arrived, Stripes reported, citing a statement from the 18th Wing at Kadena.
In a statement provided Oct. 29 after initial publication, the 18th Wing confirmed the arrival of the F-15Cs and F-22s.
Lt. Col. Alli Stormer, head of public affairs for the 18th Wing, said in the Oct. 29 email the F-15s from the 122nd Expeditionary Fighter Squadron arrived “earlier this week.” They joined the F-22s from the 525th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron at Kadena.
Independent aircraft trackers and photographs published by the military also show those planes arriving at or operating from Kadena recently.
Kadena, located on Okinawa, is the U.S.’s closest air base to Taiwan and strategically vital.
The 18th Wing at Kadena flew squadrons of permanently assigned F-15C/D fighters for years. But those legacy fighters were rapidly aging, and in November 2022, the Air Force started withdrawing them. Those fighters will be replaced with 36 permanently assigned F-15EX Eagle II jets, beginning in fiscal 2027.
Until then, the service is rotating various fighters, including F-35s, F-22s, F-16s, and F-15 variants through Kadena on a temporary basis, to maintain the base’s ability to project airpower if necessary.
The first F-15EXs had been scheduled to arrive by now, but labor disputes and other challenges slowed Boeing’s deliveries and delayed plans. The first F-15EX earmarked for Kadena left Boeing’s St. Louis factory Aug. 28, and flew to Portland, Ore., for final systems integration, software updates, and other technical preparations. After that work is done, the jet will fly to Okinawa.
Photos posted by the 18th Wing on Oct. 27 show the Alaska F-22s at Tsuiki Air Base, Japan, taking part in Exercise Keen Sword 27, which aims to improve how U.S. and Japanese forces work together.
Aircraft trackers have also observed F-15 movements to Kadena in recent weeks.
Aviation enthusiast Aux OSINT on Oct. 24 and 25 posted flight tracker images on social media of KC-46 Pegasus tankers flying Coronet missions with F-15Cs from the 122nd, inbound to Kadena.
A Japan-based aviation photographer who posts online under the handle Okadna35 posted images Oct. 24 of F-15s arriving at Kadena, bearing markings of the New Orleans base’s 159th Fighter Wing, nicknamed the Bayou Militia.
The 18th Wing said previous F-22 expeditionary squadrons that were deployed at Kadena left earlier in October. The 90th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron from Elmendorf finished departing Oct. 5, but left some of its F-22 jets behind for the 525th to fly. The 27th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron, from Joint Base Langley-Eustis, also left Kadena by Oct. 27.

Turkish engineer creates live 3D pixel map of adopted hometown Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:36:45 UTC
06:36:45 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.
The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.
The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.
While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.
Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.
The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.
The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.
Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.
Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.
An observation deck at the top of the EU's tallest building, Varso Tower in Warsaw, has opened to the public.
Located 230m up on the tower's 53rd floor, the attraction offers a 360° panorama of Poland's capital.https://t.co/VeEapOmh4s
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2025
The result is an incredible level of explorable detail, from major landmarks, such as the communist-era Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower, the EU’s tallest building, down to the seating steps and bars along the Vistula River boulevards.
The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves.
A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium.
I turned Warsaw into a flight sim 🛩️
Take off from Chopin, fly through the ring over the Palace of Culture, then land a UFO inside Stadion Narodowy as the roof opens 🛸
Desktop only for now. Can you land it? 👇 pic.twitter.com/DT2fdk1Vem
— Bedirhan (@bedcodes) October 27, 2026
Speaking to Notes from Poland, Yildirim says that he moved to Poland in 2022 to pursue a job in IT before starting his own business. Initially living in Kraków, the country’s second-largest city, he then moved to Warsaw in 2025.
Asked what his own personal favourite places in the city are, Yildirim points to Warsaw’s parks, such as Skaryszewski, Pole Mokotowskie and Łazienki. His favourite neighbourhood is Saska Kępa on the right bank of the Vistula.
The software engineer adds that his project is an example of how AI can be an “amazing tool to do 90% of the job very quickly”. The remaining 10% of human input “is what keeps it from being ‘AI slop'”.
Yildirim says that, without the use of AI, the map of Warsaw he created would have needed an entire team to build over a period of months.

Russia and Tanzania to launch joint space program (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:30:37 UTC
06:30:37 KST

Russia and Tanzania to launch joint space program (VIDEO)
Russia and Tanzania have agreed to launch a joint space program, the Russian space agency Roscosmos has said. Moscow will assist Dodoma in establishing its own national space agency and developing the infrastructure needed for a domestic space industry.
On Wednesday, Roscosmos and Tanzania’s Ministry of Information, Communication and Information Technology signed a framework memorandum on strategic partnership and cooperation on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit. The event has brought delegations from 48 African countries to Moscow this week.
“Tanzania is planning to establish its own space agency, and we are ready to provide our colleagues with expert and methodological support,” Roscosmos Director General Dmitry Bakanov told journalists. The Russian space agency has already stepped up cooperation with Tanzanian specialists in the field, with support from the Russian presidential administration, he added.
According to Bakanov, Dodoma is particularly interested in developing its own spacecraft and launching them into orbit aboard Russian rockets. Roscosmos has confirmed that Russia will launch Tanzania’s first Earth remote-sensing satellite in March 2027.
During the summit, Russian specialists demonstrated to the Tanzanian delegation the country’s capabilities in training cosmonauts and space industry specialists, as well as conducting scientific experiments in space.
The two sides also discussed sharing Earth remote-sensing data and establishing ground stations in Tanzania to receive such data. According to Bakanov, the African nation also plans to increase the number of students studying space-related disciplines at Russian universities.
Under the agreement, Russia will assist Tanzania in developing infrastructure for its space industry, while the two countries will exchange expertise and best practices in training space specialists. They have also agreed to establish joint working groups and develop road maps covering all areas of cooperation.
Moscow has been actively supporting African nations’ space ambitions. Last year, the South African National Space Agency (SANSA) hailed Russia as a key partner in advancing its national space program. Pretoria “has received most of its support from the Russian Federation,” SANSA board chairman Patrick Ndlovu told Sputnik Africa at the time. Earlier that year, SANSA CEO Humbulani Mudau announced South Africa’s support for Russia’s proposal to establish a BRICS Space Council to strengthen space cooperation among member states.
In 2024, Zimbabwe announced plans to build its first spaceport with Russian assistance. The country also said it was in talks with Roscosmos about gaining access to Russia’s cosmonaut training system, among other areas of cooperation.

Eleni Stefania Kalapoda is an ARB-registered architect and urban designer and founder of Embedded Climates. 
On a hillside in Anji, in Zhejiang province, a cluster of umbrella-like canopies steps gently down the slope, following the rows of tea bushes. There is no grand entrance, no plinth, no monumental block of stone. On October 22, at Dutch Design Week in Eindhoven, this project, Anji Hood by RoarcRenew Architects, was named Cultural Space of the Year at the Frame Awards 2026, chosen from more than 1,000 submissions by 100 jurors across 10 panels.
I served on the Frame Awards 2026 grand jury for the “institutions” categories. Three of the five projects shortlisted for the “cultural space” award were in mainland China: My Museum Beijing, Anji Hood and the Huishan Ancestral Hall Museum in Wuxi. China had 7,046 registered museums at the end of 2024, welcoming 1.49 billion visits that year.
Once a nation has built cultural venues on that scale, the question shifts from how many to what kind. The answers now emerging are quieter, lighter and more deeply rooted than the icons of recent decades.

UN votes overwhelmingly against U.S. embargo on Cuba

05:26:46 CST
06:26:46 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The UN General Assembly on Wednesday adopted a resolution calling for an end to the decades-old U.S. embargo on Cuba.
The resolution was adopted with 130 votes in favor, 17 against and 25 abstentions.
It expresses concern about the continued promulgation and application of laws and regulations, including the Helms-Burton Act enacted by the United States in 1996, whose extraterritorial effects undermine the sovereignty of other states, the legitimate interests of individuals and entities under their jurisdiction, and the freedom of trade and navigation.
The resolution calls on all states to refrain from promulgating and applying such laws and measures, and urges states that have applied and continue to apply such laws and measures to take necessary steps to repeal or invalidate them as soon as possible.
The resolution also requests the UN secretary-general to prepare a report on the implementation of this resolution and to submit it to the General Assembly at its next annual session.
Wednesday's resolution marked the 34th consecutive adoption of a resolution on the necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States on Cuba. ■

ROME, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's cabinet on Wednesday approved a draft budget worth about 26 billion euros (29 billion U.S. dollars) for 2027, featuring tax cuts and social support measures.
The package expands the 33-percent income tax bracket to cover annual earnings of up to 55,000 euros, up from the current threshold of 50,000 euros. It also raises the income ceiling for self-employed workers to qualify for a flat-tax regime from 85,000 to 100,000 euros.
Other measures include a 5-percent flat tax rate for new hires under the age of 35 and an annual state contribution of 100 euros for each newborn until the child turns 18.
Meloni said a new levy on the profits of major banks, other lenders and insurance companies was expected to generate about 5 billion euros in revenue.
The budget is the government's final spending plan before general elections scheduled for 2027. The administration faces mounting pressure to tackle the rising cost of living, as trade unions, social organizations and student groups have staged protests in recent weeks.
Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti cited rising raw material costs and borrowing rates as key challenges. However, he said an agreement with European Union authorities allowing a temporary increase in next year's fiscal deficit would provide the government with additional room for spending.
The draft budget will now be submitted to parliament for approval by both chambers before being sent to EU authorities by the end of the year for assessment under the bloc's fiscal rules. Enditem (1 euro = 1.11 U.S. dollar)

LONDON, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- European natural gas prices surged above 100 euros (about 111.50 U.S. dollars) per megawatt-hour on Wednesday for the first time since December 2022, amid concerns over disruptions to liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies from the Middle East and tightening inventories ahead of winter.
Dutch Title Transfer Facility (TTF) natural gas futures for November delivery, the European benchmark, climbed to an intraday high of 100.75 euros per megawatt-hour. Prices have risen by about 40 percent so far this month.

Market analysts attributed the price surge to continued disruptions to LNG shipments from the Gulf region and growing concerns that the conflict between the United States and Iran could escalate following the U.S. midterm elections, further tightening global supplies.
According to Trading Economics, forecasts of colder-than-usual weather in parts of Europe and Asia could boost heating demand and intensify competition for LNG cargoes between the two regions, putting further upward pressure on natural gas prices. ■

Explainer: Two deadly crashes in nine months: What's happening to Spain's high-speed rail?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:26:35 CST
06:26:35 KST

MADRID, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Just nine months after a deadly railway accident near Adamuz in southern Spain, another high-speed train collision occurred on Wednesday on the same Madrid-Seville railway line, raising renewed concerns about the safety of Spain's high-speed rail network.
The collision between two high-speed trains near Urda station in Toledo province, central Spain, has killed at least 68 people and injured 180 more.
WHAT HAPPENED AND WHY?
At around 8:54 a.m. local time (0754 GMT) on Wednesday, a Renfe-operated AVE train carrying 378 passengers struck the rear of a stationary Iryo train with 147 passengers aboard near Urda station. Both trains were heading from Madrid to Seville, according to Spain's Ministry of Transport and railway operator Renfe.
At least 68 were killed, according to the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha. More than 180 people were reported injured, with some in critical condition.
Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente said at a press conference on Wednesday afternoon that the LZB train safety system had failed at around 8:30 a.m. due to a communication problem involving three computers, affecting a 63-km section of the railway and automatically bringing several trains to a halt.
According to Puente, Adif's control center subsequently authorized the AVE train to resume normal operations at around 8:36 a.m., despite a red signal and the presence of the stationary Iryo train ahead. The AVE traveled approximately 25 km before crashing into the Iryo at around 8:53 a.m..
Under Spanish railway safety regulations, trains must remain stopped when the LZB system fails and the track ahead is occupied. Any authorized movement must follow restricted operating procedures requiring drivers to maintain a speed that allows them to stop upon detecting an obstacle ahead.
Puente described the control center's decision as "inexplicable," while railway engineering expert Ramiro Aurin told Spanish news agency EFE that human error was the most likely explanation for the collision. However, the exact circumstances and responsibilities remain under investigation.
GOVERNMENT RESPONSE AND PUBLIC SCRUTINY
The tragedy prompted the Spanish government and several major political parties to suspend their scheduled activities on Wednesday.
During a visit to the accident site in Urda, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez stressed that rescuing victims and supporting their families remained the government's top priority. He pledged a thorough investigation into the collision, saying that any negligence or failures in railway safety systems would be addressed. "We will get to the bottom of this," Sanchez said.
The government also declared three days of national mourning from Oct. 29 to Oct. 31, while the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha activated an emergency response plan and mobilized additional rescue and medical resources. Several hospitals suspended scheduled activities to accommodate the injured, while psychological support teams were deployed to assist victims and their families.
The accident also triggered calls for accountability. Opposition People's Party (PP) leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo said Spain had the right to know what was happening with its railway infrastructure. He called for immediate government and judicial investigations, as well as a comprehensive and independent review of the country's entire railway network.
In Madrid, hundreds of demonstrators gathered outside the Ministry of Transport on Wednesday evening, demanding the resignation of the Transport Minister Puente.
Railway unions also called for stronger safety safeguards. The Independent Trade Union and Civil Servants' Central (CSIF) demanded an urgent explanation of the accident, accountability for those responsible, and greater investment in railway infrastructure and maintenance.
The Spanish train drivers' union Semaf said it would proceed with a strike scheduled for Thursday, calling for stronger railway safety guarantees and structural reforms. The union also said it was considering further action following the latest tragedy.
GROWING CONCERNS OVER RAIL SAFETY
The collision marks Spain's second major fatal high-speed rail accident this year, with a crash near Adamuz, in the southern province of Cordoba, claiming 46 lives on Jan. 18.
While investigations into both accidents remain ongoing, experts have pointed to different possible causes. Jordi Vinolas Prat, a mechanical engineering professor at Francisco de Vitoria University, told Europa Press that the Adamuz disaster appeared to be linked to railway infrastructure problems, while the latest collision raised questions about signaling systems.
Jose Trigueros, president of the Association of Civil Engineers, told Spanish national broadcaster RTVE that the latest collision was particularly concerning because high-speed rail safety systems were designed to prevent two trains from occupying the same section of track. He questioned the reliability of automated safety protections and the extent to which railway operations depended on human intervention.
Concerns over railway safety had already been raised following the Adamuz disaster. Rafael Escudero, secretary-general of the Sindicato Ferroviario railway union, told Spanish radio station Onda Cero that the union had called for an audit of renovation works on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line after the January accident. He urged a review of how the more than 700 million euros (770 million U.S. dollars) allocated to upgrading the line had been spent, while stressing that the cause of Wednesday's collision remained under investigation.
The latest tragedy has also unsettled some railway passengers. Daniel, a frequent traveler between Malaga and Madrid, told Spanish radio station Cadena SER that the accident had left him feeling angry and insecure, saying recent railway incidents had undermined his confidence in train travel.
Civil engineer Martin Perea, a transport specialist and master's program director at Universidad Europea, also warned of serious damage to the reputation of Spain's railway system, calling for a thorough investigation, support for victims and their families, and a broader reassessment of the country's high-speed rail operations. ■

TASHKENT, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The World Bank Board of Executive Directors has approved a 100-million-U.S.-dollar loan to help Uzbekistan modernize its electricity distribution system, according to a bank statement.
The program will upgrade and digitalize 60 key substations nationwide to reduce energy losses, improve power supply reliability, and ease limits on integrating renewable energy into the grid.

The project, implemented by the Joint-Stock Company National Electric Grid of Uzbekistan, supports the country's target to increase installed renewable energy capacity to 25 GW by 2030. ■

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- UN humanitarians on Wednesday voiced deep concern about the intercommunal violence in the Ethiopian town of Moyale on the border with Kenya that has displaced thousands of people.
Casualties have been reported, along with disruptions to transport, markets and cross-border trade, limiting access to essential goods and services, said the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
On the Ethiopian side, the violence that erupted on Oct. 18 has reportedly displaced thousands of people in Oromia and Somali regions. This is in addition to the thousands of people who have reportedly crossed into Kenya, it said.
Local authorities in Kenya estimate that up to 50,000 people have crossed into the country since Thursday, amid reports of further crossings, it said.
Many of those fleeing are women and children. While some are staying with relatives and host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations, such as schools and churches. Food remains the most urgent need, alongside safe drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and health care, said the office.
"Continued insecurity has forced several partners to suspend activities," OCHA said. "The UN and its partners are preparing a joint assessment mission to areas affected by the violence as soon as security conditions permit."
It is critical to ensure the safety of the population, as well as safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access to all people in need, said the office.
The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has deployed an emergency team to Moyale and is working closely with the Kenyan government, UN agencies, the Kenya Red Cross Society and other humanitarian partners to support the national and local response, said OCHA.
The Kenya Red Cross Society is operating six health service points, screening for malnutrition and distributing relief items. Local communities have shared food and water, though their stocks are limited, said OCHA.
The UN and its humanitarian partners are working to scale up the response. UN agencies have deployed staff and are mobilizing additional supplies, including to prepare for potential further displacement. UNHCR is mobilizing emergency relief supplies, including essential household items and temporary shelter materials, to support nearly 12,000 people, with efforts under way to scale up assistance as needs grow, said OCHA. ■

Carvalho framed the announcement in the context of Portugal's ongoing energy crisis, saying that "freeing Portugal from dependence on fossil fuels is not a chimera: it is an essential condition for a better future and less dependence on third parties." ■

News Analysis: Britain's budget targets breathing space for households, businesses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:25:54 CST
06:25:54 KST

LONDON, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- British Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey on Wednesday unveiled the Budget 2026, aiming to give families and firms breathing space from rising costs through supporting measures in the fields including energy, income, housing, spending and business tax.
The government will provide 100 pounds (about 133 U.S. dollars) household energy payment for up to 20 million qualified households in England, with funding for similar support provided to the rest of the UK. Meanwhile, it will extend the value-added-tax cut on electricity bills to July 1, 2027, according to the budget.
The budget supports drivers by extending the cut to fuel duty for a further six months, while cutting prices at local, lower-powered public chargers to reduce costs for electric vehicle drivers who rely on them.
Earlier Wednesday, the Chancellor also abolished standing charges on household gas bills, a fixed daily fee added on top of a household gas bill regardless of how much gas has been used.
In response to the rising inflation, the government will remove tariffs from more than 100 products to lower import costs for everyday family spending such as baked beans and chocolate, and cut tariffs on kerosene and fertilizer to support households and farmers facing higher costs.
At the same time, the budget plans to increase the National Living Wage by 3.9 percent per hour on April 1, 2027.
Moreover, the budget provides a further 1.5 billion pounds (about 2 billion dollars) in funding for social and affordable housing, taking total capital investment over the next 10 years above 40 billion pounds (about 53 billion dollars).
On the front of business support, the budget backs England's high streets with a package that means all retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England will see their business rates either frozen in real terms, reduced or cut to zero.
On top of the extra 20 percent business rates cut for pubs and all but the largest live music venues, announced in July, this package will take around 70,000 more retail, hospitality and leisure businesses out of business rates by increasing the Small Business Rates Relief threshold.
To deal with the energy price hikes faced by enterprises, measures will be taken to support over 10,000 eligible businesses in electricity intensive Industrial Strategy sectors and the foundational sectors in their supply chains to cut electricity bills by up to 25 percent and bring electricity costs closer to other economies in Europe from April 2027.
However, due to the limited momentum of change brought by the budget, analysts believe there should be more ambitious plans from the government to increase living standard and boost business investment in the country.
"For this budget, the outcome for UK residents is really one in which Healey tinkers around the edges," John Bryson, a professor at the University of Birmingham, told Xinhua.
Since forecasts anticipate energy bills will rise again by as much as 27 percent in January, the government also needs to be thinking more long-term about how to protect households from rising energy bills not just in the short term but over a sustained period, said Caitlin Robinson, a professor at the University of Bristol.
This will require more ambitious investment in energy efficiency, low carbon heating and renewable electricity, Robinson added.
"This was a 'steady as you go' budget, sending the right signals to business, but lacking big calls that would really shift the economic dial," Shevaun Haviland, director general of the British Chambers of Commerce, said.
"Our key tests for the Chancellor were whether his plans would boost growth and ease costs for business. Many firms will have been hoping for a greater impact," she noted.
Tina McKenzie, national chair of the Federation of Small Businesses, hoped the increase in Small Business Rates Relief should have covered more businesses, such as manufacturers, small exporters, nurseries and office-based businesses which are not just on the high streets.
Eamonn O'Brien, chair of the Local Government Association, argued that no overall funding increase for local government means councils will continue to struggle to meet demand and provide services to their communities. ■

According to the artist, the incident occurred back in 2007, when she was just beginning to gain popularity. After the prank, the insects continued to make their presence known for several months.

21:01:16 UTC
06:01:16 KST

DETROIT — Ford Motor expects earnings next year will be roughly in line with the automaker's anticipated results this year, the company said Wednesday as it reported mixed results for the third quarter.
The Detroit automaker beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations but slightly missed revenue estimates. The company has been working to stabilize production of its F-Series pickup trucks after dealing with supplier issues for much of the past year.
"This quarter's results reflect deliberate actions to improve profitability and deliver consistent financial returns," Ford CFO Sherry House told reporters during a call Wednesday.
Ford reported third-quarter adjusted free cash flow of $4.7 billion, roughly $2 billion higher than what analysts were anticipating, according to StreetAccount.
Here's how Ford performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 49 cents adjusted vs. 40 cents expected
- Automotive revenue: $46.08 billion vs. $46.24 billion expected
The Detroit automaker also narrowed its 2026 guidance to adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $10.5 billion and $11 billion, compared with a previous outlook of $10 billion to $11 billion. Ford maintained its adjusted free cash flow guidance for this year of between $6 billion and $7 billion.
House said the company expects 2027 earnings to be roughly in line with this year's results, citing several offsetting factors in production issues this year as well as rising commodity costs.
House noted a $1.3 billion tariff refund during the first quarter of this year was largely offset by additional costs from alternative aluminum sourcing that the company does not expect to have next year, leveling out the year-over-year comparison.
She also said production of its F-Series Super Duty trucks in Canada in 2027 will make up for lost production it's expecting at its F-150 factories to retool for new models.
"Next year will be the third year on our journey of increasing and improving our warranty and material cost savings, and that's getting extended to structural costs throughout the company as well in terms of savings," House said.
Ford CEO Jim Farley called 2027 a "foundational year" for the company on its way to a previously announced target of an 8% adjusted EBIT margin by 2029. The company reported a 5.4% margin during the third quarter.
Ahead of the results, Wall Street analysts were mixed about whether Ford would be able to maintain profits in 2027.
The company has multiple efforts that will add to costs next year: It's rolling out several new or redesigned models, including its next-generation EV and Canada-produced pickups, and is enhancing its energy business that it announced earlier this year.
The missed revenue for the third quarter was a result of each of the automaker's main business units – which are broken into Blue traditional operations, Pro fleet and Model e electric vehicle segments – underperforming compared with Wall Street's expectations, according to StreetAccount.
As part of its modified guidance, Ford said it now expects pre-tax earnings of its Ford Blue unit to be $5.5 billion, which is at the high end of a previous guidance.
It's also anticipating EBIT of about $7 billion for the year for Ford Pro and Ford Model e losses of about $4 billion. Its Ford Credit unit is expected to record about $2.8 billion in EBIT for 2026.
Ford's overall revenue, which includes its credit segment, was off roughly 2% compared with the third quarter of last year, to $49.5 billion.
Its net income also was off $400 million from a year earlier to $2 billion, while adjusted earnings before interest and taxes were up slightly year-over-year to $2.7 billion.
Ford's 2025 third-quarter results included $47.19 billion in automotive revenue, net income of $2.4 billion and earnings per share of 45 cents adjusted.

Societal Complexity and the Problem of Comprehension
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:53 UTC
06:00:53 KST

Introduction. Nostalgia and the Power of Artifacts
Culture and society are on a seemingly endless trip to incomprehensibility. When I was a kid, maybe four or five, my parents would bring me to my grandparents’ house in Hillsdale, New York. My grandfather served for nearly three decades as a New York City policeman. He would tell me stories of patrolling the projects and how he would save his spare change. Eventually they escaped the city. As we pulled up to the old white house, offset from the road by a quarter-mile rocky driveway, I was reminded that this was their means of escape — to get away from the buzz of city life and decompress. Yet when we walked inside, we were hit with a cacophony of trinkets and antiques. A model plane from the 1930s hung from the cathedral ceiling, something my grandpa found at a tag sale. In the kitchen, there rose a high hutch which contained hundreds of antique vases, cups, plates, and figurines. But the one artifact — a key word for this essay — that remains in my mind is the reprint of the post-impressionist artist Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec’s work Aristide Bruant dans son cabaret from 1893. The subject, Aristide Bruant, was a famous cabaret singer and nightclub owner in Montmartre, Paris. The image was an advertisement — Lautrec was friends with Bruant. There was something both horrifying and enticing about Bruant looking over his shoulder — I would stand and stare at the image. It seemed so out of place, because in many senses it was. What was it doing on the wall of a New York City Italian’s house in Hillsdale? But their house, far from an ode to the past, penetrated my 1990s childhood with a sense that culture and artifacts not only contribute to our complexity, but in some sense are the means to find simplicity among the chaos.
I. The Inevitability of Societal Complexity
Now, many years removed from staring at Bruant, with his devilish smile and side-eye gaze, I think back on that time and wonder why the past seems so simple. My time at my grandparents’ was a simple time, full of I Love Lucy episodes as my grandfather slept on the couch, and I rested on the antique fainting chair he’d thrifted from some rich person’s tag sale. In many ways, generation after generation has posed the lament “Life used to be simpler.” On its face this is just nostalgia, with each generation thinking that life was better when they were younger. The way the sands of time move, we often look back and forget the issues of the day, instead clinging to the pleasant, simple memories, images, and smells. To some older generations, the 1950s (though in my thirties I inherited my grandfather’s love for doo-wop), with its simple life and Happy Days aura, seems to draw people back out of the complexity of everyday life. But closer to home for me, my generation does this very same thing with the 1990s, pre-smartphone, when they can think back to when life seemed…simpler. Commercials were for toys and action figures with the overemphasized male voice; video games were rudimentary, like Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 2, which I played on my Game Boy Color; and the internet was hardly the quick access point to infinity that it is today—and it was incredibly loud and obnoxious to use.
The past seems simple because society in the present seems complex.
And yet, to correct myself here, to call society “more complex” than prior generations is not quite right without defining exactly what we mean by complex. To grasp what we are getting at when we call something complex, we need to first find out, precisely, what it is that has changed. It is not simply that there are more people, or more objects, or more institutions, though there certainly are all of those things. Instead, by complexity we mean that the relationships between individuals have multiplied, and information has accumulated more than anyone can possibly take in. In the digital age there are more interdependencies, more feedback loops, more distance between any single actor’s understanding and the system’s actual operation. This distance between each other and our comprehension of the world is what we call “complex.” A village of a hundred people in sub-Saharan Africa and a global supply chain both contain “parts” that contribute to the function of the whole. What separates them is that no one inside the supply chain can hold its totality in mind the way a villager could hold the village. In other words, you cannot comprehend complex society. Complexity, in this sense, is not the pure quantity of things but the ratio between things — the ratio between the scale of a system and the scale of any single mind’s grasp of it. If thought of this way, it becomes clear why each generation longs for a prior one. That ratio continues to expand.
This distinction matters because it reframes the question from “how did society get bigger” to “how did society’s operations outrun the comprehension of the people living inside them.” For a helpful point of reference we should include Ashby’s Law. Developed in the 1950s by W. Ross Ashby, the Law of Requisite Variety holds that for a system or person to adequately control another system, the controller must have at least as much variety, or range of possible responses, as the system it is trying to control. I like to think of it as an air traffic controller. Certainly you watch one plane, but that one plane has to be understood in relation to other planes, else the whole system will collapse. Bringing this back to modern society, this is perhaps one reason government and political figures struggle to “get things done.” Certainly there is political jockeying and campaigning, but also, society is so vastly complex that one would need to understand it all to effectively address it.
II. The Mechanism of Compounding
So we’ve established that the ability to comprehend society has grown more difficult. But now we shift to another aspect of societal complexity. The compounding effect of society and culture is certainly not a new phenomenon. Joseph Tainter, in The Collapse of Complex Societies, argues that societies add complexity as a solution to problems, and as the problems grow more frequent, the complexity eventually becomes unsustainable, leading to collapse. This arguably describes the Soviet Union in the late 20th century. Hard pressed to oversee all aspects of economic and civic life, the totalitarian government was incapable of dealing with the complexity. As the need for a specific resource grows owing to more complex systems and tools, a society interlocks its markets with others overseas to acquire it; that interlocking requires new administrative roles, new specialized functions, new layers of coordination. Each of these layers costs manpower, energy, and capital, and the costs compound even as the returns on each additional layer diminish.
The same compounding shows up at the level of culture. A single people, in a single place, differentiates into subcultures, which differentiate further, until what was once “a people” is, from the inside, thousands of micro-cultures. Now, I’m not saying this is decay. That we can form subcultures within cultures is a mark of our distinctiveness as humanity — unlike all other creatures, we can create social connection that transcends purely pragmatic means. But it is also, unavoidably, the engine of the very fragmentation that makes the whole harder to see. It is this, I believe, that the older generation who longs for “better times” is really seeking — a time before the thousand micro-cultures.
Society also accumulates the artifacts of its own compounding, the leftover pieces of previous generations, which persist long after the intentions that produced them have expired. This is why I opened with the story of my grandparents’ house — their house was a storage place for artifacts from the past, like the poster of Bruant. Or think of the Roman roads: built to move Caesar’s legions into Gaul and Britain, they became the roadways for Hitler’s Panzer divisions, and later still the infrastructure of inter-EU trade. Nothing about the road’s design determined which of these purposes it would serve; the artifact outlived its author’s intent and was picked up by whatever intent came next. My grandparents fashioned their house with artifacts that were at one point in time used by prior generations.
III. The Fall of Comprehension
So far we’ve established that societies grow more complex, but we haven’t tackled the comprehension gap. Why is society harder to comprehend than before? German sociologist Niklas Luhmann has helpfully captured the reason in his world complexity thesis. Luhmann describes how, as time goes on, complexity, information, and potential compound, and this growth builds with it a support system of subsystems developed to treat each system — the siloing of knowledge and expertise. Luhmann adopted the concept of autopoiesis, a term coined by the biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, to describe how each of these siloed systems only communicates with and reproduces itself. Luhmann’s theory of complexity works like a coral reef. At the start it is just the ocean floor, but over time sediment builds and builds until there are layers and layers of compact coral. Soon, one can hardly tell where it began but can see the thriving life all around, each siloed in its own ecosystem, shared by location alone. Thus social systems, so argues Luhmann, are not people, but communication.
Of course, in the twentieth century, the sedimentary layers of society were fairly easy to grasp. A Judeo-Christian worldview and Western civics offered a shared way to understand society and each person’s place within it. But with the rise of the digital age, this has become unintelligible. Deep in the inner crevices of the internet are subcultures, subpockets of algorithmic culture that do not materialize in the real, present world like older forms of culture, but instead materialize in the mind of the individual. The loss of shared information is replaced with millions upon millions of uniquely tailored opinions. This digital media serves as a feedback loop, a simulacrum of sorts, which slowly builds up and creates a reality in and of itself — one that no longer needs to make sense of other people, but merely of myself. Society, no longer a cohesive whole, is a complex, self-optimized system incapable of diagnosing and understanding the parts for the whole.
IV. The Symptoms of Complexity
There are several important indicators of complexity that are worth exploring.
As society grows more complex, and our ability to understand it becomes more difficult, we will try to simplify it on our own terms. In other words the appeal of conspiracy theories stops looking like a failure of reasoning and starts looking like a rational response to an epistemic environment that has outrun anyone’s capacity to verify it directly. This has been a bit eye-opening for me. As society grows incomprehensible, our drive to comprehend it remains, so we seek to explain it in the most simplistic terms possible. A conspiracy theory is, in an ironic sense, I know, more legible to us than the truth. It offers a small number of actors and a clear causal chain, in place of a system with millions of interacting causes that no one, including experts, can fully trace. People are not choosing simplicity over truth out of stupidity (though it certainly can be stupid); they are choosing a story that fits inside a human mind over one that does not. Of course this does not justify a conspiracy, but merely explains its appeal in the modern world.
Hand in hand with conspiracies is the loss of institutional capital. The same collapse that has us seeking out farfetched explanations for modern phenomenon shows up inside the institutions meant to foster and produce knowledge. Academic fields fracture into sub-fields whose findings speak only to each other, no longer to the discipline as a whole, let alone to the public. It is not incidental that the reading most sociology courses still treat as canonical dates largely from the twentieth century, particularly after World War II — a period, arguably, in which society had grown complex but could still be described. Since then, the object of study may have simply outpaced the available frameworks for describing it. It is not necessarily true that we lack originality today; it is instead true that the complexity of society makes originality much harder than it has ever been. To truly be original, a person needs to somehow either shed the collective accumulation of society and knowledge, or instead channel it into a new direction. Both of these are nearly impossible to do.
Along with these points, societal complexity has fractured any shared narrative underpinnings, which has damaged our ability to value one another. This plays out often when someone is being attacked, or in dire circumstances, and instead of people rushing to their aid, they are incapable of seeing the need. This push for efficiency becomes a system of distraction and perpetual indentured servitude. The Influencer Economy, far from just another means to make money, is added complexity vying for attention and time. It’s as if we are screaming out for comprehension and clarity amidst the confusion and misunderstanding of the modern digital ecosystem. As we each live within our sub-ecosystem of culture, we are out of touch with those around us who may be in a different ecosystem. This lack of shared connection is damaging our ability to connect and find bonds.
And perhaps tying all of these points together, societal complexity traps us in a cycle of feedback loop formation. Humanity, for as much as it creates culture, likes to be around things that are familiar. We listen to certain songs, certain genres. We even listen to certain podcasts because “those people think like us.” These feedback loops actually stunt our growth. In the digital age, one can go a whole lifetime listening to voices that affirm one’s own decisions, thinking, and abilities. AI is a good example of this. AI, apart from being an algorithm, is a means of pleasing the self. It rarely pushes back, and almost always affirms us. With so much complexity, there is little need to experience things that challenge and make us uncomfortable.
AI not only feeds the feedback loop, but also serves to accelerate societal complexity beyond anything we’ve seen before. In a split second we can now synthesize billions of gigabytes of data and pull together various threads. The issue, of course, is that humanity will rely on this to export its thinking, which will only serve to further complexify society. For as understanding shrinks, the ability to process likewise fades away. AI, while being sold as a means to make work more efficient, will inevitably make it more complex. The comprehension gap is not just on the input side of the equation but on the output side as well — we are not just losing the ability to comprehend complex society, but as we export our thinking to machines, we are losing any capable function to interpret society. Our thinking no longer stems organically and with rich originality, but from a series of prompts. AI is thriving because it thrives within complexity. And the more it consumes us, the more it will flatten our comprehension.
V. The Rebirth of Simplicity
We started this essay talking about nostalgia, through the lens of my grandparents’ collection of artifacts. The means to “simplify complex society” is not a simple “return.” Society is far too complicated to simply unbuild it. The layers upon layers of social materials are not easily dissected. However, there are ways to help mitigate the complexity.
One way we can undo this is to resist the urge to fall for the minimalism of the day and instead seek to integrate artifacts from past generations within our homes and lives. Certainly you can purchase art from prior generations, but this also takes the form of listening to music from the past. I often find myself putting on Dvořák’s Slavonic Dances and connecting through the artifact of sound with a time that is not my own. This is healthy and reminds me that the present is not all there is, but we carry with us the artifacts of the past, without which we would not be who we are today.
But this also shows why reading old books matters. As C. S. Lewis argued in his essay “On the Reading of Old Books,” the ordinary reader needs old books even more than the expert does, and “if he must read only the new or only the old, I would advise him to read the old.” We don’t often think of books as artifacts, but they truly are. When you crack open a book, you basically sit yourself down across from a figure from the past and begin a discourse. This discourse has a way of piercing the complexity – cutting through the silt of culture and showing you perhaps ways of living you might otherwise never have known. Nostalgia, while often misunderstood as pure daydreaming, is a good means of reckoning with the disconnect between present and past.
Having introduced AI to this discussion, and certainly aware of its effects in making culture and society more complex, I would like to posit not a doomer narrative, but that AI can create a sort of cultural flattening. As we export thinking, writing, and the creation of artifacts, we not only lose the ability ourselves but we no longer leave artifacts for future generations. Artificially generated art will find it far harder to pierce through the silt — I highly doubt my grandparents would hang up an AI image in their antique art collection — because the artwork reminds us of the artist. Without Lautrec, I would not have the image of Bruant burned into my young mind. Certainly AI can be useful; I’m not arguing that point. But it has a way of not only introducing more information than we can comprehend, but it flattens our cultural output. The better question with AI is, is this the artifact we want to leave in the sediment for future generations? I certainly hope not.
As time moves on, society will continue to grow complex, and we certainly won’t be able to fully grasp every angle of the social sphere. But we can push back. We can resist, and seek to simplify where we can. Society is complex, yes, and we struggle to comprehend it, yes, but this means that cultural artifacts matter more now than they ever have before. So if you take anything from this essay, take this: break the complexity with artifacts from the past.
E. J. LaRow is a writer and editor whose work sits at the intersection of theology, philosophy, cultural criticism, and the moral history of the modern West. A member of the Ciceronian Society, a contributing writer for Mere Orthodoxy, and a fellow at Law & Liberty, he has published in both, as well as in First Things, Modern Age, Ad Fontes, The American Mind, and on his Substack.

British stratospheric spy flight planned for next year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:21 GMT
06:00:21 KST

Project AETHER is planning a multi-payload, long endurance flight in the 2027-28 financial year to demonstrate a broader range of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance collection from stratospheric altitudes, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress has been made in delivering the project, following up an answer given in October last year.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Project AETHER capability development is progressing under the sponsorship of the Cyber and Specialist Operations Command. Planning is currently ongoing for the delivery of a multi-payload, long endurance flight in financial year 2027-28. This will seek to build upon the previous trial events by demonstrating a broader range of Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance collection techniques from stratospheric altitudes.”
AETHER covers uncrewed aircraft operating in the stratosphere, above conventional air traffic and below orbit, where solar powered platforms can stay aloft for weeks or months and provide persistent coverage of an area at a fraction of the cost of a satellite. Earlier trials have flown from the Hebrides range, and the Ministry of Defence has worked with several manufacturers of high altitude platforms.
Cyber and Specialist Operations Command was created under the restructuring that followed the Strategic Defence Review, bringing together cyber, electromagnetic activities, intelligence and specialist capabilities under a single command.
