Powderfinger announce more shows, discuss split and joyful reunion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Powderfinger's joyful reunion was inspired by their kids and Cold Chisel
When Powderfinger broke up in 2010, their farewell tour sold 220,000 tickets.
Sixteen years later, their reunion tour has become Australia's hottest ticket. All 300,000 tickets for the Brisbane band's initial 26 shows sold out in six days.
"The response was genuinely overwhelming," guitarist Darren Middleton tells the ABC's Zan Rowe.
"As soon as tickets went on sale, we were like: 'Holy shit!'
Today, they've added nine more dates, including stops in Hobart and Canberra, to supply the intense demand.
Ticket requests have come from some unlikely places.
"It was pretty nuts," frontman Bernard Fanning says. "Not just the public response but privately.
"Like, plumbers that fixed a drain 15 years ago and still have my phone number."
Among the most beloved and best-selling Australian acts of the 90s and 2000s, Powderfinger's return was kept under wraps over 18 months of "white lies" and clandestine meetings.
In May last year, Fanning, Middleton, guitarist Ian Haug, bassist John "JC" Collins, drummer Jon Coghill and long-time manager Paul Piticco conferred to "seriously" discuss the prospect fans had longed for since the group's 2010 split.
"We got together and said, 'Let's think about if we want to do it. Is this the right time for everyone?" Middleton says.
"One idea put around was: 'No-one in the band owes Powderfinger anything.' If someone doesn't want to be a part of it, we don't do it. That's OK."
After a month away to deliberate their reasons for reuniting, they reconvened. "We got on the Zoom [call] and went, let's do it!"
Why now? Family and falling in love with the band
One of Fanning's "main reasons" for getting back together was "for my kids".
"Because they haven't seen [us perform], they'd love to be part of it … and every one of us said exactly the same thing."
"We're never very cool in our kids' eyes," Middleton adds.
Each member has taken a different path over 16 years: from raising families to pursuing solo projects, politics and other careers.
"We've all gone through different experiences, learned to stand on our own two feet again and discover who we are," Middleton reflects.
"And actually fall in love with music and with the band again."
Fanning says time apart has deepened the bonds of their friendship.
"By the end of the band, there was tension, which is natural after 21 years [together].
"But now, all those petty differences have completely disappeared in a sea of nappies and teenage angst and whatever else.
"In the last 16 years, we've had time to think about how much fun and joy there was … try and bring that into the equation again."
It's a rare opportunity whose significance isn't lost on Middleton.
"We're still alive," he enthuses. "It sounds silly, but I've lost friends in the music industry … their bands no longer have the chance to do what they did. We're super lucky."
Cold Chisel, community and nostalgia
Powderfinger's choice to headline concerts outdoors under stadium-sized tents was inspired by attending Cold Chisel's "Big Five-O" anniversary shows.
"It feels like a festival but it's indoors, it's the best of both worlds," says Fanning, who never saw Chisel the first time round, but was thrilled when he got the chance to see them reunite.
That people feel the same way about Powderfinger "makes sense," he reasons.
The group's chart-topping, award-hoovering anthems were the soundtrack to people's lives in the pre-streaming era, ruled by CDs, TV and radio, not algorithms.
"There's a warmth of feeling for that time when Powderfinger was doing well [and] people want to recapture that a little bit," Fanning acknowledges.
"I think nostalgia gets a bad rap. Because it generates good feelings amongst people, which are seriously lacking in our society at the moment.
At a time of "so much difficulty and division in the world", harnessing live music's power to foster community was a driving force for the reunion.
A multi-generational moment
Powderfinger's cross-generational popularity was evidenced by last year's Hottest 100 of Australian Songs, where the majority of voters (aged 18–29) voted in three songs.
"It's crazy," Middleton remarks.
"My 25-year-old daughter, her friends are pumped about coming. It makes me feel young again.
"People coming to see us are parents with kids who are teenagers or above. What a great experience! 'Dad, take me to see that band that you used to love …'"
Since the band bowed out in 2010, "society has devalued music incredibly", Fanning says.
Particularly Australian music, with homegrown music accounting for just 8.4 per cent of local streaming, according to a recent APRA AMCOS report.
In response to increasing festival cancellations, venue closures and declining live attendance, the frontman says there needs to be a "concentration on the arts and how important it is for our stories to be told by us".
"And that comes from musicians, from artists, authors, journalists, from whoever. It's really important to encourage that Australian storytelling to continue."
To that end, Powderfinger are committing to an all-Australian line-up of support acts for their tour, including partnering with triple j Unearthed to give emerging acts a platform to perform for tens of thousands of people. Stay tuned for details.
Will there be new music?
All five members always voted on every major career and creative decision.
Is Powderfinger still a democracy in 2026?
"Yes, unfortunately," Fanning deadpans to hearty laughter.
"It has to be. We wouldn't be able to function any other way.
"It's part of [our] DNA … sometimes there's some late-night lobbying" with JC serving as "the whip", he continues.
Beginning rehearsals in December, each member will have a say on figuring out which tunes will make the cut.
Fanning experimented with writing a set list "of what I thought were essentials".
"There were 22 songs, which is too long."
Don't expect epic four-hour long shows.
"No way. I want the quality to be really high the whole way through," Fanning says.
Middleton counters: "We'll craft a few different set lists [that] we'll revolve."
And the burning question: Will These Days and My Happiness find new company?
"I'll happily accept criticism that it's a nostalgia tour, because we're not making new music," Fanning says.
"The one thing Jimmy Barnes said to me: 'If you ever get the band back together do not make a record.'"
That said, "the chemistry of the five of us being together is very unique … [we're] never closed off to the idea of a new song, from anybody," Fanning says.
"That's what I'm excited about again. That chemistry you cannot manufacture."
But the reunion marks a new adventure.
"All of us are approaching it with so much excitement," Fanning says.
"We know it's different now, the way that we relate to each other is different.
"We obviously have to step up to a really high level or else we will disappoint a lot of people."
But Powderfinger are intent on putting in the hard work. For them, it's about proving some chemistry, between band members, between artists and audiences, between generations, is irreplaceable. And sharing that with 300,000 people and counting.
"I don't want to anticipate how it's going to feel," Middleton says.
"All I know is it's going to be an amazing end to 2027."

Quick hits: Marnus caught in ugly exchange after all-time send off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:54:18 UTC
04:54:18 KST

Marnus Labuschagne was involved in an ugly moment of DRS drama after giving a retaliatory send-off, as Temba Bavuma threw his wicket away in the shadows of stumps.
Here are the quick hits from day three of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. DRS drama and Labuschagne's ugly exchange
It was one of the most contentious moments of the series when, midway through the evening session, with South Africa 2-95 and still five runs behind, Mitchell Starc collected Marques Ackerman with a steepling, searing bouncer.
The South African lost his balance as the ball thudded into what looked to be a mixture of helmet and bat before flying to Cam Green behind the wicket.
The Australians went up and so did the umpire's finger.
Undoubtedly dazed from the contact, the batter regained his composure and met with partner Temba Bavuma.
Eventually, a referral was called for, but only as the DRS timer ticked to zero.
It was touch and go, but the officials deemed Ackerman had taken too long, despite the severity of the hit.
With the South Africans pleading their case to the umpires, the ever-vocal Marnus Labuschagne could be heard giving his own opinion over the stump mic.
"The timer's up, oh no, see you buddy!" Labuschagne said from his position at the other end of the wicket.
Meanwhile, Travis Head had made his way over to the South African camp.
"Heady, what are you doing mate? He's off!" Labuschagne could be heard saying.
Head, hands outstretched towards batter and umpire in what appeared to be a peace offering, turned back towards his team and replied.
"I'm just checking if he's alright," Head said.
Reluctantly, Ackerman made his from the middle, but spent some time at the boundary in the futile hope of being called back.
Thankfully, the replays showed the ball had collected a thick edge before crashing into visor, meaning Ackerman was doomed to be out for 62 even if the review had been permitted.
Even so, it was an ugly exchange and one unlikely to endear Labuschagne to either his opponents or those watching on.
2. Bloodied Harmer keeps South Africa in the game
With an advantage to press home at the beginning of day three, the set Australian pair of Alex Carey and Josh Inglis would have been hoping for at least another full session of batting.
The conditions were perfect, the pitch was flat, and things looked very promising as Inglis reverse-swept his way to a hugely impressive second Test century.
However, neither wicketkeeper-batter would see the other side of the first drinks break, with off spinner Simon Harmer once again doing the damage.
Only moments after ripping a nail and bloodying his fingers while attempting a low catch with his non-bowling hand, Harmer had Inglis caught behind for 102.
It was a brilliant delivery; drifting away, spinning in and kissing the outside edge of the Western Australian's blade.
Four overs later, a similarly exquisite off break had Carey (80) nudging to Aiden Markram at slip, and Harmer, a fingernail down, had dragged his side back into the game.
Australia's tail proceeded to eke out a 100-run first-innings lead, eventually dismissed for 429.
3. Marnus gives it to Bedingham
Labuschagne was in quite a mood on day three.
Before the DRS drama in the evening session, the Queenslander took quite some pleasure in giving it back to Proteas batter David Bedingham.
On day two, Matthew Breetzke had joyously celebrated Labuschagne's five-ball duck by leaping over the pitch and shouting directly at the Australian.
And when Bedingham holed out to Josh Hazlewood during the middle session on day three, Labuschagne responded in similar fashion.
The Queenslander had his chest puffed out as he ran towards the South African, face red and fist pumping, screaming what you can only imagine was something entirely considered and reasonable.
Loading Twitter content
Bedingham was out for 11 and South Africa's second innings was already beginning to teeter at 2-31.
4. A strange moment on the hill
It was a strange morning on the hill.
During the first session, the broadcast cameras found a man holding a sign that read: "Ryan Rickelton, is your mum single?"
The middle-aged gentleman received a good amount of screen time, which he used to blow kisses and adjust his sunglasses in a performance that probably wouldn't have endeared him to anyone in the Rickelton family.
Loading Twitter content
Rickelton, South Africa's wicketkeeper-batter, was stony-faced in response, before pursing his lips and shaking his head solemnly.
The commentators were lost for words at what was an uncomfortable moment for everyone involved — and especially, you'd imagine, for Ryan Rickelton's mother.
5. Bavuma throws it away in the shadows of stumps
Stumps were in sight for Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke.
The South African pair had so diligently rebuilt South Africa's innings after Ackerman's dismissal, and had just eight more balls to survive.
But with shadows lengthening at Newlands and with the pitch offering more and more for the slower bowlers, Nathan Lyon conjured a little bit of magic.
It was the perfect off spinner's delivery; drifting, turning sharply and bowling a swinging Bavuma clean through the gate.
However, it was a wildly inappropriate shot from the usually so-considered Bavuma, and the South African captain couldn't quite believe what had happened.
He grimaced and shook his head as he made is way from the middle for 35, with South Africa finishing the day on 4-140 and just 40 runs in front.

The Finnish shipbuilding company Rauma Marine Constructions (RMC) launched the third of four Pohjanmaa-class multipurpose corvettes being built for the Finnish Navy.
This was reported by RMC.
The ceremony took place on October 29 at the shipyard in Rauma. The launch of the third corvette marked another milestone in the implementation of the Squadron 2020 program.
Currently, the first two corvettes, launched in May 2025 and May 2026, respectively, are undergoing outfitting.
Meanwhile, the keel of the fourth and final ship in the series was laid at the shipyard in August.
According to RMC CEO Mika Nieminen, the experience gained from building the previous ships has allowed the company to optimize production processes and improve operational efficiency.
After the third corvette is launched, work will continue on installing equipment and shipboard systems.
In January, the RMC shipyard held a ceremony to lay the keel of the third corvette, and construction of the fourth ship in the series began.
The keel of the first ship was laid in April 2024, and the ceremony for the launch of the lead Pohjanmaa-class corvette took place in May 2025.
Finland plans to gradually commission the new ships into the fleet between 2027 and 2029. Completion of the entire series is scheduled for 2029.
The new corvettes are set to become the backbone of the Finnish Navy’s surface fleet, replacing the Hämeenmaa-class mine layers and the Rauma-class missile boats.

Societal Complexity and the Problem of Comprehension
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:53 UTC
06:00:53 KST

Introduction. Nostalgia and the Power of Artifacts
Culture and society are on a seemingly endless trip to incomprehensibility. When I was a kid, maybe four or five, my parents would bring me to my grandparents’ house in Hillsdale, New York. My grandfather served for nearly three decades as a New York City policeman. He would tell me stories of patrolling the projects and how he would save his spare change. Eventually they escaped the city. As we pulled up to the old white house, offset from the road by a quarter-mile rocky driveway, I was reminded that this was their means of escape — to get away from the buzz of city life and decompress. Yet when we walked inside, we were hit with a cacophony of trinkets and antiques. A model plane from the 1930s hung from the cathedral ceiling, something my grandpa found at a tag sale. In the kitchen, there rose a high hutch which contained hundreds of antique vases, cups, plates, and figurines. But the one artifact — a key word for this essay — that remains in my mind is the reprint of the post-impressionist artist Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec’s work Aristide Bruant dans son cabaret from 1893. The subject, Aristide Bruant, was a famous cabaret singer and nightclub owner in Montmartre, Paris. The image was an advertisement — Lautrec was friends with Bruant. There was something both horrifying and enticing about Bruant looking over his shoulder — I would stand and stare at the image. It seemed so out of place, because in many senses it was. What was it doing on the wall of a New York City Italian’s house in Hillsdale? But their house, far from an ode to the past, penetrated my 1990s childhood with a sense that culture and artifacts not only contribute to our complexity, but in some sense are the means to find simplicity among the chaos.
I. The Inevitability of Societal Complexity
Now, many years removed from staring at Bruant, with his devilish smile and side-eye gaze, I think back on that time and wonder why the past seems so simple. My time at my grandparents’ was a simple time, full of I Love Lucy episodes as my grandfather slept on the couch, and I rested on the antique fainting chair he’d thrifted from some rich person’s tag sale. In many ways, generation after generation has posed the lament “Life used to be simpler.” On its face this is just nostalgia, with each generation thinking that life was better when they were younger. The way the sands of time move, we often look back and forget the issues of the day, instead clinging to the pleasant, simple memories, images, and smells. To some older generations, the 1950s (though in my thirties I inherited my grandfather’s love for doo-wop), with its simple life and Happy Days aura, seems to draw people back out of the complexity of everyday life. But closer to home for me, my generation does this very same thing with the 1990s, pre-smartphone, when they can think back to when life seemed…simpler. Commercials were for toys and action figures with the overemphasized male voice; video games were rudimentary, like Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 2, which I played on my Game Boy Color; and the internet was hardly the quick access point to infinity that it is today—and it was incredibly loud and obnoxious to use.
The past seems simple because society in the present seems complex.
And yet, to correct myself here, to call society “more complex” than prior generations is not quite right without defining exactly what we mean by complex. To grasp what we are getting at when we call something complex, we need to first find out, precisely, what it is that has changed. It is not simply that there are more people, or more objects, or more institutions, though there certainly are all of those things. Instead, by complexity we mean that the relationships between individuals have multiplied, and information has accumulated more than anyone can possibly take in. In the digital age there are more interdependencies, more feedback loops, more distance between any single actor’s understanding and the system’s actual operation. This distance between each other and our comprehension of the world is what we call “complex.” A village of a hundred people in sub-Saharan Africa and a global supply chain both contain “parts” that contribute to the function of the whole. What separates them is that no one inside the supply chain can hold its totality in mind the way a villager could hold the village. In other words, you cannot comprehend complex society. Complexity, in this sense, is not the pure quantity of things but the ratio between things — the ratio between the scale of a system and the scale of any single mind’s grasp of it. If thought of this way, it becomes clear why each generation longs for a prior one. That ratio continues to expand.
This distinction matters because it reframes the question from “how did society get bigger” to “how did society’s operations outrun the comprehension of the people living inside them.” For a helpful point of reference we should include Ashby’s Law. Developed in the 1950s by W. Ross Ashby, the Law of Requisite Variety holds that for a system or person to adequately control another system, the controller must have at least as much variety, or range of possible responses, as the system it is trying to control. I like to think of it as an air traffic controller. Certainly you watch one plane, but that one plane has to be understood in relation to other planes, else the whole system will collapse. Bringing this back to modern society, this is perhaps one reason government and political figures struggle to “get things done.” Certainly there is political jockeying and campaigning, but also, society is so vastly complex that one would need to understand it all to effectively address it.
II. The Mechanism of Compounding
So we’ve established that the ability to comprehend society has grown more difficult. But now we shift to another aspect of societal complexity. The compounding effect of society and culture is certainly not a new phenomenon. Joseph Tainter, in The Collapse of Complex Societies, argues that societies add complexity as a solution to problems, and as the problems grow more frequent, the complexity eventually becomes unsustainable, leading to collapse. This arguably describes the Soviet Union in the late 20th century. Hard pressed to oversee all aspects of economic and civic life, the totalitarian government was incapable of dealing with the complexity. As the need for a specific resource grows owing to more complex systems and tools, a society interlocks its markets with others overseas to acquire it; that interlocking requires new administrative roles, new specialized functions, new layers of coordination. Each of these layers costs manpower, energy, and capital, and the costs compound even as the returns on each additional layer diminish.
The same compounding shows up at the level of culture. A single people, in a single place, differentiates into subcultures, which differentiate further, until what was once “a people” is, from the inside, thousands of micro-cultures. Now, I’m not saying this is decay. That we can form subcultures within cultures is a mark of our distinctiveness as humanity — unlike all other creatures, we can create social connection that transcends purely pragmatic means. But it is also, unavoidably, the engine of the very fragmentation that makes the whole harder to see. It is this, I believe, that the older generation who longs for “better times” is really seeking — a time before the thousand micro-cultures.
Society also accumulates the artifacts of its own compounding, the leftover pieces of previous generations, which persist long after the intentions that produced them have expired. This is why I opened with the story of my grandparents’ house — their house was a storage place for artifacts from the past, like the poster of Bruant. Or think of the Roman roads: built to move Caesar’s legions into Gaul and Britain, they became the roadways for Hitler’s Panzer divisions, and later still the infrastructure of inter-EU trade. Nothing about the road’s design determined which of these purposes it would serve; the artifact outlived its author’s intent and was picked up by whatever intent came next. My grandparents fashioned their house with artifacts that were at one point in time used by prior generations.
III. The Fall of Comprehension
So far we’ve established that societies grow more complex, but we haven’t tackled the comprehension gap. Why is society harder to comprehend than before? German sociologist Niklas Luhmann has helpfully captured the reason in his world complexity thesis. Luhmann describes how, as time goes on, complexity, information, and potential compound, and this growth builds with it a support system of subsystems developed to treat each system — the siloing of knowledge and expertise. Luhmann adopted the concept of autopoiesis, a term coined by the biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, to describe how each of these siloed systems only communicates with and reproduces itself. Luhmann’s theory of complexity works like a coral reef. At the start it is just the ocean floor, but over time sediment builds and builds until there are layers and layers of compact coral. Soon, one can hardly tell where it began but can see the thriving life all around, each siloed in its own ecosystem, shared by location alone. Thus social systems, so argues Luhmann, are not people, but communication.
Of course, in the twentieth century, the sedimentary layers of society were fairly easy to grasp. A Judeo-Christian worldview and Western civics offered a shared way to understand society and each person’s place within it. But with the rise of the digital age, this has become unintelligible. Deep in the inner crevices of the internet are subcultures, subpockets of algorithmic culture that do not materialize in the real, present world like older forms of culture, but instead materialize in the mind of the individual. The loss of shared information is replaced with millions upon millions of uniquely tailored opinions. This digital media serves as a feedback loop, a simulacrum of sorts, which slowly builds up and creates a reality in and of itself — one that no longer needs to make sense of other people, but merely of myself. Society, no longer a cohesive whole, is a complex, self-optimized system incapable of diagnosing and understanding the parts for the whole.
IV. The Symptoms of Complexity
There are several important indicators of complexity that are worth exploring.
As society grows more complex, and our ability to understand it becomes more difficult, we will try to simplify it on our own terms. In other words the appeal of conspiracy theories stops looking like a failure of reasoning and starts looking like a rational response to an epistemic environment that has outrun anyone’s capacity to verify it directly. This has been a bit eye-opening for me. As society grows incomprehensible, our drive to comprehend it remains, so we seek to explain it in the most simplistic terms possible. A conspiracy theory is, in an ironic sense, I know, more legible to us than the truth. It offers a small number of actors and a clear causal chain, in place of a system with millions of interacting causes that no one, including experts, can fully trace. People are not choosing simplicity over truth out of stupidity (though it certainly can be stupid); they are choosing a story that fits inside a human mind over one that does not. Of course this does not justify a conspiracy, but merely explains its appeal in the modern world.
Hand in hand with conspiracies is the loss of institutional capital. The same collapse that has us seeking out farfetched explanations for modern phenomenon shows up inside the institutions meant to foster and produce knowledge. Academic fields fracture into sub-fields whose findings speak only to each other, no longer to the discipline as a whole, let alone to the public. It is not incidental that the reading most sociology courses still treat as canonical dates largely from the twentieth century, particularly after World War II — a period, arguably, in which society had grown complex but could still be described. Since then, the object of study may have simply outpaced the available frameworks for describing it. It is not necessarily true that we lack originality today; it is instead true that the complexity of society makes originality much harder than it has ever been. To truly be original, a person needs to somehow either shed the collective accumulation of society and knowledge, or instead channel it into a new direction. Both of these are nearly impossible to do.
Along with these points, societal complexity has fractured any shared narrative underpinnings, which has damaged our ability to value one another. This plays out often when someone is being attacked, or in dire circumstances, and instead of people rushing to their aid, they are incapable of seeing the need. This push for efficiency becomes a system of distraction and perpetual indentured servitude. The Influencer Economy, far from just another means to make money, is added complexity vying for attention and time. It’s as if we are screaming out for comprehension and clarity amidst the confusion and misunderstanding of the modern digital ecosystem. As we each live within our sub-ecosystem of culture, we are out of touch with those around us who may be in a different ecosystem. This lack of shared connection is damaging our ability to connect and find bonds.
And perhaps tying all of these points together, societal complexity traps us in a cycle of feedback loop formation. Humanity, for as much as it creates culture, likes to be around things that are familiar. We listen to certain songs, certain genres. We even listen to certain podcasts because “those people think like us.” These feedback loops actually stunt our growth. In the digital age, one can go a whole lifetime listening to voices that affirm one’s own decisions, thinking, and abilities. AI is a good example of this. AI, apart from being an algorithm, is a means of pleasing the self. It rarely pushes back, and almost always affirms us. With so much complexity, there is little need to experience things that challenge and make us uncomfortable.
AI not only feeds the feedback loop, but also serves to accelerate societal complexity beyond anything we’ve seen before. In a split second we can now synthesize billions of gigabytes of data and pull together various threads. The issue, of course, is that humanity will rely on this to export its thinking, which will only serve to further complexify society. For as understanding shrinks, the ability to process likewise fades away. AI, while being sold as a means to make work more efficient, will inevitably make it more complex. The comprehension gap is not just on the input side of the equation but on the output side as well — we are not just losing the ability to comprehend complex society, but as we export our thinking to machines, we are losing any capable function to interpret society. Our thinking no longer stems organically and with rich originality, but from a series of prompts. AI is thriving because it thrives within complexity. And the more it consumes us, the more it will flatten our comprehension.
V. The Rebirth of Simplicity
We started this essay talking about nostalgia, through the lens of my grandparents’ collection of artifacts. The means to “simplify complex society” is not a simple “return.” Society is far too complicated to simply unbuild it. The layers upon layers of social materials are not easily dissected. However, there are ways to help mitigate the complexity.
One way we can undo this is to resist the urge to fall for the minimalism of the day and instead seek to integrate artifacts from past generations within our homes and lives. Certainly you can purchase art from prior generations, but this also takes the form of listening to music from the past. I often find myself putting on Dvořák’s Slavonic Dances and connecting through the artifact of sound with a time that is not my own. This is healthy and reminds me that the present is not all there is, but we carry with us the artifacts of the past, without which we would not be who we are today.
But this also shows why reading old books matters. As C. S. Lewis argued in his essay “On the Reading of Old Books,” the ordinary reader needs old books even more than the expert does, and “if he must read only the new or only the old, I would advise him to read the old.” We don’t often think of books as artifacts, but they truly are. When you crack open a book, you basically sit yourself down across from a figure from the past and begin a discourse. This discourse has a way of piercing the complexity – cutting through the silt of culture and showing you perhaps ways of living you might otherwise never have known. Nostalgia, while often misunderstood as pure daydreaming, is a good means of reckoning with the disconnect between present and past.
Having introduced AI to this discussion, and certainly aware of its effects in making culture and society more complex, I would like to posit not a doomer narrative, but that AI can create a sort of cultural flattening. As we export thinking, writing, and the creation of artifacts, we not only lose the ability ourselves but we no longer leave artifacts for future generations. Artificially generated art will find it far harder to pierce through the silt — I highly doubt my grandparents would hang up an AI image in their antique art collection — because the artwork reminds us of the artist. Without Lautrec, I would not have the image of Bruant burned into my young mind. Certainly AI can be useful; I’m not arguing that point. But it has a way of not only introducing more information than we can comprehend, but it flattens our cultural output. The better question with AI is, is this the artifact we want to leave in the sediment for future generations? I certainly hope not.
As time moves on, society will continue to grow complex, and we certainly won’t be able to fully grasp every angle of the social sphere. But we can push back. We can resist, and seek to simplify where we can. Society is complex, yes, and we struggle to comprehend it, yes, but this means that cultural artifacts matter more now than they ever have before. So if you take anything from this essay, take this: break the complexity with artifacts from the past.
E. J. LaRow is a writer and editor whose work sits at the intersection of theology, philosophy, cultural criticism, and the moral history of the modern West. A member of the Ciceronian Society, a contributing writer for Mere Orthodoxy, and a fellow at Law & Liberty, he has published in both, as well as in First Things, Modern Age, Ad Fontes, The American Mind, and on his Substack.

British stratospheric spy flight planned for next year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:21 GMT
06:00:21 KST

Project AETHER is planning a multi-payload, long endurance flight in the 2027-28 financial year to demonstrate a broader range of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance collection from stratospheric altitudes, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress has been made in delivering the project, following up an answer given in October last year.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Project AETHER capability development is progressing under the sponsorship of the Cyber and Specialist Operations Command. Planning is currently ongoing for the delivery of a multi-payload, long endurance flight in financial year 2027-28. This will seek to build upon the previous trial events by demonstrating a broader range of Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance collection techniques from stratospheric altitudes.”
AETHER covers uncrewed aircraft operating in the stratosphere, above conventional air traffic and below orbit, where solar powered platforms can stay aloft for weeks or months and provide persistent coverage of an area at a fraction of the cost of a satellite. Earlier trials have flown from the Hebrides range, and the Ministry of Defence has worked with several manufacturers of high altitude platforms.
Cyber and Specialist Operations Command was created under the restructuring that followed the Strategic Defence Review, bringing together cyber, electromagnetic activities, intelligence and specialist capabilities under a single command.

This Is What the GOP’s Final Midterms Push Looks Like
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Republicans are spending the final week ahead of the midterm elections defending historically red Senate seats that have suddenly become competitive, according to federal filings and sources familiar with the matter.
A significant focus is now on four Senate races in Kansas, South Carolina, Nebraska, and even Mississippi, all traditionally red seats, in what’s an ominous development for Republicans in their effort to at least keep control of the upper chamber.
Trump operatives tell Inner Loop that they do not expect Democrats to win those Senate seats and that they have mainly directed GOP outside groups to spend there to help boost incumbents that only have a narrow lead.
But the operatives also concede that they are having to divert an increasing amount of resources to those states—states that president Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024 and where Republicans never dreamed of having to spend tens of millions of dollars.
In total, in the penultimate week of the campaign, the Senate Republican–aligned Senate Leadership Fund spent $14 million across those four states, according to a WIRED review of federal filings. The biggest spend has been in Kansas, where SLF has abruptly dumped more than $5 million.
Trump operatives say Kansas has been a major headache since the start of October, when Trafalgar Group, a GOP pollster, found Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton one point ahead of incumbent GOP senator Roger Marshall.
Marshall, a doctor, has had an unusually tough race following a slew of negative stories about how he pursued legal action against his patients with unpaid bills and how much time he spends in Florida. Some political operatives have also complained that he has not taken his race seriously, sources say.
But the last-minute spending is also coming in places like South Carolina, where SLF spent another roughly $5 million to help incumbent Darline Graham, who has struggled to galvanize Trump's base despite having the president’s endorsement that propelled her to victory in the primary.
SLF also spent nearly $3 million in Nebraska to help Republican incumbent senator Pete Ricketts, who has been behind in some polls, and in Mississippi, the fund put just under $1 million toward Republican incumbent senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The final sprint has highlighted the fraught predicament for Republicans, who are having to patch a seemingly ever-growing number of vulnerabilities.
Trump's campaign schedule has also added several deep-red states that are flashing warning signs, in addition to the expected campaign stops in battleground states. Last week, Trump went to Kansas and South Carolina. This week, he has been in Mississippi and will return to Kansas and South Carolina, as well.
Still, several Trump operatives tell Inner Loop they have been encouraged by the fact that Democratic candidates lately have not expanded their leads in several key Senate races—a concern that has cropped up among some Senate Democratic leadership aides.
Chief among their concerns is Michigan, the best GOP pickup opportunity. Many of the most viable paths to Democrats taking the Senate majority pass through the state, but Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has suffered lingering issues with key voting blocs.
Black voters turned out in droves to help Barack Obama carry the state in 2008 and 2012, and the conventional wisdom in Washington is that El-Sayed will need similar support in order to keep the seat blue, one of the Democratic aides tells Inner Loop.
But the trouble for El-Sayed, they add, has been the decades-long animosity between Arab and Black communities in Michigan, a divide that was further strained during the primary when supporters of his challenger, Haley Stevens, ran ads featuring Barack Obama praising her earlier work during the financial crisis.
In an effort to rebuild at least part of that coalition, Obama held a joint rally with El-Sayed in Detroit over the weekend, which aides are hoping could persuade some voters. Operatives aren’t sure if it’ll be enough.
We will have to see how it pans out. See you next week, on the other side!

Microsoft stock jumps 4% as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:57:21 UTC
05:57:21 KST

Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
- Earnings per share: $4.89 adjusted vs. $4.73 expected
- Revenue: $92.28 billion vs. $90.69 billion expected
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement, with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue.
For Azure, Microsoft's finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts that she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus.
"We still have demand that exceeds supply," she said.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. "Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed," Hood said.
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues.
"In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2," she said. The delays have to do with GPU-as-a-service providers, she said.
Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it's attractive to do so, Hood said.
"We're fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our rates ratings are, and sort of we haven't been able to — we haven't yet, I would say, tapped that," she said. "And then, of course, there's other options."
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers.
Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs, and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.

Inquiry slams culture and command of Australia's SAS during Afghanistan war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:53:39 UTC
05:53:39 KST

Inquiry slams culture and command of Australia's SAS during Afghanistan war
In short:
A secretive inquiry into the culture within Australia's SAS during the war in Afghanistan has been partly made public, years after its completion.
It looked into both systemic cultural problems in the special forces unit, and whether warning signs should have been picked up at higher command levels.
What's next?
It found the chain of command in the SAS had been effectively inverted, and that senior commanders overlooked alarming warning signs like a growing number of enemy casualties.
A long-secret inquiry into the cultural and command failures of Australian special forces operators during the war in Afghanistan has found that an "abandonment of curiosity" within the Australian Defence Force's leadership and an "inversion of authority" within units helped create a culture that allowed alleged war crimes to occur.
The inquiry found deep, systemic cultural problems were rife in the ADF's Special Air Services regiment (SASR), and that the lack of intervention to correct them indicated "an absence of effective leadership at various levels".
The inquiry was commissioned in the wake of the 2020 release of the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force Afghanistan Inquiry, which found "credible evidence" of dozens of unlawful killings.
It sought to investigate the culture within the special forces units deployed to Afghanistan and any causal link to the alleged killings and other wrongdoing, as well as possible indicators that more senior commanders should have picked up on.
The inquiry report was handed to the former chief of the defence force, Mark Binskin, in 2022, but the executive summary was only published online recently.
The full report will not be made public because it contains sensitive evidence from the original Afghanistan inquiry.
The Afghanistan inquiry has been criticised by some for its finding that responsibility for alleged war crimes sat almost entirely at relatively low ranks, amid a sense that more senior ADF officers should have carried more responsibility for the actions of soldiers under their command.
This additional inquiry found an "extreme limitation" in the flow of information from SAS units to higher levels of command at the time in question, which limited what those higher ranks knew.
But it sharply criticised the ADF's higher headquarters for not taking more of an interest in some of what it considers to be clearly alarming information that was crossing its desk, like the growing number of people being killed during operations.
"There was tangible data available for higher headquarters through trends in growing numbers of Enemy Killed in Action," it found.
"This included growth and spikes in these statistics over time, as well as features such as a lack of wounded insurgents [only deaths] and the lack of ADF casualties. By historical standards, elements of this data presented as most unusual.
"Some commanders were alert to this data and rumours that accompanied it while others were not, which may suggest an abandonment of curiosity."
It suggested that the rumours circulating about the actions of the SAS in Afghanistan surely warranted investigation at the time.
"It is extraordinary that no effective action was taken given the gravity of the matters the subject of rumours," it found.
"The issues should have been escalated and effective action taken to investigate the matters or, at the least, look behind them."
Former SAS captain turned Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said he welcomed the release of the report because he believed in "transparency".
"I lived a lot of what I read in that report," he told Radio National Breakfast.
"There's almost 50 findings and a lot of it rings very true to me as a junior officer at the time.
"[The report] confirms there was unlawful conduct, that's not in dispute, but rather than focusing on individuals, it spreads responsibility throughout the chain of command."
'Arrogant', 'bikie gang' culture
The inquiry reserved some of its harshest criticism for the culture that developed within the SAS during the period.
It found a pervasive belief among some SAS operators that they were "exceptional" and, as a result, "ordinary norms and standards no longer apply".
But it places some of the blame on both the government and Special Operations Command for fostering the belief that the SAS was "superior" rather than "specialist", and it criticises the over-deployment of special forces more broadly.
It found a "tendency to arrogance" within the SAS, an "unhealthy imitation" of US special forces units and a belief among some that they were "untouchable".
It also found that operational decision-making was being influenced by "a desire to secure awards and the recognition and acclaim that comes with acts of valour", including "seeking out situations where significant contacts with insurgents was likely, or taking excessive risks for personal gain rather than mission effectiveness".
The inquiry found that the chain of command during the time was effectively inverted, with junior officers "effectively subservient" to non-commissioned officers who would ordinarily be under their command.
It found some junior officers prioritised "mateship" over "leadership", and criticised senior officers for knowingly allowing alcohol to be consumed.
"The creation of a dedicated drinking establishment within [special forces base] Camp Russell, particularly in an Islamic country, when there were clear orders that alcohol was not to be consumed, is striking," it found.
And it found when junior officers did try to challenge that structure, they would find networks of non-commissioned officers undermining them by effectively backgrounding against them.
It described the SAS as extremely homogeneous, with a largely closed culture "described by some as akin to a 'bikie gang'" with a "general intolerance of people who were not considered to be 'like us'".
But it noted that efforts toward cultural reform within the SAS were underway as the inquiry completed its work, and commended that attempt at change.
The findings of the initial Afghanistan inquiry led to the establishment of the Office of the Special Investigator, which investigated alleged war crimes.
Former SAS Corporal and Victoria Cross recipient Ben-Roberts Smith was arrested and charged with war crimes earlier this year, which he intends to contest.
Another former SAS trooper, Oliver Schulz, is also before the courts on war crimes charges, which he is contesting.

- Open Arms provides 24-hour free and confidential counselling and support for current and former ADF members and their families 1800 011 046
- Soldier On is a national support services provider for Defence personnel, contemporary veterans, and their families. Contact during office hours 1300 620 380

Bolsonaro lands in Miami with his family after fleeing Brazil: 'He is in a safe location'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:49:25 UTC
05:49:25 KST

Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing candidate who lost Brazil's presidential election this week to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, landed in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil despite a court order prohibiting him from leaving the country.
Bolsonaro arrived in the United States with his wife and two daughters after an escape route that took them through Argentina and Ecuador. AFP and Reuters reported his arrival, with the first footage showing the Brazilian politician stepping off a private jet at Opa-locka Executive Airport near Miami.
AFP footage showed Bolsonaro emerging from the aircraft with his family after its door opened. Reuters cameras also captured the family disembarking from a Gulfstream G400 jet and heading into the airport.
According to a report by NPR, uniformed security personnel escorted the family to a waiting vehicle while holding large umbrellas to shield them from journalists gathered at the scene. Bolsonaro made no statement and did not answer reporters' questions.
His arrival in the United States followed a day of widespread speculation about his whereabouts. According to flight-tracking website FlightAware, the private jet carrying Bolsonaro and his family departed Wednesday morning from Guayaquil, Ecuador, where it had stopped to refuel, and landed in Miami at approximately 9:25 a.m. local time.
The journey began Tuesday evening, when Bolsonaro and his family crossed the land border from Brazil into Argentina before boarding a private plane to Ecuador. Brazilian media also revealed that Bolsonaro used his Italian passport to enter Argentina, even though Brazil's Supreme Court had ordered him to surrender all his passports, including foreign travel documents.
According to Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, his wife, Fernanda, and their two daughters presented Brazilian documents. Argentine authorities confirmed that the family entered the country with valid travel documents and that there was no legal impediment to their entry.
Trump backs Bolsonaro's arrival as tensions with Brazil rise
Bolsonaro's entry into the United States was made possible after the State Department announced that it would grant visas to him and his family. President Donald Trump, a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, expressed support for their arrival.
The move could further strain relations between Washington and Brasília after Lula accused the U.S. administration of cooperating with the Bolsonaro family in an effort to return it to power.
Bolsonaro is expected to break his silence Thursday and publicly address his escape for the first time.
Paulo Figueiredo, a close associate of the Bolsonaro family, announced that the politician would hold a news conference in Miami during the afternoon. According to Figueiredo, Bolsonaro is currently in a "safe location" and is "resting with his family."
Figueiredo claimed that false and contradictory reports about Bolsonaro's whereabouts had circulated in the media in recent hours, some of them attributed to officials in other countries.
Election defeat, corruption investigations and a disputed escape
The younger Bolsonaro, 45, fled Brazil just two days after losing the presidential runoff to Lula, receiving 48.21% of the vote compared with 51.79% for the incumbent left-wing president. He refused to recognize the results and alleged voting irregularities, without presenting evidence to substantiate claims that the outcome had been falsified.
Meanwhile, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports amid ongoing investigations into suspected corruption and money laundering. He failed to comply, and authorities revoked the validity of his passport.
On Wednesday, Brazil's Supreme Court also denied reports that federal police had raided Bolsonaro's mansion in the upscale Lago Sul neighborhood of Brasília.
Despite the travel ban, no arrest warrant had been issued for Bolsonaro when he fled the country. According to Folha de S.Paulo, federal police did not monitor his movements after he left his home in Brasília.
The four family members also did not undergo federal police border checks when leaving Brazil, because Brazilian citizens are not required to complete that procedure when crossing the land border into Argentina.
As recently as Monday, after being ordered to surrender his passports, Bolsonaro declared that he had no intention of leaving Brazil and planned to defend himself against the allegations, which he denies. Now that he has arrived in the United States, it remains unclear how long he intends to stay.
His term in Brazil's Senate is expected to end in February, when he will also lose his parliamentary immunity from prosecution.
Argentina investigates possible assistance in Bolsonaro's escape
Bolsonaro's flight has also sparked controversy in Argentina, where a criminal complaint has been filed demanding an investigation into the circumstances of his passage through the country. 
Lawmaker Marcela Pagano called for authorities to examine whether government officials helped Bolsonaro travel onward despite the restrictions imposed by a Brazilian court. She requested the preservation of security camera footage from the border crossing and airport, passenger manifests and documents related to the chartering of the private jet.
"The Argentine border is not anyone's VIP corridor," she declared.
Meanwhile, Argentine news website Infobae reported, citing government sources, that President Javier Milei's administration helped coordinate the operation that enabled Bolsonaro's departure. According to the report, government officials were involved in examining logistical and legal options in an effort to prevent Argentine authorities from becoming entangled in legal complications.
Following in his father's footsteps
Bolsonaro's escape echoes the actions of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who also left Brazil for the United States after losing to Lula in the 2022 presidential election and refusing to acknowledge the result. The elder Bolsonaro later returned to Brazil, where he was convicted of involvement in an attempted coup and sentenced to 27 years in prison.
Flavio's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, already lives in the United States and said before the election that he would support his brother leaving Brazil if he lost.

NEW DELHI: IT & I&B minister Ashwini Vaishnaw Wednesday said the Digital Personal Data Protection Act does not infringe upon press freedom, amid concerns from news publishers that the law could hinder investigative reporting. He said the Constitution’s guarantee of press freedom remains paramount and secure.TOI has learnt that govt would be open to amending the law to explicitly safeguard journalistic work and would also invite editors and other media professionals to have a detailed discussion on their concerns.“Journalistic freedom is guaranteed by the Constitution of India. That freedom is absolutely available. There is not even an intention to affect journalistic freedom,” Vaishnaw told mediapersons. He was responding to questions over the issue in light of a legal challenge by news publishers to the new law’s potential implications for reporting on matters of public interest.Vaishnaw said the enactment of the new Act had followed a Supreme Court judgement recognising the right to privacy as a fundamental right and was framed after more than a year of consultations involving newspapers, television channels, media representatives, IT industry and other stakeholders.
He added that during the consultation process, govt had explained that the legislation would not undermine press freedom.“It was clearly explained that provisions of the DPDP Act nowhere infringe upon freedom of the press, journalism and freedom of media,” the minister said. He argued that the constitutional guarantee of press freedom could not be overridden by data-protection legislation, distinguishing the misuse of private information from its legitimate use in journalism.
Vaishnaw also said that he would invite all editors and mediapersons to have an open dialogue with govt. “We will be very happy to explain, and if there is any doubt, we will be happy to take on record any suggestion and act if there is a need to.”

Sumy Region to expand underground schools
Oleh Hryhorov, head of the Sumy Regional Military Administration, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.

Five ways out of Israel's political deadlock, and one that keeps every promise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:45:15 UTC
05:45:15 KST

The inevitable conclusion from the near-final results of the 2026 election is clear: There is no decisive winner, and for a government to be formed after the election for the 26th Knesset, someone will have to break one or more campaign promises.
For now, and probably even after the remaining absentee and special ballots are counted, neither bloc is close to securing the 61 seats needed to form a stable government on its own. Without relying on the Arab parties, which achieved a record 19 seats, the opposition's bloc for change remains far from being able to form a government to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
So, with the emerging results giving Netanyahu's bloc a slight advantage over the bloc for change led by Gadi Eisenkot, is there a way to avoid another election? The answer is yes, but in every such scenario, political players on both sides would have to break several campaign promises.
These are the possible scenarios for forming a government, based on the actual election results that defied pollsters' predictions:
Unity government under Netanyahu
In light of the election results, this has become one of the most plausible scenarios, but also the one that would require the most broken promises across the political spectrum.
Under such an arrangement, Netanyahu could break his pledge to form a government with all the parties in his existing coalition, a promise he repeated several times in recent weeks. On the other side, Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman, the potential partners in such a government, would break their promises to voters not to serve under Netanyahu, whose Likud party finished far ahead of its rivals as the largest party.
ynet reported before the election that this was the scenario President Isaac Herzog had sought from the outset. On Wednesday, Herzog commented for the first time on the emerging results, saying everything possible must be done to avoid another election, another indication of his efforts to bring about a unity government amid the political deadlock.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who made no secret of his willingness to intervene in Israel's election before Oct. 27, could also become involved afterward to help bring about such an arrangement. A unity government could make it easier for him to advance diplomatic initiatives, including expanding the Abraham Accords, the normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab countries.
Unity government with Netanyahu first in a rotation
Given Netanyahu's double victory in the election, both in leading the largest party and in heading the larger political bloc, excluding the Arab parties, it is doubtful he would agree to a power-sharing rotation. Still, the possibility cannot be ruled out entirely.
Under this scenario, the leaders of the change bloc would also break their promises to voters, having pledged not to serve under Netanyahu. Some even argued that Netanyahu was unfit to serve as a minister after the failures of Oct. 7 and therefore should have no place in any government, even one he did not lead.
Netanyahu government with defectors from the change bloc
In this scenario, the politicians breaking their promises would be members of the change bloc who chose to join a Netanyahu-led government.
All the bloc's party leaders, and apparently members of all four parties, promised not to serve under Netanyahu. Most also pledged not to cooperate with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which have traditionally been Netanyahu's natural coalition partners.
Even before the election, ynet reported that if Netanyahu emerged closer to the 61-seat threshold, as now appears to be the case, Likud was counting on the possibility of defections, particularly from Eisenkot's Yashar! party.
As ynet previously revealed, Likud even established a special team tasked with persuading lawmakers from Eisenkot's party to cross over to Netanyahu's bloc after the election.
Temporary minority government or caretaker government led by Eisenkot
Under this scenario, every leader of the change bloc except Yair Golan would break a campaign promise.
Throughout the campaign, Golan said Arab parties were legitimate partners in a future government. Senior figures in his Democrats party reiterated that position Tuesday night, saying political leaders must "show political courage" and form a government with Ra'am, the Islamist-leaning Arab party led by Mansour Abbas.
Eisenkot, too, did not rule out such a move during the election campaign, particularly when asked about Ra'am. However, he faced opposition from his main partners in the bloc, Bennett and Liberman.
All three parties, Yashar!, Beyachad and Yisrael Beytenu, have figures who are firmly opposed to such an arrangement.
Meanwhile, in statements over the past 24 hours, the Arab parties have not ruled out the possibility and have said they would help remove Netanyahu from power.
Netanyahu has already launched a campaign to delegitimize the Arab parties, even claiming they "stole the election in Israel" following their dramatic electoral gains.
Another possibility is that the change bloc, together with the Arab parties, could seek to take control of the Knesset. That would mean replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana and, at a minimum, advancing the establishment of an official state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 massacre.
In such a scenario, the Knesset could be dissolved immediately after those measures are carried out, sending Israel to another election.
Another election
That leads directly to the scenario that appeared most likely before Oct. 27: another election.
If no one breaks the many promises made over the past several months, Israel, once again caught in a political deadlock, could find itself heading back to the polls within a matter of months.
The election results revealed something most polls failed to predict: Likud's enduring support. Although the party lost some ground, it remains by far the largest in the Knesset.
According to most assessments within the political establishment, another election could primarily benefit Netanyahu.
Disillusionment within the change bloc could depress turnout in center-left strongholds and perhaps also among Arab voters, who turned out in unprecedented numbers in this election, effectively fulfilling the familiar political refrain about voters "flocking to the polls in droves."

Spain train crash survivor recalls scenes of devastation as accident unfolded
Italy

By Jaime Lopez
MADRID, Oct 29 (Reuters) - When his train drew to a halt, Sebastian Herrero thought the stoppage was due to a fallen overhead line, a problem that has increasingly beset Spain’s high-speed railway network in recent years.
But concerns about arriving late at his destination were suddenly interrupted when he found himself flying through the air and landing face-first on the seat opposite as another train slammed into the back of his.
Herrero, 46, was on his way on Wednesday to Seville from Madrid on an early-morning train operated by Iryo when a train operated by state-owned Renfe ploughed into it, sending its final three carriages careering down a raised embankment in a crash that killed 69 people.
Herrero and others in his carriage escaped by scrambling down the embankment and crossing a fence into a field. Looking back, he realised the extent of the accident for the first time.
“The scene was devastating. You saw carriages completely burnt out, as if they’d exploded. What you see coming out were people in a very bad way, and others who start pulling out the bodies of the deceased and placing them right there next to where we were,” Herrero said in an interview in Seville.
Herrero, who said he feels “born again” after surviving the disaster, was fortunate that his carriage was near the front of the train, but the impact still left many passengers with broken arms or noses.
DILEMMA AFTER JANUARY CRASH
The crash followed another accident that killed dozens in January and involved the same rail companies on the same line near the town of Adamuz. It has revived a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain’s high-speed rail network, Europe’s longest and — until recently — a source of pride for Spaniards.
Herrero remembers people asking him after the Adamuz accident whether he felt safe taking the train.
“I remember when the Adamuz thing happened because I spent a month and a half thinking about lots of things, as I had to drive there and the roads aren’t exactly in the best condition either,” he said.
“Petrol isn’t at its cheapest right now, far from it, and flying isn’t an option. So for many of us who have that connection between Seville and Madrid and whose lives depend on it, you can’t see any other solution.”
For many of the people of different nationalities and backgrounds involved in Wednesday’s accident, the prevailing feeling was one of indignation.
“It is high time for whoever is responsible to take responsibility,” Herrero said.
“I don’t know whether it is up to the courts to say so, or whether it is up to politicians, or whether it is for the Spanish people to decide, but what is clear is that it is unacceptable for this to happen and it is inconceivable that it could ever happen again,” he added.
(Writing by Charlie Devereux; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

EU pressure on Antigua’s ‘golden passport’ trade threatens budget cushion
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:38:07 CET
04:38:07 KST

By Sarah Peter
CASTRIES, St Lucia, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Antigua and Barbuda’s likely move to end its citizenship-by-investment program under European Union pressure threatens a vital revenue stream for the island nation and could test the future of Caribbean “golden passport” schemes, analysts said.
The issue exposes a vulnerability across the Caribbean, where several small economies have built government revenues and luxury developments around demand for passports valued partly for the access to Europe they provide.
Prime Minister Gaston Browne said this month Antigua would “very likely” commit to phasing out its citizenship-by-investment program after the EU gave Antigua and four other Eastern Caribbean nations until November 12 to agree to close their schemes by June 1, 2028.
The EU says the programs pose security risks by allowing foreigners with few ties to a country to obtain citizenship and visa-free entry to the Schengen area, a key selling point for passport buyers. Countries that keep the schemes risk losing that access.
The EU had initially requested the June 2028 phase-out in letters sent to Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis and Saint Lucia in June. Under a revised EU visa-suspension mechanism, operating an investor-citizenship program can itself provide grounds for suspending visa-free access, though the suspension is not automatic.
The programs, which require investments starting at $200,000, grant foreign applicants citizenship and a passport, rather than temporary residency, typically in exchange for contributions to state funds or investments in approved projects.
Buyers have included nationals of China, Russia and Middle Eastern countries who would normally need visas to enter the EU, and applicants generally have not been required to live in the Caribbean to obtain citizenship. Demand from Americans has grown since 2020, according to Kristin Surak, a London School of Economics professor who researches investment migration.
Citizenship-by-investment inflows in 2023 equaled about a fifth of the combined GDP of the Eastern Caribbean Currency Union, a group of eight Caribbean economies that share a currency and central bank, according to a 2025 International Monetary Fund paper.
The IMF estimated in a paper published in 2025 that direct investment in projects tied to the passport programs was so large that it represented between 100% to 170% of all foreign direct investment officially recorded across the five countries with such schemes.
‘EXISTENTIAL FISCAL QUESTION’
Schengen access has traditionally been an important attraction for buyers of Caribbean citizenship-by-investment passports, and losing it could reduce their value while affecting ordinary citizens too, said Surak.
A suspension could force hotels and other developments financed through passport sales to seek fresh capital, delay construction or abandon projects altogether, analysts said.
The immediate stakes are high for Antigua, where citizenship sales are the government’s largest source of non-tax revenue, according to C. Justin Robinson, director of the University of the West Indies Five Islands Campus.
The government collected about $58 million from the program in 2025 and budgeted $44.4 million for 2026, or roughly 7% to 11% of recurrent revenue, he said.
Ending the program would erase more than half of Antigua’s projected primary surplus this year, Robinson estimated.
The consequences could be even greater elsewhere.
In St Kitts and Nevis and Dominica, where such inflows have at times exceeded 10% of GDP, suspension could pose what Robinson called an “existential fiscal question.”
Antigua’s experience could also test how aggressively Brussels is prepared to use access to Europe as leverage over citizenship policies beyond its borders. The EU also withdrew Vanuatu’s visa-free access in 2024 over concerns surrounding its investor-citizenship scheme.
(Reporting by Sarah Peter in Castries, editing by Cassandra Garrison and Deepa Babington)

Analysis-Brazil’s Lula to reap gains from Bolsonaro family flight
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:37:39 CET
04:37:39 KST

By Lisandra Paraguassu and Oliver Griffin
BRASILIA/SAO PAULO, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Flavio Bolsonaro did leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva a huge favor by fleeing his legal problems in Brazil to declare himself Brazil’s rightful “leader” from his new home in the United States, analysts and Brazilian officials said.
Bolsonaro’s departure, which came after he refused to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, weakens an emboldened conservative opposition in Brazil’s Congress and lends credibility to Lula’s accusations of US meddling to help the Bolsonaro family, they said.
Bolsonaro says he was a victim of an electoral coup, but has not provided evidence for electoral fraud.
While Lula faces a groaning inbox of challenges, from taming growing debt to grooming a credible leftist successor, he now has one less Bolsonaro to worry about, allowing him to build a more transactional relationship with leaderless congressional opponents, they added.
“Considering the local dynamics, Lula benefits from Flavio’s escape to the US,” said Rodrigo Russo, a São Paulo-based partner at consultancy firm Control Risks.
BOLSONARISMO WEAKENED
Lula’s victory has been recognized by Brazil’s federal electoral court, global leaders, international observers, and Bolsonaro’s own party, which did not back Bolsonaro’s claims of electoral fraud.
On Thursday, the day after Flavio moved to the United States, his political allies sought to distance themselves from his claims of being Brazil’s legitimate “leader.”
Bolsonaro’s exit is likely to spark a power vacuum over who will now lead Brazil’s right that Lula may be able to exploit.
“There’s generally more willingness to engage with an administration that has secured a new term,” Rafael Cortez, a political scientist and partner at Tendencias Consultoria, said. “An opening for dialogue emerges.”
Flavio’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, is currently serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a 2022 coup, while his brother, former lawmaker Eduardo Bolsonaro, is also based in the United States and unlikely to return to Brazil.
Jair Bolsonaro’s three other children are not currently seen as credible torchbearers of Bolsonarismo.
Michelle Bolsonaro, Jair Bolsonaro’s wife and a prominent evangelical who appeals to millions of Brazil’s faithful, is taking her first steps in Congress after being elected senator this month.
On Tuesday, the head of Flavio Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party, Valdemar Costa Neto, posted a photo on X of him smiling alongside her, saying they had discussed “the future of our party and the challenges we face ahead.”
Flavio’s exit has weakened Bolsonarismo, a Lula aide told Reuters.
The adviser said that the right-wing opposition that remains in Brazil will likely deal with Lula more pragmatically. “It creates space for the emergence of a more democratic right, something we’ve seen the country is clearly missing,” the aide said.
US-BRAZIL TIES MAY BECOME STRAINED
Bolsonaro’s flight to the United States lends credibility to Lula’s claims of improper US support to bolster his candidacy, analysts said, while complicating relations between the two most populous nations in the Americas.
In July 2025, Washington announced a series of measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices’ visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the alleged “persecution” of Jair Bolsonaro for putting him on trial.
So far, US President Donald Trump has criticized Brazil’s election but skirted around questions over which candidate won, which experts interpret as him wanting to maintain a working relationship with Brazil, home to the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earths after China.
Bolsonaro’s departure “complicates the relationship with the US government, which will have stakeholders pushing for sanctions and tariffs,” Russo said.
The Lula adviser said Trump is likely to be more concerned about weak polls ahead of next week’s midterms than about ties with Brazil.
The US will not want to pay a high price for backing Bolsonaro, especially as it tries to limit Chinese influence in the region, including around issues like rare earths, said Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE.
“It’s a pragmatic view because Brazil is a key piece in the chess game the United States is playing as it seeks to expand its influence in the Americas,” Braga said.
(Reporting by Lisandra Paraguassu and Oliver Griffin; Editing by Gabriel Stargardter and Aurora Ellis)
