US files lawsuit claiming Google wouldn’t give employee new job following military leave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:37:00 UTC
04:37:00 KST

US files lawsuit claiming Google wouldn’t give employee new job following military leave
- The US sued Google, saying it broke USERRA by not giving reservist Mark Davisson his old or a similar job after one year of military leave.
- Davisson kept his pay and title, but Google allegedly blocked customer account work, limiting advancement. It later moved him and fired him after more military leave.
- The lawsuit seeks lost wages, benefits, and damages, and wants Google to improve USERRA training and keep a non-discriminatory workplace.
AI generated
NEW YORK - The US filed a lawsuit on Oct 29 accusing Google of failing to give an employee his old job back or put him in a similar job following one year of military leave as a US Army reservist.
The case is a rare instance of the US government suing a private employer for violating the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994 (USERRA), which protects the civilian employment of military personnel called to active duty.
According to a complaint filed in Manhattan federal court, Mark Davisson had spent two and a half years as a Google key account executive, where he handled cloud services accounts for asset manager BlackRock and hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, and managed the US business of the former Credit Suisse.
Employee fired after further military leave
Upon Davisson’s return from leave in May 2023, Google – a unit of Mountain View, California-based Alphabet – allegedly refused to let Davisson handle any customer accounts, depriving him of career advancement though he kept his pay and title.
The complaint said Google assigned Davisson in January 2024 to a cloud solutions position that also involved no management of customer accounts, and fired him seven months later following another military leave and as part of a broader workforce reduction.
Davisson has a home in Charlotte, North Carolina, but lived and worked in Manhattan while Google employed him.
Google did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Lost wages and benefits
The lawsuit was brought by the civil rights unit of the US Attorney’s office in Manhattan, with backing from Assistant Attorney-General Harmeet Dhillon, the Trump administration’s top civil rights enforcer.
It seeks to recoup lost wages and benefits as well as additional damages for Davisson, and requires Google to ensure a nondiscriminatory workplace including by improving training regarding USERRA.
“Federal law ensures that our brave soldiers, who sacrifice so much to keep us safe, are not punished by employers when they return to the civilian workforce after completing their military service,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald in Manhattan said in a statement. REUTERS

Bolsonaro stunned Brazil's political establishment on Wednesday by making the claim and alleging without evidence that Sunday's runoff election, which he lost to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by more than 4 million votes, had been marred by fraud.
Roughly an hour after sharing the document, the senator deleted it from his accounts and published a revised version, replacing the term "president-elect" with "leader of Brazil."
As Brazilian media and political observers speculated about the abrupt change, one of Bolsonaro's closest allies suggested that the explanation for the mistake was not political, but technological: the use of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
Right-wing influencer and podcast host Paulo Figueiredo, who serves as an unofficial spokesperson for the Bolsonaro family in the United States and first shared the letter with journalists, said the document had gone through several drafts and incorporated contributions from multiple people.
Figueiredo said that Bolsonaro's younger brother, former Congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, sought ChatGPT's help to finalize the letter. According to Figueiredo, the chatbot inserted an outdated version of Brazil's coat of arms and used a previous draft of the letter.
"When generating the document, AI ended up including an earlier version of the text, in which Flavio presented himself as the true 'president-elect'," Figueiredo wrote on X, adding the mistakes were noticed only after he distributed the letter to the press.
According to him, Bolsonaro ultimately opted for the term "leader" for legal and moral reasons. He added that those involved found the mistake "hilarious" and described tweaking the letter as "nothing major."
OpenAI and Bolsonaro's press officers did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
"In the end, the essential is expressed precisely by Flavio: these elections were illegitimate, he does not recognize the result, and he will continue fighting to restore democracy in Brazil," Figueiredo said.
The senator arrived in Miami on Wednesday after leaving Brazil, where he refused to comply with a Supreme Court order to turn in his passports as part of a probe into alleged money laundering, in which he denies wrongdoing.
Bolsonaro's decision to declare himself the country's rightful "leader" has failed to garner support from key figures in his political camp, leaving him increasingly isolated.

Kazakhstan and four other countries to work on QR payment integration by year-end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:36:04 UTC
04:36:04 KST

Kazakhstan and four other countries to work on QR payment integration by year-end
The central banks of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan have agreed to work out a mechanism for integrating their national QR payment systems by the end of 2026. This will allow citizens to pay for purchases abroad using their familiar banking apps, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The agreement was reached at the fourth regional meeting of representatives of the central banks of the five countries, held in Tajikistan on October 22-23, a statement from the National Bank of Kazakhstan reads.
Participants discussed the development of national payment platforms, instant payment systems, cashless transactions and remote customer identification.
The Kazakh delegation presented the progress made in developing the National Digital Financial Infrastructure, including the digital tenge, open banking, biometric identification platforms and the National Anti-Fraud Center.
Special attention was given to the Interbank Mobile Payment System, which enables users to make transfers using phone numbers and pay for goods and services via QR codes.
The participants supported Kazakhstan’s proposed approaches to integrating national QR payment systems.
In the future, citizens of the five countries will be able to pay for goods and services while travelling abroad using their banks’ mobile apps, as well as send and receive money transfers in real time.
Kazakhstan also proposed joint measures for information sharing and the regulation of digital assets.
The parties then discussed protecting payment infrastructure against cyberattacks, combating fraud, and applying artificial intelligence in the supervision of payment systems.
Earlier, it was reported that Kazakhstan plans to set up a National Cryptocurrency Analytics Center to monitor transactions involving digital assets.

Cornell begins no confidence vote over handling of alleged gang rape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:23:33 UTC
04:23:33 KST

Cornell begins no confidence vote over handling of alleged gang rape
Faculty vote will continue until next Friday and could send message that school’s president has lost their confidence.
Cornell University has begun a no-confidence vote for the school’s leadership after an alleged gang rape prompted public outcry over sexual assault on college campuses and scrutiny over the university’s handling of the case.
Faculty members started the no-confidence vote on Thursday that is expected to continue until November 6. The initiative is non-binding, but could send a message that president Michael Kotlikoff has lost the confidence of the school’s faculty.
“Hundreds of students, staff, faculty and alumni approached the sponsors of this resolution to emphasize to us that the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg,” said Paul Ortiz, the lead faculty sponsor of the resolution.
A lawsuit filed last month alleges that a female student, identified as Jane Doe, was drugged and gang raped by seven male students at a fraternity house in 2024.
The case has raised questions about whether the university acted with sufficient urgency or downplayed the alleged abuse in order to protect its reputation. The university initially shut down the fraternity and suspended the male students, two of whom were later expelled.
Faculty considered on Wednesday whether to postpone a vote of no confidence, with some urging patience and others arguing that the vote was a necessary response to institutional reluctance to take the issue seriously.
The Associated Press news agency reported that the debate took place after a group of 20 female science and engineering faculty members called on Kotlikoff to resign in a letter to trustees.
“What our community needed was clear leadership; instead, it faced a leadership vacuum,” the letter stated.
Kotlikoff sought to address the fallout in a statement earlier this month in which he listed a number of preliminary responses.
“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” he said.
Two of the men accused of taking part in the alleged rape of Jane Doe have asked for New York Attorney General Letitia James to be removed from her role overseeing the renewed criminal probe into the case over social media posts from the attorney general expressing support for the accuser prior to her appointment.
A judge on Thursday appeared sceptical of one of the challenges, which James’ office has said are “without merit”.

Trump says won’t ‘take sides’ in Brazil election, but calls it a ‘disgrace’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:21:19 UTC
04:21:19 KST

Trump says won’t ‘take sides’ in Brazil election, but calls it a ‘disgrace’
Comments come after Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro fled to Miami in the US and claimed, without evidence, that vote was stolen.
United States President Donald Trump declined to say if he agreed with the outcome of Sunday’s presidential elections in Brazil, but said he thought the contest was a “disgrace”.
“I thought the election was a great embarrassment to the people of Brazil,” Trump said in response to a question from a reporter on Thursday morning. “I watched the election. I didn’t take sides. I let it be. I was asked not to take sides by the president, the current president,” he said. “But when I watched what went down in Brazil, it was a disgrace…take a look at the market, I mean their market went down through the floor.”
Trump’s remarks came a day after former Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and his family fled Brazil and landed in Miami, Florida, in the US on Wednesday.
Bolsonaro and his family were aided in their journey out of Brazil by Trump and his administration, the New York Times reported Thursday. Officials told the newspaper that the US government would likely provide the Bolsonaro family permanent residency.
On Sunday, Bolsonaro had lost a run-off election for Brazil’s president to the left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes. The Brazilian real dropped against the dollar by 12 percent in spot trading after the election.
Brazil‘s Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports shortly after the election, in an attempt to make sure the right-wing senator did not flee the country before he could be investigated for embezzlement and money laundering.
Bolsonaro left Brazil under cover of darkness, crossing by land with his wife and two daughters into Argentina, where the government of Trump’s right-wing ally President Javier Milei had granted them visas. The family then took a small private plane to Ecuador and later on to Miami, where they landed on Wednesday morning.
Shortly after landing, Bolsonaro issued a statement saying he was “the true elected president of Brazil” and the allegations against him were “a politically motivated witch-hunt”. He asked the international community “not to normalise what is happening in Brazil” and said he would lead the country’s opposition from the US. He did not provide evidence supporting his claims.
Bolsonaro’s own Liberal Party said on Monday that it was accepting the outcome of the election.
Although Brazil and the US have had an extradition treaty for several decades, it is unclear if Washington would turn over Bolsonaro, or whether Brazilian authorities would actually indict him and ask for such a move. On Wednesday, Brazil’s Supreme Court dispelled rumours that a search warrant had been issued for his home.
Flavio’s father, Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro, undertook a very similar journey to Florida after he lost his bid for re-election in 2022. Baltic state plans universal conscription
Lithuania will introduce universal male conscription despite public resistance to compulsory military service, the country’s government has announced.
The Baltic state reinstated selective conscription in 2015, seven years after abolishing it. Under the new plan, the draft would be extended to all eligible men, while women would continue to serve voluntarily.
Annual recruitment will increase from just over 5,000 to around 7,500 men, President Gitanas Nauseda announced on Thursday following a State Defense Council meeting.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius described universal conscription as “necessary and inevitable.”
The decision follows similar recruitment pushes elsewhere in Europe. Poland is considering restoring compulsory service, which was abolished in 2009, and introducing a system covering both men and women. A recent poll, however, found that 53% of Poles aged 18–24 opposed reinstatement of the draft.
Germany has already introduced mandatory military registration for 18-year-old men. Enlistment remains voluntary, but parliament can activate compulsory service if recruitment falls short or the security situation deteriorates.
Berlin’s recruitment drive has met resistance, with some 45,000 people joining student protests across roughly 100 German cities and towns in September, with some carrying banners reading “We won’t fight in your wars” and “Russia is not our enemy.”
Applications for conscientious objector status reached over 12,000 between January and August, compared with 3,879 throughout 2025, according to figures reported by German media.
European officials have nevertheless continued discussing preparations for a possible war with Russia by the end of the decade. Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem “joked” last month that if Estonia mobilized and Russia did not attack, it would be “economically more correct to attack ourselves” rather than keep troops waiting.
Moscow has repeatedly stated that it has neither reason nor intention to attack NATO countries, describing such allegations as “horror stories” intended to prepare European populations for further militarization.
Russian officials have warned that Europe’s military buildup could itself lead to confrontation and that expanding NATO infrastructure near Russia’s borders would prompt additional security measures. Moscow has stressed that it is prepared to defend itself if attacked.

Spain train crash survivor recalls scenes of devastation as accident unfolded

Spain train crash survivor recalls scenes of devastation as accident unfolded
MADRID, Oct 29 - When his train drew to a halt, Sebastian Herrero thought the stoppage was due to a fallen overhead line, a problem that has increasingly beset Spain's high-speed railway network in recent years.
But concerns about arriving late at his destination were suddenly interrupted when he found himself flying through the air and landing face-first on the seat opposite as another train slammed into the back of his.
Herrero, 46, was on his way on Wednesday to Seville from Madrid on an early-morning train operated by Iryo when a train operated by state-owned Renfe ploughed into it, sending its final three carriages careering down a raised embankment in a crash that killed 69 people.
Herrero and others in his carriage escaped by scrambling down the embankment and crossing a fence into a field. Looking back, he realised the extent of the accident for the first time.
"The scene was devastating. You saw carriages completely burnt out, as if they’d exploded. What you see coming out were people in a very bad way, and others who start pulling out the bodies of the deceased and placing them right there next to where we were," Herrero said in an interview in Seville.
Herrero, who said he feels "born again" after surviving the disaster, was fortunate that his carriage was near the front of the train, but the impact still left many passengers with broken arms or noses.
DILEMMA AFTER JANUARY CRASH
The crash followed another accident that killed dozens in January and involved the same rail companies on the same line near the town of Adamuz. It has revived a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain's high-speed rail network, Europe's longest and — until recently — a source of pride for Spaniards.
Herrero remembers people asking him after the Adamuz accident whether he felt safe taking the train.
"I remember when the Adamuz thing happened because I spent a month and a half thinking about lots of things, as I had to drive there and the roads aren’t exactly in the best condition either," he said.
"Petrol isn’t at its cheapest right now, far from it, and flying isn’t an option. So for many of us who have that connection between Seville and Madrid and whose lives depend on it, you can’t see any other solution."
For many of the people of different nationalities and backgrounds involved in Wednesday's accident, the prevailing feeling was one of indignation.
"It is high time for whoever is responsible to take responsibility," Herrero said.
"I don’t know whether it is up to the courts to say so, or whether it is up to politicians, or whether it is for the Spanish people to decide, but what is clear is that it is unacceptable for this to happen and it is inconceivable that it could ever happen again," he added. REUTERS

Putin says Russia is ready for war with Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:50:20 UTC
03:50:20 KST

- Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 29 that Russia is ready for war with Europe but does not want one, warning there would be no winners.
- He spoke in Moscow after the Russia-Africa summit, responding to European plans to be ready to repel a Russian attack by 2030.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 29 that Russia is “ready” for a war with Europe but does not want one, and warned that a conflict between them would leave no winners, responding to European warnings that Moscow could be able to attack NATO by the end of the decade.
Putin made the remarks at a press conference in Moscow after the Russia-Africa summit, held jointly with the African Union’s chairman, Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, The Moscow Times reported, citing Interfax. He was asked about his recent phone calls with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and said Russia supports any steps to restore full relations with European countries, either with the European Union as a whole or one by one.
“Many are talking about preparing for war by 2030. First of all, we are ready, but we do not want any war with Europe. If they want to prepare, let them prepare,” said Putin.
He added that Europe had not managed to inflict a “strategic defeat” on Russia and was unlikely to do so by 2030, according to TV Rain.
“If things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that,” Putin said.
Putin also referred to tensions in the Baltic Sea, asking whether anyone wanted the region to end up like the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz, and said Russia did not want that but would respond to any challenge. He did not name any country or describe what kind of response he meant.
The 2030 date Putin cited matches the timeline European governments have set for rearmament. EU states aim to be able to repel a Russian attack by 2030, and several European officials have warned that Russia could rebuild enough military strength to strike a NATO member before then. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and the head of Germany’s armed forces, Gen. Carsten Breuer, have said Russia could be capable of a large-scale conventional attack on NATO territory by 2029, and a classified German intelligence and military analysis reported in 2025 said Moscow was preparing the conditions for a conventional war against NATO, with the Baltic states a possible target. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said Europe should be prepared for a possible major conflict with Russia as early as 2027.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected those warnings, and Putin has long said Russia has no plans to attack NATO countries. In December 2025, he said that if Europe “suddenly wants to wage a war with us and starts it, we are ready right away,” Fox News reported, while also saying Moscow did not seek war with Europe. European leaders, for their part, say Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, shows why they need to rearm.
Putin’s latest comments came two days after his calls with Stubb and Støre, which European officials have not described in detail. Neither Finland nor Norway, both NATO members that border Russia, had publicly responded to Putin’s remarks by Thursday evening.

EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
October 29, 2026
European Union and Canadian leaders are set to meet at a special Canada-EU summit to discuss critical policies like artificial inteligence (AI), climate, energy and security.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday, ahead of the summit, which begins on Friday, that the EU will continue to explore Canada's prospects for becoming the bloc's first "associate member."
But despite her comments, the summit's declaration is expected to exclude the term "associate member," a move pushed by Germany and other members.
"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," Von der Leyen clarified. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."
"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen added.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had said this week he wasn't concerned about the "associate member" status, or "specific names" to be given to the new alliance with the EU.
"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney added.
Canada's EU ties are part of a broader strategy, expert tells DW
Ottawa's quest for deeper ties to Europe is seen as a move to reduce its reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.
Frederic Merand, political expert on EU-Canada relations at the University of Montreal, spoke to DW about how the summit serves as "political impetus" to improve the bilateral trade relationship and to free Canada of its reliance on the US.
"It's not going to happen, over time, overnight. And every time we move closer to the Europeans, we realize how dependent we are on the US and how also vulnerable we are to, for example, us retaliation," Merand said.
But he added that courting the EU is also part of a broader strategy "to reinvent the Canadian economy, to create a single market, to attract more investment," as well as to diversify our partnerships with China, India and also other parts of the world.
The EU is "a natural partner" to work with, Merand said, given its existing free trade agreement with Canada, in addition to the close historical and cultural ties between the two partners.
What's on the agenda for the summit?
An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Canada and the EU sought to align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.
Canada has critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines, something for which Europe normally relies on China.
But Canada is in need of major infrastructure investment to develop its mining industry.
There are hopes that the summit can result in a plan for the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.
EU and Canadian leaders are also looking into a digital trade deal that can allow for faster and cheaper online transactions.
Additionally, Canada could be allowed to participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad.

Trains in Europe are getting safer despite recent tragedies in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:49:16 UTC
03:49:16 KST

Europe's trains are actually getting safer, despite recent tragedies in Spain
Spain was once regarded as a world leader in rail systems, but after suffering two of its deadliest train incidents in over a decade this year alone, questions have emerged.
The country has commenced three days of mourning after at least 69 people died, and dozens more were injured, after two high-speed trains collided just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday.
A computer system failure saw six trains stopped on just over 60km of track between Madrid and Seville, while another was manually given clearance to move, according to Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente.
What are the recent incidents in Spain?
Spain's high-speed rail network, operated by state-owned RENFE, is among the largest in the world, second only to China.
In January, 46 people died on the same rail network after two high-speed trains carrying around 400 passengers collided.
It was the first fatal incident along Spain's dedicated high-speed rail lines since its opening in 1992.
According to European Union data, rail fatality rates in Europe have decreased over the last decade, and last year recorded no fatalities or major accidents.
However, a series of accidents in 2023 saw a spike in those numbers.
Between 2022 and 2024, Spain had some of the fewest fatalities per million train kilometres in Europe.
University of Sydney's Rico Merkert, who specialises in European transport systems, said isolated incidents shifted people's perception around safety.
"There are so many trains, including high-speed trains, operated or run each and every day in Europe. There are millions of people travelling on those trains," Professor Merkert said.
"One incident is catastrophic and really not good and very tragic in terms of the number of fatalities.
"But statistically speaking, it's still safe due to the large volumes of passengers using trains and high-speed trains every single day in Europe."
He added that the European Train Control System (ETCS) prevented trains from reaching excessive speeds and could recognise when there was potential for a collision.
"The problem with the accident that happened [this week] is that there was a signalling sort of failure,"
he said.
"There was a system issue, so it broke down, and it's not quite clear whether that ETCS system was actually operating at all or partially unavailable. It looks like that system failure caused manual operations or signalling."
How does train safety in Europe compare?
A report into railway safety from the European Union found Australia, South Korea and the EU were among the safest railway systems between 2022 and 2024.
It also looked into passenger fatalities and found Japan was the safest, with no fatalities recorded.
Professor Merkert said it was difficult to compare Australia's rail system to Europe, because it does not have high-speed trains.
"[It] is not comparing apples with apples … high-speed trains are between 250 and 300 kilometres an hour, and you simply don't have those trains operating here in Australia," he said.
The report into railway safety said the gap in passenger fatality rates between Europe and Japan would be difficult to close in the medium term.
Professor Merkert said that was due to Japan's long tradition of running high-speed rail safely and efficiently.
"Similarly, China, they had a few incidents themselves, but overall again, the number of trains that they're operating and the number of people using those trains without having any accidents is quite remarkable," he said.
He said overall railway systems were safe, but once automated, additional safety procedures were required.
"There needs to be manual safeguards and governance structure in place that prevent things like what has happened [this week], and that simply seems to not have occurred,"
he said.

Von der Leyen’s Canada power play: Words fail the EU boss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:48:14 UTC
03:48:14 KST

Von der Leyen’s Canada power play: Words fail the EU boss
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is stirring up trouble at home during a controversial trip to Montreal, turning what should have been a straightforward trade mission into a petty argument over Canada’s fictional “membership” in the bloc.
The EU mandarin traveled to Montreal for the 21st annual EU-Canada summit on Thursday, with her tail between her legs. A month after unilaterally promising Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney “associate member” status of the bloc, she was reportedly forced to scrub all mentions of the term and downgrade her offer to one of an “ever closer association” between the EU and Canada.
When the summit closes on Friday, both sides will issue a revised joint statement that reads: “We will create an even closer association between Canada and the EU... and work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself,” according to a draft seen by Policito.
Why was the text changed?
Von der Leyen reportedly gave neither the EU’s vast bureaucracy, nor its members’ wary leaders, any warning before she told Carney in front of the European Parliament that she “would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union.”
Unilateral decisions and boundary-overstepping are von der Leyen’s calling cards, as her fellow Eurocrats have repeatedly complained to the press. “Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem,” an unnamed diplomat told The Guardian on Wednesday. The widespread anonymous briefing to various mainstream European media made it clear that France, Germany, Greece and Italy had forced von der Leyen to adopt the new, watered-down terminology.
Ursula goes rogue
In her first speech in Montreal on Thursday, von der Leyen refused to adopt the new, sanitized wording. After noting that “Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography,” she insisted that “we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union. Our idea is simple: it is an ‘association without accession’.”
Whatever form Friday’s communique will take, von der Leyen has evidently chosen to disregard the concerns of the EU’s largest member states for the sake of her own personal project. However, the difference between both statements is purely rhetorical.
What does ‘associate member’ mean anyway?
Neither “Associate member” nor “ever closer association” are defined anywhere in EU law.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz attempted to define “associate membership” in May when he suggested that it be granted to Ukraine. Under his proposal, Ukraine would participate in European Council meetings without voting rights, send representatives to the European Parliament, receive more EU funding, and become party to the EU’s mutual defense clause.
The proposal was rejected by Kiev, with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky arguing that this kind of ‘membership-lite’ would leave his country “present in the European Union, but voiceless.”
“Ever closer association” is an even more meaningless term, lifted straight from ‘Ever Closer Union’, a hagiography on EU integration by the bloc’s court historian, Desmond Dinan. Writing in 1994, Dinan argued that “European integration is a good thing,” and the phrases he used – “ever closer union” and “pooling sovereignty,” for example – have since become staples of EU speeches and press releases.
US President Donald Trump ridiculed von der Leyen’s word games last month, calling the concept of associate membership “laughable,” and threatening to “put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things” if the EU-Canada proto-alliance ever harmed US interests.
Carney – who plainly insisted last month that Canada is “not looking to become a member of the European Union” – responded diplomatically to the intra-EU squabbling. “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” he said ahead of the summit. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
However, Von der Leyen’s “membership” promise and the subsequent retraction has undermined Carney in front of his opponents. In a social media post on Thursday, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre described the concept of “associate membership” as “theater,” and dismissed the summit as “yet another grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words (catalyze, anyone?) and promises to meet again to talk more."
How long will this theatre go on? While Canadians can’t afford food and homes, Mr. Carney has distracted for months with big talk about “Associate Membership” with Europe. Now, Europe has rejected it. For the next two days, we will be distracted again from the cost-of-living crisis with wall-to-wall media coverage on yet another grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words (catalyze, anyone?) and promises to meet again to talk more. No one’s mortgage or grocery bill will come down. We already have a free trade deal with Europe, Mr. Carney. Get the 9 countries who have not ratified it to do so. And get EU countries to let our beef into the continent and cancel their planned carbon tariff on Canada. Otherwise stop wasting your time and our money. Both are running out.
— Pierre Poilievre (@PierrePoilievre) October 29, 2026
What does von der Leyen actually want?
Von der Leyen has far more riding on this summit than Carney. While the EU needs energy, minerals, and Canada’s geographic clout in the Arctic, Canada only needs to diversify some of its trade away from the US – which accounts for around 72% of its exports and 46% of its imports – in order to hedge against Trump’s tariffs and trade restrictions. At present, the EU accounts for less than 6% of Canada’s exports and 12% of its imports.
🛬 Touchdown in Montréal 🇨🇦 Rarely have I looked forward to a Summit this much. An ocean separates Europe and Canada. Yet we have never felt closer. We have a new ambition: bringing Canada closer to us than ever before, as Associate Member of the EU. And we want to take our unique partnership even further. With an Alliance for the Future, we will stand together and respond to a world of growing rivalries. Montréal, we’re about to write a new chapter in our shared history.
— Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) October 28, 2026
Although the agenda is wrapped up in the language of “shared values” and “respect for the rules-based international order,” Brussels’ priorities in Montreal are clear: the energy-starved EU needs access to Canada’s resources.
According to Euronews, the latest draft of the joint declaration includes a promise to “assess opportunities for long-term energy connectivity,” including the supply of Canadian liquefied natural gas to the EU. Remember that in July 2025 von der Leyen personally pledged to Trump that bloc members would buy $750 billion worth of US energy by the end of 2028, in a trade deal that was widely seen as one-sided.
Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne has also announced that Ottawa and Brussels intend to sign an agreement on the supply of critical minerals including lithium, nickel, and cobalt. The EU currently controls less than 4% of the world’s supply of these minerals, which are vital in the production of electric vehicles and missiles – both of which the EU intends to increase.
The Europeans also intend to sign defense production and technology-sharing deals, to squeeze cash out of Canada for the bloc’s increasingly stretched €90 billion loan package for Ukraine, and deepen involvement in the Arctic, according to the summit agenda. As the EU set out in its updated Arctic Strategy’ earlier this month, Brussels intends to increase its military presence to challenge Russia in the north, and plans to literally redraw the map of the region to increase its meager Arctic claims, and to pursue closer ties “with like-minded partners,” including Canada.
To challenge Russia in the Arctic, the EU likely has its eyes on Canada’s polar-trained military and its 20-strong icebreaker fleet, compared to the ten such vessels spread across the 27-member bloc. None of these icebreakers are nuclear powered, and even if they were to operate on joint Arctic missions, they would be outnumbered and outclassed by Russia’s fleet of 43, eight of which are nuclear powered
However, any hope von der Leyen may have had of securing preferential single market-style trade deals with Carney have apparently been dashed. According to AFP, the “associate member” version of the joint statement included an “explicit goal of deeper financial market integration.” The new, “ever closer association” communique has replaced this with a promise by both sides to “limit potential negative effects on each other.”
Von der Leyen’s unforced error
Whether von der Leyen will, by virtue of repetition and against the will of four EU member states, invent an “associate membership” is immaterial. The concept is a legal fiction, and by insisting on the word “membership,” the European Commission president set herself up for an entirely avoidable clash with the French, Germans, Greeks, and Italians.
It’s very interesting to see the Commission president goes so defiantly against the position of Germany — the biggest member state and her home country — on an issue that, as of now, remains strictly theoretical.
— Jorge Liboreiro (@JorgeLiboreiro) October 29, 2026
The argument over the statement’s wording has overshadowed the summit, but the geopolitical reality remains unchanged: the EU needs Canada’s energy supplies to keep its economy afloat, Canada’s money to prop up its Ukraine project, and Canada’s geography to legitimize its Arctic expansion. For these, it doesn’t matter how the deal is dressed up.

Ukraine’s humanitarian mission to Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has reached a key stage, with mine clearance along designated routes completed and a humanitarian convoy ready to depart, Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said on 29 October.
The mission aims to deliver humanitarian aid to civilians trapped in the occupied city facing humanitarian crisis, and provide a safe way out for those who want to leave. The operation is taking place under a localized ceasefire coordinated with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump.
Lubinets said the ceasefire has held for 54 hours without reported violations.
Aid convoy prepared, civilian evacuations planned
Lubinets said the humanitarian convoy was ready to leave and was expected to reach Oleshky’s central hospital. Residents would receive the assistance they need, he said.
Civilians wishing to leave the city would have an opportunity to do so until 2 p.m. local time, with security measures organized for their departure. Distribution of humanitarian aid was scheduled to begin after 2:30 p.m.
Delegations from Ukraine, Russia, and the United States had gathered to coordinate the next steps in the mission. Journalists from all three countries were also present, Lubinets said.
Lubinets travels to occupied Oleshky
Earlier on 29 October, Lubinets said he was still traveling toward Oleshky.
He said he wanted to be on the ground to see the situation firsthand and report on the mission’s progress. Lubinets also asked the public to rely on official sources and wait until he returned before raising further questions about the negotiations.
The Ukrainian ombudsman said the negotiations had been difficult and lengthy, adding that the mission had reached only the halfway point toward its goals.
“If I had to go for the sake of one person, I would go again,” Lubinets said, describing the mission as his duty to help Ukrainians in need.
US-mediated ceasefire enables humanitarian operation
The mission is being conducted jointly by Lubinets and Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova, with mediation and coordination by Melania Trump.
The localized ceasefire took effect on 27 October to allow mine clearance, humanitarian deliveries, and civilian evacuations.
Oleshky, on the east bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, has been under Russian occupation since 2022. Russian occupation and restrictions on access to the city have left civilians facing severe shortages of food, medicine, and other essential supplies, while access to medical care has become increasingly difficult. The humanitarian mission aims to deliver urgently needed aid and help residents who want to leave reach safety.
Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
Lubinets thanked Melania Trump and the Ukrainians and US citizens who helped bring attention to the situation in Oleshky and support the negotiations. He said the mission’s priority remained delivering assistance and helping civilians leave safely.

'They know exactly what they're doing' — What Russia gains from a ceasefire in Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:47:26 UTC
03:47:26 KST

Why did Russia agree to the Oleshky ceasefire?
An aerial view of Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, Ukraine in a photo published on Sept.16, 2026. (Dmytro Lubinets / Telegram)
Moscow's consent to a temporary ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky seems like a long-overdue and welcome concession from a country that has repeatedly rejected or violated ceasefire proposals during the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
So why is the Kremlin so on board with Oleshky? Experts, as well as information from Oleshky itself, suggest Russia's motives go far beyond addressing the humanitarian catastrophe it created itself.
Instead, the highly publicized ceasefire brokered by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump presents several opportunities for Moscow to manipulate facts on the ground, an international audience, and — crucially — the White House, all as it positions itself ahead of a new round of peace talks.
"They know exactly what they're doing," John Foreman, a former U.K. defense attache in both Kyiv and Moscow, told the Kyiv Independent.
The propaganda opportunity
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
Residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks have made safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city have frequently been targeted by drones.
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 29 accused Ukraine of "creating a humanitarian catastrophe" in Oleshky, despite the fact that Russian forces have been in control of the city since 2022.
Military analyst Vasyl Pehno said on Oct. 27 that Russia had created the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky and is now presenting itself as "heroically rescuing civilians."
The evacuation of residents from Oleshky provides the Kremlin with the opportunity to convince the world that Ukrainians under occupation would rather live in Russia than go back to Ukraine.
The Russian-installed head of occupied Kherson Oblast, Volodymyr Saldo, claimed on Oct. 27 that residents will have a choice — either to stay in Russia or to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory "to reunite with their families."
But a source familiar with the events unfolding on the ground, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, said on Oct. 29 that Russia was already taking steps to ensure as few people as possible left for Ukraine.
They said that patients at the city's only functioning hospital were being registered and told they faced filtration if they left, Russian forces had refused to go house-to-house to inform sick and immobile people that the evacuation was happening, and those living in outlying villages had been told they could be shot if they approached the assembly point.
Some residents expressed fears in local Telegram chats that they could be taken to "concentration camps."
Footage broadcast by Russian state media channel TASS also appears to show civilians being moved with only Russian forces present and before the agreed-upon date of departure, Oct. 30.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha previously warned that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there."
read also
The political gains
Despite efforts by the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and even Pope Leo XVI, a ceasefire agreement has only come about since the intervention of Melania Trump.
The first lady facilitated the ceasefire arrangement after she learned about the crisis during the United Nations General Assembly week, her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 28.
He added that her involvement in the Oleshky ceasefire was "wanted very much" by Putin, something Foreman said has obvious political motives.
"Allowing Melania to take the credit bolsters their credentials to the MAGA base as peacemakers before the midterms," he said.
Foreman argued that the temporary truce could help placate Trump, while he blamed Ukraine for blocking the peace process, Foreman added.
"The same Kremlin approach for the diesel deal, agreeing to three-way talks, and releasing a hostage in return for pausing new sanctions," he added, saying each time Russia gains something substantial without "conceding anything significant."
Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation, told the Kyiv Independent that Moscow wants to give Trump another opportunity to claim he has helped stop a war.
Russia is unlikely to violate the ceasefire this time, he said, not out of concern for civilians, but because the Kremlin would not want to jeopardize its relationship with Trump ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Despite this, the Beckman is adamant that Russia is acting in good faith.
"It's my understanding and my belief in being very close to all of these negotiations and knowing all of the parties for a long time, that everybody, the Russians included, is working in good faith," Beckman said.
"It's understood that this is a humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, and these elderly people need to be saved."
read also
Crisis beyond Oleshky
While the Kremlin agreed to the Oleshky ceasefire, it remains silent about the dire humanitarian situation across other occupied territories.
Daria Rabinovitsch, co-executive director at Helping to Leave, an organization that helps civilians leave the occupied territories, told the Kyiv Independent that calculating how many settlements are isolated is nearly impossible due to broken communications and missing internet access, but at least three other areas are known to be suffering from isolation.
These include the Kinburn Spit, settlements in the Polohy District of Zaporizhzhia Oblast where drivers refuse to go, and Enerhodar, where access has become hazardous due to intense air attacks along transport routes.
Such enclaves frequently appear when the front line shifts and Russia gains more territory, Rabinovitsch said. In some places, Russian military personnel relocate residents from active combat zones deeper into occupied lands, she added.
While the ceasefire might facilitate temporary relief efforts in Oleshky, it leaves systemic problems facing Ukrainians under Russian control unaddressed.
Across all occupied territories, civilians face failing water and electricity systems, shortages of qualified doctors, deteriorating municipal services, and mass depopulation, while specific problems differ from one occupied region to another.
"Oleshky is not the only community on the temporarily occupied territories that is experiencing a humanitarian catastrophe, and while we are happy and hopeful for the people there, we know that this evacuation will not resolve the systemic problems facing Ukrainians in the Russian occupation," Rabinovitsch said.
According to Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, the initial 30 hours of the ceasefire proceeded without incident. While Kherson Oblast had a brief chance for respite, Russian forces continued striking other Ukrainian regions and killing civilians.
As Lubinets headed to Oleshky on the morning of Oct. 29, Russian troops attacked the railway station in Dnipro, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, with a jet-powered drone, killing at least 13 people.

A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:39:43 UTC
03:39:43 KST

Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk third-party website.
The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.
“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”
A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”
“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that had been what could be characterized as an incident.
The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy, which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)
The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.
“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude.”
Accenture currently has more than $3.5 billion in contracts with the federal government, nearly $605 million of which are with the DOD. The company also contracts with other federal agencies, such as the Department of Education, the General Services Administration, and the Department of Energy, among others. Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that an Accenture contractor failed to patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group ShinyHunters getting access to the details of thousands of the Bureau’s employees. The FBI removed that contractor in early October.
Matt Triner, founder of Hunter Strategy, a Washington, DC-based IT consulting company, says that the issue exemplifies the conflicting demands government contractors face more broadly. “Organizations are often punished for reporting incidents like this, even though it’s the right and legal thing to do,” says Triner. In many cases, he says, a company could lose government contracts by admitting they’ve had a security breach, though he says that an incident like the one described is “absolutely one that would need to be reported.”
Triner also notes that the increasing pressure on contractors to deliver projects faster and at a lower price point is at odds with prioritizing safety and security. “Unfortunately, everyone is operating in a system where there are competing rules and incentives, and that existed before AI, but now it’s the same problem on speed,” says Triner.
The coding environment accessed by the Accenture contractor is run on the Non-classified Internet Protocol Router Network (NIPRNet), a DOD network used for unclassified information. While it does connect to the internet—contractors and employees can access their emails and web browsers through the network—it is heavily secured.
According to the source, in order to automate the process of writing code and spinning up cloud servers, the contractor gave their login credentials to the Claude agent. This gave the agent administrative access and allowed it to bypass the security controls enforced through the normal login process. The AI agent—which was not only writing code but also committing it or saving the code into the system on behalf of the Accenture employee—needed to connect out to the internet to perform its tasks. In doing so, it appears to have sent the contractor’s login credentials, passwords, and a map of NIPRNet out to a third party website.
WIRED is declining to name the third party website so as to protect the system from further vulnerability, but National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has previously identified it as high risk because it has a vulnerability that could let hackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials.
The system the AI agent accessed contained CUI. “Information from a CUI environment is not supposed to leave that infrastructure,” says the source. “There is no insight about what happened to the information, including the login credentials, after it was sent to [that service], whether it’s been retained”
Depending on the agency and its work, CUI can include anything from personally identifiable information (PII) to proprietary business or contracting information. According to the DOD’s website, CUI can include information on “the securing and safeguarding of explosives, hazardous chemicals, or pipelines,” documentation related to the designs of “military or space equipment or technology;” and “the exact location and quantities of radioactive material.”
Distinct from the actual data, a map of it could be incredibly valuable to a hacker. “Once an attacker understands how those things fit together, even if those things are public information, what is sensitive is how we are putting those things together and turning that into actionable intelligence,” says Triner.
While a map might not get a hacker into a system, he says, it could help an adversary move faster once they do have access and “help an attacker understand where the crown jewels are.”
Jake Williams, a former NSA hacker and faculty at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy, says that an AI agent running code in NIPRNet presents a “huge problem, and there are huge national security impacts.”
Williams notes that while individual pieces of data or information might be considered CUI, “when that unclassified information is aggregated, that can become classified itself.” For instance, the location of certain hazardous materials might be CUI, as might be information about the vulnerability of the facilities that house them. Combined, however, they could reveal information that would be kept classified.
But this is not the only way classified information may have been put at risk. Frequently, tools and code are tested in NIPRNet before being deployed into more sensitive systems like the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), the military’s secured network for classified information, and Joint Worldwide Intelligence Communications System (JWICS), a secure intranet for top secret information. Both SIPRNet and JWICS are air gapped, a security measure that means they are not connected to any outside networks. On a practical level, that means SIPRNet and JWICS would be extremely difficult for a hacker to access remotely.
But with the login credentials exfiltrated by an AI agent, a hacker could access NIPRNet and insert a backdoor or other malicious code into a tool or system. Without proper review, this code could end up deployed in one of the air gapped systems.
“The code could operate completely normally in NIPR and do something malicious and undisclosed in a SIPR network, that is 100 percent possible,” says Williams. Exfiltrating data out of these networks would be difficult, he adds, but malicious code could be used to attack the systems from the inside. “I think the most likely thing would be some kind of distributed denial of service attack,” he says.
Triner says that even something more subtle, such as slowing down intelligence operations and activities, could cause damage and make users lose trust in a tool, even once the problem is fixed.
As vibe coding, or prompting an AI assistant to write the code for a product described by an engineer, is becoming more common, vetting code is becoming more of a challenge. AI is capable of generating code at a volume that far surpasses human productivity, making it time consuming and difficult to vet.
“When you’re using an agent, you have no idea of the supply chain or even the inference chain of what has ultimately generated the code,” says Williams. “A lot of the code that these LLMs were trained on is itself vulnerable, and they can regurgitate the same kinds of architecture, and architectural issues that we see in other code.”
The government does have a way to identify flawed code in NIPRNet. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) scans code for bugs and flaws before allowing it to run. But Williams notes that a hacker-inserted “backdoor is not a vulnerability, even if we may not want it there,” and therefore would likely fly under the radar of SAST’s detection. SAST also does not usually identify structural issues in the logic chain of how code is created.
There’s no indication that hackers were able to get into a classified or top secret system. Still, Williams says, the incident should raise significant alarms. “Architecturally, any information about NIPR that you can’t see through open source intelligence, DOD considers a close hold regardless of whether something touches a classified network,” he says.
This is not the first time the DOD has been made vulnerable because of AI-related issues. Last year, ProPublica revealed that Microsoft was using “digital escorts” on its projects with the federal government, wherein American employees with security clearances would be overseeing code written by outsourced workers in China. Experts who spoke to ProPublica said that the program presented a particular security risk because the American employees were often not able to vet the code themselves, leaving openings for malicious code to be inserted unknowingly into government systems.

An Israeli soldier has been charged with spying for Iran and providing sensitive military information in exchange for cryptocurrency, The Times of Israel reported Thursday, citing Israeli security authorities, Anadolu reports.
A statement from Israel’s domestic security agency Shin Bet, police and military said the soldier was arrested in September following an investigation into suspected espionage activities on behalf of Iranian intelligence operatives.
Military prosecutors filed an indictment Thursday, charging the soldier with passing information to an enemy with intent to harm state security and maintaining contact with a foreign agent.
The investigation found that the soldier had maintained contact with Iranian intelligence operatives for approximately one year, during which he allegedly provided sensitive information about his military unit’s activities, the army’s operational readiness and military call-ups.
The information reportedly included details about his call-up following the outbreak of the war with Iran earlier this year.
Prosecutors said the soldier also shared information about military bases and their coordinates, as well as photographs of missile interceptors, military vehicles and US refueling aircraft stationed at an Israeli airport.
Authorities said he provided Iranian operatives with information about fellow soldiers and commanders, knowing that the intelligence agents might attempt to recruit them for espionage.
The investigation also found that the soldier shared access to a Telegram group used by young Israelis preparing for military service, which an Iranian operative subsequently joined.
Prosecutors said the soldier knowingly maintained contact with an Iranian handler and received cryptocurrency payments in exchange for the information.
The Iranian operative allegedly instructed him to install encrypted communication applications and offered to purchase him a mobile phone and a pistol.
The two also reportedly agreed to use coded language and prepare a cover story in case Israeli security forces discovered their activities.
The soldier was offered $200,000 to travel to Iran, according to prosecutors.
An Israeli military court extended his detention until Nov. 12, although authorities are seeking to keep him in custody until the conclusion of legal proceedings.
The case comes amid heightened tensions between Israel and Iran following the outbreak of the war earlier this year.

Netanyahu’s stalemate and the liberal fantasy of a new Israel

Open any of Israel’s liberal newspapers, or the Financial Times, or the New York Times, and one finds the same thing: the commentary on Israel’s elections arranges itself into a narrative of possible redemption. When the interpretive community that shapes opinion in the metropolitan centers speaks of the ‘struggle for Israel’s soul’ and the possibility of a new Israel arriving through the ballot box, the elections become an occasion to push a frame that attempts to ‘redeem’ the irredeemable. How is one to concede the crimes and still make room for the persistence of the settler colonial slaughter in Palestine?
Since the outset of this year, a politics of ‘redemption’ has been pushed with vigor. Many of you will have read The New Yorker (one of the worst liberal magazines in its treatment of Palestine, though the others are hardly better), which lent its pages to officials in the Biden administration who salvaged themselves through a formula of ‘good intentions, bad decisions, and missed opportunities’. It is a non-apology of a very familiar kind in the Palestinian experience: the only apology we have heard from the mouths of Zionist leaders is ‘We are sorry you forced us to kill you’. Intentions are pure, a site from which innocence can be retained even when Biden and his administration labored overtime to provision all the equipment, diplomatic cover, bombs, and financial aid necessary for a genocidal campaign in Gaza to proceed for roughly a year and a half, during which he was in a position to leverage American power to stop it.

The Israeli version follows the same logic. The ‘anti-Netanyahu change bloc’ is presented to us as a reasonable alternative, more fluent in the idiom of Western capitals, and better equipped to draw over Israel’s persistent cruelty the veil of ignorance on which the smooth operation of Western liberal support has historically depended. Seen through the prism of the liberal intelligentsia in the West, this is a necessary change: one that might wean Israel from perpetual war and return it to diplomatic and political arrangements, restoring it to the community of ‘legitimate’ states as a country guilty of nothing worse than questionable moral decisions. Decisions that remain redeemable and ultimately can secure Israel’s long-term future if it is willing to return to its old pragmatism, expand and withdraw, kill and bank in concessions.
Indeed, much is granted to the loose collection of parties in Israel’s opposition that agree on three things. Second, a vigorous hatred of Prime Minister Netanyahu, who has outsmarted them and held onto power for the past twenty years, pulling one trick after another to sustain his hold over Israeli politics. Third, the need to redefine the relation to Haredi and Orthodox community in a manner that would integrate them into Israel military machine and economy. As for the Palestinians, they can look forward to the same policies, the same day-to-day crimes, and the same massacres in Gaza, but now under a government granted a renewed license for its effort to bury Palestine because it is simply not Netanyahu’s.
What the change bloc offers is better management of the same system. It will lean more on the courts and the army to do the same job that the settlers have taken up with a sense of super-impunity in the West Bank. It is also more likely to renew the fighting in Gaza and to push the U.S. toward another round of war with Iran. It will present itself as a more credible partner for ‘normalization’ agreements that can rescue Israel from itself and from its doctrinal tilt toward embracing ‘pariah status,’ at least at the level of rhetoric. It will also offer an excuse to Western capitals that do not really want to sanction Israel and are looking for any ‘fig leaf’ to rationalize the persistence of their failure to act.
Israel’s so-called liberals, no less implicated in the structures of power, have always preferred the idiom of moderation to the blunt vocabulary of their rivals on the right. The liberals kill and perform the theatre of moral complexity. They massacre and take pleasure in possessing the capacity to utter words of guilt. They chuckle at the crimes they committed in closed rooms and in archives that only open up decades later. The substance is the same, and for all the talk of a struggle for Israel’s soul, it has been, and will remain, rotten to its core. They differ only in rhetorical strategy, and the right’s candid avowal of what the state actually does is seen by the Eisenkots as stupidity, a failure in the management of appearances.
The entire media complex around Israeli political centrism predicted a sweeping victory for its center, a narrative that wove together an infalted spin on the extent of animosity towards Netanyahu (way more popular than Haaretz would have you believe), the credentialism of the opposition leader as former chief of staff of Israel’s military with a son killed in Gaza, and the brains behind Israel’s deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure as a means to pressure and defeat resistance movements (The Dahiya Doctrine). This was the man who would unseat the Prime Minister and dethrone the king of a state so accustomed to Netanyahu that its politics has shrunk to the person himself, the polity mistaken politics for a personality. The results have produced a stalemate, with Netanyahu’s coalition coming out first with about 53 seats to around 48 for Gadi Eisenkot’s coalition. Netanyahu, declared defeated the day before, rose once again to sustain a fighting chance.
Elections and the illusion of rescue
One of the most talked-about shifts in this round of elections is the extent to which Palestinian citizens of Israel participated in the vote. Turnout among Palestinians was estimated at 80 percent, which broke the 1999 record. The Palestinian community, which makes up around 21 percent of the population and whose participation is a matter of political contestation, voted at much lower rates in previous rounds, somewhere between 40 and 60 percent. The jump in turnout should be read principally as a desperate attempt both to unseat the right-wing government and to return to a semblance of normalcy in everyday life between the river and the sea. In a tragically ironic twist, it is a desperate attempt to secure a colonial reality that is less invested in obscene forms of violence and more capable of masking it through a slow-grinding process. As a tactical intervention, it is also meant to offer Israel’s opposition a clear path towards securing a government, one in which they would have to grant some concessions to Palestinian citizens of Israel, largely on issues pertaining to everyday life and on the issue that has exhausted Palestinian political communities: the willful lack of policing that has permitted the rise of organized crime in Palestinian towns and villages inside Israel, with strong indications of Israeli intelligence sanctioning it.
Both the Joint List and Ra’am are projected to win a record number of seats, around 19. That showing compounds a problem that has already produced repeated political stalemates. Israeli politics has become so polarized around the figure of Netanyahu, and has shifted so far to the right through demographic and ideological change, that the two dominant blocs can neither govern together nor secure a majority on their own. The opposition, a largely weak collection of forces, is also incapable of truly embracing an overt political coalition with Arab parties. It is caught between its hatred of Netanyahu and its utter disdain for any political embrace of Arab parties, both in principle and out of fear that such an embrace would entail a tacit empowerment that might also push Israel towards compromises on national grounds. So the things Israelis casually fear are a Palestinian state or equal political, economic, and civic rights.
It is not a shock, then, that one of the first cynical moves by the Netanyahu-led coalition has been to invoke foreign interference in the elections, and the role of Qatar, Turkey, and the “Muslim Brotherhood” in shaping the outcome through “bribes” and influence operations, which, it claims, explain the strong showing of the Arab vote in the current electoral round. Right-wing Israeli media already call it “Ra’amgate,” a reference to Ra’am, the list led by Mansour Abbas and affiliated with the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement. Abbas, in recent years, moved to break many of the political taboos around Palestinian participation in Israeli elections, situating himself as a pragmatic leader, devoid of nationalist sentiment and interested in full civic and economic rights within the horizon of the Israeli state as it stands. Despite the many concessions, both symbolic and material, he is still treated as a “suspect” and as having a hidden agenda by many pundits and Israeli political operatives. What motivated Netanyahu, who is himself implicated in a Qatar bribery scandal through assistants who worked in his office, was to muddy the waters of any possible coalition that would see Abbas working with the opposition to unseat the Prime Minister.
But the Arab vote in Israel and its strong showing at the polls tell a different story. They speak to the sense of brokenness that has defined politics outside Gaza, and indeed in Gaza itself. The incapacity to muster an active form of resistance, and the daily assault on Palestinian life in the West Bank, in Jerusalem, and within Israel itself, have propelled a cruel push towards a protest vote built on the hope both of ousting the “Kahanist” forces from Israeli politics and of returning to a pre-October 7 sense of normalcy. It is cruel because it comes on the heels of symbolic concessions and amid the weakness of Arab political movements, which have been left wrecked as political forces and without a material and political social base. It is also cruel because it carries a sense of “cruel optimism,” in which voters know all too well that the Zionist forces on the ballot disagree on much but agree on who is on the menu – the Palestinians. But it is the desperation of the “at least” logic that stands out: at least a new government will curtail some settler excess, show more pragmatism in economic relief, and take more steps towards fighting crime. In other words, it is a symptom of a society that has lost much of its capacity to solve its own problems and is hanging its wager on forces that share the same desire to eliminate.
It is also cruel because the rise of Israeli opposition will only help whitewash Israel, sanction diplomatic relief, postpone sanctions, and open a window for the deepening of Arab normalization. It is cruel because, in the moment, it is also one of the few avenues of a cruel form of hope.
