New study challenges what we thought we knew about Long COVID
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:33:14 UTC
03:33:14 KST

in brief
- Without a reliable test, some Long COVID cases could be underreported, leading to knock-on effects.
- Australia has a handful of Long COVID clinics run by hospitals or GPs in NSW, Victoria, SA and the ACT.
New research from the United States suggests Long COVID may have affected fewer people for less time than previously thought.
Using refined data collection methods, a team from Stanford University has found that people suffering from chronic COVID-like symptoms may have been misdiagnosed or the illness overreported.
According to the Australian government, Long COVID is defined as contracting COVID-19 and experiencing symptoms for a period of at least 12 weeks afterwards.
But researchers said no clinical test exists for Long COVID, making it difficult to track its prevalence accurately.
They stress that people who were wrongly assumed to have Long COVID may still have experienced debilitating symptoms that could have been caused by other illnesses.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"These findings indicate that Long COVID may be more similar to other extended post-viral syndromes than many have thought," said co-author Steven Goodman, professor of epidemiology and population health in the Stanford School of Medicine.
The Australian government predicted there would be more than 1.3 million cumulative historical Long COVID cases nationwide by the end of 2023 and suggested between 5-10 per cent of people who contract COVID-19 still have symptoms after three months.
How was the research done?
The Stanford researchers reviewed 4.4 billion health insurance records from more than 244 million Americans and say they found a flaw in previous studies.
Older research compared people who tested positive for COVID-19 with people who were never diagnosed or tested.
The issue is that people who are more likely to test also have more records of various health issues, which can create a biased association between those health issues and COVID-19.
Professor Jure Leskovec, another author of the study, explained these discrepancies may substantially overestimate the range and duration of health effects attributable to COVID-19.
"Our new study design found 98 per cent fewer Long COVID-attributable outcomes between four to 12 months after infection compared with conventional approaches applied in the same dataset," he said.
"This doesn’t mean Long COVID is 98 per cent less common. It means that how we design these studies fundamentally changes which health effects we can reliably attribute to COVID."
By focusing only on patients who tested positive or negative, the researchers believe they have produced a more accurate picture of COVID-19's long-term health effects.
Professor Paul Griffin from the University of Queensland School of Medicine told SBS News refining our understanding of Long COVID is vital for supporting people with the illness.
"We need to make sure that we continue to look into Long COVID, manage those people, try and find tests and obviously also therapies to try and improve their situation," he said.
Difficulties with diagnoses
No diagnostic test exists for Long COVID, and Griffin explained that the criteria some experts use have shifted over time.
It's suspected there could even be different forms of Long COVID, further complicating both diagnosis and treatment.
"It's a complex constellation of symptoms that can involve pretty much every organ system in the body," Griffin said.
The disease can also manifest differently in people or be confused with other illnesses with similar symptoms.
In the worst case, some patients may have their symptoms dismissed or discounted because there is no reliable test.
"They may see some clinicians who say that they don't have anything wrong with them or that it might be due to something else or perhaps it's psychological and not an actual condition relating to their COVID infection."
Experts warn against losing sight of long COVID
Without a reliable test, some Long COVID cases could be underreported, which could mean inadequate resources are directed toward the condition.
"For a short period of time there were some resources deployed to help address that. But then I think in more recent times, a lot of those have been wound up," Griffin said.
Australia has only a handful of Long COVID clinics run by hospitals or GPs.
Dozens more of these clinics and targeted support programs have been discontinued since the height of the pandemic.
Experts said scientists worldwide will keep improving their understanding of the COVID-19 pandemic, both to better understand its impact and to prepare for future public health emergencies.
"COVID-19 had been one of the worst pandemics we face, but it certainly won't be the last. We can take the opportunity to reflect, see how we can be better prepared, and I guess also continue to manage COVID well," Griffin said.
Scrutinising and refining statistics is therefore part of building population wellbeing and resilience.
Leskovec said: "These results should complement physicians’ clinical assessments, not replace them."
"On the other hand, for data scientists, earlier Long COVID studies might need to be revisited with better controls. Our approach could improve those and future population-health studies."

Houthis say Saudi strike kills 12 as blasts heard in Riyadh
Yemen's Houthis on Thursday said 12 people were killed in Saudi strikes on residential areas in Taiz province, while explosions later rocked Riyadh.
The Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised Yemeni government have exchanged daily attacks since a years-long truce fell apart over the summer.
In the Saudi capital, AFP correspondents heard at least eight explosions as authorities warned the city was "under a hostile aerial threat" in a phone alert.
Saudi civil defence issued warnings for "potential danger" in Riyadh, Kharj and the southern city of Najran that were lifted shortly afterwards.
The Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including by launching deadly strikes on the Riyadh airport that forced its shuttering for two weeks as flagship events were cancelled - threatening the kingdom's economic diversification plans.
More than 1,600 people have been killed in Yemen since hostilities resumed, with more than 275,000 displaced, according to United Nations figures.
"As an initial toll, 12 citizens were killed and three others were critically injured when the Saudi enemy targeted the homes of the families of Ibrahim Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz and Al-Raabi Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz in Al-Barah, Maqbana district," the Houthi health ministry said in a statement Thursday shared by the group's Saba news agency.
On Wednesday, at least 14 people were killed in Saudi strikes on a petrol station and market, according to the Houthis, while the group targeted the airport in government stronghold Aden, wounding civilians.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning campaign.
The Houthis have in turn reported frequent Saudi airstrikes.
Yemen has been reeling from war since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, with a Saudi-led coalition entering the conflict a year later in support of the government.

US Jews urge Israel opposition to partner with Arab parties

US liberal, progressive Jewish groups urge Israel opposition to ally with Arab parties
Liberal US Jewish leaders are urging Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and his allies to work with parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel to oust incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, after Tuesday’s closely contested election left both major blocs short of a majority.
Several Jewish-led organisations in the US, including liberal pro-Israel lobby group J Street and activist group Israelis for Peace, have called on the opposition to embrace Arab-led parties as partners in political change.
The Joint List secured 12 seats and the United Arab List (Ra’am) seven, bringing Palestinian parties’ combined representation to a record 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The election also saw a surge in participation among Palestinian citizens of Israel, with turnout among Palestinian voters reportedly reaching a historic 80%.
J Street president Jeremy Ben-Ami welcomed their participation, saying that “their voices and votes are a vital part of Israel’s democratic fabric”.
“This is a moment for the Jewish opposition parties to demonstrate genuine leadership by reaching out to the Arab parties and working together to form an alternative government,” Ben-Ami said in a statement.
“Israel cannot build a stronger, more inclusive democracy while treating the political representatives of one-fifth of its population as illegitimate governing partners.”
New York-based Israelis for Peace also praised the high turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, describing it as “a victory to the anti-Netanyahu bloc” for helping dislodge the ruling coalition led by Netanyahu and the far right.
However, the group criticised the opposition bloc for “refusing to accept this gift, out of no other reason but deep-rooted, unexamined and systemic racism”.
The criticism comes as Eisenkot pledged to “do everything in my power to form a Zionist government” on Wednesday.
His bloc’s projected 48 seats, compared with 53 for Netanyahu’s camp, mean the opposition may need support from Arab-led parties, including the Joint List.
Formal alliances between Jewish-led parties and Arab parties have long faced resistance in Israeli politics, including since the establishment of Israel and the Palestinian Nakba in 1948.
Eisenkot’s own pre-election rejection of Arab backing could add to uncertainty following an inconclusive result, particularly amid Netanyahu’s repeated attacks on the opposition.
The prime minister warned his right-wing Jewish supporters that voting for the opposition would put Arabs in power.
Daniel Levy, political commentator and president of the US/Middle East Project (USMEP), told The New Arab that a growing minority within the Israeli diaspora, particularly in the US, as well as within Israel, was calling for a coalition that included Arab parties.
However, he argued that the decisive test would be whether opposition parties were prepared to accept Palestinian Arab parties as political partners.
He added that the issue could test whether liberal Zionism could translate its stated principles into meaningful political change in Israel.
“The question is now in the courts of the Zionist opposition, and the question is as follows: You have been telling everyone that Netanyahu is an existential threat to Israel. The continuation of his government is a disaster,” Levy said.
“Now you have the opportunity to remove it. It means partnering with the non-Zionists of the Palestinian Arab community. It means, in the words of [Democrats chairman] Yair Golan, if you like, not playing Netanyahu.”
With the election producing no clear winner, Levy said the extent to which Arab-led parties gain greater recognition, and whether attitudes towards them are shifting, would become clearer during what could be weeks of protracted negotiations over the formation of a new government.
“Even if Eisenkot can be convinced, can [Avigdor] Lieberman, who built his career on racist rabble-rousing against the Arab population, and [former prime minister Naftali] Bennett, who is a former settler leader, will they get on board with it?” Levy told The New Arab.
“Maybe the opposition bloc do go for it, or at least maybe they cooperate inside the Knesset without even forming a government. Maybe they just cooperate in the Knesset to swear in a new Knesset speaker, new committees, and to make some changes there.”
He continued: “I think many people are looking at this and saying, ‘Okay, are you going to show us all that ultimately your belief in the Jewish ethnostate and your racism towards the Palestinians is stronger than your willingness to get rid of Netanyahu?’”

Al Jazeera marks 30th anniversary with network overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:20:07 UTC
03:20:07 KST

Al Jazeera marks 30th anniversary with network overhaul
Marking three decades, Al Jazeera unveils a new structure: three channels, 33 programmes, and tech-driven innovation.
Al Jazeera is marking its 30-year anniversary with a transformation of the network, introducing a three-channel structure for its Arabic-language broadcasting operation and 33 programmes aimed at providing audiences with more in-depth coverage and analysis.
Since its launch on November 1, 1996, the Qatar-based network has helped reshape Arab journalism, challenging dominant political narratives and providing a platform for political debate rarely seen on television in the region at the time.
Reflecting on this enduring legacy during a special anniversary episode of the network’s Arabic-language Baad al-Bath podcast, veteran anchor Khadija Benguenna detailed the foundational shifts the network brought to the Arab news industry.
Benguenna said that Al Jazeera had popularised practices such as breaking news alerts, continuous live coverage, and exclusive reporting, which were subsequently adopted by other Arab broadcasters.
Former Al Jazeera news director Ahmad al-Sheikh echoed that sentiment during his appearance on the same broadcast. He described the Arab world’s media environment as previously devoid of independent voices, and credited Al Jazeera with providing an example for other Arab broadcasters to improve standards across the board.
A new era
The anniversary brings a significant restructuring of the Al Jazeera Media Network’s Arabic-language news services, separating rolling breaking news coverage, live event broadcasting, and more in-depth reporting across three channels.
Speaking to the Qatari newspaper Al Raya, Asef Hamidi, the managing director of Al Jazeera Arabic, described the changes as a “new renaissance” for Al Jazeera. “We are talking about numerous paths undergoing significant development that the audience will notice,” Hamidi said.
Hamidi, who was appointed to his current position in September 2025, said the restructuring was intended to address the growing volume and complexity of news and the need to offer audiences different ways of following events.
In an interview with Qatari newspaper Al Watan, Sheikh Nasser bin Faisal Al Thani, Al Jazeera Media Network director general, explained the philosophical necessity behind the expansion.
“From the very beginning, Al Jazeera was more than just another television channel,” Sheikh Nasser said. “It was a broader project to deepen public understanding.”
He said the strategy for the network’s fourth decade would be guided by three principles.
“Our fourth decade will be defined by three priorities: immediacy, understanding and the human dimension,” he said.
Three channels, three approaches
Under the new structure, each of Al Jazeera’s three Arabic-language news channels will have a distinct editorial focus.
Al Jazeera Mubasher, which began broadcasting in 2005, will continue its concentration on uninterrupted live coverage of events, without commentary from presenters or correspondents.
For breaking developments, the new Al Jazeera Now service will focus on developments as they unfold. But unlike a conventional news channel, it will operate without scheduled bulletins or a fixed programme grid.
Meanwhile, the flagship Al Jazeera Arabic channel will retain its news bulletins while pivoting more towards in-depth analysis and investigative journalism, as well as other programmes.
The restructuring is accompanied by plans for 33 programmes, promoted under the slogan “Your questions are our questions”.
Sheikh Nasser said the expansion was intended to provide more context on news events to Arab viewers.
“The real competitor today is not another channel, but noise – the flood of information that makes understanding harder, not easier,” he said, adding that Al Jazeera wanted to fill that gap in understanding.
Hamidi said the new programming would include investigative documentaries, discussions of political and social issues, and programmes examining the historical roots of current conflicts.
Deepening the context
The network’s ambitions extend beyond television broadcasting to strengthening Al Jazeera’s local and regional reporting through dedicated digital platforms covering Palestine, Egypt, Sudan, the Gulf and other parts of the Arab world.
The Syria Now platform, which offers documentaries, investigations, and field reporting focused on Syrian affairs, has quickly emerged as one of the primary digital outlets for news on the country.
Looking ahead, the network is also planning a project called Al Jazeera Cultural, provisionally scheduled for launch in late 2027.
The initiative will serve as a space to foster sustained debate about the Arab world’s cultural and intellectual life.
Technological integration
The expansion also forms part of a wider technological transformation, including the development of The Core, an artificial intelligence initiative announced in December 2025 in collaboration with Google Cloud.
The initiative aims to integrate AI into newsroom operations, helping journalists manage information, coordinate coverage and make better use of the network’s reporting archives.
One component, Orbit, is being designed to coordinate newsroom workflows, including monitoring developments, commissioning stories, organising interviews, translating material and managing reporting assignments.
Sheikh Nasser said the first phase of The Core is scheduled to launch on November 1.
Despite the increased use of AI, Sheikh Nasser insisted that human oversight would remain primary.
“Artificial intelligence enables the human and does not replace him,” Sheikh Nasser said. “The main standard for us is conscience and editorial judgement, and editorial judgement is human.”

apple breaks a 16-year design rule with its first touchscreen macbook pro

apple breaks a 16-year design rule with its first touchscreen macbook pro
after years of reserving touchscreens for its mobile devices, apple allows creatives to create digital content directly on the display.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Apple brings touch to the MacBook Pro after years of resistance
Apple has unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pro in Cupertino, California, ending a 16-year position on how people should interact with a laptop. Announced on October 28th, 2026, the new 14- and 16-inch models allow users to work directly on the display, reaching past the keyboard and trackpad to manipulate content with their fingers. It is a familiar gesture on an iPhone, though one Apple has long resisted bringing to the Mac.
Back in 2010, Steve Jobs argued that vertical touch surfaces were uncomfortable to use for extended periods. Speaking at Apple’s Back to the Mac event, he joked that eventually ‘your arm wants to fall off,’ explaining why the company had concentrated its efforts on developing multi-touch trackpads instead. For Jobs, the horizontal surface offered a more comfortable way to interact with a computer.
Apple maintained this thinking for years. In 2018, software chief Craig Federighi again questioned the ergonomics of reaching toward a laptop screen, suggesting that the existing trackpad offered a better experience. With the new MacBook Pro, the company has revisited that position, introducing touch as an additional way to work while retaining the familiar laptop configuration.
designers can now work directly on the screen
For designers and artists, the change opens up some interesting possibilities. Graphic designers can draw directly onto their work in Pixelmator Pro, while 3D artists can interact with digital models using their fingers. Photographs can be enlarged with a pinch, and windows can be moved across the desktop with a swipe. The screen itself becomes another working surface, allowing certain tasks to move beyond the trackpad.
Apple has integrated the touch sensor directly into its new OLED panel, reducing the distance between a finger and the content beneath it. The hinge has also been redesigned to provide greater stability when the screen is pressed. Meanwhile, macOS 27 translates touches into mouse clicks in existing applications, allowing much of the current software library to respond to the new interaction.
The MacBook Pro still operates as a conventional laptop, with a fixed screen and the familiar keyboard below. Apple Pencil support is absent, and the device has no convertible tablet mode. Touch instead joins the existing controls, allowing users to move between methods depending on what they are doing. For creative work, that could mean switching from precise cursor movements to directly adjusting something on screen.
a brighter OLED display changes the visual experience
The touchscreen arrives alongside Apple’s new PROLED XDR display, which uses two layers of light-emitting pixels to produce deeper blacks and brighter images. The screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of brightness, according to Apple, and supports both P3 and Adobe RGB color spaces. These capabilities are particularly relevant for photographers and graphic designers working across digital and printed media.
Another familiar feature has made its way over from the iPhone. Apple’s Dynamic Island now sits at the top of the MacBook display, replacing the previous camera notch with an interactive area for notifications and controls. Music playback and incoming calls can be accessed from this small section of the screen, which expands and changes according to the activity.
The physical design has also been slimmed down, with the 14-inch model now weighing 3 pounds and the 16-inch version weighing 4 pounds. Narrower screen borders create more room for the display, while a revised cooling system accommodates the smaller enclosure. Despite these changes, the overall silhouette remains recognizably MacBook Pro.
apple’s illuminated logo returns after a decade
There is also a small return to Apple’s earlier laptop designs. The illuminated Apple logo, removed from the MacBook Pro in 2016, is back on the rear of the display. For years, the glowing mark was one of the most recognizable features of Apple’s portable computers. Its reappearance brings a familiar detail to a machine introducing one of the company’s biggest changes in laptop interaction.
Inside, the new models use Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, with battery life rated at up to 24 hours. The technical upgrades extend across processing power and storage capacity, though the most immediately visible changes concern the display and the ways people can interact with it.

Paris shooting suspect admits targeting Muslims and people of African origin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:08:43 UTC
03:08:43 KST

The shooting left one dead and seven injured. The national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office highlights the premeditated nature of this racist attack.
The suspect in the shooting in Trappes and La Verrière, on the outskirts of Paris, has admitted specifically targeting people he perceived to be Muslim or of African or North African origin, anti-terrorism public prosecutor Olivier Christen announced on Thursday.
Known only as Kévin T., the 39-year-old is accused of killing one man and injuring seven other people during the attack, which was carried out both from a car and on foot on 23 October.
"He admitted having specifically targeted people who are of a Muslim or African, North African type," the prosecutor said at a press conference. The suspect is also said to have explained that he chose Trappes because he regarded it as "a hideout for Islamists".
An attack prepared over a long period
The prosecutor stressed what he described as the "very extensive preparation" of the attack.
During questioning, Kévin T. acknowledged premeditation and said he had fired "in bursts". Investigators established that from September he had bought several items intended to improve the effectiveness of his weapon, a Sten-type submachine gun dating from the Second World War. He had also bought a police armband and handcuffs.
On the day of the attack, the suspect drove between Trappes and La Verrière, shooting at several people. The man killed, Pengo Bossio Wangi, was 26 and originally from the Democratic Republic of Congo. Among the seven injured was an 11-year-old girl whose life is no longer in danger. As of Thursday, three victims remained in hospital, one of them in a life-threatening condition.
A search of the suspect's home in Plaisir, also on the outskirts of Paris, uncovered an arsenal that included magazines, two brass knuckles, a steel bayonet and a silencer. Investigators also found a Quran, a Bible and a copy of Adolf Hitler's "Mein Kampf".
Stickers bearing nationalist slogans were also discovered. Many bore the words "Long live France, RN, proud to be French", referring to the far-right National Rally party, while others carried phrases including "100% French, long live France" and "Support for the security forces". The suspect admitted having designed and ordered them online, while insisting that he was neither a member nor a supporter of any political party.
Despite these admissions, he denied intending to commit a terrorist act and considered his actions "legitimate", according to the prosecutor.
He also denied having intended to kill children, saying he may have misjudged the height of the 11-year-old victim. He nevertheless said he felt "no regret".
The suspect had reported psychological and psychiatric problems. However, according to the prosecutor, a medical examination found no acute psychiatric decompensation or signs of hallucinations or delusions that would justify compulsory hospitalisation.
The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office has opened a judicial investigation into murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist act, with an aggravating circumstance linked to the presumed origin or religion of the victims. Prosecutors have requested that the suspect be placed in pre-trial detention.
Emmanuel Macron points the finger at the far right
Appearing on the YouTube channel HugoDécrypte on Wednesday, President Emmanuel Macron denounced what he called "a racism of atmosphere" and "a disinhibition of violence".
Macron blamed far-right political movements for helping create that climate, citing National Rally and groups close to it.
The RN reacted sharply on Thursday on television channel TF1. Party MP Jean-Philippe Tanguy described the president's comments as "very problematic", accusing him of having allowed "hateful ideologies" to flourish during his time in office.
A national tribute to the victims
A national tribute will be paid to the victims of the attack. The announcement was made on Wednesday 28 October by the government, the day after a request at the National Assembly by the leader of the Green MPs, Cyrielle Chatelain.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will preside over the ceremony, minister responsible for combating discrimination Aurore Bergé told the Senate.
A date and location have not yet been announced.

Bangladesh nuclear plant gets power generation nod

Bangladesh nuclear plant gets power generation nod
Bangladesh’s Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has received the final regulatory clearance, paving the path to commence electricity generation.
Rooppur, the country’s first nuclear power plant, was given the nod to advance to Stage C by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA), the Daily Star reported on Thursday.
During this stage, the reactor’s power will be increased to produce steam, boost the turbine, and generate electricity. Capacity will gradually be increased in phases.
“Now Unit 1 will proceed with the power startup to begin the generation process,” BAERA Chairman Mahamudul Hasan was quoted as saying by the news outlet. He added that the authority would determine the startup date.
Rosatom head Alexey Likhachev earlier this month told media that the plant is on track to be connected to the national grid by end of next month.
The Rooppur plant, located 160 kilometers from Dhaka on the banks of the Padma River, was built at a cost of $12.65 billion, with Russian financial and technical support. With two VVER-1200 Russian-designed reactors, it will have a combined capacity of 2,400 megawatts. Moscow is financing $11.9 billion in state loans for the project.
Rosatom, which is providing equipment, nuclear fuel, and engineering assistance, expects to commission the second unit in 2027.
Once fully operational, the plant is expected to deliver 12% of Dhaka’s power demand.
Likhachev recently disclosed that Moscow is in talks with Dhaka to build a new phase of Rooppur’s high-capacity units.
“We are primarily talking about a possible additional phase of large units,” Likhachev said on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum, adding that Dhaka was also exploring the possibility of small-capacity units and a research reactor.

IDF may scale back Hebron presence by weekend after evacuating thousands of Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:08:23 UTC
03:08:23 KST

The IDF may exit or reduce its presence over this coming weekend from the Hebron neighborhood it has occupied since last weekend, The Jerusalem Post has learned.
None of this is certain and the situation is highly dynamic, since to date pre-elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the clear recommendation from IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir to leave the area and allow the at least 2,000 evacuated Palestinians to return to their homes.
But there is some increased expectation that Netanyahu may show more flexibility to IDF recommendations now that the election has passed and he feels in a stronger political position than expected.
The IDF occupied the area in response to last Friday morning’s deadly Hamas terrorist attack and noted that the terrorists were connected to a broader Hamas clan in the neighborhood in question, though the IDF never presented concrete evidence of how most of the 2,000 evacuees could be connected to any specific crime.
Already by Sunday-Monday, the IDF was recommending it allow the evacuated Palestinians to return, saying that it had inspected all of the relevant areas, and there was no clear military reason to remain.
Why IDF's evacuation of Hebron is different
The forced evacuations from Hebron appear to be different from other recent incidents.
Although in early 2025, Israel cleared areas of Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur al-Shams in the West Bank, evacuating close to 40,000 Palestinians, those areas had experienced well-documented mass terror incidents dating back to early 2022.
The IDF carried out multiple temporary evacuations at that time and even sent in the Palestinian Authority to fight large and organized terror groups before undertaking the mass evacuation and destroying several structures in those areas.
In contrast, this time, the IDF provided little information about the offenses of the 2,000 evacuated Palestinians, other than to say that they were familially connected to the Hamas-linked Gaza clan.
While during the 2015-2016 stabbing intifada and in earlier years, Hebron had been one of the most violent and unstable areas – and there have been some terror incidents emanating from Hebron over the past three years of war – generally, it has not been one of the leading problem spots.
In addition, the IDF said it destroyed illegally built structures that could make security operations harder to carry out. However, the military was extremely vague about what those operations were and why entire buildings needed to be destroyed to carry them out.
Pressed about how many of the 2,000 hamula (“clan”) members have records linking them to terror (or at a minimum, to rock throwing), multiple IDF sources did not appear to have any specific information on the topic.
Rather, the operation seemed to be motivated by public statements made by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz about clearing or destroying the neighborhood of the two men involved in the terror incident on Friday – apparently a collective punishment measure.
While Israel has placed closures on terror-emanating areas in the past, it has not carried out mass evacuations and building demolitions to such an extent without a specific connection to those being impacted.
Petition alleges IDF soldiers turned Palestinian homes into military positions
Meanwhile, Adalah petitioned the High Court of Justice on Thursday on behalf of Hebron’s municipality and seven residents, seeking to halt what it described as forced evacuations and demolitions during an IDF operation, and secure the return of residents ordered out of their homes.
The petition asks for an immediate order barring further evacuations and the demolition of homes, businesses and other civilian buildings while the case is considered. It also seeks safe passage for medical teams, emergency vehicles and municipal workers, arguing that sweeping movement restrictions are cutting residents off from essential services.
According to the petition, troops ordered families in the Ein Deir Baha and al-Jalda neighborhoods of western Hebron to leave their homes around 12:30-1 a.m. on the night of October 23-24. Orders were announced over loudspeakers, leaving residents insufficient time to prepare, the petitioners said.
Residents were told they could not return until further notice, without being given a timetable or conditions for their return, the petition alleges. It says some families spent the night outside and some residents were unable to take their vehicles with them.
Municipal figures cited in the petition put the number of families affected by the operation at 780, which could reach much higher than the original 2,000 estimate, up to 4,969 people, which itself was up from 488 families and 3,171 people earlier.
The petition alleges that troops took over some homes and turned them into military positions, while demolishing civilian buildings and requiring traders to remove goods from their businesses at short notice.
It says restrictions also affect residents who remain at home, hindering access to medical treatment and the movement of ambulances and emergency vehicles. According to the municipality’s figures cited in the filing, blocked access routes had prevented rubbish collection and left approximately 1,200 tons of waste accumulating across the city by Wednesday.
Adalah argues that the scale and open-ended nature of the evacuations violate international humanitarian law. Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention permits temporary evacuation where civilian safety or imperative military reasons require it, and requires evacuees to be returned once hostilities in the area have ended.
The petitioners contend that no specific justification has been provided for evacuations on this scale. They argue that barring residents’ return indefinitely, while damaging or taking over their homes, risks making their displacement lasting.
They also invoke the convention’s prohibition on destroying property unless military operations make it absolutely necessary, arguing that a general reference to security needs cannot justify demolitions across residential neighborhoods.
The petition further alleges collective punishment, citing both the measures imposed on residents and statements by Israeli officials presenting the operation as a means of exacting a price for the shooting. The convention prohibits punishing protected civilians for offenses they did not personally commit.
Adalah said it approached the authorities on Sunday and sent a reminder the following day, but had received no substantive response by the time it filed the petition.
The case names the defense minister, the head of IDF Central Command, the military advocate-general and the attorney-general as respondents. Alongside an urgent hearing, the petitioners seek immediate protection against further evacuations and demolitions, followed by orders lifting the challenged restrictions and ensuring residents’ safe return.
Already on Sunday, the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) demanded that displaced residents be allowed to return, movement restrictions be lifted, and demolitions carried out as punishment be halted. It also requested the orders authorizing the measures already taken.
It argued that public statements by ministers indicated a punitive purpose, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s description of demolitions as serving as deterrence and as exacting a price for the attack.
“No attack, however grave, gives the military license to punish an entire city,” ACRI executive director Noa Sattath said.
In an initial decision last Friday, Justice Gila Canfy Steinitz directed the state to respond and said she expected it to refrain from changing the existing situation, or demolishing addition buildings, pending a further decision.

Hold your nose: a £1.25bn subsidy for rich Rolls-Royce’s new engine had to happen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:07:27 UTC
03:07:27 KST

It wasn’t a “nothing” budget for engine-maker Rolls-Royce. The company was handed £1.25bn from public coffers to part-fund the development of a next-generation engine for single-aisle commercial planes.
The chancellor buried this giveaway in two short sentences in the stodgy middle of his speech, presumably because it would look too much like a case of corporate welfare just after he had grumbled about the £14bn extra we’ll be paying in debt interest this year.
And it’s not as if Rolls is on its uppers. The pride of Derby is the UK’s most radically improved major company of the past few years. It sits in fifth spot in the FTSE 100 index, sporting a market value of £105bn, and has enough spare cash to spend up to £9bn on share buy-backs this year.
But there had been an air of inevitability about this subsidy ever since the company’s chief executive, Tufan Erginbilgiç, talked earlier this year about how he would “appreciate” financial support from the government in developing the UltraFan engine. Appreciate? What he meant is that other governments would cough up if the UK didn’t.
That, unfortunately, is how life works in the global aerospace business. Subsidies are a down payment on the jobs and factories that can follow. Germany, reeling from the woes of its carmakers, would love to have a bigger slice of the hi-tech UltraFan action (and has a role in the gearboxes anyway). The US aerospace industry is a study in how generous defence contracts subsidise civil operations. Healey couldn’t ignore those facts of aerospace life.
What’s more, one can see how the possible long-term return on the £1.25bn could turn out very well. “The single biggest opportunity in aerospace over the next 50 years is to secure a UK engine position on next generation narrow body programmes,” said the government’s strategy document for advanced manufacturing. Aircraft engines are high-value products. About 80% would be exported, doing wonders for the national balance of payments. Projections of “tens of thousands of highly skilled jobs” eventually are credible.
The big “if” is that Rolls hasn’t yet got a slot on a narrow-body programme. The company exited that market a couple of decades ago; its civil aircraft side currently only supplies engines to the smaller wide-body long-haul market. Rolls needs to get on to either the Airbus or Boeing narrow-body programmes, and success or failure won’t be known until some time around 2030.
Thus the government is only contributing to a joint 10-year £2.5bn research and development programme, including a “demonstrator” engine to show off the gas turbine tech. There will be spillover benefits for defence capability but, ultimately, UltraFan needs to be on a civil project. It is a big bet – and Rolls, even if it wins, will need a corporate partner at a later stage.
The point, though, is that the UK government had to get behind the UK runner in this race. One trusts the guarantees on UK jobs and investment, beyond the 3,300 roles supported initially, will be written in triplicate in the final agreement. That must be a fundamental condition of support on this scale.
But this is an occasion to hold your nose. Rolls is plainly not a corporate pauper but, yes, it is justifiable to shove £1.25bn its way. Andy Burnham’s “reindustrialisation” talk would otherwise ring very hollow.

Russian publisher Eksmo alters Joe Hill’s ‘King Sorrow,’ removing a reference to Putin and replacing Russia’s invasion of Ukraine with ‘war in Europe’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:06:03 UTC
03:06:03 KST

Russian publisher Eksmo alters Joe Hill’s ‘King Sorrow,’ removing a reference to Putin and replacing Russia’s invasion of Ukraine with ‘war in Europe’
Several passages in the Russian translation of American author Joe Hill’s novel “King Sorrow” were rewritten to avoid censorship problems, changing the author’s meaning. Nikolai Karayev, who runs the speculative fiction Telegram channel Zvezdnye Mayaki Kapitana Norta, drew attention to the changes by sharing several passages from the original alongside their Russian translations.
Hill, Stephen King’s son, writes fantasy and horror. “King Sorrow” is about students who summon a dragon from another world. The Russian edition, translated by Dmitry Starkov, was published in August 2026 by Fanzon, part of the Eksmo publishing group.
Here are a few examples of changes in the Russian translation:
- In one passage in the original, a character says he has “reliable information that the Russians are farming them. They grow trolls like potatoes in the permafrost of Siberia.” Eksmo’s version reads: “I have reliable information that the Ukrainians are breeding trolls. Raising trolls like little pigs.”
- In another passage, the characters watch footage of the war in Ukraine as the novel describes a strike on a maternity ward in Mariupol. In the translation, Mariupol became Donetsk: “On March 9, something like that hit one of Donetsk’s maternity hospitals. A deafening explosion, a column of flame… One of the expectant mothers was killed in the explosion, and her baby was stillborn.”
- A reference to “Russian oligarchs who vacationed in Italy with Vladimir Putin” became simply “Russian oligarchs who vacationed in Italy.”
- Instead of “Russia invaded Ukraine,” the translation says “that night war broke out in Europe.”
After media coverage of the changes, Eksmo CEO Yevgeny Kapyev promised to “look into the situation thoroughly” and criticized Hill, writing:
So I’m wondering, this thing in Western popular culture that started with James Bond, where the bad guys are Russians or Asians, is it ever going to end? Russia could be portrayed as a wonderful country everywhere… at least in the future… Self-fulfilling prophecies are a thing, after all…
And I’m asking authors not to put “Easter eggs” about the current fraught political and military situation into their books… At this rate, they’ll be putting them in recipes soon. There are tons of other ways to get your point across…
In the spring, Kapyev was detained along with other senior Eksmo executives in the “publishers’ case.” The case concerned allegations by law enforcement authorities that Popcorn Books, another Eksmo-owned publisher, had engaged in the “distribution of LGBT literature.”

Donald Trump’s male gaze | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Adam Gabbatt’s analysis explores the seemingly odd statements that Donald Trump has made recently regarding the male anatomy of his political friends and foes (What’s up with Trump’s unhinged fixation on male candidates’ bodies?, 23 October).
These statements may seem strange, but they are not without historical precedent. Save Hammersmith Bridge – but keep it free of cars | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:54:56 UTC
02:54:56 KST

Simon Jenkins is a great defender of our national heritage, having produced many books on the subject and frequently written in the Guardian against aggressive modern architectural horrors. How shocking, then, to find him arguing for the replacement of Hammersmith Bridge simply to provide for yet more cars on the roads (Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t, 23 October). He claims that the principal cause of congestion is “London’s epidemic of roadworks”, when actually it’s the fact that there are just too many cars trying to use a road network that isn’t designed for them.
Furthermore, he says that, in its present state, the bridge “merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross it” – and yet between 12,000 and 15,000 people use it every day. Reopening it to motor traffic (and increasingly heavy cars have massively contributed to the current state of degradation of the bridge) would bring little benefit. Well over half the households in Hammersmith and Fulham don’t have access to a car, and there are very good public transport links in the area; there is even a well-thought-out plan put forward by the Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit group to run driverless electric “pod” vehicles to provide for those who are unable to walk across Hammersmith Bridge.
And quite apart from the huge difficulty involved in enabling the tearing down of a Grade II* listed structure (where’s our doughty defender of national heritage now?), there is no effective business case for replacing it at enormous cost to provide for yet more cars, when for both environmental and health reasons (particularly because of the pollution they cause), the whole emphasis should be on reducing our reliance on cars. If only someone in authority would summon up the courage to tackle the motoring lobby.
 
Dr Richard Carter
 
Putney, London
Simon Jenkins is right to castigate the different London authorities that have failed to replace Hammersmith Bridge over a period of seven years. No other capital city in Europe would allow such a prolonged truncation of a major transport artery, preventing vehicles from crossing the river. London is not a unitary authority and its mayor does not have the powers of his peers in other capitals to raise the finance to pay for the cost of a new bridge. The lack of joined-up thinking appears to be baked in to the planning processes of the different relevant authorities.
This sorry state of affairs in south-west London has led to permanent traffic chaos along the Upper Richmond Road and the hell that is Putney High Street during rush hour. Were it not for the British obsession for so-called “heritage” projects, we could have had a temporary bridge capable of carrying traffic years ago. Instead citizens are obliged to walk or pedal their way across a wonky bridge in order to get to the other side for the sake of a misplaced nostalgia for Victorian engineering feats.
 
Julian Heddy
 
East Sheen, London
The outdated photograph published with Simon Jenkins’s off-beam article on Hammersmith Bridge suggests decrepitude, when the reality is quite different. Thanks to £55m of investment by Hammersmith and Fulham council, this iconic, Grade II* listed bridge has found a successful new purpose as an active travel crossing, with 15,000 people a day walking and wheeling across its reopened main carriageway.
I know of no “growing body of opinion” calling for its replacement. On the contrary, the settled local preference has moved to build on this success with a proposal to introduce a fleet of lightweight, autonomous electric shuttles to fill the public transport gap to ensure all residents can cross comfortably and safely. Community-led Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit is working with Ohmio UK and partners to deliver this vision.
Traffic on neighbouring bridges and the wider road network is down compared with before the bridge closed to motor vehicles, while Barnes’s local economy is booming, aided by the ebike revolution.
There is no credible business case for spending hundreds of millions bringing back polluting, dangerous and exclusionary through traffic. With the mayor targeting a 27% reduction in car traffic by 2030, the priority must be to build on this success, not undo it.
 
Charles Campion
 
Chair, Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit
Simon Jenkins is a respected commentator on London’s heritage and built environment, with a deep understanding of the costs of maintaining historic infrastructure. We share his commitment to London’s bridges, but not his views on how the City Bridge Foundation’s charitable funds should be used.
We maintain five Thames bridges: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium and Blackfriars, spanning centuries of engineering history. Their upkeep requires sustained investment and commitment, demonstrated by our current £15m Blackfriars Bridge refurbishment, repairing more than 2,000 cast-iron balusters and repainting the entire structure.
Our endowment exists to meet these responsibilities in perpetuity. It is not a general fund for London’s infrastructure, nor is its value a measure of money freely available to spend.
Alongside maintaining and supporting our bridges, where there are funds available, we make grants to charities tackling inequality and disadvantage across London. These funds are made for charitable purposes and governed by the legal and regulatory arrangements that apply to our work. They cannot simply be redirected to pay for the restoration or replacement of a bridge outside our remit.
We recognise the importance of London’s bridges to the people who rely on them every day, but other Thames crossings are the responsibility of other organisations. We share knowledge and experience with those responsible through industry groups.
For nearly 900 years, the legacy of Bridge House Estates has helped keep London’s bridges standing while supporting charitable work across the city. We are proud of this legacy and the charity partners working alongside us to build a fairer London.
 
Paul Martinelli
 
Chairman, City Bridge Foundation

8 of the most atmospheric Christmas markets worth visiting
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:54:43 EET
02:54:43 KST

8 of the most atmospheric Christmas markets worth visiting
Kyiv • UNN
Strasbourg, Dresden, Vienna and other cities preserve unique Christmas traditions. This selection tells about the markets and the main festive dishes.
European Christmas markets have long since evolved from simple winter markets into a large-scale cultural phenomenon, with each city preserving its own centuries-old secrets. Every market is special, with its own fairytale atmosphere and traditions. UNN has selected for you 8 of Europe's most spectacular winter destinations, their unique traditions, and the main gastronomic symbols that everyone should try.
Strasbourg
This French city is deservedly called the "capital of Christmas." The market was first established here in 1570 under the name "Christkindelsmärik." Before that, the city had hosted a Saint Nicholas market, but when Alsace became Protestant, Catholic holidays were abolished and the market was renamed in honor of the Christ Child. You should definitely try the local bredele cookies, which are baked exclusively for the holidays, and instead of ordinary mulled wine, try hot white Alsatian wine or spiced apple juice with cinnamon.
Interestingly, Strasbourg has an entire "Christmas tree guard service." The main tree in Place Kléber is selected for months in the surrounding forests: it must be perfectly symmetrical and taller than 30 meters.
Dresden
The local Striezelmarkt is Germany's oldest market; it has been officially mentioned in documents since 1434. At first, it was simply a single day of trading, when townspeople were allowed to buy meat after the strict Christmas fast. Be sure to try authentic Dresden stollen. Today, only a few dozen local bakeries have the right to place an official quality mark on it.
The market got its name from the word "Striezel"—the term once used for a festive cake. It is also here that the world's tallest wooden Christmas pyramid stands: a 14-meter structure from the Ore Mountains.
Nuremberg
The Christkindlesmarkt in Nuremberg is a place of strict traditions. You will not see plastic garlands or loud modern pop music here. The city council closely monitors that all stalls are made exclusively of natural wood and decorated with fresh fir branches. The market is famous for Nuremberg sausages. They are very small, about the length of a finger, and are traditionally served three at a time in a sliced, crispy roll. The market's main symbol is not Santa Claus, but the Christ Child. A girl is chosen for this role by the townspeople once every two years, and she opens the festival by delivering a speech from the balcony of the Frauenkirche.
Vienna
Vienna's markets are pure classic. The very first "December Market" here was authorized by Emperor Albert I as early as 1298. It is important to note that Vienna has not just one market, but more than a dozen different locations throughout the city. Every year, the markets issue signature cups shaped like boots or hearts, which you can keep as a souvenir after paying a deposit. They are used to serve the signature hot punch. It is here, near City Hall, that the most romantic market takes place: hundreds of illuminated figures are lit up on the trees in the park, while a huge ice rink is set up among the wooded paths.
Prague
The Czech winter fairytale is centered around Old Town Square. While steam rises from stalls serving grilled sausages, the Gothic Orloj clock counts down the hours to Christmas. Prague's markets are famous for trdelník—rolled dough with cinnamon and nuts—as well as fried hermelín cheese. Traditionally, a live nativity scene with real sheep, goats, and a donkey is installed in the center of the Prague market every year, and children are happily allowed to pet them.
Tallinn
The market on Tallinn's Town Hall Square is small but incredibly cozy. The northern winter atmosphere can be felt here like nowhere else—old stone buildings, snow, and lamplight. Tallinn will surprise you with blood sausage served with lingonberry jam, cinnamon-roasted almonds, and hot mulled wine with the famous Vana Tallinn liqueur added. According to local legend, it was in Tallinn, in 1441, that the Brotherhood of Blackheads erected Europe's first public Christmas tree, around which dances were held.
Wrocław
The Wrocław Christmas market on Market Square is now considered one of the largest in Central Europe. The historic center transforms into a real fairy-tale town with two-story wooden mills. Oscypek — smoked goat cheese from the mountains, grilled and served with cranberry sauce — is a delicacy no market is complete without. If you pay close attention, you may spot the famous local bronze dwarfs hiding throughout the Wrocław market. During the holiday season, some of them are even given tiny winter hats and scarves.
Zagreb
If you thought the best markets could only be found in the north, Zagreb easily disproves that. For several years in a row, the Croatian capital won the title of Europe’s best Christmas market. Here, you should try fritule — mini doughnuts with chocolate, cinnamon, or powdered sugar, served hot in cups. The market encompasses not just one square but literally the entire city: from Zrinjevac Park with its classical music pavilion to the historic underground Grič Tunnel, which is transformed into a light tunnel with musical accompaniment.

Their presence, he said, is meant to make the next stage of the humanitarian mission as transparent as possible.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The truce, which marked a rare instance of de-escalation in Russia’s fifth year of war, initially began clouded by confusion as Chief of the Russian General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced a “silence regime” along the Kherson front beginning Oct. 27 – two days earlier than the Oct. 29 date set by the White House.
Despite fears of possible sabotage that Moscow’s unilateral announcement widely raised, the ceasefire is still holding as no incident has been reported for more than 64 hours.
Newsmax crew draws scrutiny
On Wednesday, Oct. 28 US First Lady Melania Trump, who mediated the agreement, announced that four journalists from the US conservative broadcaster Newsmax would be embedded with Ukrainian and Russian humanitarian officials in Oleshky.

Dmitriev’s growing role in Washington
Dmitriev heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), which the US Treasury sanctioned in 2022, under the previous Biden administration as it is closely connected to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Since US President Donald Trump struck a diesel arrangement with Putin on Oct. 9, Dmitriev has become not only Moscow’s main economic channel to the Trump administration, but possibly a key negotiator in the ceasefire.
The Trump administration is currently reviewing a request to lift sanctions on the fund, which helped arrange Russian diesel shipments to the US. Only a week prior, US special envoy Steve Witkoff confirmed that the US Treasury was working with Dmitriev directly.

“I know how technically the evacuation to Ukraine can take place, but I don’t know what will really happen,” Zelensky said.
Rights advocates warn of ‘human shield’
Ukrainian human rights advocates have warned that Moscow may try to keep part of the population in place.

According to Pavlichenko, there was no information available yet on whether Russian forces would subject evacuees to filtration, but warned that the risks existed. So far, he said, further details about international observers, including their number and access, remain unclear.

Human-made catastrophe
Oleshky, located on the left bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) southeast of Kherson city, has faced severe shortages of food, clean water and medicine for months, with the last food delivery reported on May 26.
According to Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha’s estimates, roughly 1,700 people remain in the city from a prewar population of 24,000, including 47 children.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets, who leads the humanitarian operation, earlier said that about 6,000 people, including some 200 children, remain across Oleshky and the surrounding settlements. In his view, up to 2,000 people could remain in Oleshky itself.
However, neither figure could be independently verified, particularly because Russian occupation authorities narrowly restrict access to information from the area.
Lubinets said on Sept. 16 that the residents had started escaping on foot independently across mined fields and under threat of constant Russian drone attacks, simply because they saw no other way out.
Before the truce was officially announced, Pope Leo XIV held a telephone discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 16, urging him to agree to an immediate ceasefire and allow the delivery of food and medical assistance to the city.
The pontiff then spoke to Zelensky on Monday, Oct. 19, reiterating his earlier request for a humanitarian ceasefire.
On Oct. 20, European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno declared a hunger strike in protest over the starvation of civilians in Oleshky.

Russia is producing ballistic missiles in volumes that exceed the global production capacity for Patriot interceptor missiles, stated Serhiy Beskrestnov (Flash), an advisor to the President of Ukraine on defense technologies.
"Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the number of Patriot interceptor missiles produced globally to counter them," he told reporters on Thursday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.

Beskrestnov noted that countering this threat requires an increase in the global production of PAC-3 interceptor missiles. At the same time, this process faces limitations, and scaling up production volumes takes time.

Six lanes and metro line under fire: Kyiv prepares about $22 million for backup river crossings after Russian strike on Southern Bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:52:25 UTC
02:52:25 KST

The Ukrainian government has instructed Kyiv to establish alternative routes after Russian attacks stopped traffic on one of the capital’s main bridges. The city authorities will bear the cost of the new crossings, with Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko saying the city needs an additional $22 million.
This year, Russia has launched tactics to spread panic among civilians and trigger more people to leave the country. In the latest attack, several Russia's ballistic missiles struck the Southern Bridge, used for vehicle and metro traffic, breaking a huge hole and paralyzing all the pathes. The bridge was closed. Now, there is a fear that more bridges can be targeted this way, dividing Kyiv in two parts.
The situation is urgent, as Ukrainian Transport Minister Mykola Kalashnyk says about 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro in Kyiv every day.
What is Kyiv’s response to the winter terror?
According to Klitschko, Kyiv convened the capital’s Defense Council on 28 October to find an answer to this difficult question.
The agenda included implementing a project to build combined water crossings over the Dnipro River and access roads to them.
“The military command will determine the locations, with approval to be granted, among others, by the Kyiv City Military Administration,” Klitschko said.
Under the government’s recommendations, the Kyiv city authorities must find $22 million for the project.
Klitschko had previously faced heavy criticism after it emerged that the city lacked sufficient shelters and last winter exposed serious shortcomings in preparing infrastructure for Russian attacks. These included a lack of alternative energy supply routes, poorly distributed energy, burst heating pipes that flooded apartments, and the inability of people with disabilities to reach shelters without elevators.
The mayor himself said the problems stemmed from the central government withholding funding, which had stalled numerous energy resilience projects and delayed their implementation.
The latest announcement also indicates that Kyiv has once again taken on the financial burden itself.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has been working with Japan on backup crossings. Tokyo has already delivered 720 meters of prefabricated bridge structures to Ukraine. The two sides are currently exploring how this equipment could be used to establish alternative crossings.
Step two: strengthening existing infrastructure
Another option is to reinforce existing bridges. City specialists are developing additional technical solutions to protect bridges across the Dnipro River, Klitschko said in his statement on 27 October, adding that proposals from the military had also been heard.
The issue of installing mobile shelters was also raised on the same day, the mayor of Kyiv said in a separate statement on his Telegram channel on 27 October. Despite intensifying Russian attacks and about, as Radio Svoboda reported in its article on 30 September, $11 million set aside in 2025, Kyiv still has only a handful of mobile shelters: LB reported in December 2025 that district tenders failed. Donors paid for the first one at a bus stop, the Kyiv City State Administration said on 15 October.
Klitschko raised the issue of shelters again after a court on 12 October ruled that local authorities must urgently install mobile shelters in public areas, including near public transport stops, parks, and squares, according to Kyiv’s Prosecutor’s Office.
Russia hits the Southern Bridge again
On 2 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times that Russian ruler Vladimir Putin had ordered the lifting of previous restrictions on airstrikes. Among new targets, according to him, were bridges, data centers, internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, and universities.
The night of 26–27 October showed what that looks like. Russia launched ballistic missile attacks in a few waves, and the second of them hit the Southern Bridge and the metro infrastructure on it, Klitschko said. The structure carries six lanes of road traffic and two metro tracks.
Zelenskyy put the night’s total at 16 ballistic missiles and blamed delays in deliveries of Patriot and NASAMS interceptors: “Every such delay is a new Russian hit on one target or another.”

Israel's election results are in: How a government is formed or new elections are triggered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:41:57 UTC
02:41:57 KST

Israel's Central Elections Committee completed the vote count Thursday, leaving the country facing a familiar political dilemma: Neither of the main blocs has secured the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Despite the inconclusive results, political consultations are already underway, with parties on both sides seeking to assemble a governing coalition and avoid another election. The next stage will place President Isaac Herzog at the center of the process, as party leaders prepare to recommend their preferred candidates for prime minister.
How does Israel form a government after an election, what happens if the first candidate fails, and when could voters be sent back to the polls?
Step by step: What happens after Election Day?
The first step is the official publication of the election results by the Central Elections Committee in Reshumot, Israel's official gazette. Under the law, the committee has eight days from Election Day to publish the results, making Wednesday, November 4, the final deadline.
The 26th Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on Tuesday, November 10, exactly two weeks after the October 27 election. But the race to form a government will begin before the new parliament formally convenes.
Once the Central Elections Committee submits the official results to President Herzog, he will summon representatives of the parties elected to the Knesset to the President's Residence. Each party will recommend the lawmaker it believes should be tasked with forming the next government.
Herzog is expected to begin consultations on Wednesday, November 4. The meetings are expected to continue Thursday and could extend into Friday.
Under Israeli law, the president has seven days from the publication of the official election results to complete consultations and assign the task of forming a government. If the results are published on November 4, that gives him until November 11, although he may make his decision earlier.
The president generally gives the mandate to the lawmaker he believes has the strongest chance of assembling a governing coalition. In most cases, that is the candidate who receives the largest number of recommendations from parliamentary factions.
The first attempt: 28 days, with a possible extension
The first lawmaker entrusted with forming a government has 28 days to complete coalition negotiations and present a government.
The president may grant additional time, but extensions cannot exceed 14 days in total, giving the candidate a maximum of 42 days.
If the candidate fails, Herzog has two options. He can assign the task to another member of Knesset, potentially the leader of the opposing political bloc, or inform the Knesset speaker that he sees no prospect of forming a government.
A second candidate would receive 28 days to form a coalition, without the possibility of an extension.
The last chance: 61 signatures in 21 days
If the president concludes that no candidate can form a government, or if the second candidate also fails, a final parliamentary mechanism comes into play.
A 21-day period opens during which at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 lawmakers can submit a written request asking the president to assign the task to a specific member of Knesset who has agreed to accept it.
If the required majority of lawmakers signs such a request, the designated candidate receives 14 days to form a government.
If that effort also fails, or no candidate secures the necessary 61 signatures within the allotted period, the Knesset is automatically dissolved and Israel heads to another election.
For now, the election may be over, but the political contest is far from settled. The coming weeks will determine whether the parties can negotiate a coalition capable of securing the Knesset's confidence or whether Israelis will once again be asked to return to the ballot box.

What Ceuta’s border crisis reveals about Frontex’s role in European security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:39:29 UTC
02:39:29 KST

A rare visit by Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia to Ceuta earlier this month has brought renewed attention to a migration crisis that continues to strain the Spanish territory on North Africa's Mediterranean coast, nearly three months after an unprecedented influx of migrants from Morocco.
Around 70,000 people crossed into Ceuta in late July, with humanitarian organisations estimating that at least 141 people died during the crossings.
Although most migrants have since left, thousands remained in the territory in October, many sleeping rough as local authorities struggled to provide shelter and essential services.
The royal visit, the first in nearly two decades, also came amid renewed tensions between Spain and Morocco, which maintains a longstanding sovereignty claim over Ceuta.
The crisis has exposed the pressures facing one of Europe's most sensitive external borders, where migration management still relies heavily on physical deterrence, cooperation with neighbouring countries, and emergency measures.
But Ceuta is neither an isolated incident nor an exception. It raises a broader question about the European Union's approach to border management: How does the bloc control its external frontiers, and who is accountable for the machinery behind them?
Part of the answer lies in the dramatic evolution of Frontex, the Warsaw-based European Border and Coast Guard Agency.
Over the past two decades, Frontex has evolved from an agency that primarily coordinates member states' border operations into a heavily funded institution with its own armed standing corps and expanding surveillance capabilities.
Yet, this technological militarisation has not delivered structural stability.
Its expanding use of aerial surveillance and cooperation with third-country authorities have also raised concerns about indirect pushbacks at sea and the division of legal responsibility between Frontex and national authorities.
Investigations into alleged pushbacks, oversight failures, and the agency's response to maritime emergencies have intensified scrutiny of whether Europe's expanding border security system is compatible with its fundamental rights obligations.
The rise of Frontex
As European integration deepened, migration and border management increasingly became matters of security policy.
The 1992 Maastricht Treaty marked an early step towards intergovernmental cooperation on migration, while the 1997 Amsterdam Treaty established the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice (AFSJ) as a central element of EU policy.
The 1999 Tampere European Council summit subsequently laid the foundations for the Common European Asylum System (CEAS).
Population movements following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the EU's eastward enlargement and the September 11, 2001 attacks further reinforced the association between migration, terrorism and border security.
Although a 2001 German-Italian proposal for a joint border police force stalled over concerns about national sovereignty, the 2003 Thessaloniki summit agreed to establish an operational mechanism to manage the EU's external borders.
The Council subsequently established Frontex under Regulation (EC) No 2007/2004, based on Articles 62 and 66 of the EC Treaty. Headquartered in Warsaw, the agency began operations on 1 May 2005.
Initially responsible for coordinating border operations among member states, conducting risk assessments and providing training, Frontex has gradually evolved into a large operational border force with armed personnel.
Its budget, approximately €6 million in 2005, has grown to more than €900 million annually, while successive regulatory changes, notably Regulation (EU) 2016/1624 and Regulation (EU) 2019/1896, have expanded its powers.
Under the 2019 regulation, Frontex aims to reach an operational capacity of 10,000 personnel by 2027, comprising 3,000 statutory Frontex staff and 7,000 personnel contributed by member states.
Equipped with uniforms, operational equipment and the authority to carry firearms under specified conditions, the standing corps represents a significant departure from the agency's original coordinating role.
Europe's expanding border security framework
The EU's increasingly security-oriented approach to migration was further reinforced by the adoption of the New Pact on Migration and Asylum in 2024.
The pact introduced a seven-day screening procedure at the EU's external borders, along with accelerated asylum and return procedures for certain applicants.
Under the framework, some asylum seekers may be treated as not having formally entered EU territory while their applications are processed, raising concerns about access to asylum procedures and legal safeguards.
The pact also expanded the Eurodac biometric database, lowering the minimum age for collecting fingerprints and facial images from 14 to six.
Its solidarity mechanism allows member states to contribute through relocation, financial payments or other forms of support, while the broader framework places greater emphasis on cooperation with third countries in managing migration.
Yet as Frontex's operational powers have expanded, questions have persisted over who bears responsibility when alleged rights violations occur.
The agency operates alongside national border authorities, creating a complex division of responsibilities between Frontex, host member states and other participating countries.
While national authorities retain responsibility for many operational decisions, Frontex provides personnel, surveillance capabilities and intelligence support.
Critics argue that this arrangement can complicate efforts to establish responsibility for alleged violations and make it more difficult for affected individuals to seek legal redress.
Pushbacks and the accountability question
Investigations by European oversight bodies and journalists have raised serious concerns about Frontex's involvement in unlawful pushbacks and how it handles evidence of alleged rights violations.
A European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) investigation found that then-executive director Fabrice Leggeri and senior agency officials were aware of illegal pushbacks carried out by the Greek Coast Guard in the Aegean Sea.
The investigation documented failures to report incidents and attempts to conceal evidence of alleged violations, including deleting records and diverting surveillance flights. It also raised concerns about interference with the agency's fundamental rights monitoring mechanisms.
Leggeri resigned in April 2022. The European Parliament subsequently refused to grant discharge for Frontex's 2020 budget, citing concerns over the agency's management and accountability.
Questions about Frontex's responsibilities also emerged following the Adriana shipwreck off the coast of Greece in June 2023, in which hundreds of migrants and asylum seekers died.
An investigation by the European Ombudsman found shortcomings in Frontex's response to maritime emergencies and raised questions about its ability to act independently when vessels are in distress.
The agency detected the overcrowded vessel by aerial surveillance before it sank, but the disaster exposed gaps in communication, coordination, and responsibility between Frontex and national authorities.
Such controversies have fuelled calls for greater oversight and, in some cases, the agency's dismantling.
The Abolish Frontex movement, a coalition of civil society organisations and activists across Europe, has campaigned to abolish the agency, citing alleged rights violations, biometric surveillance, and its role in enforcing restrictive border policies.
Frontex's growing reliance on aerial and satellite surveillance, alongside its maritime operations, has raised concerns that its border-monitoring practices could facilitate interceptions that circumvent international maritime law and search-and-rescue obligations.
Operating from bases in Malta and Pantelleria, unmanned aerial vehicles developed by Israel Aerospace Industries and Elbit Systems, alongside the EU's Copernicus satellite network, are used to detect migrant boats in the Mediterranean.
Critics argue that surveillance information can be shared with the Libyan Coast Guard or Tunisian authorities rather than civilian rescue organisations, enabling third-country forces to intercept migrants and return them to countries where they may face abuse.
Because such interceptions can occur without direct physical involvement by EU personnel, questions have emerged about whether Frontex is facilitating what critics describe as “refoulement by proxy”.
Human Rights Watch has accused Frontex of complicity in abuses against migrants intercepted and returned to Libya, raising concerns about the agency's responsibilities under the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they face serious threats to their safety or fundamental rights.
The paradox of fortress Europe
Events along Ceuta’s perimeter and unmanned patrols tracing the central Mediterranean are two sides of the same coin.
On the periphery, frontline states rely on ad hoc physical barriers, bilateral appeasement of authoritarian transit regimes, and immediate pushbacks.
Meanwhile, at the institutional core in Brussels and Warsaw, billions of euros continue to pour into an autonomous surveillance and security architecture designed to insulate the European mainland from the human reality at its gates.
As Frontex marches toward its 2027 goal of a 10,000-strong armed standing corps under the codified framework of the 2024 New Pact on Migration and Asylum, the central paradox remains unresolved.
Advanced surveillance drones, automated biometric screening, and outsourced interception do not eliminate the root causes of forced displacement; they can instead shift difficult questions of legal responsibility into a fragmented jurisdictional space.
Unless subject to enforceable judicial oversight by the Court of Justice of the European Union, independent scrutiny by civil society, and uncompromising operational transparency, Frontex will remain what the Ceuta crisis so starkly laid bare: a multibillion-euro “security illusion” that continually undermines the foundational human rights norms upon which the European Union was built.
