Syria: Flash floods kill four, collapse bridges, roads
At least four people, two of them children, have been killed after sustained heavy rainfall caused flash flooding in six provinces across Syria, local media and authorities reported on Thursday.
Heavy rain on Wednesday left at least three bridges out of service in the eastern province of Deir ez-Zor, while key roads have also been damaged.
The flooding has disrupted water supplies, while authorities shuttered schools in Deir ez-Zor, Raqqa, and Hasakeh on Thursday amid the storms.
Hundreds of families have been forced to leave their homes and the displacement camps where they reside in recent days.

Hospitals, schools, and bakeries have been affected by the flooding while disaster management teams have warned people about the risk of drowning.
Rescue teams were sent to the village of Kasrat Surour after a drainage crossing collapsed and left over 100 families surrounded by floodwater.
The flooding has caused major disruptions to traffic, including on the Aleppo-Raqqa highway.
Syrian army helicopters have been deployed across the country to help those who have been stranded.
The flooding has had far-reaching impacts, with telecommunications disrupted in Deir ez-Zor due to damage caused to fibre optic cables on the Homs-Deir ez-Zor and Aleppo- Deir ez-Zor routes.
The minister of emergencies and disaster management, Raed al-Saleh, has urged residents in eastern governorates to remain in their homes unless absolutely necessary, and to steer away from low-lying areas.
He has also called on people to refrain from trying to cross flooded roads, which comes as rescue teams grapple to deal with the situation.
Syria has been battling thunderstorms, hail, and strong winds in recent weeks, with the meteorological directorate warning that the storms and lightning are set to continue.
Syria was last hit with flooding in May, affecting scores of farmers during harvest season and destroying important wheat, barley, cotton, and vegetable crops.
The flooding in Aleppo and Idlib affected over 19,000 people and damaged over 3,400 shelters.

World Stroke Day: how to recognize dangerous symptoms, save a life, and prevent the disease
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:37:16 EET
02:37:16 KST

World Stroke Day: how to recognize dangerous symptoms, save a life, and prevent the disease
Kyiv • UNN
Stroke symptoms occur suddenly: call 103 or 112 immediately. In Ukraine, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation are covered by the NHSU.
On October 29, the world observes World Stroke Day—a disease that can cause disability or death within minutes. Its first signs are sometimes mistaken for fatigue or stress, resulting in precious time being lost. UNN explains how to recognize the symptoms, help the affected person, and receive free treatment in Ukraine.
Details
The World Stroke Organization’s campaign in 2026 is being held under the slogan Every Minute Counts ("Every minute matters"). Its aim is to teach people to recognize the danger in time and call emergency services.
What a stroke is and why it occurs
A stroke is an acute disruption of cerebral blood circulation. Without sufficient oxygen, brain cells begin to die. Consequences may include impaired movement, speech, vision, memory, and coordination. An ischemic stroke occurs because a blood vessel is blocked by a clot and accounts for the majority of cases. A hemorrhagic stroke is caused by a vessel rupturing and bleeding. Treatment for these conditions differs, and it is impossible to determine the type based on external signs: urgent diagnosis using CT or MRI is required.
Contrary to everyday myths, a stroke does not occur only in older people. If a young person has problems with high blood pressure, heart disease, heart rhythm disorders, diabetes, or vascular damage, they are just as likely to suffer a stroke as older patients.
How many strokes are recorded in Ukraine and worldwide
According to WHO estimates, 11.9 million new strokes occurred worldwide in 2021. Approximately one in four adults is at risk of experiencing a stroke during their lifetime. In addition, stroke is one of the leading causes of death and disability both in Ukraine and in most countries worldwide.
According to the Ministry of Health, 128,075 Ukrainians were diagnosed with a stroke in 2024. A statement by the Kyiv Regional Military Administration dated October 29, 2026, says that more than 90,000 cases of acute stroke were treated in Ukraine during the first eight months of this year. In turn, Ministry of Health expert Professor Yuriy Flomin reported that 68,116 hospitalizations for acute stroke were recorded during the first half of 2026. The share of hospitalizations at facilities with a contract with the National Health Service of Ukraine increased from 86% in 2021 to 96.5% in the first half of 2026.
Speaking about strokes in Ukraine, it is worth emphasizing that, despite the war, access to specialized care for people suffering from this condition is improving. According to the data cited by Flomin, thrombolysis was used in 18% of hospitalizations for ischemic stroke during the first half of 2026, while mechanical thrombectomy was performed in 3.7%. CT, MRI, or angiographic examinations were recorded in 98.1% of hospitalizations for acute stroke.
How to recognize a stroke: five warning signs that should not be ignored
Signs of a stroke usually appear suddenly. Ukrainian doctors advise remembering them using the acronym MOZOK, where
-  M - speech. The person speaks unclearly, confuses words
or does not understand the other person; 
-  O - face. The corner of the mouth droops, and the smile becomes
asymmetrical; 
-  Z - dizziness. Balance and
coordination are impaired; sometimes a sudden, very severe headache occurs; 
-  O - eyes. Vision suddenly deteriorates, and objects appear double; 
-  K - limbs. An arm or leg becomes weak or numb,
more often on one side of the body. 
You can also ask a person suspected of having a stroke to smile, repeat a sentence, and raise both arms. Difficulty performing even one of these actions is a reason to call an ambulance immediately.
A severe headache, vomiting, or sudden drowsiness also requires attention, especially if it occurs simultaneously with other signs. Sometimes the symptoms disappear quickly. This may be a transient ischemic attack—a short-term disruption of blood flow to the brain that warns of the risk of a stroke. Even if the person feels better, emergency examination is necessary.
How to recognize a stroke: Ukrainians reminded of dangerous symptoms28.10.24, 15:57 • 13579 views
First aid for a stroke: what to do before medical professionals arrive
First of all, you should immediately call 103 or 112. The dispatcher needs to be told the address, the symptoms, and that a stroke is suspected. It is also important to remember when the person was last known to be well, as the choice of treatment depends on this.
Until the medics arrive, ensure that the person remains calm and loosen any tight clothing. If the patient is conscious, help them assume a comfortable position. If the person is unconscious but breathing normally, place them on their side. This is done to prevent stomach contents from entering the lungs if the patient begins to vomit. This position also reduces the risk of choking on their own saliva.
If normal breathing is absent, begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation according to the dispatcher’s instructions.
A person suspected of having a brain hemorrhage or thrombosis of the brain’s blood vessels must not be given water, medication, or food. Because of impaired swallowing, they may choke. Aspirin is particularly dangerous among medications. It can harm the person because it thins the blood. This is life-threatening in the case of a hemorrhagic stroke.
Before the medics arrive, prepare the person’s documents, a list of the medications the patient takes, and information about any comorbidities so that dispatch to the hospital is not delayed because of this.
How to receive free stroke treatment in Ukraine
Acute stroke care is covered by the Medical Guarantees Program at hospitals that have the relevant contract with the NHSU. In August 2026, the service reported that there were 179 such facilities.
Free services include an examination by a neurologist, a CT or MRI scan, tests, round-the-clock monitoring, medications, inpatient treatment, food, and early rehabilitation. When indicated, thrombolysis (dissolving a clot with medication), mechanical thrombectomy (removing a clot through the blood vessels), or neurosurgical intervention is performed. The treatment method depends on the type of stroke and when the symptoms began. Thrombolysis is possible only under certain conditions and within a limited time, and it is not used in cases of hemorrhage.
According to international recommendations, emergency neuroimaging should be performed as soon as possible. In Ukraine, the standard provides for aiming to perform a CT or MRI scan no later than 30 minutes after the patient is admitted. The NHSU emphasizes separately that patients should not have to pay for a CT or MRI when a stroke is suspected as part of inpatient care. You can clarify the list of facilities or complain about demands for payment by calling 16-77.
Who is at risk and how to prevent a stroke
The main risk factor in this situation is high blood pressure. It may cause no symptoms while gradually damaging the blood vessels. Smoking, high cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, alcohol, and heart rhythm disorders are also dangerous.
To prevent stroke, the WHO recommends monitoring blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol; not stopping prescribed treatment; quitting smoking; limiting salt and alcohol; and eating more vegetables and fruit. At least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week is beneficial if there are no contraindications.
For heart rhythm disorders, a doctor may prescribe medications to prevent blood clots. However, taking such medications without medical supervision is dangerous.
Ukraine also has the "Health Screening 40+" program for the early detection of risks, while under the "Affordable Medicines" program, certain medications can be obtained free of charge or with a co-payment.
Life after a stroke: is recovery possible?
Although many strokes still end in the patient’s death at home or in hospital, many patients overcome this condition with the help of medical professionals and survive. However, the consequences of the illness may include impaired movement, speech, memory, or swallowing, as well as anxiety, fatigue, and depressive symptoms. Some patients require long-term—and sometimes lifelong—assistance from others. The prognosis depends on the severity of the stroke, the timeliness of treatment, and rehabilitation.
Rehabilitation begins as soon as the patient’s condition allows. A physical therapist, occupational therapist, speech and language therapist, and psychologist help restore movement, communication, and self-care. The process may take months and requires family support.
After discharge in Ukraine, a person may receive inpatient or outpatient rehabilitation, as indicated. At facilities that have a contract with the NHSU, it is covered by the Medical Guarantees Program. A doctor refers a patient for an inpatient course; transfer from another facility is also possible. The sessions are tailored to each individual: one person may need to learn to walk again, while another may need to restore swallowing or the ability to form words. It is important for relatives to help the person follow the specialists’ recommendations, but not to force them to do exercises beyond their capabilities.
To prevent a recurrent stroke, it is necessary to monitor blood pressure, glucose, and cholesterol and follow the doctor’s instructions. Unfortunately, a stroke cannot always be prevented. However, knowing the signs of a stroke according to the B.E.-F.A.S.T. formula, promptly calling 103, and managing risk factors can help save lives and reduce the likelihood of severe consequences.
Let us remind you
The Ministry of Health warns that recently more and more middle-aged people have been suffering strokes: as of 2019, more than 62% of stroke cases occurred in people under the age of 70.

Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.
Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.
The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.
The president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.
It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.
With almost all the votes counted, Netanyahu’s coalition has 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s bloc has 48, and the Joint List and Ra’am together have 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.
The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.
On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.
Voting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.
Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.
The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed the possibility of tactical voting in the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.
One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.
Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are being accused of taking Qatari money for promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.
“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.

UAE sentences eight people to life over arms supplies to Sudan’s army
Defendants handed life sentences amid tensions between Khartoum and Abu Dhabi over Sudan’s war and the RSF.
A court in the United Arab Emirates has sentenced eight people to life imprisonment over arms trafficking and money laundering to Sudan’s army, state media report.
The individuals supplied weapons and military equipment to the Sudanese army and were part of a money-laundering network connecting the two countries, the Emirati state-run news agency WAM said on Thursday.
It said the Abu Dhabi Federal Court of Appeal concluded on Thursday that the convicted individuals had participated in an integrated scheme for the illicit trafficking of weapons, ammunition and military equipment.
The accused were also found to have forged documents using companies and bank accounts in the UAE to channel funds relating to the arms deals and “conceal” their sources and destinations.
The court ordered the confiscation of ammunition and communications devices used in the crimes and the deportation of those convicted from the UAE after serving their sentences, WAM reported.
The “arms deals, money laundering endangered UAE interests”, the court order said.
Ties between the UAE and Sudan have deteriorated as the Sudanese military has accused Abu Dhabi of supplying arms to its rival in Sudan’s civil war, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group, which it has been fighting since April 2023. The UAE has denied the allegation.
The war has displaced more than 14 million people and created severe poverty and food shortages.
This week, more than 100 people – mostly women and children – were killed when military drones hit a busy city market frequented by RSF fighters in the city of Nyala in the western region of Darfur.
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said a second attack hit a civilian neighbourhood. MSF said a hospital it supports in Nyala received 36 bodies in the hours after that attack, 21 of them wearing civilian clothing, and its teams saw more than 150 wounded in the emergency room.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has previously accused the RSF of carrying out war crimes and a possible crime against humanity in its takeover of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur state, after forcing Sudan’s army to withdraw from its last stronghold in the Darfur region.

Rights groups petition Israeli court over Hebron expulsions

Rights groups petition Israeli court over expulsion of thousands of Palestinians from Hebron
Palestinian rights groups have filed an urgent petition with Israel's Supreme Court demanding the return of hundreds of families forcibly displaced from their homes in Hebron, as Israeli forces continue their military siege of the occupied West Bank city for a seventh consecutive day.
The petition calls for Palestinians expelled from the Al-Jalda, Ein Deir Bahha and Khallat Al-Maghariba neighbourhoods to be allowed to return to their homes, many of which have been seized by Israeli forces and converted into military barracks.
Lawyer Bassam Al-Qawasmi, founder of the All-Palestinian Gathering, said the court was awaiting responses from the Israeli military prosecution and army before proceeding with the case.
He explained that the legal action was launched after obtaining authorisation from Hebron Municipality and families affected by the forced displacement, with support from the city's newly established Relief and Support Committee.
The petition seeks to end the forced displacement, alleviate residents' suffering and secure their return to their homes.
Israeli forces have expelled thousands of Palestinians from neighbourhoods across Hebron since launching a major military operation last Friday after two Israeli soldiers were killed in an attack, imposing severe restrictions on movement and blocking access to residential areas.
More than 4,000 Palestinians have been displaced, while dozens of homes have been seized and converted into military outposts. The Israeli army has also demolished dozens of Palestinian buildings across the city.
Siege enters seventh day
Israeli forces continued raids and closures around Hebron's Old City on Thursday, continuing to occupy Palestinian homes in Al-Jalda and Ein Deir Bahha.
Troops also closed several iron gates surrounding the Old City, further restricting movement across the area.
The military operation has severely disrupted education, with dozens of schools suspending in-person classes and thousands of pupils forced to rely on remote learning and educational assignments.
According to Palestinian news agency Wafa, Israeli forces injured two Palestinians and detained seven others on Thursday, while settlers attacked Palestinian residents and vehicles in the Ras Al-Joura area near the city's northern entrance.
The Palestinian Prisoner's Society said on Wednesday that at least 110 Palestinians had been detained across the Hebron governorate since the operation began, including three women and seven children.
Israeli forces have also isolated 12 villages and communities in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, preventing residents from accessing markets, hospitals and essential services.
The offensive began after two Israeli soldiers were killed in a shooting near the illegal Israeli settlement of Telem last week. The Palestinian gunmen involved were subsequently killed by Israeli forces.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the closure of Hebron and instructed security forces to prepare for a wider lockdown across the occupied West Bank.
Extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich subsequently called for a military campaign in the territory similar to Israel's assault on Gaza.
UN warns of collective punishment
The United Nations and human rights organisations have condemned the operation, warning that mass displacement and sweeping restrictions on civilians could constitute serious violations of international law.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said collective punishment was a grave violation of international law, warning that threats to empty entire neighbourhoods raised serious concerns about ethnic cleansing.
Israeli human rights organisation B'Tselem described the operation as an act of collective punishment rather than a security measure.
Palestinian rights group Al-Haq also accused Israel of violating international law through its military siege.
Roland Friedrich, director of UNRWA Affairs in the occupied West Bank, warned that the displacement echoed Israeli operations in the northern West Bank in early 2025, where more than 34,000 Palestinian refugees remain forcibly displaced.

Meet the front-runners to replace Lagarde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:22:06 UTC
02:22:06 KST

A sign indicates the pedestrian way to the European Central Bank headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany on Oct. 23, 2026. | Kirill Kudyavtsev/AFP via Getty Images
FRANKFURT — The race to replace Christine Lagarde has reached fever pitch after she officially announced her intention to depart the European Central Bank in February next year.
The two leading contenders are familiar figures from the eurozone’s central banking circuit: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos, a measured economist with a reputation for quiet authority, and Dutchman Klaas Knot, a former hawk whose years on the ECB’s governing council left a more complicated legacy.
A recent Bloomberg survey of economists gives de Cos a slender lead: 12 respondents picked him, against nine for Knot. The survey offers a snapshot of expert preferences, not a forecast of the outcome. EU leaders will make the appointment, with national claims and other ECB vacancies likely to shape negotiations.
Advertisement
The choices will also be influenced by horse trading over what will likely be a package deal with the opportunity to fill the two executive board seats that will be vacant in January and May.
Softly spoken de Cos
An economist with a Ph.D. from the University of Madrid, de Cos joined the Bank of Spain in 1997, moved to Frankfurt in 2004 to be an adviser to the ECB’s executive board, before returning to the Spanish central bank. He rose through the ranks to become governor, serving from 2018 to 2024. In this role he restored the Bank of Spain’s reputation after a series of missteps before and during the financial crisis.
His achievement was implicitly acknowledged by his appointment to two terms as chair of the Basel Committee for Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for bank regulation. He now runs the Bank for International Settlements, the institution often described as the central bankers’ central bank.
His style is low-key: a modest dove, meaning that he is more attentive than hawks to growth and employment alongside inflation. Still, when inflation surged in 2022, de Cos backed the ECB’s shift toward higher rates. Equally, he has little time for governments that put off essential pension system reforms, having published a sharp critique of the Pedro Sanchez government while at the Bank of Spain.
His case
De Cos has long been groomed by Lagarde’s predecessor Mario Draghi, whose voice continues to carry a heavy weight in European economic debates and may influence the preference of some countries as they mull who to place at the top of the Frankfurt institution.
As France faces mounting debt pressures, de Cos’ experience as a senior Bank of Spain economist during the eurozone crisis could convince EU governments that he is the best fit. Galo Nuño, vice dean and professor of economics at IE University and a former alternate member of the ECB governing council, called it “a huge advantage.”
Advertisement
His challenges
The political arithmetic, however, could work against the Spaniard. France is keen to secure the role of the ECB chief economist, which becomes vacant in May 2027. Some officials may want to avoid pairing the ECB presidency and chief economist roles with candidates from highly indebted countries.
With inflation above target and the eurozone having lived through a severe inflation shock in 2022, some leaders may prefer a candidate with a more clearly hawkish record.
Enter: Klaas Knot.
Knot: Hawk turned pragmatist
Knot also has a strong economic background, boasting a Ph.D. from the University of Groningen. After early positions at the Dutch central bank, De Nederlandsche Bank, and the International Monetary Fund, he moved into senior roles at the Dutch Finance Ministry and returned to the DNB, which he led from 2011 to 2025. He has also chaired the Financial Stability Board, the global body tasked with monitoring risks to the financial system.
For much of Draghi’s presidency, Knot was a staunch hawk who publicly challenged the ECB’s stimulus measures. In September 2019, he called the package “disproportionate.”
His relationship with the ECB’s leadership was more harmonious under Lagarde. He supported both her pandemic crisis response package, PEPP, as well as the Transmission Protection Mechanism — a potentially more radical tool than any brought in under Draghi which allows the ECB to buy up unlimited debt of a single EU member country.
Advertisement
Knot remained an early advocate of raising rates when inflation took off but came to be described as a pragmatic hawk and team player.
His case
Supporters argue that a hawkish president could help the ECB support Southern European economies during a debt crisis while reassuring consumers and investors that the bank remains committed to price stability.
Knot’s former role as chair of the G20’s Financial Stability Board could also boost his case. Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding argued that “the question who may be best placed to deal with potential financial turbulences will likely play a key role in the choice of new ECB leaders.” This role was also Draghi’s springboard.
His challenges
Germany’s ambitions could be a stumbling block, as Northern European hawks will have had their turn with Knot. EFG Bank chief economist Stefan Gerlach said: “If Knot is appointed, then Germany can hardly argue that it is its turn to appoint the president after him.”
Some veteran governors still view Knot’s public break with Draghi as disloyal.
What happens now?
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said a decision would be taken by year-end, with eurozone ministers set to gather under the banner of the European Council in mid-December.
Advertisement
When it comes who will win the race, the history could cut both ways.
Nuño, who has seen both candidates in action, said each brings monetary-policy expertise and the political pragmatism needed to manage the challenges ahead.
The choice, then, will turn on which mix of policy temperament and political arithmetic EU leaders want at the top.

‘We make shit houses great again’: Visit Norway cleans up after Trump’s insult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:22:01 UTC
02:22:01 KST

Some might find it decidedly incommodious to be dumped on by Donald Trump as a “shithouse country”. Not the Norwegian tourist board, which chose instead to lift the lid on some of the nation’s loveliest lavatories.
“Are these the world’s best shit houses?” asked Visit Norway on its website, days after the US president vented his fury once more over failing to win the Nobel peace prize by describing Norway as a “shithouse country” at a rally on Sunday.
“Norway makes shit houses great again!” the agency continued above pictures of some of the country’s most striking public conveniences, adding: “These toilets are worth a visit, both when you really have to go – and when you don’t.”
Trump delivered his tirade at a rally in Michigan days before the US midterm elections. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually,” he declared, using a term he has previously applied to Haiti, Libya, Somalia and Yemen.
He added that he would welcome migrants from some countries but not Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize”. Earlier this month, Trump denounced the decision to award the prize to Navi Pillay, a former international criminal court judge.
“This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” he said. “I never heard of this person. The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited … And we will not forget, Norway.”
Along 18 designated scenic routes around Norway, Visit Norway said, leading architects had been tasked with transforming the humble wayside privy into an attraction in its own right. Several have since won international architecture awards.
The agency pictured a series of designer public conveniences, many of them architecturally striking and all offering breathtaking vistas overlooking fjords, beside rushing rivers and foaming waterfalls, and at stunning scenic viewpoints.
They “invite you to take your time and enjoy the scenery, even if you don’t have any business to take care of”, Visit Norway said, highlighting – among others – the restrooms at the Stegastein viewpoint in the Sognefjord region of western Norway.
This particular comfort station, the tourist board noted with uninhibited pride, had been ranked among the 10 best public toilets in the world by DesignCurial, the online architecture, design and interiors magazine.
Combining clean, minimalist lines with the fjord’s rugged and brooding landscape, the loos are famous for their large, black-tinted glass windows, which allow visitors a sweeping view from the throne while remaining invisible from the outside.
It also highlighted the unique, wave-shaped Ureddplassen loo on the wild coast of Helgeland, the southernmost district of northern Norway, hailed by several international publications as the most scenic restroom in the world.
Also featured are the solar-powered modernist bog at the Utsikten viewpoint, the “Instagram-worthy” Tungeneset loo (“looks pretty good underneath the northern lights”), and the world-famous triangular “golden toilet” on Senja island.
Jens Kjeldsen, a rhetoric professor at the University of Bergen, said that under the circumstances, Visit Norway’s response was well judged. “It’s like the bully in kindergarten,” he told NRK public television. “If you get too serious, the bully wins.”
Evgenia Egorova, a senior consultant at Visit Norway, told the broadcaster the response to its social media fightback had been immense. “The world needs a little laugh,” she said. “We thought: let’s meet them with kindness, and a little humour.”
Visit Norway said it had more stylish loos in the pipeline, including a forest-inspired latrine using dried wood from more than 60 trees. “Get ready for the pit stop of your life,” it urged, before signing off with a cheery: “Toodeloo!”
The Nobel peace prize is famously not awarded by the nation or even the government of Norway, but by the Nobel prize committee, which operates independently – something Trump “knows very well”, the foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said. “We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering.”

The interim report, Young People and Work, led by Alan Milburn, was published on May 28, 2026, with the final comprehensive recommendations report expected next month.
The Young People and Work report is an independent review of the increase in the number of young people who are not in education, employment or training.

Ukrainian Producer Oleg Kokhan: ‘The World Must See Ukraine Beyond War and Victimhood’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:08:29 UTC
02:08:29 KST

Oleg Kokhan is a Ukrainian theater and film producer and founder of SOTA Cinema Group, known for his collaborations with prominent Ukrainian directors, including Kira Muratova and Myroslav Slaboshpytskyi.
In 2026, he was invited to join the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, the organization behind the Oscars. In this interview with Kyiv Post, Kokhan discusses the international prospects for Ukrainian cinema, the need to decolonize the global cultural landscape, and the transition from festival success to a fully fledged global film industry.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv Post: You are one of five Ukrainian producers invited to join the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences this year. Academy membership opens up new professional opportunities. What does this mean for Ukraine? How do you plan to use this access to tools of global influence?
Oleg Kokhan: The entry of Ukrainian producers into the Academy is not simply a personal professional victory or a status symbol. It expands our presence on the world’s most influential film platform. Until now, Ukraine has more often been an object of attention for global cinema: People discussed us, sympathized with us, and foreign filmmakers made films about us. Academy membership gives us the right and the tools to become full-fledged participants and help shape the global cinematic agenda. We gain a direct voice in determining the best, but more importantly, we gain the opportunity to build a network of cultural influence.
Day of Terror: Russian Strikes Kill 20, Wound At Least 109 Across Ukraine
This means converting attention into real industry collaboration and, consequently, creating new films. It means advocating for Ukrainian films and working systematically to ensure that Hollywood is no longer surprised by our ability to make world-class cinema, but instead begins to see Ukraine as an equal, strong partner with unique experience and talent.
Hollywood has worked with Russia for decades and continues to do so despite its imperialist policies. What still prevents the global film industry from recognizing the real causes of Russia’s war against Ukraine?
Two things stand in the way: The inertia of comfort and the optical illusion in which the West has lived for more than a century.
Hollywood is an enormous, pragmatic corporate machine. For decades, Russian culture invested billions of dollars in creating the myth of “great Russian culture” – Dostoevsky and ballet. This myth was convenient, aesthetically packaged, and marketed as a universal brand of Eastern Europe. Everything around it – Ukrainian, Georgian, and Kazakh culture – was viewed by the Western film world through a Moscow-centric lens as “provincial folklore.”
When the full-scale war began, the West faced an uncomfortable realization: This “humanistic ballet” and “great literature” had produced real rapists and war criminals. Yet the inertia of thought still leads many in Hollywood to separate Putin from Russian culture, failing to understand that Russian culture itself has been and remains the principal source of legitimacy for Russian imperialism.
Our task as producers is not simply to call for a boycott, although that is critically necessary, but to decolonize the Western perspective. We must offer our own distinctive, profound, and competitive content that proves one thing: The center of European culture today is in Kyiv, not Moscow.
“War Through the Eyes of Animals” explores the humanitarian and environmental consequences of war through the eyes of different living creatures. What inspired you to create this particular cinematic testimony to Russian aggression?
The impulse came from a universal code that we did not invent but that can break through the “wall of war fatigue” around Ukraine that has formed across the world.
During a major war, the information space becomes saturated with images of violence, destruction, and human suffering. Unfortunately, the human psyche has defense mechanisms: Over time, Western audiences subconsciously shut themselves off from other people’s pain to preserve their own peace of mind.
Animals in this war are utterly defenseless witnesses and victims. They have no political convictions, do not take up arms, and cannot call for help. They are the ultimate metaphor for innocence. When we show the tragedy of this war through the eyes of a dog, a goat, or an eagle, we reach straight into the heart of any person, regardless of whether they live in New York, Tokyo, or Paris.
“War Through the Eyes of Animals” is an anthology film that shifts Ukrainian trauma from a narrow geopolitical context into the realm of a global environmental and humanitarian catastrophe. It is testimony that hostile propaganda cannot refute.
The world premiere of “War Through the Eyes of Animals” took place at the Tribeca Festival in the US last year, while its Ukrainian premiere was held at the Odesa International Film Festival on World Animal Day. Based on your observations, how have Western and Ukrainian audiences responded to the meanings the filmmakers sought to convey?
The reactions differ greatly in emotional intensity, but they are equally profound in substance.
For Western audiences, particularly at Tribeca, the film was a genuine cultural and psychological shock. It showed them that war destroys not only infrastructure but also the biosphere, ecosystems, and humanity itself. Through this film, Western viewers experienced guilt and a powerful sense of empathy, connecting with our pain through their own love of animals.
For Ukrainian audiences, the film became a form of therapy and a mirror reflecting their own dignity. In Ukraine, compassion for animals on the front lines and in de-occupied cities remains one of the key markers of our civilizational difference from the enemy. Our soldiers rescue kittens from shelling and lead horses and wild animals to safety. For Ukrainians, “War Through the Eyes of Animals” affirms our moral superiority and our love of life.
Poster of the War Through the Eyes of Animals
The world has grown accustomed to seeing Ukraine through the lens of war. What Ukrainian stories should reach international screens next to change that perception?
The world must see Ukraine not as a “victim,” but as a country of brave, progressive, and talented people. We need to move beyond documenting trauma alone. The next wave of Ukrainian cinema must offer the world:
Universal genre stories with a distinct national identity – high-quality psychological thrillers, historical dramas, and intellectually ambitious mainstream cinema; stories of our transformation – about people who, amid the greatest catastrophe of the 21st century, are building new institutions, developing technologies, rethinking ethics, and changing the world; and a profound reexamination of our heritage – stories about our avant-garde figures, from artists to military leaders and philosophers, that demonstrate that Ukraine has always been part of European modernism.
We must stop asking the world for empathy. We must give the world cinema that inspires admiration, respect, and intellectual curiosity.
You have worked with Kira Muratova, Myroslav Slaboshpytskyi, and other exceptional directors. What still prevents Ukrainian cinema from claiming its rightful place in the global market?
Working with true artists makes one thing clear: We have never lacked talent or originality of vision. Muratova represents the absolute avant-garde of world cinema, while Slaboshpytskyi made a film that transformed the global understanding of cinematic language. So what prevents us from becoming consistent players in the global market? The lack of a sustainable industry ecosystem.
There is a systemic shortage of venture-style producing expertise: Cinema is an art, but the film industry is a tough business. There is a lack of consistent state policy and institutional continuity – the market cannot develop when the rules change every year and transparent competitive procedures are replaced by chaos. There is also isolation from private capital – our business community has yet to learn to view cinema as a tool for capitalization and national branding.
Cinema is an industry. Without strong institutions, a transparent market, and international co-productions, even the most outstanding genius remains an isolated flash of brilliance rather than part of a system.
What changes are needed for Ukrainian films to secure wider international distribution and more frequent Oscar nominations?
We need a clear, pragmatic three-part strategy.
International co-production as the standard: Ukrainian films should not be developed in an “internal bubble.” From the idea stage onward, we must bring in European and American partners, funds, and international sales agents. This immediately provides a guarantee of distribution in foreign markets.
Aggressive, professional promotion – Oscar campaigns: Making an Oscar shortlist or receiving a nomination is not a lottery. It requires a costly, mathematically calculated marketing and PR campaign in the US. The state and private businesses must pool resources to finance these promotional tours and screenings.
Quality standards and market discipline: We must abandon our tendency to be lenient with ourselves. Our products must meet the highest international standards in screenwriting, sound design, and special effects.
What are your plans and ambitions for the near future?
My main strategic goal is to transform Ukrainian cinema from a film culture known for festival successes into a globally operating industry. As for specific projects, they include a cinematic tribute to Kira Muratova, a major documentary project, and two historical films. We must create cinema that does more than document the past or trauma – it must shape the image of a victorious, strong, and modern Ukraine of the future.

Only 6,000 available places for the entire Ukraine: the Ministry for Communities and Territories Development reported a critical situation with housing for internally displaced persons
Kyiv • UNN
Around 6,000 places are available for internally displaced persons in Ukraine, but new evacuations from frontline regions are expected. Over nine months, the centers received 128,000 people.
There are around 6,000 vacant places remaining in Ukraine for the temporary accommodation of internally displaced persons, and in the near future the country may face new waves of evacuations from frontline regions. This was reported by Vitalii Bielobrov, Deputy Minister for Communities and Territories Development of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
According to the official, the available accommodation may prove insufficient, given the possible increase in the number of people evacuated from regions where hostilities are ongoing.
But additionally, we can expect thousands of new refugees from the Kherson and Donetsk regions and so on. And we do not have time to create something new, something larger
He noted that the situation is being exacerbated by a significant increase in the number of people forced to leave their homes because of hostilities and the threat of shelling. In particular, over the nine months of 2026, 128,000 evacuated citizens passed through transit centers in Ukraine. This is 2.5 times more than during the same period last year. Transit centers provide initial assistance to people leaving dangerous areas, after which they facilitate their further accommodation.
At the same time, the most pressing issue remains the accommodation of elderly people, persons with disabilities, and people with limited mobility who require special living conditions and additional care.
Context
Earlier, the Ministry for Communities and Territories Development reported a shortage of places to accommodate evacuees in Ukraine's rear regions. To address the problem, the government allocated additional funding for the creation and equipping of housing for internally displaced persons. In particular, in September, the amount of the relevant subsidy to local budgets was increased to more than UAH 1.56 billion.
In addition, they want to involve international partners in the reconstruction of the housing stock and the provision of additional temporary accommodation places.
Reminder
In March 2026, the Ministry of Social Policy completed the development of a new strategy for internally displaced persons. This was announced by Denys Uliutin, who at the time was the incumbent Minister of Social Policy, Family and Unity of Ukraine. He specified that the document covers the path from evacuation to integration and the return of Ukrainians from abroad.

59% of Ukrainians read books regularly. What is the Ministry of Culture doing to grow that number?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:05:46 EET
02:05:46 KST

Tetyana Berezhna, Vice Prime Minister of Ukraine for Humanitarian Policy – Minister of Culture
Russia is burning Ukrainian books by the million. Ukrainians continue to choose books in Ukrainian: according to a new study, 87% of readers surveyed had read or listened to books in Ukrainian over the past year.
These two realities define our responsibility as a state. We must help the book sector withstand these attacks and give Ukrainians access to books that interest them. Sustaining that interest in the years ahead depends on the range of titles published in Ukrainian and how accessible they are.
The Ministry of Culture of Ukraine commissioned a comprehensive study, Reading in Ukraine: Behaviour, Motivation and Tools for Engagement, conducted by Gradus Research with support from the Believe in Yourself Foundation. The researchers combined 41 in-depth interviews with book sector professionals and people who had returned to reading with a survey of 2,200 Ukrainians aged 14 and over.
People Are Returning to Reading
Over the past year, 59% of respondents had read or listened to books at least several times a month. One-third did so at least several times a week.
At the same time, 70% of readers surveyed had experienced a break from reading lasting six months or longer. Of those who had taken such a break, 35% had returned to regular reading, while another 62% now read occasionally.
This is an important finding for policies to encourage reading. Reading habits change with people’s lives. Work, parenthood, relocation and exhaustion all affect the time and attention someone can give to a book. A change in routine, a recommendation from someone close or a compelling story can help bring them back.
Support therefore matters at different stages of life: when children first discover books, when teenagers develop their own tastes and when adults rediscover an interest in literature.
During the war, books have taken on particular emotional significance. Among readers, 32% say reading helps reduce anxiety, 30% say it helps them recover emotionally and 28% say it helps them cope with stress. Among those who returned to reading after a break, the most frequently cited reason was a psychological need for rest, support or relief from stress. This was selected by 34%.
Participants in the in-depth interviews also described exhaustion that makes it difficult to concentrate. We should take this experience into account when encouraging people to read. Some need a novel that offers a moment of respite; others need a book that helps them make sense of what they have lived through. A wide range of literature and formats allows people to choose what meets their needs at a particular moment.
Books Need to Be Within Reach
Of all respondents, 37% said that coming across an interesting book had encouraged, or could encourage, them to read more. This was the most common answer. Among those who had returned to reading after a break, 31% recalled seeing a book that caught their interest.
The opportunity to encounter books in everyday life therefore matters: to browse a title, talk to a bookseller or discover new releases on a library shelf.
Only 34% of respondents believe their town or community has enough bookshops. Another 22% say there are too few, while 21% say there are none at all. Where people live has a significant impact on their access to literature.
The Government has already adopted a resolution developed by the Ministry of Culture to reimburse bookshops for the cost of renting their premises. The first phase will cover communities with populations of up to 100,000. The first payments are planned for the first quarter of 2027, covering rent paid in the fourth quarter of 2026.
Bookshops will use the reimbursed funds to purchase books or pay for titles already sold. This will help booksellers stay in business and publishers receive payments sooner.
For a community, a bookshop can also be a place to meet authors, join discussions and discover contemporary Ukrainian literature. Supporting bookshops gives people more opportunities to participate in cultural life close to home.
Library Acquisitions Must Reflect Readers’ Interests
Among respondents, 73% know of a library in their town or community where they can borrow books free of charge. This is an extensive network that needs to develop in line with communities’ needs.
Among those who do not use libraries, 19% cited a lack of titles that interest them, while 12% pointed to a shortage of new releases. In small towns, the share of people who say libraries lack books that interest them reaches 27%.
Acquisitions should therefore begin with readers’ requests. Librarians know which authors visitors are looking for, which books teenagers are waiting for and which titles families with children borrow. This knowledge should shape library collections.
For the first time since 2021, the draft state budget for 2027 includes funding to purchase new books for libraries. The Ministry of Culture is working to replenish public library collections, while school libraries fall within the remit of the Ministry of Education and Science. We plan to build the public library programme around an assessment of communities’ needs.
Together with our partners, we are also working to improve library spaces. Libraries in Rohatyn, in the Ivano-Frankivsk region, and Bilohiria, in the Khmelnytskyi region, became the first pilot sites for the Libraries for All programme. Up-to-date collections, welcoming spaces and professional advice should help people find books they connect with—and return for more.
Supporting Readers’ Own Choices
Among readers aged 18–24, 91% had read or listened to books in Ukrainian over the past year. The state has an important role in sustaining this interest and giving young people the means to choose their own reading.
From the launch of the eKnyha programme in December 2024 to the end of June 2026, young Ukrainians purchased more than 549,000 books through the scheme. State support translated into books that readers chose for themselves, while also supporting the book sector.
We are working to extend eKnyha to parents of newborns. We look to the Verkhovna Rada to support this expansion so that families can receive assistance to buy books from the beginning of a child’s life. After all, a child’s introduction to reading often begins with time spent with their parents, the sound of their voices and a first favourite story.
As children grow, they need room to make their own choices. Contemporary literature for reading for pleasure should therefore also be available in school libraries. The opportunity to try different genres, discover authors and share impressions with friends helps children develop their own tastes as readers.
In 2027, we also plan to expand the Tysiachovesna programme to include the book sector. Support for new Ukrainian publications should go hand in hand with the development of bookshops, libraries and interest in reading.
I measure the results of this work by the opportunities it creates for people. Can a child choose an interesting book at the library? Can a young person afford literature that reflects their own tastes? Can an adult reader find the title they need in their community?
The study gives us a basis for making decisions and assessing their results. We need to understand how bookshops perform after receiving support, whether readers borrow newly acquired library books and how young people’s interest in reading develops.
Ivan Franko wrote:
Books are the depths of the sea:
Whoever dives down to the bottom,
Though the effort be great,
Brings wondrous pearls to the surface.
For every reader, these “pearls” are different: new knowledge, a better understanding of themselves or support through a difficult time. Ukrainian literature gives us the opportunity to reflect on our experiences, discover the world and form our own opinions.
Our task as a state is to broaden that choice. To ensure that libraries receive the books their readers are waiting for, that bookshops can operate in communities and that literature for different ages and interests is published in Ukrainian. To help everyone find the book that sparks a love of reading—or brings them back to it.
We cannot choose the book that will captivate someone. But we can give them more opportunities to find it.

Ukraine heads for first economic decline since 2022 as Russian strikes take their toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:51:28 UTC
01:51:28 KST

Ukraine heads for first economic decline since 2022 as Russian strikes take their toll
Intensified Russian attacks on Ukrainian businesses have pushed the economy into decline for the first time since 2022’s invasion shock, choking key industries as inflation hits a three-year high.
Ukraine’s National Bank said on Oct. 29 that the country’s economy will shrink by 0.4% this year, after revising its previous forecast of 1.8% growth. The last time Ukraine’s economy contacted was the year of Russia’s full-scale invasion, which saw its gross domestic product (GDP) plummet by an astonishing 30% before gradually recovering the following year.
The bank said the decline was caused by Russia’s months-long blockade of seaports and escalating attacks on logistics and production facilities. The metallurgy industry has particularly suffered, with steel production shutting down across the country amid the heightened risk of deadly Russian strikes.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's Agriculutral Ministry said that farmers wont see any profits from crop production this year, as they cannot export goods via the Black Sea, while costs for autumn sowing, fuel, fertilizers, and land rental payments have increased.
The attacks, combined with the fuel crisis caused by the war in the Middle East, have also caused inflation to surge to double digits, jumping to 10% in September, the bank said.
The NBU predicts that annual inflation will reach 12.5% by the end of 2026 — a three-year high. To help cool the economy, the bank hiked its benchmark interest rate from 16% to 16.5%, the highest level since October 2023. The rate is expected to remain in place until spring 2027, the NBU said.
"Taking the consequences of the destruction into account, the NBU forecasts a slow recovery in economic growth in 2027-2028," the bank said.
"Economic activity will be supported, in particular, by public and private investment in the defense industry, the localization of weapons production financed through the Ukraine Support Loan, and projects to restore critical infrastructure."
The bank predicts that next year, Ukraine’s foreign partners will provide $52 billion in direct budget support and $37 billion for defense needs through the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan program, after the country passed several laws this month to unlock funding from the EU and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The funding will help Ukraine cover core budgetary needs, although the country faces a projected deficit of nearly Hr 1.7 trillion ($37 billion) next year.
This year has been one of the hardest for Ukraine’s economy, with businesses expected to lose some $10 billion in the wake of the attacks, creating a Hr 70 billion ($1.5 billion) tax shortfall.
As Russia shows no sign of slowing its attacks, the country is adapting to a new phase of the war. Ukraine’s Economy Ministry is developing support programs for companies, including a multibillion-dollar war risk insurance fund to help cover businesses starting in January.

Israel completes vote count, Netanyahu bloc retains 53 seats

Şahin Demir
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has completed counting votes in Tuesday’s parliamentary elections, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc securing 53 seats, opposition parties 48 and Arab parties 19, the Ynet newspaper reported Thursday.
The committee said it had completed counting special ballots, known as double envelopes, but would release the final results later.
Results from 12,644 polling stations have been entered into the system, totaling 5,589,836 votes, including 5,564,764 valid votes and 25,072 invalid votes, it said.
The special ballots include votes cast by soldiers, prisoners, diplomats, and hospitalized voters who could not vote at their regular polling stations.
The overall distribution of seats among the three political groupings remained unchanged from Wednesday’s results, despite changes in individual parties’ seat allocations following the counting of special ballots.
Netanyahu’s Likud party rose from 26 to 27 seats, while the ultra-Orthodox Shas party fell from seven to six.
Among Arab parties, Ra’am gained one seat, increasing its representation to eight, while the Joint List dropped one to 11.
Netanyahu’s bloc includes his Likud party and allied far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
The opposition bloc, led by former Israeli Army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, includes his Yashar party, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s Together alliance, Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid, Yair Golan’s Democrats and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu.
The two Arab parties, the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am), secured a combined 19 seats, potentially putting them in a pivotal position in negotiations to form the next government.
Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc reached the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Voter turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999 and up 7.1 percentage points from the 2022 elections, according to the Central Elections Committee.
The official results are expected to be announced Nov. 4.
President Isaac Herzog will then consult parliamentary factions before appointing a lawmaker to form the next government.
The new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10.

USA: GMLRS Missile Successfully Redirected in Flight and Hit Moving Target for the First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:50:20 UTC
01:50:20 KST

Lockheed Martin, in collaboration with the U.S. Army, successfully tested the ability to re-target a GMLRS guided missile after launch from a HIMARS rocket system, striking a moving target.
This was reported by Lockheed Martin’s press office.
The tests took place at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. During the test, a GMLRS rocket was launched from a standard M142 HIMARS launcher, after which updated target data was transmitted to it directly during flight.
The Strigo data link and the Remote Interceptor Guidance-360 (RIG-360) system were used for this purpose; the company funded the integration of these systems at its own expense.
After receiving the new data, the missile adjusted its guidance and successfully destroyed the moving target.
According to the developers, implementing this capability does not require a fundamental redesign of the GMLRS missile itself. Instead, the technology involves integrating existing reconnaissance assets, launchers, and target-acquisition systems into a single network.
Lockheed Martin notes that the data transmission system used can also be adapted for the ER GMLRS long-range rockets and the operational-tactical Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs).
Lockheed Martin has been working on the capability to update target coordinates in flight since at least 2023. At that time, the company first demonstrated the transmission of new coordinates to an experimental GMLRS communication channel using the RIG-360 system.
During the test, the equipment was mounted on an aircraft that simulated the missile’s flight path.
The next phase consisted of the current tests, during which the technology was tested using an actual GMLRS missile and against a moving target.
In August 2026, Lockheed Martin also unveiled the Strigo family of technologies, which includes radio-frequency sensors, data links, and guidance heads for missiles of various types.
Technologies from this family are already being used in the development of the PrSM Increment 2 missile guidance system, designed to engage moving ground and sea targets. In September, the U.S. Army ordered PrSM Increment 2 missiles from Lockheed Martin worth $1.2 billion.

01:50:07 KST

By Isabel Teles
SAO PAULO, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro’s decision to declare himself the country’s rightful “leader” has failed to garner support from key figures in his political camp, leaving the right-wing lawmaker increasingly isolated in Brazilian politics.
Bolsonaro made the claim in a letter he posted on social media after arriving in the United States on Wednesday, having left Brazil following his defeat to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by more than 4 million votes in Sunday’s runoff.
Bolsonaro has cited the fact that a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice extended voting by two hours due to Lula campaign allegations of voter suppression in left-leaning northeastern states, though Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought a voting extension due to rain in conservative southern states.
He alleged he was a victim of an electoral coup, but did not provide evidence for electoral fraud.
Lula’s victory has been recognized by Brazil’s electoral authority, global leaders, international observers, and Bolsonaro’s own party.
“I did not like it,” the head of the senator’s Liberal Party, Valdemar Costa Neto, told reporters on Thursday when asked about the letter.
“Flavio went through a difficult situation — we understand that — but we do not approve of it. We want to move the country forward,” he said later.
Sao Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas, a prominent Bolsonaro ally who campaigned vigorously for the lawmaker, told newspaper Estadao that Brazil’s election results must be respected and that it was time to move forward.
US President Donald Trump, who confirmed his administration had allowed Bolsonaro to enter the country, declined to comment on Thursday when asked who he thought was the legitimate winner.
“I watched the election. I didn’t take sides. I let it be. I was asked not to take sides by the president, the current president,” he said.
PARTIES RECOGNIZE LULA’S WIN
Aecio Neves, head of the center-right Brazilian Social Democracy Party and a vocal critic of Lula’s Workers’ Party, described Bolsonaro’s behavior as “incomprehensible” in a statement, adding that opposition politics must be conducted from within the country.
Center-right party Uniao Brasil, which backed Bolsonaro in the second round, said it was essential that institutions “remain greater than any individual.” The election was conducted with integrity and its results must be respected, it added.
The centrist Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB) party, which also supported Bolsonaro in the runoff, struck a similar tone.
“The MDB reaffirms its total confidence in the Brazilian electoral system and, therefore, in the legitimacy of the result of the election last Sunday,” it said.
‘FLAVIO IS VENTING’
In his letter, Bolsonaro pledged to lead the opposition from abroad and “assume the risks” that local politicians could not, adding he would support a potential bid by Senator Rogerio Marinho for Senate president in 2027.
Marinho, who served as Bolsonaro’s campaign manager, told reporters that Bolsonaro remains “a leader” and ”the most prominent figure on the right” in Brazil, given the support he received from nearly 60 million voters.
But Marinho also rejected allegations of electoral fraud.
“The Liberal Party cannot make that claim, nor can I make that claim, because there is no evidence to support it,” he said. “Flavio is venting in response to the second-round election results, which were unexpected for all of us.”

17:50:02 CET
01:50:02 KST

Oct 23 (Reuters) - The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.
Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US midterm elections.
Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.
The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7. The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known.
Post publication, Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Limited (EASTMED), the manager of the Agioi Fanendes tanker, said that the vessel was awaiting orders while sailing towards the North Atlantic but its destination had not been determined as New York.
“The discharging port or country is not yet nominated and finalised,” an EASTMED official told Reuters.
The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.
Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.
A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.
“As far as I’m aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.
The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.
RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTSSince the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.
It also supplies Central Asia by rail.
Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.
It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, LSEG data showed.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.
Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.
That account was not accurate, a source familiar with the matter said.
Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end.

Yemen’s hospitals buckle as fighting escalates
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:49:54 CET
01:49:54 KST

TAIZ, Oct 29 (Reuters) - In a hospital in Yemen’s Taiz, a 25-year-old pregnant mother of two lay immobilised after a bullet lodged in her spine while she was trapped inside her home without food or water for two days.
The UN and aid agencies say health needs in the besieged city of Taiz are critical, amid acute shortages of medicine, oxygen, surgical gloves, anesthetic and fuel. Hospitals near Yemen’s front lines are facing large influxes of patients, treating up to 700 war wounded in a single week, according to the Red Cross.
Amal al-Sabri said she was injured by a sniper bullet in the village of al-Shaqb — perched on the slopes of Mount Sabir overlooking Taiz — as an escalation in fighting between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement takes a devastating toll on civilians.
Medics at Al-Thawra hospital in Taiz said they could not perform a scan because she was over four months pregnant.
“The bullet entered from the side and is now lodged near the spine. They (the doctors) couldn’t remove it because of the fetus,” Sabri told Reuters. “Now I am giving up the fetus.”
HEALTHCARE SYSTEM ‘AT BREAKING POINT’
Taiz governorate, which hosts about half of the 281,000 people who have been newly displaced in Yemen since the start of August, has been largely isolated since October 3, with fighting preventing humanitarian supplies from entering and civilians from leaving.
Taiz, Marib and the Red Sea coast are seeing some of the highest casualties, with patients arriving at hospitals with gunshot wounds and complex blast injuries, according to the Red Cross.
“The healthcare system across Yemen is at a breaking point,” said Red Cross spokesperson Hachem Osseiran.
Even before the latest fighting, more than 40% of hospitals and healthcare facilities across the country were already either closed or partially functioning following years of protracted conflict, he said.
There are also concerns about the outbreak of disease as water runs short and rubbish accumulates on the street.
MEDICAL FACILITIES UNDER ATTACK
Throughout Yemen, primary care for pregnant women is disrupted. In some hospitals near the front lines, maternity wards are being converted into emergency rooms, Osseiran said.
“Some of them (doctors) have to make a very difficult and painful choice: Do I help this woman deliver her baby, or do I rush to a person who is bleeding out because of a gunshot wound?” he said.
In Taiz city, the UN says community midwives have stopped working due to restrictions on movement.
Not only are health services stretched, they are also under attack. A hospital in Taiz’s Sabir Al-Mawadim district was hit by mortar fragments for the second time this month, while a strike on an ambulance killed its driver and a paramedic, according to the UN.
On Monday, another strike that hit near Mocha General Hospital — where medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières supports the maternity and pediatric wards — damaged the building and triggered panic among patients.
“Such incidents are preventing patients from coming to the hospital for fear of their lives,” MSF said.

Russia to extend diesel export ban, use quotas to fulfil US deal, sources say

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:49:13 CET
01:49:13 KST

Oct 29 (Reuters) - Russia will extend its diesel export ban until the end of the year while allowing some companies to ship fuel under a quota system to meet its new export commitment to the US, two people familiar with the discussions told Reuters.
Moscow and Washington agreed a diesel supply deal after Presidents Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump spoke by phone earlier this month. The energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine announced alongside the agreement has allowed Moscow to increase fuel production. At the same time, fuel shortages earlier this year have prompted the government to maintain tight controls on oil product exports.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Tuesday that three tankers carrying Russian diesel to export markets were already under way and that a fourth would sail on October 28.
Novak also said Russian refineries were recovering quickly from repairs. The sources said refinery utilisation had risen 25% at the end of October from the start of the month after drone attacks on facilities subsided.
Under the current diesel export ban, the government permits limited exports through a quota system. Those quotas will quadruple from October levels to 2 million metric tons, or about 0.5 million barrels per day, in November, the sources said. Shipments under existing intergovernmental agreements will also continue.
The Energy Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The current ban on diesel exports is due to expire on October 31.
In October, the government exempted several refiners from the ban and granted them export quotas totalling 0.5 million tons, the sources said. A new government order expected in early November would expand the list of exempt refiners and set new export limits. If the quotas are used up quickly, the government could consider increasing them further, the sources added.
Nominal diesel production in Russia exceeds domestic consumption by about 40%. As refineries return to normal operating rates, they will need export outlets to prevent a domestic glut.

Oct 29 (Reuters) - Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez said on Thursday the government has made progress in identifying state assets to be offered to the private sector and former owners, a move that could reverse widespread nationalizations ordered by former President Hugo Chavez.
“I have instructed that non-essential assets held by the state be assessed to determine which can be offered to the private sector or returned to their former owners. This process is already well advanced,” Rodriguez said in a televised address.
In April, Rodriguez appointed a government commission to audit and evaluate state-owned assets, including infrastructure in key industries such as energy, power and mining. They have been working on asset classification since, according to sources.
She did not provide further details on how the process may be carried out. Under Chavez, the nationalization of key projects and industries left over a dozen international arbitration claims, which mostly remain unsettled by the government.
In her speech, Rodriguez said that 44 energy contracts are currently being negotiated under the state’s new oil law approved in January. The government has stated that 61 oil agreements have so far been signed, without providing details.
“Similarly, important negotiations are underway in the mining sector, specifically regarding gold, aluminum, and iron,” she added.
The president also said that she has instructed law enforcement agencies not to arrest people without a warrant, and vowed to defend the right to “peaceful protest” in the country, which has a history of political repression and last week saw its first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years.
“The responsible exercise of political rights is guaranteed for everyone. Our doors are open,” Rodriguez said.
In her address, Rodriguez also said that the government has planned four quarterly increases in the national minimum wage in 2027.

EU frees up over 20 billion euros to potentially help Ukraine's defense
