Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:48:43 UTC
01:48:43 KST

BRUSSELS, Belgium — EU countries were invited to pitch 20 billion euros' ($22 billion) worth of defense projects on Oct. 29, and the European Commission emphasized that those plans should ideally prioritize Ukraine.
The 21.3 billion euros ($23.8 billion) on the table is part of the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument, which includes 150 billion euros ($167.5 billion) in favorable loans freed up in May 2025 that EU countries can draw on to help them beef up their defense and support to Ukraine.
The scheme proved quite successful, with 19 countries submitting proposals for the loans.
However, the full 150 billion euros was not used, chiefly because Italy and Hungary scaled down their borrowing plans, allowing the Commission to issue its new call.
"Along with their needs and national defense priorities, member states are also encouraged to use the funds from this second call to strengthen cooperation with Ukraine," a European Commission press release reads.
For the Commission, that means EU countries engaging in joint defense procurement with Ukraine and spending to address Ukraine's "urgent needs," for example, in "air and missile defense systems, drones and counter-drone systems, and ammunition and missiles."
That new call for submissions also comes as Ukraine-EU defense cooperation has gained momentum.
Among the spending plans already foreseen for the SAFE loans are many plans for joint production with Ukraine, even for countries seen as less pro-Ukraine in the bloc, such as Bulgaria, which has a plan to co-produce drones.
The EU has since then also launched its EU-Ukraine drone alliance, which brings together manufacturers from both sides to deepen cooperation, and the bloc has moved forward on five pan-continental defense projects, in which Ukraine has been deeply embedded.
The same day the European Commission issued the new call for SAFE proposals, EU-Ukraine defense cooperation was a key topic at Brussels' annual defense and space conference, organized by the consultancy Logos.
Panu Routila, CEO of Finnish defense manufacturer Patria, told the Kyiv Independent he is excited about a new joint venture between his company and Ukrainian drone producer General Cherry.
For Routila, the cooperation will allow the two companies to advance together on first-person view (FPV) drones and interceptor technology.
Patria is now looking for "direct collaboration" with Ukrainian companies across a range of "emerging capabilities," following that first positive collaboration, Routila told the Kyiv Independent.
Former Prime Minister and head of the Kyiv Security Forum Arseniy Yatsenyuk told the Kyiv Independent at the same event that his message for defense manufacturers in Europe is simple.
"Press your national governments to support Ukraine and to provide more," Yatsenyuk said.
He characterized the situation as a win-win, because if countries provide financial support to Ukraine, it can continue to procure from European defense manufacturers.
The SAFE loans are a concrete line of funding through which national governments could boost financial support at low borrowing costs.

HK housing chief quits after fire probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:54 UTC
01:42:54 KST

Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee (李家超) yesterday apologized and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the territory’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight.
The massive fire that broke out in November last year engulfed seven buildings in an apartment complex in a northern suburban district, killing 168 people and displacing thousands of others.
Many former residents of Wang Fuk Court have spent nearly a year waiting to see how the government will address accountability for the disaster that claimed their loved ones and their homes, which were undergoing maintenance work.
Photo: AP
At the opening of the news conference, Lee and seven other top officials bowed in apology.
Lee said that Hong Kong Secretary of Housing Winnie Ho (何永賢) “should bear political responsibility,” although no personal wrongdoing was found.
He said that Ho had resigned on Wednesday.
An independent committee found that the Hong Kong Housing Bureau’s independent checking unit failed in its duties supervising the maintenance work.
The Buildings Department, the Fire Services Department and the Labor Department had shortcomings in supervision over fire hazards of the apartment complex, Lee said.
A three-month investigation would be conducted into the four government agencies to determine whether staff were derelict in their duties, he said.
Officials also proposed a series of measures, including criminalizing bid rigging.
The committee’s report said evidence pointed to a lighted cigarette being the cause of the fire, which started on the flat roof between two apartments on the first floor of Wang Cheong House.
The committee heard substantial evidence that construction workers had smoked on site, including on the scaffolding, while a few cigarette butts and some partially burnt materials, such as cardboard boxes, were found on the flat roof.
Experts found the use of foam boards, non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets and canvases contributed to the fire’s spread, among other factors, the report said.
A majority of the deaths were caused by smoke inhalation rather than burns. The replacement of some staircase windows with movable aluminum composite panels or wooden boards for workers’ convenience allowed smoke to infiltrate residents’ escape routes, it said.
Opaque foam boards that covered the apartments’ windows blocked residents’ views, delaying evacuation, it said.
The shutdown of the fire alarm system was also a factor in the heavy death toll, the report said.
The committee said evidence clearly demonstrated that Will Power Architects Co, the consultant for the maintenance project, and Prestige Construction & Engineering Co, the main contractor on the project, had cut corners.
“There is no doubt that they are the main culprits responsible for the occurrence of the inferno and the high fatalities in the tragic incident,” the report said.
Evidence also revealed an array of registered contractors and building professionals who conducted no substantive work and were only asked to lend their names to “rubber stamp” statutory forms in return for a fee, it said.
The private contractors and consultants had deceived the regulators, it said.
“However ... deception succeeded because the regulators’ own practices enabled it,” the report said. “In each case, the regulator’s reliance on the good faith of the regulated parties left obvious fire hazards uninvestigated.”
The committee found that the Housing Bureau’s independent checking unit and the Buildings Department, as the two agencies primarily responsible for supervising the execution of the maintenance work at Wang Fuk Court, had failed in their supervisory duties in ensuring the safety of such work.
Among the shortcomings were the lack of proper investigations into the use of the foam boards and the fire-retardant quality of the scaffolding nets despite multiple complaints.
The Independent Checking Unit should be criticized for adopting the practice of giving prenotification to consultants and contractors about site inspections, it added.
The committee’s work is separate from criminal investigations in which seven people and two companies, Will Power and Prestige, were charged with offenses including manslaughter and conspiracy to defraud over the fire.

The US and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi said late on Wednesday.
Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference in the Philippine central province of Cebu, where he met with US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of ASEAN defense chiefs, and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
The missiles that are to be produced as part of a joint effort called “Operation Supercharge” are “essential for the F-35,” Koizumi said, without elaborating or providing other details of the agreement.
Photo: AFP
The US-made F-35 jets are one of the world’s most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.
During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he “shared a sense of crisis ... regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-US alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before.”
“We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means,” he said.
Their discussions were not directed at any specific country, he said.
Hegseth said in a separate meeting with ASEAN defense ministers that the US is committed to help deter aggression in the region.
“The approach we’re taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear,” Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. “Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves.”

Tragedy and triumph intermingle on the peaks of Nepal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:50 UTC
01:42:50 KST

Hike up and ski down was Jim Morrison’s relatively straightforward dream, albeit not on your typical ski hill.
Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson aspired to summit Mount Everest’s north side, something only five people had ever done. None had ever skied down it. Given the long stream of mountaineers that queue up on the south face, you could call it the most drastic feat ever of avoiding a lift line.
Everest: The Other Side, by Free Solo filmmakers Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, is the big-screen chronicle of Morrison and Nelson’s mission. Theirs is a quixotic aspiration: climb the world’s highest peak and then coast down.
Photo: AP
But Everest: The Other Side is as much a document of tragedy and grief as it is one of extreme sport. On a similar expedition in 2022 while biding their time for Everest, Morrison and Nelson — partners in love and adventure — reached the top of a Nepalese mountain. But after just a few turns on her skis, a sheet of snow dislodged underneath Nelson. She died in the avalanche.
Nelson’s death reverberated through the mountaineering world and it reshaped the film Vasarhelyi and Chin were making. In Free Solo, which documents Alex Honnold ascending El Capitan in Yosemite without ropes or a harness, the filmmakers had to contemplate the possibility that Honnold might fall to his death.
In Everest, that awful possibility comes to pass. Nelson’s fatal fall, as well as Morrison’s recovery of her body two days later, is captured with agonizing IMAX clarity. If Free Solo was about an unmitigated triumph, Everest wrestles with a darker side of such perilous exploits.
“This movie, the worst happened,” Vasarhelyi says in a brief moment on screen.
Risk tolerance is a common topic for Vasarhelyi and Chin, filmmakers who have intrepidly fused nature documentaries with adventure drama. Chin is himself a decorated climber; he summited and skied down the south face of Everest in 2006.
But in Everest, questioning whether it’s worth it is front and center. The movie lingers on the moments when Morrison and his team leave their homes, parting with children for two-month stints during which they’ll risk their lives on desolate peaks on the other side of the world. When Nelson dies, she leaves behind two boys. As the years tick on in the documentary, we watch them grow up without their mother.
Yet within months of her death, Morrison, from his lakeside Tahoe home, resolves to push ahead with the Everest climb. Tragedy isn’t new to him. Years earlier, he lost his wife, Katie, and two children, Wyatt and Hannah, in a plane crash. After first finding a walk down the driveway an insurmountable hike, Morrison resolves to live for them.
So his aim to reach the top of Everest and ski down may be a daredevil feat, but it’s also a grieving, heavy-hearted quest. He describes his yearning to ride down “the raddest ski line in the world.” But what’s compelling him is also something that can’t be easily articulated.
Everest: The Other Side is, to a certain extent, alive to these quandaries. The filmmakers even share in them. Chin accompanies Morrison on both an aborted ascent and the successful attempt last year.
Deciding to continue with the project is its own debate for Chin and Vasarhelyi. They have two children of their own. Their proximity to extreme expeditions has already brought tragedy close to home.
“How many people who have eaten at our dinner table have died?” Vasarhelyi asks him.
The couple divorced last year, though their separation goes unmentioned in the film.
While these debates are often present in the documentary, Everest grows increasingly shy of them. The higher Morrison climbs, the less inquisitive the movie gets. On the first attempted ascent, some of the Sherpas grow wary of the risks involved. Their sensible hesitations don’t put Morrison, handsomely outfitted by his North Face sponsor, in the best light.
By the time Morrison realizes his dream, it feels as though many have, off camera, moved on with their lives. The families back home fall out of the movie. Everest: The Other Side becomes a mournful and increasingly solitary march.
Maybe that’s appropriate. Morrison’s extreme compulsion inevitably pulls him away from us, leaving behind a more disquieting film. Even he can’t help but notice while hiking up that the snow conditions he’ll be skiing down are rock hard and terrible. The descent, lasting four hours, is a feat of skill, perseverance and bravery. Even on a bad day, he’d have to grant, the skiing would have been better back home.

Polls do not dictate the winners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:50 UTC
01:42:50 KST

Amid the fervor of an election campaign, many treat poll results like a report card, scrutinizing every percentage-point change and growing anxious or panicking when numbers fluctuate. Some notice wide discrepancies between polls conducted by different organizations and question whether the methodology is flawed or the figures have been manipulated.
However, all of this is unnecessary. Polls are, after all, merely sample surveys — the real winner would ultimately be determined by each vote cast on election day.
In the past few years, polling has faced a fundamental problem: Few people answer landline calls, and many no longer have landlines at all. Yet local election polls often rely on landline numbers to identify a respondent’s location and confirm whether they live within the electoral district, which leads to insufficient coverage. That makes sampling impossible.
Even among those who still have landlines and are willing to answer, figuring out how to weigh their responses to accurately reflect the views of an entire electorate has become a major challenge for pollsters.
Imagine that only one person in a particular age group answers the phone. If that person’s views are weighted to represent the entire age group, any difference between their opinion and that of other voters could cause a dramatic shift in the overall results of the poll.
That is why polls should be taken with a grain of salt. There is no need to be discouraged by polls, and those who are in the lead certainly should not become complacent. Polls do not decide elections — votes do.
With less than one month until election day, candidates should not get carried away or disheartened by poll results. To achieve victory, they should make the most of the remaining time, work pragmatically to win votes and ensure that every vote is counted.
Some voters fixate on the polls while others dismiss the results as an illusion; some rush to interpret the numbers and others get into arguments or demand that the campaign teams of the candidate they support respond in specific ways.
As others descend into chaos, we should stay calm, take time to reflect on our chosen candidate’s strengths and think carefully about how to communicate those strengths to our friends and family — and even those we have only just met. We should engage with them sincerely, explaining why they need to vote and why they should vote for the candidate we are supporting.
One of the most important reasons for this is that China is always closely watching Taiwan’s elections. Election results reflect public sentiment and morale in Taiwan.
In Taipei, for example, Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) — who advocates for resilience — would deal a serious blow to China’s will to wage war.
That is because China can only afford — and wants — a quick and decisive victory; otherwise, it risks the collapse of its regime. The more Taiwanese demonstrate their resilience and determination to resist, the more carefully China must weigh its options before acting and the less likely it is to launch a war.
While some candidates scramble to cover up their deeply flawed public image, dismiss unfavorable polls as illusions and spend their days cooped up at home “analyzing” poll results, we should put the polls aside for now. Whether the numbers favor us or not, the election outcome would be determined by actions.
There is no need to get emotional over poll numbers; instead, we must focus on steadily winning one, two or even 10 more votes each day. When the day’s work is done and you go to sleep, you can feel at peace knowing you have met your goal.
Each person’s small efforts, day after day, all add up to something much greater. The victory that ultimately matters most is the one achieved on election day.
Tommy Lin is chairman of the Formosa Republican Association and director of the Taiwan United Nations Alliance.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

The shocking rise of rib remodelling: ‘I wanted that hourglass shape’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

Daniela Cesin was 14 when she began thinking about her looks.
“I was a little bit chubby and I started to work out at home and lose weight. I saw the difference in my body: my abs, the muscles in my arms, and I started liking it,” she says.
By 31, she had the slim, toned body she had hoped for, but something was still missing.
Photo: AP
“I wanted to have that guitar hourglass shape,” she says.
In August, Cesin travelled from Miami, where she has lived for the past 15 years, to her native Venezuela for liposuction and a fat transfer to her hips. She met her cosmetic surgeon for the first time the day before the procedure, and he realized she didn’t have enough fat to go ahead with it. Instead, he offered to perform RibXcar: a rib remodeling surgery that would involve fracturing three of her lower ribs on each side and binding them in a corset for three months, to set the ribs in a new position and give her a wasplike waist.
“I was like: ‘No, no, no, I don’t want to do anything with the ribs,’” she says.
The idea of breaking the bones around her vital organs sounded a lot more invasive than a breast augmentation, which she had 10 years ago, or a rhinoplasty (nose surgery) and blepharoplasty (eyelid surgery), which she had two years ago. Also, she had never heard of the procedure.
But after the consultation, she decided to trust her surgeon. Cesin had already paid for flights and taken three weeks off from her job as a sales director. The next day she was anesthetized, and her surgeon used an ultrasound to locate the ribs, made six small incisions in her back, and inserted a vibrating tool to create greenstick fractures — an incomplete bone break — on each rib. When she came to she was wearing a black corset with small knobs on each side that she could tighten to her preferred measurements.
The recovery has been uncomfortable. It was initially hard to stand or lie down without help, and there was soreness from the incisions. The first week, Cesin barely slept.
“Your body doesn’t get used to any position, so every hour I would wake up.”
But the worst part has been eating while wearing her corset, which must remain on for 23 hours a day; this causes acid reflux. Despite her discomfort, when we speak six weeks after her surgery, she is pleased with the eight centimeters she has shaved off her waist.
Cesin is one of a small but growing number of women choosing to fracture their ribs for an hourglass shape. To achieve this look, women previously underwent riskier rib removal techniques, which reduce the protective bone barrier for the liver and spleen.
Kazbek Kudzaev, a plastic surgeon in Russia, realized in 2017 that he could achieve similar aesthetic results when he moved the ribs with a drill until one side fractured, then bound the body in a corset while they healed. Since his discovery, surgeons in countries including Colombia, South Korea and France have refined the technique. Today, it takes about an hour and is performed under general anesthesia as a day-surgery treatment.
NON-INVASIVE PROCEDURE?
It is touted as a noninvasive procedure, but many of the women I interviewed described feeling as if they had been “hit by a bus” after surgery. And there are serious risks. These include standard surgical complications, such as allergic reactions to the anesthesia, blood clots, wound infections and seromas (pockets of fluid that build up under the skin). But also more specific dangers, including a collapsed lung, known as a pneumothorax; and a haemothorax, where blood collects in the space between the chest wall and the lungs. Both of these are potentially fatal.
Sandip Hindocha, a consultant plastic surgeon at the Private Clinic on Harley Street in London, is skeptical about the procedure.
“If a patient came to my clinic and said this is what I want to do, I’d be asking the question: ‘Why do you want to do that? And why do you want to make such a permanent change to your body?’”
He references a paper published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, which states that between 2018 and 2024, out of 2,351 patients who had rib remodeling, there was an overall complication rate of 3.7 percent.
“That’s not a small number,” he says. “If we did a breast augmentation, you wouldn’t expect a complication rate like that.”
The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), doesn’t endorse the procedure. Former president Nora Nugent points out that it is relatively new, “with limited data available on long-term results and it requires advanced body contouring skills as well as the ability to treat any potential complications. It may be something that UK/BAAPS plastic surgeons bring into their practices in due course but it is not available at the moment.”
The procedure isn’t typically offered to cisgender women over the age of 40, because of the increased chance of them having osteoporosis, which can cause the bones to fully break rather than fracture. Another complication for patients is that gaining weight can cause your body to change shape again, so pregnancy can affect the results. The procedure “needs to be done with a surgeon who has a lot of experience in it,” says Hindocha. “Maybe a surgeon that also does chest wall reconstruction.”
In the UK, plastic surgeons are advised to give patients a cooling-off period of at least two weeks to weigh up the risks and potential consequences of having any procedure. But Hindocha worries that patients are sometimes opting for rib remodeling with less time for reflection, despite the permanence of the change.
“If you put an implant in and later you don’t want it, you can, worst case scenario, remove it,” Hindocha says. Whereas the ribs are “a structural, rigid part of you that you cannot reverse.”
WAISTLINES THROUGHOUT HISTORY
Throughout history, waistlines have expanded and shrunk. Between the 16th and 19th centuries, corset wearing and tight-lacing became a symbol of beauty for the “leisure class” (the restrictive garments made physical labor impossible). The engineered hourglass shape fell out of fashion in the 1920s, but made a comeback with Marilyn Monroe, before slender, androgynous frames gained popularity from the 60s to the 90s. In the 2010s, the extreme curves of the Kardashians became the defining silhouette.
In recent years, tinier, waif-like frames have become popular on TikTok and Instagram, but a highly defined waist is also considered desirable. This is thanks, among other things, to the multibillion-dollar shapewear industry; global access to Instagram and filters; and easily streamed online workout videos that focus on creating a slim, hourglass silhouette through targeted training. But now there are adverts on social media for permanent surgical options too.
In July, 10 Australian influencers, who have made names for themselves globally on shows including Married at First Sight and Below Deck, prompted headlines with a trip to Bali. They were there for a brand collaboration with a rib recontouring practice called Snatched Waist. The clinic they visited looked more like a spa than a surgeon’s office and, post-surgery, the influencers were soon lounging by the pool, showing off their narrow waists on Instagram.
Not everyone is sunbathing in a bikini after the procedure. When Sophia woke up from her rib remodeling procedure in November last year, she expected to be transferred to her Beverly Hills hotel room, a little sore but ready for recovery. Instead, she was surrounded by emergency medical technicians, who were putting her on to a stretcher to take her to hospital by ambulance. The next thing she remembers is lying in a hospital bed, hooked up to an electrocardiogram and an intravenous drip.
A CT scan showed Sophia had suffered a pneumothorax: 25 percent of one of her lungs had collapsed. She was put on oxygen and monitored for six hours before being released. Although she had signed all the consent forms for the procedure, “it was completely shocking to me,” she says.
For at least a month, Sophia had a deep pain in her lung and some shortness of breath. She had to return to the hospital after some fluid build up, but eventually started feeling better. The pain from the surgery itself subsided after about three weeks: coughing and sneezing was no longer agonizing. And she was able to return to her office job and hike in her corset at the weekends.
Sophia is transgender and chose the procedure to feminize her body, by narrowing her torso, which she felt was too wide. She began consultations for the procedure in August last year, with the surgeon planning to fracture ribs 10, 11 and 12. But by the time of her surgery in November, the surgeon felt confident he could achieve better results by going even further up the ribcage, ultimately operating on five ribs on each side. Sophia knew this would increase her risk of a pneumothorax, but was willing to take the chance.
“I didn’t start transitioning until I was 47 and I feel as if I’m playing catch up, because I’m so old, and testosterone was running rampant all those decades,” she says. “That’s why gender-affirming procedures are really important to me.”
’IT WAS A BIT UNDERWHELMING’
The final results weren’t what she had hoped for though. “It was a bit underwhelming.”
Last month, she went for a second round of rib remodeling with Leif Rogers, a different surgeon in Pasadena and Beverly Hills, California. Rogers removed cartilage from the anterior side of her ribcage on ribs three to 10. On rib four, he cut sections out and secured them with titanium plates and screws. Sophia had a breast augmentation at the same time, as the inframammary incisions were already open. When she e-mails to update me a week and a half after her second surgery, although there has been no collapsed lung this time, she says: “Recovery has been significantly more painful, and I am experiencing more shortness of breath.”
Despite the risks, Rogers expects skeletal remodeling to take off: that includes rib remodeling, clavicle shortening and pelvic widening.
“Versions of it have existed for quite some time,” he says. “Limb lengthening and shortening has been around for a long time. Of course, we change the bony skeleton of the face all the time, but other than that we haven’t changed the torso very much. The changing of the skeleton of the body is a little bit newer, as for a long time people used to just put their hands up and say: ‘Too bad, this is the way you’re built.’”
So why now?
“The techniques have got way better. And there’s marketing for it out there.”
In the US, he says, medical insurance often covers the procedure for transgender patients, “because they consider it a medical condition to have gender dysphoria. And I think on top of that, it’s just social media. Social media makes everything explode.”
Rogers says the Kardashians have been highly influential.
“I think Kim was part of why we wanted a big butt, and then she lost a lot of weight, so everyone wants to be like Kim, right?”
In 2022, Kim Kardashian attended the Met Gala after losing a considerable amount of weight, in a sparkling dress once worn by Monroe. Her slender figure coincided with a growing movement towards thinness, a rejection of the body positivity movement of the 2010s, and the advent of the Ozempic era, when the diabetes drug became popular as a weight-loss treatment. A controversial 2022 New York Post article was headlined: “Bye-bye booty: Heroin chic is back.” On TikTok, people had begun measuring their waists using A4 sheets of paper, phones and Apple headphone wires, showing off their Barbie-like proportions.
“We have always done very demanding things for beauty,” says Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and author of the 2018 book Perfect Me, who mentions foot binding and extreme corsetry. “But they were always about adornment. I think what’s different with the global ideal now is that increasingly things are becoming normalized and naturalized. We’re seeing things that are purely about adornment being recategorized as health and hygiene, and then they become invisible, and if you don’t do them you start to look abnormal,” she says. “It becomes about standard presentation.”
As we move from a text-based culture to a visual culture, increasingly, “who we are is how we look,” she says, “and that is a form of identity that is a massive and dramatic change, but one that’s snuck up on us, that we don’t talk about enough. So the visual is becoming the dominant way of presenting ourselves, being ourselves and thinking about ourselves.”

Pakistan reverses Taiwanese airlines ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

The first Taiwanese commercial aircraft since restrictions were lifted flew over Pakistan yesterday morning following an abrupt U-turn by authorities to approve permits that were briefly revoked due to Islamabad’s “one China” policy.
EVA Airways (長榮航空) Flight 65 from Taipei to Vienna entered Pakistani airspace at about 3:30am local time, Flightradar24 tracking data showed.
All other Europe-bound EVA Air and China Airlines (華航) flights that departed late on Wednesday night into early yesterday morning opted to use Russian airspace, or go via India.
Photo: EPA
The airlines had been forced to detour, including flying over Russia, since Sunday, after Pakistan shut its airspace to Taiwanese carriers, citing support of Beijing’s “one China” policy.
However, just hours after Bloomberg News reported the move, Pakistan’s Civil Aviation Authority hastily renewed the permits for the Taiwanese carriers.
They would now be allowed to fly through Pakistani airspace until March 27 next year, documents dated on Wednesday showed.
EVA Air declined to comment, while China Airlines did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
No country had previously said it would deny all Taiwanese carriers use of airspace.
Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) yesterday said that the Cabinet “deeply regretted” Pakistan’s brief closure of its airspace to Taiwanese airlines.
“We deeply regret Pakistan’s behavior, including pandering to China by compromising flight safety, disregarding international rules and reality, undermining our national sovereignty, and politicizing and weaponizing airspace,” Lee said when asked about the issue at a Cabinet news conference.
“The Republic of China, Taiwan, is a sovereign country. It and China are not subordinate to each other. This is an undeniable, objective fact and the status quo in the Taiwan Strait,” she said.
A Ministry of Transportation and Communications official said that the access period coincided with the International Air Transport Association’s winter schedule, and that an application for continued access would be filed for the summer schedule that follows.
The ministry would remain in close contact with the airlines about any changes in airspace access, the official said.
“We suspect China [was] behind this,” Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) told Bloomberg Television.
“China Airlines and EVA received a notice from the Pakistan authorities that they will lift the ban, but only temporarily ... until the end of the winter,” Chen said.
“We condemn Pakistan, and if China is behind this, I think that is a very bad practice to use its leverage over the countries in the global south to do that,” he said. “I think that gets in the way of the safety of the passengers and the smooth operation of the global supply chain.”
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun (郭嘉昆) told reporters that “as far as we are aware, there are no obstacles for residents of the Taiwan region to travel internationally.”
In April, the Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar revoked overflight permits for President William Lai’s (賴清德) flight to Eswatini, forcing him to postpone the trip.
At the time, Taiwan blamed “intense pressure” from China for the revocation.
“China now learned that this could be an effective way to block our airspace access and therefore sort of further isolate Taiwan,” Chen said. “We see this is the discovery that they can weaponize the airspace assets.”
Many like-minded countries had assisted Taiwan over the airspace closure, he said.
“We are afraid that this might be a practice that spreads to other global south countries,” he said. “I think that is a major concern for not only for Taiwan, but also for other countries in the region and beyond.”

AI rise could fuel China invasion threat: Palantir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:47 UTC
01:42:47 KST

Palantir Technologies Inc’s head of defense Mike Gallagher on Wednesday warned that advances in artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities have made it more compelling for Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) to seize control of Taiwan.
Gallagher, a former Republican member of the US Congress who led a House of Representatives committee focused on US strategic competition with China, said that Taiwan’s importance to AI development has grown to the point that Xi might need to act on Beijing’s designs toward the nation — especially in light of the competition between the US and China to dominate the technology.
“The logic of Xi Jinping sacrificing enormously to take Taiwan is getting more compelling,” Gallagher said at a defense policy event in Indiana with US Senator Jim Banks.
Photo: Bloomberg
Chinese embassy in Washington spokesman Liu Chang (劉暢) said in a statement later on Wednesday that Beijing “brooks no external interference” and suggested the US “act prudently” on Taiwan.
“The Taiwan question is China’s internal affair,” he said. “Stronger cooperation between enterprises on both sides of the Taiwan Strait in semiconductors and other fields is the right path toward mutual benefit and win-win outcomes.”
As Taiwan is the home to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), it makes it a chokepoint that China could exploit to halt US progress in AI technology if authorities in Beijing found the US was gaining too much of a lead, Gallagher said.
“If China takes Taiwan, they will control TSMC or disable TSMC — they will have the ability to hold the rest of the world economically hostage,” said Gallagher, who left Congress in early 2024 and joined Palantir later that year.
While some prominent US officials have previously warned that China was seeking the capability to invade Taiwan by next year, the US has backed away from that projection, including in March with an intelligence assessment that concluded an invasion “would be extremely challenging and carry a high risk of failure.”
Even so, China has stepped up patrols by its coast guard off Taiwan’s east coast, highlighting the risk that a blockade would pose to global supply chains in the event of a Chinese invasion.
The patrols add to the regular military drills conducted by Chinese forces in the region.
Palantir plays a critical role in the US military as a key provider of technology for the Pentagon, including its Maven Smart System, which uses AI for surveillance and targeting.
During his remarks, Gallagher said that companies in Silicon Valley have increasingly talked about the inflection point where AI models begin to improve themselves, calling it the kind of super intelligence that could get China’s attention, characterizing it as being on par with the development of nuclear weapons.
“If that is true, that we’re at an inflection point, and this technology is a game changer on par with the advent of nuclear weapons in the 1940s,” he said.

Samsung Electronics Co plans to increase spending more than 60 percent this year after selling out of high-end chips for next year, yet its stock fell after the company failed to outline plans to share ballooning profits.
The world’s largest maker of memory chips expects capital expenditure to jump to 84.4 trillion won (US$63.1 billion) this year, targeting market share from SK Hynix Inc. and Micron Technology Inc.
However, chip-division operating income fell about 2 percent shy of estimates and the company withheld plans for future shareholder payouts until January.
Photo: Bloomberg
While Samsung’s semiconductor profits surged 15-fold — reflecting a severe shortage of storage for servers and smartphones — investors had expected more after SK Hynix soundly beat expectations a day prior. Samsung let the market down after its smaller rival announced total new payouts of US$45 billion.
Longer-term, the world’s biggest memory maker is trying to mobilize its financial resources to catch up in securing lucrative long-term contracts, particularly for the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) essential for Nvidia Corp’s accelerators.
Samsung sees the next-generation of such advanced chips — to work with Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform — as a once-in-a-decade chance to catch up to SK Hynix.
“Samsung is also lifting capex by around 60 percent this year, so until it spells out how this windfall gets split between new capacity and shareholders, there’s a genuine question mark over how much actually comes back to investors,” eToro lead analyst for Asia Pacific Josh Gilbert said. “That turns January into a must-deliver moment.”
Samsung yesterday reported that group-wide net income also missed estimates.
While earnings are bounding ahead, the shortfall versus expectations coincides with growing doubts about the extent and durability of the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom, as well as Samsung’s ability to sustain higher margins.
The company has secured 10 long-term supply agreements with key customers, executives said.
However, while SK Hynix said its HBM was sold out through 2029, Samsung said its HBM was sold out only through next year.

Samsung also announced additional shareholder returns for this year.

US Army outlines Pacific deployments for possible 2027 China-Taiwan conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:19 UTC
01:42:19 KST

The US Army Pacific (USARPAC) is deploying forces and equipment across the region based on the assumption that Beijing could possess the military capability and the intent to invade Taiwan by next year, a top US commander said on Tuesday.
Speaking at the TechNet Indo-Pacific conference in Honolulu, US General Ronald Clark said that the threat posed by the so-called “Davidson window” is “still valid,” US military newspaper Stars and Stripes reported on Wednesday.
The term stems from a 2021 warning by Admiral Philip Davidson, then-head of the US Indo-Pacific Command, that the threat of Chinese military action against Taiwan could materialize within six years.
Photo: AP
The six-year timeframe has driven US defense budgeting and strategy in the Pacific with the goal of deterring or obstructing an invasion, Stars and Stripes reported.
Asked whether the Davidson window was still relevant, Clark said: “The answer for us at USARPAC is yes.”
The six-year window is “a period of time for which we’re snapping the chalk line to say we need to be ready by this date,” he said in the report. “So we’ve embarked upon a strategic approach to setting the theater that we refer to as Army Ready Forward.”
Under the Army Ready Forward initiative, USARPAC has placed equipment, materiel and personnel on a rotational basis west of the International Date Line on the island chains closest to China, Clark said.
The most pressing issue for the military is finding the right balance between “exquisite high-end systems and affordable, mass-producible alternatives,” particularly regarding autonomous systems, he said.
The 2027 timeline has been a focal point for US defense planning, although assessments of Beijing’s immediate intent vary.
In 2023, former CIA director William Burns said US intelligence indicated that Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) had instructed the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) to be ready by next year to conduct a successful invasion.
However, an annual threat assessment issued in March by the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence assessed that Chinese leaders did not currently plan to invade Taiwan in 2027.
“Chinese leaders do not currently plan to execute an invasion of Taiwan in 2027, nor do they have a fixed timeline for achieving unification,” it said. “Beijing almost certainly will consider a variety of factors in deciding whether and how to pursue military approaches to unification, including PLA readiness, the actions and politics of Taiwan, and whether or not the US will militarily intervene on Taiwan’s behalf.”

Following the scent to Singang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:16 UTC
01:42:16 KST

Several years ago, the Ministry of Economic Affairs began encouraging legacy manufacturing enterprises to reposition themselves as tourist factories. In these places — which draw busloads of Taiwanese tourists but few international travelers — visitors can learn about the history of particular industries, observe production, join DIY workshops and gain an appreciation of the unglamorous but valuable skills that underpin Taiwan’s economy.
Among the country’s most successful tourist factories are sites which make balloons, braised foods, cookies, fishing gear, ribbons and whisky. Few are so closely tied to local traditional culture, however, as Singang Incense Artistic Culture Garden (新港香藝文化園區) in Chiayi County.
The small town of Singang (新港) is best known for its principal place of worship, Fengtian Temple (奉天宮). Each year, the massive nine-day Mazu pilgrimage that starts in Taichung’s Dajia District (大甲) arrives at the temple, then turns around and resumes its homeward trek.
Photo by Steven Crook
Han Chinese have been burning incense made from agarwood, sandalwood and other fragrant ingredients since at least the Song dynasty (960–1279 AD), and incense has long held a central role in Taiwanese religion and temple culture. The burning of incense establishes a symbolic connection between the human and spiritual realms. Incense smoke is believed to carry the prayers and gratitude of the pious up to the deities they worship. Pioneers wishing to consecrate a new shrine carried with them ash taken from the censer of an established temple in their home region — a ritual known as fenxiang (分香, “dividing the incense”).
These traditions are familiar to anyone versed in Taiwanese popular religion, yet a visit to Singang Incense Artistic Culture Garden offers additional insights to those who can read Chinese or use their smartphone’s translation function.
Originally a thoroughly traditional incense making operation led by three brothers surnamed Chen (陳), the site became a tourism factory in 2008. It now includes an exhibition area, a demonstration workshop, a shop and a restaurant for visiting tour groups — as well as a large production area which is off-limits to the public.
Hoping to get some good photos of incense makers at work, I peered through the murky glass that separated me from two middle-aged men. They were busy dipping thin sticks in powder, shaking off the excess, then placing them in a machine that rolls the sticks to ensure they’re evenly coated.
To my surprise, neither man wore a respirator mask or eye protection. Even if the materials being used were 100-percent natural, the sifting and shaking generates plenty of dust. It can’t be healthy.
‘NINE SKILLS OF INCENSE MAKING’
I clambered around to the other side of the building, where a couple of doors had been left open, presumably to ventilate the workshop. Pictures taken, I headed for the air-conditioned comfort of the exhibition hall.
One display focuses on the “Nine Skills of Incense Making” that were essential before machines became available. The skills are, in order: dipping (in water, to moisten the bamboo splints); twisting (in natural gum, which ensures the incense powder stays on); resoaking (with water, to activate the adhesive); spreading (holding sticks in a fan-like shape, then tossing aromatic wood powder over them); twirling (rotating the sticks so the powder coating is even); tapping (to shake off excess powder); air drying (until they’re partly but not entirely dry); dyeing (each stick’s handle using red or pink pigment); and sun drying. Even then, the work isn’t done, as the finished sticks have to be inspected, bundled and packaged.
INCENSE MOTHER
One panel tells the story of Jiutian Xuannu (九天玄女), the putative inventor of incense sticks. Myth has it that her father was desperately ill and unable to swallow the bitter herbal medicines prescribed by traditional physicians. One day, she dried the medicinal herbs and ground them up into a powder. After adding a binding paste made from tree bark, she rolled the mixture onto narrow strips of bamboo. These she lit and placed in her father’s bedchamber, so he could breathe in the herbs.
The therapeutic aromas eventually cured him — and his daughter earned an additional name, Xiang Ma (香媽, “Incense Mother”). Over the past thousand years, beyond her role as the patron deity of incense, Jiutian Xuannu has also been worshipped as the goddess of warfare, longevity and sexuality.
Another part of the exhibition concedes that Taiwan’s incense-making industry has been in decline since the 1970s, yet it doesn’t offer any explanations. Rather than any decline in the amount of incense being burnt, I suspect it’s a consequence of cheap imports from China and Southeast Asia taking market share.
Several display cases contain exceptional woodcarvings and objects crafted from incense dough. Similar works of art can be purchased on site. They’re stunning but hardly cheap; I saw one carrying a price tag of NT$398,000. More affordable purchases come in the shape of aromatic sachets, essential oils, fragrant soaps, sandalwood shampoo and various types of incense. In addition to joss sticks of different calibers, there are incense coils, incense yuanbao (元寶, the shape gold and silver ingots used in the China of yore), incense powders and jingxiangfen powders (淨香粉) used in purification rites.
Returning to the car at the end of our visit, I poked my head into the company’s production area. Being a Sunday, the machines were quiet, but outside a pair of workers moved back and forth, turning over incense coils as they dried under the sun. If I learned one thing at Singang Incense Artistic Culture Garden, it’s that incense making — like many other traditional trades — brings its participants both daily tedium and economic stability.
In 1986 I entered the US Peace Corps in Kenya. As a US government volunteer we had a special US government ID for use in Kenya. Because of our position, we received extensive training in how to behave. This had special urgency for my group of volunteers: we had originally been slated for Nepal, but a US Peace Corps volunteer in another country had criticized that nation’s authoritarian president in public, and all of the Peace Corps volunteers were kicked out. As a result, the next group for that nation got sent to Nepal, and we got bumped to Kenya. The
On Oct. 2, after years of delays, Taiwan’s air force took delivery of the first two F-16V Block 70 fighter jets at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung County. In a sign of how eagerly anticipated this arrival was, speculation and rumors had been flying as to why they had been sitting for weeks in Hawaii en route to Taiwan. These are part of a total of 66 F-16V Block 70s on order. There are hopes the rest will arrive by the end of next year, but no one will be surprised if that extends into 2029 or even later. Worse,

Getting less attention is that across the board the relationship is growing stronger, and both sides appear to be planning to put more of their eggs in each other’s baskets. Debate in Ivory Coast spills into concert halls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:42:14 UTC
01:42:14 KST

Ivorian reggae star Alpha Blondy abruptly interrupted his concert’s chilled-out vibes to wade into a far less laid-back subject — the coups in his country’s unrest-riven Sahel neighbors.
His comments swiftly went viral on social media, in a sign of how Ivory Coast’s poor relations with the military-led governments in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have spilled over into popular culture, with artists caught in the crossfire.
“To my Sahel brothers ... no more coups d’etat. That’s enough,” the singer, known for his political bent, told the crowd in Ivory Coast’s economic capital, Abidjan.
Photo: AFP
The past few years’ toppling of democratic governments in west Africa is “destabilizing the region,” Blondy said, leg propped up against a loudspeaker. “Africa has no time to waste.”
Since the coups, all three have turned their backs on France — and therefore on Ivory Coast, which the juntas consider far too close to their shared former colonial ruler for comfort.
Several Internet commentators from the Sahel countries accused Blondy of attacking their leaders while turning a blind eye to Ivory Coast President Alassane Ouattara’s largely uncontested election to a fourth term — a criticism echoed by some Ivorians.
With the climate tense, musicians and promoters have found themselves ensnared in controversies that have led to dozens of canceled concerts or boycott calls.
In the latest example, Burkinabe singer Issouf Manem-Yam was forced to apologize for remarks seen as insulting toward Ivorians after his Abidjan concert planned for the middle of this month was axed.
“He’s an artist; he shouldn’t take sides, even if his remarks were made out of patriotism,” a Burkinabe cultural figure told reporters.
The tipping point can be traced back to 2022 at least, when Mali detained 49 Ivorian soldiers for six months. With social media awash with calls to target the other country’s artists, Malian singer Mariam Ba had her Abidjan concert canceled, weeks before the same happened to Ivorian rapper Didi B’s planned gig in the Malian capital, Bamako.
The tit-for-tat cancelations have only become more frequent, with Malian artists targeted in Abidjan while Ivorian musicians have received at-times frosty welcomes in the Sahel capitals.
“We’ve documented a dozen cases of Malian artists who have fallen victim,” a Malian culture ministry official told reporters, adding that the subject was on the agenda when Ivory Coast’s security chief visited in the middle of this month.
Every political remark is under scrutiny.
For backing Ouattara during Ivory Coast’s presidential campaign last year, Malian artist Sidiki Diabate has been slated within his home country.
On the other side of the border, Ivorian diva Aicha Kone has frequently raised hackles in Abidjan for backing the Sahel juntas.
Blondy’s fellow Ivorian reggae singer Tiken Jah Fakoly also found himself mired in the squabble after criticizing clampdowns on free speech in Ivory Coast’s neighbors.
Under criticism by supporters of the three juntas, he replied in 2024 that the Sahel states “thought I was going to be their minstrel.”
Several months later, the affair took a bizarre turn after his beloved “Rasta Bambi,” a doe he had lovingly raised on his farm in Mali, went missing.
Supporters of the juntas on the Internet swiftly seized on Rasta Bambi’s disappearance to mock the singer, with one commenting ironically that the deer “is demanding democracy from you” and had “just broken the chains of slavery.”
Despite the tensions, Ivorian and Sahel artists have continued to criss-cross the border to play gigs in each other’s countries, with cultural ties proving stronger than diplomatic ones.
“Artists are truly above taking sides in politics,” the president of a cultural association in Abidjan said.
Instead of the Ivory Coast-Sahel row, the official blamed the political situation in the Sahel countries — which are all wracked by a long-running and bloody jihadist insurgency — for “reducing the mobility of artists”.
One Ivorian musician who has kept the music playing on in the junta-run nations is Serge Beynaud, who performed near the Burkinabe capital, Ouagadougou, at the end of last month.
Sole hitch of the evening: with the bouncers clearly intent on making sure no disorder disrupted the gig, one of his dancers was whipped by an over-zealous security guard.

The Office of the Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights refutes reports that Russian occupiers have begun evacuating residents of the town of Oleshky in Kherson region, without waiting for the announced arrival of representatives of the American media and teams from both the Ukrainian and Russian human rights commissioners.
"We currently have no confirmation of such actions on the part of the Russian side," Director of the Department of Information Policy, Communications, and Protocol Events at the Ombudsman's Office Tetiana Shelest told reporters on Thursday.
Earlier, Russian propaganda media published a series of photos and videos showing civilians from the city sitting on military buggies driving through the streets of Oleshky. It was reported that civilians are currently being gathered and preparations are underway to receive the humanitarian convoy.
As previously reported, according to Fox News, the humanitarian operation in Oleshky was coordinated through the mediation of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump. The agreement was signed on October 23 by Dmytro Lubinets, the Verkhovna Rada's Commissioner for Human Rights, and Russian Ombudswoman Yana Lantratova. A ceasefire in Oleshky area went into effect on Tuesday, and the mission will last about a week. Four American journalists from Newsmax will be stationed directly in the occupied city to document the humanitarian mission, the U.S. First Lady said.
Lubinets himself reported earlier on Thursday that he was already on his way to Oleshky. Commenting on social media posts claiming that he was allegedly in Russia, specifically in Anapa, he wrote: "There are many questions and provocative posts circulating. So I want to clarify: I am going there to be on the ground in person and see what is happening. To keep you informed about the mission's progress. Please trust official sources and do not draw conclusions from unverified reports."
Humanitarian aid for residents of occupied Oleshky was scheduled to be delivered to the city on October 30; demining of the routes for the mission is currently underway. However, Russian propaganda media are reporting that the first batch of humanitarian aid was delivered to the town as early as Thursday.

Eight of England’s nine water companies still failing on environment, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:39:48 UTC
01:39:48 KST

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has summoned water industry bosses to Whitehall after a report found that the environmental performance of the big companies has worsened despite investment.
“People are sick of excuses,” Dame Angela said, after the Environment Agency joined the Drinking Water Inspectorate, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat for a joint report that rated eight of the nine water companies in England as “poor” or “requiring improvement”.
There were 74 serious pollution incidents, the category that causes significant harm to the environment, the report said. That was just one fewer than the previous year, despite billions of pounds of investment, bans on bosses’ bonuses and a public outcry. The watchdog’s environmental performance assessment ratings of water companies added up to 16 “stars” out of a possible 36, a fall from 19 the previous year, and the lowest score since the process began.
Changes could be imposed on the industry, Eagle warned: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and-branch reform cannot wait.”
The UK is one of only two countries in the world where the provision of water is fully privatised. The other is Chile, where water privatisation was imposed in the 1980s by a military dictatorship.
Overall, there were 2,666 pollution incidents in England in 2025 – a 40% increase on 2016, the EA said. Thames Water had the most, followed by Anglian Water, United Utilities, Yorkshire Water and Southern Water.
The Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Eagle was preparing to take “further action”, with “tougher consequences” for executives at failing companies.
Defra said it would “set out a clear set of improvement actions”, such as “tackling leakage”, “reductions in pollution incidents” and “improving customer satisfaction”. Rules that took effect last year would block bonuses for executives at companies receiving a one-star rating.
Environmental campaigners called for stronger action. “This is a system that rewards shareholders and creditors while our rivers, wildlife and bill payers lose out,” said James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action.
Thames Water, the worst offender, ought to go into special administration immediately, he said. “Ministers must end the failed privatisation experiment, review alternative models including public ownership, and give regulators the power to make polluters pay not the public.”
The four agencies have pooled their data in a joint report for the first time – a step towards combining currently fragmented regulatory responsibilities under a single watchdog. But Richard Benwell, the chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said a new regulator “must be more than a merger of existing institutions”.
“It needs a clear legal duty to restore nature, strong environmental targets and the powers and resources to enforce the law across the water industry, industrial agriculture, and chemical companies,” he said.
Water UK, the industry trade body, said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history, as well as other areas of good performance. However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough.
“While more than half of all pollution incidents last year were caused by blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies, there is clearly more work to do.
“It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth and end sewage entering rivers and seas.”

India increases growth forecast for fiscal year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:30:00 UTC
01:30:00 KST

India increases growth forecast for fiscal year
October 29, 2026
India's Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review.
The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.
India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.
The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm."
The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter.
Inflation, fueled by El Nino and geopolitics, poses a threat
However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season.
It said that external factors like oil prices and "global uncertainties" — seemingly a reference at least in part to the instablity in the Middle East — continued to pressure the rupee's value and pose inflationary risks.
Consumer price inflation (CPI), the wholesale price index (WPI), food cost prices and fuel and power prices were all rising month for month, albeit at very different rates.
The CPI was up 5.54% year-on-year in September, but the WPI had risen more sharply at 11.39%. Food index inflation was up by 8% in rural areas, and a slightly more modest 7.18% in urban centers.
But, as in many other countries, fuel and power costs increases were in an entirely different league, at 25.85% inflation in September 2026 comapred to the same month a year earlier, prior to the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East.
Ministry says FX reserves ample, rupee's decline appears manageable
Although it has been a comparatively slow decline, the rupee has been consistently losing value against the US dollar over the past five years, threatening the country's relative purchasing power internationally. This slide has picked up pace in the last 15 months or so.
But the ministry pointed to foreign exchange reserves worth some $721 billion and said that India was "well-positioned" to weather such risks and sustain its expansionary trajectory..

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Some 50,000 Ethiopians have fled into neighboring Kenya, seeking safety following violent clashes in southern Ethiopia, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has said.
The UN migration agency warned, in a statement issued Thursday, that further arrivals could place additional pressure on already stretched local services and resources.
IOM data showed that an estimated 50,000 people had arrived in Moyale, Marsabit County, as of Thursday. They are staying with local communities along the border or sheltering at five temporary sites.
As the situation continues to evolve, IOM said the Kenyan government and inter-agency partners are planning a response for up to 80,000 people, anticipating further arrivals and growing humanitarian needs.
"The situation remains fluid, and the number of arrivals could increase in the coming days," IOM Kenya Chief of Mission Nomagugu Ncube said in the statement.
Noting that most of the displaced are being sheltered by local communities, Ncube stressed that meeting their immediate needs, while also supporting the communities who are now hosting thousands, is "an urgent priority."
The UN agency stressed that newly arrived populations urgently need basic supplies, safe water, emergency shelter, healthcare services, critical protection and sanitation support.
The arrivals follow a week of deadly intercommunal clashes between Ethiopia's Somali and Oromo communities in and around Moyale, a border town. Media reports have linked the violence, which has reportedly killed scores of people on both sides, to tensions over a flag dispute. ■

China's Zhang wins 53kg total at weightlifting worlds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:29:06 CST
01:29:06 KST

NINGBO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's Zhang Haiqin won the women's 53kg title at the Weightlifting World Championships here on Thursday, holding off American Miranda Ulrey by one kilogram in the total standings.
Zhang lifted 98kg in the snatch and 123kg in the clean and jerk for a total of 221kg. Ulrey matched Zhang's 98kg in the snatch but managed 122kg in the clean and jerk for a 220kg total.
The two traded successful lifts throughout the snatch, both opening at 95kg before making 98kg. Both failed at 100kg on their third attempts, with Zhang taking snatch gold by virtue of her lighter body weight.
"I really wanted to make 100, that weight was over the record and I wanted it, but I rushed it a little," Zhang said. After the snatch, she initially thought she had finished second. "I didn't realize at the time, I thought I was second, and then my coach told me I was first."
Rosegie Ramos of the Philippines took snatch bronze with 97kg.
In the clean and jerk, Ulrey missed her first attempt at 119kg before making 120kg and 122kg. Zhang made 120kg and then 123kg on her second attempt, a lift she knew was crucial.
"The second lift is key. If you fall behind on the second lift it's very hard to come back," Zhang said.
Zhang then attempted 126kg on her final lift, which would have given her clean-and-jerk gold and broken the total world standard of 223kg, but she was unable to complete the lift.
"On the third lift I pulled too hard off the floor and my whole frame kind of collapsed, the weight just crushed me," Zhang told Xinhua. "I tried to stand up but I really gave it everything."
Clean-and-jerk gold instead went to Kim So Hyon of the DPR Korea, who lifted 123kg in the afternoon's Group B session before the Group A competition. Kim finished with a 214kg total, enough for bronze overall.
Because Kim reached 123kg first, she ranked ahead of Zhang in the clean and jerk. Zhang said she did not watch Kim's afternoon session.
"I was resting in the back, I didn't see it, it didn't affect my rhythm, I just focused on myself," Zhang said.
The world standards for the new 53kg category, which took effect Aug. 1 under the Los Angeles Olympic cycle, are 99kg in the snatch, 126kg in the clean and jerk and 223kg in total. Zhang lifted 101kg in the snatch and totaled 227kg at a national Grand Prix in August, but came up short of those marks on Thursday.
"Of course there's regret, the world record felt right there, but regret gives me even more motivation," Zhang said. "I just need to take it one competition at a time, make every lift, and go back and build a stronger, more solid base."
The men's 70kg Group A competition is scheduled for Friday. ■

Sweden's Center Party leader nominated for PM amid political deadlock
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:29:05 CST
01:29:05 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Swedish Parliament Speaker Andreas Norlen on Thursday nominated Center Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist as the country's next prime minister (PM), with a parliamentary vote scheduled for next Tuesday, marking the latest attempt to break the political deadlock following September's general election.
Norlen said the Nov. 3 vote would test parliamentary support for a proposed five-party coalition government comprising the Center Party, Social Democratic Party, Christian Democrats, Green Party and Liberal Party.
Thand Ringqvist confirmed to Swedish Television (SVT) that she had accepted the nomination, saying the Center Party would "continue to take responsibility and contribute constructively to ensuring that Sweden gets a government."
She said the speaker had decided to nominate her following their discussions, although she had also pointed out that other possible ways forward remained.
Norlen thanked Thand Ringqvist for her efforts to explore possible governing arrangements, saying they had helped deepen understanding of the political situation.
Drawing on lessons from Sweden's prolonged government formation process in 2018, Norlen said he wanted to link exploratory talks more closely with parliamentary votes to maintain momentum and gradually increase pressure on political parties to resolve the deadlock.
He also outlined the next step should Thand Ringqvist's nomination be rejected. Ulf Kristersson, leader of the Moderate Party and outgoing PM, would then be given one week, from Nov. 3 to Nov. 10, to explore the possibility of forming a government.
The latest development follows weeks of unsuccessful attempts to form a government after Sweden's Sept. 13 general election. On Oct. 15, parliament rejected Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson's bid to become the PM. Andersson had previously failed to secure sufficient support for a government after two rounds of exploratory talks.
On Oct. 19, Norlen tasked Thand Ringqvist with exploring the possibility of forming a government. However, after holding talks with other parliamentary parties, she reported back to the speaker on Monday that her efforts had failed to break the political deadlock.
The Social Democratic Party, Left Party, Green Party and Center Party together won 176 seats in the 349-member parliament in September's election, giving them a narrow majority but leaving them divided over the composition of a new government.
Under Sweden's constitution, a prime ministerial nominee is rejected if at least 175 members of parliament vote against the proposal. If four consecutive nominations are rejected, a new election must be held within three months. ■

China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative named UN World Restoration Flagship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

01:29:00 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative was named a World Restoration Flagship by the United Nations on Thursday during the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia.
The initiative is jointly led by China's Ministry of Natural Resources and Ministry of Finance. This marks the second time a nationwide ecological restoration initiative from China has received the United Nations Decade on Ecosystem Restoration recognition, making China the first country to achieve the distinction twice.
Chosen from over 200 applications and more than 80 government-submitted nominations, the Blue Bay Restoration Initiative was recognized as one of the world's most promising, ambitious and inspiring examples of large-scale ecosystem restoration, said Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme.
The initiative aims to restore more than 150,000 hectares of coastal wetlands and over 2,000 km of coastline by 2030, bringing lasting benefits to local communities, she added. ■

Interview: More than an expo, Rwanda sees CIIE as a link to Chinese market, says official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:28:59 CST
01:28:59 KST

KIGALI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Rwanda's regular participation in the China International Import Expo (CIIE) reflects a strong desire to maintain a long-term close connection with the Chinese market, an official said.
In a recent interview with Xinhua ahead of the ninth CIIE from Nov. 5 to 10 in Shanghai, China, Rwanda Development Board (RDB) Deputy Chief Executive Officer Juliana Muganza said that rather than viewing the expo as merely an exhibition, the government recognized that the event offers a platform to promote Rwanda as an investment destination.
This view is backed by the growth in bilateral trade between Rwanda and China from approximately 300 million U.S. dollars in 2019 to 849 million in 2025, according to RDB data. Meanwhile, Rwanda's exports to China have also seen a significant surge from approximately 35 million dollars in 2019 to 227 million in 2025.
Calling China one of Rwanda's most important economic and trading partners, Muganza mentioned that for a country like Rwanda, the CIIE provides a vital opportunity for local companies, including small and medium-sized enterprises, to present their products directly to Chinese buyers, distributors, e-commerce platforms and consumers.
However, she added that Rwanda's participation goes beyond selling products during the six-day expo.
"We use the CIIE to build long-term commercial relationships, better understand developments in the Chinese market, promote Rwanda as an investment and tourism destination, and strengthen the broader economic partnership between Rwanda and China," she said.
Rwanda has participated in the CIIE since the first edition in 2018.
Muganza said the exhibition has also been instrumental in expanding investment cooperation.
Data from the RDB showed that registered investments by Chinese companies in Rwanda rose from 460 million dollars in 2024 to 548.5 million dollars in 2025. Chinese companies in Rwanda are increasingly active in sectors such as manufacturing, infrastructure, construction, energy and real estate.
Muganza said that while the achievements cannot be attributed to the exhibition alone, the CIIE contributed by providing Rwanda with a major platform every year to promote local products, investment opportunities and tourism.
During this year's CIIE, Rwandan exhibitors will showcase some of the country's most competitive and distinctive products, including specialty coffee, premium tea, chili and chili products, macadamia nuts, and other agricultural and value-added Made-in-Rwanda products.
Other products with considerable potential include honey, avocado, dried fruits and nuts, as market access for additional Rwandan products continues to expand.
Muganza emphasized that the CIIE, an exhibition dedicated specifically to imports, "sends an important message that China is not only interested in exporting to the world, but is also actively creating opportunities" for companies from around the world to access the Chinese market.
Pointing to win-win cooperation, Muganza said the exhibition helps foreign companies gain access to the scale and opportunities of the Chinese market, while Chinese companies and consumers benefit from a wider range of international products.
On China's zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries, which came into force in May, Muganza said Rwanda considers the policy a very important development for Africa-China trade.
Muganza also noted that China's high-level opening up "sends an important and positive signal," creating opportunities not only for major multinational corporations, but also for producers and businesses from developing economies. ■

Russia to Extend Diesel Export Ban, Use Quotas to Fulfill U.S. Deal, Sources Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:21:05 UTC
01:21:05 KST

Russia will extend its diesel export ban until the end of the year while allowing some companies to ship fuel under a quota system to meet its new export commitment to the U.S., two people familiar with the discussions told Reuters.
Moscow and Washington agreed a diesel supply deal after Presidents Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump spoke by phone earlier this month. The energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine announced alongside the agreement has allowed Moscow to increase fuel production. At the same time, fuel shortages earlier this year have prompted the government to maintain tight controls on oil product exports.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Tuesday that three tankers carrying Russian diesel to export markets were already under way and that a fourth would sail on Oct. 28.
Novak also said Russian refineries were recovering quickly from repairs. The sources said refinery utilization had risen 25% at the end of October from the start of the month after drone attacks on facilities subsided.
Under the current diesel export ban, the government permits limited exports through a quota system. Those quotas will quadruple from October levels to 2 million metric tons, or about 0.5 million barrels per day, in November, the sources said. Shipments under existing intergovernmental agreements will also continue.
The Energy Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The current ban on diesel exports is due to expire on Oct. 31.
In October, the government exempted several refiners from the ban and granted them export quotas totaling 0.5 million tons, the sources said. A new government order expected in early November would expand the list of exempt refiners and set new export limits. If the quotas are used up quickly, the government could consider increasing them further, the sources added.
Nominal diesel production in Russia exceeds domestic consumption by about 40%. As refineries return to normal operating rates, they will need export outlets to prevent a domestic glut.
