Israeli settlers target journalists, Palestinians in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:20:11 UTC
01:20:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Armed Israeli settlers threaten West Bank families, attack journalists
Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank faced renewed threats of forced displacement on Thursday, as armed Israeli settlers raided homes in the Jordan Valley and allegedly assaulted journalists and activists in Masafer Yatta, days after Israel's parliamentary election.
UK-based charity Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) said masked, armed settlers entered the Palestinian community of Al-Shuneh, near Jiftlik, at around 2am, surrounding three homes and threatening to expel residents unless they left "voluntarily".
The settlers allegedly damaged a resident's car and stole a 1.5-cubic-metre water tank before returning to a nearby hill, where they appeared to have established an illegal outpost the previous day.
Aseel Baidoun, MAP's deputy director of advocacy and campaigns, told The New Arab that the outpost posed an immediate threat to the community's survival.
"For Palestinians in communities like Al-Shuneh, an outpost can spell the end of their community and displacement from their homes. What starts as a few caravans, tents or a settler farm can become a permanent settlement with full backing from the Israeli state," she said.
"Outposts can spread onto more land, link settlements and cut off Palestinian communities from basic services and healthcare. For families already facing attacks and threats, and unable to reach their grazing land for two years, every new development makes it harder to stay."
"That's why the speed of work on the hill overlooking Al-Shuneh is so alarming."
Around 80 families face uncertainty over whether they can remain in their homes, with residents already struggling to access basic services, according to MAP.
Settlers have reportedly spent several days clearing land and carrying out construction on the hill overlooking the community. More than three settler families have arrived at the site and begun installing what appear to be water pipes and electricity cables.
MAP also documented earlier threats against Al-Shuneh residents, including an August incident in which armed settlers allegedly assaulted a family and threatened to burn their homes and seize their livestock unless they left.
Baidoun warned that the outcome of Tuesday's Israeli election was unlikely to improve conditions for Palestinians.
"Whatever the outcome of Israel's election, there is little reason to expect a change in the policies driving settlement expansion and settler violence," she told The New Arab.
"All of Israel's major political parties support the settlement project, and Palestinian communities cannot rely on a new government to protect them from the violence and displacement it actively encourages and enables."
Journalists and activists assaulted in Masafer Yatta
In a separate incident, Russian activist Adele Shoko reported that Israeli settlers attacked her and two colleagues, US journalist Jasper Nathaniel and Israeli-Russian activist Andrey X, in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, in Masafer Yatta.
Shoko said armed settlers beat the group, threatened them and stole equipment and personal belongings.
"Jasper and I were also beaten. Jasper was then pepper-sprayed and arrested," she wrote on social media, adding that Israeli forces had taken Nathaniel into custody.
"Andrey was severely beaten and lost consciousness several times in front of police. Despite this, he was denied hospital treatment. He was put in an ambulance – but instead of being taken to hospital, he was taken to a police station. He is still there, arrested and being denied medical care," she added.
Footage circulated online appeared to show several men, some armed, beating Nathaniel and Andrey X. Other footage showed Israeli authorities leading Nathaniel away as he shouted that he had been assaulted.
In later updates, Shoko said both men were "physically okay" and were "having their court hearing" following their detention.
Activists subsequently reported that Andrey X had been released after Thursday's court hearing. Nathaniel's status had not been publicly confirmed.
The attacks follow a warning on Monday from UN-mandated investigators, who accused Israel of committing "extermination" in the occupied West Bank.
Palestinians across the territory have faced escalating violence by Israeli settlers and soldiers, particularly since the start of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

German serial rapist sentenced to 12 years as police investigate 44 more cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:19:58 UTC
01:19:58 KST

Frank S. was sentenced to 12 years in prison, followed by preventive detention. The 69-year-old from Berlin systematically drugged and raped 14 women and filmed the assaults. A further 44 cases are expected to be examined in a separate trial.
The court sentenced Frank S. to 12 years in prison, followed by preventive detention. The 69-year-old is unlikely ever to be released.
One of the worst serial rapists in German criminal history is believed by investigators to have drugged and raped 58 women, filmed his crimes and shared the footage online with other men. It was this that ultimately led to his capture.
After his chat partner was arrested, police tracked down Frank S., searched his flat and found the video recordings.
Frank S. had filmed a total of 58 women after drugging their drinks and sexually assaulting them. Some of the women were still conscious and begged him to stop. Afterwards, many were unable to remember what had happened because of the heavy sedation. As a result, Frank S. was not reported to police, while other women suppressed memories of what they had experienced.
It was only when police visited some of the women at home during the investigation that they first learned what Frank S. had done to them.
On Wednesday, Berlin Regional Court sentenced Frank S. to 12 years in prison, followed by preventive detention, for 22 rapes involving 14 women. In nine cases, he also violated their intimate privacy by recording them.
During the three-month trial, all 14 women testified as witnesses, with six also participating as joint plaintiffs. The perpetrator's videos were also used as evidence.
According to the court, the women were completely helpless and defenceless because they had been sedated with various medications. The judges found that Frank S. took advantage of this. The now 69-year-old filmed his acts and is said to have stored the video recordings digitally "like trophies in a cabinet". The court described his actions as particularly "contemptuous towards women".
Despite the confession delivered by S.'s defence lawyer at the start of the trial, the court ordered preventive detention after he serves his sentence. This measure is considered one of the harshest tools available to the judiciary. By the time he could be released from prison, he will already be over 80 years old.
The court did not consider his advanced age sufficient reason to conclude that S. would not reoffend. The presiding judge stated that the defendant had not fully understood what he had done to the women or the serious consequences his actions had had for them. The verdict is not yet legally binding, and S. can still appeal.
Frank S.'s devious methods
Over a seven-year period from 2016 to 2022, the now 69-year-old met the 14 women through dating platforms and deceived them. He gained their trust in a way that was, according to a court spokesperson, "particularly devious". He told one woman he was a police inspector and another that he was a helicopter pilot. Ultimately, the trained electrician invited the women to his flat and offered them drinks.
However, the alcoholic drinks were laced with substances that, combined with alcohol, left the women helpless and unable to resist. Some still tried to protest verbally, but S. ignored them. "What really mattered to him was to exercise power over these defenceless women," a court spokesperson explained. S. raped the sedated women, in some cases several times, in his bedroom, where a video camera was permanently installed.
The judge described S.'s methods as systematic and highly organised. His crimes followed a pattern. The court also stated that he acted like an archivist and, as became particularly clear from the videos examined, carried out his crimes in a calm and routine manner. He is said to have rewatched some of the footage while smoking a cigarette.
Four expert witnesses, including specialists in IT, toxicology and psychiatry, provided evidence during the trial. Six of the victims participated as joint plaintiffs during the three-month proceedings. Two of them attended the sentencing but declined to speak publicly.
Women avoid public attention as organisations show solidarity
"What is very important for me and also for my client is the preventive detention that has now been ordered, because the propensity to offend and the danger he poses, at least as things stand today, are very clear," said Silke Studzinski, lawyer for one of the joint plaintiffs.
Laura Leogrande, a lawyer for another joint plaintiff, also said "that there was indeed a reluctance to speak in public". She stressed that this was not a criticism, however. At the plaintiffs’ request, the closing statements were delivered behind closed doors. They decided to speak about the rapes they had suffered without members of the public present.
"I do find it remarkable that there was so much shame," Leogrande said, "about having been in this situation, about having become a victim of this crime, and having trusted this man enough to go home with him, and then something like this happens." The victims were not to blame.
Outside the courthouse, organisations such as Terre des Femmes and initiatives like "Die Scham muss die Seite wechseln" ("Shame must change sides") showed their solidarity. They called for protests and rallies.
"Terre des Femmes is here because we stand in solidarity with those affected and because we want to send a signal against sexualised violence," explained Sina Tonk, a department head at the organisation, in an interview with Euronews. "We know that only around three percent of rapes are ever reported to the police, and that happens out of fear or shame, or because many obstacles are placed in the way of those affected."
Another trial could follow. Police now believe there are 58 victims, and investigations into a further 44 cases are ongoing. Ten women believed to appear in the videos have not yet been identified.
Leogrande stressed that this is not a new phenomenon. Rather, rape after a victim has been drugged is "something that has only now come to the surface, that is only now being talked about and that is only now being investigated in real detail". The Pelicot case in France has drawn particular attention to the issue.
Berlin police became aware of Frank S. after officers in Lower Saxony passed on a tip based on a chat log. S. had exchanged information about his crimes with a suspected rapist in Verden, Lower Saxony. He was arrested in March 2026 and has remained in pre-trial detention since then.
The series of rapes is considered the largest case to date involving drug-facilitated sexual assault before the Berlin Regional Court. Germany has also recently tightened its laws on sexual violence, including provisions concerning the use of incapacitating drugs and the recording of crimes.

‘If this works, it will be the first real ceasefire across a large stretch of the front’: Russia and Ukraine maintain truce in occupied Oleshky for more than two days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:05:56 UTC
01:05:56 KST

‘If this works, it will be the first real ceasefire across a large stretch of the front’: Russia and Ukraine maintain truce in occupied Oleshky for more than two days
Russia and Ukraine have halted hostilities around the occupied city of Oleshky since October 27. The Verkhovna Rada’s human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed on the morning of October 29 that the ceasefire had held for more than two days. Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, said humanitarian aid — “food, fuel, medicine, and hygiene products” — had been sent to Oleshky.
Lubinets and Lantratova set out for Oleshky on the afternoon of October 29. Lubinets will be the first Ukrainian official of such rank to visit Russian-occupied territories. Both commissioners said their main task is to deliver humanitarian aid to residents and ensure the safe evacuation of those who want to leave.
Sources who spoke to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda and were involved in organizing the ceasefire said the ceasefire around Oleshky is meant to test whether Ukrainian and Russian military commanders can carry out political agreements to end hostilities.
Organizing a halt to the fighting turned out to be “an extremely difficult task,” according to the outlet’s sources. A political order to cease fire does not by itself guarantee automatic compliance on the front line, a source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s administration told Ukrainska Pravda. Even Ukrainian troops demanded guarantees several times that if they stopped, “nothing bad would happen afterward,” the source said. The source explained:
We want to get the military — both our General Staff and the Russian one — used to the idea that if the political leadership has decided that in a given sector of the front we stop, freeze in place, and no one opens fire, the military can make that happen. They can guarantee it. Not a situation where the political leadership has reached an agreement and the military says, “Sorry, we can’t stop, we’ve got something going on.”
It is easier for the Russian side than for the Ukrainian side to organize and maintain a ceasefire, according to Ukrainska Pravda’s sources. “They [the Russians] have a rigid military vertical. We have a decentralized army. And someone — some well-known military blogger — could stir up the mood on air so much that everything falls apart afterward,” a source said.
If the ceasefire in Oleshky can be maintained, as planned, until the evening of November 1, the Ukrainian side expects to repeat this kind of local ceasefire later along other parts of the front. “That’s precisely so the military can learn how to do this: stop, ensure safe passage, and so on. So that later, if there’s some major agreement, we could implement it right away,” a source who spoke to Ukrainska Pravda said.
If this works, this will be the first example of a real ceasefire across a fairly large stretch of the front. It’s come at such a cost — the military, Russia’s Federal Security Service, and everyone else are doing nothing but trying to sabotage it. But we believe it will work out and that this will set a precedent.
The war in photographs
Russia’s Defense Ministry announced that it had begun clearing mines from roads leading into Oleshky and published photos and video of sappers at work. Russian President Vladimir Putin, speaking at a plenary session of the Russia–Africa summit underway in Moscow, claimed it was Ukraine that had mined the approaches to Oleshky, creating “practically a humanitarian catastrophe.”

HAIKOU /China/, October 29. /TASS/. China’s southern island province of Hainan increased its international trade in services by 11.7% year-on-year to 56.95 billion yuan ($8.48 billion) in January-September 2026, the region’s Department of Commerce said.
According to the department’s WeChat page, the province’s services exports increased by 14.9% to 40.41 billion yuan (around $6.02 billion) in the reporting period, while imports reached 16.54 billion yuan ($2.46 billion), up 4.7%.
The department said that the cross-border maintenance sector (for vessels and aircraft — TASS), inbound tourism and computer game exports demonstrated particularly impressive results over the nine months. Key transport and logistics companies such as COSCO Shipping played an important role in developing Hainan’s freight sector.
The Department of Commerce forecasted that Hainan’s international transport services sector would grow significantly by the end of 2026. The department highlighted the key role of the visa-free regime and air traffic growth, which have brought far more tourists from Russia, Kazakhstan and South Korea to the island.
In addition, the department noted that the quantitative growth in Hainan’s international services trade came with structural optimization, driven by both traditional and new factors. According to the published data, the Chinese special administrative region of Hong Kong, the United States, Russia, Ireland and Singapore are Hainan’s top five partners in this field. According to estimates, they accounted for more than 57% of total commercial activity in this segment of the island’s economy in the first three quarters of 2026.
The department also stated that the Hainan Free Trade Port would continue to use institutional and other advantages to strengthen the regional transport sector and inbound tourism and to introduce new types of services trade. At the same time, the province’s authorities plan to diversify the entry of local companies into foreign markets and ensure the high quality of their economic interaction with partners from other countries and regions.

Hidden ADHD common in women seeking treatment for depression and anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:00:01 UTC
01:00:01 KST

A recent study reveals that nearly one in five women seeking treatment for anxiety or depression also have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, with nearly half of those cases having never been previously diagnosed. The research highlights how overlapping symptoms can obscure the underlying attention condition in adult women. These findings were published in The International Journal of Psychiatry in Medicine.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition involving inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. During childhood development, hyperactive traits often fade, while inattentive traits tend to persist. Medical professionals historically diagnosed the condition much more frequently in males, and in clinical settings, the ratio of diagnosed males to females is roughly ten to one.
Population surveys show a much narrower gap, suggesting the condition often goes unrecognized in female populations. Women frequently display more subtle, internalizing symptoms like emotional sensitivity or internal restlessness. These internal struggles are easily mistaken for mood or anxiety disorders. Because conditions like major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder share traits with ADHD, such as difficulty concentrating, the underlying attention disorder is frequently missed.
An additional feature commonly reported by people with ADHD is hyperfocus. This phenomenon involves episodes of intense, prolonged concentration on specific tasks, often to the exclusion of everything else going on around the person. Though not an official diagnostic criterion, hyperfocus is well-documented and can substantially affect daily functioning.
Psychiatrists Hazal Yavuzlar Civan and Tonguc Demir Berkol from the Bakirkoy Prof. Dr. Mazhar Osman Training and Research Hospital for Psychiatry, Neurology and Neurosurgery in Istanbul, Turkey, conducted the research. They wanted to understand how ADHD manifests in women already seeking help for mood problems. They also examined hyperfocus to see if it could help clinicians distinguish these conditions.
The researchers recruited 170 female patients at outpatient psychiatric clinics. The participants first completed the Beck Depression Inventory and the Beck Anxiety Inventory, which are standard questionnaires that measure the severity of depressive and anxious symptoms. Women scoring above the threshold for clinical depression or anxiety then took additional surveys.
These follow-up surveys included the Wender Utah Rating Scale to measure childhood ADHD traits, a separate screening tool for adult ADHD symptoms, and the Hyperfocus Scale. Following the questionnaires, a trained psychiatrist conducted a structured clinical interview with each participant. The final diagnoses were based on standard psychiatric guidelines.
The clinical interviews revealed that 33 of the 170 women met the criteria for ADHD. Within this group, 15 patients had no prior ADHD diagnosis. ADHD was especially prevalent among women experiencing social anxiety disorder and a condition called double depression. Double depression occurs when a patient experiences a severe depressive episode on top of a chronic, long-term baseline of low mood.
The women with ADHD reported distinct life experiences compared to the participants who only had mood or anxiety disorders. They had more disciplinary issues in school, more frequent job changes, and a higher rate of family members with ADHD. The rates of past suicide attempts did not differ in a statistically significant way between the two groups, but the women with ADHD reported higher levels of current suicidal thoughts and feelings of failure.
When looking at specific depressive symptoms, the two groups diverged. The group without ADHD reported more concerns about physical health and changes in sleeping habits. The authors suggest this health-related worry reflects a somatic focus, which is a heightened awareness of bodily sensations commonly seen in anxiety and depression.
Conversely, individuals with ADHD often experience impaired interoception, meaning they have a harder time recognizing internal physical states. This altered awareness might reduce how often they notice or report physical symptoms like poor sleep.
ADHD was highly prevalent among women experiencing social anxiety disorder. The researchers suggest social anxiety in these patients may be driven by ADHD-related executive dysfunction, which impairs the brain’s ability to plan, organize, and interpret social cues. Difficulties in self-regulation often lead to repeated interpersonal failures, which can eventually create lasting feelings of shame and a fear of social evaluation.
The researchers also identified distinct patterns regarding symptom overlap. In the group without ADHD, higher attention deficit scores correlated with worse depression. Higher hyperactivity scores correlated with worse anxiety. Hyperfocus scores also rose alongside general ADHD-like symptoms in these women.
The women diagnosed with ADHD did not show these same statistical correlations. While their overall hyperfocus scores were substantially higher than the group without ADHD, the severity of their hyperfocus did not track directly with the severity of their mood or anxiety symptoms. The findings suggest hyperfocus may serve different roles depending on the diagnosis, acting as a coping mechanism in ADHD but manifesting as a maladaptive trait in mood disorders.
The study details how similar symptoms stem from different root causes. Both ADHD and anxiety can involve restlessness, distractibility, and tension. In anxiety, inattention usually stems from excessive worry, with mental energy consumed by ruminating or anticipating threats, and this type of distractibility often improves in relaxed environments.
In contrast, inattention related to ADHD is consistent across different settings and typically appears early in life. It is usually associated with poor task initiation, organizational difficulties, and mind-wandering that is completely unrelated to specific fears. The authors note that thorough developmental histories are required to distinguish primary ADHD from secondary attention problems caused by mood disorders.
The research relied on a cross-sectional design, meaning the assessments occurred at a single point in time. The methodology cannot determine the sequence of symptom onset. It remains unclear whether ADHD symptoms preceded the depressive and anxious symptoms, or vice versa.
The sample focused entirely on women seeking outpatient psychiatric care. The prevalence rates and symptom patterns might look different in men, people not seeking psychiatric help, or individuals treated in inpatient hospital settings. The group of women diagnosed with ADHD was also much smaller than the group without the condition, which limits the statistical power of certain comparisons.
Future research should follow patients over extended periods to track how these overlapping conditions develop over a lifespan. Incorporating biological markers or tracking symptoms in broader populations could further clarify how hyperfocus operates across different mental health diagnoses.
The study, “ADHD Comorbidity in Women With Depression and Anxiety: Prevalence, Clinical Features and Hyperfocus Dynamics,” was authored by Hazal Yavuzlar Civan and Tonguc Demir Berkol.

Cabinet gathers to weigh right-wing bloc’s new joint demands

Top members of the Dutch cabinet have gathered to discuss demands made on Thursday by a newly formed alliance of right-wing parties that could determine the future of the government’s tax plan.
On Thursday morning, leaders of the far-right JA21, orthodox Protestant party SGP, and farmer-citizen movement BBB announced they are banding together to force concessions in the tax plan negotiations.
They set out their demands – mainly concerning asylum, nitrogen and abortion – in a letter to the cabinet on Wednesday evening.
If their demands are met, the group says, it will support the cabinet on the rest of the tax plan and take a “constructive” approach to the budget.
The parties want to scrap plans to raise taxes to fund defence spending for NATO, as well as a planned VAT rise on flowers, and they want profit exemptions for small businesses raised.
Adjustments to the nitrogen plans demanded by BBB, harsher measures against asylum by JA21, and a pause on late-term abortions, home abortions and surrogacy demanded by the SGP are now joint demands by all three parties.
The move makes prime minister Jetten’s plans for broad support in which parties across the political spectrum back his plans, even more unlikely.
So far, opposition parties on the left and the right have said the coalition must choose a direction: side with left-wing parties like PRO and Volt, or with the right wing. Within the coalition, D66 and CDA prefer the former option, but the VVD has been leaning rightwards.
The letter contains a number of potentially intractable policies. Ending an obligation to the so-called “spreading law”, which requires all councils to house a fair share of asylum seekers, is something asylum minister Bart van den Brink (CDA) has said he cannot commit to.
Dropping the defence tax is particularly sensitive for the CDA. The SGP’s demands on abortion and surrogacy will clash with D66’s stances, broadcaster NOS reported.
The nitrogen proposals also conflict with agreements the cabinet has said are needed to get permits issued again, and PRO has said it will withdraw its support if the nitrogen plans are substantially changed.

Letter from Mideast: At 16, I carry a rifle and dream of home
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:35:30 CST
00:35:30 KST

by Ali Ahmed
ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- I once imagined myself in a doctor's white coat. Poverty and war put a rifle in my hands instead.
My name is Ali Ahmed. I am 16 years old. Since June 2026, I have been a soldier in a Yemeni pro-government force.
My first monthly salary -- 265 U.S. dollars -- seemed to prove that I had made the right decision.
As the eldest of seven children, I felt useful for the first time in a long while. I sent money home to cover my father's medical bills and help feed my younger siblings.
My mother was relieved, but frightened, too. She understood before I did that the salary came at a price. I knew how to pull a trigger, but little about fighting a war.
About a month after enlisting, I was sent to the front in Hays district, Hodeidah governorate. One night, Houthi fighters surrounded our position, and gunfire tore through the darkness. I could barely see where the shooting was coming from. I aimed at the flashes and fired in panic.
My hands shook. My legs shook. My heart felt as though it were trying to escape my chest.
Two young men from southern Yemen, like me, were killed that night.
I could not stop picturing my mother. For the first time, I truly understood that I might return home not as a son, but as a body.
The war soon taught me another lesson. Four of my friends were killed in a drone strike, and we had to gather what remained of them.
Until then, danger had meant noise: gunfire, explosions, and shouting. After that day, I learned to fear silence, too. Death can arrive without warning.
The life at home I had once hated became the life I longed for. I would gladly have spent all day delivering orders on my motorbike under the scorching sun, earning almost nothing, if it meant coming home alive.
The war followed me into my sleep. Even on quiet nights, I lay waiting for something to happen. Eventually, I saw a doctor because I could no longer sleep properly. The medication helped me sleep, but it could not give me back the peace I had known before the war.
I also began to see the war differently.
Before enlisting, I had never met a Houthi fighter. Then I saw Houthi prisoners. Some were young; others looked exhausted or frightened. But they looked familiar. They looked Yemeni.
I could not help wondering: Did they have sick fathers, too? Younger brothers waiting for food? Had they once imagined another future, as I had?
When you see the other side from a few steps away rather than across a battlefield, war stops looking as simple as it once did.
If the fighting ended tomorrow, I could sit with a Houthi fighter and drink tea. Without rifles between us, we might discover how much our families had in common, and how little we had known about the people we feared.
At the front, we talked more about home than politics. We talked about mothers, wives, children, and food. Sometimes, we asked one another for a final favor: if we were killed, find a way to break the news gently to our mothers.
I do not know when the fighting will end. But I know what I want if I ever make it home for good.
I want to sit with my family by the sea, with a plate of white rice and fish and a glass of red tea. Nothing more. Just all of us, together and safe.
Editor's note: Ali Ahmed is from Yemen's southern port city of Aden. He joined the Giants Brigades in 2026.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Xinhua News Agency.

China Focus: China expands, diversifies launch infrastructure to meet rising space industry demand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:35:21 CST
00:35:21 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China is expanding and diversifying its launch infrastructure to meet the growing demand from the commercial space industry, with its offshore launch platforms, commercial spaceports and dedicated launch pads opening up new avenues for private rocket makers to send spacecraft into orbit.
A typical example is a commercial rocket carrying nine satellites that lifted off from a ship in the East China Sea near Shanghai in September this year. Although the densely populated economic hub has no traditional rocket launch site, sea-based launches are able to connect Shanghai to the country's growing space industry.
China's first sea launch took place in 2019, off the coast of Haiyang in east China's Shandong Province. The coastal city has since built a spaceport for rocket assembly, testing and launch operations. Teng Yao, chief engineer of the spaceport, said sea launches offer greater flexibility in choosing launch locations and trajectories, and allow rocket debris to fall into waters that are unpopulated.
Wenchang in south China's Hainan Province, which hosts a launch site tasked with missions of launching space station modules and lunar probes, has added facilities specifically for commercial rocket and satellite launches since 2024.
Meanwhile, the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone near the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China has developed launch pads tailored to private rocket makers.
Access to launch pads has been a challenge for China's commercial space sector. Wang Lifeng, a professor at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, cited limited launch capacity, tight schedules and long distances between launch sites and rocket assembly facilities as constraints on growth.
Large satellite networks like Qianfan (or Spacesail) and GW constellations, which each have more than 10,000 satellites, further increase the need for a steady flow of launches.
Diversified facilities not only boost launch numbers but also make launch operations more efficient.
Wenchang's commercial spacecraft launch site has put its first two pads into regular service. The second pad alone can accommodate more than 20 rocket types and can be prepared for another launch in 66 hours. The third and fourth pads in the second phase are scheduled to be operational by the end of the year. Upon full commissioning, the site is able to handle about 60 launches annually.
Haiyang offers another route to greater efficiency. Peng Haomin, co-founder of Orienspace, said the private company's facilities are clustered in Haiyang's spaceport, allowing rockets to be assembled, tested and loaded onto a launch ship within 5 km.
"This has replaced usual transportation over more than 1,000 km, drastically cutting logistics time and cost," Peng said.
Dedicated facilities can also streamline rocket operations. Meng Xiangfu, deputy chief commander of Lijian-1 rocket of commercial spaceflight company CAS Space, said that with its tailored launch pad and technical facilities at the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone, the company can complete the testing and preparation of a rocket in 10 days.
The expansion of launch infrastructure not only benefits the space industry, but also helps boost local economy through investment.
With more than 30 aerospace projects landed, Haiyang has attracted 33.5 billion yuan (around 5 billion U.S. dollars) in related investment. Wenchang's space industry park hosts over 700 companies, while Shanghai is developing a commercial spaceport-related terminal to link rocket assembly with port logistics and sea launch services.
These developments fit into a broader global trend of investing in space capabilities to support the sector's growth, as the United States aims at expanding its space transportation capabilities and Russia calls for efforts to upgrade its industrial and ground-based space infrastructure.
A 2025-2027 action plan issued by the China National Space Administration calls for coordinated development of commercial space launch sites and supports new types of commercial launch systems, including sea-based launch and recovery facilities.
At the same time, China is pressing ahead with the development of heavy-lift and reusable launch vehicles to further expand launch capacity and improve cost efficiency.
Analysts note that efficient operation of these facilities could equip China's commercial space sector with the launch capacity and operational flexibility it needs. ■

Finland and Varjo test virtual counter-drone training for soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:13:44 UTC
00:13:44 KST

- The Finnish Defence Forces and Varjo are piloting mixed reality counter-drone training with a brigade-level unit using XR-4 Series headsets.
- Varjo says the headset can show a five-inch FPV drone clearly enough for training at realistic distances, with preparations starting in February 2026.
The Finnish Defence Forces have teamed up with Helsinki-based headset maker Varjo to test and develop mixed reality training that prepares soldiers to spot and counter small attack drones, the military’s Innovation Unit and the company announced on Oct. 29.
Varjo is working with a brigade-level unit of the Finnish Defence Forces on the pilot, using its XR-4 Series mixed reality headset. The partners did not name the unit, say how many headsets are involved or how long the pilot will run, or disclose any contract value. Preparations for the partnership began in February.
The project is aimed at the threat from first-person-view, or FPV, drones and loitering munitions, the small explosive-carrying drones and one-way attack weapons that both sides have used in huge numbers in Ukraine. The Finnish Defence Forces said soldiers need to understand what drones can do and how to operate under that threat, and that training has to be realistic, repeatable and readily available.
Mixed reality headsets use outward-facing cameras to show the wearer the real world around them, then add computer-generated objects into that view. In this case, that lets soldiers practice detecting and engaging virtual drones in a real training environment without flying actual drones. Varjo said the XR-4’s image is sharp enough to train against a five-inch FPV drone, a common size class named for its propellers, at realistic distances, which matters because such drones are hard to see until they are close.
“The drone threat is one of the critical challenges of the modern battlefield, and training must keep up with the changes,” said Timo Toikkanen, CEO of Varjo. “Partnership with the Defence Forces makes it possible to improve training and make it match operational needs. We are proud to see Finnish technology at the forefront of this work.”
“We at our end are also proud of our partnership with Varjo. Virtual technology offers a possibility to train and prepare for drone threats in a realistic and repeated manner without consuming real resources. This partnership brings together a real operational need and Finnish technology. This pilot gives us valuable insights into how virtual training can be put into even better use in the Finnish military training,” said Maj. Ville Kuparinen, Head of the FDF Innovation Unit.
Varjo’s headsets are already used across European militaries and defense companies, mostly for vehicle and flight simulators. In March, Varjo and Norwegian firm Fynd Reality began fielding 39 XR training systems in Ukraine for Leopard 2A4 tank crews and other armored vehicle training, paid for by Norway’s defense materiel agency. In June, Varjo said it had added a counter-drone simulator to the training gear it supplies to the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Rheinmetall also builds Varjo’s XR-4 into its deployable land training simulators.

One of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's longtime ultra-Orthodox allies is considering a dramatic political shift, offering to support opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot as Israel's next prime minister in exchange for legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service. The proposal comes as Israel's election count nears completion, with neither political bloc securing the 61 seats needed to form a government.
A senior United Torah Judaism official confirmed to ynet on Thursday that the party intends to propose supporting a government led by Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, on the condition that legislation granting military draft exemptions be advanced.
"Gadi has the option of forming a government with Netanyahu, but then Netanyahu would be prime minister and he would be a senior minister," the official said. "We are offering him the premiership. That's better than being No. 2 or going to another election."
The proposal signals a possible break between United Torah Judaism and Netanyahu, whose right-wing and religious alliance has relied on the ultra-Orthodox party for parliamentary support. It also underscores the political leverage the party hopes to gain from an election that has left neither major bloc with a governing majority.
The obstacle, however, is substantial. During the election campaign, Eisenkot identified mandatory military or national service as one of his conditions for potential coalition partners, directly conflicting with United Torah Judaism's demand for draft exemptions.
Even with United Torah Judaism's projected seven seats, Eisenkot's current bloc would control only 55 of the Knesset's 120 seats, six short of a majority. Shas, another ultra-Orthodox party, is projected to win six seats, but no agreement involving the parties has been announced.
The proposed arrangement could also face resistance from Eisenkot's existing political partners, particularly Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Liberman, who has opposed forming a government with the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds 53 seats as 99% of votes counted
The political maneuvering comes as Israel's Central Elections Committee announced Thursday afternoon that 99% of votes had been counted, with no change in the balance between the main parliamentary blocs.
According to the latest figures, Netanyahu's bloc is projected to win 53 seats, Eisenkot's bloc 48 and the two Arab parties a combined 19, leaving both major political camps short of a majority.
Netanyahu's Likud remains the largest party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar! with 21 and the Beyachad (Together) party with 12.
The Joint List is projected to receive 11 seats, while the Arab-led Ra'am party and the Democrats are each projected to receive eight. United Torah Judaism, Yisrael Beiteinu and Otzma Yehudit are each on seven, while Shas and the joint Religious Zionism-Zehut list are each projected to win six seats.
The Reservists and Economic Party remains below the electoral threshold and is not currently projected to enter the Knesset.
Double-envelope count completed, but results remain unofficial
Earlier Thursday, the Central Elections Committee announced that counting had been completed for the special double-envelope ballots, a voting procedure used by soldiers and others voting away from their designated polling stations.
The committee said results had been entered from 12,644 polling stations, representing 5,589,836 votes. Of those, 5,564,764 were valid and 25,072 were invalid.
The final batch of double-envelope ballots, representing 24,713 votes, had been transferred for data entry and verification. Their results will be published only after those procedures have been completed.
The committee emphasized that the figures remain provisional and that official results will be published Wednesday, November 4, following an additional election integrity review.
The preliminary outcome leaves Israel facing complex coalition negotiations, with United Torah Judaism's potential offer introducing another possible route to a government led by Eisenkot. Whether he would consider compromising on military service legislation, or secure enough parliamentary support even with the ultra-Orthodox party's backing, remains unresolved.

ECB's Lagarde resigns early so she can speak freely on topics beyond monetary policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

ECB's Lagarde resigns early so she can speak freely on topics beyond monetary policy
FRANKFURT, Oct 29 - European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said on Thursday she had decided to step down eight months before her term was due to expire so that she can speak more freely on issues beyond monetary policy.
Lagarde, 70, has led the ECB since November 2019 and previously headed the International Monetary Fund. Her term would otherwise have run until October 2027.
"There is never a good time to leave," Lagarde told a press conference. "But it's embedded in the governance of the ECB that presidents, board members have to leave because they cannot be up for renewal."
Lagarde said the decision to leave early was driven by a wish to engage on issues outside the ECB's mandate.
"I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters," she said.
She noted that ECB officials are bound by strict rules of neutrality: "We have an obligation of neutrality, we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy," Lagarde said, adding that the mandate is "the price we pay for being independent."
Lagarde said she no longer felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. "I'm interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation," she said, without elaborating.
Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, Lagarde said she believed she had something to contribute beyond central banking. "There are things that I can say — whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I should say those things and I cannot do so in my current position," she said.
Lagarde sought to reassure markets and staff that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank's operations. "A process has already started to identify my successor," she said, adding there were "plenty of excellent candidates — much better than me, actually."
She dismissed concerns about continuity. "Don't worry about decision making in limbo — no, absolutely not," Lagarde said. "The institution is solid, strong, like a rock, and it will continue being so." REUTERS

As Delhi-NCR braces for Diwali celebrations, concerns over firecracker emissions and worsening air pollution put the spotlight on the festival’s environmental cost.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday said it was not inclined to impose a complete ban on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR, but warned authorities against pushing it to take a "very harsh stand" by failing to enforce its orders on the ground.A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale said repeated judicial directions would serve little purpose unless authorities ensured compliance, stressing that air pollution affected "every living being"."We are not inclined to completely ban but don’t push us to take a very harsh stand," the bench said as reported by news agency PTI. The Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati outlined measures taken by the Delhi government and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) to tackle pollution.“There is no point in passing orders and directions unless you give effect to them on the ground, otherwise, it becomes a mockery,” the bench observed.The court said the matter was not adversarial and called for serious action and cooperation from all stakeholders to regulate the use of firecrackers.“Every year we are trying to balance it out but unless there is cooperation from everyone, it can’t be done,” the bench said, adding that the concerned officers must be present on the ground to monitor implementation.
The bench also suggested roping in prominent personalities, including sportspersons, to spread public awareness about the harmful effects of firecrackers.Bhati told the court that the Delhi government had drawn up an extensive plan to tackle the pollution season. Measures scheduled to come into effect from November include curbs on older vehicles and construction and demolition activities, along with staggered office timings.
The Centre informed the court that internal consultations on the use of barium in firecrackers were still under way. Bhati sought three weeks to complete the process, and the bench said it would consider the issue after that period.The Supreme Court was hearing two petitions, including a suo motu case on air pollution in the National Capital Region covering firecrackers, stubble burning and solid waste management. The other petition seeks a ban on the manufacture of firecrackers.

Details
As noted by Ukrzaliznytsia, an air-raid alert was announced in advance at Dnipro railway station and the station itself. Orders to suspend traffic were immediately issued both to locomotive crews and to the station.
An evacuation was announced on the electric train that was due to travel to Zaporizhzhia (more than 10 minutes remained before the strike). Voice announcements began, and, in accordance with the protocol, the assistant driver walked through every carriage of the train (in the electric train, each carriage has a poster, and the announcements also clearly indicate the need not merely to leave the train but to leave the platform as quickly as possible and move at least 200 meters away). The train's locomotive crew evacuated in advance. At the same time, evacuation announcements were being made at the station. They were repeated several times. Passengers were told that train departures would resume after the alert ended and that everyone had to remain in shelters. Unfortunately, despite all this, many people were in the immediate vicinity of the train at the fateful moment of the strike, resulting in such a significant number of people killed and injured

The European Central Bank kept its key interest rate unchanged on Thursday, while warning that rising energy prices pose a growing risk to inflation.
“Although the full consequences of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has so far remained largely stable, and wages at present show no significant reaction,” the ECB said in a statement.
The decision follows rate increases in June and September.
Tore Stramer, chief economist at the Danish Chamber of Commerce, said uncertainty surrounding French public finances and a broader rise in market interest rates had given the ECB room to pause.
However, he cautioned that further increases remained a possibility.
“The ECB is certainly not in a situation where it can shelve the interest rate hammer for now,” he wrote in a comment.
Stramer expects rising energy prices to prompt another rate increase at the ECB’s next meeting in December.

PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.
Direct flights from Copenhagen to Ilulissat cleared as Greenland airport opens
Travelers heading to western Greenland will no longer need to change planes in Nuuk after aviation authorities approved the opening of Ilulissat’s expanded airport on Thursday.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority granted final safety approval overnight, following inspections and a test flight.
“Following a long series of inspections and a test flight, we have approved that the airport meets the necessary level of safety required to operate a modern, international airport,” said deputy director Lars Korsholm.
The approval comes with temporary restrictions during the airport’s initial operating period. These will gradually be eased as the airport gains experience.
Korsholm said the restrictions were unlikely to affect scheduled flights, particularly outside the tourist season.
The airport’s runway has been extended from 845 meters to 2,200 meters, allowing larger aircraft to land in Ilulissat, a town on Greenland’s western coast near Disko Bay.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen had to connect through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.
Initially, Air Greenland will generally operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday, with additional weekly departures during busy periods, including Christmas and New Year.
Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.
The expansion forms part of a multibillion-krone investment in Greenland’s airports, which also includes improvements in Nuuk and a new airport near Qaqortoq in southern Greenland.
The projects aim to improve transport connections and support economic development, particularly through increased tourism.

Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.

ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.

The recall covers the following four products:

Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.

Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.

Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.

Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.

People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.

Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.
The practice occurs on a limited basis at a slaughterhouse in Tarnow in southeastern Poland, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.

Danish Crown said the Polish facility slaughtered 69,000 cattle in 2025. The company said only “a minority” were slaughtered using the kosher method but declined to provide a specific number.

Sokolow chief executive Przemyslaw Gostkiewicz said Poland has a particular tradition of kosher slaughter that allows Jewish people to follow their dietary rules.
“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.

“Parents should take it seriously and check the rules before saying yes to an electric scooter,” council chief executive Jakob Bøving Arendt said.
Emergency departments in Odense and Svendborg have treated 811 people injured in electric scooter accidents since 2021. Twenty-five percent suffered serious injuries.
Odense University Hospital physician Jens Lauritsen said crashes can cause severe injuries even at legal speeds.
Modified scooters capable of traveling 60, 80 or 100 kilometers per hour could endanger both riders and others, he said.
Denmark to cull 27,000 turkeys after bird flu outbreak on Lolland
Danish authorities will cull 27,000 turkeys Monday after highly pathogenic avian influenza was detected in a flock in Stokkemarke on the island of Lolland.
It is Denmark’s second confirmed outbreak of the highly contagious disease within one week, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration said.
Another outbreak was identified Friday in a flock in Bøgelunde in Slagelse Municipality.
“It is therefore extra important at this time of year that everyone who keeps poultry or other birds does everything to prevent contact between their animals and wild birds,” agency veterinarian Mette Kirkeskov Sie said.
Owners should prevent wild birds from reaching their animals, drinking water and feed. The agency also recommends changing footwear before entering areas where birds are kept.
Authorities have established protection and surveillance zones around the infected flock on Lolland. Poultry owners within those areas must follow stricter disease control requirements.
The restrictions will remain until authorities complete their investigations and determine that the risk of further transmission has declined.
The agency said avian influenza only very rarely spreads to humans.
However, people should avoid touching sick, weakened or dead wild birds.
Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.
Source: Ritzau

The granting of citizenship in particular has taken up a significant amount of the political debate recently.

Rusal will acquire a majority stake in two joint ventures to be established to develop a bauxite deposit and build an alumina refinery in Ghana, the Russian aluminum producer said after signing of an agreement with the Ghana Integrated Aluminium Development Corporation (GIADEC).
