Under Sanctions, Russia Turns to Africa With Plans to Relocate Industrial Production
Russia is ready to move part of its industrial enterprises to Africa, Russian leader Vladimir Putin announced on October 29, The Moscow Times reported the same day.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"This fully corresponds to Russia's interests, especially today, when numerous sanctions are being applied to the Russian economy and Russian enterprises," Putin stated at the Russia-Africa forum. He described the investment potential of Russian companies as "fairly high" and added that "there is work to be done here."
Putin stressed that investments in African countries must be "reliable and protected." Plants would then operate "regardless of the foreign policy situation," he explained.
He was responding to Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who argued that Africa must go beyond exporting raw materials and importing finished goods.
"We must develop our own industrial potential, modernize our agriculture, strengthen our energy infrastructure and logistics routes, and invest more in research and technology development," Ndayishimiye told the forum. He emphasized that Africa should become "a real market for production and sales" rather than remain a consumer market.
A day earlier, Putin told 22 African leaders, including those of Ethiopia, Zimbabwe and Mali, that Russia had achieved "impressive results" in high technology. He said Moscow was ready to share its know-how with its "African friends." Competitors "have to catch up with us in some areas and copy our developments," he emphasized.
Russian ministers and state companies have since set out their own offers. Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov announced that Russian companies were ready to manufacture goods in African countries under industrial cooperation.
"The main message we bring to Africa is: let's ensure sovereign development together," he stated. Reshetnikov proposed cooperation in pharmaceuticals and IT solutions. Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov expressed readiness to develop automobile manufacturing in partnership with African partners.
Rosatom proposed building floating nuclear power plants in coastal African countries. "As a starting step, a source such as a floating nuclear power unit could be a good entry point to both solve their tasks and join the nuclear club," a representative of the state corporation explained.
Russia's largest liquefied natural gas producer, Novatek, offered African countries its own production technology, proven on Arctic projects. Aluminum giant Rusal signed a memorandum with Ghana on a joint venture to mine and process bauxite, the raw material for aluminum.
Moscow's push into African markets follows steep losses in its traditional energy trade since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Gazprom has lost more than half of its exports outside the former Soviet Union, with Russian gas exports expected to total about 77 billion cubic meters in 2026, down from 185 billion in 2021.
Exports are projected to fall to 72 billion cubic meters by 2028 once the EU gas embargo takes effect, a level last seen in the second half of the 1980s. Efforts to offset the losses through a major new supply deal with China have stalled over pricing, leaving talks on the proposed Power of Siberia 2 pipeline suspended.

Russia Revives World War II-Era Arctic Shipping Route to Export Grain
Russia has begun using an Arctic maritime route dating back to World War II to export grain for the first time, Reuters reported on October 28. The move comes as Moscow seeks alternatives to traditional shipping corridors through the Black and Baltic Seas amid growing security risks stemming from its war against Ukraine.
To address these difficulties, Russia has been redirecting grain shipments from its southern agricultural regions to Baltic Sea ports, offering subsidies for rail transportation. At the same time, Moscow has begun exploring the Arctic as an alternative export corridor.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On October 28, the Murmansk Commercial Seaport and Demetra Holding, one of Russia’s largest grain trading companies, announced that the first shipment of 3,400 metric tons of grain, transported from the country’s main agricultural regions, was being loaded onto a vessel at the port.
According to Reuters, the vessel is expected to carry approximately 28,000 metric tons of wheat from Murmansk to Casablanca, Morocco.
Located nearly 2,000 kilometers north of Moscow, near Russia’s border with Norway, Murmansk offers access to international waters. The port also has historical significance, having served as a major entry point for Allied supplies delivered to the Soviet Union during World War II.
“At a time when traditional export routes are facing restrictions, Murmansk Commercial Seaport is swiftly opening up an alternative route to foreign markets for Russian farmers,” the port said in a statement.
The development comes as Russia increasingly relies on Baltic Sea ports to maintain its grain exports.
According to Reuters, Russia exported approximately 1.2 million metric tons of grain through Baltic ports in September alone, accounting for more than 60% of its total seaborne grain shipments that month.
To accommodate the growing volumes, Russian companies have been converting port terminals previously used to handle fertilizers and coal into facilities capable of processing grain exports.
Russia has permitted grain-carrying vessels to leave the Sea of Azov for the first time since July, temporarily authorizing departures from the commercial ports of Temryuk and Kavkaz.
Citing three sources familiar with the situation, Bloomberg reported that the clearance was issued on October 26, with at least one vessel having already crossed the Kerch Strait into the Black Sea.

Researchers develop AI tool to identify bacterial DNA in soil
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:49:12 CST
23:49:12 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Israeli researchers have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) tool that can identify bacterial DNA in tiny genetic fragments found in soil, the Hebrew University of Jerusalem said Thursday.
Researchers extract DNA from soil samples to study the microorganisms living there, but identifying the source of many genetic fragments remains difficult.
The tool, called BBERT, is an AI model designed to process highly fragmented DNA/RNA sequences as short as 100 DNA letters and learn patterns in bacterial DNA, the university said in a statement.
In their study, published in Nucleic Acids Research, the researchers showed that the tool can identify bacterial DNA, including genetic material that can't be matched to existing reference databases.
The tool helps distinguish bacterial DNA from that of other organisms and identify fragments containing protein-making instructions, they said.
In tests, BBERT distinguished bacterial from non-bacterial DNA with around 90 percent accuracy, identified protein-making fragments with 88 percent accuracy and their correct reading frames with 96 percent accuracy.
Tested on 1,969 publicly available soil DNA datasets, the tool identified many fragments that existing methods had left unclassified.
The researchers said that the tool could help uncover previously overlooked genetic information and better understand the diversity of life in soil. ■

FIFA expects a record $5 billion from ticket sales and hospitality at the 2026 World Cup

FIFA expects a record $5 billion from ticket sales and hospitality at the 2026 World Cup
Kyiv • UNN
FIFA expects around $5 billion from tickets and hospitality at the 2026 World Cup — five times more than in Qatar. The tournament was attended by 6.81 million fans.
FIFA is expected to receive around $5 billion from ticket sales and hospitality services at the 2026 World Cup — more than five times what it earned at the tournament in Qatar four years ago. UNN reports this, citing The New York Times.
Details
FIFA President Gianni Infantino previously announced that this year's World Cup, co-hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico, generated $15 billion in revenue, $2 billion more than expected.
This means that one-third of this revenue came solely from ticket sales and hospitality services, although the $5 billion figure is part of an ongoing audit, so it could be slightly higher or lower.
The 2026 World Cup included 40 more matches (104) than Qatar (64), while ticket sales and hospitality services at the 2022 tournament generated $929 million in revenue.
The governing body of world football was widely condemned for its ticketing policy at this year's tournament, introducing dynamic pricing for the first time and also receiving a 30 percent commission on any resale.
One consequence of FIFA not allowing a traditional secondary ticket market in the United States and instead permitting resales only through its own platform was that it prevented money from going to advertising intermediaries and, as the governing body says, from being reinvested in world football.
The initial prices announced before the tournament were the highest in World Cup history, with tickets for the final at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, United States, on July 19 starting at $4,185 — seven times the price of the cheapest ticket for the 2022 final in Qatar.
In response to what they called "sky-high" prices, Football Supporters Europe and Euroconsumers, a consumer protection organization, filed an official complaint with the European Commission. FIFA has consistently defended the prices, pointing out that any revenue generated from ticket sales will ultimately be reinvested back into football, and also noting that they reflect the North American market, where it is not uncommon to pay hundreds of dollars to attend sporting events.
However, following widespread negative reaction, they introduced a limited number — 1,000 tickets priced at $60 — for each of the 104 World Cup matches.
FIFA emphasized that the tournament was attended by "an unprecedented 6.81 million fans" and that the "attendance rate" was "99.7 percent across all matches."
"The revenue generated by the tournament will provide unprecedented resources for FIFA's member associations to invest in the game, such as supporting the development of men's, women's and youth football across all 211 FIFA member associations every day of the year," a FIFA spokesperson added.
"As announced earlier this month following the FIFA Council meeting in Zurich, the FIFA administration presented the FIFA Council with a proposed initiative called the \"FIFA Surplus Solidarity Program\", which envisages using part of FIFA's reserves to more than double the level of planned funding for the 2027–2030 period to $6.35 billion," the statement said.

In a statement, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu and his allies of carrying out an “improper influence operation” aimed at delaying the results beyond their scheduled announcement and creating pretexts to delegitimise the work of the incoming Knesset.
He also called for a “comprehensive, immediate and impartial investigation” into suspected “foreign interference.”
The dispute followed a letter sent by Judge Noam Sohlberg, the chair of Israel’s election committee, to Shin Bet security agency chief David Zini asking him to investigate “serious suspicions” of “hostile” foreign influence on the election in favour of Arab parties, Haaretz daily reported.
Netanyahu’s Likud party seized on the request, saying no Zionist party should cooperate with the United Arab List or the Joint List, the two Arab parties.
Likud also said Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a member of the party, should not be replaced by votes “bought with money", and that no government posing a danger to Israel should be formed.
Eisenkot also accused Netanyahu of responding to political developments with “lies, manipulation of public opinion, and the spread of chaos".
Ridiculous allegations
The Israel Hayom daily reported that Israeli police found no evidence supporting election fraud allegations by the Likud party, while the Central Elections Committee sees no current grounds for concern over the integrity of the vote.
Meanwhile, Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson rejected accusations "made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media" that his country had interfered in the Israeli elections.
"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," said Majed Al Ansari.
"They accuse Qatar of buying off Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli political left, and now, in this latest campaign, the Arab vote. These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure."
With all regular ballots counted, Netanyahu’s bloc had secured 53 seats, compared to 48 for the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot, while Arab parties won a combined 19 seats.
Neither main bloc reached the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset, leaving Arab lawmakers potentially pivotal in efforts to form a government.
The new Knesset is expected to be sworn in on November 10, while the official election results are due to be announced next Wednesday.

The net profit of Russia’s “PhosAgro” fell by 37% in the third quarter of 2026 — intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
PhosAgro’s net profit in the third quarter of 2026 fell to $156 million. Costs rose by more than 30%, while debt reached $4.5 billion.
Net profit of one of Russia’s largest fertilizer producers, "PhosAgro," fell by 37% in the third quarter of 2026, to $156 million, while production costs and debt are rising. This is reported by Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, reports UNN.
Details
Over the nine months, gross profit fell by 27%, to $1.7 billion, while net profit declined by approximately 67%, to $389 million. The cost of production rose by more than 30% year-on-year. Sulfur and sulfuric acid, which are essential for producing phosphate fertilizers, became more expensive: about $503 million was spent on them in six months
According to available information, the company sells mainly for export, particularly to India, Brazil, and African countries, and therefore depends on global prices, demand, and delivery costs.
Last year, it produced 12.2 million tonnes of products for more than 100 countries, but large volumes do not generate profit if selling prices lag behind costs
At the same time, the company’s debt is also increasing. In particular, according to the intelligence service, debt at the end of the third quarter amounted to about $4.5 billion, 11% more than at the end of 2025.
Last year, capital expenditures amounted to about $836 million, while free cash flow was only $253 million. If profit continues to decline, modernization will have to be financed through loans.
A similar picture can be seen throughout Russian industry: large production and export volumes are increasingly failing to translate into profit

Ukrainian charged over death of Monaco royal
A Ukrainian man living in Monaco has been charged in connection with the death of Antoine de Massy, a relative of Prince Albert II, the ruler of the wealthy European principality.
The 42-year-old suspect, whose identity has not been disclosed, has reportedly lived in Monaco for three decades. Prosecutor General Stephane Thibault announced a judicial investigation on Wednesday.
According to local media, the Ukrainian national has been charged with involuntary manslaughter and failure to assist a person in danger. He denies wrongdoing and has been remanded in custody.
De Massy, 29, whose father is a first cousin of Prince Albert II, was found dead on Sunday evening after apparently falling approximately 13 meters from an elevated section of the coastal Boulevard du Larvotto into a garden behind a luxury residence.
The former competitive tennis player was reportedly last seen alive overnight Saturday into Sunday, leaving a nightclub apparently intoxicated and accompanied by another man. His family alerted authorities when he failed to attend a gathering, triggering a search that led to the discovery of his body in the secluded garden.
Thibault said CCTV footage showed the suspect accompanying de Massy along Boulevard du Larvotto. The Ukrainian national was arrested on Monday, although it remains unclear whether he was the man who reportedly left the nightclub with the victim.
Earlier this year, Monaco, known as a haven for millionaires, was rocked by a bombing targeting Ukrainian-born businessman Vadim Ermolaev, who was injured alongside members of his family.
The alleged bomber was identified as a Ukrainian woman who was later found dead in her home country, reportedly killed by her handlers. Investigators identified the suspected masterminds as an active operative of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, and an unofficial agent of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU). Both are now in Ukrainian custody.
Kiev portrayed the bombing as a profit-driven crime carried out by rogue agents. However, one suspect claimed the operation had been authorized by the Ukrainian state as a legitimate act of war against Russia.
The case resurfaced this week when former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said the Monaco bombing “echoed” an alleged Ukrainian intelligence plot against him that Austrian law enforcement had thwarted.
Kravchenko fled Ukraine for Vienna last month and was subsequently dismissed by parliament after a subordinate was accused of running a protection racket on his behalf. The Austrian authorities confirmed the arrests of suspected Ukrainian intelligence operatives in early October.

The return of veterans to work requires systematic support, particularly from trade unions, says the head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, Byzov
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:18:11 EET
23:18:11 KST

The return of veterans to work requires systematic support, particularly from trade unions, says the head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, Byzov
Kyiv • UNN
The head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, Serhii Byzov, spoke about how trade unions help military personnel and their families, facilitate the professional adaptation of veterans, and cooperate with employers to create proper working conditions.
The return of veterans to civilian work requires not only employers’ willingness to hire people with combat experience, but also systematic support — from physical and psychological recovery to workplace adaptation and the protection of labor rights. Trade unions can play an important role in this process by helping service members and veterans obtain the necessary support, find jobs, and protect their interests after employment. UNN spoke with Serhii Byzov, Head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, about how the trade union system is helping defenders return to working life.
Details
The FPU emphasizes that support for a veteran should not end after medical assistance has been provided or employment has been secured. It is important for a person to be able to return to professional activity, receive a decent salary, have proper working conditions, and be able to count on the protection of their rights.
The trade union’s main task is to help the veteran. After returning from the war, a person may need not only rehabilitation, but also support with employment, adaptation to civilian life, and the resolution of labor-related issues. Therefore, a trade union should be there not only when a problem arises, but also when a person begins a new stage of their life
From rehabilitation to returning to the workforce
One of the areas of support for service members within the trade union system is medical rehabilitation and psychological recovery. According to the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, nearly 50,000 service members and their family members received rehabilitation and psychological recovery services at the sanatorium and resort facilities of PJSC "Ukrprofozdorovnytsia" from 2022 to October 1, 2026. In addition, since the beginning of the full-scale war, more than 25,000 people have found shelter at the company’s facilities.
We had one case when a service member approached us after suffering an open traumatic brain injury and requiring further rehabilitation. The trade union helped resolve the issue of injury payments and payment for 21 days of recovery at a sanatorium in Myrhorod. After rehabilitation, the service member returned to his brigade and continued his service
At the same time, the return to civilian life for those leaving the service does not end with health recovery. The next challenge may be finding a job, changing professions, or adapting a former workplace to the person’s new needs.
According to the FPU head, the trade union helps service members who are forced to leave the service due to their health condition find employment through cooperation with the State Employment Center. Another area is cooperation with business representatives who can offer veterans jobs, decent pay, and opportunities for professional development.
For a veteran, it is important not simply to find a vacancy, but to have the opportunity to work in accordance with their skills and state of health. Therefore, support should begin with dialogue: clarifying the person’s needs, determining whether the employer is ready to adapt working conditions, and understanding what opportunities exist for this. Trade unions can help establish such cooperation so that returning to work is not a formality, but a genuine restoration of professional life
Protecting rights after employment
Finding a job is only part of the reintegration process. After employment, questions may arise regarding working conditions, workplace organization, pay, and interaction with management or colleagues. For veterans who have been wounded or have a disability, it may be necessary to create an accessible workspace or adapt their job duties.
Particular attention should be paid to psychological adaptation. After the experiences they have endured, veterans may find it difficult to work in a noisy environment, among large numbers of people, or under constant stress. However, people are not always ready to speak openly about such needs, fearing biased treatment.
As Serhii Byzov emphasized, in such situations, a trade union can represent an employee's interests in dialogue with the employer, help protect labor rights, and seek solutions that take into account the person's needs and the enterprise's capabilities.
Our task is to represent the interests of employees and help find solutions that take into account the needs of veterans and the enterprise's capabilities
Among the approaches to reintegration, Serhii Byzov mentioned individual support for veterans, mentoring by colleagues, flexible working hours, and access to psychological assistance. According to him, it is also important to prepare not only the veteran themselves for their return, but also the team — so that interaction is based on respect and understanding rather than stereotypes.
Why cooperation between trade unions and employers is important
As the European Business Association reported, a noticeable trend has emerged: Ukrainian companies are gradually developing practices for employing and adapting veterans. In particular, businesses are training teams to interact with colleagues who have combat experience, introducing retraining and adaptation programs, and in some cases creating special positions to support veterans.
However, businesses' willingness to employ veterans must be accompanied by systematic support. It is important for an employer to understand how to organize an employee's return, what state assistance opportunities are available, and how to respond to a person's needs without violating their rights.
Trade unions can complement businesses' efforts through the direct representation of employees. They can participate in discussions on the conditions for veterans' return to an enterprise, monitor compliance with labor guarantees, help resolve conflict situations, and contribute to ensuring that support programs work not only formally but also in practice
In his view, it is also important to develop partnerships between trade unions, employers, government institutions, and organizations that provide rehabilitation and retraining services. Such interaction makes it possible to combine various support tools — from restoring health to professional fulfillment.
One of the tools that can be used to formalize the relevant guarantees is a collective agreement. The FPU is working to include provisions concerning veterans in sectoral agreements and has developed a model section for collective agreements at enterprises. This includes, in particular, workplace adaptation, retraining opportunities, psychological support, and assistance with employment after leaving military service.
This approach makes it possible to move from situational assistance to clear rules under which an employee can count on support, while an employer can plan the necessary changes. At the same time, specific mechanisms must take into account the nature of the work, the veteran's state of health, and the enterprise's capabilities.
Veteran reintegration is a shared responsibility
The return of veterans to civilian working life requires consistent efforts at various levels. The state must ensure effective support programs, employers must create proper working conditions, and trade unions must represent employees' interests, help protect their rights, and promote social dialogue.
For the FPU, this area means an opportunity to combine practical assistance to service members and their families with work on the conditions in which veterans return to working life. After all, successful reintegration is not only about employment but also about the opportunity to work with dignity, safely, and without discrimination
Successful veteran reintegration is not only about the opportunity to find a job. It also means fair pay, safe conditions, respect for human rights, and the opportunity for professional development. That is why it is important that support for veterans not be limited to individual programs but gradually become part of labor relations and the everyday practices of enterprises.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:16:18 UTC
23:16:18 KST

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alleged on Oct 29, without providing evidence, that Arab parties’ record gains in an election this week were driven in part by voter fraud, a charge rejected by Arab leaders, who accused him of incitement.
The allegation represents an escalation of anti-Arab rhetoric by Netanyahu and his far-right partners after high Arab turnout in a national ballot on Oct 27 effectively blocked a smooth path to power for either him or his main Jewish rivals.
Israeli election officials said on Oct 29 that there was a probe into fraud allegations, though the election’s integrity was not “systematically compromised”.
Analysts and critics say that by stepping up attacks on Arab parties, Netanyahu may be trying to ensure his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, feels unable to even consider forming a minority government with Arab help that could oust him from power.
Netanyahu’s goal is “delegitimising any Arab-Jewish cooperation”, said Eytan Gilboa, professor of politics at Reichman University.
Election officials were expected to finish tallying votes later on Oct 29, in a tightly fought election that has produced no clear winner and is likely to be followed by weeks of protracted negotiations over a new government.
With nearly 93% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious bloc held a modest lead in seats over a bloc of right-wing and centre-left parties led by Eisenkot, with both men’s coalitions short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Parliament.
Parties representing Israel’s 21% Arab minority were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot’s bloc, with 48 seats against Netanyahu’s camp of 53, with no realistic path to power without broad Arab backing, an option Eisenkot has so far ruled out.
However, Eisenkot’s camp could also try to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside, without including them in a governing coalition.
Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of fraud; Arab parties call it incitement
Ahmad Tibi, one of the leaders of the Arab Joint List party, said Netanyahu was on an orchestrated, toxic campaign meant to undermine the election results.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told Reuters.
During and after the Oct 27 election, Netanyahu and his allies warned against rising Arab turnout, and his right-wing Likud party issued statements accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the vote”.
It demanded police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service investigate incidents of suspected election bribery and intimidation at ballot stations in Arab towns. It said it possessed evidence of such activity but has not presented it to the public.
The police say they have arrested at least seven people since Tuesday in Israel’s south, where many Arabs live, on suspicion of voter fraud. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan said they were suspected of attempting to bribe voters to cast ballots for the Arab-dominated party Ra’am, which has Islamist roots.
On Oct 29, the head of Israel’s Central Election Committee, Supreme Court jurist Noam Sohlberg, said he had asked the Shin Bet to investigate suspicions that unidentified foreign players had tried to intervene in the election.
Likud seized on Sohlberg’s request, alleging an attack on Israel’s democracy, “an Islamisation of Israel and the toppling of the right-wing in order to bring about IDF withdrawal and defeat on all fronts, foremost Iran”.
Likud said Qatar was behind the alleged election intervention, which Qatar later denied.
Ra’am head Mansour Abbas said on Oct 29 that his party was not involved in the reported suspicious conduct and urged a full investigation. He said that Netanyahu was on an incitement campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens.
“We have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimisation he is waging against Arab citizens: Nothing will come of it, because there is nothing there,” Abbas said in a statement.
In a letter sent to a parliamentarian and published by the Central Election Committee, the committee said that there was “no base for claims that there was systematic harm to the election’s integrity”.
Israeli President: ‘We must not tarnish an entire community’
After vote tallying is completed, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with party chairs and choose a candidate who he thinks has the best chance to form a government.
The coalition that last toppled Netanyahu, in 2021, relied on Abbas’ Ra’am party. But Eisenkot’s underperformance means the opposition would now need backing from the Arab-dominated Joint List, which includes an explicitly anti-Zionist party. Most Jewish leaders have shunned formal alliances with Arab parties since Israel’s founding.
Eisenkot called for an investigation that would protect election integrity but said Netanyahu was exploiting the suspicions to “spread chaos”.
He said in a statement that Netanyahu’s aim was to “challenge the official election results, in which the Israeli public voted against the government”.
Herzog said the allegations must be investigated.
“But even at a moment like this, we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy,” Herzog said in a statement. REUTERS

2 dead as ‘fairy chimney’ rock spires collapse at tourist site in Turkey’s Cappadocia
ISTANBUL – A landslide triggered by heavy rainfall caused a rock spire to collapse in Turkey’s Cappadocia tourist region on Oct 29, killing at least two people, the local governor said.
Turkey’s Cappadocia region, a magnet for tourists from around the world, is home to rock formations known as “fairy chimneys”, created by ancient volcanic activity.
“According to initial findings, two people were killed and five others injured in the incident,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on X.
“Search-and-rescue teams are continuing intensive, coordinated operations to locate any other victims who may be trapped under the debris,” he said.
The incident occurred at 3.15pm when a landslide triggered a rockfall in the town of Goreme near the open-air museum, local governor Huseyin Kok said.
The area was closed to the public following the collapse, according to reports.
Eyewitnesses reported hearing a loud noise as the rock spire near an open car parking lot fell.
Television footage showed heavy machinery digging through the rubble as rescue teams gather at the site in an effort to recover people trapped beneath the debris.
“Our search-and-rescue operations at the scene are ongoing. The government is continuing its efforts at the scene with all available resources,” Kok said.
Turkey’s culture and tourism ministry has launched restoration work in the region to help preserve the fragile rock formations from climate-related damage, natural erosion and human activity.
In 2024, another rockfall was reported in Cappadocia, although no deaths or injuries were recorded.
The Cappadocia region, a major tourist attraction known for its rock-carved underground cities and early Christian churches, is also famed for hot-air ballooning, a thriving industry that sees dozens of balloons take to the skies on clear mornings.
But concerns have been raised about safety following a series of accidents. AFP

- Finland launched the third Pohjanmaa-class corvette at Rauma on Oct. 29, putting three of the four new warships in the water.
- All four corvettes are due to be completed by 2029 and will replace seven older Finnish Navy ships.
Finland launched the third of its four new Pohjanmaa-class corvettes at Rauma on Oct. 29, putting three of the Finnish Navy’s largest warships in decades in the water, the Finnish Navy said.
The ship was moved out of the construction hall at the Rauma Marine Constructions shipyard on Finland’s west coast, where fitting out will continue afloat. The Navy said all four corvettes are due to be completed by 2029 and will enter service in phases, and it has said it expects to take the ships into service between 2027 and 2029. The Navy did not say when the third ship will begin sea trials.
“The launch of the third vessel shows the progress of long-term and persistent work. This is an extensive undertaking that brings together the Navy’s future capability, domestic industrial expertise and close cooperation between different parties,” said Rear Adm. Tuomas Tiilikainen, commander of the Finnish Navy.
Construction has picked up pace across the four hulls. The first corvette, whose construction began in 2023, was launched in May 2025 and is now being fitted out. The second was launched on May 21 this year, less than a year after its keel was laid. Rauma Marine Constructions laid the keel of the third ship and started production of the fourth in January, putting all four under construction at the same time, and the fourth ship’s keel followed in July.
The corvettes are being built by RMC Defence, a subsidiary of Rauma Marine Constructions, for the Finnish Defence Forces Logistics Command under a program known as Squadron 2020. At 117 m (384 feet) long with a crew of about 70, the ships are the largest surface combatants the Finnish Navy has ordered since its coastal defense ships of the 1930s. Each is designed to stay at sea for 14 days and has a range of about 3,500 nautical miles.
The Pohjanmaa class combines several jobs that the Finnish Navy now spreads across older vessels. The four corvettes will replace seven ships: the four Rauma-class missile boats, the two Hämeenmaa-class minelayers and the minelayer Pohjanmaa, retired in 2015, whose name the new class carries. Each corvette carries anti-ship missiles, Evolved Sea Sparrow surface-to-air missiles in a vertical launcher, a 57 mm gun, torpedoes for anti-submarine warfare and rails for laying sea mines, an important task in the shallow, mine-friendly waters off Finland’s coast.
The ships also have ice-strengthened hulls so they can operate year-round in the northern Baltic, where the Gulf of Finland and the Gulf of Bothnia can freeze in winter, and they are fitted with composite ballistic armor to protect key areas. The Navy said the corvettes will give it new capability to defend Finnish waters and operate within NATO, which Finland joined in 2023.
The Navy plans to keep the Pohjanmaa class in service into the 2060s. The first ship is due to be handed over to the Navy in 2027, with all four in service by 2029.

A brewery with a 270-year history is closing in the Czech Republic due to falling demand for beer

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:13:50 EET
23:13:50 KST

A brewery with a 270-year history is closing in the Czech Republic due to falling demand for beer
Kyiv • UNN
Velké Březno will cease production due to falling demand and rising costs. The Březňák brand will be moved to other Heineken breweries.
One of the Czech Republic’s oldest breweries, Velké Březno, will cease production after nearly 273 years of operation amid falling demand for beer and rising costs. At the same time, the Březňák brand will be preserved, while its production will be transferred to other Heineken group breweries. Bild reports, UNN writes.
Details
One of the Czech Republic’s oldest breweries, Velké Březno, located in the town of the same name in the north of the country, is ceasing production. Beer has been brewed at the company’s current site since 1753, while the history of brewing here dates back to 1606. As Robert Kičina, a representative of Heineken Czech Republic, told Ústecký deník, production was gradually reduced throughout 2026, and the remaining capacity will now be permanently shut down.
At the same time, the Březňák beer brand produced by the brewery will not disappear. Its production will be transferred to other Heineken group breweries, to which the Czech brewery has belonged since 2008. The logistics and sales divisions will remain at the former site. The reasons for the production shutdown include declining beer consumption in the Czech Republic, as well as rising energy and raw material prices.
Breweries in Germany are experiencing similar problems. In 2025, beer consumption in the country fell by almost 6%, and sales continued to decline in 2026. Amid falling demand and price competition, companies with decades-long histories are closing. For example, the Eichbaum brewery in Mannheim stopped production on September 30 after nearly 350 years of operation, while the 165-year-old Rupp brewery in Lower Saxony faced bankruptcy.

Israel elections: What the record tally by Arab parties means for Zionist politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:13:23 UTC
23:13:23 KST

Arab parties, which are mostly supported by the Palestinian citizens of Israel, received a resounding victory in the October 27 election, changing the balance of power in the Knesset.
With roughly 90 percent of ballots counted as of Thursday, the two main Arab-led parties – the Joint List and Ra’am – are on track for a combined count of 19 seats.
Their total is nearly double the previous count of 10 and well above the 2020 record of 15 seats.
According to the latest tally, Netanyahu’s right-wing and ultra-Orthodox bloc is expected to win 53 seats, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot is set to bag 48 seats.
Neither Zionist bloc is expected to reach the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government in the 120-member Knesset.
The projected 19 seats give the Arab-led parties significant leverage in coalition negotiations, but they do not guarantee a place in government.
It creates an opportunity for the two Arab parties to assert their democratic credentials in a country where Palestinian Israelis have long been treated as second-class citizens.
The community, which lives in separate towns, consists of the people whose ancestors stayed put during the Nakba, the mass expulsion of over 750,000 Palestinians following the creation of Israel in 1948.
The level of discrimination against Palestinian Israelis, who now make up roughly 20 percent of the country’s population, has risen dramatically since the October 7 attacks three years ago.
Towns dominated by the Palestinian Israeli community saw a significant shift in voting patterns. Their turnout hit 80 percent, the highest in decades.
They voted in large numbers because of deep frustration with the most right-wing government in Israel’s history and its far-right ministers, who have vowed to “Judaise” parts of Israel populated by Palestinian Israelis.
Experts say Arab parties made electoral gains despite Netanyahu’s campaign strategy, which centred on delegitimisation of Arab political participation in coalition-building.
Netanyahu’s Likud party has already claimed that the election was “stolen by Arab parties” that “support terror and the elimination of the Jewish state” through bribery, threats, violence, forgeries and the use of illegal software.
Main members from both Zionist blocs have said they wouldn’t include Palestinian Israelis in a coalition.
Ferit Belder, associate professor of international relations at Istanbul’s Marmara University, tells TRT World that opposition leaders largely deferred the question until after the vote to avoid the political costs of “normalising” Arab politics in the first election after October 7, 2023.
“Despite their electoral success, it is not guaranteed that the Arab parties will be able to translate this success into concrete gains and become part of the ‘legitimate circle of coalition-building’,” he says.
The Central Election Committee’s moves against Arab parties – left to the Supreme Court to resolve – further underscored the reluctance of Zionist parties to defend legitimate Arab participation, he adds.
Ozgur Dikmen, a scholar of Jewish politics, tells TRT World that Zionist politicians are more likely to frame the Palestinian Israeli gains as an element of insecurity and threat.
In a possible new cycle of elections, as seen between 2018 and 2022, such an “Arab threat” narrative would remain a useful tool for the right, he says.
A political force to reckon with
Numbers show the Zionist blocs’ dependence on Arab parties to reach a majority, raising the political costs of exclusion.
Gokhan Cinkara, director of Necmettin Erbakan University’s Global and Regional Studies Application and Research Centre, tells TRT World that the election results mark a significant turning point in Israeli politics.
He says the Arab parties have become a political force that can no longer be ignored.
“Anyone seeking to form a government will have to engage with the Arab parties in some way,” he says.
The two Arab parties approached the election with different strategies.
Ra’am, under Mansour Abbas, insisted on formal coalition membership to address the concerns of the Palestinian Israeli community.
Ra’am also joined the 2021 Bennett-Lapid government. Its integrationist approach and moves, such as placing former Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz on the Knesset candidate list, already positioned the party as a potential coalition partner.
The Joint List, a union of communist Hadash, secularist Ta’al, and nationalist Balad groups, offered only external support for any anti-Netanyahu government in exchange for concrete improvements: stronger action against violence and crime, better housing, and the rollback of discriminatory policies of Netanyahu’s government.
Dikmen says that the chances of “formal inclusion” of Arab parties in the coalition remain limited.
It might be slightly more possible for the Eisenkot bloc to accept a coalition supported by the Arab parties, particularly with figures such as Abbas willing to serve as supporting partners, he says.
“I do not think it would be very realistic to expect seeing a Palestinian-Israeli minister,” Dikmen says.
Belder notes that the main task for the Arab parties is to convert their Knesset seats into material improvements in the daily lives of the Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Abbas of the Ra’am party has long argued that parliamentary presence without executive power confines the parties to the “world of slogans”, Belder says.
In the Knesset, a larger and more confident Palestinian Israeli caucus can at least be expected to reshape debates on equality and minority rights, even if fundamental arguments over the character of the state remain largely unchanged.
Dikmen points out that since December 2022, the Ministry of National Security under far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir has made serious reductions in the security budget of Palestinian Israeli-majority towns, contributing to skyrocketing crime rates – one of the drivers of the high turnout.
“I think such a reaction would reflect itself in the attitudes of Palestinian members in the Knesset,” he says.
Belder anticipates that far-right efforts to undermine judicial authority and policies that harm Palestinian Israelis’ daily lives – performative home demolitions and the humiliation of residents under Ben-Gvir – can be reversed or restricted.
Settler violence in the occupied West Bank might also come under closer government scrutiny, he adds.
Cinkara notes that the Arab parties will play an important role in advancing opposition priorities, including the election of the Knesset speaker and the allocation of committee seats.
“The key challenge for the Arab parties will also be to offer their voters practical policies,” he adds.

buying the plant.

Feature: Revving up dreams, Libyan woman builds career in engine modification
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:55 CST
22:53:55 KST

TRIPOLI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- In a workshop humming with engines in Mayah, 40 km southwest of the Libyan capital Tripoli, 25-year-old Rawan Abu Aisha is building a career uncommon for Libyan women -- turning a childhood passion for cars into a business modifying engines.
Growing up, Abu Aisha often watched her father work as a mechanic. "The workshop environment was familiar to me from childhood because I grew up watching my father work with cars," Abu Aisha told Xinhua.
"Over time, that interest became something I wanted to turn into a profession," she explained, saying the opportunity came through an entrepreneurship competition in Libya that invited participants to present innovative business ideas.
Drawing on her family background, she proposed modifying car engines to meet owners' specific needs. The idea became real when a customer agreed to an engine replacement. The project subsequently grew into a company established in 2022, whose primary business is modifying engines using its own custom-built units.
"My father's support and practical experience helped me take my first steps in this field," she said. "His encouragement gave me the confidence to develop my skills and turn an idea into a real business."
Her studies in entrepreneurship also equipped her with knowledge of business management, marketing and accounting, helping the company move beyond its technical roots toward a more structured management approach. What began as a business relying largely on customer recommendations later expanded its reach through an online presence and social media platforms.
According to Abu Aisha, the company's social media page has attracted over 50,000 followers, and demand for its services has grown so rapidly that her current team can barely keep up.
"The growing number of followers and the rising demand for our services show that there is considerable interest in what we do," she said. "Our next step is to expand the business and improve our ability to meet customers' needs."
Abu Aisha also hopes to partner with companies abroad, stressing the importance of long-term planning and continuous development.
"Building a sustainable business requires more than providing a good technical service," she said. "It also requires organized management, continuous improvement and a clear vision for the future."
While she believes social acceptance of women in the workplace has grown in recent years, Abu Aisha's greatest lesson from entrepreneurship is that young women must take initiative and pursue their ambitions, rather than let stereotypes dictate their choices.
"Women should not allow stereotypes to decide what they can or cannot do," she said. "They should be willing to try, learn and discover their abilities through practical experience."
For young women considering careers in mechanics, engineering or other nontraditional fields, her journey shows how personal interests can be turned into professional opportunities through determination, learning and hands-on experience.
"I want to continue developing the business and provide services that customers can trust," she said. "I believe that competence and expertise, rather than gender, should determine whether someone can succeed in a particular profession." ■

Across China: New study traces evolution of terrestrial animals on Qinghai-Xizang Plateau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:45 CST
22:53:45 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A new study has reconstructed the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, offering a clearer picture of how the unique fauna of Earth's "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years.
The research, led by a team from the Chengdu Institute of Biology (CIB) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, was recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
"Overall, the study deepens understanding of how mountain animal life evolves and provides a framework for studying how biodiversity forms in mountain regions worldwide," said Li Jiatang, a researcher at CIB.
Home to many species found nowhere else, the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, covering about 3.07 million square kilometers and ranging in elevation from 88 to 8,848 meters, according to the researchers.
The plateau platform, the Himalayas and the Hengduan Mountains are the plateau's three major subregions.
Scientists have long been interested in how the plateau's tectonic history and monsoon systems shaped the evolution of local biodiversity. However, earlier studies mostly looked at plants or single animal groups, leaving the overall development of the plateau's land animals poorly understood.
To fill this gap, the researchers combined time-calibrated evolutionary trees covering more than 20,000 species across invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. They then reconstructed the evolutionary history of 527 endemic terrestrial animal species on the plateau.
The study found that most of the plateau's endemic land animals did not arrive from elsewhere and then become new species. Instead, many evolved locally, splitting into new species right where they were, something scientists call in situ diversification.
The plateau was also a major receiver of species. The study found that animals moved in nearly twice as often as they moved out. The Qinghai-Xizang Plateau therefore played two roles at once: it was a place where new species formed, and a biogeographic sink that took in more species than it sent out.
The three subregions played very different roles. The Hengduan Mountains were the main source of local species formation, producing many new species. The Himalayas were both a source and a sink, producing new species locally and receiving species from elsewhere. The plateau platform produced very few new species locally, with most of its animal life coming from immigration, making it an important sink and a major receiver of species.
The researchers also examined how geology and climate shaped this evolutionary history. They found that a major climate transition about 34 million years ago marked the onset of sustained species diversification and biological exchange. However, the timing of these processes varied across the three subregions, reflecting differences in their uplift histories and monsoon systems.
The study also found a consistent "plants first, animals later" pattern. By comparing animal evolution with plant studies, the researchers identified this pattern across the plateau and its subregions. Early-colonizing plant groups created suitable ecological niches, laying the foundation for later animal immigration and diversification. ■

====================================================================================================

Antarctic sea ice loss disrupts ocean freshwater system: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:28 CST
22:53:28 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW) has rapidly become saltier and denser as Antarctic sea ice loss reduces freshwater input, potentially affecting deep-ocean warming and sea levels, according to new research.
The AAIW, a vast layer of fresh water spanning much of the Southern Hemisphere's ocean, helps store carbon, supply oxygen and drive global ocean currents. It plays a role in heat, freshwater and carbon redistribution around the planet, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of Melbourne.
The study, published in Nature Climate Change, found that Antarctic summer sea-ice melt helped maintain the AAIW from 1995 to 2015. From 2016, Antarctic sea ice declined to record lows. Between 2016 and 2024, reduced freshwater input led the water layer to become saltier, denser and deeper.
The team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of about 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, along with satellite and atmospheric datasets.
Researchers said the last time the AAIW underwent a similar shift was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica. However, that transition took thousands of years, rather than two decades.
The researchers said changes in the AAIW could affect the ocean's ability to store carbon and push more excess heat into deeper waters, meaning existing models may underestimate deep-ocean warming and miscalculate regional sea-level rise. ■

Croatia reports 25 West Nile virus cases, 1 death

ZAGREB, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Croatia has confirmed 25 cases of West Nile virus infection this year, including one death, the Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ) said on Thursday.
Of those infected, 19 developed symptoms, including two having West Nile fever and 17 with the more severe neuroinvasive form of the disease.
Zagreb and the surrounding areas accounted for 15 cases, making the region the hardest hit. Most West Nile virus infections in Croatia are recorded between mid-July and the end of October. The HZJZ said the transmission season is expected to end as temperatures drop.
Since the beginning of this year, Croatia has reported more West Nile virus cases than last year, when it recorded six cases, but still less than the highest annual total of 63 confirmed cases, reported in 2018.
Speaking to local media, the HZJZ said that the European Union has experienced its most intense West Nile virus season to date, with the virus spreading to more northerly areas. ■

2026-10-29

Internationally recognised site selection consultants whose recommendations influence global companies’ decisions on where to locate new manufacturing facilities, technology centres and other investment projects will gather in Riga this week. On 29 October, Latvia’s capital will host the Site Selectors Guild European Conference for the first time in the Baltic States. The Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) sees the event as an important opportunity to strengthen Latvia’s position in the international competition for investment.
The Site Selectors Guild brings together internationally recognised site selection consultants who help multinational companies evaluate different countries and make investment location decisions. Eleven Guild members will visit Riga, including representatives of international consulting firms such as JLL, Newmark, BCI Global and IBM Plant Location International. Their recommendations can be decisive when companies are choosing between several countries competing for the same investment project.
“Investment does not begin with the construction of a factory. It begins with a decision about which country a company should choose for its development. And the people who have come to Riga this week play an important role in making those decisions. The fact that they have chosen to meet in Latvia is significant recognition of our country’s visibility, but making a good impression alone is not enough in the competition for investment. Companies need to know how quickly they can start operating, what support is available and who can help resolve specific issues. Latvia’s advantage lies in its ability to make decisions quickly and ensure direct cooperation with the people responsible. Our task is to make sure that the next time these consultants are looking for a location for a new factory or technology centre on behalf of their clients, Latvia is among their first choices. That is why, during the conference, LIAA will also present concrete opportunities and advantages that Latvia can offer international companies seeking to expand their operations and implement new investment projects here,” emphasises Ieva Jāgere, Director of LIAA.
Latvia’s competitiveness in attracting investment is also reflected in its results to date. In 2025, 31 investment projects with a total value of €1.01 billion were launched with LIAA’s involvement. Meanwhile, during the first nine months of 2026, the total planned value of investment projects attracted by LIAA reached €886.8 million, representing almost 90% of the agency’s €1 billion target for the year.
LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere will attend a meeting with conference participants on 28 October. During the conference, LIAA will use the opportunity to establish contacts with international consultants and present Latvia’s investment environment. Key elements of Latvia’s investment proposition include access to the European Union’s single market, a skilled workforce, the exemption of reinvested corporate profits from corporate income tax, and the opportunity for eligible investment projects to benefit from the Green Corridor initiative, which accelerates access to certain public administration services.
According to LIAA, maintaining cooperation after the conference will be particularly important to ensure that consultants have access to up-to-date information about investment opportunities in Latvia and direct contacts to facilitate future projects. This will help Latvia become involved at an early stage in the evaluation of new investment projects and compete for their implementation.
The second Site Selectors Guild European Conference will take place on 29 October at the Radisson Blu Latvija Conference & Spa Hotel in Riga. It will bring together site selection consultants and representatives of economic development organisations from Europe, North America and Asia. The conference programme will feature discussions on global investment trends, the impact of artificial intelligence on site selection, energy availability, clean technologies and the semiconductor industry.
The conference is organised by the Site Selectors Guild, with the Riga Investment and Tourism Agency (RITA) serving as the host partner.
More information about the conference is available here.

When Philosophers Reinvent The Wheel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:33:17 UTC
22:33:17 KST

You may not believe this, but philosophers sometimes work in ignorance of research programs, bodies of literature, methodologies, and findings outside of philosophy that could be relevant to their work.
In a post at his blog, Ethan Landes (Eindhoven) shares how he recently discovered that the relatively young philosophical subfield of conceptual engineering, to which he contributes, appears to have reinvented a wheel produced 50 years ago by scholars in the field of sociolinguistics.
Neat find. But ouch.
He writes:
There is an entire literature that discusses things at a level that I (we?) all thought was unique to conceptual engineering. An entire literature the conceptual engineering literature could have drawn on for ideas and knowledge. But no one looked carefully, so we have a decade of literature of us forging our own paths.
It reminds me of the time I spent an hour fighting my way up an English hill through thick, knee-high heather, only to discover at the top that [there] had been an unmarked path 20 meters to my right the whole time.
Some degree of ignorance of other fields is a cost of disciplinary specialization for creatures who sometimes have to do things that cut into their research—like sleep, or die. Since specialization has its benefits, some ignorance is expected.
And its worth noting that philosophy is increasingly interdisciplinary, and on some measures, the most interdisciplinary field in the humanities.
Still, philosophy’s remit is about as broad as can be, so perhaps it has a greater risk of interdisciplinary ignorance leading to research which duplicates work done elsewhere, or research which would have been significantly advanced in light of awareness of very similar research already conducted outside of philosophy.
Dr. Landes gave us one example, but I’m sure there are others, both contemporary and historical. Let’s hear about them.

Western Europe is falling apart – we should prepare for what comes next
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:32:30 UTC
22:32:30 KST

Western Europe is falling apart – we should prepare for what comes next
For Russia, developments in the rest of Europe matter primarily insofar as they affect our national interests. Above all, this concerns security given that, for centuries, Russia has faced its greatest challenges from the West, and there’s little reason to assume that this historical pattern has disappeared.
Western Europe’s leading countries now stand at a crossroads, yet the choice confronting them isn’t simply between competing models of domestic development, it’s between war and peace with their neighbors, foremost among them Russia, whose size and historical role have repeatedly made it the principal obstacle to Western European expansion.
The unrest sweeping several European countries this autumn marks a new phase in the continent’s systemic crisis as it reflects the convergence of two long-term problems that much of Europe’s political establishment has proved incapable of resolving.
The first is the exhaustion of the socioeconomic model that sustained Western European prosperity throughout the Cold War and its aftermath. That model depended on Europe’s privileged position in the global economy and the absence of serious competitors beyond the Western world, but China’s rise, combined with increasingly limited resources, has undermined those advantages.
Closer economic integration with Russia, and access to its enormous natural wealth, might have offered Western Europe a final opportunity to preserve its exceptional position, but instead regional leaders allowed their own arrogance to prevent an accommodation with Moscow because they couldn’t accept that Russia wished to live peacefully with its neighbors, but on terms consistent with its own interests.
The second problem is Western Europe’s longstanding absence of genuine sovereignty.
Integration into the American-led NATO system has deprived even major powers such as Germany, France, and Britain of the freedom to pursue fundamental political change and one of the alliance’s practical functions has been to preserve the existing political order within its member states.
Any serious attempt to transform that order would require a reassessment of relations with Washington and such independence is something these European governments have long been unwilling, or unable, to contemplate.
Together, these structural weaknesses have left Western Europe’s political and economic establishments effectively paralyzed.
For nearly two decades, governments have substituted the appearance of activity for meaningful reform. Successive emergencies, involving migration, the pandemic, hostility towards Russia, and preparations for military confrontation, have allowed leaders to avoid addressing deeper problem and this helps explain the temptation to interpret today’s unrest as another exercise in political manipulation. Emmanuel Macron, for example, has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to survive the consequences of disastrous decisions through tactical maneuvering.
Yet it would be a mistake to dismiss the protests as artificial or orchestrated.
In France, the initial demonstrations were driven by schoolchildren and university students demanding more teachers and improvements to an education system suffering from declining standards, but these grievances are hardly unique to France and they reflect broader weaknesses in modern education, including funding arrangements that encourage institutions to compete for pupils rather than concentrate on teaching.
By early October, the French protests had expanded as other groups affected by Macron’s liberal economic policies joined the demonstrations. The authorities blamed the political left, while unrest escalated into rioting and looting.
Similar discontent emerged in Spain and Portugal, where soaring housing costs became the immediate trigger. Both countries have spent years occupying subordinate positions within the European Union, with little influence over its economic priorities, even as their former politicians find comfortable positions in Brussels.
Western Europe has consequently entered a period in which conventional political competition is increasingly accompanied by mass protest and the participation of young people is particularly significant.
In France, the EU’s most important military power and its only nuclear-armed member, it was students who provided the initial momentum. While much of the adult electorate has descended into political apathy under Macron, younger generations retain aspirations for a better future and their grievances are genuine. So, too, is the wider crisis that has brought people onto the streets.
There are therefore grounds to believe that public dissatisfaction may eventually bring new political forces to power, which from Russia’s perspective raises an obvious possibility in that perhaps Western Europe’s next generation of leaders will prove more reasonable on questions of security and relations with Moscow.
Such hopes, however, may be premature because they reflect less our actual experience of European politics than our desire to imagine a Western Europe capable of recovering its political judgement.
Indeed, the objective nature of the present crisis makes its possible consequences especially troubling and European history offers little reassurance that profound domestic upheaval produces peaceful relations with neighbouring countries. On the contrary, revolutionary transformations have repeatedly generated external aggression, and the French Revolution provides one example.
The upheavals of the late 18th century were followed by wars against neighboring states and, eventually, Napoleon’s attempt to dominate Europe.
The extraordinary energy released by revolution demanded an outlet, while new rulers also needed resources and opportunities for enrichment beyond their borders.
As Henry Kissinger observed in his early historical work, the internal foundations of Napoleon’s expansionism helped prevent a lasting accommodation with Russia after the disastrous campaign of 1812.
Germany offers an even more destructive precedent, where the political upheavals of the 20th century ultimately brought to power a regime whose ambitions extended far beyond Germany’s borders. The conquest of neighboring countries was followed by an attack on the Soviet Union and the most devastating war in human history.
Again, internal political transformation was accompanied by an effort to direct national energies towards external expansion and the consequences of that war fundamentally altered Europe’s position as many of its leading states lost much of their effective sovereignty and became dependent on the United States for their security.
Paradoxically, that dependence may now offer some protection against the most dangerous consequences of Europe’s internal crisis because governments that lack genuine strategic independence may also lack the freedom to embark upon adventures of their own choosing.
Nevertheless, Russia can’t base its security on the assumption that European political upheaval will produce more sensible leaders even if the temptation to hope for a peaceful transformation of Europe is understandable. Hope isn’t a strategy, and history provides ample grounds for caution.
Russia must therefore prepare not for the miracle of a Western Europe reconciled to peaceful coexistence, but for the possibility that its internal crisis will once again find expression in confrontation abroad.
Whatever political forces eventually emerge from the present turmoil, preparing for a military confrontation with our European neighbors must remain one of Russia’s central strategic priorities.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

Higher energy prices trigger surge in inflation now at 5.26%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:31:51 UTC
22:31:51 KST

Inflation, the figure that reflects the general rise in the price level, has risen to 5.26 per cent this month. The cost of living in Belgium has risen mainly due to the sharp increase in the price of natural gas and electricity.
Inflation in Belgium continues to rise: whilst the cost of living rose by 4.69 per cent last month, inflation has increased to 5.26 per cent this month according to the statistics agency Statbel.
Anyone following the news on energy prices knows the cause all too well: the sharp rise in energy prices is caused by the ongoing tensions in the Middle East, which have been putting pressure on gas and oil supplies to Europe for months.
Following the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, inflation saw its first significant spike in April, rising to over 4 per cent. After a slight dip in June, inflation has been on a steady upward trend again since July.
Inflation has not been this high since April. Back then, too, sky-high energy prices were to blame.
Natural gas more expensive too
Compared with a year ago, energy inflation this month stands at 33.22 per cent, compared with 24.37 per cent in September.
Electricity is 23.7 per cent more expensive than in October last year, heating oil 30.8 per cent and natural gas as much as 52.5 per cent.
In addition to price rises for natural gas, electricity and heating oil, rising rents, higher tuition fees for higher education, more expensive clothing and airfares are also driving inflation.
The sharp rise in the price of external storage devices is also striking: +48.7 per cent. As a result of the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) computer applications, high global demand has led to a shortage of hard drives and memory cards.
Trigger index not exceeded
The health index, on which any indexation of wages and benefits is based, rose from 4 per cent in September to 4.53 per cent in October. The rise is not sufficient to trigger a 2% top-up.
The last time this happened was the case was in June. As a result, benefits and the salaries of civil servants got a 2% top up in September.
According to the Planning Office’s inflation forecasts from last month, the reference index was set to be exceeded again in November. The Planning Bureau will publish new inflation forecasts on Tuesday.

Details
"You can look at my quotes from January 2023, when we began working, and I said that we would do exactly what we are doing now," the head of DC Studios wrote in response to a since-deleted post.
"I said that some stories would stand alone, like the Guardians films (Clayface is exactly that), while some would be part of a larger narrative structure, which is the Superman saga. At the same time, every part of the larger story must work on its own, regardless of whether you need to watch everything else," Gunn noted.

The originally proposed ‘8-10 year roadmap’ included not only storylines (although that was part of it), but also a plan for DC’s development as a whole, including a focus on diamond characters (Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman), as well as lesser-known characters whom we could turn into diamonds (Krypto, John Stewart, Peacemaker), how we would foster filmmakers’ freedom and allow for different tones and ratings, the influence of ‘Star Wars’ and George R. “Thirteen people were killed as a result of the Russian attack on Dnipro. At least five others were wounded. Medics are providing all necessary assistance,” Hanzha said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later reported that the number of injured in the Russian strike on a railway station in Dnipro increased to 10 people.
Ukraine’s state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said Russia used a jet-powered UAV to strike the railway station in Dnipro.
“The strike hit one of the platforms, where train No. 866 Dnipro-Zaporizhzhia was located at the time. Despite the heightened danger alert, people were on the platform. There are dead and wounded,” the company said.
Earlier, Russian ballistic missiles struck the territory of a university campus, Kyoto Park, areas adjacent to a metro station, and nearby residential quarters in Kyiv. One person has been killed and nine injured, most of them students living in a university dormitory.

Shell rakes in $12B profit as Middle East war drives up prices
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Oil and gas giant Shell has recorded $10.8 billion in adjusted quarterly profits – double what it made in the same period last year – as war in the Middle East boosts energy prices.
Since the US and Israel began attacking Iran this year, Shell’s fuel products have risen in value, largely due to strikes on competing refineries in the region that produce petrol and diesel.
The corporation, which moved its headquarters out of The Hague to London in 2022, made record profits after Russia invaded Ukraine the same year, and has seen profits surge again since the outbreak of war with Iran.
MPs have called for a windfall tax to prevent Shell or other energy conglomerates from profiting from geopolitical conflict.
Shell’s move to London makes placing a levy on the profits harder, however, and the European Commission has also ruled out an EU-wide windfall tax, saying it’s a matter for individual nations.

And also, based on the percentage of use, I can see that they really are trying to build some kind of stockpile in order to attack us in winter, which is logical. They produce somewhere up to 3,000 jet-powered Shaheds per month, and we can also add the Geran-5 to that — it is a separate weapon, around 700

They are planning tens of thousands per year

Ukrainian intelligence reveals the size of Russia's Su-34 fighter-bomber fleet
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:05:00 EET
22:05:00 KST

Ukrainian intelligence reveals the size of Russia's Su-34 fighter-bomber fleet
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine has published data on the number of Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers, their production rates and the vulnerabilities of Russia's aircraft fleet.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU)
Quote: "As of 22 October 2026, the Russian Aerospace Forces had approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service, including upgraded Su-34M (Su-34NVO) aircraft."
Details: According to DIU, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed since the start of the full-scale invasion, while another seven have been damaged.
DIU noted that these losses are significant for Russia's military air fleet, as replacing the aircraft requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources and specialised industrial cooperation.
"By way of a comparison, the number of Su-34s destroyed is equivalent to approximately 2½-3 years of production based on an estimated capacity of 14-18 aircraft per year," the intelligence agency explained.
DIU said Su-34 fighter-bombers were one of the key components of Russia's strike aviation in its war against Ukraine. Their use as carriers of guided aerial bombs has enabled the Russian military to expand its ability to strike ground targets, particularly in areas of active hostilities and frontline settlements.
"Despite significant combat losses, Russia continues to produce and modernise the Su-34, attempting to maintain the size of its aircraft fleet and sustain the intensity of its missile and bomb strikes," the intelligence agency emphasised.
Meanwhile, according to DIU, Russia's ability to further expand this capability depends on production capacity, the availability of technological components and the Russian military industry's ability to compensate for its losses.
Background: In October, Russian state corporation Rostec announced that a new batch of Su-34 aircraft had been delivered to the Russian Aerospace Forces. The number of aircraft delivered was not specified.

Kiev loses 1,155 troops along engagement line in past day - latest figures
The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,155 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 260 troops and two armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, more than 220 troops and a field artillery gun in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and over 145 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost over 340 troops and seven armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, more than 175 troops and an armored personnel carrier in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and roughly 15 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.

Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 220 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy field artillery gun in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup West units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Mayaki and Bogorodichnoye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, Podvysokoye, Glushchenkovo, Studenok and Monachinovka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said.
