China Focus: AI drives digital transformation in China's primary care
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:05:51 CST
21:05:51 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China is introducing AI-powered tools in community health centers to speed up the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare, improve primary care, expand equitable access and enhance public well-being.
Artificial intelligence (AI) assistants that support voice-based consultations, automated medical records, medication-risk screening, follow-up reminders and health education are appearing in community health centers. They are becoming a key part of the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare.
The push comes as family doctors in China take on a wide range of duties, from resident registration and chronic-disease follow-up to initial screening and public-health record keeping, often burdened by heavy paperwork and limited staffing.
AI-assisted family-doctor services have been introduced in many cities and provinces this year.
In May, the Longgang District of Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province launched the "Ant Afu" app, allowing residents to check medical reports, obtain AI-assisted interpretations, sign up for family-doctor services and link family members' health information.
In Beijing's Fengtai District, the Majiapu Community Health Service Center has deployed an AI family doctor and an AI health steward. Built on large models and AI-agent technologies, the system supports chronic-disease management, wearable-device monitoring and automatic risk alerts, with high-risk cases forwarded to contracted family doctors.
In Wuxi, east China's Jiangsu Province, AI was used in a citywide cancer screening campaign. Residents completed risk self-assessments through a mobile app or an AI-powered voice questionnaire, and big-data models identified high-risk groups for follow-up screening at 49 institutions equipped with AI-assisted imaging, ultrasound and endoscopy systems.
According to the Wuxi Municipal Health Commission, the AI-enabled screening significantly improved cancer detection among high-risk groups, with liver and lung cancers detected at markedly higher rates than in the general population.
Industry insiders say the most significant shift is that AI is moving from isolated add-on tools into routine clinical workflows in some community health centers. Earlier systems often required doctors to open separate applications for image reading or diagnostic support. The newer AI systems are being integrated with hospital information systems and health-checkup platforms, so that AI prompts appear within the interfaces doctors already use.
"AI used to seem lofty and unrelated to primary care," said Nie Chunlei, vice president of the Community Health Association of China. "But now we can see it has taken root at the grassroots level."
With growing demand and expanding real-world deployments, more tech companies are entering the sector, further driving the digital upgrade of grassroots healthcare services.
Ant Group's Ant Afu health app has rolled out its "AI agent plus human doctor" model in more than 40 cities. Tens of thousands of grassroots doctors use the platform, and it had served more than 5 million residents by mid-August this year.
The push is not limited to Ant Group. JD Health, Runda Medical and others are also ramping up investment in primary-care AI, each drawing on its own strengths.
Policy support has become more explicit. In October 2025, five national agencies issued guidance identifying intelligent clinical decision support, AI-enabled family-doctor services and coordinated chronic-disease management as priority areas. The guidance sets a goal of basically achieving full coverage of AI-assisted diagnosis and treatment in primary care institutions by 2030.
Still, industry insiders caution that scaling AI across primary care requires careful adaptation. AI cannot simply be transplanted into primary care; it must be tailored to frontline needs, embedded in daily workflows and built into applications that are replicable, scalable and can be regulated -- challenges that will take time to resolve.
Sun Dehui, R&D director at the Beijing Medical Robotics Industry Innovation Center, said primary-care AI is a clear long-term direction for public health. With policy support increasingly focused on the grassroots level, the sector is poised for rapid growth in the coming years, offering significant market potential while continuing to ease the burden on frontline clinicians and benefiting residents with chronic conditions. ■

Lithuania to introduce universal military conscription in 2032, president says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:55:00 UTC
20:55:00 KST

Lithuania plans to introduce universal military conscription in 2032, requiring a larger number of young people to serve in the armed forces amid security concerns, President Gitanas Nausėda said Thursday.
The State Defence Council, which comprises the country’s political and military leadership, agreed on the timeline at a meeting, Nausėda told reporters afterward.
Women would continue to be able to perform military service on a voluntary basis, he said.
Lithuania currently drafts more than 5,000 young people into the armed forces each year. Under universal conscription, the annual number would rise to about 7,500, accounting for demographic trends and the fact that some young people are deemed medically unfit for service, the president said.
Nausėda said the 2032 target would give the country time to invest in adequate accommodation for the larger number of conscripts and train enough instructors.
The authorities also need to balance conscript training with refresher training for reserve personnel to ensure both are carried out effectively, he said.
“I think implementing conscription from 2032 is optimal,” Nausėda said.
According to Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, the government wanted a quicker transition to universal conscription, but were convinced by the military to push back the date to 2032.
“You could say there is political will, but at the same time, there is the question of the military’s readiness. The military has clearly stated that they would be ready by 2032,” Sinkevičius told reporters after Thursday’s State Defence Council meeting.
The date for introducing universal conscription was discussed “at length and in detail, with lively debates” at the council, the PM said.
“Everyone agreed that this isn’t a race, nor is it a matter of setting a specific date in stone – that we must move toward universal conscription and that it is inevitable, but needs to be done when you’re prepared,” he said.
The preparations would include training some 300 instructors and building suitable facilities to house the young draftees, he added.
The council also agreed to expand the range of service options available to conscripts. These could include training as drone operators or assisting the State Border Guard Service and firefighting and rescue services, the president said.
After trying to switch to fully professional armed forces, Lithuania restored partial conscription in 2015, citing increased security threats following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014.

PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, October 29: Spanish papers discuss Wednesday's deadly train collision. The New York Times investigates whether a "safest seat" in the event of a train crash exists. Next, we look at a report about "the shocking rise of rib remodelling". We end with some photos from the Arctic and Antarctica.
Spanish papers are reacting to the devastating train crash that killed dozens of people on Wednesday. Both El Mundo and El País emphasise that it's not the first time this has happened – the last train accident in Spain was only nine months ago. El País also has a first-person story: "I travelled on this train", writes a journalist who works for the paper. He happened to be there during the crash. He already covered the Adamuz disaster in January and now he writes: "I had that feeling again of living through a nightmare". He also describes the strange calm and how he and other passengers managed to free themselves from the last carriage.
The New York Times asks the question "Is there a safest seat in a train crash?" The answer is not so simple. There's a rough consensus that it's best to sit in the middle of the train, in case of a hit from the front or the back. Some experts are even more precise, saying the best bet is sitting in the middle, in an aisle seat facing backward – that's because if the train suddenly stops, the whiplash would be less brutal and there's a smaller chance of being hit by flying objects. But experts told the paper that there are too many variables in train crashes to say for certain. This time in Spain, for example, the hit was from the back, so the safest place to sit would have been in the front of the train. But of course passengers couldn't have known in advance of the nature of the crash.
The tragedy is still very recent, but it could already have political repercussions. According to Democrata, it could harm Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's reputation before snap elections that are happening in only a month's time. The weak link among his ministers is Oscar Puente, the transport minister, who was already in post in January during the first train crash. According to the paper, he has three options: "continuity, resignation or dismissal". Puente is under fire, and not only because of the actual crashes. Some time after the previous rail disaster, he appeared in a comedy video in which he imitated a derailing train.
Next, The Guardian reports that rib remodelling surgery is on the rise. First, the patient's ribs are fractured, and then the person has to stay in a corset for three months, almost 24/7. The idea is to give the person a wasp-like waist. The Guardian spoke to people who went through it, who say it's extremely painful and feels like "being hit by a bus". One lady who did it couldn't sleep comfortably for more than a week because she was in constant pain. Although the procedure remains rare, more and more people are deciding to do it. Between 2018 and 2024, there were more than 2,300 patients, with an overall complication rate of 3.7 percent, which remains quite high for beauty procedures.
Finally, a new photography book by polar specialists Sue Flood and Ian Dawson captures the Arctic and Antarctica. The Times shows its favourite photographs that "document life at the frozen edges of the world".

Hackers expose US immigration surveillance network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:53:26 UTC
20:53:26 KST

Hackers expose US immigration surveillance network
Personal and operational details of more than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors, including undercover immigration agents, have been leaked online, reportedly exposing the department’s internal structure and surveillance operations.
The disclosure comes amid growing public anger over President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign, with the department’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facing growing criticism over aggressive raids, detention conditions, and the use of force against migrants and protesters.
Released on Wednesday by transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), the files contain names, contact details, job titles, and internal system access groups across ICE, Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and other DHS agencies.
DHS confirmed to the media that it is “aware of a potential breach” and is working to address it, adding that it will protect employees and update the public “when more information is available.”
What’s in the files?
Dubbed ‘Icepick’, the archive was supplied to DDoSecrets by a hacktivist group called ‘Department of Peace’. It contains around 21,300 CBP records, 6,600 linked to ICE, and 3,400 to Homeland Security Investigations, along with records from immigration services, cybersecurity, and other DHS divisions. Some records match employees’ social media profiles, but others exposed internal organizational charts and previously undisclosed programs and operations.
According to Wired, the files reference undercover investigations, wiretapping, and immigration databases, with internal access groups linked to surveillance tools including Palantir’s Falcon software and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition system used by immigration agents. Other groups reference AI services including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Elon Musk’s xAI chatbot Grok. Access groups are lists of employees authorized to use particular systems, which means the records could help identify which employees have access to surveillance tools and how DHS operations are organized.
“This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” investigative journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew, who developed a searchable version of the archive, said in a statement accompanying the release. She called it “a complete game changer for anyone investigating DHS,” arguing that it could help identify agents and their chains of command.
DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said the files go beyond an ordinary employee directory.
“Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations,” she said, pointing to officials overseeing covert investigations, efforts to identify government leakers, and deportation programs.
The hackers claim to have obtained the records through DHS’s Okta employee login system, though Okta denied that its systems were compromised.
Why now?
The hackers linked the leak to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s pledge to intensify immigration enforcement. Speaking after two fatal ICE shootings in Texas and Maine, Mullin said federal agents are “turning up the heat on the streets,” despite growing criticism of their tactics. “On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ‘turning up the heat.’ This is what happens to ICE when you do that,” a Department of Peace spokesperson said in a statement published by DDoSecrets.
The disclosure comes amid growing backlash over Trump’s immigration crackdown, a central priority since his return to the White House in January 2025. His push for mass deportations, expanded detention, and tighter border controls has sparked protests over aggressive raids, masked agents, and alleged racial profiling.
Anger intensified after federal agents fatally shot US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota in January, followed by other violent incidents involving ICE officers. Just this month, federal agents shot and wounded a Dominican migrant during an arrest in New York, prompting further demonstrations.
ICE has also faced scrutiny over detention conditions, with at least 52 deaths in its custody during Trump’s first 500 days back in office, according to Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights.
The administration maintains that its operations are necessary to enforce immigration law and remove dangerous criminals. The Icepick publishers say the records can help journalists, lawmakers, and civil liberties groups investigate DHS activities. Emma Best argued that the disclosure can enable investigations, congressional inquiries, and legal challenges by replacing the administration’s “anonymity with accountability.”
Yet another breach
The disclosure adds to a series of US government data security incidents.
In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed that it stole personal data on nearly all FBI agents and their spouses, including sensitive job details and medical information. The group said the attack was “not financially motivated” and demanded that the FBI withdraw a cybersecurity advisory published in May that it claimed contained false allegations about it.
Separately, a Pentagon personnel system breach reportedly exposed Social Security numbers, personal details, and military job records belonging to more than 3 million people, including service members and their families. The incident prompted a class-action lawsuit last week.

Ukraine has a national typeface called Zakon — what makes it distinctive
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:51:52 EET
20:51:52 KST

Ukraine has a national typeface called Zakon — what makes it distinctive
Kyiv • UNN
The Zakon typeface was created based on Ukraine’s artistic tradition for documents and the visual identity of government institutions. It will be introduced gradually.
Ukraine has unveiled the national typeface Zakon. It was created based on the Ukrainian artistic tradition. The Ministry of Culture of Ukraine reported this on October 29, UNN writes.
Details
"The new national typeface Zakon was presented publicly for the first time in Kyiv. It was developed by Ukrainian designers based on the historical heritage of the country's lettering tradition. The new typeface is intended to establish Ukrainian identity in the state's visual space and gradually replace typefaces of Russian origin in official documents," the Ministry of Culture noted.
The development of a national typeface is provided for by Resolution No. 4764-IX of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine dated January 2026, "On Strengthening the Role of the Ukrainian Language in Establishing the Ukrainian State."
"We continue to establish Ukrainian identity in the visual space. The creation of a national typeface is an important step toward ensuring that state institutions represent Ukraine through our artistic tradition and contemporary Ukrainian design. A typeface is part of a state's recognizable image. Through the form of its letters, it conveys the character of our culture and makes it present in everyday life. We seek to ensure that Ukrainian design shapes the image of our state and that cultural heritage becomes a source of new solutions," said Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy — Minister of Culture of Ukraine Tetiana Berezhna.
What the typeface is for
The initiative, the Ministry of Culture noted, is aimed at creating the state institutions' own visual language. After all, certificates, letters of appreciation, diplomas, awards, and plaques are still designed using typefaces of Russian origin, including Izhitsa and Petersburg, as well as typefaces Cyrillicized by the Russian studio ParaType.
The Ukrainian typeface tradition in contemporary design
Zakon is a classic Ukrainian antiqua that combines national graphic traditions with modern requirements for document design.
The development was based on the legacy of six outstanding masters of Ukrainian lettering. Heorhii Narbut was the author of the first Ukrainian banknotes and the coat of arms of the Ukrainian State under Hetman Skoropadskyi, and one of the founders of the Ukrainian Academy of Arts. Many of his typographic solutions remain part of Ukrainian identity to this day.
Vasyl Krychevskyi was the author of the coat of arms of the Ukrainian People's Republic and left a significant typographic legacy.
Yakiv Hnizdovskyi lived in emigration but sought to bring the Ukrainian alphabet closer to the Western typographic tradition. His work also helped contemporary masters.
Robert Lisovskyi was a graphic artist, a master of Ukrainian book type, and a follower of Mykhailo Boichuk and Heorhii Narbut.
During the Soviet era, Vasyl Khomenko created a Ukrainian typeface that was used virtually until the end of the Soviet Union.
Vasyl Chebanyk is a luminary of contemporary calligraphy who designed the ceremonial copy of the Constitution of Ukraine and left a rich typographic legacy.
The typeface incorporates characteristic features of Ukrainian graphics: asymmetrical serifs, diamond-shaped dots above the letters "і" and "ї," and the distinctive mark above "й" in the tradition of Heorhii Narbut. Its proportions also draw on the European tradition of classical antiqua typefaces.
Four Ukrainian type designers worked on the creation of Zakon:
-  Oleksii Chekal is a calligrapher, a research fellow at the Museum of Books and Printing of Ukraine, and the author of typefaces for the Orthodox Church of Ukraine; 
-  Hennadii Zarechniuk is a researcher of Ukraine's typographic heritage and a co-author of the Kobzar KS, Zahar, and Dnipro typefaces; 
-  Dmytro Rastvortsev is the author of the e-Ukraine typeface and a co-author of UAF Sans for the Armed Forces of Ukraine; 
-  Andrii Shevchenko is the author of the Arsenal typeface, which won a competition for a contemporary Ukrainian typeface for official business use. 
The project manager is Taras Ishchyk, a serviceman and the author of the graphic style of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Three typefaces for the state's different needs
The Zakon typeface family consists of three typefaces:
-  Zakon Text is intended for office work, official documents, and everyday text work. It is freely available for use; 
-  Zakon Decor was created for designing ceremonial documents, awards, and inscriptions; 
-  Zakon Letterpress is intended for printing original copies of regulatory and legal acts of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. 
The two latest typefaces are available under a closed license to a limited number of users. The font includes four styles: Regular, Italic, Bold, and Bold Italic.
How the national font will be implemented
The transition to Zakon will take place gradually, without additional costs for the mass replacement of existing signs, forms, and other materials.
After the presentation, the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine will provide government institutions with the font and instructions for installing it. At the first stage, Zakon Text will be tested during the preparation of letters, orders, forms, and other documents. The feedback received will help the developers improve the font.
At the same time, the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine is working to make Zakon the font used for the official publication of regulatory legal acts.
You can learn more about the national font, download it, and leave feedback on the website of the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine.

these glowing amber sculptures begin with a natural polymer produced by tiny insects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:50:05 UTC
20:50:05 KST

these glowing amber sculptures begin with a natural polymer produced by tiny insects
ori orisun merhav explores a future of multispecies design, where biological processes inform how we manufacture and inhabit the world.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
insects make the material for ori orisun merhav’s sculptures
Brussels-based designer Ori Orisun Merhav is experimenting with a natural polymer produced by tiny lac insects, transforming their resinous secretions into glowing sculptures and sculptural furniture. Through her research practice Made by Insects, she heats and blows the amber-colored material into clusters of translucent bubbles, some perched on branching steel structures, others suspended as elaborate chandeliers.
The material is known commercially as shellac, a substance typically used as a protective coating. Here in Merhav’s hands, it takes on a completely different spirit.
Her latest works extend the research into 3D printing and large-scale installations, imagining how an insect-produced material might become part of our built environment. After years of research into the insects themselves, the designer has received a 2026 Dutch Design Award for her experimental approach to material production.
the tiny insects behind an unlikely design material
The insects that produce this shellac are known scientifically as Kerria lacca, and are roughly the size of a grain of sand. They attach themselves to the branches of host trees and feed on their sap, converting sugars into a natural resin that hardens around their bodies. This protective enclosure allows the insects to develop and reproduce. The hardened resin can then be collected from the branches, washed and processed into shellac, a material humans have used for centuries in furniture finishing and other applications.
Designer Ori Orisun Merhav first encountered the insects while researching ecological relationships during her studies at Design Academy Eindhoven. She was fascinated by their ability to manufacture a polymer through their own biological processes, and she traveled to Thailand to study lac cultivation and meet the communities who harvest it. There, she learned about the insects’ life cycles and the agricultural practices surrounding their production.
The research became her 2022 graduation project, The Lac Lab Open Source, an evolving archive of material experiments that eventually grew into Made by Insects. It also introduced her to the economic realities of shellac production, as synthetic alternatives have steadily reduced demand for the natural resin.
learning to build from the insects themselves
Back in her studio, Merhav began testing what the material could do beyond its traditional applications. Shellac softens when heated and hardens again as it cools, allowing her to stretch it into thin membranes and blow it into hollow forms using techniques borrowed from glassmaking.
Her earliest experiments produced large, individual bubbles, but their delicate walls made them brittle and difficult to transport. Looking more closely at the insects’ protective structures, she discovered that their enclosures comprised many smaller, interconnected cells.
The observation changed her approach. Merhav began blowing smaller volumes and joining them into larger structures, developing a new language of clustered forms that draws directly from the insects’ construction methods. In works such as Branching Insects Chandelier and Meet Me Under the Insects Tree, the amber bubbles grow along slender metal supports, casting warm light through their uneven surfaces.
The finished pieces have an almost botanical appearance, although their structural logic comes from the resinous shelters of insects.
3D printing a polymer made by another species
Merhav’s experiments have since expanded into digital fabrication. Working with Ginger Additive, Reflexlab and Aeditto, she produced her first 3D-printed shellac objects in 2023, later continuing the research with material engineer Tom Samson and the Bio-Polymer Lab at Avans University of Applied Sciences in the Netherlands.
The process explores how a naturally occurring polymer can move through a printer without chemical modification. Temperature and the material’s behavior during extrusion influence the forms as they take shape, leaving behind uneven surfaces and visible layers of hardened resin.
Her Morphopoiesis vessels offer a closer look at this emerging technique. The objects rise in irregular, cellular walls, with ridges of deposited material forming dense networks around their hollow interiors.
a woven insect canopy takes shape in london
At Sarah Myerscough Gallery, Merhav’s ongoing research has grown into an environment visitors can move through. Portal Into The Multi-Species, on view from October 14th to November 7th, 2026, occupies the gallery’s entrance corridor with delicate shellac bubbles attached to steel branches. Further inside, the forms become larger and more textured.
In The Woven Insect Canopy, palm sheaths coated in insect-produced resin are held within sculptural steel supports, their fibrous surfaces illuminated from within by LEDs.
The series includes Awakening, Regeneration and Bifurcation, the latter reaching 140 centimeters in height. Light passes through the shellac-coated fibers to reveal their interwoven structure beneath the amber surface. The works point to an interior shaped by biological processes. A material originally created as a protective shelter has become part of an imagined architecture.
who makes the materials we live with?
Merhav’s interest in mutualism runs through the project, beginning with the relationship between lac insects and the trees that sustain them. The insects depend on their hosts for nourishment, while cultivation involves managing the trees’ health and the insects’ reproductive cycles.
Human participation adds another layer, through the farmers who maintain these environments and the makers who work with the harvested resin. The ecological relationship itself is complex, yet the research draws attention to the many participants involved in producing a single material.
These sculptures, for Merhav, are part of a much longer exploration of how these relationships might inform design. The work remains experimental, with the material’s fragility and the demands of fabrication continuing to shape its possibilities. Still, her lamps and vessels offer a tangible glimpse of an unusual manufacturing future. An insect produces a polymer to protect itself on a tree branch. Generations later, a designer studies that structure and finds a way to build with it.
project info:
designer: Ori Orisun Merhav | @ori_orisun
research practice: Made by Insects

How two high-speed trains collided in central Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:50:00 UTC
20:50:00 KST

Two high-speed trains collided just before 9 am on Oct 28 in Spain, killing at least 68 people and leaving more than 50 injured. Rail services between Madrid and the southern Andalusia region have been suspended. It is Spain’s deadliest train crash since 2013.
An Iryo express train had stopped at a red signal when it was struck by a Renfe high-speed train between the towns of Los Yebenes and Urda, near Toledo, about 118km south of Madrid by rail. The trains were both heading south from Madrid to Seville.
The crash is the second collision between high-speed trains on the same line in nine months. An accident between trains operated by the same two companies killed 46 people in January. Iryo is a private high-speed rail operator, while Renfe is owned by the Spanish government.
Addressing reporters in Madrid, Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said a computer malfunction had automatically stopped all traffic on part of the line. Puente said the fatal train crash occurred after the central command centre erroneously told the Renfe train to restart, without any speed restrictions.
Authorities said there were 147 passengers on the Iryo train, and 397 were on the Renfe train.
Prior to the crashes in 2026, Spain’s last major rail disaster occurred in 2013, when 80 people were killed and 145 injured after a high-speed train veered off the track on a sharp bend as it approached the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

mcdonald’s recycles happy meal toys into wireless mouse shaped like french fries

mcdonald’s recycles happy meal toys into wireless mouse shaped like french fries
developed with lenovo, this french fry-shaped wireless mouse brings a familiar red carton to the desktop, giving recycled toy plastic a new day job.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
MCDONALD’S AND LENOVO PUT FRENCH FRIES ON THE DESKTOP
McDonald’s China is giving its fries a place beside the keyboard. Developed with Lenovo, the brand’s French fry-shaped wireless mouse translates its familiar red carton and yellow contents into a computer accessory, incorporating plastic recovered from old Happy Meal toys. The collaboration brings together two recognizable features of the fast-food experience: the packaging that holds lunch and the small plastic object that tends to outlast it. This time, the latter gets something useful to do.
The design keeps the visual shorthand intact. A red lower shell carries the Golden Arches, while molded yellow fries rise across the top, giving the mouse an uneven silhouette that departs from the anonymous curves of conventional office hardware. The food reference determines the object’s shape as well as its colors, turning a piece of takeaway packaging into something intended to stay on the desk.
RECYCLED HAPPY MEAL TOYS FORM THE MOUSE’S PLASTIC SHELL
According to the product information, more than 60% of the exterior casing is made from recycled plastic sourced from collected Happy Meal toys. Lenovo describes a process involving sorting, shredding, purification, and material modification to produce recycled ABS suitable for manufacturing. The toys lose their original forms along the way: their material returns to production, eventually taking on another distinctly McDonald’s identity.
The collaboration sits within McDonald’s China’s Reimagine Good Things initiative, launched in 2021 to explore new uses for recovered materials. Previous products have included trays and flowerpots, extending the program into everyday objects. Here, the shift from toy to computer accessory also changes the intended user and setting. Something once handed out with a children’s meal reappears among the equipment of adult working life, retaining a little of its former playfulness.
WIRELESS CONNECTIVITY HIDES BENEATH THE FRENCH FRY SHAPE
Behind the sculpted fries, the mouse offers Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless connectivity, quiet-click buttons, and three adjustable sensitivity settings. A 380mAh rechargeable battery powers the device. Its accompanying carrying pouch unfolds into a mouse pad, allowing the accessory’s protective cover to become part of the desktop setup. The specifications give the novelty object a practical role, although its distinctive outline alone says little about comfort over a full working day.
This limited release places the mouse between functional equipment and branded collectible, with its appeal resting on an immediately legible transformation. A carton normally associated with a brief stop for food becomes an object designed for repeated use. Whether that makes answering emails more appetizing is another matter.
project info:
name: French fry-shaped wireless mouse
brands: McDonald’s and Lenovo | @mcdonalds and @lenovo
location: China

Estonia's volunteer rescuers send 146th aid shipment to Ukraine
The Estonian Rescue Association (Päästeliit) has sent aid to Ukrainian rescuers, funded by donations and the Foreign Ministry, providing shelter, power and heating for over 30,000 people this winter.
The Kyiv consignment has included a minibus, two high-pressure tents with trailers, diesel heaters, power stations, lighting towers and heated blankets, enough to set up two emergency centers, Estonia's Embassy to Ukraine announced.
"This was our 146th shipment to Ukraine. Every time we hand over new equipment, we hope the situation will improve. Unfortunately, the head of Kyiv's rescue service confirmed that the situation is already worse than ever, and that the coming winter will put civilians — especially children — in an even more difficult position than last year," said Piia Kallas, head of the Estonian Rescue Association, a volunteer organization which complements the Rescue Board (Päästeamet).
Estonian Rescue Association delivered emergency tents and equipment to Ukraine's rescue services @SESU_UA. The aid will provide temporary shelter, electricity and heating for more than 30,000 people during the winter. The package was funded by @MFAestonia and donations. https://t.co/fOGAZI2tOy
— Estonia in Ukraine (@EE_Ukraine) October 28, 2026
The shipment delivered to Kyiv included a minibus, two high-pressure tents with trailers, diesel heaters, battery power stations, battery-powered lamps, lighting towers, heated blankets, folding tables and chairs, fast chargers, thermos flasks, changing mats, children's toys and play mats. With this equipment, rescuers can set up two emergency centers where residents can find temporary shelter and warmth, charge their devices and receive psychological first aid.
A second delivery reached rescuers in Rivne oblast in southeastern Ukraine, including an off-road vehicle, a generator, battery power stations, lighting towers and heaters. The generator was donated by a private donor who decided to give their equipment to those who need it most.
Since the start of the invasion in February 2022, with support from donors and partners, the Rescue Association has delivered nearly €7 million worth of rescue equipment and vehicles to Ukrainian rescuers.

Firehawk raises $150M at $1.4B valuation to build more rocket motors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:26:16 UTC
20:26:16 KST

- Firehawk raised more than $150 million in a Series D led by Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, valuing the company above $1.4 billion.
- The funds will expand its Oklahoma propellant plant and Mississippi missile integration site to scale rocket and artillery motor production.
Dallas-based rocket propulsion firm Firehawk has raised more than $150 million in a Series D round that values the company at more than $1.4 billion, money it will use to scale up U.S. production of rocket propellant, solid rocket motors and artillery motors, the company said on social media on Oct. 28.
Private equity firm Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, co-founded by Dallas investor Kyle Bass, led the round, with new and existing investors and strategic partners also taking part. Firehawk said the round was upsized and oversubscribed, and the Dallas Morning News reported its original target was $100 million. The company did not disclose how much each investor put in.
The money will fund the build-out of Firehawk’s propellant and rocket motor plant in Lawton, Oklahoma, and its missile integration facility in Crawford, Mississippi, along with new research and development sites and more hiring, the company said in its funding announcement. Firehawk plans to produce more than 100,000 artillery motors in 2027 under a commercial agreement with General Dynamics, and its Oklahoma plant is expected to start low-rate production by mid-2027.
Firehawk was founded in 2019 by CEO Will Edwards to make hybrid rocket engines powered by 3D-printed fuel, and it now describes itself as covering the whole chain from propellant to motors to complete rounds. Its pitch is volume: the U.S. military’s appetite for rockets and missiles has outrun the small number of established solid rocket motor suppliers, and Firehawk says its patented manufacturing process can produce propellant faster and at larger scale for smaller tactical weapons.
The company broke ground on its Great Plains Arsenal rocket motor and propellant plant in Lawton in April. Its Crawford site can integrate 40,000 tactical rockets a year, and Firehawk says it plans to raise that to about 120,000 at full-rate production.
Much of that work centers on the Hydra-70, the 70 mm unguided rocket fired from U.S. Army attack helicopters and other aircraft. This summer the U.S. Army picked Firehawk as one of four new companies to build Hydra-70 rockets, alongside iRocket, Nammo Perry and Albers, with each required to deliver 24 prototype M151 rockets within 18 months. In August, Firehawk fired six Hydra-70 rockets at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, all of which worked as intended.
The Series D follows a $60 million Series C that closed in September 2025 and a strategic investment in November 2025 aimed at speeding up solid rocket motor production and integration.
Firehawk has not said how many Hydra-70 rockets or rocket motors it has delivered to the U.S. military so far, or when its Oklahoma plant will reach full-rate production.

====================================================================================================

Mathematicians find an infinite number of Ramanujan equations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:19:15 UTC
20:19:15 KST

The legendary mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan and Yifeng Huang, a postdoctoral researcher at Emory University, have something in common: they will not be ignored. In 1912 Ramanujan, a 24-year-old clerk at what was then the Madras Port Trust in India, began mailing pages of new, unproven formulas to mathematicians across England. One of his letters eventually reached British mathematician G. H. Hardy at the University of Cambridge, who recognized Ramanujan as a visionary, invited him to visit and helped launch his groundbreaking career.
More than a century later, Huang, while a graduate student at the University of Michigan, began e-mailing mathematicians letter after letter—more than 40 in total. He scarcely heard back.
Huang’s ideas concerned two formulas that appeared in Ramanujan’s letters and are now known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. In September 2026 Huang and a few collaborators uploaded a proof that the historic equations represent a single case of a much grander geometrical theory. In particular, the work showed that the Roger-Ramanujan identities correspond to a trefoil knot in a certain space. The trefoil, known as the shape of the familiar Celtic knot, is one of the simplest mathematical knots. And related knots, they found, reveal an infinite number of previously unknown identities.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Everything about this subject, even the original discovery, is a surprise,” says George Andrews, a mathematician at Pennsylvania State University and an expert on Ramanujan’s math. Ramanujan, Hardy and their collaborators “were all unable to prove this,” he adds. “So the things that have cropped up from knot theory were a total surprise to me.”
The Roger-Ramanujan Identities
Hardy was responsible for shaping much of early 20th century number theory. Initially skeptical when he received a letter from Ramanujan, Hardy later wrote that he recognized the letter’s author as “a mathematician of the highest quality, a man of altogether exceptional originality and power.” It was a pivotal moment.
Two of Ramanujan’s formulas were startling: they represented an infinite series of sums on one side and an infinite series of products on the other, with no visible reason for the two to agree. By 1916 British mathematician Percy MacMahon had found a way to read them. These two equations were similar to ones studied two centuries earlier by mathematician Leonhard Euler. Euler had a neat trick for sidestepping such complexity: he connected the equations to a type of counting problem known as a “partition.” A partition of a number is a way of writing it as a sum. MacMahon transformed Ramanujan’s formulas into two kinds of partitions that looked nothing alike, but whose counts always came out identical.
Here’s how one side of a Ramanujan equation was partitioned: count the number of ways to sum up to a certain value using numbers that are at least two whole numbers apart. For instance, 6 can be written as 1 + 5, 2 + 4 and 6. So there are three partitions.
On the other side, sum using only numbers that end in 1, 4, 6 or 9. For 6, the answer is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 4 and 6, which also gives three partitions.
The formulas say these two very different counts agree for every number. Before Ramanujan could prove them, he came across an obscure proof by English mathematician Leonard James Rogers in an old math journal. Thus, the equations became known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities.
“It was regarded, for most of the 20th century, as an isolated gem,” Andrews says. No one suspected it lay at the heart of a much larger theory.
In the early 1970s Andrews uncovered an infinite family of the identities. “I discovered them only to learn that [mathematician] Basil Gordon had done them first,” Andrews says, “which was a huge disappointment for me.”
The new family came to be known as the Andrews-Gordon identities.
Since then the identities have turned up in strange places: in representation theory, in the study of symmetric functions, even in physics via the “hard hexagon model,” which describes how gas atoms can settle onto a surface in a triangular pattern.
“Who would have thought that the Rogers-Ramanujan identities were related to how liquid helium behaves when poured onto a graphite plate?” Andrews says.
A Pinch to Build a Conjecture
Yifeng Huang had a hunch.
Matrices—little spreadsheets of numbers—can undergo operations such as flips and transpositions, which must be done in a certain order to get the correct result. But if the values of the matrices are chosen such that the order of operations doesn’t matter (meaning they “commute”), then the matrices behave like coordinates and can be used to describe curves. Take any smooth curve, such as the parabola y = x2, and replace y and x with pairs of matrices. A textbook-level problem might ask: How many pairs of matrices make the equation true? A math student can find the answer.
But what happens if you use a curve that isn’t so smooth—one that has a “pinch” in it, also known as a singularity? Now textbook theory breaks down. These matrix counts had neverbeen studied.
While he was still a Ph.D. student at the University of Michigan, Huang started counting matrices on pinched curves such as y2 = x3, which comes to a sharp tip when x and y equal 0. Before long, his counts reproduced a familiar formula: one side of the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. “Already this discovery is fascinating,” Huang says. “I’m wondering what is going on. It can’t be a coincidence.”
From that single example, Huang made a bold, vague guess: What if every pinched curve hid a new identity, with its matrix count collapsing into a neat formula? Hoping to discuss the idea further, Huang wrote letters to a small group of mathematicians—around five to 10 people.
University of Virginia mathematician Ken Ono received one of those letters. But thinking Huang’s idea was “crazy,” Ono dismissed it.
Another letter recipient was Alexei Oblomkov, a mathematician at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, whose work connects algebraic geometry and knot theory. “I thought it was kind of a great idea, and later we met at one of the conferences, and I liked the idea even more,” Oblomkov says.
By then, Huang and Ruofan Jiang, now a mathematician at the University of California, Berkeley, had devised a systematic way to count how many matrices make the formulas for pinched curves true.
Oblomkov brought geometry to the table. Zoom in on the pinch in y2 = x3, he advised, and surround it with a tiny sphere in four dimensions, where mathematicians say such curves naturally live. The curve pierces the sphere along a closed loop in a “trefoil” knot. Both counts lead to the classic Rogers-Ramanujan identities. What about another curve? It also led to another knot, which was hiding another family of identities. And another curve led to yet more.
The team’s ideas crystalized into the Huang-Jiang-Oblomkov (HJO) conjecture. Simply stated, pick any two numbers a and b that are greater than 1, with no common factor. The conjecture predicts that for the curve xa = yb, a count of the matrix solutions will always collapse into a Rogers-Ramanujan-type identity. This translates into infinitely many families of identities, one for every value of a. The case a = 2 is the family Andrews and Gordon found. Every larger value of a was uncharted. And each curve comes with its own knot: the trefoil for a = 2 and b = 3 and more intricately wound torus knots for the rest.
The Proof
Again, Huang began sending out e-mails—more than 40 in 2023—and gave a circuit of seminar talks.
This time, when Ono received one of Huang’s letters, he found the idea “mind-blowing,” he says. “That’s when I joined this chase.”
By then Ono had signed on to the artificial intelligence company Axiom Math as its founding mathematician. He, Huang and another Axiom mathematician, Kenny Lau, worked for seven months in tandem with AxiomProver, the company’s math-focused AI system.
Because the ideas were so new, Ono says, they couldn’t simply ask an AI model to solve the problem—there was no literature for it to learn from. Instead AxiomProver worked like a research assistant, testing a far more expansive space of ideas than would be humanly possible. It also translated the proof into Lean, a machine-friendly language for automated proof checking. In the end, the quartet made of humans and AI stitched together ideas from five different areas of math to prove the conjecture.
Ono’s take on AI in math is more hopeful than many in his field. “Everyone talks about the end of math,” he says. “But someone had to invent this structure. This is what we should be doing.”
The team members posted their HJO conjecture to the preprint server arXiv.org in August 2026. And in September, the three followed up with the conjecture’s proof.
Recast as geometry, the old identities now point toward unmapped territory, raising questions that mathematicians are eager to explore.
“We found something exciting,” Oblomkov says, “a way to extend the geometry in the case when it’s not a trefoil knot, but a so-called Hopf link—basically you have two circles tied together. So that will be the next paper.”
Oblomkov also says Fields Medalist Peter Scholze has published a few papers that take some of Huang’s ideas even further. The pinched curves xa = yb are only the beginning. The equation is, Huang says, “only the first example of a singularity I would write down.” Oblomkov agrees: “It’s just the first case, and there will be many more.”

German industry groups urge Berlin to join defence bank initiative
BERLIN, Oct 29 - German business and industry associations on Thursday urged the government to join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), saying membership was needed to close financing gaps for companies in the defence sector and protect their access to future projects.
The joint statement was signed by groups including the German Security and Defence Industry Association (BDSV), aerospace association BDLI, the chamber of commerce DIHK, engineering association VDMA, savings banks group DSGV and the Startup Association.
The proposed multilateral institution, backed by Canada, seven other NATO countries and Ukraine, would provide long-term, low-cost financing for defence, security and resilience projects.
"The geostrategic threat situation urgently requires new answers and approaches: financing for the defence sector must be secured sustainably over the long term," said Elisabeth Hauschild, managing director of BDSV.
The associations said the bank could offer guarantees for commercial loans to small and medium-sized companies, including startups, as well as long-term loans, venture capital and equity financing for capacity expansion, innovation and critical raw materials.
"As a multilateral development bank, it provides the decisive risk buffer through guarantees and long-term financing instruments—particularly where established banks have so far been reluctant to support long-term contracts for the Mittelstand," Hauschild said.
The DSRB, which will be based in Canada, has faced challenges securing support from larger European nations. Reuters was first to report in September last year that Britain had declined to join the project.
A spokesperson for the German finance ministry told Reuters on Monday that Germany was an observer in the negotiations on DSRB's charter and was reviewing open questions.
Germany should participate in the bank's founding process and join the group of founding states as soon as possible, the business associations said.
The groups warned that companies from member countries could receive preferential access to procurement projects financed by the DSRB under its planned charter rules. If Germany stayed outside the institution, its companies could be excluded from market opportunities or face a competitive disadvantage against rivals from member states, they added. REUTERS

Christine Lagarde: The outsider who led the ECB her way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:11:13 UTC
20:11:13 KST

Christine Lagarde: The outsider who led the ECB her way
FRANKFURT, Oct 29 - Christine Lagarde's decision to step down early as European Central Bank president ends an eventful seven years at an institution she was never expected to lead.
The former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund arrived in Frankfurt in 2019 as the first ECB chief with no formal economics training or central banking experience — prompting some market participants to label her a "credibility risk."
In fact, she knew so little about the institution that Lagarde, 70, later said she had accepted the job thinking the presidency was a five-year mandate, rather than eight.
Yet after a tenure dominated by a pandemic, two energy shocks and the worst inflation spike in the euro zone's history, Lagarde leaves with a record that defied the sceptics.
"Her seven years at the ECB have been, on the whole, pretty good," said Willem Buiter, an economist and former Bank of England official, noting that the ECB managed to bring inflation back down faster than peers in Britain and the United States.
Her exit, however, threatens to be as political as her arrival.
By walking away before her eight-year term ends, Lagarde gives European Union leaders a chance to pick her successor before a French election next spring that opinion polls suggest far-right candidate Marine Le Pen will win, replacing President Emmanuel Macron.
For an institution that fiercely guards its independence from political meddling, the timing has drawn sharp criticism from central bank watchers.
"This is debasing the institution and just following the purely political calculus of the French president," said Paul De Grauwe, a professor at the London School of Economics.
Lagarde and Macron have not addressed such criticism directly. Lagarde has said she would not be a candidate for the French presidency but would advocate for pro-European values in her home country "in whichever capacity" she deemed most efficient.
'BETTER WITH BUTTER'
Throughout her career, Lagarde has stood apart from more technocratic colleagues through a mix of charm, consensus-building and folksy pragmatism.
Favouring plain-speaking homilies over dense economic theory, the then-IMF chief famously declared that "everything is better with butter" when discussing growth and told governments to "fix the roof while the sun is shining".
Unorthodoxy was a hallmark of Lagarde's career, and the subject of her upcoming autobiography "Lady First".
A former corporate lawyer who spent years in Chicago, she entered French politics in 2005 as an outsider. Early missteps earned her the domestic moniker "Madame Lagaffe," but she soon became one of then-President Nicolas Sarkozy's sharpest operators, steering French banks through the 2008 crash.
She led the IMF through Europe's debt crisis, navigating a messy Greek rescue that imposed harsh austerity, and sparked outrage in Athens when she bluntly urged suffering citizens to "pay their taxes".
Her appetite for high-stakes bets showed again in 2018 with a record $57-billion lifeline for Argentina to back then-President Mauricio Macri. The gamble unravelled, failing to halt a currency collapse or avert a deep recession, and left the IMF bound to its most troubled debtor.
THE SPREADS CRISIS AND THE TRIBAL CLIQUE
Her occasional unfamiliarity with the nuances of central banking still peeked through.
In March 2020, as the pandemic rattled sovereign debt markets, Lagarde told a press conference the ECB was "not here to close spreads" between Italian and German borrowing costs.
The comment triggered an immediate selloff in bond markets and forced her to swiftly walk it back.
Under Lagarde's watch, the ECB swiftly rolled out emergency bond-buying that stabilised markets as COVID-19 spread. It launched its fastest series of interest-rate hikes to bring inflation under control following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, although it later acknowledged it had been slow to recognise the full impact of spiking energy prices.
As ECB president, she once described economists as a "tribal clique" — a provocative jab at the profession's establishment, though she later softened the blow by saying she hoped to join the tribe.
A 'MORE POLITICAL' ECB PRESIDENT
Lagarde used her political skills to repair rifts. Unlike her predecessor Mario Draghi, whose top-down style embittered some hawkish northern European peers, she worked to build consensus among the euro zone's 21 national central bank chiefs.
Her willingness to wade into politics remained evident: in January, Lagarde walked out of a World Economic Forum dinner in Davos during a speech by US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that criticised Europe, an episode that underscored fraught transatlantic relations.
Whoever succeeds her when she leaves the ECB on February 7 will face fresh challenges including strains in French bond markets ahead of next year's election and a Middle East conflict that threatens a new bout of inflation.
Ultimately, Lagarde's legacy may be a paradox: an outsider who showed that political diplomacy could steer a central bank through historic shocks, but whose early departure served as a final reminder of her political instincts.
"She was put there for a reason: being more political than her predecessor and, on that mission, I think she largely succeeded," Frederik Ducrozet, head of strategy and macro research at Pictet Wealth Management, said. REUTERS

Four more arrested in election bribery probe as Likud seeks revotes at Arab polling stations

Police arrested four more suspects Thursday in an investigation into alleged vote-buying on behalf of the Arab Ra'am party, including three school principals from Bedouin communities in southern Israel, as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party prepared to challenge election results at polling stations where it alleges bribery and other violations occurred.
Three of the four newly arrested suspects were subsequently released to house arrest.
The arrests bring the number of people detained in the investigation to seven since Tuesday's parliamentary election. The case centers on allegations that money and other benefits were offered to voters in exchange for supporting Ra'am, an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas.
The developments come amid a separate investigation into suspected foreign interference in the election, possibly involving tens of millions of shekels from Qatar. That inquiry is being conducted by the Shin Bet domestic security agency at the request of Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, chairman of the Central Elections Committee.
The two investigations are distinct, and no connection between the suspected Qatari funding and the alleged vote-buying involving Ra'am has been established.
Likud, meanwhile, is escalating its challenge to the election results as part of a broader political campaign against cooperation with Arab parties following an inconclusive vote that left neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition with a clear parliamentary majority.
The party is preparing to seek the annulment of results at polling stations where it claims voters were bribed or prohibited methods were used to influence the vote, ynet has learned.
Cash payments, fuel vouchers and allegations of vote-buying
A Bedouin source from the Negev, familiar with political activity in the region, described what he alleged was a system used by Arab parties, particularly Ra'am, in the days leading up to the election.
According to the source, political activists visit the homes of low-income residents and offer financial assistance ranging from 200 to 300 shekels ($65 to $95), including to families affected by home demolitions and residents of unrecognized Bedouin villages.
He alleged that the payments are presented as assistance to needy families, while recipients are asked in return to support a particular party at the ballot box.
In other cases, he claimed, fuel vouchers worth 100 shekels ($32) are distributed to people who transport residents to polling stations.
The amounts can vary depending on family size, he said, with payments allegedly distributed one or two days before the election and sometimes on Election Day itself.
The source argued that some residents do not view such payments as election bribery but rather as financial assistance, particularly given the poverty and lack of basic services affecting disadvantaged Bedouin communities.
"I don't understand what all the fuss is about," he said. "We learned this from Shas, which has been doing it for years and even distributes money in synagogues."
Shas is an ultra-Orthodox Jewish political party that has long been part of Netanyahu's governing alliances.
"So why all the fuss now? Just because we're Arabs? Because we turned out to vote and became a powerful political force?" the source asked.
His allegations against Shas were not substantiated in the account.
Likud prepares legal challenge to election results
Senior Likud officials said the party intends to petition election authorities in the coming hours over polling stations where it suspects bribery or the use of prohibited methods.
"New elections must be held at these polling stations," senior party officials said.
Attorney Ilan Bombach, Likud's legal adviser and a deputy chairman of the Central Elections Committee, is preparing the petition based on material the party previously submitted to the committee.
Likud alleges that the material documents election bribery and the use of prohibited methods, including applications that tracked the identities of voters at polling stations.
The planned challenge is separate from the Shin Bet investigation into suspected foreign financing.
Likud maintains that the evidence it has already submitted is sufficient to invalidate results at certain polling stations and require voting to be repeated there.
Bombach is not alleging that ballot papers were forged or that vote totals were falsified. Instead, the petition focuses on alleged bribery, the use of prohibited election methods and the distribution of money or other benefits to voters in exchange for their support.
The party's allegations have not been established in court.
Under Israeli election law, election results can be challenged through a separate legal process. Courts may order voting to be repeated at specific polling stations if violations are established and could have affected the results.
The planned petition comes as Arab parties have emerged with potentially decisive parliamentary influence following Tuesday's election, intensifying political disputes over whether the opposition could form a government with their support.
Seven suspects detained, including three school principals
The latest arrests follow the detention of three suspects on Election Day by investigators from Lahav, the Israel Police's national investigations unit, on suspicion of election bribery and conspiracy to commit a crime.
The original suspects were identified as Ibrahim al-Gharibi, 42, from the Al-Azazmeh community; Hussein Masaudin, 63, from Segev Shalom; and Saif Abu Riaash, 38, a physician from the Al-Sana tribe.
A magistrate's court initially extended the detention of al-Gharibi and Masaudin until Sunday while ordering Abu Riaash released to house arrest.
Police appealed the physician's release, however, and his detention was subsequently extended as well.
During court proceedings, a Lahav representative said Abu Riaash had organized gatherings at private homes to encourage residents to vote for Ra'am.
"He holds meetings in people's homes to get them to vote for Ra'am, even though he is a doctor, and that is problematic," the police representative said.
Al-Gharibi is suspected of violating election law after investigators searching his home discovered cash. A search of his vehicle also uncovered envelopes bearing Arabic writing, green shirts and flags, and Ra'am ballot slips.
Masaudin, meanwhile, accused authorities of politically motivated persecution.
His defense attorney said envelopes discovered at his home bore the name of the Islamic Movement, the religious and political movement associated with Ra'am, and that each contained 1,000 shekels ($320) intended as charitable donations to low-income families.
Investigators also seized another envelope containing 12,000 shekels ($3,840). Masaudin said that money belonged to his son.
The suspects have denied wrongdoing, and the allegations remain under investigation.
'The Bedouins came out to vote because they feared for their lives'
A relative of Abu Riaash rejected suggestions that the surge in Bedouin voter turnout resulted from improper financial inducements.
Instead, he attributed the increase to anger over National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose policies toward Bedouin communities in the Negev have drawn criticism.
"The increase in voter turnout in this election is because of one thing: the failed minister who caused damage in the Negev, Ben-Gvir," the relative said.
"Of course the Bedouins came out to vote. They feared for their lives. There's also no sense of security."
The relative said his own experiences during the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack had strengthened his determination to influence the country's political direction.
"I was at the gas station in Kfar Aza on Oct. 7. I am officially recognized as a victim of a terrorist attack, so of course I want to influence this government and change it," he said. "That's how everyone is thinking."
Separate Shin Bet investigation examines suspected Qatari funding
In a parallel development, Sohlberg, who also serves as deputy chief justice of the Supreme Court, sent an unusual letter to Shin Bet Director David Zini calling for an investigation into suspected foreign funding and election bribery involving foreign actors.
The letter followed a meeting between Sohlberg and Zini on Wednesday.
The suspected interference reportedly involves an attempt by Qatar to influence Israel's election through transfers estimated at tens of millions of shekels.
The intelligence underlying the suspicions has been described as "solid," although the precise nature of the alleged payments, their intended recipients and whether any election bribery actually occurred remain unclear.
According to information obtained by ynet, the Shin Bet had possessed the intelligence for several days but waited to determine whether the suspected bribery would take place.
The agency declined to comment on the investigation.

Teledyne FLIR wins $48M to turn 10 Bulgarian Strykers into CBRN scouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:06:36 UTC
20:06:36 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Teledyne FLIR Defense a $48 million contract to equip 10 Bulgarian Strykers with upgraded CBRN reconnaissance sensor suites.
- The work runs through 2028, with the sensor suites integrated in Bulgaria after the vehicles are delivered.
Teledyne FLIR Defense has won a $48 million U.S. Army contract to fit Bulgaria’s new Stryker fleet with the same upgraded chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear reconnaissance sensor suite now going to U.S. Army units, the company announced on Oct. 26.
U.S. Army Contracting Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, awarded the contract under a Foreign Military Sales agreement, the government-to-government route through which allies buy U.S. defense equipment. Bulgaria will equip 10 of the nearly 200 Strykers it is buying with the Nuclear, Biological and Chemical Reconnaissance Vehicle (NBCRV) Sensor Suite Upgrade, turning them into dedicated vehicles for detecting contamination ahead of other troops. Work will run through 2028 at several Teledyne FLIR sites in the United States, and the sensor suites will be fitted in Bulgaria after the vehicles arrive.
The NBCRV is the CBRN reconnaissance version of the Stryker. Its crew drives into or near a suspected contaminated area, detects and identifies hazards from a distance, collects samples and reports what it finds so commanders can decide where units can safely move. Teledyne FLIR is the lead integrator for the U.S. Army’s upgrade of that system, which adds more automated sensors and an unmanned aircraft, and the company began delivering the new suites to U.S. Army units in 2025.
Among the third-party sensors in the package, the upgraded vehicle carries Teledyne FLIR’s R80D SkyRaider drone fitted with the company’s MUVE B330 biological detector, which lets the crew sample the air for biological agents away from the vehicle. The U.S. Army tested a Stryker launching the SkyRaider with the MUVE B330 during development. A Teledyne FLIR command and control system ties all the sensors and platforms together and automates part of the analysis to reduce the workload on the crew.
“The upgraded Stryker vehicles will provide Bulgaria with the most advanced mounted CBRN reconnaissance capabilities in Europe,” said Dr. JihFen Lei, President of Teledyne Defense and Aerospace Group and Senior Vice President of Teledyne Technologies.
“Together, our two Stryker modernization efforts highlight the breadth of sensor solutions Teledyne FLIR can deliver to NATO allies and partners, helping warfighters detect, identify and respond effectively to an array of battlefield threats,” Lei said.
The new award is Teledyne FLIR’s second Bulgarian Stryker contract this year. In January, the company won a contract worth up to $32 million to supply thermal sights and radars for Bulgaria’s Stryker fleet, giving crews 360-degree visibility and long-range threat detection.
Bulgaria is buying the Strykers to replace its Soviet-era tactical vehicles and to operate equipment compatible with other NATO forces. The first five combat vehicles arrived at the Black Sea port of Burgas on Feb. 14, along with eight more provided free of charge through a U.S. assistance program, and the fleet is going to the 61st Mechanized Brigade.
Teledyne FLIR said it has received contract vehicles worth more than $240 million for the NBCRV Sensor Suite Upgrade program since 2024. In June, it also won an $11.2 million U.S. Army contract for more than 45 SkyRaider-based CBRN sensor drone kits for dismounted units operating away from the reconnaissance vehicles.

As criminal networks spread in Latin America, Quito is new battleground
QUITO, Oct 29 - For years, the neighborhood watch group in the working-class area of Solanda in Ecuadorean capital Quito had patrolled their nighttime streets armed with little more than whistles and sticks, on the lookout for cellphone snatching and other petty crimes.
But then they realized the criminals were changing. Members of notorious national gangs began to move into the area, and shootings, contract killings and extortion took hold. The watch suspended the patrols, fearful they might be targeted themselves. Their place was taken by heavily armed troops, sent by the national government.
Ecuador's importance as a transit point for cocaine exports from Colombia and Peru has spiked over the last half-decade, stoking an explosion in violence and crime in the once tranquil South American country that has caught up everyone from Pacific fishermen to politicians, journalists and grandmothers forced from their homes.
President Daniel Noboa, an ally of the administration of US President Donald Trump, has responded with a widespread military, police and legislative crackdown on crime, sending soldiers into the streets and hardening sentences, among other measures. The government has notched several major captures or killings of gang leaders, but that has led to fragmentation, creating vicious internecine violence and splinter groups seeking new territory.
That now includes Quito. This historic Andean city, with its whitewashed colonial buildings, cobbled streets, and backdrop of cloudcapped volcanoes, has long been a draw for tourists and digital nomads. But it is becoming an increasing focus of criminal activity, residents, police and analysts say. Gangs are using local drug sales to gain a foothold in neighborhoods, taking advantage of the capital’s strategic location to distribute drugs to the country’s ports, from where cocaine destined mostly for Europe and the US is shipped.
“Criminal organizations have tried to establish themselves in certain neighborhoods through small-scale drug trafficking," police Lieutenant Colonel Juan Chacon told Reuters as his team conducted a raid on an alleged drug distribution site in central Quito. "That connects them to a range of other crimes."
Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones, all gangs which the US has designated as foreign terrorist organizations, are present in Quito, according to police.
Solanda, built as a public housing project in the 1980s, with a busy commercial district and narrow streets of modest houses, appears on a national government list of high-risk Quito areas. Residents have installed a surveillance camera system on every street corner and metal gates at entrances to side streets to prevent unknown people from entering.
“With the cameras, you can identify the criminal and avoid exposing yourself,” said Maria Eugenia Alban, a community leader in Solanda. “Now criminals are no longer acting alone, and they are armed.”
GANGS 'TRYING TO ESTABLISH A FOOTHOLD'
The pushback from authorities has had some success. An increased security response in Solanda lowered violent death figures to just two between January and September of this year, down from 13 in the same period of 2025, according to government records.
Violent death figures in Quito overall fell in 2024 and 2025 from a high of 294 in 2023, according to Interior Ministry data, as Noboa sent soldiers onto the streets. And violence still remains below that of Ecuador's port cities like Guayaquil and Duran.
But, the armed forces say, it is a constant battle.
“Organized crime groups are trying to establish a foothold in Quito,” Lieutenant Colonel Miguel Saavedra, head of a tactical army brigade which is responsible for controlling guns, ammunition and explosives in the capital, told Reuters at a checkpoint where his unit was checking cars for weapons. His troops were seeking to "safeguard and restore security" in the city, he added.
About 4,000 police and military personnel were deployed at entry points and along strategic corridors in Quito as part of a security plan announced by Noboa in August. The city has been under a 60-day state of emergency since September.
During the first six weeks of the plan, police arrested more than 300 people, according to national police figures. The military joined police operations to check for weapons at entrances to high-risk neighborhoods and conducted targeted patrols.
Drug seizures in Quito were up nearly 500% between January and September, compared with the same period a year before, according to police figures.
Military and police operations across Ecuador cost gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining and fuel and arms trafficking nearly $20 billion in losses between January and July, according to the Defense Ministry.
However, crackdowns in one place can prompt criminal groups to seek out more favorable territory where residents are less wary of crime, said Colonel Mario Pazmino, a former head of army intelligence and current security analyst.
He said Quito is part of the “cocaine triangle," serving as a transit and temporary storage point for drugs coming from the Colombian coastal city of Tumaco and Putumayo province, before being transported across Ecuador along Pacific and Amazon road corridors.
The capital’s strategic position has been exploited by a growing number of criminal groups over the past year, said Tiziano Breda, an analyst at conflict-monitoring organization ACLED, although its status as a "transit point" lowers the risk of it being the focus of the sort of violent disputes between groups seen elsewhere.
“In Quito’s case, international cartels and national gangs are beginning to converge and establish themselves,” Pazmino said. “Quito is a hub city. The gangs come to protect the merchandise and look for other activities.” REUTERS

In Lebanese village near Israeli troops, farmers brave danger to harvest their olives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
