In Lebanese village near Israeli troops, farmers brave danger to harvest their olives
ZIBQIN, Lebanon Oct 29 - In a field overlooking a lush valley in southern Lebanon, residents of the village of Zibqin balanced on branches picking their olives while Lebanese Army soldiers stood nearby.
Zibqin is adjacent to Israel’s self-declared “security zone” in southern Lebanon, where Israeli troops have demolished dozens of villages, saying armed group Hezbollah had embedded itself in civilian infrastructure — a claim the group denies. Israeli shelling frequently strikes the valley below the olive groves despite a June ceasefire between the two sides.
As Palestinians, Israeli rights groups and the UN report increased violence and olive thefts by Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Lebanese farmers also fear for their safety, illustrating how conflict is again upending the annual harvest.
Despite the danger, Lebanese farmers are returning to fields they have tended for generations, determined to harvest a crop that is one of their main sources of income and nutrition.
Ali Bzieh, a 65-year-old farmer from Zibqin, said he had no choice but to come to the fields. “This is my land, this is my livelihood, this is a harvest we wait for from one year to the next,” he said, sitting under the branches of an olive tree. “We have an attachment to this land, to the plants, and to the crops — we don't leave them.”
LIMITED PROTECTION
Many families came back to Zibqin after the ceasefire between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah. But the situation remains unstable, Raef Bzieh, a local official, said. “The ongoing bombing and the aggressions taking place on the outskirts of the village have of course caused worry and panic among the people.”
The danger prompted residents to ask the Lebanese Army to accompany them to their fields. But Mustafa Barakat, a 50-year-old carpenter, said that even with the army, the villagers did not feel safe. “But if the Israelis decide to cause harm, they can harm us, and the army,” he said. “They have struck the Lebanese Army more than once.”
Israeli attacks have killed 26 Lebanese soldiers in 2026, according to statements posted by the Lebanese Army on X. The Lebanese Army is not party to the conflict between Hezbollah and Israel.
In response to questions from Reuters, the Israeli military said its strikes in Lebanon are against Hezbollah and its infrastructure and are not directed at the Lebanese Army or civilians. It also said it is working to "enable the olive harvest and assist residents in carrying it out".
Thirty-eight Israeli soldiers have been killed in southern Lebanon in 2026, according to posts on the Israeli military's website.
WAR CHANGES HARVEST’S RHYTHMS
Barakat's days in the olive grove used to start in the early morning and stretch until sunset. Now, he limits his time in the field to when the Lebanese Army is present.
The danger has reshaped what was once an occasion for families to gather and share the hard work of harvesting olives.
“In the past, we used to treat this (harvest) season like an outing," he said. He used to come with his family to the fields and prepare food together. "Now, you can’t bring children… bombing could occur, and they could get hurt," he said.
The conflict has affected the harvest in other ways too: “We weren't able to tend to our olive trees, so our olive trees did not yield as they usually do,” said Ali, who was displaced for several months. He said the harvest was half what it normally was.
Ali said that he hoped the situation wouldn't escalate further and force his family to flee again. But many in Zibqin were bracing for that possibility: some residents continue to pay rent for apartments in areas further north. Others have already reserved a place to stay in the event of further escalation.
Yet as war casts its shadow over the harvest for the fourth consecutive year, the farmers refuse to abandon their fields.
“This land is our identity, it is the passport we carry," said Barakat. "If we abandon it, we are truly left without an identity." REUTERS

Written Danish exam grades fall across Denmark’s upper secondary programs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:56:47 UTC
19:56:47 KST

Grades in written Danish have fallen across Denmark’s upper secondary education programs, according to the latest exam results released by the Education Ministry on Thursday.
At general upper secondary schools, known as stx, the average grade in A-level Danish, the highest subject level, fell from 6.8 in 2018 to 6.2 in 2026.
Across upper secondary programs, grades declined both compared with last year and over the longer term.
Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said the figures worried him and raised concerns about students’ use of artificial intelligence.
“Artificial intelligence has in a very short time changed the students’ everyday lives,” he said in a press release.
“And we cannot ignore what it can mean for their academic proficiency. Because if AI becomes a shortcut around the work of writing, analyzing, and expressing oneself, then we risk that the students learn less,” he said.
The figures follow a PISA international student assessment published in early September that showed declining performance in reading, mathematics and science among 15-year-olds, renewing debate about academic standards in Danish schools.
Police announce stop-and-search zone for Copenhagen derby
Copenhagen Police will introduce a stop-and-search zone around Parken on Sunday, 8 November, when FC Copenhagen face Brøndby IF in a match classified as high risk.
The zone will be in force from 06:00 to 20:00 across parts of Østerbro, including Trianglen, Blegdamsvej, Jagtvej, Østerbrogade, Svanemøllen Station and Strandboulevarden.
Within the zone, police can stop and search people without suspecting them of a criminal offence. The measure is intended to prevent unrest surrounding the derby.

“We will also be present in large numbers so that we can intervene if there should be signs of unrest brewing,” he said.

PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.
Direct flights from Copenhagen to Ilulissat cleared as Greenland airport opens
Travelers heading to western Greenland will no longer need to change planes in Nuuk after aviation authorities approved the opening of Ilulissat’s expanded airport on Thursday.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority granted final safety approval overnight, following inspections and a test flight.
“Following a long series of inspections and a test flight, we have approved that the airport meets the necessary level of safety required to operate a modern, international airport,” said deputy director Lars Korsholm.
The approval comes with temporary restrictions during the airport’s initial operating period. These will gradually be eased as the airport gains experience.
Korsholm said the restrictions were unlikely to affect scheduled flights, particularly outside the tourist season.
The airport’s runway has been extended from 845 meters to 2,200 meters, allowing larger aircraft to land in Ilulissat, a town on Greenland’s western coast near Disko Bay.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen had to connect through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.
Initially, Air Greenland will generally operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday, with additional weekly departures during busy periods, including Christmas and New Year.
Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.
The expansion forms part of a multibillion-krone investment in Greenland’s airports, which also includes improvements in Nuuk and a new airport near Qaqortoq in southern Greenland.
The projects aim to improve transport connections and support economic development, particularly through increased tourism.

Five municipalities in Jutland have volunteered to accommodate more Ukrainian refugees than their allocated share, offering some relief to municipalities facing pressure elsewhere in Denmark.
Haderslev, Horsens, Skive, Struer and Viborg will receive a combined 133 additional refugees, according to the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Viborg will take the largest share, with 65 additional arrivals, while Skive will accommodate 18.
Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov, from the Social Democrats, welcomed the decision, noting that Copenhagen and municipalities in its western suburbs are particularly stretched.

More than 47,000 Ukrainian refugees currently live in Denmark, compared with the 100,000 arrivals authorities prepared for in 2022.
Despite the lower number, Bødskov said pressure on municipalities justified tighter admission rules.
He acknowledged the difficulties involved while emphasizing Denmark’s continued military, civilian and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine.
Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

Danish tax agency faces further scrutiny over identity theft cases
Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.

Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.

Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.
“The interest rate fluctuations do not change the fact that pensioners can count on receiving the pension they are guaranteed, and a robust bonus capacity allows us to increase pensions for all members,” Præstegaard said.
ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.
Electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex recalled over electric shock risk
Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.
According to Epiq ApS, the affected products lack child safety protection covering the socket openings, creating a potential electric shock hazard.
The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.
Customers will receive a full refund even if they no longer have their receipt.
The recall covers the following four products:
Scoop ledningssæt med tre stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with three sockets. EAN code: 5713359129661.
Basis ledningssæt med fire stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with four sockets. EAN code: 5713359131749.
Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.
Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.
The company has instructed customers to return affected products to their original Bilka or Føtex store for a refund without requiring proof of purchase.
Veteran Venstre lawmaker expelled over party discipline dispute
Preben Bang Henriksen has been expelled from Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, after refusing to promise that he would follow the party’s position in future parliamentary votes.
The lawmaker confirmed his expulsion Tuesday following a meeting at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing.
“The conclusion of a vote was that I am expelled,” he said.
Henriksen will continue as an independent member of parliament but said he had hoped to remain in Venstre.
The dispute followed a September vote on legislation concerning fertilizer use, when five Venstre lawmakers opposed the party’s position over concerns about its impact on agriculture.
Venstre chairman Troels Lund Poulsen subsequently sought stronger party discipline, receiving support from the party’s national executive committee Sunday.
“Once the debate has taken place, and a majority has decided on a direction, the expectation is that the majority backs it, even if one wished for a different result,” Poulsen said Tuesday.
Henriksen refused to make that commitment, arguing that lawmakers should retain their independence.
Under Denmark’s Constitution, members of parliament are bound only by their own convictions.
However, Venstre’s internal rules prevent lawmakers expelled from its parliamentary group from remaining party members.
Henriksen, a former lawyer from Aalborg, entered parliament in 2011 at age 57.
He has served as the party’s justice spokesperson and chaired parliamentary committees overseeing legal affairs and intelligence services.
Known for following his own conviction, he has previously gone against the party line. In 2021, he voted with eight members against launching an impeachment trial against Inger Støjberg, who ended up being convicted. The members were granted a free vote when they voted.
In the 2024 book “Ærlig talt – Borgen indefra”, he described that he was close to leaving Venstre because of Lars Løkke Rasmussen’s purchase of clothes with party money. The book also contains criticism of political conformism and the workflows at Christiansborg.
With Preben Bang Henriksen’s departure, Venstre loses another one of its vote-magnets, as he received the fifth-most votes in Venstre in the election in March 2026.
Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

Norwegian to cut 123 jobs at Copenhagen Airport as it reduces locally based aircraft
Norwegian will lay off 123 employees at Copenhagen Airport, including 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew members, as it reduces the number of aircraft based in the Danish capital.
The decision follows talks with Flyvebranchens Personale Union, or FPU, the union representing the employees, according to Danish business outlet Finans.
Most affected staff will leave at the end of January next year, with the remaining departures planned 10 months later.
“It is a sad day for Norwegian, and I am incredibly affected on behalf of the affected employees,” Sara Neergaard, the airline’s country manager in Denmark, told Finans.
“But there is no other way. The redundancies are happening out of necessity.”
Norwegian plans to reduce its Copenhagen-based fleet during the summer season from 16 aircraft to 14. The airline says demand varies considerably between seasons, requiring 16 aircraft during the summer peak but only 10 in winter.
The change will not reduce the number of summer departures from Copenhagen. Some summer routes will instead be operated by aircraft based in Spain.
Union challenges the decision
FPU Chair Thilde Waast described the layoffs as an attempt to “undermine Danish working conditions.” In a written response, she accused Norwegian of seeking to replace Danish employees with “cheaper Spanish labor.”
Neergaard said the union had rejected options that could have reduced the number of layoffs, including seasonal contracts under which staff would work more in summer and less in winter, as well as voluntary leave.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline by passenger share last year, according to the airport’s latest financial report. It carried 15% of passengers, behind SAS at 38% and ahead of Ryanair at 9%.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest base after Oslo. The airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen last year.
EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

The University of Copenhagen (KU) shut down several administrative systems Monday after another cyberattack, just days after hackers gained access to personal information belonging to approximately 525,000 people.
The university confirmed the latest attack on its website, reporting disruptions to several administrative systems and difficulties accessing university websites on Monday evening.

The minister summoned leaders from Denmark’s eight universities to a meeting Monday to discuss cybersecurity.

New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news
A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.
Editor-in-chief Michael Dyrby describes the content as AI-assisted rather than fully automated.
Human editors select stories, determine their angles, review AI-generated drafts, make revisions and choose images before publication.
“We could have made it so that AI did everything. But it doesn’t,” Dyrby said.
AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.
The aim is to produce more journalism with fewer resources while maintaining editorial control.
“We will find out,” Dyrby said, describing Projekt Y as an experiment in journalism’s future.
Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.
Its target audience is primarily adults aged 28 to around 60.
Dyrby, who graduated from the Danish School of Journalism in 1989, previously helped launch TV 2 News in the mid-2000s.
Projekt Y has received media subsidies and will also generate revenue through advertising.
Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.
“The ambition is to create a technology that is so simple that everyone can use it and create their own media outlet, and in that way help democratize the use of media,” Dyrby said.
Additional publications are planned throughout the remainder of this year and into 2027.
Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.

People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.

Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.
Source: Ritzau

The announcement comes as the government seeks to restrict residence permits for displaced Ukrainians arriving from 14 areas it considers less affected by the war.
Parliament has already passed legislation excluding Ukrainian men aged 23 to 60 from obtaining residence under a special law, aiming to prevent them from avoiding military mobilization.
Several Jutland municipalities previously offered to accept additional refugees, citing available accommodation and demand for workers.
However, only Skive proceeded among the five municipalities that initially expressed interest.
Brønderslev requested additional funding, which Bødskov rejected, saying municipalities willing to help must operate under existing financial arrangements.
More than 47,000 Ukrainian refugees currently live in Denmark, compared with the 100,000 arrivals authorities prepared for in 2022.
Despite the lower number, Bødskov said pressure on municipalities justified tighter admission rules.
He acknowledged the difficulties involved while emphasizing Denmark’s continued military, civilian and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine.

Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.

He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.
“The interest rate fluctuations do not change the fact that pensioners can count on receiving the pension they are guaranteed, and a robust bonus capacity allows us to increase pensions for all members,” Præstegaard said.
ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.

Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.

The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.

The recall covers the following four products:
Scoop ledningssæt med tre stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with three sockets. EAN code: 5713359129661.
Basis ledningssæt med fire stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with four sockets. EAN code: 5713359131749.
Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.
Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.

Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.

Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.

“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.

Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:56:39 UTC
19:56:39 KST

Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.

Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.
Direct flights from Copenhagen to Ilulissat cleared as Greenland airport opens
Travelers heading to western Greenland will no longer need to change planes in Nuuk after aviation authorities approved the opening of Ilulissat’s expanded airport on Thursday.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority granted final safety approval overnight, following inspections and a test flight.
“Following a long series of inspections and a test flight, we have approved that the airport meets the necessary level of safety required to operate a modern, international airport,” said deputy director Lars Korsholm.
The approval comes with temporary restrictions during the airport’s initial operating period. These will gradually be eased as the airport gains experience.
Korsholm said the restrictions were unlikely to affect scheduled flights, particularly outside the tourist season.
The airport’s runway has been extended from 845 meters to 2,200 meters, allowing larger aircraft to land in Ilulissat, a town on Greenland’s western coast near Disko Bay.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen had to connect through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.
Initially, Air Greenland will generally operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday, with additional weekly departures during busy periods, including Christmas and New Year.
Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.
The expansion forms part of a multibillion-krone investment in Greenland’s airports, which also includes improvements in Nuuk and a new airport near Qaqortoq in southern Greenland.
The projects aim to improve transport connections and support economic development, particularly through increased tourism.
Denmark among 36 countries confirmed for Eurovision 2027 as boycotts continue
Canada will make its Eurovision debut next year, while several European countries remain absent amid disagreements over Israel’s participation in the international song contest.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organizes Eurovision, announced that 36 countries, including Denmark and Israel, are registered for the 2027 competition.
Ireland and the Netherlands have withdrawn for the second consecutive year, citing Israel’s participation and concerns over the humanitarian situation in Gaza and restrictions on press freedom.
Spain, Iceland and Slovenia also boycotted this year’s contest over Israel’s involvement.
Iceland will remain absent in 2027, while Spain and Slovenia have until December to decide whether to participate.
“As the EBU acknowledges that the matter is complex, it has agreed to give both broadcasters a deadline until December,” Eurovision’s official website stated.
The Czech Republic has also withdrawn, with national broadcaster Česká televize citing budget adjustments.
North Macedonia, meanwhile, will return for the first time since 2022.
Next year’s competition will take place in Burgas, Bulgaria, following Dara’s victory in Vienna with the song “Bangaranga.”
Denmark finished seventh this year with Søren Torpegaard Lund’s “Før vi går hjem,” its best result in 13 years.
The 2027 contest will feature semifinals on May 11 and 13, followed by the grand final on May 15, when 25 countries will compete.
Bulgaria, as the defending winner, qualifies automatically alongside the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy, which make the largest financial contributions to the competition.
Viewers and professional juries will determine the results of both semifinals and the final.
Five Danish municipalities agree to take additional Ukrainian refugees
Five municipalities in Jutland have volunteered to accommodate more Ukrainian refugees than their allocated share, offering some relief to municipalities facing pressure elsewhere in Denmark.
Haderslev, Horsens, Skive, Struer and Viborg will receive a combined 133 additional refugees, according to the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Viborg will take the largest share, with 65 additional arrivals, while Skive will accommodate 18.
Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov, from the Social Democrats, welcomed the decision, noting that Copenhagen and municipalities in its western suburbs are particularly stretched.
“It is a shared task to ensure that the Ukrainians who come to Denmark also gain a proper foothold in our local communities,” Bødskov said.
The announcement comes as the government seeks to restrict residence permits for displaced Ukrainians arriving from 14 areas it considers less affected by the war.
Parliament has already passed legislation excluding Ukrainian men aged 23 to 60 from obtaining residence under a special law, aiming to prevent them from avoiding military mobilization.
Several Jutland municipalities previously offered to accept additional refugees, citing available accommodation and demand for workers.
However, only Skive proceeded among the five municipalities that initially expressed interest.
Brønderslev requested additional funding, which Bødskov rejected, saying municipalities willing to help must operate under existing financial arrangements.
More than 47,000 Ukrainian refugees currently live in Denmark, compared with the 100,000 arrivals authorities prepared for in 2022.
Despite the lower number, Bødskov said pressure on municipalities justified tighter admission rules.
He acknowledged the difficulties involved while emphasizing Denmark’s continued military, civilian and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine.
Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.
