An order from the Danish Transport Authority led to additional baggage checks from October 8. Some passengers missed flights, and SAS reported rebooking 352 travelers.
Copenhagen Airport introduced additional security checks following an order from the Danish Transport Authority and underestimated staffing needs on some days in October, the airport said Wednesday after long queues caused passengers to miss flights.
The airport received the order on October 6 and introduced the measures two days later. The changes meant more passengers had their baggage checked manually, it said in a press release.
The airport did not explain why the authority issued the order or give details of its requirements.
There were periods of long waits on October 8, October 22 and October 23, the airport said. Passengers also faced waits of up to an hour early on Saturday, October 24.
Danish media have reported lengthy queues, particularly over the past five days, with some passengers reaching their flights too late to depart as booked.
The airport acknowledged that it had underestimated staffing needs on some days during October. It said “it is naturally not satisfactory” that some passengers had had “a bad experience”.
SAS said on October 23 that it had rebooked 352 passengers because of the long waits. Passengers were also urged to arrive earlier than usual and allow extra time for security.
Norwegian also offered affected customers rebooking.

Danish tax agency faces further scrutiny over identity theft cases
Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.

Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.
The group reported a third-quarter profit after tax of 397 million DKK.
Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.
“The interest rate fluctuations do not change the fact that pensioners can count on receiving the pension they are guaranteed, and a robust bonus capacity allows us to increase pensions for all members,” Præstegaard said.
ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.
Electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex recalled over electric shock risk
Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.
According to Epiq ApS, the affected products lack child safety protection covering the socket openings, creating a potential electric shock hazard.
The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.
Customers will receive a full refund even if they no longer have their receipt.
The recall covers the following four products:
Scoop ledningssæt med tre stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with three sockets. EAN code: 5713359129661.
Basis ledningssæt med fire stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with four sockets. EAN code: 5713359131749.
Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.
Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.
The company has instructed customers to return affected products to their original Bilka or Føtex store for a refund without requiring proof of purchase.
Veteran Venstre lawmaker expelled over party discipline dispute
Preben Bang Henriksen has been expelled from Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, after refusing to promise that he would follow the party’s position in future parliamentary votes.
The lawmaker confirmed his expulsion Tuesday following a meeting at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing.
“The conclusion of a vote was that I am expelled,” he said.
Henriksen will continue as an independent member of parliament but said he had hoped to remain in Venstre.
The dispute followed a September vote on legislation concerning fertilizer use, when five Venstre lawmakers opposed the party’s position over concerns about its impact on agriculture.
Venstre chairman Troels Lund Poulsen subsequently sought stronger party discipline, receiving support from the party’s national executive committee Sunday.
“Once the debate has taken place, and a majority has decided on a direction, the expectation is that the majority backs it, even if one wished for a different result,” Poulsen said Tuesday.
Henriksen refused to make that commitment, arguing that lawmakers should retain their independence.
Under Denmark’s Constitution, members of parliament are bound only by their own convictions.
However, Venstre’s internal rules prevent lawmakers expelled from its parliamentary group from remaining party members.
Henriksen, a former lawyer from Aalborg, entered parliament in 2011 at age 57.
He has served as the party’s justice spokesperson and chaired parliamentary committees overseeing legal affairs and intelligence services.
Known for following his own conviction, he has previously gone against the party line. In 2021, he voted with eight members against launching an impeachment trial against Inger Støjberg, who ended up being convicted. The members were granted a free vote when they voted.
In the 2024 book “Ærlig talt – Borgen indefra”, he described that he was close to leaving Venstre because of Lars Løkke Rasmussen’s purchase of clothes with party money. The book also contains criticism of political conformism and the workflows at Christiansborg.
With Preben Bang Henriksen’s departure, Venstre loses another one of its vote-magnets, as he received the fifth-most votes in Venstre in the election in March 2026.
Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

The layoffs are expected to be completed by the end of November. There will also be voluntary departures, though the company declined to say how many.
CEO Christian Jensby said Rambøll’s growth had made the organization more complex.
“In many areas, the organization has become difficult to navigate, decisions take too long, and areas of responsibility are not sufficiently clear,” he said in a statement.

Norwegian to cut 123 jobs at Copenhagen Airport as it reduces locally based aircraft
Norwegian will lay off 123 employees at Copenhagen Airport, including 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew members, as it reduces the number of aircraft based in the Danish capital.
The decision follows talks with Flyvebranchens Personale Union, or FPU, the union representing the employees, according to Danish business outlet Finans.
Most affected staff will leave at the end of January next year, with the remaining departures planned 10 months later.
“It is a sad day for Norwegian, and I am incredibly affected on behalf of the affected employees,” Sara Neergaard, the airline’s country manager in Denmark, told Finans.
“But there is no other way. The redundancies are happening out of necessity.”
Norwegian plans to reduce its Copenhagen-based fleet during the summer season from 16 aircraft to 14. The airline says demand varies considerably between seasons, requiring 16 aircraft during the summer peak but only 10 in winter.
The change will not reduce the number of summer departures from Copenhagen. Some summer routes will instead be operated by aircraft based in Spain.
Union challenges the decision
FPU Chair Thilde Waast described the layoffs as an attempt to “undermine Danish working conditions.” In a written response, she accused Norwegian of seeking to replace Danish employees with “cheaper Spanish labor.”
Neergaard said the union had rejected options that could have reduced the number of layoffs, including seasonal contracts under which staff would work more in summer and less in winter, as well as voluntary leave.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline by passenger share last year, according to the airport’s latest financial report. It carried 15% of passengers, behind SAS at 38% and ahead of Ryanair at 9%.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest base after Oslo. The airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen last year.
EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.
University of Copenhagen rules out second cyberattack, but system disruptions continue
The University of Copenhagen says it was not hit by a second cyberattack Monday, reversing its initial assessment after shutting down several administrative systems.
Activity that appeared to signal another attack prompted the shutdown. By Monday evening, the university had determined that no new attack had occurred, it said on its website.
However, a controlled shutdown remains necessary as a precaution linked to the original breach, and some systems continue to experience disruptions.
The university disclosed the first attack Friday. Outsiders gained access to information about approximately 525,000 people, including details such as full names, CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers, telephone numbers and private email addresses.
The breach also compromised ID card PINs belonging to about 20,000 employees and students. The university temporarily restricted physical access to selected critical locations following a security assessment.
Those locations have reopened after all affected cardholders received new PINs.
The University of Copenhagen, the Technical University of Denmark and Aarhus University have all faced cyberattacks within a few weeks.
Christina Egelund, Denmark’s minister for research, higher education and digitalization, previously told Ritzau that leaders from the country’s eight universities had been summoned to a meeting Monday to discuss security.

“But there is no other way. The dismissals are happening out of necessity.”
Last week, aviation news outlet Check-in.dk reported that 125 employees at Norwegian’s Copenhagen base were at risk of losing their jobs.
The airline plans to reduce the number of aircraft based in Copenhagen during the summer season from 16 to 14.
According to Norwegian, the decision reflects significant seasonal differences in passenger demand.
The airline currently needs 16 aircraft during the busy summer months but only 10 during winter.
Despite the reduction in Copenhagen-based aircraft, Norwegian says it will maintain its existing number of summer departures from the Danish capital.
Some routes will instead be operated using aircraft based in Spain.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline last year, accounting for 15 percent of passengers, according to the airport’s latest financial statements.
SAS held the largest share at 38 percent, followed by Ryanair in third place with nine percent.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest operating base after Oslo.
Last year, the airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen Airport.

Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.

People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.

Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

- The systems will support counter-drone and ground defense, and Smart Shooter helped set up local installation and maintenance capability.
Israeli company Smart Shooter has delivered the first batch of its SMASH Hopper MG remote weapon stations to an unnamed integrator in Asia, which is building them into a defense system for an Asian military to shoot down drones and engage ground targets, the company said on social media.
Smart Shooter did not identify the country, the armed force or the integrator, and it did not say how many systems were in the first batch, what the contract is worth or when further deliveries will follow. As part of the project, the company also helped the customer set up local installation and maintenance capability.
The SMASH Hopper is a lightweight remotely operated weapon station that lets a soldier aim and fire from behind cover or from inside a vehicle, and the MG designation refers to the version configured for a machine gun. It uses Smart Shooter’s SMASH fire control technology, which tracks a moving target and releases the shot only when the computer calculates a hit, an approach the company built for hitting small drones that are hard to engage with ordinary iron sights or optics.
Earlier SMASH Hopper versions carried an assault rifle, including the configuration inside the company’s SMASH DOME portable counter-drone system, which pairs the weapon station with radar and optical sensors.
Israel Defense Forces units have used the SMASH Hopper for several years, Smart Shooter said in June, when Israel’s Defense Ministry placed a new order worth up to $2.5 million with delivery by the end of 2026. That followed a separate ministry contract in May for SMASH Hopper systems, spare parts and services, which Israeli media linked to the drone threat on the country’s northern border.
Most of Smart Shooter’s sales come from its rifle-mounted SMASH 2000L and SMASH 3000 fire control sights, which are used by U.S. forces, and in September the U.S. Army included the company’s U.S. subsidiary in a group of 10 counter-drone suppliers sharing $4.15 billion in contracts, with Smart Shooter receiving $150 million. The company says the SMASH family is also used in Britain, Germany and other NATO countries.
Smart Shooter described the Asian integrator’s system as a layered defense against threats in the air and on the ground, but it did not say which other sensors or weapons the system includes or when the armed force expects to put it into service.

Plenum adopts resolution on Party self-governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:54:48 UTC
19:54:48 KST

The Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee has adopted a resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance as it concluded its fifth plenary session, according to Xinhua News Agency.
The Politburo presided over the meeting. 
President Xi Jinping, who's also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, delivered an important address, and a communique was issued after the session.
At the session, participants considered and adopted the Resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance. 
Xi delivered explanatory remarks on the draft of the resolution.
The CPC Central Committee gave a highly positive assessment of the great achievements the Party has made in exercising full and rigorous self-governance in the new era, Xinhua reported.
"It was stressed that many favourable conditions are now in place for advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance, while we also face many new circumstances and new issues in this endeavour," the communique said.
Profound changes in global, national and Party conditions have made the CPC's tasks of uniting and leading the people in safeguarding China's sovereignty, security, and development interests, of uniting and leading the people in promoting reform and development and maintaining social harmony and stability, and of maintaining its advanced nature and integrity even more formidable, it added.
Systematic plans for persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance were also made at the session, according to the communique.
Strict management of officials is the key to full and rigorous Party self-governance, it noted.
"We will build up the ranks of high-calibre officials with firm political commitment, outstanding professional competence, excellent work conduct, and strict discipline," it added.
Party organisations at all levels play the principal role in exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance, said the communique, adding that it is therefore essential to systematically advance the development of Party organisations at all levels and in all sectors to strengthen their political and organisational functions.
"It was noted that taking integrated steps to ensure that officials do not have the audacity, opportunity, or desire to commit corruption is both an important strategy for full and rigorous Party self-governance and a fundamental guideline for our fight against corruption," the communique said.
"We must take systematic steps to address both symptoms and root causes of corruption and adopt a holistic approach that combines severe punishment, targeted remedy, and effective prevention, carrying this fight through to the end."
Strengthening Party regulations and institutions represents a long-term, fundamental strategy for ensuring full and rigorous Party self-governance, said the communique.
The CPC Central Committee decided at the session that the Party will convene its 21st National Congress in Beijing in the second half of 2027 and stated that this congress, which is to be held at a critical stage for basically realising socialist modernisation and on a new journey toward the Second Centenary Goal, will be a highly important meeting and an event of great political significance for both the Party and the country.
The session elected Zhang Shengmin as a new Politburo member.

Without electricity, food or medicine – civilian evacuation planned in Russian-occupied Oleshky

Residents of Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's Kherson region, who wish to return to Ukrainian government-controlled territory after evacuation will first be transported to Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar region, according to a ceasefire agreement reported by Fox News.
From there, they will be flown on a Russian Ministry of Defence aircraft to Gomel in Belarus before being transferred to Ukraine.
The evacuees travelling to Ukrainian-controlled territory will be accompanied by Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets, two representatives of his office and two Ukrainian journalists.
Representatives of Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and members of the humanitarian mission coordination group will also travel with them to Belarus.
On Wednesday morning, both Lubinets and Lantratova announced that no ceasefire violations had been recorded during the 30 hours since the truce began in Oleshky.
Oleshky is located in the Russian-occupied part of Ukraine's Kherson region.
The town remains under constant shelling, while residents who have stayed behind have been forced to survive for months without electricity or adequate medical assistance.
Food and medicine are in short supply, and roads leading into the town have been mined.
According to volunteers, approximately 1,500 people, including around 40 children, remain in Oleshky.
Including neighbouring villages, the total number of people in the affected area is estimated at approximately 6,000, including around 200 children.
Lubinets reported that the ceasefire in Oleshky began at 3 a.m. on 27 October.
The Russian Ministry of Defence confirmed that the ceasefire had been implemented.
The ceasefire is expected to remain in effect until 10:59 p.m. on 1 November.

🔴 Suspect in deadly shooting near Paris admits racist intent, French anti-terrorism prosecutor says

Paris shooting suspect admitted to targeting Muslims and Africans, prosecutor says
A shooter suspected of killing one person and wounding five others, including a child, last week in the town of Trappes, near Paris, admitted to targeting Muslims and Africans, France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor said. The 39-year-old was on Thursday charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
A man arrested after a gun attack in the Paris suburbs, killing one person and wounding seven including a child, has admitted to "targeting individuals who appeared to be Muslim, African, or North African", prosecutors said Thursday.
Last Friday, the 39-year-old, identified as Kevin T., opened fire with a submachine gun from a moving vehicle as he drove through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière, west of Paris. He was arrested later that day. Most of the victims were of foreign origin.
The attack came in an increasingly tense political climate, with presidential elections just six months away and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leading opinion polls.
On Thursday, the suspect was charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, said the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office (PNAT).
Read moreSuspect in racist Paris shooting transferred to psychiatric unit, had drugs in his system
Earlier this week Kevin T. had contested the racist nature of the attack.
National terrorism prosecutor Olivier Christen told reporters Thursday that Kevin T. now claimed he had chosen the location for his actions because it was "a hotbed for Islamists".
The suspect has been held in police custody, Christen said, noting that he had requested that he be held in pretrial detention.
'No regret'
Authorities initially said five people, including an 11-year-old child, had been wounded in the attack, but later revised the toll to seven injured.
Three victims were still in hospital Thursday, one of them in life-threatening condition.
Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French national of Congolese origin, was killed in the attack.
Kevin T. rejected suggestions he had "intended to kill children", but that he "might have been mistaken due to their size".
He stated that he "feels no regret", Christen said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The prosecutor noted the "very high level of preparation" behind the attack, including the acquisition in September of "several weapon components designed to enhance the tactical effectiveness of a Sten submachine gun, as well as a police armband and handcuffs".
Kevin T. denied any "terrorist intent", viewing his actions as "legitimate", the prosecutor said.
A search of the suspect's home had uncovered "weapons or weapon components, specifically a magazine, two pairs of brass knuckles, a steel bayonet, and a silencer", Christen said.
Also found were several books, including a Quran, a Bible, and Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf, as well as stickers celebrating Le Pen's far-right National Rally (RN) party.
'RN provided ideological ammunition'
Christen said the stickers bore slogans such as "Long live France, RN, proud to be French", but they were not produced by the RN party.
Kevin T. had told investigators he had designed them himself, then ordered them to be manufactured via Amazon.
The suspect told investigators he was neither a member of nor a sympathiser with any political party, Christen added.
According to a source close to the investigation, Kevin T. had become increasingly radicalised by far-right ideology over the past decade, blaming Arabs and Black people for "everything".
Romain Ruiz, a lawyer for one of the victims, said: "What this man's statements show is that the National Rally provided him with ideological ammunition, and that this ammunition is what came out of his gun on Friday."
Kevin T., who has four previous convictions, said he had suffered from psychological problems and had used drugs since the age of 13.
The attack has triggered protests against the normalisation of racist hatred.
In an interview on the YouTube channel HugoDecrypte on Wednesday, Macron suggested that "certain political movements on the far right" – including the RN and "those close to them" – had allowed a climate of racism "to take root".
RN lawmaker Jean-Philippe Tanguy retorted that it was the president himself who had allowed "hateful ideologies" to flourish.
Authorities banned a far-right, radical-leaning symposium on "remigration" – scheduled for Saturday in the suburbs of Paris – and a demonstration planned for Sunday in the capital.

Germany news: Merz says North Korea threatening Europe's freedom

- VW has been struggling to keep pace with competition from China and to transition to electric vehicles
- Berlin's mayoral candidate Elif Eralp is under fire over her interview with Der Spiegel
Here are the main headlines from and about Germany on Thursday, October 29, 2026:
Elif Eralp: Berlin's potential next mayor caught in dispute over private interview remarks
A German news magazine's decision to publish private interview notes has sparked a controversy surrounding Berlin's potential next mayor.
On Thursday, Der Spiegel published internal comments on an interview by Elif Eralp, who led the socialist Left Party (Die Linke) to victory in September's state election. Her office had accidentally included the remarks while approving an interview for publication.
In the notes, Eralp expressed fears for her family's safety if she publicly named Ibrahim Ibrahim, a pro-Palestinian activist who is reported to have links to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which the EU designates a terrorist organization. Ibrahim had attended the Left Party's election-night celebrations and was photographed with prominent Left Party Bundestag member Ferat Koçak.
Eralp also cited advice she received from Berlin police against publicly naming individuals linked to organized crime, though that advice was reportedly related to a separate case. Der Spiegel questioned whether her fears could affect her independence as mayor. Eralp rejected suggestions that she could be intimidated and pledged firm action against terrorism and organized crime.
She is reportedly considering legal action against the magazine and a complaint to Germany's Press Council. The magazine has also faced criticism for publishing remarks intended for internal use, raising questions about the balance between public interest, privacy, and journalistic ethics.
The timing is significant. Eralp, the daughter of Turkish immigrants, could become Berlin's first Left Party mayor and the first woman of Turkish descent to hold the office. Her party won 25.7% of the vote in September's election and hopes to form a government with the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens. Both prospective partners have approved formal coalition negotiations.
The Left must decide whether to follow suit at a party conference this Saturday, October 31. The far-left party is also facing accusations of antisemitism involving some of its members. Newly elected lawmaker Vanessa Emde faces possible exclusion from the Left's parliamentary group following comments questioning whether states, including Israel, have an inherent right to exist. The Left has been part of Berlin coalition governments before but has never led one. The controversy comes at a pivotal moment in its effort to do so.
German diplomacy: From Asia to Latin America
Germany's leaders are on a foreign relations push, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz on a trip to South Korea, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul in Panama and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier in China.
Merz spoke of the threat North Korea posed to Europe's freedom by supplying troops to fight in Russia's invasion of Ukraine. He wraps up his visit with a trip to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, meanwhile, is in Panama where he is visiting ahead of traveling to Atlanta for the G20 meeting.
Wadephul is there to promote free trade and also handed over humanitarian supplies to his Panamanian counterpart Javier Martinez-Acha Vasquez.
And then German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities in China and picked up a ping-pong paddle for a game with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll, who is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.
Wadephul visits Panama ahead of traveling to the G20 meeting in Atlanta
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul landed in Panama on Wednesday evening for a visit.
After his arrival at Panama City airport, Wadephul handed over humanitarian supplies to his Panamanian counterpart Javier Martinez-Acha Vasquez.
The aid shipment is made up of about 20 tons of supplies. Panama was hit by a powerful earthquake earlier this month.
The supplies include water filters, blankets, tarpaulins, cots and kitchen sets worth over €150,000 ($167,000).
More than 5,000 people are still being housed in emergency shelters, weeks after the magnitude-7.7 quake on October 9, which resulted in injuries and damaged hundreds of buildings.
Wadephul also thanked the Central American country for maintaining the Panama Canal "so responsibly and ensuring it is fit for the future, as well as more generally focusing on preserving balance in the region."
Restrictions on other sea routes due to the conflict in the Middle East has meant that the Panama Canal is more important to global trade than ever.
Wadephul is due to hold talks on Thursday with Martinez-Acha Vasquez and President Jose Raul Mulino.
Wadephul will travel to the US state of Georgia for the G20 summit in Atlanta on Friday and Saturday.
IN DEPTH: The search for President Steinmeier's successor
Several names are being floated to replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's ceremonial head of state — including some that could be the first woman to hold the post.
Read our full report here.
Ping-pong vs. politics: Steinmeier takes on German Olympian Boll
After delivering his speech at Peking University, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities to play ping-pong with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll.
In the university sports hall, the two faced each other, accompanied by two Chinese participants — a referee and the university president. Right from the start, Steinmeier downplayed his chances, and subsequently lost 1–7.
Boll, who won silver at the Beijing Olympics in 2008, is the most successful German table tennis player of all time.
He won several Olympic medals, as well as titles in World Cups and World Championships during his storied career, which saw him ranked as the number 1 player in the world in 2003, 2011 and 2018.
To this day, Boll remains one of the best-known Germans in China, where ping-pong is unofficially considered the national sport.
Boll is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.
Steinmeier calls for fair trade in China during Bejiing visit
Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Thursday called on China to reduce economic imbalances between the two countries, as well as between China and Europe.
Steinmeier, who was speaking at the renowned Peking University, also urged China to work with Germany and other European nations to strengthen the international, rules-based order and "to advocate for peace and free global trade."
The German president, who holds a largely ceremonial role, spoke of his respect for China's rapid development in its economy, technology and politics, calling China a "defining world power."
But Steinmeier added, "With greatness and power comes great responsibility."
"We are not concerned about China's rise. We are watching how China rises," he said.
"We do not want to decouple from China; on the contrary, we want to structure trade in such a way that it continues to benefit both sides." This, he said, requires fair and uniform rules.
Steinmeier was referring to the high barriers European companies face when trying to operate in the Chinese market. Since China heavily subsidizes its exports to Europe, the European market comes under pressure too quickly.
This poses "the danger of one-sided vulnerability," Steinmeier said. Europeans cannot want this for their economy, just as "China does not want it for its economy."
What did Steinmeier say about China and the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East?
He also called on China to exert more influence on Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.
According to Steinmeier, China's interests are also at stake in this war, just as they are in the Middle East. As a major trading power, China also needs free sea lanes, intact supply chains, and a secure energy supply.
"The longer these conflicts persist, the weaker the global economy as a whole becomes — and with it, one of its largest economies: China," the president said.
Steinmeier addressed future issues in which China should take a particular interest: climate change and artificial intelligence. He appealed to his hosts, saying that when it comes to AI, "we should jointly establish international guidelines so that the technology remains under human control," he said.
On the final day of his state visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership and hold talks with, among others, President Xi Jinping.
Steinmeier is making his first visit to China in eight years, as he seeks to boost bilateral ties.
Friedrich Merz accuses North Korea of threatening Europe's freedom
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday said North Korea was threatening "freedom throughout Europe" by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Merz highlighted that Russia was supplying weapons to North Korea.
The chancellor said this arrangement therefore shows how "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects Korea's security."
North Korea has boosted its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pyongyang has provided Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. It has also, according to South Korean intelligence services, sent about 15,000 soldiers to fight alongside Russian forces.
In exchange, Russia provides financial backing, military technology and security guarantees to North Korea.
Before Merz's arrival on Thursday, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, according to the South Korean military.
At the start of his visit, Merz said he hoped that Korea would eventually be unified. The peninsula has been split along the 38th parallel since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953.
Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen their two nations' strategic and security ties, which includes joint military exercises and exchange of intelligence.
The chancellor is expected to conclude his trip to South Korea with a visit to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.
WATCH: Can Germany's pivot to Asia end its reliance on China?
Germany is looking for new partners in Asia. As Chancellor Friedrich Merz travels to Singapore, Japan and South Korea, Berlin is trying to reduce its economic dependence on China while adapting to a changing global order. But can countries in the Indo-Pacific, besides China, help Germany diversify its trade and security partnerships?
This week on Berlin Briefing, DW's Giulia Saudelli speaks with DW Business Reporter Steven Beardsley and DW Chief Political Correspondent Nina Haase, who is traveling with the chancellor.
They discuss Germany's push to "de-risk" from China, growing security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, and whether middle powers can work together to shape the future global order.
Germany, South Korea upgrade ties to 'enhanced strategic partnership'
Germany and South Korea on Thursday pledged to work together on the economy, energy and security and high-tech industries, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said.
The South Korean leader made the announcement after a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Seoul.
At a joint press conference, Lee told reporters that he had asked Merz for Germany's backing in securing favorable treatment for South Korea as part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act.
The two leaders also agreed to improve bilateral ties to an "enhanced strategic partnership," Lee said.
8-year-old girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German zoo
An eight-year-old girl sustained serious injuries after she was attacked by at least one wolf at a wildlife park in Brandenburg in east Germany.
The child was brought to hospital by a rescue helicopter on Wednesday.
Local officials said a zookeeper had helped prevent other children from being attacked.
Police are investigating how and why the attack occurred, which took place during a special program for children.
Police on Thursday said their investigation was centered on a staff member who was in the enclosure with the children, a spokeswoman said.
The Teltow-Fläming district administration said the incident happened before the wildlife park's regular opening hours as part of an "Animal Keeper Day" for children.
The administration also said the attack had taken place in the polar wolf enclosure.
"While the animals in the wildlife enclosure were being watered, the wolves kept there attacked a girl and seriously injured her," the district administration said.
The zookeeper's quick action prevented "further harm to two other girls" who were also at the scene, the district added.
The park will remain closed for the time being, officials said, as authorities launch a safety review at the wildlife park, which is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin.
Police are still probing the circumstances that led to the children being inside the enclosure.
The Johannismühle Wildlife Park said it was cooperating with authorities but could not provide further details due to the open investigation.
"We deeply regret the incident, and the affected family has our full support," the park said.
The wildlife park was closed until further notice "due to technical reasons," a sign at the entrance said on Thursday.
A wolf bit a woman in a busy shopping area in Hamburg this year, in what is thought to be the first such attack since wolves were reintroduced to the country in 1998.
German Chancellor Merz says he hopes for Korean reunification
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is visiting Seoul, said at the start of his visit that he hopes North and South Korea will eventually be reunited.
The Korean Peninsula has been divided into two states since the Korean War ended in 1953.
Merz pointed to his own country's division between West and East Germany for much of the second half of the 20th century.
"Korea and Germany are united by the painful experience of division," he wrote in the guest book during his meeting with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
"I also wish for the people of Korea what we are fortunate to experience in Germany: unity in freedom."
North Korea is a largely isolated dictatorship ruled by Kim Jong Un, while the South is a democracy that has close ties with the West.
The two Koreas technically remain at war since a truce ended hostilities.
Merz is set to visit the demilitarized zone (DMZ), which divides the two countries, on Friday.

Hong Kong leader John Lee apologised Thursday and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the city’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight.
The massive fire that broke out last November engulfed seven buildings in an apartment complex in a northern suburban district, killing 168 people and displacing thousands of others.
Many former residents of Wang Fuk Court have spent nearly a year waiting to see how the government will address accountability for the disaster that claimed their loved ones and their homes, which were then undergoing building maintenance work.

The committee's report said evidence pointed to a lighted cigarette being the cause of the fire, which started on the flat roof between two apartments on the first floor of Wang Cheong House. The committee heard substantial evidence that construction workers had smoked on site, including on the scaffolding, while a few cigarette butts and some partially burnt materials, such as cardboard boxes, were found on the flat roof.
Experts found the use of foam boards, non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets and canvases contributed to the fire’s spread, among other factors, the report said.
A majority of the deaths were caused by smoke inhalation rather than burns. The replacement of some staircase windows with movable aluminum composite panels or wooden boards for workers’ convenience allowed smoke to infiltrate residents’ escape routes. Opaque foam boards that covered the apartments’ windows blocked residents’ views, delaying evacuation. The shutdown of the fire alarm system was also a factor in the heavy death toll.

The committee said evidence clearly demonstrated that Will Power Architects Company, the consultant for the maintenance project, and Prestige Construction & Engineering Co., the main contractor on the project, had cut corners.
“There is no doubt that they are the main culprits responsible for the occurrence of the inferno and the high fatalities in the tragic incident,” the report said.

It said the evidence also revealed an array of registered contractors and building professionals who conducted no substantive work and were only asked to lend their names to “rubber-stamp” statutory forms in return for a fee. The private contractors and consultants had deceived the regulators, it said.

Financial Times refuses to correct Putin call ‘disinformation’ – media
The Financial Times has refused to correct an anonymously sourced article about a recent phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and the leaders of Norway and Finland, despite objections from both Nordic governments.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb spoke with Putin earlier this week, drawing criticism from some of Europe’s more Russia-hawkish politicians. Store has since demanded the FT retracts its reporting on teh conversation.
The British newspaper claimed that Putin spent significant time “lecturing” the Nordic leaders on “medieval Slavic history” and its relevance to the Ukraine conflict. Citing three anonymous sources described only as “familiar with the conversation,” the FT portrayed the Russian president as “fixated” on history.
Store’s government told Norwegian daily Verdens Gang (VG) that the characterization was inaccurate and that Finland had contacted the FT on behalf of both countries to challenge its account. Finnish media also covered the joint refutation, with the newspaper Helsingin Sanomat citing its own sources to dispute the British paper’s description of the call.
Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov said later in the day that the FT article is “some invented information, or rather disinformation” and that the Nordic leaders were correct to call out the publication.
The FT, however, rejected the request, telling VG that it stood by its reporting.
Its article, published on Tuesday, was written by three journalists.
One of them, American national Christopher Miller, previously worked for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, a US government-funded international broadcaster originally established with covert CIA funding to conduct anti-communist propaganda operations during the Cold War. Miller went to Ukraine in 2010 as a volunteer with the US Peace Corps.
His co-authors, Max Seddon and Henry Foy, head the FT’s bureaus in Moscow and Brussels, respectively.
Last week, the newspaper published a lengthy article by Seddon titled “The Putin whisperers,” recounting a dramatic but difficult-to-verify story of American and German nationals attempting to avert a “nuclear Armageddon” through backchannel diplomacy with Moscow.
Foy, notoriously broke a story in 2025 alleging that a plane carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had experienced suspected Russian GPS jamming. The FT journalist was himself aboard the aircraft when it landed in Bulgaria.
Key elements of the story were challenged almost immediately by flight-tracking service Flightradar24. Bulgarian authorities subsequently debunked the core claims relayed by FT.
Despite the discrepancies, the FT insisted it stood by its reporting. Foy did not respond to requests for comment from fellow journalists who questioned the account.

====================================================================================================

Can the world’s religions survive the existence of aliens?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
10:26:37 UTC
19:26:37 KST

One of the greatest mysteries of life is whether we are alone in the cosmos. The laws of probability suggest we aren’t, but despite centuries of searching, we have never seen any clear evidence of life beyond our planet. Still, the world’s religious leaders are already formulating how they would respond to extraterrestrial life—and some have more interesting approaches than others.
These discussions took center stage at a Capitol Hill gathering called the Disclosure Forum that took place earlier this year on a sunny day in June. A gaggle of lawmakers, retired military personnel, academics and businesspeople crowded into the Russell Senate Office Building’s Kennedy Caucus Room with me. As I listened, they spitballed ideas on how to handle what they believe are the increasingly likely chances of first contact with alien life.
Several speakers at the event stressed that a revelation that Earth has been visited by intelligent extraterrestrials would raise immediate questions about planetary defense. Others theorized hopefully that there could be enormous economic opportunities.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
There would also be enormous societal impacts: Carlos Eire, a historian and religious studies professor at Yale University, told event attendees that finding out humanity isn’t alone in the universe could shake us to our very souls—religious leaders would need to contain the fallout, he said.
Eire serves on the advisory board for the Disclosure Foundation, a nonprofit that organized the event and is dedicated to transparency around unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) and aliens.
“If disclosure reveals that there are nonhuman intelligences,” Eire told me later in an interview, “it remains to be seen who these intelligences really are and what they do, or what they’re hoping to accomplish, with human beings.”
“There won’t be a single reaction,” he adds. “For some people, it will confirm all sorts of things. For some people, it will demolish certain beliefs.”
Reactions could be split along religious lines—and some belief systems may be better equipped to deal with aliens than others, experts say.
For example, Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and other religions that originate in the Global East “have always conceived of the universe as vast, as going through many cycles of existence,” says Jeffery Long, a religious studies professor at Elizabethtown College.
Hinduism, Long tells me, has many deities, some of whom are described in religious texts as traveling through the cosmos on “vimanas”—flying chariots that could, to some, be read as akin to spaceships.
“If you start reading ancient Hindu literature and about different deities and then other species of intelligent beings, it’s very sci-fi,” Long says.
Meanwhile, the Abrahamic religions—the largest of which are Christianity, Judaism and Islam—are largely accepting of the idea that conscious life might exist that isn’t human, but none of these religions are monoliths.
The sheer scope of Christian belief systems makes attitudes to aliens among believers difficult to pin down, Eire says. Some theologians are optimistic: in his 2023 book Astrobiology and Christian Doctrine: Exploring the Implications of Life in the Universe, which received some NASA grant funding, Andrew Davison, now a divinity professor at the University of Oxford, wrote that he believes Christianity would be more “robust” in accepting alien life than some might think.
Certainly, leaders in the Roman Catholic Church have hinted at being open to extraterrestrials—the late Pope Francis once said he’d happily baptize an alien if they asked—Eire points out that within certain forms of Christianity, such as Protestantism, there can be incredible diversity in beliefs.
“There are Bible-thumping antievolutionists in parts of the U.S. that call themselves Evangelicals, and there are Evangelicals that are damn close to Catholics,” Eire says. “Predicting what Protestants will do is just impossible. The spectrum is so wide and contains so many different kinds of Christianity.”
The Abrahamic religion that may be the most open-minded about aliens, Long says, is also the oldest. Jewish scripture, while making no mention of spaceships, does include repeated mention of angels with a higher consciousness than that of humans. Even the most devout followers would perhaps be accepting of aliens because the religion’s dogma is “more about ethics and living your life here and now than it’s about ‘if you do this, you’ll go to heaven,’” Long says.
Academic explorations of how religious belief might influence attitudes to potential alien life are spotty at best, but that dearth of research could change. Aliens have become less taboo for scientists beyond astrobiology; the possibility of extraterrestrial life is no longer a punch line.
At the June Disclosure Forum, I heard more about how the White House is approaching the issue by setting up an advisory group on UAP, led by Harvard professor Avi Loeb. Loeb said at the event that he hopes the UAP Science Advisory Council will go on to publish scientific findings in reputable journals. That may include research in the field of exotheology—the study of religion and theological ideas related to alien life, Eire says.
“The academic community is readier now than it was 10 years ago for various reasons,” he says. Eire points to the Pentagon’s recent publishing of several tranches of previously classified UAP-related documents and media as a reason for this increased openness.
As to whether a kind of spiritual malaise or panic might result from aliens revealing themselves, that’s unclear. According to one recent poll, a third of Americans believe at least some UAP sightings were actual spacecraft; another poll found about half the country believes aliens probably exist. But drilling down more formally into specific religions is more murky: A 2021 poll revealed that among U.S. Christians, people who said religion was very important to them were less likely to believe that intelligent life might exist on other planets, as were those who attended religious services at least weekly. Belief in alien life also varied by denomination.
Much could also hinge on what kind of alien life is out there. While most people imagine intelligent beings that are in the best case friendly and curious like E.T., or, in the worst case, here to annihilate humanity, like in Independence Day, that’s not what most exobiologists are searching for. Instead they are on the lookout for distant exoplanets that exhibit signs of life closer to Earth’s microbes than humans.
“If there was amoebalike life on other planets, that would be a significant thing,” says Shoaib Malik, a science and religion lecturer at the University of Edinburgh and co-editor of the book Islamic Theology and Extraterrestrial Life: New Frontiers in Science and Religion. But while microscopic life would “definitely show proof of concept,” Malik adds, it wouldn’t fundamentally shake people’s faith.
“I think the real challenge really is if there’s something equivalent or something more advanced than the human being, particularly if you associate human uniqueness with rationality and spirituality,” Malik says.
Other scholars aren’t so sure. David Weintraub, a retired astronomer and author of Religions and Extraterrestrial Life: How Will We Deal With It?, says the difference between a microbe and, say, a primate is only a matter of degree.
“I think it would only make a difference to someone who does not believe in evolution, and that’s where we start drilling into the religious aspect of this,” he says. “If you accept evolution as a natural part of the way the universe works, then if you find microbial life of any sort, a possibility exists that that microbial life could evolve into intelligent life someday.”
Although there are no direct comparisons of similar evolutionary situations arising in modern history, says Paul Gutjahr, a professor at Indiana University Bloomington and author of the book Faith in Space: American Religious Belief in Extraterrestrial Life, there are many examples in human history in which religion and new knowledge of the cosmos has collided. When evolution was an emerging theory, for example, it presented a major challenge to Christianity.
“What you find is that people within that tradition find ways to adapt,” Gutjahr says. “It’s not like everybody becomes a friend of evolution, but there are there are very smart, capable and vocal people that start to think about if evolution is just the way that God worked his magic.”

Life magazine, the inspiration for &quot;The Secret Life of Walter Mitty,&quot; is being revived again
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:25:18 EET
19:25:18 KST

Life magazine, the inspiration for "The Secret Life of Walter Mitty," is being revived again
Kyiv • UNN
The iconic Life magazine will resume print publication next month as a quarterly with the backing of Karlie Kloss. The publication will also develop video, films, and events.
The iconic magazine Life, a chronicler of 20th-century America known for its visual storytelling, is being revived and will return next month in print as a quarterly, despite challenging business conditions. The New York Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
"Nearly two decades after the last edition ceased publication, Life magazine is coming back to life," the publication says.
The iconic publication, known for its red-bordered logo and commitment to visual storytelling, will begin publishing again next month as a quarterly print edition. It is returning to a fragmented media landscape that exists in a very different world from the height of the publication's popularity in the mid-20th century, before the internet, social media and artificial intelligence upended the business model of magazine publishing.
But Karlie Kloss, the model and entrepreneur who is supporting the project through her company Bedford Media, says the brand's legacy deserves to be revived and adapted for the 21st century. In addition to a website and social media presence, Life plans to expand its activities to include short films, documentaries and events.
"What made Life magazine special was its ability to bring the world closer together," Kloss said. "And it is our responsibility to preserve and protect that legacy."
The magazine's history
Life magazine was founded in 1936 by Henry Luce, the founder of Time and Fortune magazines. The cover of the first issue featured a black-and-white photograph by Margaret Bourke-White depicting the concrete Fort Peck Dam in Montana, United States, which was part of U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt's "New Deal." The issue sold out immediately.
Life magazine, which became a monument to the power of photojournalism, documented mid-20th-century American life, including World War II, the space race and the civil rights movement. It published the work of photographers such as Robert Capa, Alfred Eisenstaedt and Gordon Parks, resulting in such unforgettable images as the sailor kissing a woman in Times Square on V-J Day in 1945, as well as portraits of Marilyn Monroe and James Dean. The magazine also was the first to publish Ernest Hemingway's complete novella "The Old Man and the Sea" and commissioned Norman Mailer to cover the Apollo 11 crew's 1969 Moon landing.
The magazine's circulation peaked in the 1960s, exceeding eight million copies. But as television's popularity began to upend the magazine industry, Time Inc. discontinued the weekly magazine in 1972. Its life was revived in 1978, this time as a monthly magazine, and continued until 2000, when Time Inc. announced the end of regular publication.
The magazine played a role in the adventure film "The Secret Life of Walter Mitty" (2013), in which the protagonist - Walter Mitty (played by Ben Stiller) - works as a manager of the photo negative department at Life magazine.
