"No politician is irreplaceable" – Mieriņa delivers a significant message as Latvia's 14th Saeima concludes its work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:59:56 UTC
17:59:56 KST

As Latvia's 14th Saeima concluded its work on Thursday, Speaker of Parliament Daiga Mieriņa of the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) called on lawmakers to maintain respect for the Saeima and democratic values, stressing that the country is always greater than any political party, parliamentary group or parliamentary term.
In her final address to the outgoing parliament, Mieriņa acknowledged that the past four years had not been easy and had required considerable work, patience and compromise. Nevertheless, lawmakers had managed to maintain dialogue even when their opinions differed.
The Speaker recalled that during the 14th Saeima's term, parliament held 219 sittings, conducted 7,911 votes, adopted 1,060 laws and held 3,555 committee meetings.
She emphasised that the Saeima is a mirror of society, reflecting what Latvia has been and what it is today.
Mieriņa thanked lawmakers for their contributions to strengthening parliamentarism, democracy and the Latvian state, noting that every member of parliament had left their mark over the four years, whether through adopted legislation, initiatives or parliamentary debates.
She stressed that in a democracy, there are no small or large mandates, only the trust of voters granted for a limited period.
Addressing lawmakers who will continue serving in the next parliament, Mieriņa encouraged them to retain the ability to listen not only to their own voters but also to those who hold different views.
She also urged them to respect parliamentary traditions and the people on whose behalf decisions are made.
At the same time, Mieriņa noted that society is changing and a new generation is knocking on parliament's doors, bringing its own perspectives and expectations of politics.
She stressed that politicians must be willing to listen to this generation and make room for new representatives.
Mieriņa emphasised that no politician is irreplaceable, as members of parliament serve for a limited time, while Latvia, democracy and the people they serve remain.
Concluding her address, the Speaker wished lawmakers success in both their political careers and personal challenges.
She also quoted author and speaker Neale Donald Walsch, saying that a true leader is not someone who has the most followers, but someone who creates the most leaders.
Mieriņa ended her speech with the traditional Latvian wish: "May Latvia live as long as the sun!"

US reporters to monitor Russia-Ukraine truce in frontline town – Melania Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:59:04 UTC
17:59:04 KST

US reporters to monitor Russia-Ukraine truce in frontline town – Melania Trump
American journalists will observe a humanitarian mission under a Russia-Ukraine truce in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Kherson Region, Russia, US First Lady Melania Trump has said. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has confirmed that the reporters are expected there, and that demining operations are already underway.
Alyoshki, located on the left bank of the Dnieper River, was largely cut off from essential supplies and basic services for months under a Ukrainian siege, with drone attacks and remotely laid mines hampering aid deliveries and evacuation efforts from a town where an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 civilians remained.
Russian Foreign Ministry envoy Rodion Miroshnik described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods,” accusing Ukraine of obstructing humanitarian efforts.
However, after US mediation spearheaded by the Slovenian-born US first lady, Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the area starting October 27 to allow humanitarian assistance to flow in and evacuations to proceed. As of Thursday, both Russian and Ukrainian officials reported no truce violations. The pause is scheduled to last until Sunday.
Writing on X on Wednesday, Trump said four American journalists from conservative US outlet Newsmax will arrive in Alyoshki and accompany Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian leaders. “Serving as neutral observers, they will independently record and permanently document this historic humanitarian mission,” she said.
Dmitriev confirmed that Newsmax reporters will be there, adding: “Humanity and peace must prevail.”
Speaking to reporters before departing to Alyoshki, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said other foreign journalists are also expected to arrive, without providing further details.
Both Trump and Lantratova confirmed that Russia and Ukraine have begun clearing mines to secure aid routes. “It is now crucial to make the roads safe so that people can leave the town,” Lantratova said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said on Thursday that most Ukrainian mines found near Alyoshki were scattered by drones, and that they are predominantly Western-made. It also released a video showing a large-scale demining effort involving remotely-controlled robots.
The Alyoshki crisis was discussed during an October 9 phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, the leaders agreed that Russia’s human rights commissioner would maintain direct contact with Melania Trump’s office. US envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently met with Putin in St. Petersburg last week to discuss proposals for ending the Ukraine conflict.

Flora U-19s draw 2-2 with 9-man Chelsea in UEFA Youth League
Tallinn FC Flora's U-19 side drew 2:2 at home with English Premier League giants Chelsea's youth team Wednesday.
The game was the first leg of the UEFA Youth League second qualifying round, played at the A. Le Coq Arena in Tallinn.
After a sending-off, the visitors were down to 10 men early on in the second half, falling to nine players shortly before full-time after a second sending-off, but held on for the draw
Midfielder Sander Alamaa put Flora ahead in the fourth minute, but Chelsea striker Jashayde Greenwood equalized a quarter of an hour later and then Chizaram Ezenwata put the visitors in front shortly before half-time. Flora's equalizer came on 60 minutes, when Alamaa converted a penalty won by left-back Karel Isok.
"Before the game we said Chelsea are vulnerable on the counter-attack. For the first goal I got a good run at the center-back and took my chance. It was a good start to the game. For the second goal I'm not sure it was a penalty, but at least it was given our way. I saw the goalkeeper dive one way and just put the ball calmly in the other corner," Alamaa told ERR after the match.
Chelsea finished with nine men: center-back Dante Waite was sent off on 55 minutes and midfielder Isaac Silva collected a second yellow on 89.
"In some ways you could feel the difference in level with players from a Premier League club's academy. They were technically very high-quality players. In midfield their players played some unbelievable passes. But if you go into duels the way we did today, we can take down anyone," Alamaa added.
The second leg takes place in London next Wednesday, November 4.

Spain, Portugal work with Kiev to develop weapons for strikes against Russia — politician
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:52:07 UTC
17:52:07 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The authorities in Spain and Portugal, together with Kiev, are working to develop weapons for strikes against Russia, while their own citizens are grappling with a housing and economic crisis, Viktor Medvedchuk, head of the Other Ukraine movement and former leader of the Opposition Platform - For Life party banned in Ukraine, said.
"While the two countries on the Iberian Peninsula are trying to cope with a housing crisis and rising costs of living, their governments are engaging in increasingly extensive military cooperation with Ukraine. Behind the familiar phrase ‘support for Ukraine’ lies a far more specific reality: Spanish and Portuguese companies, together with Ukrainian manufacturers, are launching projects in the fields of missile technology, strike drones, guidance systems, and other weapons designed to strike Russia," he wrote in an article posted on the movement’s website.
According to the politician, Spain's military-industrial cooperation with Ukraine primarily concerns missile technology and long-range drones. "Portugal also emphasizes long-range drones, though in addition to aerial systems, this includes sea-based unmanned vessels," he added.
Companies cooperating with Ukrainian firms include Tekever UAS, S.A., a Portuguese drone manufacturer whose AR3 and AR5 systems have been used by the Ukrainian armed forces since 2022, as well as the Spanish companies Sener Aeroespacial, S.A. and Escribano Mechanical and Engineering, S.L.U., and others.
"As a result, the political choices made by Madrid and Lisbon seem highly contradictory. On the one hand, there is condemnation of military actions in the Persian Gulf. On the other hand, these countries are being drawn into the war in Ukraine, which requires funding and cuts to social service budgets. While Spaniards are being forced to live in tents due to the housing crisis, and Portuguese authorities acknowledge the lack of affordable housing as one of the most pressing social problems, the governments of both countries are at the same time allocating state resources, industrial capacity, and technological expertise toward expanding arms production for Ukraine," he concluded.

Purges at the Pentagon: Hegseth fires top military planner

Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed from his position as director of J5 without an immediate replacement. The dismissal came amid possible U.S. strikes on Iran.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired the Pentagon’s top military planner. A Pentagon representative said this on October 28, UNN reports, citing AP.
Details
This is the latest in a series of generals being dismissed, and it comes even as U.S. President Donald Trump is considering resuming strikes on Iran in the eight-month war.
U.S. Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed as head of the Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff. He became the second general dismissed from the position, known in military circles as "J5," under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee, was forced to retire in October last year.
A Pentagon representative said there was no immediate replacement for Sylvia and that no reason for his dismissal had been provided.
A representative of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff said: "The Chairman, Joint Staff and Joint Force express their deep gratitude to Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia and his family for 32 years of distinguished service to our country" and "wish him and his family all the best."
Typically, the J5 director and his staff are responsible for developing and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the U.S. president. Sylvia’s dismissal came amid Trump’s repeated statements about launching new military operations against Iran.
Trump vowed to "finish what was started" in Iran after the war with Israel began eight months ago and said new strikes could take place after next week’s midterm elections.
According to two diplomats familiar with the situation, U.S. officials warned a number of Middle Eastern countries and regional allies that they needed to be prepared for the possible resumption of hostilities after Tuesday’s election, as well as possible retaliatory measures by Iran. They said Trump had not yet made a final decision on new strikes.
A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are heading to the region.

Türkiye hosts 13th OTS summit to advance Turkic unity and cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:33:53 UTC
17:33:53 KST

Türkiye is hosting the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara to further “unity in language, thought, and deed” among its member states.
The summit kicked off on Thursday with the Meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the OTS.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hosted the meeting, according to diplomatic sources.
Foreign ministers of the OTS posed for a family photo ahead of the meeting.
The two-day summit is hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan under the theme Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.
Established in 2009, the OTS, formerly known as the Turkic Council, adopted its current name during its eighth summit held in the Turkish metropolis Istanbul in 2021.
While Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are members, Turkmenistan, Hungary, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, and the Economic Cooperation Organization hold observer status.
The organisation said on October 24 that the summit will bring together the heads of state of its member states, as well as high-level representatives from observer states and its secretary general, to “discuss the current state and future prospects of cooperation within the Organization,” among other issues.
It said in a statement that the heads of state are expected to review the progress achieved across the OTS’ priority areas, and that particular emphasis will be placed on “further strengthening unity and solidarity” among the Turkic states and advancing cooperation under the Turkic World Vision 2040.
It added that the summit will also mark Türkiye’s assumption of the OTS’ chairmanship from Azerbaijan, and is expected to address the appointment of a new secretary general and the organisation’s strategic priorities “for the forthcoming period.”
“The Heads of State are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, together with a number of decisions and documents aimed at deepening cooperation and further strengthening the institutional framework of the OTS,” it added.
The leaders’ summit will be held on Friday.
‘Unity in deed’
Turan Gafarli, a non-resident fellow at the Baku-based Topchubashov Center, defined support among Turkic states and bolstering their political solidarity as the significant aspect of the Ankara summit.
Noting that they are living through a period in which the world faces “increasing uncertainty,” Gafarli told Anadolu that the Turkic world is evolving into a political structure that is “developing the capacity to act in unison in the face of international developments.”
“Naturally, this is a long-term process. Yet, the true meaning of brotherhood is not just coming together during good times, but standing by one another during difficult ones,” he said, noting his belief that the summit in Türkiye will further solidify the “atmosphere of trust built to date.”
Gafarli highlighted the term of unity used in the summit’s theme as “highly significant,” as well as expressed belief that the summit will give momentum to developments particularly in the realms of economic relations, transport corridors, and political coordination.
He stated the growing strategic importance of the Middle Corridor presented a “historic opportunity” for the Turkic states to become more closely interconnected economically, but that this requires a number of steps, including bolstering trade between member states.
“Furthermore, it is essential that the Turkic states engage in closer consultation on international issues and advocate more robustly for their shared interests,” he said, adding he believes Türkiye’s chairmanship could bring fresh dynamism in this context.
Meanwhile, Shairbek Dzhuraev, the president of the Crossroads Central Asia research institute based in Bishkek, shared the belief that tangible progress has been observed most evidently in the economic sphere, underlining transport and transit in particular.
“The development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route depends on the harmonisation of tariffs and the simplification of customs procedures. In this context, results can be measured by the time and cost involved in transporting goods,” Dzhuraev said.
Dzhuraev further underlined digitalisation as a second promising area, which he defined as the focus of the organisation’s informal summit held in Turkistan in southern Kazakhstan in May.
“The most substantial outcome of the Ankara summit would be the establishment of concrete timelines and mechanisms for implementing decisions already reached – particularly those concerning transport and trade,” he stated.
As part of the OTS Ankara summit, sports is also an area where unity is expected to be shown “in deed.”
During a news conference in Ankara ahead of the summit, Kursad Zorlu, the ruling Justice and Development (AK) Party's deputy chair in charge of relations with Turkic states, said the event includes plans for players from Turkic states to be classified as domestic rather than foreign in one another’s leagues, saying the initiative would foster a football ecosystem across the Turkic world.

Thousands of years of knowledge, struggle shaped India as cultural nation: Gajendra Singh Shekhawat

Sekhawat was addressing a gathering at the launch of the book 'Timeless India: Protection & Revival of Indian Cultural Identity under the Leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi'
NEW DELHI: Union Culture Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat on Wednesday said India is not merely an entity confined within geographical boundaries but a cultural nation shaped by thousands of years of continuity, knowledge, struggle and experience.Shekhawat was addressing a gathering at the launch of the book 'Timeless India: Protection & Revival of Indian Cultural Identity under the Leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi' at the Dharohar Bhawan, the headquarters of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), which hosted the event along with the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA).The book has been published by IGNCA and Subhi Publications and edited by former Rajya Sabha member Tarun Vijay.
"India is not merely an entity confined within geographical boundaries, but a cultural nation shaped by thousands of years of continuity, knowledge, spiritual practice, struggle and experience. India's civilisation and cultural consciousness have flowed uninterrupted through centuries," Shekhawat said."India has established connections with civilisations across the world through dialogue and cultural exchange.
Its knowledge traditions, architectural heritage and cultural legacy have attracted many countries around the world," he added.During the colonial rule, "efforts were made to weaken Indians' sense of pride" in their civilisation, culture and traditions. This also influenced the way Indians viewed their own knowledge traditions and cultural ideals, an IGNCA statement quoted the minister as saying."The distinctive feature of Indian civilisation is its ability to draw inspiration from the past while moving towards the future. Ideals represented by Lord Ram and Lord Krishna, along with the traditions of sages, thinkers and seekers of knowledge, remain important foundations for India's cultural consciousness," he said.The book explores the role of monuments in preserving and revitalising India's cultural identity, alongside the discourse surrounding the nation's historical memory.It gives particular importance to monument preservation and the idea of "decolonising the nation's memory", highlighting the need to understand India's cultural heritage through its "own historical experiences, traditions and cultural outlook", the statement said.Union Minister of State Jitendra Singh, former Rajya Sabha member and ex-president of the Indian Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR), Vinay Sahasrabuddhe, were present on the occasion, among others.In a separate statement, the tourism ministry said the Indian Culinary Institute (ICI) on Wednesday signed an MoU with the Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), providing for the recognition of ICI's BBA and MBA programmes by the JNU, enabling the university to award degrees to students completing these courses at ICI.
The MoU was signed by JNU V-C Santishree Dhulipudi Pandit and Gyan Bhushan, Director, ICI, in the presence of Shekhawat and Tourism Secretary Bhuvnesh Kumar.The recognition of ICI's BBA and MBA programmes by JNU, commencing from the next academic year, is expected to enhance academic and professional opportunities for the students, the statement said.

SEOUL, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's tech giant Samsung Electronics set records in the third-quarter operating profit and revenue, powered by an explosive performance in its semiconductor business, the company said Thursday.
Its operating profit skyrocketed 783.1 percent from a year earlier to hit an all-time high of 107.4 trillion won (about 80.4 billion U.S. dollars) in the July-September quarter, beating market expectations of about 105.7 trillion won.

It marked another record-breaking performance on surging demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
The company said it managed its product mix with a focus on AI products while scaling up sales of high-bandwidth memory 4 (HBM4), expecting industry-wide competition for AI leadership to boost AI infrastructure investments in the fourth quarter.
Samsung forecasts that AI infrastructure capital expenditure will reach a historic level in 2027 amid an expanding AI ecosystem, predicting that AI-driven demand will far exceed the industry supply compared to 2026. ■

Singapore factory, domestic supply prices rise in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:42:30 CST
16:42:30 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's manufactured product prices and domestic supply prices rose in September, driven by higher oil prices and costs of electrical machinery apparatus, including electronic integrated circuits, the Department of Statistics said on Thursday.
The Singapore Manufactured Products Price Index (SMPPI) increased 5.3 percent month on month, accelerating from 4.4 percent in August, marking its third consecutive monthly gain. The oil index rose 7.9 percent, while the non-oil index increased 4.8 percent.
The SMPPI surged 47.5 percent year on year, up from 40.1 percent in August. The oil index climbed 58.9 percent, while the non-oil index rose 45.8 percent.
The Domestic Supply Price Index (DSPI) increased 7.3 percent month on month, compared with 4.1 percent in August. Its oil index rose 15.9 percent, while the non-oil index gained 4.1 percent.
On a year-on-year basis, the DSPI jumped 48 percent, up from 38.8 percent in August. The oil index surged 78.9 percent, while the non-oil index increased 38.2 percent.
The increases in both indices' oil components were mainly due to higher prices of petroleum and petroleum products, while gains in their non-oil components were largely driven by higher prices of electrical machinery apparatus, the data showed. ■

Font size
None of the 18 crew members - 14 Filipinos and 4 Ukrainians - aboard the container ship CONTSHIP JET, which was struck by maritime drones in the Black Sea around noon yesterday, was injured. They arrived at Varna’s Sea Station last night, and the ship’s owner had already arranged hotel accommodation for them through his local agent. The crew will undergo medical examinations.
Varna Regional Governor Mario Smarkov described the successful rescue operation as “the most wonderful news”, but declined to comment on whether any containers had fallen from the vessel or whether there was a risk to the environment until the relevant authorities had carried out the necessary inspections.
Mario Smarkov
PHOTO Rumen Sarandev
Later, Bulgarian Navy Commander Rear Admiral Kiril Mihaylov announced that the vessel had been carrying 421 containers, 20 of which had fallen overboard and were drifting at sea. Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:10:08 UTC
16:10:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign said Thursday that cyberattacks using overseas IP addresses had breached a campaign server and flooded a platform with more than 70,000 fake sign-ups.
CNA reported that Shen’s campaign office said hackers targeted several campaign websites starting last Friday. The attackers exploited a security flaw to gain control of a server, created fake administrator accounts, and installed software to access the system remotely.
The hackers then tried to obtain access to Shen’s main campaign website but failed. The campaign said the website ran on a separate server and its login credentials were not stored on the compromised server.
The campaign team discovered the breach early Wednesday and completed repairs that evening. It removed the malicious software, deleted fake accounts, changed passwords and security keys, and tightened server access, per CTS News.
The second attack targeted a new platform where supporters could sign up for sections of campaign vehicle routes. Within an hour of its launch Wednesday evening, automated programs using overseas IP addresses flooded the platform with more than 70,000 fake sign-ups, per Tai Sounds.
The campaign said it quickly required users to log in before signing up. The change blocked the automated submissions and allowed the platform to resume normal operations.
Shen said cybersecurity had always been a priority for his campaign. His office said all affected websites were operating normally and that it would continue to guard against further attacks.

It focuses on three key areas: real-time intelligence sharing, personnel training, and joint investigations, according to CNA.
Lee added that despite Taiwan’s unique international circumstances and its inability to participate in Interpol, it continues to maintain direct contact with international law enforcement agencies through bilateral and multilateral channels.
NPA International Affairs Division Director Lin Miao-ling (林妙齡) stressed that crime knows no borders, and law enforcement agencies should be able to cooperate without restrictions, CNA reported. Otherwise, they will always be one step behind criminals, she said.
The international community needs Taiwan’s expertise and contributions, Lin added.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Digital Affairs Minister Audrey Tang (唐鳳) said AI can help people bridge political divides and have a greater say in government decisions, the Financial Times reported Wednesday.
Speaking with Financial Times Innovation Editor John Thornhill, Tang explained how Taiwan uses technology to bring people with opposing views together. Digital platforms, she said, help officials find ideas with broad public support and turn them into policy.
Tang pointed to the country’s efforts to fight AI-generated investment scams in 2024. Fake videos featuring public figures, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳), had spread online to promote fraudulent investments.
As digital affairs minister, Tang sent text messages to 200,000 randomly selected phone numbers to seek public input. Officials then randomly selected 447 people to discuss solutions in small online groups, where AI helped summarize ideas and find areas of agreement.
Participants called for stronger checks on online advertisers and rules holding platforms responsible for losses from scam ads. Tang said more than 85% of participants supported the proposals, which helped shape laws passed within months.
Tang cited official figures showing that deepfake investment scam ads fell by more than 94% in 2025. She argued that the country had shown how public input could help fight online fraud without limiting free speech.
Tang also recalled the 2014 Sunflower Movement, a student-led protest against a proposed trade deal with China that led to the occupation of the legislature. Protesters feared the agreement would give Beijing more influence over the country, and Tang said public discussions helped people develop common proposals despite their differences.
Taiwan used a similar approach in 2015 to address disputes between taxi drivers and Uber over the ride-hailing firm’s services. Online discussions helped both sides reach agreement on proposed rules, offering an early example of how technology could help resolve disputes.
Tang said the country’s approach has drawn interest abroad, and she has visited 29 countries over the past two years to share its experience. In Germany, she has worked on a project that uses AI to help people find shared solutions to problems with transport and public services.
Tang said government action alone was not enough to make public participation work. She urged journalists, educators, and citizens to help turn shared ideas into practical solutions.

U.S. Navy pays $23 million to shield warship power grids from hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:01:11 UTC
16:01:11 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Integer Technologies a $23.1 million contract to research zero trust cybersecurity for shipboard power systems.
- Integer will work with Florida State University’s Center for Advanced Power Systems, with research running through October 2030.
The U.S. Navy has awarded South Carolina-based Integer Technologies a $23.1 million contract to research how zero trust cybersecurity can protect the electrical power systems that run its warships, without slowing the split-second controls those systems depend on.
The Office of Naval Research awarded the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract for a program called Threat Resilient Integrated Defense for Enhanced Naval Technologies, or TRIDENT, the Department of War announced in its daily contract list this week. Integer is teaming with Florida State University and its Center for Advanced Power Systems, and work will take place in Columbia, South Carolina, through October 2030. The award is a science and technology effort, meaning it funds research and prototyping, and it does not put a new cybersecurity system on any ship.
The contract calls for investigations into “threat-informed” zero trust architecture frameworks tailored to the cyber-physical security needs of shipboard power systems. Zero trust is a security model that drops the old assumption that anything already inside a network can be trusted. Every user, device and command has to prove it is legitimate each time it asks for access. The Navy wants an architecture that lets a ship monitor the cyber and physical state of its power plant, change its defensive posture as threats change, and keep fighting through an attack while the electrical system keeps performing.
The funding structure is more complex than the headline figure. The contract has a 36-month base period and a 36-month option that would begin 12 months after award and run alongside the base, which is why the whole effort ends about four years from now. The Navy obligated $10.1 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds at award, enough to pay for the full base period, leaving about $13 million tied to the option. Navy research money is available for two years, so the fiscal 2026 funds expire at the end of fiscal 2027, the government’s current budget year. ONR bought the work through its long-range broad agency announcement for Navy and Marine Corps science and technology, an open solicitation that accepts proposals year-round, so the Navy could not say how many bids it received.
The problem TRIDENT is meant to study comes from how warship power has changed. Older surface combatants such as the Arleigh Burke-class destroyers use gas turbines geared directly to the propeller shafts, with separate, smaller generators for electricity. The three Zumwalt-class destroyers were the first U.S. Navy surface combatants built around an integrated power system that generates electricity for both propulsion and weapons. Two Rolls-Royce MT30 main turbine generators and two smaller auxiliary generators produce about 78 megawatts, which feeds the electric motors that turn the shafts and a shipwide grid for sensors, combat systems and hotel loads. The Navy’s planned DDG(X) next-generation destroyer is designed to use a similar integrated power system.
That architecture lets a ship shift power between propulsion and weapons on demand, which matters as electrical loads grow. L3Harris, which builds power distribution equipment for Virginia-class submarines, said this month that advanced radars, directed energy weapons and next-generation propulsion will place extraordinary demands on shipboard power. Laser weapons such as the 60-kilowatt-class HELIOS installed on USS Preble (DDG 88) in 2022 draw their “ammunition” straight from the ship’s electrical system.
It also means a single, software-managed grid now sits underneath nearly everything a warship does. Power is controlled by networked switchboards, power converters, protective relays and a machinery control system that decides how to route electricity and how to isolate a fault before it spreads. Those are operational technology systems: computers whose job is to move physical equipment. If an attacker could send false commands or corrupt the data those controllers rely on, the consequences would be physical, from tripping generators to cutting power to weapons or radars in combat.
The contract identifies two constraints that make zero trust hard to apply aboard ship. The first is latency. Integrated power systems rely on very fast control loops to protect equipment and keep the grid stable, and enterprise zero trust tools typically add checks, such as authentication, encryption and traffic inspection, that take time. A security layer that delays a protective trip or a power transfer by even a short interval could cause the damage it was meant to prevent. The second is the mix of legacy and modern equipment. Ships stay in service for decades and are upgraded in pieces, so a single power plant can contain older controllers that were never designed to authenticate commands alongside newer networked devices. The contract does not say which ship classes or systems the research will model.
Florida State’s Center for Advanced Power Systems is one of the Navy’s main university laboratories for electric ship research. Established in 2000 in Tallahassee, the center operates one of the largest real-time digital power system simulators along with 5-megawatt AC and DC test beds for power hardware-in-the-loop testing, in which real equipment is connected to a simulated ship grid so engineers can stress it under realistic conditions. Cybersecurity for power systems is one of its listed research areas, and it leads the Navy-funded Electric Ship Research and Development Consortium of universities. In June, Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the center an $88 million contract for modeling, simulation and testing of advanced shipboard electrical power and energy systems through 2031.
Integer Technologies is a small business founded in Columbia in 2021 by Duke Hartman and Josh Knight. It has built a portfolio of Navy research work focused on cyber-physical systems, often in partnership with universities. In September, ONR exercised a $10.2 million option on a separate Integer contract with Louisiana State University to develop a cyber-physical resilience framework for Navy maritime platforms, with work running through March 2030. The company was also among more than two dozen firms placed on the Navy’s $982 million multiple-award contract for its Unmanned Surface Vehicle Family of Systems in 2024.
The threat the Navy is preparing for has moved from theory to documented activity on land. In a February 2024 advisory, CISA, the National Security Agency and the FBI assessed with high confidence that Chinese state-sponsored hackers known as Volt Typhoon were pre-positioning themselves on IT networks to enable movement into operational technology and disrupt critical infrastructure in a crisis. The agencies said the group had compromised organizations in the continental United States and its territories, including Guam, a key hub for U.S. forces in the Pacific, and had kept access in some networks for at least five years.
Earlier cases showed what attacks on control systems can do. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, sabotaged Iranian uranium enrichment centrifuges by manipulating their industrial controllers while showing operators normal readings. In December 2015, a cyberattack on Ukrainian power distribution companies cut electricity to roughly 225,000 customers, the first publicly confirmed blackout caused by hackers. Both targeted fixed infrastructure on land, and a warship differs in important ways: its networks are smaller and more tightly controlled, and it often operates with limited outside connectivity. Ships still connect to shore networks in port and receive software and hardware updates from contractors during maintenance, which gives an attacker possible ways in.
The Department of the Navy has led the military services in applying the Pentagon’s 2022 zero trust strategy to enterprise IT, and its officials said in early 2025 that they were preparing zero trust standards for operational technology, the category that includes ship machinery and weapons platforms. TRIDENT is aimed at that harder category, where a security tool has to work within the timing and reliability limits of physical equipment.

CEO of one of Australia's top cultural events becomes French knight

Biennale of Sydney CEO Barbara Moore appointed Chevalier of Ordre des Arts et des Lettres
The CEO of the Biennale of Sydney, Barbara Moore, has been appointed Chevalier of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, or a knight of the French Order of Arts and Letters.
"I'm pretty shocked by it," she told ABC Arts, ahead of the ceremony at Sydney Town Hall on October 29.
"It's a big deal and admittedly I have a bit of impostor syndrome. Like, I'm still young!
"But these endorsements mean a lot … they say we're doing something that's contributing in a positive way."
Moore, who moved to Australia from Canada in 2007, has been CEO of the festival since 2019.
The French Order of Arts and Letters is one of the country's highest cultural honours, awarded to someone for their contribution to arts and culture in France and around the world.
Past recipients include musicians Nick Cave and Kylie Minogue, actor Cate Blanchett, artist Tony Albert, the late film critic David Stratton, and former Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron.
"I think the point of these things is to encourage relationships and bonding," Moore said.
"I'm an untrained diplomat, where I'm just trying to bring people together and break down barriers.
"When the world is so used to shouting at each other and we're losing the art of listening, art helps us connect and learn from each other."
It is a poignant statement in a year when the biennale, curated by Hoor Al Qasimi, was subjected to community, commercial and political pressures, including the withdrawal of sponsors and accusations of antisemitism.
Asked how arts festivals like the biennale should navigate a charged political climate, Moore offered plainly: "Boldly, like warriors."
She continued: "If we operate through fear, if we're part of burning books and over-censoring, we have a problem.
"People are going to have feelings and opinions, especially in divisive times. But that doesn't mean we cancel organisations and we shut projects down.
"We have to remember what we're there for and that's to bring people together."
Taking Australian arts and culture abroad
Earlier this month, Moore was in France for the contemporary art fair Art Basel Paris, which was cut short in response to education and cost-of-living rallies that escalated into rioting.
She was there to take a group of biennale patrons to see a new exhibition by Ghanian artist Ibrahim Mahama. His work featured in the 2020 Biennale of Sydney, which was forced to close after 10 days by the COVID-19 pandemic.
His exhibition opened at the Cartier Foundation gallery, which partners with the biennale to platform First Nations artists and curators.
The partnership has inspired another celebration of Australian artists on the world stage, with Australia announced as guest of honour at next year's Art Paris contemporary art fair.
Art Paris director Guillaume Piens saw the large-scale work of First Nations artists including Kaylene Whiskey and Dylan Mooney at the newly reopened White Bay Power Station during the 2024 Biennale of Sydney.
"He'd never seen anything like that before, and he thought he wanted to bring First Nations artists to the fair," Moore said.
What that means for the place of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art on the world stage, Moore suggests, is more than its popularity with collectors.
"It's a reckoning," she said. "[People are asking:] 'How do we make the world a better place? How do we get through these tumultuous times?'
"Maybe looking at the oldest continuous living culture could be a good start, to think about how to exist on this planet and where the humanity is.
"Maybe there's some things we forgot we need to remember again."
The next Biennale of Sydney is scheduled to start on March 21, 2028, and will be led by Singaporean curator Low Kee Hong.

Afghanistan opium production jumps fivefold as farmers find ways round Taliban ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:45:16 UTC
15:45:16 KST

Afghanistan opium production jumps fivefold as farmers find ways round Taliban ban
Opium production in Afghanistan has risen fivefold in a year. According to a UN survey released on Thursday, it’s the first significant increase since the Taliban banned poppy cultivation in 2022.
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) found that the area planted with opium poppy grew by 330 per cent, to more than 43,000 hectares, up from about 10,000 hectares in 2025.
Estimated production rose by 400 per cent, from about 300 tonnes to just under 1,500 tonnes.
Both figures remain well below levels before the ban, when some 232,000 hectares were under cultivation.
For decades, Afghanistan was the world’s biggest source of illicit opium. Before the ban, it accounted for around 80 per cent of global supply.
The Taliban seized power in August 2021. In April 2022, they outlawed poppy cultivation and all narcotics, citing religious grounds.
Hidden in cereal fields
The de facto authorities say they eradicated 22,000 hectares of poppy this year. But UNODC said many farmers appear to have adapted to evade enforcement. Some are hiding small plots within cereal fields or inside walled compounds. Others are planting and harvesting at staggered intervals to avoid detection.
“The fourfold increase in opium poppy cultivation shows the difficulty in sustaining decreases in illicit opium cultivation when poor farmers have no alternatives to feed their families,” said UNODC Executive Director Monica Juma.
She urged the de facto authorities and the international community to work together to support farming communities, by investing in livelihoods, farm infrastructure and access to markets.
Shift to the northeast
Cultivation spread to 16 of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces, five more than last year. Three in every four hectares were in the northeast, now firmly the country’s main growing area. Before the ban, most poppy was grown in the southwest.
Prices dipped from $570 a kilogramme last year to $500 but remain far above pre-ban levels of under $100. UNODC said large regional price differences may encourage trafficking from the northeast to the southwest.
Stockpiles running low
The survey said traffickers in the region appear to have relied on opium stockpiles to keep supplies moving since the ban.
But recent seizure data suggest those stocks are running down. The 2026 World Drug Report also found early signs that heroin supplies in Europe are falling.
With demand holding up and prices high, shrinking supplies could push cultivation in Afghanistan higher still.
“International cooperation is needed to investigate and dismantle transnational drug trafficking networks both in Afghanistan and the rest of the world,” Ms. Juma said.
UNODC said continued monitoring would show whether this year’s jump is temporary or the start of a resurgence in opium and heroin production.

From Atoms to Universes: The Architecture of Everything in the Age of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

AI has become a consumer product faster than it has become a discipline. Each week brings new models and more information than anyone can absorb, and the easy response is uncritical consumption. Architecture needs a different strategy, built on criticism and method. AI is now acquiring spatial intelligence, the capacity to understand how physical space behaves, and architects can test a project against its environment while they design it. Used with judgment, AI can bring architects closer to nature and its complexity, and make them better builders. We simulate the world to learn how to inhabit it.
Tool as designer of human
How many times will the present generation have to revolutionize their daily way of being? Historically humanity has experienced drastic reprogramming of a lifestyle once every few centuries. With the industrial revolution it dropped down to once every few generations. AI has compressed this interval in ways we're still bound to find out.
As Jean-François Lyotard wrote, "technology wasn't invented by us humans. Rather the other way around." In a time when humans are being designed by their tools faster than ever, how are we supposed to program our own evolution in order to reach a symbiosis between natural intelligence and the artificial? What are the means of acquiring the necessary skills to allow AI to shape us for the better?
Artificial intelligence is an opportunity to enhance once again the possibilities at hand of every individual. From the first books that allowed broad education, to accessibility to infinite information through the internet, to access to navigation and creation through AI.
Language models to World models
Large language models learned the world through its descriptions. They merely predict text from statistical regularities. They mimic human speech and thought based on large databases and simple probability. World models, on the other hand, are systems that learn how an environment behaves, its physical rules, spatial dynamics, causal states and functional structures, so that they can predict new behaviors. Fei-Fei Li calls current LLMs "wordsmiths in the dark", eloquent about a three-dimensional world they have never had to move through, and argues that spatial intelligence is the field's next frontier. For architecture the difference is decisive. A model of text cannot anticipate how physical and social reality responds to a project, while a model of space enables simulating scenarios, testing how a project responds to gravity, wind, sunlight, wear and human use. Thermal diffusion, moisture absorption, pollutant dispersion and the flow of people become feedback the project responds to, and design proceeds through interaction with these dynamics instead of imposing a form on them.
Simulation can inform a decision. It cannot take over the responsibility of making it. We need now more than ever professionals with criteria, who use AI responsibly as an analytical tool, rather than a mere burst of productivity. The architect becomes less an author of forms and more a designer of knowledge systems, measured by the capacity to anticipate consequences in a dense and often uncertain reality. What remains human is the process.
Mindhub for Intelligent Artificial Worlds
Spatial AI is a call for hybrid profiles that cross design with computational engineering and materials science. The Mindhub for Intelligent Artificial Worlds (MIAWS), at ETSAM, Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, is a digital hub for the whole AEC sector built around that change. It combines original research with a worldwide network of practitioners and institutions, and its Foundations program runs online across ten modules that carry one project from AI modeling and simulation to data visualization and integration. The aim is to keep pace with the technology without handing over judgment. We invite you to get to know the program and take part in the change.

North Korea launches missile salvo toward the Sea of Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:42:45 UTC
15:42:45 KST

- North Korea launched suspected ballistic missiles at about 12:36 p.m. on Oct. 29, Japan said, with nothing reaching its territory or exclusive economic zone.
- South Korea said around 10 short-range ballistic missiles were fired from the Wonsan area, North Korea’s first ballistic launch in 17 days.
North Korea launched what may have been a ballistic missile at about 12:36 p.m. local time on Oct. 29, and it is presumed to have fallen near the east coast of the Korean Peninsula without reaching Japan’s territory or exclusive economic zone, Japan’s Ministry of Defense said on social media.
Tokyo said Japan, the United States and South Korea are working closely to analyze the launch, and that so far there have been no reports of damage to aircraft or ships operating nearby. The exclusive economic zone is the band of sea extending up to 200 nautical miles (370 km) from Japan’s coast, where Tokyo controls fishing and resources.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was briefed immediately and gave three instructions: gather and analyze information and keep the public quickly and accurately informed, thoroughly confirm the safety of aircraft and ships, and prepare for any contingency. The government’s North Korea task force at the prime minister’s crisis management center pulled together information from ministries and convened an emergency team to discuss the response.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi then ordered the Self-Defense Forces to work closely with the United States and South Korea on collecting and analyzing information and to keep up surveillance in case of further developments. The Japanese government said North Korea’s repeated missile launches threaten the peace and security of Japan, the region and the international community, and it promised to release more details as they become available.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff gave a fuller picture, saying North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area on its east coast toward the sea at about 12:30 p.m., SBS reported. Neither government has yet said how far the missiles flew or how high they climbed, and North Korean state media had not commented on the launch by Thursday afternoon.
The launch is North Korea’s first ballistic missile firing in 17 days and follows a busy October. On Oct. 3, it fired a missile from near its east coast that Japan’s Defense Ministry said flew about 680 km (420 miles) at a peak altitude of about 90 km (56 miles) before landing outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone. On Oct. 12, Pyongyang fired several ballistic missiles from near its capital, some of which flew more than 900 km (560 miles), and later called them tactical ballistic missiles, short-range weapons meant for battlefield targets. Two days later, it test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea east of the peninsula.
The launches come as tensions remain high along the inter-Korean border. In early October, South Korea and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded that North Korea had deliberately planted the mines that wounded three South Korean soldiers inside the Demilitarized Zone on Sept. 21. South Korea’s National Security Office held an emergency meeting after Thursday’s launch and said the repeated ballistic missile firings violate United Nations Security Council resolutions, which bar North Korea from testing ballistic missiles.

'We must learn so that it doesn't happen again': Oct. 7 veterans prepare soldiers for the next war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:39:37 UTC
15:39:37 KST

On Oct. 7, 2023, as Israel awoke to an unprecedented nightmare, these four company commanders were still serving in more junior positions. They rushed from the officer training school, private trips and weekend leave straight into the chaos in communities near the Gaza border, including Be'eri, Kissufim, Nir Oz and the Re'im junction.
They rescued civilians under heavy fire, witnessed scenes they had previously thought existed only in movies and, in some cases, suffered serious injuries. Now, after three consecutive years of intense fighting in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank, they command companies at the Givati Brigade's training base, the Nahal Brigade's training base, the Paratroopers' training program and the squad commanders' course.
The officers are bringing hard-earned operational lessons and insights gained at great personal cost to the training grounds, where they are responsible for educating and shaping the next generation of combat soldiers.
"On Oct. 7, I was a team commander in the Gefen Battalion at Bahad 1," recalled Capt. Y., now a company commander overseeing recruits in the Givati Reconnaissance Unit, referring to the IDF's officer training school.
"We started that morning at 7 a.m., and I drove south with my father to reach the assembly point. I spent my first hours of fighting with two officer cadets, and from there we drove to the Re'im junction area, near the site of the music festival, and then to Nir Oz.
"I separated from the cadets to join my team because I understood that I was responsible for my unit and couldn't let my soldiers fight without me. We brought combat equipment from Bahad 1 and then headed into fighting in Sufa, Nir Yitzhak and the Yesha junction. We spent three or four days restoring control."
One moment from those first days remains particularly vivid.
"There was a moment when we stopped the Humvees, quickly prepared ourselves and the company commander told us to forget what we knew and understand that we were entering a combat zone," Capt. Y. recalled.
"When you're in the Gaza or Lebanon sector and someone tells you that, you understand. But I looked around and saw kibbutzim and Israeli communities. That really struck me. It was a period of tremendous shock and disbelief."
A generation that did not experience Oct. 7
Serious injuries and prolonged combat have become inseparable parts of the commanders' stories.
Capt. N., now a company commander in the Paratroopers' 890th Battalion training program who is set to be promoted to major, fought in Be'eri during the first days of the attack as part of a force known as "Ben-Mosh."
"We ran through Be'eri for two consecutive nights, going from house to house, rescuing residents and fighting in firefights until the community was declared clear," Capt. N. said.
"From there, we moved on to preparations for entering Gaza. A week after the ground offensive began, I was seriously wounded by friendly fire. Shrapnel cut into my windpipe, I was sedated and placed on a ventilator, and I underwent two months of rehabilitation. As soon as I could, I went straight back to my company."
Three years later, the new generation of soldiers is one that did not experience Oct. 7 firsthand as combat troops.
"Today, apart from my deputy company commander, no one serving under me was there on Oct. 7 or at the beginning of the ground offensive," Capt. N. said.
"My job is to help the soldiers imagine what it looked like. We were there, and we remember the initial shock. Our responsibility is to make sure that shock doesn't happen again next time."
Capt. A., a company commander in the IDF's squad commanders' course, puts the cultural and disciplinary lessons in stark terms.
"When I apply Oct. 7 to the training of commanders, I tell my trainees one thing: We must never forget. We must not forget what happened to us and what was done to us, and we must not forget that we failed in our mission," Capt. A. said.
"Alongside heroic battles, there were quite a few professional lessons we must learn so that it doesn't happen again. And it could happen tomorrow morning.
"My trainees were schoolchildren on Oct. 7, and now the responsibility rests on their shoulders. If they forget, we'll fall back into the same assumptions that made us less effective.
"At the tactical level, when I say there could be a war tomorrow morning, it's not a cliché. It's a belief I translate into daily preparations: maintaining constant readiness with ammunition, drills, defensive procedures and readiness at dawn.
"In my view, operational culture is the greatest lesson. Where that culture was lacking, that's where we failed."
'We failed in our mission to defend'
These lessons are shaping the next generation of soldiers from the ground up.
Capt. Y., a company commander at the Nahal Brigade's training base who is currently leading recruits through a week of field training, recalled the moment everything changed for him.
"We entered Kissufim into a full-scale battlefield, with gunfire coming from every direction and rockets in the air," he said.
"As we were driving, a friend who was in the vehicle with me was speaking on the phone with his family in Be'eri, explaining how to tie a shirt into a tourniquet to save their younger brother, who had been shot.
"We went from house to house under fire to rescue families and act as human shields for them. Our mission was to make sure no civilian was harmed, and we failed in that mission."
Capt. Y. of the Nahal training base said today's recruits arrive with a profound sense of responsibility. They understand that they are the country's protective vest, he said, and are eager to learn from the combat experience their commanders have accumulated.
Capt. Y. of the Givati Reconnaissance Unit described his company as part of a "generation of victory," a generation that has fought continuously for three years across multiple fronts, including Gaza and Lebanon, and demonstrated levels of resilience and capability rarely seen among soldiers performing mandatory military service.
All four commanders agree that the operational experience gained at such a heavy cost will, in their view, leave the next generation of combat soldiers better prepared to face the most demanding challenges.

Putin and African leaders chart new course for cooperation: As it happened
The third Russia-Africa Summit has concluded in Moscow, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and African leaders adopting a joint declaration and agreeing on priorities for cooperation in the coming years.
The second and final day of the gathering at the Kremlin focused on international affairs, Africa’s growing global role, economic cooperation and security. Putin and African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye addressed the summit before holding a joint press conference.
The leaders adopted a declaration covering issues ranging from UN reform and sanctions to maritime security, trade and infrastructure, alongside a cooperation action plan for 2027–2029. The declaration also called for greater African representation in international institutions and opposed neocolonial practices that undermine national sovereignty.
Putin held a series of bilateral meetings with African counterparts, discussing investment, energy, infrastructure and educational cooperation. Speaking to reporters, he also addressed Russia’s relations with Europe, international maritime security and Moscow’s role in resolving conflicts across Africa.
Wednesday’s opening economic forum focused on expanding trade, strengthening financial independence and supporting industrial development across the continent. Putin called for Russia-Africa trade to reach $50 billion, backed reform of the IMF and World Bank, and offered to share Russian digital technologies.
RT followed the summit’s final day, bringing you the key announcements, agreements, and footage from Moscow.
This live feed has now ended.
- 29 October 2026 19:37 GMT Western countries attempted to discourage African leaders from attending the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, Kremlin presidential aide Yury Ushakov has said. “There were many opponents of this summit among Western countries. They tried to persuade some leaders not to come, citing various difficult conditions in Russia,” Ushakov told RT. Despite these efforts, the summit attracted substantial representation, he said, adding that participants were interested in expanding cooperation across multiple sectors.

The initiative, announced by Synergy Corporation in partnership with Innopraktika, will provide applicants with assistance in choosing universities, learning Russian and obtaining visas. The first centers are expected to open in Morocco and Nigeria, while a separate network of vocational colleges will begin operating in Tanzania this November, offering training in professions including welding, electrical work, and mechanics. 
Watch the full RT report below.
- 19:17 GMT Russia and African countries have adopted a joint declaration at the conclusion of the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, setting out priorities for cooperation on security, international affairs and economic development. 
Key points of the declaration:
· Maritime security: Oppose the unjustified detention, seizure or arrest of civilian vessels, including African-flagged ships, in violation of international law.
· Sanctions: Oppose unilateral coercive measures that violate international law, including sanctions imposed outside the UN Security Council, and work to reduce their economic impact.
· Sovereign assets: Oppose the freezing and attempted confiscation of sovereign assets, as well as political and economic coercion against sovereign states.
· Colonial reparations: Pursue legal mechanisms to assess and compensate for damage inflicted on African countries during the colonial era.
· International justice: Counter the politicization and misuse of international criminal justice mechanisms, including their use to exert neocolonial pressure on African states.
· UN reform: Work toward reforming the Security Council to increase African representation.
· Counterterrorism: Strengthen cooperation against terrorists’ use of drones, encrypted platforms and digital finance.
· Arms control: Oppose the politicization of international arms control, disarmament and nuclear nonproliferation mechanisms.
· IMF and World Bank: Push for reforms to give African countries greater representation and influence in decision-making.
· G20: Call for South Africa’s full and active participation in the group to be restored as soon as possible.
· Cultural heritage: Support the return of cultural objects and historical artifacts taken from African countries during colonial rule.
· Space cooperation: Expand peaceful space exploration, satellite technologies and joint research.
· Trade and infrastructure: Develop cooperation in precious metals and expand maritime, river, road, rail and aviation infrastructure.
· Climate policy: Oppose discriminatory protectionist measures introduced under the pretext of combating climate change.
· Sovereignty: Counter neocolonial practices that undermine states’ independence, restrict their decision-making or facilitate the exploitation of their natural resources.

- 18:18 GMT Putin has warned against disruptions to shipping in the Baltic Sea similar to those in the Strait of Hormuz, saying Russia would respond to any challenge. Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc holds lead
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 29, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- Latest vote count at 99% shows Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc holding the lead at 53 seats
- Anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot at 48 seats
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election.
READ: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims.
Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”
A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.
Read more in depth coverage of that story, right here.
Israel elections: Where things stand on Thursday afternoon
With the final tally of votes in Israel's high-stakes parliamentary elections expected on Thursday evening, we take a look at today's events thus far.
- Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party doubled down on allegations that the election has been stolen by Arab parties.
- Netanyahu said that evidence would be handed to police, Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee.
- Netanyahu also referred to statements about the "involvement of foreign entities that interfered and bribed voters in favor of Arab parties," saying they were "an unprecedented shock."
- Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, said political actors should not "exploit the information" that had yet to be clarified "in order undermine the official results."
- Qatar meanwhile, has denied any involvement in such allegations: "We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," it said, adding it is accused of buying off the Arab vote.
- Qatar’s foreign minister spokesman Majed Al Ansari spoke of "accusations made by certain Israeli politicians" and said they had "launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes."
- Sami Abu Shehadeh, chair of one of the parties in the Arab-led Joint List, called the claims a new phase of "incitement" against Arab-led groups.
- The head of the Arab-led Ra'am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed any investigation into election interference. He said his party had nothing to do with it.
- Israel's Central Elections Committee poured cold water on vote fraud allegeations saying "there is no basis."
- "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity," The Times of Israel quoted acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne as having written in a letter.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end
With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.
That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.
The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.
Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.
The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.
Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.
Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.
According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.
This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.
The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.
UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law.
"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.
"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."
Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.
He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW
Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.
"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."
Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.
"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.
Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.
WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock
Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.

Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.

Ousted defense ministry chief to run for Parempoolsed at Riigikogu election
